Simply put, this is the best space sandbox out there.
Want to play a police fighter pilot and combat pirates and hostile aliens? You can. Want to go rogue and become a mercenary and work for the highest bidder? You can. Want to be a trading tycoon and amass a massive merchant fleet that controls the entire economy of dozens of worlds? You can. Want to build your own private space armada and watch the glorious space-fireworks fly while personally commanding your own fleet of capital ships? Yep, you can.

an incredible space sim with in-depth combat, well modeled trading, impressive graphics, immersive soundtrack and large ship variety. Reccomended to any with an interest of space sims/sci-fi games. Be aware that this game has a steep learning curve, however, and the combat system is strict and unforgiving. Some parts of the game, such as liberating ships and collecting cargo are a bit clunky, but are understandable in context.
Despite these flaws, this manages to be one of the best space games of all time.

I have more or less kept up to date with the development of this game and was quite impressed by the steady improvement the updates delivered. However, I still think it's quite pricey for what the game has to offer. I waited for a sale to buy it.
Even though the game feels like something new and features plenty of well-thought-out mechanics, the big problem is that it's all aimed at one thing: creating a big, secure and profitable prison with lots of prisoners and rooms.
That's why there is little room for creativity - after a (short) while you just figure out the most effective way of building and handling things and there's no reason to do it any different than in your last game. Whenever you try something new you do it knowing that you're just making it more difficult for yourself and without any in-game motivation.
I've been a long time fan of Rimworld. It feels very similar in some parts but doesn't suffer from this problem of routine building up since there are more factors that you can't control and more possibilities overall, thus giving you a pretty different story each game.
I would not recommend buying Prison Architect for more than 10€ (that's about 0.8€/h for me) and only if you really, really need to build a prison instead of something you can do in other simulations.

I got this game from the Humble Bundle Monthly service. This game is definitely my favorite out of the month! Really, what a surprising and unbelievable mini-adventure! Wuppo is a simple action-adventure game where you explore various hub towns, talk to friendly wum NPC's, work for CREDIT, catch the train, and fight crazy bosses. Gametime clocks in at around 6-8 hours after defeating the final boss.
Combat is performed with a gumgumgun and a bazooka (each are customizable) that you control with your mouse or right stick. Menus are simple and intuitive, and there's not too much "game" to it outside of talking to people and figuring out how to complete whatever the main objective is. You might accidentally walk into rogue boss encounter, or find yourself doing oddjobs that just pique your curiosity! Lots of stuff for completionist to sink their teeth into, while still being straight-forward for those of us that just want to experience the story and thrill of defeating the boss.
You need to keep an open mind, however, Graphics aren't everything, and I know you want to go back to playing whatever carrot on a stick fps or moba but this game really can be enjoyed if you give it your time. If it's on sale, and you really liked games similar to Super Paper Mario or point-and-click games then download the demo?

Spec Ops: The Line begs the question, 'can a video game be good without being fun'? And in my opinion the answer to that question is a resounding yes.
Now to be fair, the gameplay is solid - uninventive and a bit slow, maybe, but undeniably functional and no detriment to the experience as a whole.
However the story is where this game becomes unique. It ventures through the horrors of war in ways the bog standard shooter just shrugs off. It is incredibly difficult to talk about this game without spoiling it, but ill do my best. It is, fundementally, an analysis of the shooter genre (specifically modern military varieties) carried out in the medium it critiques. Its dark, grisly, but it also has its moments of levity, though these become rarer the more you progress.
I'm nominating this game for 'Haunts My Dreams' because it has done just that. Its a game I'll remember in the dead of night and just think about until I've fallen asleep. It causes you to think about the actions you carry out in the game until you finally say, 'is it worth it'? And the moment a game begins to make its players question the actions they take as the main character, is a game worth playing, discussing and sharing with those who haven't yet experienced it.

Right off the bat: this game probably has the best story I've ever seen in video games.
Everything is dripping with leans into the fourth wall, symbilism, and meta-narrative.  One can go so far as to say the monotonous and over-the-top violent gameplay coincides with the generally psychological theme of desensitization to violence.
If you're on this page, you've probably heard it before.  This game will tear your heart out in many ways, and it won't be like any other shooter you've played.  There are shooters you should play for the enormously fun gameplay (Doom 4, F.E.A.R.), hell there are shooters you should play for a good story (Wolfenstein: The New Order, Half-Life 2), this one is different.  This one you need to play for the pure potency of its themes and allegories, for the introspection into the human heart at its darkest.  This game will emotionally thrash you, have you questioning your own actions and motivations, and most of all the character you play as.  No surprise it was inspired by Heart of Darkness, but it still does play like a modern tragedy.  A story of mental instability and PTSD consuming a mind, a story of guilt and vengeance.  All of it coelesces into a narrative masterpiece.  Play this game.  Clear six hours from your schedule and play it, you owe it to yourself to experience this.
It's true, the gameplay is nothing to write home about.  It's actually quite frustrating at times.  Getting it first for the Xbox, I couldn't get very far into it, I kept getting frustrated and putting it down.  Personally I found playing it on PC easier just because it was easier to control so I was able to plow through it a lot faster.  The beginning can be a bit of a slog, but there's a turning point in the story close-ish to the beginning that will grab you and never let go.  Push through to that point and you'll be glad you did.  So to speak.
It's not a pleasant game in the same way that Saving Private Ryan or Schindler's List aren't pleasant movies.  But it's probably one of the most important.  Not only is the story beautiful in its own tragic way, it's also a very important example of a game being used as an interactive medium to drive a point, with a very heavy emphasis on player action and intervention that makes it miles more effective.  And as you play through this spiral of madness, distrust and helplessness, remember that stuff like this happens all the time in the real world...
P.S. For the Steam Awards, I wrote in a category for this one, "Most Criminally Overlooked"

For those that missed the first episode of Sonic 4, this is a 2D platforming game staring everyone's favorite blue hedgehog. The plot is the same as its always been, but with a twist. Dr. Robotnik, the evil antagonist of most every Sonic game has now teamed up with Metal Sonic! The dude with 90s attitude isn't alone though, he now has Tails to go with him. With Tails, come new mechanics, such as jumping into the air, and calling Tails to lift Sonic like a helicopter. If you're on the ground and use the tag button, it summons Tails to combine the two for a super fast attack. If you need to use the helicopter ability, the game will have a little billboard to tell you. This game feels more a kin to the Game Boy Advance games than the original Genesis games which the first episode clearly drew inspiration from.
In Episode 2, you have four zones with three acts each followed by a boss fight as a fourth act. Not just that, but later into the four hour game, you unlock a playable Metal Sonic with four zones and one act each. These zones use assets from the first episode. So in all, there are 16+ levels for you to master. These levels feel a lot longer than the first episode and the Genesis games as a whole. Some levels feel like six minute marathons with no end in sight.
The levels are big and offer many paths to the exit. You'll have to avoid an array of enemies, spikes, and even death traps. You'll collect rings everywhere and these rings aren't just because dullards love shinny things, but as long as Sonic has at least one ring, he can take another hit. Even if you have 100 rings and get hit, only 30 will spray out of Sonic. When you get hit with no rings, it means death for the fuzzy blue guy. There are plenty of check points in each level if you die. A game over simply means that you'll need to start the level again. If you collect 100 rings in a level, you get an extra life. If you have 50+ rings at the end of the level, a giant ring will appear that will take you to a special bonus stage.
These bonus stages are updated versions of the old Sonic 2 bonus stages. You'll follow Sonic running down a 3D half pipe. You can boost and jump. There are a few check points that need X amount of rings to get past. So as Sonic, you'll solemn down the tube moving left and right, collecting rings and dodging obstacles that will lose you rings. At the end you'll find a chaos emerald.... that somehow isn't green. Whatever. Collect all seven to unlock a yellow Super Sonic.
New to the Sonic 4 series is local co-op and even online co-op, but since the game came out in 2011, good luck trying to find a partner. There are online leader boards for time attacks. It adds to the replayability I guess, but more than that, the game has a red star ring on each level to collect. These rings are either tough to find or tough to get. Its an extra challenge for veterans.Sonic and Metal Sonic play the same. Left and right to move, with a single button to jump. Hold down to duck and hit the jump button to start a spin dash to get momentum to go up slopes. You still need to charge it which takes time. That's why the airborne dart attack is not only a much better way to gain speed instantly, but you can also lock in on targets accurately hit them no matter what the angle. Episode 2 didn't make as much use of the homing attack as the first episode, but it does make travel easier, darting for an enemy or a springboard. The only difference between Metal Sonic and the ordinary version is lack of an ally. No helicoptering around or bowling through enemies.
Calling Tails just feels slow. Tails automatically zips right back to Sonic wherever he is, unless he just died, but it just halts the game to wait. The Sky Fortress kicks off with an airplane mission that has Sonic atop Tail's plane that gives you full control to move the plane left, right, up and down. Complete with Sonic able to jump and attack. Under normal circumstances, I'd think it diversifies gameplay having a plane dodge enemies and twirl through barricades to destroy them. This felt like a slow auto scrolling level (act). There was still a part where the 2D platforming returned, but then it was just back to being on top of a plane. It felt dull, slow and boring. Then having to fight the boss on the plane was unfun.
The real snag that I have for this game is how long and dull the boss battles are. They take traditional, classic boss battles and completely twist them around into mega bosses. See I like the twists and fighting giant bosses, I just don't like how tedious every boss was. Having to damage each boss for three minutes before the final phase of the boss fight left me clueless and dead ate up most of my 4 hours in the game. These 3 minutes on each attempt felt like 10 and I was never in any real danger. It wasn't a challenge surviving the 3 minutes, it was just a delay for the real challenge. At least the game takes full advantage of having Metal Sonic as an enemy. You get three boss fights against him.
The game has other down sides too, like a timed race against sand flooding an area. Sonic needs to go up, breaking through barriers, then down. This would separate the casual players from the hardcore. It ate up two dozen lives and was quite the difficulty spike. Then on the final two levels, when Sonic went down hill or uphill, the entire screen would shift so Sonic wasn't running downhill, he was on a horizontal plane. It was disorienting, and might cause someone motion sickness.
Water areas feel better in this game than they have in the past. Sonic jumps higher and Tails can carry him, so you have more maneuverability. Under water still slows down Sonic and he can't swim. If you're underwater too long, Sonic will need to get oxygen from big air bubbles that drift their way up.
The soundtrack feels Genesis in a good way. Percussion and synth horns. Its all upbeat happy game music. The graphics are bright and vibrant. There is a good color pallet here. A dusty yellow castle with an aquatic greenish blue moat. A winter wonderland theme park, lit up for a holiday with blue ice water. A metallic sandy red oil rig in a yellow desert. A yellow sky fortress with fans to propel Sonic into the air. Dr. Robotnik's gray and purple metal lair. As each zone progressed, the acts would change their color pallets so you'll see day turn to dusk. It all adds to making each of the three acts feel different. Having Metal Sonic's 4 different zones with 1 act each adds a lot of diversity, even if 3 acts each would have been nicer.
Even with all the bad, its still a good game. Better than most other 2D platforms out there for $15. I enjoyed the first episode better, but it felt like they took the gameplay a step in the right direction. If its on sale, take a risk.

The sequel to the mixed recieved Sonic 4 Episode I is simply amazing. The story is that Little Planet from Sonic CD has returned and with it, the return of Eggman's greatest creation: Metal Sonic. It's up to you as the dynamic gaming duo of Sonic and Tails to stop him. The graphics look amazing as it's a full on 3D graphics engine played from a 2D perspective (Also known as 2.5D) and the music and sound design is simply amazing in it's Sega Genesis limitations. The gameplay is the same old Sonic the Hedgehog 2D high speed platforming, but this game introduces 3 new abilities for Tails: The fligh, the swim, and the rolling combo, all activated by pushing the action button at the right time. The levels are designed well and the bosses are pretty fun to fight. The weak points is that it's still a short game with 4 zones (3 acts each) and the final zone with one boss for each zone. The verdict is that this game is a must buy for fans of 2D Sonic, worth $15. If you're not big on the series, buy when it's on sale

Don’t be put off by the game’s lack of commercial success. First it should be said the both parts of Sonic 4, Episode 1 (4.1) and Episode 2 (4.2) seem to have an identity crisis. They are officially sequels but in reality they are something of an updated remake, 4.1 and 4.2 borrow and reference Sonic 1, 2, 3&K and CD heavily; 4.1s bosses are all remakes of the originals, a fault 4.2 even references with the first boss originally appearing to mimic the Aquatic Ruins’ Boss before transforming into something new. However even it borrows the later levels and boss fights. The level design 4.2 is also much better than 4.1’s. As 4.2 has original zones; Sylvanian Castle, Winter Park Zone and the Oil Desert (whose features resemble 3&K’s Sandopolis much more than Sonic 2’s Oil Ocean which it would appear to be a copy of at first glance). After this 4.2 does fall into copying the final zone which is just an amalgamation of Wing Fortress, Sky Chase and the Flying Battery zones, taking features from each but making them worse (in the Sky Chase knock off for example Tail’s Plane can disappear leaving the player plummeting to earth).
There are problems with both games; they both insist on the use of Sonic’s homing attack to access ledges which I find it unnecessary for a side-scroller. Again Physics does not seem to apply in Sonic the Hedgehog’s universe, he can walk up walls when travelling at fairly low speeds (although not as badly as he could in 06), while the homing attack creates momentum from nothing.
Even the traditional saving grace of the Sonic game, the soundtrack, is poor which is disappointing. In addition, the game also has a very short life span, 4.1 failed to keep me attached for more than 5 hours, and while 4.2 actually saw me to completion, it only has at most 5-12 hours of gameplay depending on how quickly you can master it and I doubt either has much in the way of replay value unlike the games they are based upon.
This said however, for once Sonic actually controls well (which he never does in 3D Games). 4.2 itself still contains a number of very good features. The inclusion of team mechanics was a great idea as it makes Tails a valued partner to Sonic, his abilities have made him an essential part as he can get Sonic through traps and defeat opponents. 4.2 also did well with the special stages, which like 4.1s are copies of the original games (this time the tunnel runs of Sonic 2,) unlike 4.1 however, 4.2 improves the originals. Tails is no longer a dead weight, he doesn't drop rings when hit and a new power up (a chaotix ring type feature) can give new interesting challenges, it is just a pity they weren’t used more often.
Therefore although neither are great like the games they were trying to emulate, they are ok and I generally do not see why they have been so badly received as they’re worthy successors to the original Sonic. 4.1 may be distinctly average but 4.2 is a big improvement upon it. The current price tags are not value for money but if you pick them up in the Steam sale (as I did) 4.2 is certainly worth a fiver. 4.1 should only be purchased if you want the bonus Metal Sonic Mode which works when you own both parts.

This game is more then just pay to win, it's pay to play. Your cash rewards, experience, and so forth are all dramatically reduced if you don't buy their VIP. It's not just that though, they refuse to make any new guns that you can actually unlock in the game. Every new gun is one you have to pay for! Not a single new gun has been released to public aviablilty since the restart of the actual game from APB, All Points Bulletin. If that doesn't make it bad enough, to truely enjoy yourself in the game you need to be a VIP. Why? Better and longer trials for weapons and cars, not to mention the ability to customize yourself and vehicle, emblems, and more to higher extents. The only game worse then this with a worse pay to win system is WarZ now known as "Infestation Stores." It is though fun to play once you're a high enough level, hackers are dealt with much easier now because of the anti-hack system known as Fair Fight was installed. There's without a doubt of equalization in weapons, but that equalization is in the ones you pay for. The graphics aren't bad, controls, mechanics, and interest isn't bad at all actually. From climbing ladders to driving off ramps from unfinished highways, civilians actively moving about the map to simply running over criminals or enforcers to catching criminals in acts of crime. There's a lot of innovation, tons of little areas to be found even when you think you know all the maps and secret locations. I can honestly say if it wasn't for the pay to win system this would be without a doubt the greatest game ever made. It's like Grand Theft Auto 4 and Need For Speed: Most Wanted (the original for Xbox 360.) You can steal a civilan car for the lulz of it, or make your own from a fairly wide range of choices and if you decide to dump cash into this game that customization can truely be starstriking. If this game allowed you to unlock everything over time it'd be an absolute reccommendation, but it not only doesn't try to do this but HEAVILY avoids it. Potential never met.
Did I mention they made it so you have to buy upgrades for your friend and ignore list, or that new content is never given to those who don't pay...?

I can't quite fully get into this game. It is for people that like Megaman X/Megaman type games obviously... but this game is a little too insane for my tastes. the hit sprites for the enemies and attacks are so huge, that hit detection isn't quite perfect. There were plenty of times I was trying to avoid a big fireball or enemy, and then I jumped forward - and thought I would take damage, but didn't because the hitbox of everything isn't the entire sprite. You eventually get a feel for it and can compensate, but I really think that if you visually touch a sprite border, you should take damage.
Also, I think because of the nature of the random levels, it relies too much on cheap hits from huge groups of weak enemies and environment hazards. I much prefer more thought out levels created by real people - like the Megaman games. It just feels more fluid and challenging on a fair level, as opposed to a bunch of thrown together hazards. I feel like they need to tweak the level generation process to allow for some more cohesive levelsthat don't have pit drops and environment hazards constantly.
All that being said, I don't hate it - and I can enjoy it to a small degree. My biggest complaint is there is no real feeling of progression overall. I think it would do well to add something like usable energy tanks, and maybe a few items that hold over even after dying (if even only for a few runs after instead of forever.) So far it's super frustrating to be having an excellent run, then getting screwed by a bad level or a crazy difficult boss, then to start literally over from the beginning with no nuts, and your base abilities.
Also, the few music tracks are pretty good - but they need a LOT more. They get repetitive much quicker than Megaman music does for sure.
Lastly, I feel like the main characters still need a slight redesign. They look kind of cheap to me. Something is missing, but I can't quite put my finger on it.
I'm glad it's still early access, which means they can hopefully polish some of this into a more enjoyable game. As it is, I find myself screaming after every death and have to turn it off for a few hours before I feel like subjecting myself to it again.
I recommend it to anyone wanting a good Megaman type shooter, at the $8.99 price I got it at. At this point though, I wouldn't be able to justify it's $11.99 early access price, and definitely not the $15 release price it will be.

One of the snow zone acts ends in a tails swimming test that, if failed, kills you by trapping you underwater until you drown. I got this game for free after voting in the Golden Joystick Awards in 2016. While I'm not particularly into third-person shooters, I quite enjoyed this gift.
PROS
+ The storyline is powerful with some thought-provoking and often harrowing twists. Major decisions are genuinely challenging.
+ Fantastic character development with strong voice acting.
+ Gameplay is good, and the AI provides a reasonable challenge.
+ The Dubai setting and architecture looks great, not to mention realistic. The sandstorm mechanic is done well also.
+ Great soundtrack, featuring a handful of 60s/70s classics.
+ Good variety of weapons, from firearms to grenades.
CONS
- I played through the story twice (on the lowest two difficulty levels) to get the multiple endings. After that, though, the game offers little replayability, and it sounds like multiplayer is to be avoided.
- Speaking of difficulty, I saw little difference between those first two settings when it came to AI strength.
- Cutscenes are rendered very poorly, which is a shame, considering the game itself looks graphically sharp.
- Movement can be clunky, as can the controls.
- If you're the squeamish sort, this is a game to be avoided.
The pros outweigh the cons for me. Even five years after its release, and even though it was a commercial failure, it is still a quality game for fans of TPS games or even just story-driven titles.

Upon completion of this game.
All I have to say is that it's amazing.  I really enjoyed the pacing of the game from start to finish.
There was never a moment where it felt really slow.  And most missions as in the original DMC series can be revisited in second playthoughs.
While it's very hard to gauge this game since it's on it's own spin.
I was one of many who outcried due to the change in Dante and after finishing up this I feel that he's something that I've grown used to.
This game very well does parallel the personalities albeit Dante kinda is weird at the beginning of the game. But anyone who's ever really followed the series from 1st game should understand that Dante is the 'rebel' between his twin Vergil.
At first it seemed as this game heading towards a very stupid plot but later on as the game unravels you start to witness the polar opposite personalities between Dante and Vergil.  They do bring back the nolstagia, the sense of rivalry betweeen the two and what they stand for which makes it a great game.  Maybe, comparable to DMC3 which is a classic and also my fave DMC game.  And this DmC however does beat out DMC4, as DMC4 had a very lackluster plot and very little character development.
In DmC though, I never encountered or felt the game was very haphazard in the sense that it didn't feel like .. "oh this, is the part where I play Dante.." which was a weird cut-off in the original series.  This game however doesn't do that.  It transitions cutscenes, combat and characters all in one.  It's a very smooth, very wonderful experience.  Almost every character in this game get their time to shine in their own spotlight.  Which didn't go too well on DMC4.
Now, on to the gameplay.  Yes, this game does carry on elements from the previous titles and then some.  It does it in some ways better than others.  Having Dante being able to use a multitude of weapons which do have their lineage in playstyle (*helm breaker*etc.) makes for a variety of choice on fighting your enemies.  They even introduce certain enemeis that are only vulnerable to certain types of weapons as well.
The greatest thing about this game though is the non-existent Nero. Of which I very much despised in DMC4.  Because this game carries the grab/grapple moves into Dante's kit. So there's never a need for a Nero.  Which is something I wish they implemented instead in DMC4 for Dante rather than shoe horning an unpleasant character to play as.
I'm not ragging DMC4 in any way, loved the game but this DmC fixes everything that was wrong in DMC4 and delivers in a very fluid, dynamic and then some. The music is awesome it definitely delivers in that department.  I love industrial music and they way they mixed dubsteps in certain fights (bosses included) made battles feel funny and enjoyable.
But seriously if you're a hardcore DMC fan like I am I suggest picking this up.  Even if it's just on a steam sale, you won't regret it. But opinions are opinions .. I mean I picked it up expecting to hate it.  In the end the whole just took me by surprise.  Vergil's cold, egotistical yet primmed ego is very well existent in this game.  Felt good to have that opposing ego to Dante's more punk♥♥♥♥♥attitude. Overall, feels like a DMC game. 10/10
tl;dr this game is about Two Brothers .. Two Brothers!
SPOILER: Dante's hair turns all white at the end.  ALL OF IT! so stop crying already!

Early Access Watcher Reviews 20XX
Update Version: 0.954b
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the reviewer. I try my best to judge a game by the technical and core aspects, but even with my review I still believe these games are not for everyone.
The one genre I never had much skill for would have to be the side-scrolling platformer. There are a variety of famous games that have immortalized the genre and each one has left me dead in he corner. I should probably be the last person reviewing this type of game, but when I noticed 20XX was on sale and that "Inafundme" had his game coming out next week, I thought it would be nice to see what a small group can do to recapture the feel of the genre. As I expected, I was not very good at it, but that doesn't mean the game is bad - just me.
It is a good thing to note that a controller would probably save you some major heartache. When I switched over from keyboard, my survivability skyrocketed, problem due to the keyboard button layout. You start off with a tutorial that introduces the key button responses and fight one of the beginner bosses. It is quick, informative and leads you to the main hub where you can purchase items, switch characters, attempt challenges and jump into the main game. Daily challenges are up for grabs and the items for sale can be purchased with soul nuggets you acquire during missions. Two unique play styles are offered as Nina (blue armor) utilizes a blaster that only shoots left or right (without upgrades) and Ace (red armor) wielding a sabre. A collection of all the items you obtained is also present, which helps keep track of the beneficial qualities each item brings to the table.
Similar to the old school style games 20XX seeks to emulate, the visual appeal has a very retro aesthetic in level design. Character models and enemy textures look a little more three dimensional, but they complement the scenery quite well with bright color helping detail projectiles. Music is top notch with upbeat tempos helping keep the tension high as the clock in the top left counts down. Blaster shots and sword swings carry that classic "pew pew" noise you expect from these kinds of games with explosions and fire bursts rounding out a simple, but effective sound design. It is what one would expect from a Mega-man game and it really lives up to that expectation well.
Blasting enemies and collecting power ups is the primary objective in overcoming the challenges this game has to offer. Each level has a platform run filled with potential upgrades, such as stat boosters and main weapon changes, that help deal with the boss fights found at the end. Once the boss is defeated, you are given a reward and able to select from one of three portals leading to the next level. The further you manage to go the more difficult enemies and level layouts become. Added challenges are also available in the form of skulls that make each level harder, from denying health drops to selecting the next level you proceed to after the boss. It can be as hard or as easy as you want in 20XX, which makes it very accessible to hardcore veterans or new inductees alike.
Unlike other Mega-man esq games, 20XX manages to fuse rogue-like elements into the mix and pulls it off rather effectively. During each run, blue versions of typical enemies will appear and have the chance to drop soul nuts, which you use upon death to purchase items from the main base. This provides a small leg up and if the soul nuts are not used, then they are lost forever. The randomization of level layouts have been consistently different throughout my entire play through with only one or two levels feeling familiar in parts. There are also infrequent portals to challenge rooms that can appear along with vending machines used to replenish health and energy for bolts. Luck can be a deciding factor in terms of running into off setting platform formations that will unfortunately lead you to be stuck in an inescapable position. Other than that, the rogue like elements really keep the game fresh and challenging to what could have easily been just a eight boss campaign.
Co-op is present in the game over online service or locally, but I only jumped in once to ensure it was functioning. It worked rather well, but things can get a bit chaotic on screen with all the enemies. Challenges for weekly and daily variations have a set restriction mode and a standard version to give an extra difficulty setting, but they generally play like a normal run. There are some issues, however, that creep up from time to time. Hit box detection for some enemies is extremely picky and can have you easily killing a something normally while the same monster requires you to be on it completely just to hit it. Enemy types are rather limited with a standard color change used as a resin for tougher foes. Some of the background images can be misleading when placed behind platforms, making it difficult to tell if a slice of land is actually there or not. Levels are relatively short, but this can be a pro or a negative depending on your approach. I had an issue with some of the randomized platform jumps, but those were very far and few between. The one aspect of the game I can happily support is how well it runs at this point in time. It can still use some optimization, but this has to be one of the best frame rates I have seen with a early access title.
I do not regret purchasing 20XX and have a good feeling it will surpass the expectations of eager platform enthusiasts still hoping Might #9 will have a shred of playability. It can eat away a good chunk of time and keeps things fresh with the randomized levels. It is one of the few games I have experienced during my harsh journey into Early Access that manages to remain operational. It has a bug here and there, but overall 20XX pulls off a stellar charged shot into a genre held hostage by nostalgia. I look forward to seeing how the game manages to evolve further down the line.

I have owned and played approximately 2,000 hours in Rust since early November of last year. Yes, if you do the math on average I've been playing almost 40 hours a week of Rust. Yes I have a job, and No I am not a neckbearded basement dweller. During this time I have played Vanilla rust on US East 1 with some time spent in 100 Airdrops and Combat Tags for gun practice.
Rust is a very difficult game. A VERY difficult game both to play and get started in. Especially if you are a solo player. A popular Rust Youtuber, KCMO said, "Rust has to be one of the most frustrating games I have ever played. But I also find it to be the most rewarding game I have ever played because of how hardcore it is." For those of you that may be new to Rust, check out this video from December 2016 a little under two months after I started playing.
Rust at it's core is a great game, great concept, good mechanics and interesting story. I've got so much time in Rust because I felt it was a great game, and I loved it. I played it almost exclusively since I purchased it and I genuinely care about the direction it is going. Unfortunately that direction is not good.
Being that the game is still in development coming up on 4 years now (You are not in "early development" anymore as your banner claims), a lot has changed since November of 2016. Those changes unfortunately have been, in my opinion, for the worse.
I joined the game at a time where the XP system and blueprints 2.0 had been scrapped and the component system was coming into it's own. What a time to play Rust. I was able to make some friends and we began playing as a group. I have some very fond memories of solo bases in November, December, January and playing at odd hours to ensure uninterrupted farming as I was still very new. As I grew in experience, I got better, my base designs became more impenetrable and I have gone several month long wipes without being raided.
Since then, alot of positive new static content has been added to the game but the game mechanics have changed so much that the game is completely stacked against the solo and small group players and now favors large groups of people known as "zergs" and clans. This is even more so than it did before. They are able to farm faster, build larger and get top tier weaponry and crafting supplies faster as a result of reimplementing the blueprint system and the absolutely cancerous hunt for scrap. The game is no longer fun and has become way to much of a grind. There was natural progression prior to this. There is just a slog now where a set back is monumental. A solo player can collect approximately 120-150 scrap per hour by running a road or visiting the larger rad towns and recycling EVERYTHING they get their hands on. With the implementation of the new blueprint + scrap system it is just too much and no longer rewarding. Prior to this there was a real sense of investment in time and reward. That is now gone as the time investment is just too much and this is coming from a guy who spent 40 hours a week on this game.
The other huge issue is hackers. Rust is plagued with hackers. Active hackers using aimbots, auto aim, ESP, speed hacks, quick mining hacks and everything else. And passive hackers that are using hacks to gain a situational advantage. It's awful. The reports are not handled fast enough and there are no admins on official servers. (I've offered to be one multiple times given my time on the server). It's really a detriment to the game and Facepunch doesn't seem interested in fixing or addressing the issue.
In closing, I cannot recommend this game any longer. I have brought a couple friends into the game since I started but now it's just no longer fun.  I hope that Facepunch, Gary Newman and Helk (Devs) wake up tomorrow and see theses issues for the game killers that they are and revert to the November, December, January, February, March timeframe when Rust had it's highest peak players and things were awesome.
TL;DR
Rust was great in the Nov-Dec 2016 and Jan-Mar 2017 time periods and has gone downhill since. Changes to core game mechanics have been terrible. Some good static content has been added but the changes to the mechanics heavily outweighs that. Revert the mechanics, fix your hacking issue, staff your servers, stop making the game into a grind, balance your loot tables, nerf the zergs, blueprints and scrap system is cancer.

From best to worst
Metal Sonic: maximum good
The art assets: A magnificent transition of classic sonic stage elements reimagined in 3D, every stage is a nostalgic combination of themes I fondly remember as a child.
The zones: Three acts per zone, though with substantually more variety in both the mechanics employed by the stage and the art assets and set pieces uses to create the surroundings. It's a more lovingly crafted subtle progression than previous games were able to render.
The special stages: Out of seven the first five are amazing. Prepare to smash your face against the monitor as you retry the last two relentlessly. FORTNUATELY you can restart the special stages if you know you're going to fail without the arduous task of beating a level with 50 rings, dodged a real bullet there Sega.
The bosses: Suprisingly inspired (for the most part), they employ using cooperative attacks with tails.
Tails: No longer sabotaging your special stages. There's a rather large startup delay for the Sonic/Tails combination attacks and going SSJ I mean Super Sonic was a bit jarring. While flying with him he is prone to dropping sonic if you shear the two of them on a cliff's edge while trying to scale it. He will literally pull a Yoshi on Sonic by dropping him into an endless void pit unless you soar overtop the edge.

- Speaking of bosses, most of them are huge, well balanced, and unique
- The gameplay is tight and platforming feels smooth
- The various races and surprisingly deep lore really make the world feel alive
- The writing is light and silly but still manages to touch of some important social issues
- There are a bunch of Easter Eggs and minigames
- Great music
- Devs are still active on the Steam forums, and were quick to help me with a problem I encountered (not a glitch or bug, just my own idiocy)
- It's a generous 8-10 hours long, depending on how much exploring and non-main story stuff you do.
Cons:
- Combat is simple and has little variety.  You can upgrade your gun when you reach a certain shop, but none of them really change the shooting mechanics that much.  Also, the rapid-fire upgrade seems a little OP.
- Waiting for trains.  I get that Wuppo's world is very much alive and the train operators are doing their best, but waiting for them to reach your station is about as much fun as it is in real life.
- The Menu system.  I got used to it after several hours, but found it really irritating until that point.
Overall, Wuppo is an incredibly fun and joyful game.  At it's best, it feels like the best Nintendo game Nintendo never made, and at it's worst, it's still pretty fun.

Wuppo is a mixed bag, the game has amazing characters, a great world and a nice general story but it lacks in gameplay, pacing and interface. At first i absolutely loved this game, because the introduction of the game is really well done, the interaction between the main character and the hotelier is hilarious. My love for the game quickly faded when it turned out that the gameplay is mostly superficial platforming and point & click style puzzles with a couple of nice bossfights thrown in there.
Gameplay:
The first puzzle was already confusing, there are 4 pictures of different races below a switch puzzle, however you had to throw random items on these. I really don't know how they thought a cooking pot resembles a race that looks like a potato.
Sure you have a bird that can sometimes be helpful he basically tells you what to do for the first puzzle but as often he can obfuscate the solution even further. In a later puzzle where you need to summon a dude the bird says the dude can't be summoned right now, so i thought well maybe i have do something else first, turns out he could be summoned you just need to turn off the lights again.
That is how i generally felt about the game, i had no idea where to go or what to do most of the time, so i just wandered around aimlessly until i found something to do, reminding me more and more of point and click games – a genre i hate.
Other gameplay issues are that you can run out of money to buy an item that is necessary to beat  the game. In Popocity you need to buy an item and there are some jobs you can do to get money, however eventually these jobs become unavailable and then you have no way to get enough money other than going back to old areas and gather some money there which is boring and slow and i was almost ready to abandon the game right there.
Pacing:
While the characters and the story are amazing, the pacing isn‘t. Throughout the game you can find filmstrips and because money is always tight you have to pretty much watch all of them because you get money as a reward for watching them, they are usually long and boring reading sections, wouldn‘t be so bad if it was voiced or funny cutscenes but it is just huge textboxes with a little picture in the background. Right before you are ready to fight the final boss they slap you in the face with a 10 minute read about how the Wuppo world functions.
User-interface:
I wouldn‘t recommend playing this game with a controller, i couldn‘t find a good keybinding steup to make the platforming and using items work in a good way. It is better with mouse and keyboard because you can assign hotkeys to items but it still feels off. Probably because the mouse-wheel scrolls through every single item you have ever collected instead of just the ones you have hotkeyed? Or maybe i dislike it because you can‘t aim properly in this game and you can‘t hit an enemy that is directly in front of you? Or maybe i dislike that they designed some menu-items for a controller and others for mouse and keyboard? Maybe a little bit of all of these, it just doesn't feel right.
To summarize my experience in one sentence: In Wuppo you go through a bunch of frustrating puzzles for two hours to have a 2 minute fun interaction with an NPC and a cool 5 minute boss fight.

As a huge fan of Action Platformers like Megaman X and Super Metroid, it was tough to find series that were very similar and just as awesome. After watching a gameplay video of this at the recommendation of a friend I ended up buying it immediately.
20XX is very much like the Megaman X series of games where you fight bosses, get powerups, dash, wall jump etc. etc. but with a Rogue-Like twist on it. It even controls pretty much exactly like MMX, except your boss weapons are mapped to their own buttons instead of being able to change to them.
Graphically the game is in 2D and uses sprites, but it looks kinda like a flash game. The music however is pretty cool. It's all chiptune music and sounds great.
You've also got access to two different characters (Nina and Ace) which play very similarly to X and Zero.  Nina uses a chargeable Arm Cannon but only fires straight, and Ace uses a beam saber.
Being a Rogue-Like game, there's a lot of Replay value to be had. Each level is generated from scratch to be different. Every run is littered with different powerups that augment one or a combination of abilities. Aside from boss abilities there are powerups that change the function of your main weapons too (like a triple shot for Nina). There are also skulls you can activate that make the game harder too much like Halo's skulls or Gears of War's Mutations
Perhaps the best thing about this game IMO is the Co-op. The game supports both Online and Couch Co-op. To me this is probably the best thing about the game. I doubt I would've enjoyed this game as much as I did if it was single-player only. I think it's a great game so far and I think anyone who wants to fill that void left by Megaman should give this a try
Tl;dr version
Megaman X meets Roguelike with co-op
I highly recommend this if your a fan of MMX or similar platformers

Once again, expanding on the Arkham series started in 2010, Origins has entered the fray (as of 2013).
This game, once again, like Arkham City, expands on the great system presented in Asylum.
The world is once again, open.  Arguably more so than before, yet still restricted based on story progression in some areas, understandably so for a game with a linear plot.
The boss battles got much better and less frustrating than before, but still challenging.
In the three years since release, the graphics have aged just as well as the first two games, and still holds it's own today.
Once again a console -> PC port, but it seems to have worked well, with minor issues with possible crashing, but nothing game-breaking as far as I'm concerned.
The cutscenes are ripped from the console version directly, so resolution will not looks a crisp as it could have, but still acceptable, as it doesn't break any immersion or anything.
The story, is once again stellar, exceptionally so given it's linear nature and the predictability of the universe it takes place in.
Once again, unfortunately, the collectible system has been masisvely inflated and there are much too many of them, but they still offer interesting lore to the universe: concept art, challenge maps, interview tapes from villains, background stories for characters, etc...
The combat system didn't change much, aside from some new gadgets and their mechanics.  If it isn't broke, don't fix it.
The Cold, Cold Heart DLC is pretty good and expands on the story behind Mr. Freeze, but the rest of the DLC is mostly filler and stuff for replayability in the form of challenge maps and challenge campaigns, which don't interest me, personally.
Overall, the game is definitely worth trying out, even more so if you're familiar with the previous installments in the franchise.

I had heard of this franchise over the years, but I hadn’t ever played it myself before. DmC – Devil May Cry is an action adventure platformer from Ninja Theory and Capcom. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
The first thing that really struck me about DmC was how good the graphics looked. I was playing on lower graphical settings (for the sake of performance) and the game still looked better than a good handful of games that are brand new. They were seriously well done.
After gawking at the graphics, I next came to the actual animations. Everything is incredibly fluid: combat, walking, jumping, everything. Even if you’re the laziest, most pathetic mortal on the face of the planet, you can’t help but to feel badass while you’re playing this game. That is just how good the animations make everything look.
The next thing that I came to that just impressed the hell right out of me, was the upgrade system. While you are in the store upgrading your abilities or your weapons, I discovered the best upgrade system I had ever seen in a game like this. First of all there is an option for you to try out the upgrade before you commit points to it. That’s right. The game let’s you try out the ability or upgrade before you buy it. Secondly, once you’ve purchased the ability/upgrade, if you end up finding out that you don’t like it or you don’t ever use it you can take the points out (free of charge) and immediately put them into something else. Every game should have this.
The music is pretty good. I recall seeing Combichrist being mentioned in the credits and another band, but I can’t remember who. That being said, Combichrist was an excellent choice for this game as their contributions to the soundtrack really went well with all the action.
Enemy design was pretty cool. Normally, when I think about demons, I’m thinking about big, fleshy, horned monsters that run amok and torment everyone in their path. This was not even close to the case in DmC however. Demons (while some do have fleshy bits) are mostly made from what looks like metal, ceramics, and bone. It was a very interesting take on demonic entities (and, albeit, a refreshing one).
Boss design (with the exception of Mundus) was also really cool. Let’s just say that the Succubus is not going to look like your expectations in the slightest.
The Bad
DmC started out with a great story. There were great cutscenes, dialogue, a giant Hunter Demon with a ridiculously cool voice. However, as the game went on, the quality of the dialogue and the story went steadily downhill. By the end of the game things had become so predictable that I felt like I was watching some edgy 90’s teen movie.
The Meh
The game is pretty short. I blazed through it in right around seven hours.
There is a marked lack of gore in most of the game. I suppose this makes sense as (I mentioned above) most of the demons you fight are made from materials other than flesh and blood.
Verdict: Yea
DmC is a great game and a great addition to any collection. If you’re a fan of the franchise, you’ll no doubt love it. If you’re new to the franchise, I’m pretty sure that you’ll love it all the same. It has a bit of a steep price tag (especially for how short it is), but, if it went on sale, I’d most certainly snag a copy. As always, thanks for reading.

Not a bad game at it's core but for a "finished" product, the game lacks a lot of refinement. As it is now, it's very rough in terms of UI and how game elements are explained and structured.
An example is the "Bureaucracy" board, which serves as the sort of research element of the game. Research is very simple, requiring only a modest sum of cash up front and time. However, whereas in other games research is designed to increase effectiveness or open up alternative strategies, a large amount of the research in Prison Architect is there just to cost time. Laundry, for example, is a required service in your prison. Otherwise, inmates will become increasingly hostile and it will give them reason to riot, initiate violence, destroy property etc. But laundry is locked behind another research, the Foreman, and you only get laundry incidentally from researching prison labor. There are many other research topics that are absolutely necessary to running your prison even moderately effevtively, such as janitors, guard deployment/patrols and basic finances. In effect, this forces you to research a decent amount before you can even think about accepting prisoners.
Another alarming issue is the lack of clarity in gameplay elements. A large amount of rooms or objects lack descriptions entirely. The sorting table, for example, is to be used in the library. (Why do I want a library anyways? It says inmates are shipped books and tasked with sorting them onto shelves. Is this a punishment? Can they read in the library eventually? When does this take place, during freetime, work time or some other time? Nothing I could find in the game would explain any of this.) But theres no description for the sorting table. In fact, there's no indication what this object is used for at all from the object page. The only way to find out what it's used for in game is if you decide to build the library, which the game never prompts you to do or gives you any reason to do so, and then view the requirements that pop up when the room comes up as invalid.
Some elements that were intended to be used together just dont mix period, for whatever reason. The game features grants, which are usually cash in advance and on completion of some sort of objective, such as expanding your prisoner capacity or building a certain facility. One of these grants is for visitation and requires you to build a visitor's table and some entertainment objects in a visitation room. (I'm not sure why I need a TV in a visitation room however.) However, in addition to the visitor's table (Which is basically just a table with 4 chairs, not very secure.) there's also a traditional visitation booth that features the glass pane between the prisoner and visitors and the telephone for talking to one another. The catch is that building the booth doesn't satisfy the requirements of having a visitation room. You can have your prisoners talking with friends and family all day from 8AM to 8PM with the booths but the game still refuses to acknowledge you have a working visitation room, at least in terms of the grant. Even if you were to build a table instead, you still need a TV for whatever reason to complete your grant.
There's a handful of other issues with the game too. One of my favorites is staff refusing to use the toilet unless it's labeled as a staff room, even if it's outside of the prisoner area. They'll even use it if the game tells you the staff room is invalid, which defeats the entire purpose of having a notification that the room is invalid anyways.
Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game at it's core. It just lacks a lot of clarity and polish for it to be a complete game in my opinion. I'd say it's worth it if you can get a 50% off deal on it but otherwise I'd pass it up. If you do get it then I'd advise you to have the wiki or some other reasource ready. This isn't a game that has a built in resource for you to consult when you need help and neither is it a game that prompts you to learn through discovery. It expects you to know what you're doing at the get go but offers no assistance in figuring it out.

Insanity's Blade is exactly what it looks like: a fairly uncomplicated, gratuitously violent, good ol' retro romp. If you're looking for a few hours of satisfying pixelated horror-fantasy carnage that occasionally might also make you break a sweat, but not too much, you should definitely give it a go.
Pros:
Extremely satisfying carnage - a retro game where you will definitely not feel underpowered. With the exception of trickier sections and bosses, you can just keep rolling onwards and mowing down everything in your path. I don't know about you, but sometimes, I don't want puzzles or tactics or anything else of that sort to get in the way of pure, straightforward slaughter in a game I'm playing. You will find plenty of that here. The art and sound contributes a lot to the experience, too.
Challenging platforming sections - not too many of these, but the trickier ones might pleasantly surprise you if you like this kind of thing.
Beautiful retro art - absolutely lovely pixelated horror-fantasy scenery and monsters. Nothing too fancy or super duper original - but everything looks just as good as it should.
KILLER soundtrack - the music is absolutely
. That epic track in the trailer? Almost all of the OST is on that level of awesome. You can also set it to be 8 or 16 bit, which is a nice touch.
Story - this isn't Dragon Age, obviously. But for a game of this caliber, the story does its job perfectly.
Controls - this game gets right what many old games got wrong: difficulty should not lie in bad controls.
One-machine coop mode - unfortunately I had no one around to try this with, but it looks like it could be a lot of fun.
Cons:
Inventory and shop system look like they were originally meant to hold more significance - in their current form, they're unnecessary.
Difficulty is uneven - one of the early levels is so relentlessly lengthy and hard even on normal that I rather opted to restart the game on casual (you will know the one. f***ing wizards). The boss of the same level is the hardest in the entire game. There are a handful more sections later on that will definitely test your mettle - but apart from these, there isn't much of a challenge for the most part. In fact, the game gets mostly easier as it goes on because of the attack upgrades.
Repetition - the less complicated levels may get boring for some people pretty fast. I still enjoyed them for the undisturbed carnage myself.
Final verdict: It's a fairly simple, extremely satisfying oldschool platformer. Definitely worth the price, and a good way to take a break from overcomplicated modern games.

It's hard to explain why this game is fun, but it's fun nonetheless. At first glance it looks like some sort of strategy game, but in reality it's a relatively mindless clickfest in the spirit of Farmville. It's sold by Big Fish Games, where the first one is available, and falls into the sort of casual clicky games category they're known for. Now, I never play those sorts of games, which is why this may seem like a novelty to me and therefore "fun."
You control up to four workers who are able to work on one command at a time, but you can queue up commands and the next available worker will take the next available task. Basically, things pop up on the map and you tell workers to collect them and then tell workers to take them from the main building to somewhere else or to go fix or upgrade something. While you're busy a-railroadin', a train will come by every so often that you need to service. The real "strategy" is to balance between collection and building. My personal battle was to not queue up so many commands in advance. When there are 10 things to click, I want to click them all, but you'll learn to let some lumber or stone sit while you prioritize ticketing a train. It's always good to keep one worker close to home for when trains come by or you realize you need to do something now (commands can only be canceled if a worker hasn't already undertaken the task). If you send all four workers out, you may have to wait 5-15 seconds for them to make it back and, well, time is money.
There are 40 maps and it took me about five hours to beat. At the end of each map, you get to work on a structure in a town. It doesn't do anything to the game and completing all the structures doesn't award you anything. You just need to get 80% of the town built before level 40 or the banker will...do something to you that makes you lose the game. I'm not sure why the bank is making you build a whole town.
As far as I can tell, the story makes no sense whatsoever. You're fixing up an old railroad with your uncle while a banker follows you around mocking you after he personally lent you the funds to take on the project for the second time. The story is identical to the first game. I can't tell if the dialogue is poorly written or poorly translated, but it's pretty boring and the subtext is hard to follow.
I played it in the morning while I was having my coffee and waking up before work. It hit the ol' cerebral spot. It was just what my brain needed.
There's a demo of the first one floating around out there if you're curious. I did that before I bought it here.
Do I recommend it? Yes, but just know it's casual city, USA.

I had heard of this franchise over the years, but I hadn’t ever played it myself before. DmC – Devil May Cry is an action adventure platformer from Ninja Theory and Capcom. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
The first thing that really struck me about DmC was how good the graphics looked. I was playing on lower graphical settings (for the sake of performance) and the game still looked better than a good handful of games that are brand new. They were seriously well done.
After gawking at the graphics, I next came to the actual animations. Everything is incredibly fluid: combat, walking, jumping, everything. Even if you’re the laziest, most pathetic mortal on the face of the planet, you can’t help but to feel badass while you’re playing this game. That is just how good the animations make everything look.
The next thing that I came to that just impressed the hell right out of me, was the upgrade system. While you are in the store upgrading your abilities or your weapons, I discovered the best upgrade system I had ever seen in a game like this. First of all there is an option for you to try out the upgrade before you commit points to it. That’s right. The game let’s you try out the ability or upgrade before you buy it. Secondly, once you’ve purchased the ability/upgrade, if you end up finding out that you don’t like it or you don’t ever use it you can take the points out (free of charge) and immediately put them into something else. Every game should have this.
The music is pretty good. I recall seeing Combichrist being mentioned in the credits and another band, but I can’t remember who. That being said, Combichrist was an excellent choice for this game as their contributions to the soundtrack really went well with all the action.
Enemy design was pretty cool. Normally, when I think about demons, I’m thinking about big, fleshy, horned monsters that run amok and torment everyone in their path. This was not even close to the case in DmC however. Demons (while some do have fleshy bits) are mostly made from what looks like metal, ceramics, and bone. It was a very interesting take on demonic entities (and, albeit, a refreshing one).
Boss design (with the exception of Mundus) was also really cool. Let’s just say that the Succubus is not going to look like your expectations in the slightest.
The Bad
DmC started out with a great story. There were great cutscenes, dialogue, a giant Hunter Demon with a ridiculously cool voice. However, as the game went on, the quality of the dialogue and the story went steadily downhill. By the end of the game things had become so predictable that I felt like I was watching some edgy 90’s teen movie.
The Meh
The game is pretty short. I blazed through it in right around seven hours.
There is a marked lack of gore in most of the game. I suppose this makes sense as (I mentioned above) most of the demons you fight are made from materials other than flesh and blood.
Verdict: Yea
DmC is a great game and a great addition to any collection. If you’re a fan of the franchise, you’ll no doubt love it. If you’re new to the franchise, I’m pretty sure that you’ll love it all the same. It has a bit of a steep price tag (especially for how short it is), but, if it went on sale, I’d most certainly snag a copy. As always, thanks for reading.

APB Reloaded is a bit of a mixed bag. If you've played Grand Theft Auto before and any of its multiplayer mode renditions, you'll feel at home. You can choose one of two sides; criminal or enforcer. Enforcers get less-than-lethal weapons and can start police chases with criminals caught in the act of theft or mugging. Criminals can steal/mug for extra cash. The catch is that enforcers need criminals present to really initiate any open world gameplay. Criminals, well, they can just mug/steal with or without enforcers around. It makes for some very lopsided income generation.
Aside from open world, you can play missions. All missions are PvP in nature. There are no bots, AI or PvE content. The game ranks players by green, bronze, silver and gold. The issue however is that, if you queue by yourself, it is very common to find yourself playing against 4-5 gold players while being paired with silvers. If you want to enjoy APB more, make sure you get a few friends together to round out your team. That way, win or lose, you'll probably enjoy the game a lot more.
There is a *lot* of customization in APB. You can color clothes, unlock cosmetic parts for your car, create playlists for your car's radio and the music played for enemies when you kill them. Most of the customization is unlocked through normal, grind-heavy reputation gameplay (ie. play missions while pledged to a contact, level them up, unlock more, etc.).
The free to play aspect is both well-rounded.... and lop-sided. The starter weapon is a very versatile weapon and you may find yourself using it longer than you might expect for good reasons. It won't win a sniper fight, but it is a mixed range weapon. Vehicles can be a little unbalanced, but usually you can find an NPC vehicle that will get you 80% there compared to an upgraded one (I'm probably being generous with that statistic though). Where things can, and will, get out of hand is character modifications and weapon upgrades. Unless you grind the game out and toss some money into the cash shop, you will likely never, ever win against a leveled/ ranked gold. Normally, this would be expected. But you will encounter missions against them in your first 30 minutes of play. Not at max level, not days into the game but from the very start.
So, know that going in...
And last, cheating. It is present in this game in the form of aimbots and wall hacks. It isn't anywhere near as bad as it used to be, but you'll know the players when you see them. The new anti-cheat system can take hours/days to sift through and ban players, but it is there where it used to be completely absent.
Can you I recommend APB? Yes. It is free to play so you should give it a shot and make your own opinion of the game. But if you're looking for a game where you can level in peace, without a grind and be comparable to paying players, this is not your game. If you're looking for a game that you can invest time in, learn to be better at and make minimal, smart purchases to reach the top, APB may fit what you're looking for.

Wuppo is the most charming game I got to play in years. The world the characters and the gameplay is all really solid, the only thing that didn't really grasp me was the combat but Wuppo will go down as one of the best indie games I ever got the pleasure to play.

It's hard to describe Wuppo, but the thing that left a nagging feeling after the ending credits rolled was the combat. Wuppo doesn't need a combat system.
The things the game does best are most certainly not combat based. It's the world building, the quick characterizations that leave you attached to so-and-so. The facial expressions used to convey an idea or a feeling, and the dialogue that is pretty genuinely inspired. The different races and their history and the borderline feeling of awe as you discover what the game is actually going to be about.
Slapped on to all of that is a platformer-shooter combat system that could have been a fairly direct rip from any game of the NES era. But the controls aren't tight, your aim is clunky, and your mobility is lacking (so you can't dodge some of the bullet-hell-ish attacks you'll be dealing with). You have different weapons, but even though you can bind them to number keys, switching is kind of inconvenient given the number of other important items you'll want to have on that row. So really, you're more or less trading blows and stat checking against every opponent you fight. It just doesn't belong.
And that would be forgivable if the combat weren't so large a part of the game. But you probably spend about a third of your time in combat, about a third of your time walking from one place to another, and another third in conversations and actually exploring your current objective.
Wuppo does a lot of things right. But it's a short enough game that those bright spots are insufficient to carry a $15 price tag.

Not a bad game at it's core but for a "finished" product, the game lacks a lot of refinement. As it is now, it's very rough in terms of UI and how game elements are explained and structured.
An example is the "Bureaucracy" board, which serves as the sort of research element of the game. Research is very simple, requiring only a modest sum of cash up front and time. However, whereas in other games research is designed to increase effectiveness or open up alternative strategies, a large amount of the research in Prison Architect is there just to cost time. Laundry, for example, is a required service in your prison. Otherwise, inmates will become increasingly hostile and it will give them reason to riot, initiate violence, destroy property etc. But laundry is locked behind another research, the Foreman, and you only get laundry incidentally from researching prison labor. There are many other research topics that are absolutely necessary to running your prison even moderately effevtively, such as janitors, guard deployment/patrols and basic finances. In effect, this forces you to research a decent amount before you can even think about accepting prisoners.
Another alarming issue is the lack of clarity in gameplay elements. A large amount of rooms or objects lack descriptions entirely. The sorting table, for example, is to be used in the library. (Why do I want a library anyways? It says inmates are shipped books and tasked with sorting them onto shelves. Is this a punishment? Can they read in the library eventually? When does this take place, during freetime, work time or some other time? Nothing I could find in the game would explain any of this.) But theres no description for the sorting table. In fact, there's no indication what this object is used for at all from the object page. The only way to find out what it's used for in game is if you decide to build the library, which the game never prompts you to do or gives you any reason to do so, and then view the requirements that pop up when the room comes up as invalid.
Some elements that were intended to be used together just dont mix period, for whatever reason. The game features grants, which are usually cash in advance and on completion of some sort of objective, such as expanding your prisoner capacity or building a certain facility. One of these grants is for visitation and requires you to build a visitor's table and some entertainment objects in a visitation room. (I'm not sure why I need a TV in a visitation room however.) However, in addition to the visitor's table (Which is basically just a table with 4 chairs, not very secure.) there's also a traditional visitation booth that features the glass pane between the prisoner and visitors and the telephone for talking to one another. The catch is that building the booth doesn't satisfy the requirements of having a visitation room. You can have your prisoners talking with friends and family all day from 8AM to 8PM with the booths but the game still refuses to acknowledge you have a working visitation room, at least in terms of the grant. Even if you were to build a table instead, you still need a TV for whatever reason to complete your grant.
There's a handful of other issues with the game too. One of my favorites is staff refusing to use the toilet unless it's labeled as a staff room, even if it's outside of the prisoner area. They'll even use it if the game tells you the staff room is invalid, which defeats the entire purpose of having a notification that the room is invalid anyways.
Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game at it's core. It just lacks a lot of clarity and polish for it to be a complete game in my opinion. I'd say it's worth it if you can get a 50% off deal on it but otherwise I'd pass it up. If you do get it then I'd advise you to have the wiki or some other reasource ready. This isn't a game that has a built in resource for you to consult when you need help and neither is it a game that prompts you to learn through discovery. It expects you to know what you're doing at the get go but offers no assistance in figuring it out.

This is a better Mega Man game than anything Capcom has made in the past ten years. Seriously, ZX came out ten years ago, the last X game was twelve years ago...
20XX evokes nostalgia for the Mega Man X series and the era of challenging platformers, while not aping the early 1990s. The art is clean and aesthetically pleasing, the soundtrack is phenomenal, and procedural level generation coupled with the game's roguelike-like permadeath make for a fantastically difficult, non-repetitive action platformer that feels like a modern take on a long past world of video games.
I don't think I've ever played a classics-inspired game on Steam that felt so right. It feels like being a kid again. Though if I had played more of the Mega Man series as a kid, maybe my runs in 20XX would last longer than a few levels.
In simple, simple, simple terms; The game is HELLA fun and HELLA hard.

Even though its still in early access, 20XX is a fantastic Mega Man X style roguelike that is constantly evolving. The level elements are randomly generated, giving a new experience each time you play. Collecting augmenting items, aquiring armor, and obtaining bosses weapons all enhance your robotic warrior as you blast your way through the game.
Pros:
Gameplay: The game feels very similar to Capcom's iconic JUMPANDSHOOTMAN franchise. While the physics are not completely identical, it's accessable enough for veteran players to jump into the action.
Items: The variety of collectables breath life into the genre, changing the game in fun and exciting ways.
Music: The score is top notch.
Difficulty: The game starts off very friendly for beginning players, but scales up in difficulty after progressing through each stage, reaching brutally punishing levels late game, just like Mega Man games are known for.
Support: The developers are constantly updating the game (and do so every other Wednesday), adding new content and responding to user feedback. It's refreshing to see how involved the creators are.
Cons:
Randomly Spawning Items: This game is a roguelike, so random powerups come with the territory. But it can be very frustrating when you cannot find powerups that are relevent to your current character build.
DIfficulty: As I mentioned, this game can be downright punishing. Especially if you don't have the proper items and equipment, some of the late game stage hazards seem cheap and infuriating. The laser traps in the Sky Temple in particular will make you want to throw your controller if you couldn't find anything to help you deal with them.
Learning Curve: This isn't a con so much as a statement, but there is a definite adjustment period needed to get use to the game mechanics; especially if you're a Mega Man veteran. For example, the fact that your health doesn't replenish at the start of each new level seemed very strange at first, but once you get a feel for the game, these adjustments become a nonissue.
All things considered, I love this game, and am continuously impressed by how far its come. I can't wait to see the finished product.
9/10 Would definitely recommend.

Super-tight controls. This takes the freedom of movement it took all the way up to Megaman Zero to perfect, and then makes it even better. Get ready to dash-wall-jump off a wall, over an enemy, turn, shoot, backtrack, and grab onto a small platform with your head for another wall-jump.
Excellent platforming play. Ground? What ground? While it can be a bit frustrating in the Sky Temple, with its countless traps, the game fully has you making accurate leaps from one tiny platform to another, or going up and down walls, or doing disappearing block puzzles. What more, the randomly generated levels prevent you from getting too "muscle memory" with the jumps. While the levels are still primarily linear, they do have you going left, right, up, and down. You're not just going screen by screen clearing enemies, but also having to watch your movement at the same time.
The soundtrack! Oh, the soundtrack! Brandon Ellis is a genius. I could spend pages explaining it, but it'd be faster if you just looked it up and listened to it.
They have a reddit in which they take user input into consideration. The game is seeing improvement after improvement, with regular updates still coming out.
Plus, there's something to be said about how Roguelikes can have you coming back to the same game, time after time, and still having fun.
Oh, and it has cool power ups and graphics and whatnot. But seriously, how did you make it all the way down here and STILL haven't bought this game? BUY THIS GAME!!
Also, coop multiplayer: SO AWESOME! Buy copies for all your friends!
