Tails also reeeally likes landing on ledges and dropping Sonic off them. Which leads to a fair number of cheap deaths, especially in bottomless pit-heavy stages.
The stage design still also has "haha surprise you died" issues from time to time. Oil Desert Act 3 and Sky Fortress Act 1 spring to mind especially but there's a good bit of it throughout. Really Sky Fortress Act 1 does literally everything wrong and destroys any good will towards Sky Chase zone as well.
The graphics are better, the music is a bit better, the physics are a bit better. It's all just slightly better and on the low end of a positive review for me.

A game has to be fairly unbearable for me to not want to finish it.  Well, congratulations Sonic 4, you've landed in that small list of games I just straight up hate.
The parts that broke me?  Lots of them, but most specifically the Oil world part 2: the  Oil world has a mechanci where you run across sinking sand and have to jump in order to not sink into it and die, right?  Fine, that's fair.  At a certain point in the stage I was then forced to run along this sand, but in a low corridor where while on top of the sand Sonic's head would be touching the roof of the corridor.  This immediately slowed my progress to a grinding halt.  It gets better, though, because as you get further down the corridor, the roof is raised BUT Spikes are placed at the bottom of the roof!  The spike tips reach exactly where the ceiling of the corridor was before, so if you jump too high you just die.  This isn't ok but I could have at least gotten through the area if it wasn't very, very long or if there had been any rings whatsoever in it, but no, I got hit once, all of my rings disappeared in the sand, and then I had to go through the rest of this insanely long corridor without any protection.  ♥♥♥♥ that.
The boss of the Winter world -- really cool looking level by the way -- was also full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  Alright, cool, I'm racing Metal Sonic and I have to catch up with him and hit him, awesome!  This is awesome!  Wait, two minutes into the fight -- seemed like a long time for a sonic game -- he just hits the platform that I'm running on, breaking it.  I immediately ran into the hole and fell to my death, restarting the fight.  Alright, whatever, that was really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because I didn't have the time to react, and it's dumb that I have to restart the boss fight but at least I know that's coming now and it won't happen again.  Oh wait no, he just does that attack so fast and it's right on top of where you're running that you're just ♥♥♥♥ed if you don't anticipate it.
Elsewhere in poor design land is anything to do with Tails.  Alright, so you occassionally have to press a button to join up with Tails for a special ability.  Cool.  Except for, you know, these abilities being so limited in utility that the only times you use them are when the game halts your progress unless you use the abilities. Hey game, if you think I can't figure something out because I'm not using it frequently enough then I'm pretty sure you designed these abilities poorly.
Tl;dr: there are some cool parts to the game but they usually get ♥♥♥♥ed up with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design, horrible enemy placement and just straight up terrible choices.

Sonic 4 Episode 2 is a game I'm completely inconsistent with. I played it for half an hour and thought it wasn't worth playing through, played it again from beginning to end and hated it, and then played it through again and honestly thought it was on par with the Genesis games.
In comparison to Episode 1 it's definitely better. The physics are improved and the graphics no longer look like New Super Mario Bros. but worse. A lot of people complained that classic Sonic was absent from the first game, and took it way overboard, but I kinda do agree that modern looks really unnatural here. Thankfully there's a mod for that anyway if it bothers you that much.
The game controls a lot better than Ep1 and it's at least satisfying in this game, but still not quite as solid as in the classic games or even Generations. Sonic feels like he lacks weight on the ground and momentum building isn't quite right, sometimes requiring homing attack spamming just to reach your max speed on the ground.
The level themes are all blatantly reused concepts with the exception of White Park which while I can compare it to some levels it doesn't outright copy anything. I hate the fact that a game selling itself as Sonic 4 is almost nothing but recycled levels and enemies, but the levels themselves have so many new concepts that it's still pretty fresh as a whole, and the likenesses of Episode 2's levels to classic levels isn't as offensive as in Ep1... with the exception of Sky Fortress which is nearly identical.
The game's visuals are absolutely gorgeous. I'd say Sonic 4 Ep2 is the most scenic game in the series. It's incredibly polished visually. I can't say the same about the soundtrack, though. While I initially really hated it, I realized on subsequent playthroughs with Super Sonic available I never used him for just one reason; I didn't want to stop the level music. While I do actually really love the compositions themselves, the instrumentation is horrid. They clearly went for a Genesis style tinny-ness to the synths but it just sounds awful on some tracks, specifically Sky Fortress Act II and the Death Egg's theme, two songs which I would actually really like if they used better synths.
Oh yeah it's also really short. This game has five zones in total and 25 levels in all if you count the boss levels and special stages. I think with a casual runthrough of both this and Sonic 2, Sonic 2 would still be longer, but I consider Sonic 2 to be fairly short for a Sonic game I dunno. Completing the game without all of the Chaos Emeralds yields a message to go collect them, but there's really no reason to, because it does nothing to the ending. Little Planet is still stuck inside the Death Egg while Sonic and Tails feel good about themselves in their escape pods. This could be thought of as a lead-in to Episode 3, but as of now Sega has no plans for one. One of the developers has said that they might make one if Ep2 sold well. Did it? I dunno but I certainly don't want the Sonic 4 series to end like this.
The game was actually short enough that I turned to achievement hunting to elongate it. Which was odd as this was after I'd already had my fill of this game and dismissed it as another bad Sonic entry. I actually WANTED to come back to collect achievements and actually found a lot of fun with the game, both in gathering the achievements and just playing the game itself. However I will say that the achievements are absolutely pointless. Certain gameplay elements like the Red Rings and presence and abundance of rings before boss encounters were clearly just implemented for the game's achievements on release, but getting said achievements has no bearing on the actual game whatsoever. Collecting all the Red Rings or getting the last hit on every boss as Super Sonic, none of this affects the game at all. It doesn't even have a list of the achievements in game so really it's questionable why they're even there other than to make this short game slightly longer.
All in all though I did find a lot of fun with this. The game's length as well as reused settings are the biggest problems, but they're pretty well made up for with a beautiful presentation, pretty enjoyable music and most of all a lot of good level gimmicks and physical designs. Is it as good as the classics? Eh, probably not, if only because it's not completely orginal, but I had just about as much fun with it anyway.

Insanity's Blade is an arcade-inspired platformer where you control Thurstan, a retired warrior that have it's village attacked by a horde of demons and it's family killed in the process leaving him as the sole survivor of the tragedy. After that Thurstan embarks in a journey to find the cause of the demonic horde while slowly giving in to the hatred of demons and mental degradation of the loss of his family.
If that summary got you interested in the game it's because at the very least it's story, while simple in premise and execution, is very well told and never stops been entertaining even if it is very thin and almost bare bones. In this case you could even say it has no fluf, only the very essencial for the plot. I have to admit, this is what saved this game for me and made me continue to play up until the end of it's story mode. While I enjoyed it, I understand many others might give this game a pass because of the next point: Gameplay.
The gameplay is simple but there's little to no variety in it, so it dulls very quickly. The mechanics aren't very well thought for what the game intends itself to be, evident by the fact that the game gives the player projectiles for a hand to hand platform brawler. Screenshots are beautiful, but the game is very poorly animated and most stuff in motion isn't really all that good and that leads into the fact most stuff that fly on screen and hits the player could be deemed as unfair. Because of the poor animations enemies also have very poorly telegraphed attacks and some enemies don't even have the required animation to convey what they actually do (most notable for weapon-throwing enemies).
Thurstan controls a little too abruptly for confort and really doesn't have any sort of momentum to his movement or combat. He has an attack and a grab for his offensive options and they aren't really nice to use. The attack button stops Thurstan on spot to make the attack motion and hit the enemies and the same goes for the grab with the only diference been that Thurstan flip-jump over the enemy and throws it forward. The attack has another characteristic that makes it the superior choice on almost every situation: it can be upgraded on certain shops throughout the game to have increasingly powerful projetile knives been thrown everytime you attack. This should be awesome but it gives away the fact that it was a patchwork for everything else that didn't work in the game. Enemies don't stagger or flinch when hit, some of them don't have attack animations and there is a sensation that there is no weight to anything you do or is done to you because the animations and sound effects don't convey properly what is going on.
Maybe none of that is very concerning to you and you are loving the game so far, but remember what I said on the beggining summary of the game? "Insanity's Blade is an arcade-inspired platformer..." And that also apply to it's core design: ENEMIES EVERYWHERE AND RESPAWNING!!! That is what I consider to be what made aparent to me this game didn't really know what it wanted to be. In one hand you have a very breef but powerful story and a pair of protagonists that are really easy to simpatise due to their intermission banter. On the other you have a game wanting to be so arcade-hardcore that it passes some very outdated, clunky, poorly thought AND made design decisions as integral to the experience that it is really hard to imagine how this game even holds itself together. At least the soundtrack is nice, nothing really special, just nice.
Do I recomend this game? Only if you can stomach the gameplay for long enough to enjoy the story and if you are a really BIG fan of stories, although this may be way too bare bones for you. If you are after some interesting characters, this may also be an interesting one since there is enough time to develop the characters alongside the story. Bonus points for been short (took me 3hrs to beat it). But if you are someone who value your gameplay as paramount and don't really regard story and characters as important or is one who are looking for deep and rewarding gameplay or you simply can't stand arcade design principles, you should avoid this one.

Insanity's blade sure is insane! Ha ha, get it? I'm funny!
I may have also become partly insane when playing this game or maybe that was the lingering effects of playing Corgi Warlock, I'm not sure. Regardless this game is an experience and not a good one.
What is good is the presentation, everything about this game is inspired by earlier video games from the 90's and it is clearly a homage to those types of games even down to the 'how to play'. The music is also servicable and I think I liked one song but I'm not sure, I would have to hear it again to be sure which is difficult because that would mean playing the game again which I am not doing!
I would like to point out that I did infact beat the game and unlike a lot of the positive reviews with only 30min or less playtime, the early game is almost the same as the end game in terms of monsters you fight, how you fight them and general game progression. There are very few tricks and surprises along the way which is both a blessing and a curse since I reached a point where I just wanted the game to end but some variety might have made me re-invested in the game.
Lets talk about the bad now because there is a heafty amount. First of all the game was not tested in multiplayer so having a second player breaks the game. Both in terms of removing all challenge except for the last stage and also in terms of breaking the actual game. The game has a lot of glitches, some amusing and others annoying for example I, as player one died but player two was still alive. No problem right? Well when I died we were just about to enter the boss chamber and this caused the boss to not spawn and the room to also not spawn correctly so there was no boss. Just a half black screen while we waited for time to run out just on the off chance that would fix the issue.
Then there is the final stage itself, now when you play in multiplayer player two
player one will teleport to one another if either one strays too far. On the last stage you need to climb falling platforms and if you touch the bottom of the stage you will die. This would not be so difficult except unless you both jump together,
then one of you will pull the other backwards and you will both die! This is never an issue anywhere else in the game either.
Now to complain about the bosses. They are boring. They recycle 3 bosses all through the game and then the final boss is a recycled boss but with a new skin and that is it.
The bosses also offer no challenge and here is a tip (if you are fooling enough to buy this game!) the bosses ONLY target player one, so as player one, pull a boss to the wall and let player two go all ham on it. Any time this doesn't work, simply climb the wall and shoot, none of the bosses have attacks that will kill you if you do this, unless you fall asleep or something.
And the final cardinal sin, the game ends with a sequel hook. The developer? Working on a new game. Is it part two? HA HA HA HA of course it isn't!
I recommend watching this game, either on youtube or twitch or vimeo, whatever, watch it and enjoy the visuals because they are great but never, ever buy and play this game. It is awful.

Picked this up during the summer sale for $1.19, I believe, and I have not been disappointed.  If you were a fan of SNES platformers like Castlevania, ActRaiser, and Demon's Crest, then you'll enjoy this game quite a bit because that's exactly what you're getting with Insanity's Blade: a solid, old school, dark fantasy themed platformer.
The story follow Thurston, a retired soldier whose town, along with his wife and children, are slaughtered by a demon.  Branded by the demon and blamed for the destruction of his town, Thurston is now on a quest for revenge accompanied by Finn the dwarf, one of the few people who believe that Thurston is innocent.
The gameplay couldn't be simpler or easier to get the hang of.  One button attack, one button jumps, and the other button allows you to grab a monster and, depending on what direction you're holding when you grab them, Thurston either throws them, punches them to death in the balls (not joking), or rips one of their arms off to use as a weapon.
Throughout the game Thurston will level up which will increase his max HP.  In addition, you also collect gold that you can use at shops that appear during the game.  In the shops you can purchase upgraded attacks: shooting a spray of three daggers, then five, three and five again, but this time the daggers are on fire.  You can also purchase 1Ups, and upgrade your max HP.
The music is pretty great to and taps into that nostalgia of old school side scrollers.
There are two modes to the game: story and arcade.  Story mode, obviously, follows the set story line of the game.  It allows you to save between stages and offers side quests to go on to find treasure.  Arcade mode plays like a traditional game of this type: no saves, just 3 lives.  I haven't played this mode yet as I'm still working my way through story mode, so I'm not sure how many continues you get.  Arcade mode also does away with the side quests.
I only have a few complaints so far.  One is that the game is kind of buggy sometimes.  The one I've run into the most is sometimes the screen will go crazy.  By this I mean that sometimes the screen will just quickly scroll in a random direction for a few seconds before flicking back to where I'm currently at.  Hasn't been a major issue so far as it seems to mostly happen at the beginning of boss fights after they finish speaking.  The other one I've run into is specific to one particular stage, and that is stage 2.  Right in the beginning of it, after to jump off the moving platform, there are merfolk jumping out of water at the bottom of the screen.  The floor appears to be solid.  But, if you try to walk straight over the floor, you will fall into the water an die.  Not a major problem if you know to look for it, all you have to do is jump over to the torch.
My only other complaint is with the side quests, and that is I don't really know how they work.  They will appear on the map and you can select them but most of them I've run into just have people telling me about some treasure in one of the stages, or some spot I'm supposed to look for.  However, when I go to that stage I can't find them.  And once you complete a stage you can't replay it.  So, maybe I'm just missing them, I'm not sure.

At first I wasn't sure about this title. It started off well, but at one point became extremely difficult. I thought I was doing something wrong or hadn't found the right items or something. I was worried that if I lost all of my lives I wouldn't get a continue, or if I did, I'd have to restart from the beginning anyway. Turns out, you don't need to worry about lives much at all. Even if you lose all of them, you can continue right where you would had you have merely lost a life. I'm not certain, but I think you have unlimited continues as well, at least in story mode. So this would seem to make lives pointless. So don't even worry about that. Just keep playing and you'll be fine.
That being said, the game itself reminds me of the classic Castlevania games and Super Ghouls n Ghosts. There are multiple subtle references to such past video games if you are paying attention. You can find new weapons to use along the way, but no matter which weapon you have, you still have the ability to shoot multiple "daggers" at enemies. The damage you do is based on your level and choice of weapon, so kill everything you can to level up and get money. Money is most useful for buying upgrades to your throwing daggers, so don't worry too much about buying lives or health so much. It costs too much anyway, and you keep your money and exp even if you die.
With the worry of losing lives out of the way, you'd think that would make the game too easy, but you'd be wrong. It has very challenging platforming levels, and onslaughts of enemies coming at you. There's also secrets and on my first playthrough, I didn't find every weapon, so that is a reason to go back and play again. There's also an arcade mode that has no save feature or side quests. Its just a linear level-by-level run like it would play if you were actually playing it in an arcade cabinet. This game plays just like a classic 16-bit arcade game would have. There were a few glitches I noticed though. Mainly graphical ones where things would studder or a sprite would grow to enormous size while the game is paused, but nothing too major. Nothing game breaking.
All in all, its a fun game for a decent price. I recommend it if you like classic games like Castlevania, Ghouls n Ghosts, Magic Sword, or Black tiger. Its longer than you think it would be, but not too long. You get a decent amount of play time for your money, and that's a good thing. Looking around online, I found little to nothing about this game. It certainly deserves more attention and love. I do hope they can make the sequels to this game they wanted to at some point. I think they can be even better.

Even though its still in early access, 20XX is a fantastic Mega Man X style roguelike that is constantly evolving. The level elements are randomly generated, giving a new experience each time you play. Collecting augmenting items, aquiring armor, and obtaining bosses weapons all enhance your robotic warrior as you blast your way through the game.
Pros:
Gameplay: The game feels very similar to Capcom's iconic JUMPANDSHOOTMAN franchise. While the physics are not completely identical, it's accessable enough for veteran players to jump into the action.
Items: The variety of collectables breath life into the genre, changing the game in fun and exciting ways.
Music: The score is top notch.
Difficulty: The game starts off very friendly for beginning players, but scales up in difficulty after progressing through each stage, reaching brutally punishing levels late game, just like Mega Man games are known for.
Support: The developers are constantly updating the game (and do so every other Wednesday), adding new content and responding to user feedback. It's refreshing to see how involved the creators are.
Cons:
Randomly Spawning Items: This game is a roguelike, so random powerups come with the territory. But it can be very frustrating when you cannot find powerups that are relevent to your current character build.
DIfficulty: As I mentioned, this game can be downright punishing. Especially if you don't have the proper items and equipment, some of the late game stage hazards seem cheap and infuriating. The laser traps in the Sky Temple in particular will make you want to throw your controller if you couldn't find anything to help you deal with them.
Learning Curve: This isn't a con so much as a statement, but there is a definite adjustment period needed to get use to the game mechanics; especially if you're a Mega Man veteran. For example, the fact that your health doesn't replenish at the start of each new level seemed very strange at first, but once you get a feel for the game, these adjustments become a nonissue.
All things considered, I love this game, and am continuously impressed by how far its come. I can't wait to see the finished product.
9/10 Would definitely recommend.

After playing the main game to 85% completion I unfortunately feel compelled to give Ori a marginal thumbs down.
If you don't already know, Ori is described as a Metroidvania game. Except this isn't entirely accurate. Metroidvania - ie. Castlevania and Metroid, would imply a lot more combat than what we see here in Ori. Chiefly this is a PLATFORMING game, with certain areas 'walled' off, either literally or metaphorically, behind abilities you need to acquire to access them. Most of the skills you get are going to be movement related. All the usual suspects are here; wall climb, double jump, ground stomp, etc.
There isn't anything wrong with Platforming games per se, in Ori's case however there isn't enough to keep your interest when the platforming is interspersed with incredibly dull combat. Defeating enemies usually amounts to spamming X and dodging projectiles until whatever you are attacking dies. Ori has his own heat seeking projectiles that does most of the work for you. There's a charged version of weapon but it's effectively the same thing. You will find a myriad of pallet swapped enemies, but it always comes down to spam X and dodge.
So is the platforming good enough? In parts it can be, but on the whole Ori feels more like a chore to get through. Jump here, glide here, run there, etc. x 4 different sub worlds until done. The complete lack of boss fights doesn't help things either. Instead, each level is concluded with an escape sequence. You know the one; run as fast as you can before the fire/water/falling rocks gets you. And if you die, go back to the beginning. Do people actually like these events?
Ori has a lot going for it. It runs very well, Ori controls well, graphically it's 2D but very colorful with a fair amount of variety between worlds. The story is fine but mostly skippable. With better combat, more interesting enemies, and more skills that aren't just movement based there could have been a winner here. As is there are better games of this genre you could be playing.

I can't really recommend this in its current, early access form. A friend bought it for me to play together, and it was noticable right away that it's far off from its inspiration (or at least, its similarities in character design and control remind me vaguely of Megaman, but of a weaker version.)
Some points:
-The online co-op is decent, and was what I derived most of my enjoyment from.
-The game has daily challenges and such, which could suggest some long term replayability.
-The level design is kind of terrible. It really just likes to throw a bunch of enemies at you and pretend it's hard, when a charge shot wipes out everything in a line anyways. The platforming is basic, and relies heavily on poorly timed hazards like lazers that always turn on at the time you actually need to jump.
-Disappearing block platforming, constantly. If you didn't like those parts in megaman, you'll hate them here. They're strewn throughout the levels like a weed on fertilizer.
-The random generation really feels like the same thing over and over. Most of the items are basic "more damage, more drops, higher jump, max health, max energy", with a few interesting things mixed in.
-I repeat my earlier point on hating the level design. Perhaps randomly generated platforming is only good on paper, especially when that naturally means a lot of repeated platforming sections.
-Don't really like how the character controls. That may just be personal.
Hopefully it tightens up before the end of its early access phase. The game is generally well reviewed so hopefully it gets the support it needs, as it looks like it will be more or less successful regardless.

First it has to be said - don't listen to the DMC fanboys who hated on this game since the reveal trailer. They hate the game no matter what, and their oinions can't be taken seriously.
How do you know if they're a biased fanboy? Telltale signs include called Dante 'Donte', and outright hatred and vitriol towards the games existance.
Now that we have that out of the way and the baggage of a much loved franchise is put aside, is this game good or not? The answer is yes, it's a very good game, in fact it's one of the best action games I've ever played.
Devil May Cry 1 was an instant classic, it was my first PS2 game and is still my favourite DMC game. I've played every game in the series, including the terrible sequel, and in my opinion DmC is easily the second best game in the series. Arguably it's the best.
Note that many consider DMC3 to be the best, and that's perfectly agreeable, I ultimately prefer 1 because of the atmosphere, and Dante in DMC3 was a little too over the top, OK a LOT over the top.
DmC has the best combat and platforming in the series, the most well told and interesting story (it fleshed out the characters in a way that the entire tetralogy never did), and it also has one of the most striking and interesting visual designs I've seen in a AAA game.
Ultimately this game is pure fun, as with most straight up action games, you know what you're getting - linear level design, fast and furious combat, in your face characters and a rocking soundtrack.
I've played all major franchises in this genre - DMC, God of War, Bayonetta and Ninja Gaiden; DmC is easily the best of the genre available on PC.
The goal of these games is to make you feel like an all-powerful badass, and have fun while you do it, DmC delivers.
Get it, have fun, kick♥♥♥♥♥- win.

Underneath a bizarre (albeit very cute) title and exterior lies an exemplary adventure game. Its world and characters bear a charm that evokes memories of old LucasArts point & click games.
Majority of my playtime was spent exploring, platforming, talking to characters and solving small puzzles. The occasional bouts of combat seemed to be tuned for those more familiar with action games, though there's also an Easy difficulty if you're less interested in combat.
Some puzzles might leave you perplexed as you wonder what items you might need, but paying attention to item descriptions and dialogue should help you through eventually. I felt that the game didn't suffer from point & click "moon logic".
The game helps you immerse yourself into the world by having no loading screens and by filling populated areas with characters which constantly go about their business interacting with the on-screen environment. Public transports also move in real time, reinforcing the illusion that the world doesn't always just wait for you to show up.
In the end, I was just pleasantly surprised to have found a game world that was easy to get invested in, and to have found a game that just made me feel happy.

It's a solid shoot-em-up / bullet hell, but the camera is a bit lacking. I'd suggest grabbing it, but wait for 50% discount.
XenoRaptor is a bullet hell game where you actually control a mechanical dragon and fight flying chainsaws in space. The game offers a pretty straightforward bullet-hell / shmup gameplay. If you play the campaign mode, it throws you into different levels. The levels differ not only in background pictures, but in actual amounts and types of obstacles. This really adds a good variety to the gameplay. The first levels don’t offer much resistance from environment, but it gets tougher as the game progresses. There are meteors and explosive barrels to make your life much harder. Ouch.
Your ship has 3 weapons. Two of them are main weapons that produce “heat.” If you gain too much of it – the ship overheats and can’t fire. It feels like a good solution. On one hand, the player is forced to decide when to press the fire button. On the other hand, it opens up space for different strategies: if some users like heavy weapons that shoot once in a while, they can go for it. The others can go for the ones that can fire rapidly, aren’t as deadly, but generate less heat and can be used much more often. The third weapon requires special pickups, ammo, as it generally tends to be a bit stronger than the other two. I have to admit that I’ve rarely used the third weapon, as you can generally fulfill all your destructive needs with the other two.
One of the features of the game is the ability to customize your ship and your weapons: adding special effects, firing patters, reducing the heat generated or increasing the ship durability. There are lots of options for customization. Most of them are locked from the start, so you get to unlock them by defeating bosses and minibosses during campaign.
The gameplay itself feels very fair: although there’s plenty of random in enemy / obstacle placement and health drops, you always have the feeling that you’re in control. After enemies kill you, you can backtrace to the exact moment where you messed up or maneuvered poorly. Pretty straightforward. You get rewarded for skill, and punished for mistakes. The difficulty itself is pleasantly challenging: enemies swarm around you, leaving you no time to rest. One downside is that the waves take lots of time to clear before you meet the miniboss. If you fight for more than 5 minutes and then die, you’ll have to restart everything from scratch without any actual gains.
The game is well polished: explosions look pretty, the guns feel heavy. The enemy models look a bit bland and due to fast pace of the game it often gets hard to distinguish the roles of enemies.
The biggest issue for me was the weak camera controls: your ships stays in the middle of the screen all the time, which feels very lackluster compared to other action games. Usually, in action games like these, the camera leans forward, towards your aim reticle or ship flight direction. This serves two purposes: it adds ‘action’ feeling to the game, making player feel in the middle constant movement and maneuvering, but also improves the gameplay quality: when you are going forward with your ship, it’s much more important to know what’s going on in your movement direction than what stays behind your ship.
Overall, the game is well done, but the it could have been much better with improved camera controls. So yeah, I suggest grabbing it, but maybe wait for 50%+ discount.

Negatives
-Some weapons are flat-out better than literally all the rest, and you'll find yourself coming back to the same few setups, especially if you want to progress. Using the asteroid-throwing flamethrower, mind-control beam, plutonium gatling beam, etc. just results in a less enjoyable experience. They do less damage and/or are highly conditional in their use, and when you switch it up, you get destroyed by the difficulty when you can no longer dodge in any direction, or your weapon can only hit something 2 feet in front of you. after talking with the developers, i can honestly tell you i now udnerstand where aLL my issues were coming from. so i'm changing my review a bit. as well as going in a bit more detail

Rating: Very Positive <3
Game progress: Main story complete [2016-12-25, same day I got the game]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
When I saw the screenshots of the game on the steam page I thought to myself, GEE that looks like Castlevania X Dracula! (One of my favourites by the way) so I don't see why not! The game looks highly interesting and atmospheric. And wow I wasn't wrong. First time starting the game it felt amazing just seeing those pixels like OH MY GEE! The intro was very nice, title screen is just simply amazing and the overall feeling of starting the game felt like nothing before. And the gameplay just felt very much like Castlevania X Dracula, maybe a bit TOO MUCH but why the living heck would I mind that :3? The game ran super smooth, pixels and sprites were amazing and the overall style was great!
This is the fun part. The part where I will complain, heh. Well you see the gameplay is great but I think it could be greatly amazing with more variation by possibly offering alternative attacks (Such as magic, swords) yes the game has different weapons but it has the same style. It's like you're throwing knives with a sword, axe or mace. If the game had melee for close range & high knockback, magic for splash damage and throwables for long range instead of weapons shooting orbs/throwables then it would have way more variation I'd say. But it's still fun anyway. Enemies had very similar properties. Just walking towards you and dealing melee damage. For lore reasons it can slip away if they're weak and such but I gotta say it's way more fun dodging the enemies that shoot fire at you and try to chase them down in order to survive. In terms of life & death I think it's a great deal that you get 4 lives (Yes 0 is a life) to add more to the difficulty of the game. I think it's great when a game pushes you to be careful and scared to death when you are nearly defeated by something because it adds a greater reward feeling once you get past an obstacle. Most enemies are very easy to avoid and defeat because some are too slow, too weak and very easy to forget about over how easy they are. Though it doesn't stop the game from being fun at all! In fact the game had tons of different looks and gameplay changing enemies which made the game change pace from time to time. Alongside the snow storm in a later level where you had to pay attention where the storm was blowing in order to jump over a few gaps without the storm pushing you down. Bosses in the game turned predictable very quickly and barely held much of a challenge. But what I do LOVE SO MUCH is the fact that each boss had different moves! The last level is what I truly love. Okay, it's time do get rated unhelpful by all the diehard fans of this game who don't actually read the review.
It should be noted that I have reached the final stage of the game (I think), the volcano area that I don't remember the name of. I gave up because of how tediously difficult the game became, and this is coming from someone who loves the dark souls series to death.
Ori and the Blind forest is very overrated, but any game that people like has some redeeming factors. The art, sound design, and movement is all very fluid. I really liked the animations of Ori, and thought they were very adorable. However, the combat is dull and unskillful. It basically boils down to press X to shoot homing projectiles and hope you don't get hit. The enemies are pretty basic and there really aren't that many of them. The game does a poor job at indicating what can hurt you. Many times I die to thorns that I didn't even realize were there. The abilities, like ground pound, double jump, and glide are mostly uninspired, with the exception of one interesting ability that would allow you to sling yourself from projectiles, launching the projectile in the opposite direction as you, which created some neat puzzles and movement sections. The exploration felt very limited and boring, as there weren't enough times where I felt rewarded for exploring. The map didn't feel too memorable like Dark Souls or Symphony of the Night. There were a few good scripted moments in the game, and overall, it's alright.
If you read to the end, and you disagree with my points (which based on the helpful to unhelpful ratio, that probably is the case) please explain why you disagree with them or what I missed when I was playing this game in the comments section. I really would like to know since this game is widely regarded as amazing, and obvoiusly, my opinion differs.

This game is so sleek and fun and polished, and it's still only in Early Access! 20XX is extremely fun, whether you're by yourself or whether you're playing with a pal. Also the platforming and controls are so smooth and actually play just as good, if not better, than a certain platformer series that this game may or may not be based off of COUGH Mega Man X COUGH.
The items and armor upgrades are all cool and unique, and it feels so rewarding when you earn them, whether it's through completing battle challenges, or platforming challenges. 20XX is also a roguelike, meaning it changes every time you play, and you get to choose which boss to take on next. New weapons also give new fun ways to use the character, allowing you to develop your own strategies to clear enemies and finish the stage. This game honestly has me more hyped than Mighty No. 9 ever could get me, and the soundtrack for this game is absolutely beautiful, and just SCREAMS Mega Man X. I actually need to listen to the full title theme before I start the game and exit the game. All the time.
Another feature that adds even more replayability are the leaderboards and daily/weekly challenges, which are premade 20XX runs, and they're solid, clean fun. The game also has a casual mode which increases accessibility to people who aren't hardcore platformer players, and lets everyone have a good time. Also, did I mention you can bring a friend and you can both have a grand old time?
This game nails everything down hard. The platforming is solid, the gameplay is fun with rewarding challenges, and there's just so much diversity and upgrades that you'll just keep on playing.

It is with some reluctance that I give this  a thumbs down.  The game is too crass, the writing is, at times, shoddy and uncreative, and the story line is cliché and predictable.  All that is not to say that you can't have fun while playing.  The fighting, if you enjoy a button mashing frolic, is good.  The monsters demand different methods of attacking and you have to learn how to switch your fighting style on the fly.  Not my normal style of playing but one that I ultimately enjoyed.  Most game level where interesting if mostly linear.  There were several disappointing levels as well as ones that were truly creative and fun to play.  The game seems to allow for plenty of replay.  After your first play through you can go into different modes.  You can revisit the levels to find all the goodies, as well as trying to complete the different secret missions.  Personally I found the secret levels to be tedious.
Ultimately the game could have used a bit more polish in terms of story and dialog.  A couple of levels need to be scrapped and redone.  A good game was brought down by these misses.

I'm not sure about all of the changes and patches that proceeded its release, but DMC was far better than I expected after reading all of the negative reviews from journalists.
When it comes to action games I typically prefer the more methoiodical approach to combat over frenetic twitch combat. That said, DMCs combat is just as well designed as many other similar games I have enjoyed in the past (such as Darksiders). DMC has a non-pretentious story and the world is filled with interesting, creative, often psychedelic levels. Dante's douchbag o-meter was far lower than I expected too; so that was great suprise (I thought he was a real POS clown in the older DMC titles).
My only real complains are two fold. The camera is constantly getting stuck on the environment; in a fast paced action game this is an absoloute no-no. And all of the extra weapons you acuire beyond mid-game are a distraction and superfluous.
Overall DMC is a well made, well paced action packed ride.

Wuppo was an adorable, original, and fun adventure game that is a strong rec. It reminded me a lot of Yoshi's Island and other great SNES games. It's story-heavy and character-heavy, with a super-cute art style and I really just loved it. It's genuinely one of the most heartfelt games of its type I've encountered in these sales -- when so many games feel like exersizes in bland, emotionless mediocrity, Wuppo clearly was made with a lot of love, and it shows. I also thought it hit that sweet spot of being challenging and requiring quick thinking, but never getting frustrating. It also (also) feels finished, while a lot of these games feel like they rush to wrap up because the dev ran out of time/resources, Wuppo is very much finished and feels finished, and even has an extra area that's totally optional but has some lore. Spill the ice cream, save the world!

Anyway, these bugs i am talking about exist mostly in two forms.
-The i can't fly bug as i call it. Simply put, the game can't decide whether i'm pressing space bar to fly off a roof. So it alternates between flight stance and standing whilst slowly drifting to the ground.
-The can't counter this bug. Batman games are oriented around the unseen predator and massive melee brawler playstyles, for the latter one has the ability to either attack or counter an enemy attack. Now wouldn't it be usefull if that counter butten would actually work? Unfortunately it does not about 40% of the time, even more so the fix for this(putting the game into directx9 mode(yes, this really is a fix)) only worked for the directly upfollowing playsession for me.
As i see it, this means that already 2 of the game's core systems do not properly function for some users. The counter issue i think is the worst of these, as this bug has been around for at least 3 years now and was affecting numerous players.
Unlike it's predecessor i have not tried to play this game on my laptop, this is unfortunate as i with this I haven't found whether WB has once again ruined the performance of AMD videocard users.(Arkham city ran better on a GT650M(mid-high range laptop card), than on a Radeon HD 7950(2nd most powerfull desktop AMD card of the same year))

This would be a "neutral rating" if I had the option so please read for why it's a "not recommended" from my side.
At first glance the game is pretty nice, solid, stupid fun. The farther the game progresses the weirder the ballancing gets, though. You can shoot unlimited daggers and every melee weapon you find can be selected free of charge at any given point without apparant disatvantages. So plowing through most enemies is easy enough. The game offsets this by introducing odd (near) one-hit kill attacks from larger monsters and instant kills from traps and pitfalls.
The latter is the really annoying part of the game as there are passages with spiked crushers coming from the ceiling and from the walls instantly kiling you. The two problems here are that you often can't really see where the crushers will come from exactly so sometimes it's a guess/hope situation of being in the right place. The other thing is that these passages can be very, very, very frustratingly long without checkpoints. you have unlimited continues - so basically unlimited lives but ulimately trying again and again in levels where it's stop and go or die and repeat over and over again simply is no fun.
If I could I'd give the game a neutral review because the rest really is a lot of fun. the music is pretty good and pushing and the graphics are also very nice. The atmosphere ranges somewhere in the ballpark of ghosts 'n' goblins while the animations oddly remind me of Altered Beast.
If you can live with some wonky hit detection and a few annoying levels with crushers and insta death pittfalls you get a very solid and fun retro game for a good price - then by all means buy it.
Ultimately I found myself ragequitting a few times too often to really recommend it, personally.

Don't fret, they're easily dispatched by walking up to them and pressing Y (after, again, rebinding the moronic default setup).
But after dying to a wizard firing fireballs at me off screen as I was trapped between two falling ceiling spikes, I kind of just lost patience with it.
I thought the i5 Sandy Bridge in the recommended system specs was a joke. I tried playing it on my 6700HQ and was getting around 40 FPS without plugging in to the wall and enabling the boost clock. Just let that sink in. Running natively on a platform throwing tens of thousands of times more MIPS than a Sega Genesis or Saturn, drawing pixel art that's about as graphically  complex as Ghost n Goblins, this game somehow manages to run worse.
At least the pixel-art is actually good, faithful to the sort of stuff you'd see on the 16-bit consoles in their hay-day, albeit without dynamic lighting, particle effects or any of the other sort of eye-candy that remotely justifies needing more than a sewing machine to run a modern pixel-art game, but you could probably tell that much from the screenshots. Ideally the developers would be hired as artists by a better company to churn out more, leaving the programming and design to someone with a clue.

It's very hard to tell when one of these retro styled games is going to be good or bad. I'm very happy to say that the last two Dark Fantasy, Retro titles I've picked up are great games in there own ways. But on the pluss side, the game it still quick and easy to learn, with various ways for you to deal with the on coming hoards of deamons, undead, and a slew of other monsters they throw your way. And the "Rip off there arm and beat them with it" graple option is interesting in of it's self.

Insanity's Blade takes you through a wormhole,  dropping you right into the SNES/Sega Genesis era.
My nostalgia was accompanied by pleasant surprise, as I don't remember any games on SNES being quite this good...  of course at that point in my life I seldom had the determination to actually finish a game, so my recollection of them it's mainly limited to the first few levels.
It seems that having the benefit of a modern processor and GPU allows the overall speed of the given effects and the complexity of the graphics to be a significant improvement over past console games even if the developer here has nailed the Retro vibe.
You even have the opportunity to choose how retro you want to go, at least as far as the sound design goes.  You have the option to choose between 16 and 8 bit music.  ( I choose 16 bit.)
The game is a 2d side-scrolling platformer with hack and slash combat, quests, upgradable weapons, an inventory, unlockable abilities, and at least one instance juvenile tongue-in-cheek humor.  ( which I still find hilarious)  You can track your progression and location through a menu based world map.
I've heard many 2D games dropped into the sub classification of metroidvania, but in my opinion that feel wasn't overwhelming on this title.  In hindsight though it's almost impossible to deny the similarities...  I also saw a fairly heavy Ghosts and Goblins influence.  (Full disclosure I never beat those games either)
In general I'd prefer not to divulge too many details about a game's story, so here I'll stick the same did the story from this game was nothing revolutionary, but it was interesting and serve very well to care either gamer from beginning to end of the experience.
You play as Thurston who has to fight through the literal forces of hell... in an effort to save your loved ones and your own sanity.  As is usual, these roads are treacherous.
The atmosphere is pure dark Gothic fantasy.  The game play feels fast and gritty.  Blood, Fire and whirling blades.
The replayability is definitely there, but this isn't a title that you can look forward to sinking hundreds of hours into...  I don't know though, perhaps someone will.
There's a steep ramp up and difficulty between the "easy" mode and the rest...  even "normal" provides a stiff challenge.
I'm pretty sure that I got the game on sale and in my opinion that made it a steal, but even if I paid full price I would have felt that I got my money's worth.

I first played the original game when it was released, but never finished it, and forgot about it to be honest. I'm so glad I picked up the Definitive Edition of Ori and the Blind Forest. Everything about this game is excellent and there are really no decent complaints that could be made.
The story is compelling - this is an achievement in its own right, given that the story is told through a fictitious language, very brief one-to-two line snippets of text, and the stellar audio-visual presentations throughout. The soundtrack can feel a little mediocre at times when viewed on its own, coupled with the cinematic displays though, it is more than stunning. Some of the tracks worked so perfectly with the visuals, that when I listen to the soundtrack, the images and feelings of the accompanying cinematic are immediately seen and felt again. Needless to say the soundtrack now lives on in my Spotify library.
In terms of its visual performance, again, I have trouble faulting it. The use of oversaturated colours is a pet hate of mine, as it makes me feel like I am playing a game for three-year-olds. In this case though, the artists have juxtaposed drab desaturated areas with gleamingly hypersaturated areas. The result is an impressive aesthetic experience that will leave any viewer wanting more
The developers have chosen to employ a traditional metroidvania design to the levels. This is done in an elegant enough way that going back to find collectibles previously not accessible is done with relative ease. The game also balances the tutelage of newly acquired skills, with self-discovery on the player’s part. Whilst sometimes difficult on the ‘normal’ setting, with some perseverance, it can be passed reasonably quickly in 5-6h. One common complaint is that saving the game on low health where you can’t back-track to restore health, can lead to an unfinishable save; I don’t accept that. I found myself in many frustrating situations… but again, with perseverance, the challenge was overcome.

Just like other reviews say, this is randomly generated Mega Man X with items you can buy to show up in shops during your runs.  Most of these items have passive effects such as boosting attack power, increasing health item drop rates, raising max health and fully restoring current health, etc. There are also equipment pieces for head, body, boots, arms, and weapons.  The X-style character can swap out her normal buster for weapons like a spreadshot, and the Zero-style character can find axes, spears, and other weapons to swap with his saber if you're lucky enough to find them during your run.
The dev has been great about adding consistent, large content updates throughout the Early Access period.  20XX continues to get better, and I look forward to seeing the final version.
Basically, this is an incredibly good, randomly generated Mega Man X game. If you like Mega Man X or platformers in general then this is definitely worth your money.

This game is a rare 10/10 from me. I will heap praise upon it for days because it's a unique experience, unlike anything else I've played. It's also a very clever and insightful game, the world and mechanics constantly surprise and impress me. The story is rivetting, the gameplay is tough and satifying, the progression is meaningful. The world is full of endless secrets, surprises and fascinating subplots to explore and characters to meet. Most of all, despite its unassuming appearance, Wuppo feels like a real, living world. Like a microcosm of the earth, complete with separate populations, nations, war, intrigue and politics. You begin as a simple face in the crowd (in fact it's easy to become literally lost in the crowd, to forget which little guy is you among the hundreds of onscreen characters) but over time you work with or against the various parties, tribes, nobles, organisations and gods to make the world a better place.
It would be difficult to play this game without immediately falling in love with the strange and charming world of Wuppo. If you like your games as a plain single scoop of vanilla then perhaps you'll be turned away, and some may find the combat/platforming too difficult. Some younger players may also be confused or overwhelmed by it all. But otherwise I can't recommend it highly enough. Do yourself a favour: grab your best hat or favourite object, wear it on your head, take off your seatbelt (and your trousers) and dive right in to the world of Wuppo, it's a truly priceless experience!

I feel pretty conflicted about whether Insanity's Blade is actually good or not. It has a really classic feel, providing instant nostalgia with the old-school basic gameplay of spamming attacks and basic platforming, accompanied by some really nice arcade music and sound effects; but it's not as enjoyable as it could be, simply because it's lacking a lot of polish.
Where Insanity's Blade doesn't cut it:
- It's glitchy, but nothing game breaking.
- The difficulty curve is really unusual. The second boss fight was pretty much the hardest fight in the game - to the point that I was considering giving up because replaying the cave level was getting so repetitive. After getting past that boss everything was pretty simple; even the final boss took me less tries.
- The gamepad controls are not well thought out. A is melee AND ranged attack, B is jump, X is throw. You can remap the buttons, but if you make attack B, then it also becomes "confirm" in menus, which was even more confusing.
- Melee and ranged attacks are combined. As it is you'll mostly just mash A to progress through levels when you're not having to do some of the platforming. Occasionally throw is worthwhile when an enemy blocks your attacks, but spamming melee/ranged is usually the safer option.
- In story mode you progress through a map, and collectible weapons are hidden (sometimes not very well) within the stages you play through. Despite having a map where you can select the level from, you can't revisit a level you've already completed - so if you miss a weapon, you can't go back for it. Why even bother making me select dots on a map?
- Level design isn't great. The worst level design element is the moving spiky blocks as there is no consistency to how they appear. Sometimes they'll be completely hidden in the ceiling and you'll only know there is one that might be coming down when you see falling particles, but those particles don't line up properly, and if the particles started falling while there were off-screen, they won't appear as you move across under it resulting in being suddenly and unavoidably crushed.
Despite all it's faults I really enjoyed playing Insanity's Blade. I wish there was more polish on Insanity's Blade, but then the glitches, unbalanced difficulty curve, and unfair deaths make it feel even more accurate to the old-school style they were going for.

Gotta give the reccomend. Side Scrolling hack n slash done in 8 bit pixel art, but with alot of modern touches. The action is simple but satisfying, your charecter sports  a button for attacking/launching projectiles and a second  one for grapple moves. add in a jump button and that's essentially it.  They help to keep combat interesting though by having a series items and weapons you can find which can offer better range or power.  There are also upgrades for throwing axes, including launching several axes at once or launching axes on fire for better damage.
Success in play is all about timing, knowing when to launch in for a melee strike, or throwing an enemy. Also the enviroments offer plenty of traps that can lead to instadeath, so tread carefuly.
All in all, the game channels the hack and slash classics from old like golden axe or dungeons and dragons.  Would highly reccomend if you like similar old style games.

Insanity's Blade is not an awful game, and it may entertain you for a couple of hours if you need a dose of old-school sidescrollers.
The problem is the general pacing and level design (not to mention the story, which, coupled with the pacing, makes it a very disorientating game... for me, anyway).
The game is very unbalanced, in a similar way to Jets N' Guns: the difficulty peaks at the second or third level, but once you get past that point, you snowball out of control. Now, Jets N' Guns kept being interesting (somewhat) by its huge selection of guns and the joy of trying all the different combinations, which is something not present here. While there are weapons, they're all the same (maybe with a different damage stat? it was never relevant).
The levels seemed like an excuse to throw enemies at you, with irregular terrain to give an illusion of change. But, since most of the enemies don't do much aside from walking straight into you, it quickly becomes a matter of pressing forward while continuously attacking.
The bosses follow a similar pattern -- while the first couple of bosses were cool, and you actually had to predict what he was going to do -- most of them will die by spamming attack, once the snowball effect sets in.
Not much more to say about it. The levels didn't really have a rhythm to them, or a reason. You simply choose the next stage and blast your way through 15 times. It's unfortunate that there isn't more to it...
The music was cool, and the visuals had some strengths as well. It was enjoyable for a bit! But, overall, I don't see this as worth a purchase, if you're looking for a
game. If you just want to pass the time, why not?, give it a go.
P.S.: The second level, despite being much harder than the others, in my opinion, was by far my favourite. It wasn't a stellar level, but it did seem to have a more careful design. My problem with it was due to having 0 lives, and thus a miss-step would end up with me repeating the whole level (a level with instant spike deaths and a bossfight, etc. etc.)... Despite all that, it had some simple platforming sections, and had you fighting enemies in a corridor where you did have to do some manoeuvering to succeed in.
Not perfect, but certainly where I would point to, if I needed to explain the presence/lack of level design.

It's the little things that make this game good for me. It's satisfying to blow things up, and knowing that there's a variety of ways you can do so. The sound and hit physics effects are my favorite part. The sound effects are beefy. Bullets and missiles crash into metallic hulls, explosions really shake the subwoofer, and there's a lot of pewpew for good measure too.
For most weapons, the target may not explode immediately, and they blow up later. During this time you might even see them wobbling out of control. A hard hit from most weapons will knock them off their path, possibly crashing into something. This combined with the great sound effects really feels good, so much that I often find myself trying to set up good angles so that I can inflict maximum carnage per shot.
The weapons have a lot of variety and some of them are quite entertaining. If you're patient you can even drag asteroids or bigger enemies around to smash into groups of smaller enemies. It's arguably not as damaging as simply blasting enemies straight up, but it's very fun. Also, as people have mentioned, you can teleport fighting bears into an enemy cockpit. It's crazy damaging and the target ship will float around unpowered and out of control for a time after the bear has done its work, giving you an easy shot to finish it off. You can also replace the "payload" with bees and stuff, if bears aren't your thing.
The enemies you encounter have a fair amount of variety. There's swarms of little enemies that you can't ignore, bigger enemies that often have heavier fire power, and annoying enemies that dodge or go invis. They also use a variety of weapons and tactics, from straight up ramming you to long-ranged missile barrages. That said, it's probably wise to make sure you bring a weapon for various situations within a level, as the enemy types will often vary per wave in a level.
Friendly fire is always on, even for enemies. That said, you can use it to your advantage. Enemies crashing into each other, hitting each other with their bullets and explosions, etc., means that your movement and positioning are important.
Speaking of which, the controls are super responsive. Turn rate doesn't seem to be an issue at all (unlike some twin stick shooters I've played), as your ship will immediately face/shoot where your mouse pointer is. The pointer is also fairly easy to spot even in the midst of bullets, explosions and debris, which is important since some weapons are designed to travel or explode where your mouse is currently located. All in all it's designed very well in this aspect.
All in all it's a solid buy even at full price. It's the kind of pace with customization that I'm looking for, and if this were an arcade game I'd probably be sinking way more money into this than its asking price on Steam.

Well, good luck with that.
However, the game can be challenging sometimes. And that can, depending on what games you enjoy, really get to you.
The learning curve... It's kind of in the middle. The basics are easy to grasp, pilot your ship around, kill enemies. Easy enough. But mastering the dodging, without killing yourself in that asteroid you forgot was there, now that takes time.
I'd say it's a good game. I find it overly addictive. I can't say much about the multiplayer yet tho, as I haven't tryed it, but shooting up aliens with your friend, both as powerful spacedragons? Not every game lets you do that... I'm just saying...

Like all games, StH4 has its problems, but I don't think that ruins it for the game. While it's very true that you're going to have far easier a time with a controller than a keyboard/mouse, overall, the game is very well put together. Piece by piece, here's what I think.
The music, like for all Sonic games, is very well done and feels very fitting. Every single stage sounds appropriate, from White Park Zone sounding very much like a snowy wonderland to Oil Desert Zone sounding like an intimidating desert factory. The music itself is composed fantastically, with nothing in it that would grate on the ears, and even the new power-up music doesn't sound too bad.
The controls and physics take some getting used to, especially if you haven't played a game with Sonic's acceleration need; thankfully, it's been improved somewhat from Episode 1, making it less bothersome. They can also be frustrating at times, but once you get over the slight learning curve, it never feels rage-inducing or overly frustrating. Annoying at times, yes, but at least here, it won't ever feel like the game is actively hating you and all you stand for. Sky Fortress' changed controls can take a bit to adapt to, especially if you're playing co-op, but other than that, failures mostly feel like skill or mistakes rather than bad controls.
The Zone desgins are wonderful as well. Each Zone gives a feel of some of the older games' Zones, but at the same time, they also have unique little twists or tricks that makes them feel like their own unique places as well. From White Park's snowy theme park feeling to Oil Desert's very industrialized setting, even if there aren't as many of them as in other games, they leave a mark.
The game is, despite some claims, not that much shorter than the other four games it emulates (Sonic 1, 2, 3, S&K). While there are only 4 normal Zones, every Zone has 3 Acts, plus a stand-alone "act" that's the boss of that Zone (not counting the final Zone). As an added bonus, you can replay any Special Zone you've beaten for fun, or to practice for harder ones.
Speaking of the Special Zone, the special stages from Sonic 2 make a return! And to add to the fun of the "friendly competition" of the ring gathering, the animation played when going between checkpoints is actually different depending on which character has the most rings. The stages, as usual, can be easy or hard depending on how good you are at picking up rings while dodging, but they definitely have the same feel as the old-school ones.
The co-op for the game can be either a blessing or a curse, depending on if you have someone to play with or not. The game feels very much like it was built specifically FOR two players to work together on it, which means if you do have two people, you can do a lot you wouldn't get to do or pull off some neat tricks. At the same time, if you're playing alone, it can sometimes be a little frustrating or difficult precisely because of the build intending two people.
All in all, it's definitely not a perfect game by any means... but it's a game that those who enjoy that style of gameplay should, in my opinion, pick up if they can, regardless of whether they're a Sonic fan or not. Those who are fans of the old-style Sonic, however, will definitely find even more enjoyment in it with all the throwbacks. However, I would DEFINITELY reccomend a controller if at all possible.
SEGA managed to make something that felt both old-school and unique with Sonic 4 Episode 2... and how many games can claim that?

A huge improvement over the first "episode". If I have any criticism of Sonic 4 at all, it's that it's too eager to simply bask in the series' past glories. "Hey, remember this from the old games?" "How about this?" "And this?". Even the special stages use the same sequence of colours to tap into your nostalgia gland. Mind you, Sonic Generations did this successfully, but that whole game was one big homage. This feels like a game with no identity of its own.
Still, at least they got the physics more or less right this time.

This is a good, albeit slow-paced, sandbox space simulator with a fully realized intersteller supply-and-demand based business economy. X3 offers plenty of eye candy all around; its universe is a beautiful place. Follow the main story, or break away and come back to it as you please. Fully customize your starting ship(s) with upgrades to weapons, navigation, optics, etc. as you can afford them.  Work your way up in the corporate world by purchasing manufacturing spacestations, cargo vessels to transport goods and fighters to defend stations or escort vessels; build a financial empire, be your own Builderberg Group. Eventually, you can purchase an armada of capital ships and support vessels that you can use to supplement your firepower inside and outside of the main plot. You can helm any vehicle you purchase (provided you're close enough for a short spacewalk), and then, with upgradable ship computer software, issue orders to the rest of your fleets from the comfort of your captains seat. Maintain diplomacy with a variety of alien species, some of whom are mortal enemies, neutrals, allies, and still others who will eventually warm up to you after you invest some cash in their economies or shoot down enemies inside their sectors. Chilled out game-relaxing at times-that you can play with one hand on the mouse, or using the keyboard only, or both if you choose; it works however you want to play it. It's a complete change of pace from FPS games, and there can be long dull intervals between exciting firefights. Think of it as Elder Scrolls: Oblivion in space. Epic. Be who you want to be: Trader, Fighter, Fleet Commander, Pirate, Business Mogul. The choice is yours.

is a single-player 2D action platformer with a touching story. There's only half a dozen characters taking part in the plot, and you only control Ori (a "guardian spirit" who looks like a little white monkey) restore balance and harmony to the Great Forest.
The game boasts magnificent graphics and atmospheric music, with a distinctive world design evoking oriental mythology and ecological/Miyazaki themes. There's no dialogue and only a little voice-over in some strange language (possibly Japanese?) in the cutscenes that advance the story, which is fairly linear.
The gameplay is fluid with all one can expect from a well-balanced action platformer: There's enemies to defeat, missiles & traps to dodge, mini-puzzles to solve (levels and the like) and lots and lots of acrobatics to be performed! As Ori explores the world around the Great Forest he unlocks new abilities that allow him to do even crazier acrobatics. The theme of the game is non-violent, so, instead of boss fights there's "escape stages" at the end of each level (there's ~7 of them), where you gotta flee rapidly from chaotically escalating situations while executing the aforementioned acrobatics with precision!
The game autosaves in all the major locations of the map and after all key events, but you can also save almost anytime using some sort of an ability that depletes your Energy (Mana). Finally, the map is almost totally interconnected so that Ori can travel anywhere in the world "on foot"; fast-travel is always an option (in the "Definitive Edition" only), accessed from several key locations called "Spirit Wells". That is helpful for completionists who back-track to uncover all secrets and explore all optional zones.
I completed the "Definitive Edition" of the game in about 12 hours, on mouse+keyboard, playing two thirds on Normal and then switching to Easy. My only real complaint is that the Easy difficulty setting wasn't as easy as I expected, meaning that the acrobatics (the most challenging part of the game for me) still had to be performed with accuracy; I think that poor Ori died several hundreds of times until the Forest was restored!
I am not planning to replay the game, as I've seen most of the content and all the story: I got over 50% of the Steam achievements without any special effort, and the remaining ones are all for hardcore players. Please note that the "Definitive Edition" does not have Steam Cards; for these, you can always play the regular edition but it has no fast-travel and no difficulty settings. I did not encounter any technical difficulties with the game (bugs, lock-ups, crashes) and the menus etc were all fine.
In overall, I can safely recommend this beautiful game to players that like action-platformers without violence and who enjoy a cute story. If I were to grade the game, it'd be in the 8.5-9/10 range.
If you enjoy platformers, you owe it to yourself to pick this game up.

It's difficult to describe Wuppo. Essentially you're a white fluff ball trying to save the world with a Gumgumgun. It is a unique and entertaining 2D RPG.
- Quirky but great art style and music.
- Love the small details, like how certain words shake or are bold when an NPC speaks (for emphasis or emotion) or that you can't cut the line at the amusement park.
- This game does not hold you by the hand. There are no arrows telling you were to go. No quest log. No map. You have to figure things out by yourself. Talk to NPCs, read what they say.
- So many side-quests and little interactions. This game really rewards you for exploring.
- Filmstrips will give you more background information about their world. If you're not interested, you don't have to watch them.
- Bosses can be challenging. You really need to learn their patterns.
- Every death is fair. You need to dodge those projectiles or position yourself properly. Get good, scrub.
- I love that the NPCs are active. They're constantly running around, changing hats, buying items/food.
- Shoutout to the Dutch developers who sneaked in Dutch words into their game. Big respect.
- Your happiness is important.
- Boss run is hard and shows you no mercy.
- Large number of items, hats, consumables.
- I came across some bugs. Nothing game breaking.
- Waiting for the train and trams can be boring (but the NPCs have places to go too, the world doesn't revolve around you).
- I would have liked to have a map.
Wuppo feels like a testament to older games: (1) you're expected to figure things out by yourself, (2) if you die, it's your own fault. I love it that the developers decided to create their game in this way. I'm sure that not everyone will feel this way but I really enjoyed Wuppo.

Wuppo:
~~~~~~
Who would have believed that eating ice cream could earn you an eviction notice? Well, to be fair with Carlo, the Wum at the Wum House service desk, it’s not fun at all cleaning ice cream off the beautiful rugs at the entrance and on the fourth level. Especially now, when all the cleaners have run away to Popocity. It’s only part of the reason; the real reason is that Carlo dislikes cleaning (I’m with you, Carlo), but throwing a Wum out of the Wum House for this, it’s a tad extreme. Hey Wuppo! Did you hear what I say? You have to find a new place to live. Well, start cracking!
Wuppo is a platformer/adventure game with good puzzles where you control a cute, round character who has four legs and can make great double jumps. He is part of the Wum race, who are the most intelligent of four main species in the world, but lack of abilities.  The other three races are the Blussers, Splenkhakkers and the nasty Fnakkers.
You’ll meet a bird, “Denksnavel,” fairly quickly in the game. This bird will give you hints every time you select him. The Allesweters is another character who you will be talking a fair bit with and can be found in different locations. He has a projector and can play the filmstrips collectable items you’ll find within the world.
The world is extremely well-designed with great locations to discover, and it’s not hard to navigate. Within the main places, you’ll have to help other Wums or species to move forward in the game. Some will be challenging puzzles and others will lead to a fight with big, scary monsters! Please don’t scare the kawum out of me! When you successfully help these characters and make them happy, you’ll be rewarded with extra health points and items which in turn will help you to resolve the next puzzle or challenges in the world. There is a fair bit of reading in this game and you really need to take your time to go through it or you will miss important information. Bear in mind that you can come back to individuals and re-asked questions. The dialogue is really fun and you can select different answers when you interact with each creature.
In some of the destinations, you’ll find stores where you can buy or sell items using the smurt currency. You can obtain additional smurts either by helping other individuals, or when you kill enemies.
For me the game shines in the puzzles. However, you’ll be fighting interesting bosses and some are not that easy to eliminate. Oh, by the way, you’ll be armed with a GumGumGun which shoots coloured gums. There is a place where you can upgrade your weapons at a specific store in Popocity.
Splendid artwork and the soundtrack is very cute. For the controls, whether you use the mouse and keyboard or the gamepad, they work fine and it is very easy to allocate binding keys to your inventory.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Splendid artwork
-	Well-designed world
-	Great puzzles
-	Fun fighting bosses
-	Fun dialogues
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	 I think the fighting bosses could be a notch harder
This game is a gem - thoroughly entertaining and fun to play!
