What may seem like a generic shooter involving mass genocide on the surface, is actually a well-paced strategic fight for survival that tests your morality. Spec Ops: The Line conveys the truth about why we engage ourselves in this genre of gaming and makes us ask what we would actually do if we were placed in this depressing narrative.
From the start, you are thrown in to explore the new barren geography of a decimated Dubai, where a massive sandstorm has swept through, killing most of the population and leaving survivors with little to no resources to live off of. The plot puts players in the boots of a special forces operative: Captain Walker, who leads his squad to recon for survivors, that is until they encounter a group of hostile refugees. They then get sucked in after receiving a distressed call from surviving American forces of a battalion that has stayed behind to look after the local populace. From there, the gravity of the situation forces you to betray your orders and embark through rough terrain to desperately find answers, even if you have to kill for it. As you traverse through the city with each horrific scene you witness, you notice your own character become progressively more unhinged and violent. The game, through all the characters, speaks to the player and reflect about your recent actions, as if you are Walker yourself. This direct engagement with the player makes it immersive and hooks you in.

For how much destruction is in the game, the visual presentation is very welcoming as you traverse through nicely textured ruins only to see the beautiful skyline all around you. Although the level design is quite linear, it’s nice to see that there is attention to every corner you pass.
The environment drives the story, shapes the environment, and changes your approach in completing your mission. From being in a helicopter chase with a minigun chewing up pursuers to various sandstorms that will limit your view and mostly relying on the muzzle flashes from the enemy to know their location. There are buildings stuffed full of sand and if an armored machine gun turret were unlucky enough to be near one, the player could shoot out the glass and crush them, getting Walker out of tight spots. You are not always afforded this though, flanking and team command may be required, making reliable gameplay very important.

Although the controls take some getting used to, the gameplay is quite mediocre. You will find yourself hitting keys by accident that can expose you and both friendly and enemy AI will inexplicably do the same or sit in cover uselessly. Being cover based, it good to see that this is done flexibly, since you are able to swap cover, peek over and to the side, and destroy other cover. There are 18 weapons to use, most of which are balanced out and I found myself constantly changing weapons to try, considering none were really overpowered. Other gadgets like frag and stun grenades can also be used to help progress further. The types of enemies you encounter will affect your strategic approach. Heavy units may require you to fall back and use explosives while snipers can easily be taken out by your teammates when given the command. Again, this encourages players to take advantage of their surroundings. There is a difficulty setting that accommodates all player skill levels and playing on harder difficulties will demand critical thinking, putting more stress on you but making victory much more rewarding.

Some of the logic is flawed, whether its falling out of a building and surviving to having water tankers decimating a full city block. There is a lot of evidence that did not add up with the reality, but it is possible that a lot of what the player sees are the hallucinations that Walker experiences, but it’s never explicitly confirmed. There were some clichés and exaggerated behaviour amongst your team as though the game was trying too hard to generate emotion, but these were rare cases and won’t put you off once the bullets fly again.

The sound was invigorating and helped to make up for the gunplay. From a slow breeze walking through a deserted highway and metal cranking from billboards to crisp gunfire flying overhead with a slice of screaming carnage. There are strong metal tracks while also some soft moments where appropriate. The voice acting feels authentic to the situation and gets tense, especially when your team shouts aggressively between a volley of gunfire. Nolan North does an exceptional job in his lines as Walker who sounds real and emotional in all aspects.

I had only managed to play a few games of both multiplayer and co-op, but I felt I did not miss out on it much. It uses conventions already seen in games like Call of Duty and Counter Strike and there are only a handful of players still playing. That is not to say it is unplayable, but it lacks in innovation leaving players with no motive to continue when there are so many other shooters that do multiplayer much better. Multiplayer involves your standard level progression system which unlocks new weapons and cosmetics and the game modes are heavily inspired from existing shooters, establishing a sense of “I’ll give it a go” to experienced shooters and not "Woah, what's this?". Co-op has you team up with another friend and completing missions that consist of going from point A to B fighting off hordes of enemies much like Left 4 Dead.

There was never one point that I was not invested in the single-player. I finished the campaign in one play through, since I was so eager to uncover what happened as well as the future complications that came with it. The ending left me thinking afterwards about what soldiers really look for in a mission. That being said, it was also confusing about what actually happened and I think it was wrong to not provide a clear explanation of what was real and not. There are collectibles and intel that help fill some of the holes about the story as well as character history. This, along with the achievements will encourage a second or third playthrough.

Spec Ops: The Line’s greatest values are its story and presentation. While the controls had a frustratingly unusual layout to get used to, coming to grips and developing experience makes you more of an effective player, giving off a sense that you are really a special operative who needs to take tactical consideration, which the dev’s took care in the level design. As I usually recommend with older games, wait for this to go on sale for about 5 to 10 dollars, especially if you want to host games with your friends. Considering the current online population, I’d recommend this to anyone looking for a single-player decent shooter that, although involves violent gameplay, addresses the repercussions of war which is a fresh take from what we are so used to. Mainly because it was not a sales success, Yager development are not going to make a sequel, making this the second time the series has been put on halt, after the original games that started from 1998 to 2002. I think it is important however that this game is remembered for how it portrays violence which future games should consider and if done correctly, can drive a really beautiful and interesting narrative.

Insanity's Blade is a 2D Action game centered around Thurstan in his quest for revenge against a demon that slaughtered his entire village and his family. It has quite a strong opening and you are thrust into a village up in flames and citizens are desperately running for their lives before you even start to play. You can save a few villagers that are tied up or have something that you need to progress but most are on their own as Thurstan continues onwards with only vengeance on his mind. Throughout most of your adventure you will be accompanied by a dwarf that fights by throwing axes but will only show up in cutscenes if you are not playing local coop making him seem like a rather unimportant character if you are playing solo. Thurstan himself fights by throwing daggers but can also pick up a multitude of weapons like shovels, torches and swords to name a few. He can also grab enemies to throw them out of the way, but the range of grabbing is way too short, ensuring you will nearly always take damage so I only used it when I was standing under a trap and needed to get the enemy out of the way  immediately. Your enemies will mostly be composed of the undead and a few demons, most are just cannon fodder and go down without posing much of a threat. Most of my deaths were by being knocked back after taking some damage and being pushed back, it is a very real threat that you should be careful of since enemies love waiting at the corner of a cliff to do you in. You have a health bar and can take multiple hits but a misplaced jump or not seeing a trap will instantly kill you and set you back to the checkpoint, assuming you have any lives left.
Before you start your quest you will be able to pick either Story mode which has side quests and the story is told before and after levels or Arcade mode that gets rid of side quests, saving the game and most of the story. The side quests are my biggest issue with the game. The story is not the most interesting one around but it is serviceable but the side quests break up the flow of the narrative badly. First off most are not optional and you will have to replay some levels over a few times before being able to move on to the next level. It may not sound like a big deal but imagine this scenario. You have traveled  a vast frozen wasteland in the middle of a snow storm with no clothes, no way back and very dangerous terrain, and you now stand at the gates of hell, all to save your loyal comrade who was dragged  into it's depths to aid you in your quest. And then you have go all the way back to the Swamp stage to collect some useless item, dwarf be damned. It's stuff like this that made me care little for the story which is unfortunate since Insanity's Blade is the first part of the planned series. Arcade mode has very little story, no saving and best of all no side quests. I vastly preferred this mode even though it does have a bit too much useless dialogue such as in the second level where a random man stands and says that “you are now entering the dungeon of …..” and that doesn't really mean anything without  the context of the story mode. Would be way less annoying is you could skip text instead of waiting for it to go away.
There are four difficulties which are Casual and Normal, both have unlimited continues and then we have Manly and Hell which have no continues and is suggested for those that like the threat of actually being able to lose the game and want to fully experience Arcade mode. A rather neat feature is the ability to play either the 8 bit or 16 bit soundtrack. You may want to switch soundtracks over time because while the music is awesome at first, it has very little variation from song to song and the constant need to replay levels in Story mode makes it much more annoying though not unbearable. Overall there are 16 levels including the opening and most feel very unique as the environments are constantly changing, like the first level being set in the after mentioned burning town while the second is in a swamp stage with giant fighting trees. One level even turns the game into a shoot em up where you ride a dragon and breathe fire onto your enemies. That was fun though the dragon does move too slow to confidently dodge projectiles and some enemies were very damage spongy. In fact a lot of the enemies can feel bullet spongy throughout the game since they added  an experience system where you level up after killing enough enemies and become more powerful, though progressing to another level without killing much and the enemies will feel like they soak up too much damage until you level up. On the other hand it can make the game an absolute breeze if you kill enough enemies, though the timer in levels discourages this. Even arcade mode has this leveling up system which is unfortunate.
Another RPG aspect of this game is that enemies drop money that you can use in a weapon shop that allows you to buy more lives or allows you to throw more daggers each attack. Gathering enough money to finally be able to throw 6 flaming daggers at once was a pleasant experience. Money feels perfectly balanced and actually valuable making each purchase decision a potentially fatal if you don't want to buy any lives to save up for a more powerful attack. You will have to be quick on your feet to pick up loot since it does disappear rather quickly. There is also an inventory system in which you can carry six weapons and swap them out at will. You do lose the ability to switch weapons once you pick up the Insanity Blade pretty late in the game though it is far more powerful than anything you had before it and necessary to defeat the forces of hell. Most of the challenge lies with the enormous screen filling bosses that you must defeat. To give an example of a boss, at one point you fight an immobile and imprisoned titan whose only source of attack is to swing his eyeball at you and occasionally blast energy out of it. It is much more of a challenge then you might imagine (until you learn pattern) and craziest of all he swings his eyeball in a room filled with spikes. It's that absurdity that leaves me excited to face the next boss awaiting me though toward the end you do face the same boss in a few stages with no differences to his attack pattern. Unfortunately that blighted leveling up system does make some boss fights far easier than they should be. While it is pretty cool to see Thurstan become a killing machine by the end it would be nice to be able to turn it off.
Another issue I would like to bring up is with the artstyle. There are too many foreground objects blocking your view. They do become transparent when you stand behind it but that's not so with the enemies causing you to attack blindly just in case there is something behind them. When all is said and done this is still a very good game. While the RPG aspects of it like side quests in story mode and leveling up subjectively harms the game, it more than makes up for it in the sheer fun of it all.  As long as you set it to “hell” difficultly and play in Arcade mode it will surely challenge you till the end despite the leveling up system. It is a dark, no nonsense game that really feels like someone mixed together both Conan the Barbarian and Berserk. When you beat the game you can turn off the thrown daggers in every attack and slay your enemies with pure melee giving the game a whole new feel. Insanity's Blade has it's flaws but I truly believe it to be a hidden gem and worthy of any fan of the Action genre. If you are terrible at Action games this would be a great one to get you into them.  At it's low price it is an easy recommendation to anyone that is even slightly interested in Insanity's Blade. It will be very interesting indeed to see the direction of this new series.

After finally beating the game today I've got several things to say about it. First one: I actually liked the game. The story is ok, the characters are not half bad, gameplay brings back memories of good old times, mixing platforming fun with a non stop action and the soundtrack is really awesome. However bajillion of bugs and some frustrating moments because of lack of polish ruins the game, in a way. Single player mode is more or less stable, but co-op mode is a buggy hell.
When you bind your controls in the options, you have to choose who will use a certain device. I wanted to play as player one on my Xbox360 controller, while the second player uses keyboard. So I set Player one: Gamepad/Player 2: Keyboard. And I ended up playing as player 2, while player 2 played as player 1(Thurstan). When I changed this vice versa (Set myself as player 2) - poof, for some reason it worked. Bizarre.
On the Plague Island there were some enemies that could not be killed at all, after throwing them they were stuck in the air upside down. Next thing, the fallen (into the pitfall) comrade will teleport to where you stand, so that you don't part ways too far, well that helps a lot actually, but not during the last stage, where you can teleport right into the abyss because your buddy failed. During the pre-final boss battle I was stuck in one place and could not move. So my fellow 2nd player had to do all the work. Oh, and the next one (SPOILERS BELOW):
When Finn accidentally teleports to hell, 2nd player has to play as the priestess. But there will be a side quest around that time where you will have to return to the swamp stage, and the 2nd player will again play as finn. He came back from hell? Or maybe priestess used her awesome magic to turn herself into a dwarf? Meh, whatever.
Anyway, I had fun with the game and I liked it. I hope it will be properly patched and polished, especially the coop mode. But anyway I want to thank the developers for adding this coop mode, because local coop retro arcades like this are golden, and I was glad that a game like this could be played in coop (Always wanted a coop castlevania in the past).
So, right now I give this game 6/10. I like it, but it can be a lot better if developers will polish it enough.

A lot of games in the (city) building genre tend to all have a similar theme - while Cities:Skylines and Planetbase are fundamentally different in terms of gameplay they still offer very similar objectives - building a systainable city/colony where everything works.
I know Planetbase is not the best example for this, it does convey my point tho.
Here is where Prison Architect enters the field: It offers a completely new take on building something. Rather than managing big-scale cities and traffic you manage a Prison with all it's contents - cells, cell quality, laundry, cleaning, health.
The game starts small, as many others, but you can rapidly expand and create huge Prisons.
It is one of those games where you inevetably need to take multiple tries before finally getting it right as you usually run into problems. It is entirely possible to build a decent prison first try, but to get it running better you will need more tries and experience.
The game has a great pacing, you can begin expansion shortly after getting your first prisoner intake, but at the same time too rapid expansion is effectively limited by staff count and money.
Overall I can recommend this game as it is good fun and really enjoyable because it offers a unique concept and implementation.

This is the 1st Arkham Game in the series. (Chronological Order) Released in October 2013. Being the first game, it  serves as the Action-packed Origin Story where (A Fresh from Training.) Bruce learns many new skills and meets many vital characters in the Arkham Storyline! (Note that this is Rocksteady's adaptation so it will be different to any origins or sagas from the comics! This is a Videogame Dammit!)
Also i wont Spoil anything from the story here because im reviewing overall content and mechanics, not specific parts of the plot. You can find a neat summary on the games page for this. ;)
Without further ado, lets get to the Black and the White, the Strengths and the Reserved Judgement that is the...
Pros and Cons.
+Pointy Bat-ears Strike Fear into Dumb thugs! xD
+The Plot is done in such a way that its almost episodic and gives each character a balanced time in the spotight! (Before being beaten up by Batman.) Lots of new enemies are introduced especially, their origins are also given an arkham game spin. This is the origins game of the series and revelas lots and lots about the people of gotham! No spoilers here but there are many plot twists and interesting turns for the story, though they  could take a while to be revealed.
+Graphics are good for the time, couldnt ask for more here. Its what you would expect from 2013, nothing more, nothing less. Lots of little effects like snowfall and chilled breaths give gotham a true Christmas feel.
+His Cowl
Snowflakes=<3
+Bigger Map Size which is surprisingly dense with activities. It expands on Arkham Cities map and adds south gotham to The North, connected by the gotham pioneer bridge. Gliding across the snow capped rooftops of The Major Areas of Gotham is a really unique feeling. Especially for a Batman game.
+Collectibles will keep any gamer busy for at least a few days! (Maybe too many...)
+The Boss battles are Balanced and shouldnt take too long to complete. Although many of them use repeating sequences, they will be beaten quickly so its not too much of a problem!
+The Origins of the Characters are generally really well done! If you cant see this game as a big new entry to the series, you can at least view it as a backstory to other games in the series. (As it is the First.) Bruce's story about developing into a more solid and refined figure of justice is given to us in an immpressive way. The Pacing of the plot is done well, but you are reminded often that this is far from a cinematic experience. I wouldnt imagine seein this as a film at all (Which is probably for the better.)
+Many new Features to gameplay include: Enhanced Detective Mode with the ability to "rewind" scenarios, new gadgets and interface additions. (Keep in mind that he gets all of these NEW features before Arkham Asylum!!)
+It has Added Multiplayer for the first time! I've tried it only a few times so i cant say much but it does have some good modes and progression. But im betting people will buy this for the story, combat and thrill of being Brucey boy!
+Story is about 12-16 hours without touching on any of the other fun Activities! This is definetely long enough for gamers and it is the average length for the Arkham games too, so thats good!
+Once again, the combat system is done so well, its just so smooth! It seems like Batman is just dancing at some points, he feels in the zone at some times! Although, saying that, the targetting can get a bit off a completely ruin a huge combo..The Combat system is simple enough to understand quickly but complex enough to put major effort into strining together some Badass combos! The Mechanics of Hand to Hand (To Gadget too!) Combat in the Arkham Games are a true marvel of third person Action games, and many games (Of the same genre) have tried to dupicate aspects that stood out. Watch some gameplay of challenge maps if you still arent convinced. (I do wish there was a mode where a comic balloon would pop out and say Kapow! or Wack! with every few punches and kicks. ;D)
-Its Riddled (See what i did there) with bugs and even some crashes at times. Although the main offender is frame drops in graphically busy sequences. These are minor issues but people have been known to have much worse. Obviously on Launch there was some Large problems that arose, but they were quickly patched by Rocksteady. (Every game will have issues on launch! just depends how much coverage they get really!)
-A Gloomy Gotham leads to Brightness issues and an annoying fog thats makes it hard to see long distances.
-Mission objectives often include much Backtracking, Many Dull Dialogue scenes and timed sequences that seem far to easy to the average gamer.
-Linear Environment around the City. Like Doors that you cant open at all, Blank and boring walls, Slow Animations and No Miscellaneous Interactive objects to find!
-Repetitive boss battles! The Deathstroke one is the worst offender!its really only3 different Counters and then a simple beatdown for one of the best mercenaries in DC!? A Skillful Meta-human gets given this disgraceful Repeat of actions? Quite sad really. Boss battles actually have variation between each major VIllain, taking a new apporach to defeat them really uses all of Batmans Skill and Gadgets. However i felt that they were generally better in the other Arkham Games.
-The New detective mode has difficult controls and slows down the story a bit too much at times. You know  exactly where B is but you havent found the right Clues  to find A beforehand... The Hiding of Evidence is a bit too easy as well.
Give us a bigger Challenge Rocksteady!
-The Pacing was a bit strange as well! After a huge boss battle, it would be nice to follow up and see how alfred is doing (And join him for a cuppa!) and fix up your suit right? Instead you will get a call from Enigma and will have to deactivate some bombs straight away! Ignore the fact that Batman is a human being and even he has a bedtime! He must have adrenaline built into the suit...
-The Plot would have been better with some emotional scenes or bonds built with certain figures even!
A Sequence about Bruces life, A flashback to when he is training on a mountain. This comes back to pacing and where the story is going...It does have Lots of Plot twists!
-Among others, Bane is a very different Character, same as many villains. Although this can be excused due to origins and all that. Some Personalities or even costumes for Batman's Foes were a bit of a strange choice. But then again, i read the old school comics so i keep comparing their personalities, etc.
-Some Gadgets you will hardly use outside of missions and thir uses were too specific to stand out as a true Batman Toy. The Electrical Charge or disrupter (Although useful for armed thugs!) will never match the various functions of the Grapple hook or the Remote-Batarang.
-The Colour theme seems dull compared to the other games i the series, this is obviously due to the season and the industrial design. But interiors should be more plentiful and have more Variety too!
Overall I give this Plot-Packed Arkam experience a
Light on the New Features and Colours, but heavy on the Origin stories and Combat (Once again) this is a must-by for Batman lovers, just to see Rocksteady's take on the Caped-Crusader's rough side...and the familiar line up of Villains that we all know and love. Athough it does have numerous technical Issues and repetitve missions that will be noticeable.

After being disappointed with Sonic 4 Episode I, a return to Sonic's 2D roots that featured some ugly art design and a brutal phsyics engine, I wasn't expecting much from Episode II. Surprisingly though, I ended up having quite a bit of fun with the sequel. The physics engine is upgraded considerably and, while still not perfect, now feels much closer to the Genesis-era games. The hideous cel-shaded character design from the first episode was also ditched in favor of a cleaner look. Level design and boss battles are also improved from Episode I. The newly-introduced "Tag Actions" feel fresh and make for some nice platforming sequences as well. On the downside, the soundtrack is hit-or-miss (mostly miss) and a little more zone variety would've been nice.
While still not on the level of the the 2D Sonic games from the Genesis days, Sonic 4 Episode II manages to hold its own and provide an enjoyable experience that retains that classic Sonic feel while tossing in a few fresh twists here and there. Worth playing if you're a fan of the series.

And once you've gotten really good at the game, there are plenty of upgrades and skill mods to play around with, plus local and online multiplayer support.
Overall, this is a very fun game that I enjoy immensely and recommend highly. As of writing this review, there is currently a sale going on, so I would definitely buy it now. Seriously, this game is good, and if you have a controller, you should play it.

Great game! Plays like the old NES games that I would spend hours and hours playing in order to beat back in the day. I like that it has RPG elements like a leveling up system to get stronger, different weapons that can be found and equiped, and stores to purchase permanent upgrades. There are also side quests that can be taken on to flesh out levels.
Although the game sports an old school graphical look, the graphics are detailed enough that it boarders on PSone era 2d games. It looks good and I have no complaints.
Some other cool things about the game are the bosses which are huge and require some intense footwork to master and the varied enemies that show up in different stages. The stages themselves are huge and really varied. This keeps the progression fresh and interesting.
Some negatives I found: the combat is fairly basic and doesn't get much past dodging and spamming the attack button. Also, the instant kill pitfalls and spikes can be seriously annoying, especially on longer levels.
Overall, I really like this game and recommend it.

Ingredients
1/3-1/2 cup sugar
1 tablespoon cornstarch
4 cups frozen unsweetened pitted tart red cherries
1 cup crumbled shortbread cookies
2 tablespoons butter or margarine, melted
1/4 cup chopped pecans or almonds, toasted
Ice cream (optional)
-------------------
Directions
1. In a small bowl, combine sugar and cornstarch. In a large saucepan, sprinkle cornstarch mixture over cherries; stir to combine. Cook and stir over medium heat about 10 minutes or until thickened and bubbly. Cook and stir for 2 minutes more.
2. Meanwhile, in a medium bowl, thoroughly combine crumbled cookies, butter, and nuts
3. Divide cherry mixture among four dessert dishes. Sprinkle cookie mixture over cherry mixture. If desired, serve with ice cream.
------------------------

The Verdict: I give No More Room in Hell a 9.8/10 for it's deep approach at survival and realism

Quick review:
Pros:
- Realistic but fun gameplay
- Scary as hell atmosphere
- Excellent multiplayer
- Great developer support (constant patches and good community too)
- FREE! And completely free too, none of this "free-to-play but not really because infinite pay-to-win DLC muahahaha" bullcrap
Cons:
- Animations could do with a bit of work (but this IS a mod)
- Steep learning curve
- Sometimes buggy (although as I said, there are constant patches. Finally I can switch to my torch while holding a crowbar!)
Overall score: 8/10
Full review:
No More Room in Hell is one of, if not the best mods I have ever played. Zombie games definitely aren't scarce nowadays; hell, zombie mods for Half-Life 2 aren't exactly hard to find either. The zombie genre is getting kind of old, but NMRiH is so fresh and unique in its gameplay that even the tired concept of flesh-eating hordes doesn't detract from the awesome experience.
So, what makes NMRiH so unique? Its realism. Realism and zombies don't usually go together, as infected people biting one another and slowly turning the world into an apocalyptic wasteland isn't exactly realistic. But the attention to detail here is astounding. You can become infected, a concept which has barely been touched upon in most zombie games (other than Resident Evil: Outbreak, which did pretty poorly anyway) and choose whether or not to reveal it; you can pop some pills to keep you going or ask your mates to pump you full of lead to stop you from turning. Ammo is scarce - very scarce. Melee weapons are your best bet, but firearms handle realistically and each weapon has their own ammo type. Teamwork is another aspect of NMRiH which works fantastically. Covering each other's backs feels actually genuine; a highlight of the game for me is the dynamic lighting system, in which a player with a torch lights up an area for all the other players in the game as well. This means that one player can be on light-shining duty, and another on zombie-mauling duty. Sharing resources is also crucial. Health is also very realistic. The two seperate game modes also allow for some variety. Survival is your typical "board up the house, kill waves of zombies, await extraction" fare, but the Objective Mode is where the game shines. Objective Mode is basically "go from point A to point B, overcoming various obstacles and puzzles along the way." The randomisation of objectives and the sense of achievement when you FINALLY complete a map are what makes Objective Mode great. There's no charging guns blazed in NMRiH, unless you want to be instantly pummelled or bitten to death by an angry horde. This is a true survival-horror game, and that's what makes it great.

It's a series of sandbox assassination missions where the meat of the game lies in the exploration of the games's stages, mechanics and areas. It's about replaying it's content to try different approaches.
Poison his drink? Shoot him in front of 50 people? Sabotage a wire to  ignite a patch of oil leading to an explosive barrel as he walks past? Drown a him in the toilet after tricing him to eat years old food? Will you sneak around? Will you replace one of the target's guards? The game is about exploring possibilities.
Story is not the focus in this game, it's more happens in the background as you go about your job (assassination) but there are a cutscene tied to this story unlocked with each cleared mission that show a connection behind your main hits in the game.
*Note: The story of Hitman (2016) seems to be crafted like a TV series, the end of season one does not bring any kind of conclusion it only set up season 2.
There are currently only 6 main missions+ 2 smaller training missions (season 1) but each mission have a large sandbox type area to explore and poke at.
All game modes are set within these sandboxes but non-main missions might change things up a bit.
The game periodicly have time sensitive targets. You only have 1 shot at getting them and a limited window of time to attempt the assassination. These targets will be unavailable after completion (failed or otherwise) or after a certain amount of time.
*Note:There are cosmetic rewards tied to success in this mode.
Unless they recycle rewards in the season 2 Elusive targets then these cosmetic rewards could remain exclusive to players that got them before the end of the season1 elusive targets.
A multi-replay of a assassination. First attempt might ask you to kill a spesific target. Second might ask you to kill the same target while wearing a spesific disguise and without being discovered. Third might add a target and spesify that no non-targets die and that anyone killed or otherwise taken out are hidden within 20 seconds.
It's somewhat a mixture of a training mode and a challenge mode.
These are player created assassination missions. Players can mark any NPC in the game as a target, if they kill said NPC (or NPCs) they can choose to add their method of assassination to the contract requirement before submitting the contract to the Hitman server where other players can play said contract.
The episodic releases got some flak on release. There was player confusion, not helped by a mishandled PR campaign.
My initial reaction was that this hurt and would continue to hurt the game.
My current thoughts are that spacing out the releases of main missions gave the developers both the time and feedback needed to make a better product.
In addition the releases of minor content throughout the season, like Escalation missions and elusive targets was a good fit for this model.
You are awarded XP for doing new stuff like killing the target a new way or using a new entrypoint/infiltration method.
This XP is applied to a progression system tied to the spesific level, each main level can unlock stuff like new weapons, start points, dropoff points and misc gear. (Weapons and gear carry over to other missions and game modes)
Note: The game was originally released with an always online system that made it so you could not access anything unlocked within the progression system if you could not access the servers. This has been a minor annoyance upto now, the servers are not offline often but it has happened.
Note2: The always online system was scaled back a bit after the developer regained it's independence. My initial test of this showed that I could now still play with unlocked content but could not unlock any new content without server access.
Note3: At least this change ignites hope that the server requirement will be removed when they are someday permanently taken offline thus not rendering the game unplayable.
A 4 mission campaign that adds new targets in 4 of the existing cities, more details and thoughts below.

Reworked part of an existing mission with targets, NPC's and a minute of other changes. Feels more like a well done elusive target than a new mission.

A caveat to this: I only have less than 8 hours on record on Steam, but I've played it much more extensively on both the 360 and the PS3.
I was excited for this game. Ridiculously so. I was introduced to the series by its 4th installment, which is still my favorite action game to date and I still attest as the most mechanically precise and polished DMC title in the series. Everything is frame-perfect and crisp, and you can feel the depth of detail and opportunities you have to pull off amazing combos, regardless of how proficient you are at executing them.
DmC falls short in this regard; it took me a while to admit this, but once I did it was obvious. The combat is still precise, but not to the level the series has promised. However, the main issues with this game lie in the arsenal of abilities it gives you. A massive damage buff on dodging attacks, single high-power moves with a far greater reward than risk, and the ability to freely pull all non-huge enemies into melee range and dominate them with wide-range moves are the biggest culprits. It allows for extremely easy domination of the battlefield with no penalties to style with only a moderate amount of practice.
But.
I still think this is a fantastic action game. Does it measure up well to its predecessors? Maybe not. But the flair and style is unique and - in my opinion - pleasing, giving the game a feel that no other game on the market has. And if its mechanics aren't superb, they are still great, letting you pull off lots of really cool combos even if easier moves will do the job just as well. You have plenty of options for flowing from state to state, air to ground, close to far, and vice versa. The ability to attack an enemy below you and bring them up to aerial state is notably unique and fun. The weapons are super cool and responsive. Hitting enemies is satisfying and full of feedback, something most action games fail miserably at.
The story is good, but not great. It definitely shines in the beginning of the game, where dialogue and character body language is nothing short of fantastic. Some of the early conversations are fantastic, making the world feel incredibly believable. From there it devolves, unfortunately, into more typical fare, but the presentation remains satisfying and still provides an experience better than most short games manage to get across.
If you're expecting this game to provide the hundreds upon hundreds of hours the other games could potentially offer, don't. But it's well worth its price to explore some solid action gameplay and should keep you occupied throughout the entirety of its content, including every difficulty level and DLC, making it a great purchase.
It's unfortunate that the Definitive Edition hasn't come to PC. From what I've read, it fixed a lot of balancing issues the game had, but I never got a chance to play it. I can only offer a review for the vanilla version available here. If you don't think you'll -ever- have a chance to play the DE on XBox1 or PS4, and your aching for an action game, I'd still recommend this one. Especially on sale. Otherwise grab the DE for consoles. Though I'm certain it didn't cure the core downfalls of the game, it solves some of the more annoying issues.

I went into DMC: Devil May Cry not knowing what to expect.
What I found was an exceptionally fun, addictive and well executed video game.
Importantly, this title is a departure from previous DMC titles. Nowadays, you'd call it a reboot. Really, it's something of a re-imagining of the beloved series. It acts as a great/ accessible entry point to newcomers and does away with any of the convoluted lore found in it's predecessors.
This is a fresh start, and while it isn't necessarily the DMC you're accustomed to, that is by no means, a bad thing. What you'll discover here is essentially the refinement of the DMC formula and honestly, it's never been better!
DMC: Devil May Cry is an over-the-top, action blockbuster.
It's insane, it's self-indulgent but miraculously, never looses it's way.
It knows exactly what it is and really plays to it's strengths.
Perhaps the game's greatest strength is in it's storytelling.
DMC's plot is simple but very effective. Cutscenes connect each chapter but never do they feel unnecessary, nor do they detract from the action. Sure, Dante's cheesy one-liners are still here in abundance, but the game is exceptionally well written! Everything just flows - particularly, the dialogue!
Character exchanges are genuinely emotional. In a fantastical world of demons and angels, these characters are surprisingly well grounded in something oddly believable! Some great subtleties in the animation, accompanied by some truly outstanding vocal performances really help differentiate DMC: Devil May Cry from other titles in the genre. Dante and his allies are legitimately likable - exhibiting some real depth. You'll undoubtedly find yourself invested in their tale.
Gameplay-wise: The action is intense.
You'll unlock new weapons and new combos as you progress, allowing Dante to unleash devastating new attacks. It's a legitimate power-rush!
Combat is as basic or as complicated as you'd like it to be and caters for genre veterans and newcomers alike.
In addition, a loud, heavy metal soundtrack perfectly compliments and heightens the intensity.
Platforming here is great fun too.
As you progress, you'll unlock new abilities to help Dante scale ever-changing environments.
Level layout is more or less linear, but the art design is ripe with creativity - always interesting.
This quality of design and innovation is constant throughout DMC - in all aspects.
DMC: Devil May Cry is a truly great 'Hack 'n' Slash' experience.
It's easy to pick up and a ton of fun! If you're a fan of the franchise or the genre, you wont wanna miss this one!

This game has a great potential to be a fun little distraction, when having flashlights and lasers shone into your eyes is too 'realistic' for you, or when WoW is too 'click-to-win' for your taste.
Mixing MMO and TPS in a pretty strange mix, the action, customization, and open world feel you can find in this game have impressed me. For a free to play, pay to win game it turned out to be rather enjoyable even without transactions.
However, the only reason I can NOT recommend trying this game, is its match making system. You, as a new player, must not only understand your chosen role, criminal or enforcer, but also your role as fodder. The match maker feeds you to higher levels quite readily, and to make sure you, as the fodder, can't leave the trough it drops you into, you are not permitted to leave a mission once you've been pulled into it.
Feeding higher ranks isn't avoidable. You have cheap guns and no armor, they have very powerful guns and armor that grants them greater health than you. In a CQC fight between yourself, wielding an SMG made for CQC, and a high level enemy, wielding a high power rifle made for sniping, the higher level will win due to the fact their armor soaks your bullets, and your lack of armor doesn't soak their far stronger bullets.
Ultimately, the choice you must decide on before you pick up this game is this: Do you want to be a feeder, or do you want to be a competitor? If you chose the latter, hit the back button on the store browser and find another free game.

If you love Mega Man, Mega Man X, or Mega Man Zero.... Get this game immediately. Seriously, don't even read the rest of this review, it's a waste of your time, you could be playing 20XX. If you aren't hooked already, don't worry, this game is definitely good enough to stand on its own merits.
Mega Man X (or Zero, if you play Ace like me) meets roguelike: the game in a nutshell. You play through the game as Nina or Ace. Nina is a ranged character with a buster capable of charged shots, while Ace is a melee character with a three hit combo, though he can also charge the first swing of his sword for double damage. The characters function the same, essentially, though Ace has just a tiny bit more natural mobility and hp than Nina to accomodate his gameplay style (go fast, kill, repeat).
You go through a tutorial run which does a very nice job of explaining the gameplay mechanics via gameplay and small sections of on screen text, but after that... heheh. During runs you come across chests. Break these suckers open to acquire: health/energy/nuts, upgrades that can give you boosts to stats, such as attack or speed, upgrades that can grant new abilities, like double jumping, mid-air dashing, orbital shields, etc., or switch out your standard weapon for something a little more shiny, all of which can dramatically change how you play the game from that very point forward, or at the very least keep you alive ;) You may also find vending machines for health or energy. They'll keep you in good condition... provided you have the cash. At the end of your run you fight a boss! Go figure. Beat his♥♥♥♥♥and then you can either take his power, some cash, or a low-tier upgrade. Beat the stage before the bonus timer runs out and you get an additional chest with who knows what inside!
What keeps things interesting? As you beat levels, the following levels become more difficult. More enemies.TOUGHER enemies. More obstacles. Harder platforming. Stronger bosses. The longer you go, the harder it gets, in every way. Hopefully you've been stacking those upgrades and earning some nuts... However if you find the normal run too easy, or just not enough fun... Turn some skull modifiers on. Double the length of all levels, make even MORE enemies spawn, make those enemies act faster and hit harder, turn level obstacles into instant death, do a run with no nuts (hahahaha...), no stat boost drops, make it so the game doesn't end until you die or are done with being immortal. It's up to you.
CO-OP?!?!?! That's right, you can do two player runs, either locally or online! You can choose either character, there is no "You're Tails, I'M SONIC" bs. In local co-op, the screen will expand to fit both players according to the distance between them (similar to Smash Bros. if you've played that), but online, you get your default screen view. Items drop for players the same way but will be labeled with "P1, P2" for their respective player.  Right now the game is in beta, so online play... it's not perfect, but by no means should you avoid it entirely. There's a bit of lag, and some bugs in the safehouse, but a solid experience nonetheless.
USE A CONTROLLER. It says to use an X360 but... anything similar is probably okay (I use a logitech f310 gamepad). The controls are super tight, exactly like the titles that inspired this one. The level design can honestly be a tad frustrating at times, but if you remember to open your eyes, breathe, and think about what you're doing, you'll get through it (also unlock double-jump as soon as you can lol).
Yeah right now the game is $11.99? Final sale price will be $15. Worth every penny now, and this game is trending up. There is a lot care put into this game and it shows. Buy it, add me as a friend, and I'll wreck shop with you.

In the year 20XX.......
(and at the bottom for those who prefer TL:DR)
It was the intro to one of our favorite side scrolling robot blasting platformers for many years. A series that endured and always delivered what it promised. Hard as nails difficulty over a wonderful soundtrack delivered with the same gameplay time and again. In todays market, many complain that games are "too similar" or "Don't do anything to advance the series" in an accusation of being stale. This is true in some cases, but I've never felt it a negative for others. Megaman was one such series that never grew stale for me. From 1 to 8, then X through X3. I was late to the playstation, so X4 and X5 were missed for me in the beginning. Later, the series would return in the form of Collectors packages (The Megaman Collection, and the X Collection). Again, it proved that there was a desire for these old games, even though mostly unchanged (They did some amazing work with the music in those collections). Then, radio silence. Megaman was abandoned by the company (certainly not the creator, who fought hard for it) and a wonderful idea was thrown away. Megaman Universe. It was a sore disappointment to hear of a game that would play like Megaman, with huge crossover potential and player created levels would be here for limitless potential of fun. Though, it seems that dream lived on in this game.
Batterystaple Games picked up the torch that Megaman universe attempted to produce, and began running as hard as they could. For an indie developer, I'm personally amazed at how well they've done here. The game controls as great as any side scrolling platformer of yesteryear or even today. Better than most others. Controls are tight and gameplay is fluid. Never have I felt a cheap death through bad hit detection or input. The only advice I can give, is that the controller is a necessity. Keyboard just isn't going to cut it here. That said, controls on some indie games are shoddy and clearly needed fine tuning in early access or alpha stages. Not so here. Even in Alpha, Batterystaple nailed it.
Level design is another area I was nervous about. Roguelikes are a popular breed right now, but often a voxel world is used. Easy enough to procedurally generate, it's significantly harder to do this with side scrolling, non-voxel elements. I was concerned many levels and layouts would look the same. While, Yes, there are a few times in my five hours (and growing) I saw a usual layout, it was always blended into a previous layer or later layer seamlessly. Thankfully, the level design also doesn't reuse different platform layouts in the same level. Meaning it won't be a direct mirror of somewhere in the same level. Speaking of level design, again this is quality stuff from indie developers. Batterystaple really captured level design here, and staged the levels based on how many bosses you've beaten. Level 1 is short with one boss. Level 2 is longer, with a sub boss station. The station features a challenge such as no boosting, not getting hit, or timed completion to give you a reward. Then, later levels have the same layout, but spike throwers added in. By Level 5, the enemies are getting upgrades too. With changed colors (Oh, good ol' pallette swap) come added fireballs. 3-way shots turn to 5. One burst of lasers turn to three. Again, the level ramp-up just proves that rogue like runs in a procedural generation can be done, and done well, if the developer has the right formula to use. These guys sure did.
Graphics and Music. This areas great in one, and pretty good in the other. Graphics are perfect to me. They recall the classic 16-bit era with perfection and at no point did I feel the enemies were complete copies of the game that inspired this. Instead, they were the developers own take on them, and done well with their imaginative creations. The music is pretty good, but the one thing I feel could use some help. Not that they're bad, but the same four tunes seem to stand out, especially when certain levels are reused for two bosses. This isn't a negative, by no means, but something that Batterystaple can surely hit on with their race to release. Whats in here is great, to be sure. I just feel theres room for more.
Overall, I know it's early alpha, but for the price, I can't argue buying it right now. Help these developers along and get them to release day on this with the money they deserve for putting such a great game into our hands. They took a classic that was once amazing and revitalized it in the way it's own parent company refused long ago. Mighty No. 9 is due to come out soon and while I'll be playing that as well, I feel there are things Batterystaple did here in 20XX that Mighty No. 9 hasn't done yet (and i'll certainly be playing both of these). Perhaps an endless mode is in the cards for that game too, but i've yet to hear of it. 20XX though, it's like an endless mode every time you start. With powerups to buy that drop in the generated levels, daily and weekly seeded challenges to play for fun or bragging rights via leaderboards, Co-op, modifiers that change the game with significant things like "spikes make you die" mode, and a second playable character with a laser sword to alternate with, I honestly cannot say anything better about 20XX than i've already said. This games entirely worth it, if you have any love for sidescrolling platformers, and especially the forgotten Megaman franchise, don't wait for a sale. Buy this game and show the love. You won't be disappointed with this.
Pros:
-Revitalized side-scrolling platformer genre with the perfect 16-bit look and feel
-Procedural Generation of levels combined with Rogue Like power up system make each new playthrough different.
-Perfect controls and perfect accuracy of side scrolling just "feels right"
-Co-op, Daily, Weekly, and Modified Weekly challenges make a great way to keep interest.
-Price is great for this. At 12 bucks, it seems a steal. If on Sale, it pretty much is. The games fully playable with almost no problems found in most Early Access/Alpha games. Polished right from the start.
Cons:
-Layouts can sometimes start to feel a bit samey if the generation puts some similar components together a few times in a row.
-Music is the same four to five songs. While nice, it will be noticable in a longer run including same areas.
A final statement. Cons are included just as some feedback. In no way do I find these actually negative, as I have played right through and enjoyed every single thing. I merely put them for points where improvement could be done (and most likely will be, given the developers excellent track record of updates.). Overall, it's feedback and not meant to dissaude anyone.

As soon as I laid eyes on this game, I had to have it. It called out to me. Now I've beaten it, and it was good, but not quite what I had hoped for. Having grown up on the games that this one draws its inspiration from (Rastan, Golden Axe, Ghouls n' Ghosts, Castlevania, Magic Sword, Willow, Magician Lord, etc.), I feel that I can provide a classically educated view of Insanity's Blade's quailty.
Now altogether, I greatly enjoyed my initial playthrough of Insanity's Blade. About half of it was played with a friend by my side, and the other half was solo. It's fun, and I would recommend it to anyone who likes the dark medieval fantasy flavored platformers. This game really shone amongst the darkness in terms of visual design and Music. It looks spectacular, and sounds great. The animations lack fluidity and the sound effects sounded like stock samples, but this doesn't detract from the game's charm.
This game also does a wonderful job of storytelling. I felt for the hero, Thurstan, from the beginning to the end. His one friend along the way, Finn the Dwarf, was a welcome sidekick who brought a necesarry heaping of personality (as well as a heaping of butt-kicking.)
Where this game suffers is in the gameplay itself. Not that it was bad. It actually exceeds the expectations of the 16 bit era platformers that it tries so hard to emulate. However, by today's standards, a bit more fine tuning would be expected. This genre has been around for approximately 30 years, which is ample time to dissect and perfect, yet with this game we find frustrations in rigid controls, easy levels, and hard bosses.
Playing multiplayer mode changed the dynamic a bit. Double the firepower made the enemies laughably easy, especially the bosses that I thought had been hard in single player mode. However, playing through the stages themselves became much harder as I had to share the screen space and field of view with my companion. Any level with death traps became much more challenging to navigate due to said sharing.
The length of the game was nice. Long enough to beat in three casual evenings, and the fact that the ending alludes to a sequel gives hope that things will be improved the next go around. Until then, I hope for some updates to turn this decent game into an unforgettable gem.

I never thought I'd say that any new Hitman game would even get close to attaining the level of quality Blood Money achieved (especially after the disaster titled "Hitman: Absolution" was released...) but well, Hitman™®© 2016 is definitely a serious contender for the "Best Hitman" title!
I actually think it's quite a bit better than Blood Money, in all honesty. Since Hitman 2016 goes back to the old non-linear style of gameplay, with huge maps and dozens of ways to achieve each objective. In addition to that, it also brings in a lot of modern functionality and accessibility features (similar to what's seen in Absolution) but in such a way as to not impact/hamper gameplay, so it still retains that "old Hitman feel".
Additionally, although we all have many memories of the great missions in Blood Money (and Silent Assassin, etc.) Hitman 2016 isn't lacking in that department, either. Although it doesn't have the same quantity of missions as Blood Money (six compared to BM's dozen), they're all just as carefully-crafted and aren't dumbed-down; which is honestly great to see in this day and age - especially compared to games other AAA devs release.
But also, I would argue that the individual maps in Hitman 2016 is more replayable than the maps in the past Hitman games, too. Since not only does each map have multiple objectives, (which can be completed in any order, and depending on how you complete the first, it may impact how you approach your other objectives) there are also a lot of additional missions that use the same maps (Escalation Contracts and Elusive Targets) which force you to navigate the map in different ways, putting an interesting twist on a map you might already know like the back of your hand.
So in all honesty, if you're a fan of other games in the genre (old Hitman games, Death to Spies, etc.) or if you simply enjoy assassinating people with methodical precision in general, (although if you enjoy the latter, I would suggest seeking help from a professional psychologist...) I strongly recommend this game - even when it's not on-sale!

Edit: IO removed Denuvo when they went indie a few months ago, and they're in complete control of the franchise, so I'm once again hopeful for the franchise.
I haven't played this since Dec 2016 or so, so this is mostly from memory. Pretty good entry into the Hitman franchise. The levels are wide open and nice to explore, with lots of detail. The player-made Contracts sounds interesting, but I never tried them. Releasing one episode (level) at a time was a gamble, but I also got this on sale for $30 so I feel that I got my money's worth. The amount of time that went into each level is clear. The episodes are large and meant to be replayed and experimented on, so if you're the type to just rush to the objective, this may not be for you.
The always-online + Denuvo thing didn't pose a problem for me, but the online-only elusive targets and extra costumes may no longer be available? Or maybe they rotate them. I/O owns the Hitman franchise now since Square Enix shot themselves in the foot and dropped them. I really hope I/O reconsiders the always-online DRM now that they're free, too much negativity around it to taint a good series like Hitman. I look forward to the new levels that come whenever, but I'm also going to wait until they're all out before I consider buying.
Couple cons from memory:
- Voice acting. No variety at all. You'll hear the same handful of VAs in Italy, Japan, etc. which is really jarring. Was this a budget issue? Need to pay more attention to this, it can't be that hard to find native VAs.
- This might've been on my rig (and might've been patched), but throwing the coin was laggy for me (the coin itself stuttered and chugged along the ground). I've since installed a new SSD + GPU since then and haven't replayed it, so who knows.
- No suitcase + no elevator because the game engine can't handle it? Bizarre limitation, but it didn't affect my gameplay. I like high-rise levels, though.
Overall a great Hitman game.

Not many games have the same story style as this one. Most games put you in as a hero,  saving civilians and shooting bad guys. But in Spec Ops: The Line... are you a hero? Who are you saving? Who are the bad guys?
All-in-All, this is the best game I've ever played, I highly reccomend this to anyone who likes military shooters, a good campaign, or if you just want to hate yourself after playing it.

It looks awesome. You can screenshot any random frame in the game and it results in a fantastic image.
The gameplay is amazing. Controls feel fluid and action-loaded. It's really fun to run around! There is always something new, new enemies, new environment, new mechanics, new skills. Nothing gets recycled.
Level design is really cool! At first I had to learn that some areas are inaccessible at first - I tried like 30min to reach a higher spot I saw on the map and just couldn't do it, because the proper skill was missing. But I didn't know about that. Maybe a little hint would have been nice (aka "come back later"). But besides that, amazing world design. Not only that lots of areas are connected in surprising ways (e.g. you can suddenly reach the spawn from the other side), but also just this feel when you go through an area one way, get some skill or something else at the end, and then you have to backtrack everything, but it's all of a sudden a totally new experience. So cool! Also really cool is, that you are often not fighting against enemies, but against the environment. For example there is the hot floor, where you can just stand on for one second. Ouch ouch ouch.
I also like the skill tree to customize your experience. Just as it needs to be. No crafting and resouce-gathering, no, just experience and skills, like in the good old days. Love it! Many other games get stuffed with some overloaded customization junk, that doesn't fit the spirit of the game. Just mentioning Tomb Raider as an example. That resouce-gathering, baw. It's just not fitting the game. Here this mistake was not made and the skill system was kept simple.
Music is lovely, voices are cool, and Ori is just cute. Love her. Just sweet! The story is nothing special, but doesn't need to be.
The difficulty is very high, but the more rewarding it is. And yes, I've sworn alot during play. "Why do you even have live containers when everything is oneshot anyway!!", to mention one example ;-) But after you've done it, it's even more rewarding! And I really loved not being sold for dumb and get some game, where you just walk through and press some buttons from time to time. Nope, really challenging. But they thought well about the difficutly and gave you benefits to compensate that. You can use your energy resource to save any time, in other words, you basically have a resource for saving the game. Can't exagerate that way, but can place some savegames whereever you have trouble. Did the really hard jump? Just drop a save before is, try until you get it, then save again. There is also no 10sec death-anamiation or so, just an instant respawn, so it's fine to die! Died about 400 times btw and saw that I'm quite on average in the leaderboards ;)
In the early concept videos, you see some elements that remind you quite a bit of Mario or other classic platformers, but in the game, they don't appear. Yup, it's something new and not just a Mario or Yoshi or whatever remake. Bravo! The closest is probably MeatBoy. In some interview they say indeed, that they started to develop at a time where MeatBoy came out. You notice that, but I didn't mind the analogy. The Escape-Scenes, that remind you of MeatBoy, are well done and fun.

This is one of the only games I have ever reviewed. It is AWESOME, and it is being ACTIVELY DEVELOPED. If you are reading to make a decision, I am here to tell you that
However, in the interest of being informative (as you, the discerning review reader desire), here are some flaws with the current state of this EARLY ACCESS game.

Megaman with only one life and a slew of diverse upgrades to help you survive.
Fast gameplay.  Randomly generated levels.  Daily challenges.  Extra difficulty modifiers should you feel normal game is too easy.
CO-OP!  ONLINE CO-OP!!!
Insane value if you're looking for a fun game for <30 min play sessions!!!
20XX stays true to the feel of Megaman.  I have played and beaten every Megaman and X game, and this game feels like a close cousin, nearly at home in the collection.
The jumping feels tight.  Enemies are well animated and interesting. Battle is fair but can quickly be overwhelming if using incorrect strategy.  The hidden boxes make level exploration an exciting adventure.  The timed bonus upgrades keep you clipping along towards the boss.
I wish you could keep all the boss weapons you earn instead of being only limited to 3 at once.  (You can choose your reward after each level & it doesn't have to be the special weapon).  Sometimes enemy placement in randomly generated levels cause almost no angle of safe attack.  You should be able to save soul nuts throughout multiple runs.
Highly recommended!

I can only comment on the technical quality of this PC port -- which is extremely poor -- rather than the gameplay. That's because this was so unplayable on my fairly powerful system that I didn't successfully get to the gameplay. So much so I requested a refund. I had heard terrible things about the Arkham Knigh port, but figured this earlier game wouldn't suffer these same issues. particularly after a few years in the wild. Nope, same low quality control.
First of all, even the opening cinematic -- and every area after that -- had extremely low framerate and juttered and stuttered constantly, even after adjusting my settings. This on a system which has easily run smoothly even graphically demanding and UNOPTIMIZED code like Ark or Star Citizen. This doesn't even account for items like Injustice from the same publisher which run fine. Strike 1.
Strike 2: While for many games on a PC I do do KB+M, for brawlers and like -- particularly ones designed for console -- I like using a controller. Every game I've installed on Steam and outside it has had no problem recognizing the controller if it's supported. Overwatch, TF2, Injustice, etc. However, while this game did RECOGNIZE a controller, it didn't respond to it's inputs in any way. So another case of this game failing a technical task that many other publishers seem to be able to do. I've been playing Overwatch Beta, and that -- in BETA -- is 1000% more technically polished and stable than this. Heck, it even recognized my Blackwidow keyboard and changed lighting in response to game actions. Even WB's Injustice, while buggier than most non-WB games I played, is acceptably ported.
WB should be embarassed at the low technical quality of their port here, and one wonders if they are going to do such a poor job of it, why they even bother.

After playing the first mission, I thought the game had potential but it quickly turned into a buggy slog. Fine game, awesome blend of Magic Sword, Ghost N' Goblins, and some Splatterhouse :)

Edit: Changed my rating to an 8/10. Devs listen to players and address issues quickly, including some of my complaints.
I choose to give this a Yes, but I rate it as-is at 6/10; it often felt like I was playing an Early Access game. With some polish, this would be greaaaat. As it stands, I would only recommend buying this when it is on sale.
The underlying story and art are both great. I got a very well-done vibe from the setting. It felt dark, gritty, violent, and dirty, as if I was playing the original Splatterhouse games. If Berserk had a retro game, this would be it. One suggestion is to change the HP bar from the extremely dull red line, to a segmented structure akin to Castlevania or Zelda.
However, I have many smaller gameplay complaints that resulted in the Early Access feeling.
1) Inventory and upgrades. It is entirely unclear if weapon choice makes a difference. Damage numbers look incredibly small, are seemingly variable, and often blend in with backgrounds, and enemies typically seem to take the same number of hits. With upgrades, around the time you can afford the 6 fire daggers, the upgrade will become useless shortly after. It is unclear what the HP upgrades do -- max HP increases or simply healing? I bought one once, didn't notice a difference; found myself without anything else worth buying after maxing the daggers. How about weapon upgrades? Also, the fact that weapon collecting becomes pointless later on is a drag.
2) Damaging enemies. I often (1/15-1/30 attacks or so) found non-blocking monsters to not take damage from the knives. Also found a few instances of stronger mobs (e.g. the level 2 orcs, or the giant fat ogres in later levels) taking way too much damage, while also swinging at me and not actually being able to damage me. 20 seconds later, they just died.
2) Backtracking and progression. You can't go back through most levels, and there is a completion % tracker. This is a huge negative to me. You need to restart the entire game if you didn't find a weapon or whatever optional quest. The game is short, but it is still annoying. Consequently, I recommend running dual save slots if you play this and are a completionist -- one to allow you to replay a level if you accidentally finished it without finding the optional quest. The game autosaves, so dual saves will give you an extra chance. Tying into 1), it's unclear what benefit there is to the optional quests and the weapons.
3) Quest tracking. There is simply no method for quest tracking. There is nothing that says you did or did not do something on a level already, or which quests are brand new. There are simply orbs on the main map that you need to drag your cursor over each time to check and see if it is active or not. I found myself noticing a blue orb on the third island at some point before ever reaching that island, which I am not sure I ever interacted with, and I did not feel like restarting the game a second time to figure out when it became active. I missed the 5th weapon, so that must have been it.
4) Level design. Some of the beginning levels are good. There is legit platforming, from spike traps to rope climbing, and numerous pits. However, later levels are too linear and the amount of platforming became almost nonexistent. Credit for the very last level, though -- *really* well done.
5) Graphics. Numerous instances, especially in the monastery, where graphics overlapped and just looked buggy. Ledges sticking through walls, etc.

Snes/Nes/Genesis era half-castlevania, half-beat-em-up type action platform jumping game.   If you're looking for your retro fix, this game has it.  8-bit or 16-bit toggle-able soundtrack to suit your taste!  You may play in arcade mode or story mode which gives a little more open-ended bit on exploration but either is suitable for the action-game lover of yesteryear.   Just a simple game like they made 25 years ago - if that is what you want, this is your fix.  While it's no Castlevania, it certainly does have it's charms - honestly I can't really find complaint in the fact that it cost just a few American dollars to buy.  A few times were quite NES-era [cussword] difficult so it's definitely up to par on challenge.  A must on any retro-gamer's list of games to check out.

-The most glaring issue with the game is a seemingly the weapons not having any balance which is kind of an issue witha  game predicated upon smashing through countless waves of ghouls. You start off with just bunches and the ability to perform wrestling moves, however you quickly get to start throwing blades, which is what the issue is. There's really no reason not to just run through the entire levels tossing blades constantly and it will kill anything in a cone in front of you.  making those cool wrestling moves superfluous.
Althought you get some other weapons the blades still do most of the damage, and arguably the best additonal weapon you get is only about 2 levels in, a flail. Although it seems to do slighly less damage than the sword/mace (as far as I've collected, there's still 3 more weapons to collect) it has range about 2.5x the length of them. Again I don't see much of a reason not to just mash attack button as you progress. Making it rather dull.
-You'd think with such a simplistic combat they'd at least throw a variety of enemies at you, but frankly this isn't true. You get a few enemies that make you think and jump to avoid their attacks, but for the most you get a barrage of slow moving enemies popping up inches from you, and the ones that don't follow this  pattern are still easily beaten by just mashing attack and throwing blades.
-The levels themselves don't boast much in the way of creativity. Although they aren't terrible, there's very little in the way of actual variation. a Few walls to scale here and there, the odd pit (you have trouble distinguishing from regular terrain causing unnecessary deaths)
-Those enemies popping up out of the ground mere inches from you? They aren'y really much of a challenge but they still will hit you often enough to be really just annoying. While it's welcome difficulty, it happens so often it becomes mundane very quickly. The difficulty I feel should come from elsewhere.
-The difficulty. It's true I have died quite a few times in the game, it's very rarely from me failing to defeat enemies, it's usually just something cheap that one shots you like a missing element of terrain that for some reason has you fall to your death, or a spiked cinder block on a chain falling down on you. A platformer does need these things, but I just wish they weren't nearly the only means of dying.
- I love the asthetics of this game, fantastic looking environments and enemies
- Not amazing music, but still very nice.
- You'll get a few chuckles out of the wrestling moves/throws
-An interesting story
- If you want a somewhat mindless game to occupy your time, it does it well. It is, and unashamedly a casual game.

This game is a bit of a mixed bag.  Sega fixed the problems from episode 1 with the way Sonic moves and tried some new ideas, but a number of them failed miserably.
The good things first:  The graphics are definitely improved and they got rid of the ugly fake 16 bit look from Sonic.  Sonic moves better and doesn't feel so sluggish.  Sega tried a lot of new ideas and came up with some pretty unique levels which are a pretty nice change from previous games.
Now the bad:  A lot of that new unique stuff is terrible, flow breaking, and annoying.  Some new enemies seem to be designed to always hit you if you're going fast like Sonic should.  Some parts of the new level designs are rather annoying, especially the way they ham-fisted the Tails combo abilities in.  In order to reach the fast path in a lot of levels you seem to be required to use Tails' flying ability to reach places you can't even see.  There's also a combo rolling attack which is required to break down some barriers.  The game prompts you every time you're required to use them to continue in the level, and they mainly serve as an annoyance.  And the other problem with the levels...they actually added a scrolling level in the game.  That's right, in a game where the whole point is to be as fast as possible, they added a slow scroller (and Sonic becomes extremely sluggish on this level as well).
Now the biggest problem with the game: the bosses.  Without exception, the bosses are all extremely annoying and tedious fights.  Bosses are a lot more complicated than previous games, take many more hits to kill, and of course require Tails combo abilities at certain not-so-obvious spots.  They also tend to have very long start and transition sequences that you have to wait through every time if you fail.  One of the bosses even uses the scrolling level set up to make it as annoying as humanly possible to fight him.
I got to the final boss, and fighting him is so annoying that I can't even be bothered to finish the game.  Do yourself a favor and just get Episode 1 and Generations.  This one isn't worth it.

To start of simple, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is one of my all time favourites of the GTA franchise so when I found the old disk, I though to myself, "Well, haven't seen you in a while!"
As I grew up my sister introduced me to GTA San Andreas. We used to have a PS2 where me and my sister used to sit for hours just running through the ginormous world of GTA, looking for what we could do and what we could shoot down next. I know it sounds violent, but you have to see it from my point of view. My parents were always screaming (well, as I think about it, it was my father who was the rude one) and the only person I could trust was my sister. So when she first showed me the wonderful world of videogames I had a world I could escape to, if I didn't wan't to think about reality.
So back to the review. Sorry for getting emotional for a moment.
It just brought back so many memories.
SO!
As I was staring at the disk my brain instantly though about taking my old PS2 my sister left behind as she moved to her own apartment. A few hours later I was through half of the story, took over some areas for my gang, spend way to much money at AMMO-NATION (The gun shop. Sorry if I spelled it wrong). So I thought to myself, "Hey! So after the story was done I messed around with some mods and DAMN IT IS SO AWESOME!
Sometimes it is a bit buggy though.
But what do you expect from a game this old? :)
If you see it on sale, then get it. It's a great game!
