Astroneer is a planet and space exploration game with a mixture of crafting and survival elements on procedurally generated planets. It was finally released in Steam's Eearly Access in 16th December and I have been anxiously waiting for this game for a long time. When I saw the first pictures and trailers, it instantly gave me the sense of freedom and exploration on a grand scale that I have been craving. And of course, I have been very excited these past days when we all can finally set out to seek our destiny in this curious universum.
As I'm writing this review the game is still in very early development stage and weird bugs and nasty surprises are bound to happen. I was fully aware of this and knew the current annoyances would not keep me from having fun!
Gameplay
So, it all starts with you selecting your hero and landing down to an unexplored planet. Game briefly gives you couple tips how to do things and after that you're on your own. When I got the game, it wasn't even released yet and I enjoyed very much the fact that there were no guides around or too much hand holding within the game. You had to figure stuff out yourself and the system on the background is quite unique and requires at least some focusing for it to be mastered.
Your tasks in the game vary between material collecting for crafting, base building and expanding, researching new types of tech and building more complex stuff. At first you jog around like a humble space peasant, dropping down lifesaving tether lines that lead into resource sites and tunnels. Then you start driving around in small rovers, then bigger trucks and you can even hook these into each other to make trailer combinations. Soon your tether worries are over and your vehicles own life support is enough to keep your lungs well oxygenized!
All the vehicles and the various gizmos you can install into them require power of course and you can juice them up with solar panels, wind turbines and extra batteries to keep going on. You can scoop up some energy nodes from ground too - or use a bio fueled generator on your vehicle to give it a boost of energy.
What I like especially in Astroneer is how your vehicles have certain type of equipment slots and the possibilities of you micro managing them. You can play around with them whenever you like, tear your cargo and items down and change everythings' places on a whim.
I had this scenario dozen times, where my truck was full of supplies, miles deep in the underground tunnels and heading back home. The vehicles store up only so much energy, so eventually I ran out of juice. I tear down a fully loaded cargo module, drop it on the ground while I grab a generator from my suit's shoulder, slam it in the truck's side and give it some time to recharge batteries. Once I'm good to go, I snap the cargo module back on and keep on truckin. Later on, I of course fine tuned my truck with solar panels, a wind turbine and a generator with enough biofuel to go with it.
The World
The graphic style, animations and visual effects are all very appealing. I love the edgy, simplified and clean style of the game and it all ties well together with the soundtrack. The soundtrack is there, but it's not really stealing away your attention from the game itself - and yet after hours and hours of listening to it you still don't get annoyed by it.
I visited all the seven planets the game currently has and they all have their own biome and special weather effects and dangers. The terrain on a barren planet is dusty, sandy and well… Barren, with little vegetation. Arctic planet has a chilly and very rough terrain, where moving around in vehicle is pretty much impossible. And all this time when you adventure on various planets, you can see the other planets in midst of starts when you look up into the night sky.
It took me 24 hours in 3 different days to rummage through most of the current content and to figure out all the bells and whizzles. I would have done it probably sooner too, but I had to start a fresh game 3 times due to one savegame file not loading up anymore and on the second savegame my character was stuck inside a building. (Can't destroy buildings or anything you build at least for now) Again, nasty early access symptoms but nothing major to worry about. System Era has been pushing out solid patches on daily bases and they DO listen to your troubles as long you report the bugs on a proper channel: their own forums.
Crafting & Building
Crafting in Astroneer in pretty simple and straight forward. You build various kinds of workstations and they all serve their own purpose. Smelter smelts ores, Printer "prints" various modules and items on resource materials, Vehicle Bay allows you to build Rovers, Trucks, Shuttles and even Spaceships that can punch through starting planets' orbit to expand your colony into other planets. Research station unlocks new technologies like new vehicles, gear, modules etc.
Like vehicles, these workstations require energy too - and of course resources depending on what you're about to build. You can fine tune your bases energy needs with solar panels, wind turbines and extra energy bank. Solar panels don't generate energy at night, wind turbines won't spin if there's no wind. Yeah, duh. But I like the attention to these details. And these are all detachable, movable items so you can switch their places depending on your base needs and they fit in vehicles too.
The starting planet's surface has more than plenty of basic materials available. The harder metals are underground and there's tunnel entrances almost everywhere to be found. The rarest materials can only be found via researching various strange items found in the world. They can be in a form of giant seeds, roots, crates, glowy rocks etc. Once you get off the starting planet, these rare materials can also be found on planet's surface areas and they require more advanced drilling mechanisms for you to collect them.
--
At the moment - once you have unlocked all the tech and built most things, there's really no "need" to leave the starting planet. Not much will change in the game - the planets all have the same materials so the only valid reason at the moment is to see the sights and explore new areas. I have no idea about the game's future plans, but I do see it brightly lit. Astroneer is one of those 'good vibe games', where you can truly relax, have fun by yourself or with friends and family. Game has no violence: you don't shoot or smack or kill anything in it - though the nature and elements on planets vary and they can kill you if you're not cautious enough. Luckily death is no permanent, so just jog back to the unlucky previous You and you can save your precious items and continue your adventures.
I am eagerly waiting for some minor bug fixes that gave grey hairs to my cute Astronaut and of course more content - any and all kinds of! I want to keep playing Astroneer more.

This is the most emersive and pure iteration of the Hitman series yet. Hitman: Absolution was more of a story-focused and linear third-person shooter, and that didn't really play to the strengths of the Hitman series, but the confusingly named 'HITMAN' manages to capture exactly what a Hitman game should be. There is still a narrative, and while it is mysterious and interesting, you could enjoy the game just as much without paying attention to any of the story. The game was originally released in an episodic format (though I bought the whole thing after everything was already available), with each episode providing its own huge and detailed sandbox map. The maps are absolutely packed with detail and beautifully crafted; Sapienza being my favourite. Each episode has a contract connected to the main plot, these have their own challenges and special opportunities to go for. This is where the game shines. There are multiple ways to assassinate each target, and you will want to try at least all of the more elaborate plans; they are all so much fun to figure out and execute. 'Opportunities' act as hints to give you an idea of what options might be available in each episode, you can decide to what extent you want them, if at all.
As you complete challenges you unlock new equipment, weapons, and starting positions. A progression system like this might seem unnnecessary to some, but personally I like to gradually unlock new things. All of the unlockables are optional extras that may aid you if you feel like using them, but each map contains everything you need. The gameplay has been refined, and the gunplay (if you choose to use it) is great. All of this adds up to what I believe is the purest and most immersive Hitman game in the series.

I have to ration how often I load this game, as I'll start playing it and then wonder how I've invented time travel, 6 hours passing in the blink of an eye. It also made me realize I'm a bit of a cruel dictator when it comes to human rights. I build the smallest possible, cramped yet efficient rooms, give the bare necessities in visitation and entertainment, lock up prisoners who complain and make the rest work 10 hours a day, all whilst banking fat cash into my account and cackling maniacally.
This is a somewhat realistic simulation of the basics of human life in a prison. Each prisoner has needs, and you have to meet those needs by building a variety of rooms and filling them with objects. It sounds simple, but the gameplay is fairly complex, with emotional, psychological and physical needs all coming into play.
The mechanics are straight forward seeming, but it's easy for riots to start and things to escalate wildly out of hand. Oops, turns out people reeeeally don't like it if you don't feed them. There is a deceptive amount of strategy and forward thinking required that makes each prison you create more efficient as you build up your knowledge. My first one burned to the ground and resulted in a few dozen guards getting shanked whilst the prisoers escaped... yeah okay, not only should I have fed them, I guess I should have built prison walls too. Live and learn (unless you're a guard in Prison Athravan, RIP!)
Add to this research trees, staff management, educational and recreational programs, managing addiction, guard rotas and pathing, shakedowns and security, visitation, resources and financial stress and you have one hell of a deep simulation game.
On top of the pretty much endless simulation, the modding community for this game is fantastic. Thousands of people have poured their heart into prison and object design, as well as scenarios and additional features, and it's all available free. The game was great to begin with, but kudos to all those who have submitted to the workshop, and to the developers for providing the tools for the people who are way smarter than me to share their creations. All I can do is scroll through page after page in awe of their dedication and skill.
Shut your mouth you mediocre architect hater.

Ok, you can just get an idea of how much the developer cares about this game by taking a peek to its title and its game store page - everything is spelled wrong, without capital letters, with wrong spaces (like achievements : darkness with spaces before and after the colon); the description of the game keeps on calling it "amaze achivements" without the "e" in the second word, "rubins" instead of "rubies" and so on.
So yeah, this is definitely a game that match its premises.
Basically, you're put into a labyrinth with a top down point of view; your character is a glowing spark that you can slowly maneuver with WASD keys. Actually, even if the controls are sloppy, it doesn't matter since there are no enemies at all and you get no harm by hitting the labyrinth walls.
The levels, in succession, consist of random labyrinths in which there are lots of dead ends and sometimes you'll spot in those dead ends some dark red polygons - they are those which will trigger the achievements and, when collected all in the same level, let you progress to yet another level which is the same as the one before.
Plus, the achievements aren't related to the levels or the objects you can collect.. and there's no menu either, just a pre-game menu in which you can choose resolution and game quality (as with other tons of games). So you can't replay previous levels.. even though it would be quite pointless, since they're all the same.
And the achievements (if they're not working for you, you need to copy the "Managed" folder from Amaze Achievements - Forest to the corresponding folder in this game, look in the Steam discussion for more information) will unlock (around 50 at a time, but not in tray) only by touching those dark ruby colored polygons. So that you can complete everything on level 1, and actually there's no point in going on with the game since the levels are all the same.
Anyways, if you want to go deep in the game and if you are aware that you won't be able to get back to the previous level, by touching the last ruby of the level (there are no marks at all, you can't view nor maps neither how many stones you have yet to collect or how many of them you've already collected) - I say "ruby" 'cos they're dark red and look like bad-drawn rubies, but they're just rotating dark polygons - you will be automatically transported to the beginning of the new level.
As I said, the fact that your spark-character is slow and the labyrinths are quite large (mainly due to the dead ends) it can be frustrating to go on with the levels and get nothing in exchange.
As with many reviews I took some screenshots (I don't know why but some games, when I press the usual key combination, open me some kind of F12 Chrome debug screen and don't allow me to take in-game screenshots) but what you see in the game hub page is what you literally get - the same dark maze over and over.
Of course, going on with the levels means that there are more rubies but really, there's no point in going on and on since the game has nothing to offer.
So, if you're here for the achievements and they aren't unlocking, take a look in the Steam discussion and guide sections. If you're here for a maze/puzzle 3D game, well you won't find anything enjoyable at all. And being the first reviewer also gives me the chance to write an extensive explanation of what you're going to buy and to warn you if, as I said, you'd like to get a real "action/adventure/indie/casual" game as the game store page wants to think you about.

DmC: Devil May Cry, the "reboot" of the original Devil May Cry games set in a more contemporary setting.
Just a basic run-down of my relationship with the franchise and with this game:
I've played DMC2 and 3 to completion and only bits and pieces of DMC4. As for this game, I got it for 9$ as part of a Humble Bundle and personally that's the only way I'd be able to recommend this game to anybody, at the time of me writing this, I have 7 hours on the game. A little less than 6 of those hours were a complete playthrough of the game on Demon Hunter (Normal) and the rest were me being afk so needless to say I stand to give a review of the game.
As for Pros and Cons,
Pros:
-The Combat System feels great as it should in a hack and slash type game, it seems that even though the game was made by a different studio than normal, they definitely captured the Devil May Cry feel in the gameplay.
-The music is amazing, extremely blood pumping, encouraging players to want to do better in the game and overall makes combat 10x more enjoyable.
-Tons of replayablity with numerous collectables, unlockables, and the variety of difficulty settings going all the way to "Hell to Hell" mode where Dante dies in one hit but everybody else is significantly stronger.
-Great Social Commentary
Cons:
-The story is trash, even by Devil May Cry standards. I totally understand that they were trying to make the story more "modern" if that makes any sense, but they blew it, big time. One of the more popular reviews on Steam explains it beautifully:
"The story of a man and his brother who dream of destroying Mountain Dew and Fox News just so they can kill the owner of Bank of America." -stikas
That's the whole story, take it or leave it.
- The game really cheaply tries to force players to use/mix up their combos by incorporating the other weapons. This is a bit of a tough one to explain because you really have to play the game to comprehend how bad a solid half of the weapons are, yet they still try to force you to use them. "Dante" (I use that name VERY loosely) has 9 weapons he can use, only about 4 of them are actually useful.
Rebellion, the default sword, Eryx the second demon weapon you get (huge fists), Aquila, the second angel weapon you get (some glave shuriken type things... they just stun people), and Kablooey, the third gun you get toward the end game (stops enrage). Idk where I'm going with this, but if you buy the game for whatever reason, trust me you'll agree with me
- The characters (Dante and Vergil) and watered down hollow shells of their former selves. To put it bluntly, Dante is an annoying prick that's gotta make a stupid remark about everything, now that's pretty much the old Dante, except imagine if it was a 7 year old and his vast vocabulary doing it. Vergil on the other hand is pretty close to the original, except for the fact that he throws honor completely out the window and just does what he wants.
- Boss Battles are lackluster, idk what more I need to say.
In Conclusion, the only way I can possibly recommend this game is if you get it on sale or part of a bundle, as there are plenty of other hack and slashes (like the original games) that do what DmC: Devil May Cry does, but extremely better.

Wuppo is a cute and charming game that goes against using conventional means of guiding the player, and instead requires you to be observant and to pay attention to what the enviorment and its inhabitants tell you. This causes the game to feel much more rewarding when you figure out how to advance. There are also optional collectibles in the game in the form of film strips. Even though they are optional, I highly recommend that you find as many as you can, as they reveal information about various characters and places in the game, and some of that information can be very helpful.
The platforming is solid, it has tight controls and proper physics on rounded bouncy platforms such as mushrooms. The combat is also good, although simplistic, with unique and challenging bosses that appear in the most unexpected places. The only real criticism I have with Wuppo is that if you're somewhat of a completionist like me, aquiring everything is a massive undertaking, specifically when it comes to buying all the unique items from all the shops. Grinding out all of the smurt (the in-game currency) takes a very long time, and the process becomes very tedious very quickly.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in adorable creatures, and games that reward thoughtful observation as well as good platforming skills.

Welcome to the strange world of Wuppo. A world filled with Wums, Blussers, Splenkhakkers, Fnakkers and a handful of other races. You are a Wum living in the Wumhouse, a house where every Wum can live in leisure, but seeing more and more Wums leaving to the new underground city of technical development Popocity. After you've made a mess of the hallways in the Wumhouse, AGAIN, you've been thrown out of the house. Now homeless, your adventure begins where you meet other characters, fight strange bosses, solve enviromental puzzles, help communities, save the world, and find a new home.
Strong Points:
+ The world - Building a world ain't easy, especially one with races and technologies so different from ours. But the developer managed to not only create a consistent world, but one that feels very alive and full of things to explore. A great achievement.
+ NPCs and their interactions - The world is filled with small little creatures with small little lives. They don't feel like static objects that speak the same sentence their whole lives, but as real and alive creatures. Big plus for writing and coding all these dialogues for all the little interactions, even when they are insignificant to the plot, just to keep the immersion.
+ Music - The soundtrack is gorgeous and fits to every situation our little Wum is thrown into. A great achievement by the composer.
+ Animations - Very fluid. Love how the expression of our little Wum changes at different dialogue options.
+ Difficulty - The bosses and environmental puzzles are sometimes hard and challenging, but never unfair. Great job.
Average Points:
T Gameplay - You don't play Wuppo for it's inventive gameplay: it's your average Indie Metroidvania. But that isn't needed for a game like Wuppo, the gameplay is the medium you use to explore and interact with the world, and it does that just fine.
Weak Points:
- Art style - Sorry Lars, but most of it looks like it was made in MSPaint. Sometimes it looks nice, and sometimes it's just plain ugly. However, the art style is consistent throughout the game, so it doesn't break the immersion.
Conclusion:
Wuppo is a charming game with a great world to explore that feels very alive. Recommended!

Wuppo is an incredible game to be brought to us by just two people. WITH THE EXCEPTION OF ONE MAJOR ISSUE.
I think about games that hit the closest to real, honest classic gaming. Authentic and not forced or fabricated. For example, I think Bleed is the closest an indie game has gotten to a legitimate Gunstar Heroes successor. With Wuppo, I think this is the first indie game I've played to feel, in its presentation, with its cast of quirky characters, with its music, its gameplay systems, etc. like a Nintendo-made game. It may not LOOK like one (The art is more like a very cute spin on An Untitled Story), but it sounds, acts and feels like one in just about every way. If you don't like the direction the Paper Mario series has gone, this game is not Paper Mario, but it has that same kind of writing, and worldbuilding, and overall fun and adorability.
There is a huge amount of bosses (17!!), a theme park with rides you can ride on, an underground city with jobs (we'll get to that), an apartment complex full of nutty people, a forest tribe of flower people, islands in the sea to find, another dimension entirely-- the world of Wuppo is enormous. Not quite the size of a game like Opoona (another similarly quirky and wonderful game), but much larger than you'd expect on first playing the game.
The combat and general interface are relatively simple. Point and click to fire, WASD to move. You can throw items on pedestals and give items and money to people for trade. Part of the fun of the game is finding things in shops that you have no idea what they are, and sometimes you might need them. Why does a city sell a diving helmet? Why does an apartment sell rocks? You'll find out!
Okay, let's talk about the elephant in the room, and I haven't read reviews lately so I dunno how people will feel about this, but: THE POPOCITY SECTION OF THE GAME IS REALLY TEDIOUS. You will spend about 3 hours in Popocity, an underground city underneath the Wum village, trying to build Credit for the city in order to finance the city's big expansion. This means getting jobs, performing tasks, buying items from shops, staying in the hotel, etc.
This is all fine, and I liked the concept INITIALLY. The problem is that there just isn't enough to do here. You can sell newspapers (and after doing it 8 times you unlock a side quest, which-- by the way, that tells you something about the tedium doesn't it? Doing the same minigame 8 times?) but the only change is how many papers you deliver, and whether it's to Central or to Old Town. You can participate in debates at City Hall once a day, but there are very few topics (we already decided on the painted ♥♥♥♥offel!! Three times!!) . You can find Kneft monsters for Credit once a day, which only varies slightly in how the enemy waves spawn. You can buy items from a seedy shop at outrageous prices for 1000 credits a pop. And you can work in the factory, which consists of jumping up and down on a seesaw over and over again.
There's just not enough to any of these jobs to make grinding out the credit fun. Each time you do several jobs and go back to the Credit final tally you'll be left with a feeling of "really?? I still have that much to go??". I feel like this can be fixed either by increasing the credit that jobs give or by providing more variety to the jobs. For example, why not more topics at City Hall? Why not a police job tracking down criminals in the city? What if a machine breaks down at the factory and you can get extra Credit for fixing it? If the message is "work is supposed to be tedious", then it comes across the same as the infamous treadmill from Super Paper Mario -- in the end, it's still tedious and that's all that matters.
ALL THAT SAID, Wuppo is a fabulous game. I can't not speak about that section because it makes up a third of the game, but the other two thirds are so weird, so wild, so wonderful, so witty, so silly, that it kept me smiling all the way to the end. It's one of my top 3 indie games of the year, to go along with Copy Kitty and Rive as the best experiences I've had on Steam in 2016.

I like to describe this game as "Multiplayer Grand Theft Auto". You're in a large scale city environment with traffic, NPCs, and other characters, and its third person shooter style. The storyline behind the game makes it somewhat believable: the city has deteriorated and crime is rampant, in a last ditch effort to save the city the mayor deputizes anyone who wants to help enforce laws, thus the creation the two major factions enforcers and criminals. Characters are grouped (typically groups of 2-4 or up to 8 if you call in backup) to help each other with missions that are assigned by a dispatcher depending on their faction. You can create your own groups with friends or be auto grouped. There will usually be around 80-100 people running around on any particular server, and dozens of servers, so you get to find a wide range of different people and skills. The missions fit well with the back story (eg, enforcers have to raid doors and crims have to stop raids, etc; criminals have to spray graffiti and enforcers have to stop graffiti, etc) but do lack some depth and can be repetitive.
Another good aspect of the game is the visual customization for clothing and vehicles. With an in-game mini graphics designer, its possible to create almost any design for your vehicle or clothing.
The game can be very addictive and has lots of continual play value as you constantly unlock weapons, vehicles, and perks.

The popularity of this game is beyond good and evil, pun intended. How can anyone except a 12 year old find this enthralling? The shooting does not feel particularly good. The story while trying cringeworthy hard to make a powerful statement, feels like it's written by hollywood washouts with a mental handicap. It fails on every level to attain the power a story like this could become. Dialogue is super cheesy, you don't feel you are making a real difference in the overall story, despite the game desperately wanting you to feel like you would.. Everything feels dated. After all the hyping, I was sorely disappointed in this game. There are far better shooters with a powerful message out there. This game is only remembered for it's shock value, which is the easiest and cheesiest way to attain publicity.

What I always liked about the Hitman games was that the developers tried out new things in every new release. Some worked out well, some didn't, and I think often times whats good or bad is a matter of personal taste. Nearly every title had some flaws for my taste (the one with the least amount for me was "Blood Money"), but I always liked and recommended them.
This one is different. Although the levels are beautiful designed, the missions are diverse and the voice work is fine as always (exception below), there are some really annoying flaws that prevent me from giving a thumbs up, and, since thumb sideways is still not an option, i have to go for the negative one.
- The "always online" function is bu*****t, at least for the SP mode. I get that there are people who want to compete with others around the world and upload their personal records and create and share challenges. I am not one of them, but I‘m fine with that. These are MP functions and can be handled separately like in countless other games. But why the hell are my personal level statistics only saved as long as I play online? I played the game roughly ten hours before the first "can not connect to server" message came, so it asked me if I wanted to continue offline. So, the savegame becomes an offline one and i won‘t be able to upload my statistics for competition, fine. Don‘t care. But this is a g****mn single player game, one where my character gains experience based on my performance! That means an offline SP can not unlock more items to make new playthroughs interesting. You may start a level in online, but as soon as you switch to offline it erases all score and data you collected in this level. Thats a no-go, and don‘t tell me that it‘s a technical problem to store my level data offline or something.
- All unlocking functions of items and weapons are tied to this levelling system. So, if you want to play and gain more stuff for future playthroughs, you have to see that the server is online. If it‘s not, you‘re out of luck. Which also means that if the developer closes down sometime in the future (a thing that sadly happens from time to time) the game is gone for everybody.
- Statistics are massivly reduced compared to earlier games. Just the numbers for target kills, innocent kills, being seen and time are given. No detailed listing of weapon use, cause of death, etc. Sad!
- One storytelling thing that bothers me is that no matter where you eavesdrop, be it on servants in Bangkok, streetfolk in Italy, Marrakesh or Paris they all talk in perfect american or british english.
Why? They used native speakers in the previous games. I get that you need to understand the dialogues. Make 47 understand every language and give subtitles! This game is already over the top, but the exotic flair is part of the charme. If everyone sounds the same (and they use just a handful of actors that don‘t use any variation in their voices), it becomes dull.
- Some mission clue was misleading and made me search about 3 hours for a person at a specific place ("dongle" in Sapienza), not giving me a clue to realize that this person had already left. A case of very bad mission design.
- The inventory system is worse than in previous games. You basically have a scroll wheel you have to open and scroll through for every single item (even lockpicks are not automatic anymore). No quick slots, no "next item" key, nothing. Very impractical.
In conlusion I have to say it‘s not a bad game per se.
It is actually quite good. But compared to the previous hitman games and their high standard, for me it is clearly a step down in quality.

Hm, what can I say about rust? I mean sure the game's community is a majority of horribly toxic players who kill new players on sight for no logical reason, there is nearly no sense of wildlife in the gane except for the rare deer or bear, and that the game is horribly unoptimised, but these are just minor set backs right? Ehhh, kinda? The game has a $20 price tag which rarely goes down on sale which means its difficult for people to try out this game without paying the extremely high price. Unfortunately, this game can be quite tedious and just an openworld PvP FPS most of the time with next to none of the "survival" aspect that Facepunch was going for. The game itself is quite enjoyable with a larger group of friends or even a clan but playing alone is a nearly impossible task as if you are alone and farming resources to upgrade your base, and a small group of players ambushed you. Bam, everything is lost. Oh and if you try to join a group of players to survive with they'll either kill you or they'll....uhhh no actually they'll just kill you. Luckily, this game has got decent players that help new players and aid they're attempt of survival and these players are what give you hope to take down the toxic and fight for the good. Now why am I giving this game a positive review? It's because of how the game has a way to keep bringing you back to make you think 'I want to build a fort and start a clan." Or " I should check back on my base and upgrade it" or just " man, I wanna play some Rust ". Sure, the game needs many updates and improvements to become a full game, sure the players need to stop being so toxic so the game stops having a bad reputation for it's community and sure the price should drop more often for players that don't want to buy a non developed game for $20. These things may happen overtime but at this point, I believe that Rust was worth my money and was *mainly* good fun.

Existe cara nova na cidade. Carl Johnson - ou CJ para os outros membros da gangue - é o mais novo membro da família mafiosa de "Grand Theft Auto". Aliás, cidade não é o termo correto - San Andreas, diferentemente de Liberty City e Vice City, é um estado e esse salto é uma boa analogia para compreender a escala da mudança na mais nova obra-prima da Rockstar.
Assim como "Grand Theft Auto III" explorou o mundo de "O Poderoso Chefão" e "Vice City" revisitou a história de "Scarface", "San Andreas" não esconde sua inspiração nos filmes que retrataram a violenta situação das brigas de gangues na Califórnia dos anos 90. Surpreendentemente, CJ é provavelmente o mais honesto de todos os protagonistas da série: depois de passar cinco anos trabalhando em Liberty City, ele volta para Los Santos (inspirada em Los Angeles) para o enterro de sua mãe - e encontra os habitantes do bairro sofrendo nas mãos de outras gangues. A sua prioridade é, antes de mais nada, defender as famílias de Orange Grove, o que nem sempre é feito da maneira mais pacífica e educada possível.

I've only cracked the surface of Wuppo and I'm loving it.  The controls and animations are fluid and feel natural, and there's so much to discover and learn in the early game that I have to give it a quick review for those curious.  Wuppo has the same charm that I would expect from an entry in Yoshi's series of games or better yet, Kirby.  The world is immediately presented to you as being well-established and it makes no apologies for bringing you, the player, in before you have any clue as to what it's all about.  Tutorial nonsense is kept at an absolute minimum, with only the most obtuse details being presented in easy to digest comments from NPCs.  The music is brilliant and adds a level of depth you'd think was only reserved for games in much different calibers; the soundtrack is refreshing and simply breathtaking, with some elements being pseudo-rhythm based.  The first couple boss (I think?) encounters were super hard but gave off that lightbulb moment when I realized the pattern and how the arena had to lend itself to my advantage.
An open world that doesn't hold your hand but also doesn't try to diminish your abilities at every turn- why can't more games understand this simple concept?  Yes, there is a gap between Nintendo Hard and Tryhard Hard.
Wuppo is not a game that panders to anything, really.  It is brave, and dares to be it's own entity without selling itself out to tired gimmicks or lazy tropes.  It even forces on you its own, wildly different
and at first I was searching for ways to rebind my controller but after 20 minutes or so I realized that this beautiful game was asking me to try something new, and that, right there, is when I realized the scope of Wuppo's depth.
Finally a game for Nintendo platformer lovers, one that wraps you up in the brilliance of its design instead of substituting creativity with cheap, artificial difficulty.  I had no idea what it was when I bought it, and I still really don't understand even a small percentage of what this game actually
, but man, I'm glad I gave it a chance!

I'll mostly be summing up the singleplayer and multiplayer gameplay in this review and leaving the technical part mostly alone until the end, but first, let's start with the Campaign, then Multiplayer and Zombies(in their current states on PC).
Compared to the other games in the franchise, Black Ops 2 has one of the best campaigns on offer, particularly for the addition of decisions you can make in the story that can change how it all ends, this mechanic has unfortunately not been implemented in any CoD games after this one. The story in itself, is a continuation of the first Black Ops and while you don't miss out on a good deal of actual storyline without it, it helps to add a bit more connection to some of the characters.
One feature that did hang around in future games was the ability to modify your loadout in the Campaign, which was first implemented in Black Ops 2, and added a bit of extra content to unlock after the story was completed in the form of special weapons to mess around with. All in all, it's pretty solid if you're a new-comer or a veteran of the franchise, although certain scenes can be quite confronting to some players, thankfully, there'a an option for that in-game.
(This should be interesting)
If you've played Call of Duty before at least once, you'll know the basics of what to expect here; ultra-fast, chaotic gunfights that will constantly be on the move, but still attempt to be accessible to just about everyone.
Currently, you can expect to see a player peak of just under or equal to ~2,202, which... is not a lot at all, to say the least, Off-peak however is a lot worse, with an average that regularly reaches and can go under... 500 players. For comparison, Team Fortress 2, a game which a part of it's community thinks is dead, has a ~40,000 average player peak. Yikes.
Unfortunately, the low playercount can make the gameplay suffer, for example:
Let's say you open up Public Match and have a look through of what people are playing see Combat Training, for example and- oh, only 30 people are playing that, let's look at something else... maybe... Party Games- oh, wow even less are playing that. A few more people are playing in Hardcore, but they're all playing TDM, except for one or two people trying to play CTF. Now, you may be thinking "Well, where are the other 400-1600 players?" Let's see...
They're all in Core. Team Deathmatch. Out of all the gamemodes available. And guess what?
THEY PLAY NOTHING ELSE, AND HALF THE PLAYERS YOU'LL FIND THERE WILL SWEAT THEIR BALLS OFF AND USE ALL THE GIMMICKS AND TRICKS IN THE GAME TO DO SO.
If you're a casual player or a new-comer, go to Combat Training, you'll get less rewards, but the experience will be much more enjoyable, and while it tends to have a low player count, you'll only need 4 players in a lobby to start a match, so it balances out.
Or, if you have the Nuketown 2025 DLC and a strong internet connection, try Nukejacked, full matches there are often the most chaotic and over the top out of all of them, the spectacle alone makes things enjoyable.
I can't really speak for the veterans of the franchise on this one, since, well... my total kill/death ratio of 0.46 speaks for itself, even though i got the game at launch.
Now for the Zombies part of Black Ops 2, revolving around co-op play.
...
Unfortunately, not a lot of people play this version of Zombies on PC, Only a hundred or two play it which is a shame as it's more accessible than Multiplayer, but still allows you to play with your friends.
If you don't have any DLC, you'll have access to three locations in the area of Green Run, the Town, the Bus Depot, and the... Farm, was it? Yeah, the Farm.
The Town is the most beginner friendly of the three locations, housing the two gamemodes Grief and Survival, which are shared by the Farm as well, but with different properties that make it more difficult.
People generally only Survival in the Town and Farm and leave Grief alone, i don't think i actually haven't managed to play Grief but i remember playing it once, and i'm gonna say you aren't missing out on much, it's essentially Survival but instead of dying upon being mauled by zombies, you turn into a zombie and are free to kill the remaining survivors as you see fit. It can be entertaining, but also rage-inducing.
The Bus Depot is the real meat in the Zombies section of Black Ops 2 if you have no DLC, housing it's own unique gamemode: Tranzit, it's the most complex and technical on offer, taking you on a tour around a large town that has 5 locations inside it by means of an upgradable automated tour bus that can somehow... drive over a... river of lava...
If you don't want to get on the bus, however, you'll either be stuck at the location you're at, or having your head ripped apart by a face-hugging demon baby because you wondered where the bus was going.
...No. I'm not kidding.
Anyway, the gamemode centers around building machines out of various parts you find around the area and using them to go deeper into the various locations in the world and to help combat the never-ending zombies, parts can be very hard to find without prior knowledge, but since the game itself is nearly 5 years old, it won't be too hard to find an experienced player who can show the ropes.
All in all, the Campaign is great, the Multiplayer is a bit of a sweat-fest in Core and not many people play, and Zombies is solid, but has almost no-one playing.
However, it is one of the better CoD games of this decade without a doubt, the graphics do hold up surprisingly well and it's relatively easy to run on modern PCs, as long as you can cope with the low chance of the game crashing every few hours, but it usually isn't infuriating.
(...Except when you're carrying the flag and are going head to head with the enemy flag carrier, and you crash just as you take the first shot while catching him off-guard, but that's just me...)
The game's solid, and a great time if you've got friends who play as well.

This game is quite unlike any other game because of the terrain tool that lets you raise / lower / smooth the terrain. There is a bit of a learning curve with the game because  there are no tutorials. But once you have spent some time, you can have a lot of fun with the tool. For example, you can point the tool at your feet and use the 'raise terrain' to lift you into the sky. Or, you can use the 'lower terrain' to dig a tunnel straight to the center of the earth. The graphics are absolutely beautiful. This game has a great amount of promise. But, in its current state, it just has too many bugs for me to recommend. I will sit down and play for a couple of hours and have a ton of fun. But then I encounter a game-stopping bug and wanted to pull my hair out.
For example:
1. Using the 'raise terrain' tool, you will frequently find yourself floating in the middle of the planet. You then die and and are unable to recover your items. If you are very careful, you can sometimes avoid this.
2. The game will randomly "lose" items when you pick them up or put them down. For example, if you pick up a tether, it will often disapper. In addition, I have had instances where I was carrying an item, and between picking it up and putting it down, the item would just disappear. There are some workarounds for the tether. For example, you can put the stack of tethers in the top left slot. Also, you can check the number of tethers in that slot and know not to pick any up if the top left slot is full. These workarounds are annoying but help a bit. However, when an item you are carrying from Point A to Point B just completely disappears, there just isn't any workaround for that!
3. The game has random problems where items stop working. This seems to be related to partial items. For example, I often had an energy item in my backpack that was partially used. I moved the item from my backpack to a platform, and the item stopped working. Shortly thereater, ALL energy resources stopped working. The only solution was to delete the save game and start over from scratch.
4. The Smelter will often bug out and produce items that cannot be picked up. Or, the smelter will just "lose" items while smelting. Again, there is no workaround.
I am sure these bugs will be fixed in the near future. But, as these are essentially "game stopping" bugs, I cannot recommend the game at this time. I will keep an eye on the patch notes and update my review once these problems are resolved.

Ori and the Blind Forest is amazing and I would highly recommend trying it out, although there are a few flaws, this is easily one of the best games I have played in a long time. The art and atmoshpere are spectacular, the world is colorful, the characters are interesting, and the soundtrack is amazing enough to even compete with games like Halo. One flaw I noticed was that there were a few difficulty spikes, most of the game is fairly easy even on hard mode, but I usually died quite a few times during the escape sequences. Personally I have no problem with a few difficulty spikes, it just makes beating it even more rewarding, however this may be something that others would not enjoy. Speaking of the escape sequences... they are just amazing, they are fast paced and the music is always top notch during the escape. Ori and the Blind Forest has some of the best platforming I have ever played, it's smooth, fast, and all the skills you unlock adds so much more to the platforming. You visit certain trees in the game to unlock new skills that will help you in combat and allow you to enter places you couldn't go before. These skills are unlocked at a nice, steady pace and are all extremely fun to use. The platforming bit where you have to carry the ball in Black Root Burrows was a bit annoying to me at first becasue you move so slow and you cant use Ori's abilities when you carry the ball. But when it came time to carry the ball again in the Forlorn Ruins, it was actually pretty fun because the ball affected gravity in a way that changed the platforming up a bit. The story is the weakest point of the game but still isnt neccisarily bad. If you don't think about it too much, then the story is pretty good, but the more you think about certain things that happen in the story the more you realize, "Wait, that shouldn't work..." or "That doesn't make too much sense". I wont spoil anything, but if you finished the game you probably know what I'm talking about. It wasn't anything that completely ruined the story or anything, the ending was still very good. The only other flaw I noticed was that you couldn't set up a custom keyboard layout, and becasue the charge jump key was "w" it just felt kinda awkward to me, but I couldn't change it becuase you can't re-bind your keys. Luckily I got used to it for the most part but it was still a bit annoying. I'm sure I didn't cover everything there is to talk about, but hopefully I got the point across that you should definetly try this game out if you haven't already, it's an amazing experience!

The Cuban Missile Crisis, also known as the Caribbean Crisis (Russian: Карибский кризис, tr. Karibskij krizis), or the Missile Scare, was a 13-day (October 16–28, 1962) confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union concerning American ballistic missile deployment in Italy and Turkey with consequent Soviet ballistic missile deployment in Cuba. The confrontation, elements of which were televised, was the closest the Cold War came to escalating into a full-scale nuclear war.[1]
In response to the failed Bay of Pigs Invasion of 1961, and the presence of American Jupiter ballistic missiles in Italy and Turkey, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev decided to agree to Cuba's request to place nuclear missiles in Cuba to deter future harassment of Cuba. An agreement was reached during a secret meeting between Khrushchev and Fidel Castro in July 1962 and construction of a number of missile launch facilities started later that summer.
The 1962 midterm elections were under way in the United States and the White House had denied charges that it was ignoring dangerous Soviet missiles 90 miles from Florida. These missile preparations were confirmed when an Air Force U-2 spy plane produced clear photographic evidence of medium-range (SS-4) and intermediate-range (R-14) ballistic missile facilities. The United States established a military blockade to prevent further missiles from entering Cuba. It announced that they would not permit offensive weapons to be delivered to Cuba and demanded that the weapons already in Cuba be dismantled and returned to the USSR.
After a long period of tense negotiations, an agreement was reached between President John F. Kennedy and Khrushchev. Publicly, the Soviets would dismantle their offensive weapons in Cuba and return them to the Soviet Union, subject to United Nations verification, in exchange for a U.S. public declaration and agreement never to invade Cuba again without direct provocation. Secretly, the United States also agreed that it would dismantle all U.S.-built Jupiter MRBMs, which were deployed in Turkey and Italy against the Soviet Union but were not known to the public.
When all offensive missiles and Ilyushin Il-28 light bombers had been withdrawn from Cuba, the blockade was formally ended on November 20, 1962. The negotiations between the United States and the Soviet Union pointed out the necessity of a quick, clear, and direct communication line between Washington and Moscow. As a result, the Moscow–Washington hotline was established. A series of agreements sharply reduced U.S.–Soviet tensions during the following years.

What I always liked about the Hitman games was that the developers tried out new things in every new release. Some worked out well, some didn't, and I think often times whats good or bad is a matter of personal taste. Nearly every title had some flaws for my taste (the one with the least amount for me was "Blood Money"), but I always liked and recommended them.
This one is different. Although the levels are beautiful designed, the missions are diverse and the voice work is fine as always (exception below), there are some really annoying flaws that prevent me from giving a thumbs up, and, since thumb sideways is still not an option, i have to go for the negative one.
- The "always online" function is bu*****t, at least for the SP mode. I get that there are people who want to compete with others around the world and upload their personal records and create and share challenges. I am not one of them, but I‘m fine with that. These are MP functions and can be handled separately like in countless other games. But why the hell are my personal level statistics only saved as long as I play online? I played the game roughly ten hours before the first "can not connect to server" message came, so it asked me if I wanted to continue offline. So, the savegame becomes an offline one and i won‘t be able to upload my statistics for competition, fine. Don‘t care. But this is a g****mn single player game, one where my character gains experience based on my performance! That means an offline SP can not unlock more items to make new playthroughs interesting. You may start a level in online, but as soon as you switch to offline it erases all score and data you collected in this level. Thats a no-go, and don‘t tell me that it‘s a technical problem to store my level data offline or something.
- All unlocking functions of items and weapons are tied to this levelling system. So, if you want to play and gain more stuff for future playthroughs, you have to see that the server is online. If it‘s not, you‘re out of luck. Which also means that if the developer closes down sometime in the future (a thing that sadly happens from time to time) the game is gone for everybody.
- Statistics are massivly reduced compared to earlier games. Just the numbers for target kills, innocent kills, being seen and time are given. No detailed listing of weapon use, cause of death, etc. Sad!
- One storytelling thing that bothers me is that no matter where you eavesdrop, be it on servants in Bangkok, streetfolk in Italy, Marrakesh or Paris they all talk in perfect american or british english.
Why? They used native speakers in the previous games. I get that you need to understand the dialogues. Make 47 understand every language and give subtitles! This game is already over the top, but the exotic flair is part of the charme. If everyone sounds the same (and they use just a handful of actors that don‘t use any variation in their voices), it becomes dull.
- Some mission clue was misleading and made me search about 3 hours for a person at a specific place ("dongle" in Sapienza), not giving me a clue to realize that this person had already left. A case of very bad mission design.
- The inventory system is worse than in previous games. You basically have a scroll wheel you have to open and scroll through for every single item (even lockpicks are not automatic anymore). No quick slots, no "next item" key, nothing. Very impractical.
In conlusion I have to say it‘s not a bad game per se.
It is actually quite good. But compared to the previous hitman games and their high standard, for me it is clearly a step down in quality.

20XX looks like Mega Man, and  also impressively feels like Mega Man with its tight controls, but there are some rough edges that I would like to see get smoothed as Batterystaple Games’ project transitions from Early Access to full release. Nina and Ace only have two “alternate” main weapons, and one for each is ridiculously rare. Ace’s range-reducing, but theoretically more powerful, multi-slash feels more like a nerf than a buff. Thematically, the differences between Nina and Ace are limited to gun vs “knife”; in arguably my favorite MMX game, MMX4 (You can’t make  me pick just ONE, okay!), X reflects the classic Mega Man character with special powers based upon defeated enemies manifesting themselves as projectiles, in addition to my favorite feature of MMX, hidden upgrades; Zero, on the other hand, gains Street Fighter-style powers, including a “Dragon Punch”-style flame sword, an ice stalactite “spike” move, or a somersault slash. Ace gains none of these things, and his powers beyond his basic attacks are identical to Nina’s. I would like to see more variance.
Another flaw to 20XX is its randomization algorithm. I have unlocked many things after several deaths, but I encounter the same upgrades over and over in a single run. To play with the more fun stuff that requires large sums of soul nuts, I have to start a “casual” run and select three of my powerups as defaults. It is one thing to be difficult, and normal mode is no more challenging than casual besides gaining three powerups to start; if I don’t care about leaderboards and just want to enjoy the game, why would I ever select a mode beyond casual? “Skulls” add objectives to runs, but I would currently not bother to attempt them until I felt confident that good powerups would spawn.
Overall, I think 20XX has the potential to be an adequate proxy for a licensed Mega Man game. We shall see in the near future if it will be remembered as flattery or artifice.

It's Mega Man for 2015 and beyond. Take everything you enjoyed from Mega Man Classic (tight controls, difficult bosses, variety of bosses/level design) and mix it with Mega Man X (expansive open level design, fast platforming, great animations for enemies, more overall mobility of characters). It's fast paced, fun, and still requires the skill of the original Mega Man series to succeed.
Levels are procedurally generated so in theory theres an infinite number of ways to start a run in 20XX and you also have daily/weekly challenges in two difficulties (normal/hardcore). Pair that with the skulls (basically each skull increases difficulty in some crazy way like "no powerups" "enemies require 2x damage" etc) and you can challenge yourself in a variety of ways.
There are two playable characters: one that's like X and another that has a sword weapon. DID I MENTION YOU CAN PLAY CO-OP? Cause you can...and it's awesome.
Seriously, stop reading. If you like Mega Man X or Classic, just go. Buy the game.

I've been an early supporter of 20XX (previously Echoes of Eridu) and each new transition the game makes has been towards a better end. The art style is striking and distinct, the music addictive and catchy, the controls have always been very tight which makes the platforming and combat really shine. The playstyle distinction between Nina and Ace is very well established and makes for two solid experiences. The co-op is a very welcome addition as well, distinctly adding to the experience without bogging down the core game.
Over all this is a game I love seeing grow. The devs are incredibly friendly, have been hugely open to feedback and are making something you can tell they love. They're awesome with communication, and the title screen even displays planned drop times for updates. This is a game that definitely does Early Access right, and you won't spend days wondering "What did my money go to, anyway?" - this coming from someone who backed it on kickstarter ;)
I would very much recommend this game to anyone with a love of Mega Man, specifically the X series; the obvious inspiration is used tastefully, and feels like an appropriate ode to the things that made the X series fun to play. If you're weird and have never played Mega Man X, then I'd say if you like faster paced platformers, you'll enjoy this as well.

I've known absolutely nothing about this game until a few days ago when my friend--who had been following the game's development--told me to check it out.  I had nothing but her word to go off of, and boy am I glad I gave this game a shot.  Going in, the first thing you'll notice is that this game is hilariously cute.  But the deeper you fall down the rabbit hole, the more you realize how much this game has to offer. It has a lot of charm and a lot of heart, especially seeing how it mostly comes from only two indie developers, and the soundtrack is very engrossing (I'd recommend getting the ultimate edition if you've got the money for it).  The puzzles can be very tricky at times, but they're never too overwhelming--especially since you have an in-game guide that can toss you hints if you're stuck.
The game has quite a few bugs here and there, but there are save spots all over the place and it literally takes a second to save, so as long you don't forget to pop into one, you should never lose more than a couple minutes' progress from a crash.  The devs have been VERY involved with taking feedback from players and are actively seeking out bugs to fix for their next update, and it just goes to show how much they care about the game and their fans.
All in all the game will take up about 13 hours on your first playthrough, many more if you're a completionist or want to give one of the higher difficulties a shot.  Between the cute characters, beautiful scenery, enchanting soundtrack, and fascinating story, I'd say this is definitely worth a buy.

I think there hasn't been another military shooter that subverts the genre as it progresses in this way. The way The Line flopped money-wise might've also made sure none like it are ever going to show up either.
The soundtrack is GREAT: old-fashioned rock and roll aplenty. The Black Angels, Mogwai, stuff that sounds like Vietnam protest rock. The voice work is also great: there's Paul "Colonel Campbell" Eiding, Bruce Boxleitner, Jake Busey as the most messed-up radio jockey you've heard and groan yes, there's also Nolan "grouchyvoicing every game" North. Okay, so the thing is – The Line is surreal, it's got a flawless art direction and the game's just honestly good, but the caveat is that you have to give it some leeway especially if you can't take shooters or slow burn. You'll get bored with what it's doing if shooters aren't your thing.

The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these issues, to realise that they’re not just scarring- they say something deep about WAR. As a consequence people who dislike Spec Ops truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn’t appreciate, for instance, the humour in the white phosphorus scene, which itself is a cryptic reference to COD style on rails segments. I’m smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Yager's genius wit unfolds itself on their computer monitors. What fools.. how I pity them. :joy:
And yes, by the way, i DO have a spec ops tattoo. And no, you cannot see it. It’s for the operators’ eyes only- and even then they have to demonstrate that they’re within 5 mental problems of my own (preferably lower) beforehand. Nothin personnel kid :sunglasses:

I would give it a solid 9/10 overall, but keep reading if you want more in-depth explanations and ratings on stuff.
~
~
Borderlands 2, if you haven't heard of it already, is a first-person shooter with a story that'll give some headache-inducing laughs at some parts, and some gut-wrenching feels at others. There's plenty of backstory for each character and enough lore about the areas that you could keep digging for a handful of hours past completion of the game, if you went straight for the end. If sidequests are your thing, you're in luck, because Borderlands 2 has quite a few.
~
~
I enjoyed the story, but it wasn't much that popped out to me. There were certainly some twists and turns, and it had good writing, but it didn't really grasp me like some other games have. Due to this being an FPS where running around shooting s*** constantly will progress the game, I don't feel like this affected the game too terribly much.
The characters themselves are pretty good and have a decent chunk of depth and backstory. The only character that I have an issue with is Tiny Tina. As fun as Tina is, they made her come on a little strong when you first meet her, but she's pretty cool and funny in her DLC.
7/10 for the story.
~
~
Since this is an FPS, and a lengthy story-based one at that, I feel inclined to speak a bit about the gunplay.
If you're looking for traditional guns that shoot normal bullets and put holes in stuff, you're gonna be slightly disappointed. A lot of the guns in the game have modifiers that make them burst fire when zoomed in, or alter the accuracy as you fire the gun in succession more.
If you're looking for guns that have unique twists on nearly all of them, you'll love Borderlands 2. Almost everything has some sort of modifier. From burst fire on your sniper rifles, to faster fire rate as you shoot more. Being able to electrocute, set people on fire, corrode them, or cover them in slag, an element in the game that makes it so anything covered in it takes more damage, or mutates it in some way.
I personally like the gunplay, since it's so varied and fresh when you get a new gun that fits nicely in your loadout.
9/10 for the gunplay.
~
~
Apart from gunplay, there is a lot of stuff in between all of it, including movement, driving, and some others.
As for movement, it felt pretty nice. Nothing really clunky, and it was pretty smooth overall. I will note that the world clips (where you can stand) and the models (what you can see) don't match up perfectly in some areas, but the world is pretty freakin' big, so I can let that slide for the most part.
7/10 for the movement
Driving is not a favorite here. You use forward and backward like any other driving game, but you turn the car with your camera. I personally don't think that was the best move here, since the terrain is best navigated with some more precision controls than your camera. This didn't really affect me much though, since driving isn't a massive part of the game. It's mostly a means of transportation between one area to another.
4/10 for the driving
Menu navigation wasn't the best I've seen, but it wasn't the worst thing I've seen either. I'm very indifferent about the menus. They look good, and I like the idea of the panels switching out between skill trees or your inventory and your current loadout. I like the visuals, not so much the actual navigation.
6/10 for the menu navigation
~
~
The in-game soundtrack is fantastic. It brings a great fighting vibe when you're in the midst of battle, and it also fits very well when you're between fights out in the wasteland. I don't really have much else to say about it other than that it's very broad and goes very very well with the different areas of the game.
10/10 for the music
~
~
I always have to consider the achievements in a game to see if it's worth going for 100%. Borderlands 2 is not a game I'd be willing to 100% right now due to the fact that a decent portion of the game's achievements are locked behind DLC, and I'm not willing to dish out the money for DLC that I don't really want to play just for the achievements. Apart from the DLC wall, the achievements are pretty fair, and you would get a lot of them on a single playthrough, even though some may take a bit of extra effort and searching to get.
6/10 for the achievements

Pretty, easy, boring platformer.
Positives:
Wonderful artwork, both aesthetically and technically very well done.
Negatives:
Boring autotargeted combat.  You have no control over your abilities (other than stomp), you just mash X to damage enemies.  Why even have combat if all that's required is pressing one button?
Repetitive platforming challenges.  Avoid enemies and spikes, use their projectiles to gain height, double jump to platform.  Then do this over, and over, and over.
No bosses, just "escape sequences" which are at least semi-challenging, but are just a faster version of the same platforming stuff you do in the rest of the game.
Minimal exploration.  Everything is mapped out for you so there's no sense of exploration, just following the map to the next story beat.
A year or two ago I would have given this a thumbs up, but too many much better platformers have come out in the meantime.  I'm hoping for the sequel the devs spend as much time on the gameplay as they did this time around on the visuals.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a very good game. The gameplay is fun and challenging, the visuals are stunning, the music is amazing, and the story is good. I'm reluctant to throw around the word "masterpiece", because it holds so much meaning to me. Still, this game came pretty close in achieving that title.
I think this game would really benefit from a fixed difficulty, like the game Hollow Knight has. I think it would rule out any and all complaints about inconsistent and unbalanced difficulty. While I understand that a consistently hard game would not draw as big of an audience, I'd still love to see it.

I have gotten so much play out of Prison Architect since buying it. I was on the fence about buying it for a long time because I wasn't really connecting the graphic look I was seeing to a semi-serious game, and was kind of worried it would be too Roller Coaster Tycoon cutesy (which is GREAT for that setting but would be out of place here). But as a game it actually works pretty well and it's amazing how into it you can get watching your prison run. It's a really fascinating game that manages to be fun but also give the smallest odd insight into prison life. There's a good variety of settings. The escape mode is a laugh too, though I think it's better in a downloaded prison by someone else than using your own because you know your own prison's weaknesses TOO well.

There have been times I've found certain control elements slightly frustrating, or wondered "why is this happening", but there is basically always a logical explanation that makes sense once you find it. It's just that Prison Architect doesn't hold your hand as much as we've all become accustomed to in the last 15 years of mostly challenge-less gaming. Pretty much everything has a logical explanation, it's just not a game with flashing arrows saying WIN BUTTON HERE STUPID.

Also, it's nice to see a game that was actually in Early Access at one point that (1) wasn't a blatant scam or (2) was bought by 14 people and a dog in the Ukraine that has been abandonware for 14 months. A real, honest to goodness development success story that is still getting updates.
I've enjoyed games in the past like SimCity, Civilization, Tropico 4, Roller Coaster Tycoon 1 & 2, and I think if that's anywhere in your wheelhouse you really can get a lot out of this game. It's a unique setting executed well, and one of those games you'll go "well this is okay" then look up and realize it's 5 hours later.

You may not have heard of Introversion’s prison sim, but only if you yourself have been in prison for the past half a decade. It is a game in which you lay down a prison piece by piece, from the armory and the cells, to the toilets in the cells, to the pipes that connect the toilets to the sewer, and so on. It plays a little bit like traditional management games and a little bit like PC gaming legend Dwarf Fortress. Thankfully, the creators have forgone the ASCII horror of the latter and given it a cutesy comic book art style. This sometimes clashes with the strangely serious tone of the introductory chapters, which see you execute a prisoner on death row by electric chair. These opening “missions” are called a campaign but they are more of a tutorial, easing you in and letting you play around with optional tasks at the close of each level.
And if ever a game needed a tutorial, it’s this. PA in its final form is complex, refreshing and sometimes frustrating. It will take you hours to get to a state of semi-comprehension and days to fully understand every little cog of the machine. In fact, I still can’t brave the use of logic switches or pressure plates, which can be used to micromanage every tiny movement of your prisoners and staff. I have just about got my head around installing a viable back-up generator and plumbing system, for when my primary power centre explodes and several janitors burn to death (this has happened twice).
That brings us to the core of what makes Prison Architect so appealing. Things can and do go wrong. A recently added events system throws disasters at you while you build. So you may be in the middle of scheduling a drugs programme to relieve addicts of their dependencies when suddenly the mayor calls you and tells you that a news story has broken about visitors smuggling heroin into a nearby prison, and we can’t be seen to be complacent. Shut down your visitation rooms or face fines, he will say. And you will look at your prisoners, trapped in their cells, shouting about their families, and wince.
Sometimes multiple things will go wrong at once. A fire broke out in the central power hub of my facility, knocking out both water and power to the maximum security wing. It was 2am in the morning and the firefighters I called in worked through the night to douse the flames. But at the same time, the mayor called me and told me casually that I was to remove all the weights benches from the prison because of public pressure. In my mind, I threw the phone to one side and thought: “I will do that later, for God’s sake, we are on fire here.” But as the dawn broke, power and water had still not been restored to the maximum security wing. The kitchen staff were unable to cook breakfast and as the prisoners woke up and roamed from the showers to the canteen, all they found were empty serving trays. The riot began almost at once. Five chefs were murdered.

This game is much better than it should rationaly be. And that's saying something about the tremendous depth that it has.
On the surface, it's a simple turn-based one vs all on a grid (sort of like fox board games). All positions have their basic ability (hammer, teleport, heal and a few others) that slowly level up as more enemies get killed on this position. I'm not sure if this upgrade system is its main draw (choosing which upgrade to get is hard, but in an interesting way), or the looming death at almost every turn. You see, you only have two lives. Get hit twice without healing inbetween, and it's game over. And you can push enemies off the board, but some can do this to you as well. So all the game comes down to is "how do I avoid getting in a situation where I'll die?". Weighing offense versus defence, ease of movement around the board versus weapons is a pretty complex task that really outweighs the simplicity of what is really ON the board.
Perhaps equally interesting is what this game DOESN'T do/have. There's no music, only minimal sounds and visuals, no options or tutorials (okay: you can always check what tiles or enemies will do) and no other gameplay modes than the main one. There's no gamepad or keyboard support, and perhaps most surprising for a game with these credentials: no mobile version (seriously: this game would be awesome on android or iOS). So for the designers out there: it's games like this that prove that if your main mechanics are strong enough, you don't even need those things that are taken for granted in almost all video games.
I got this game from a friend (so for free), but it's easily worth the asking price (to the point where I'd be hard pressed to find something as good for 5 bucks). So...an easy thumbs up. :-)

Morphblade is one of those games that straddles the line between "casual" and "strategy": you can play through a quick game when you have five minutes of free time and you're not feeling particularly thoughtful; or you can set aside a few hours and try to best your high score as you try to set up the perfect combination of tiles to keep one step ahead of your enemies. It plays like some sort of calvinball-chess, each tile having its uses and drawbacks, and you need to use all of them as the insectoid enemies swarm the board and overwhelm you. I enjoy the strategic aspect as much as I enjoy its throwaway nature - if I'm not feeling particularly motivated I'll throw this on for a few minutes and play around, but when I really focus on it I'm pushing to try and get the highest score I can, working out the best combination of tiles and upgrades to keep the swarm at bay. Each new game is a learning experience.

Wow, currently my favourite game. The introduction says it is in Alpha, even pre Alpha, but they are doing beta testing. I think it is further along than many beta games I have played. Many people say it is similar to minecraft, I don't play minecraft so I wouldn't know. What I do know is that I quite often find myself playing till 2-3 am in the morning losing track of time and playing for 8 hours. While it is in alpha/beta, there are few bugs left and reporting them gets them fixed.
In reviewing this, I decided to describe the game, so you get a gist of what it is like.
So basically you start with a landing capsule on a planet and build your base up. At first you have to stay in range of your base because you need oxygen and energy, the latter is not essential. You need compounds (which you mine or trade for) to build tether lines which link you to the base and provide constant oxygen and energy, the latter provided you have built energy collectors. You can upgrade your character so you can carry more oxygen and more energy. Energy is produced in 3 ways, you can mine it, you can regenerate it with your suit by building mini solar collectors or a little wind turbine, or even carry a little generator around with you in your backpack or you can build vehicles and mount solar collectors on them. Your suit stores oxygen, but you cannot produce it in there. Vehicles have constant oxygen in them it seems, but without energy in them they won't run :), they can be used to weather out storms.
So basically you mine, explore, build in this game, mining is simplistic as you find the item called compound, mine it until you have enough to make one stack and then depending on the number of stacks you need of a particular mineral, you can build firstly the extension to your base (with resin) then build the work top for example, smelter to melt minerals - raw copper into stacks of copper etc., trade centre, vehicle station, research etc.
Uou power these buildings by building additional power generator/collectors in your base, these are different from your suit, but suit versions can be used in your base initially. It takes energy to mine, and you can basicallty dig minerals out and dig further under ground into whole cave structures with minerals and find hidden items, research items, crashes space ships with techniology you can then research.
There is a multiplayer option, I have not really encountered anyone.
You can build vehicles link them together so you have more space to carry things, build upgradews, cranes, winches, build additional storage, power etc.
So you build the main base, then you find the research for say, rover, truck, shuttle, spaceships :p Yes you can use a shuttle to land elsewhere start a second base, or you can find the research for a spaceship and build on a new planet.
So far things that have killed me, storms throwing rocks at me, poison underground, and falling off a cliff into an area underground.
No monsters thankfully, I hope they don't add any, Ossiris New Dawn is a similar game thopugh more realistic graphics it has monsters. this game uses anime style graphics, beautiful tundras, vibrant colours etc.
Pros - Explore, mine, research, build, craft, grow more advanced tech, use vehicles, build shuttles and ultimately a sapce ship, vibrant colours, beautiful landscapes, very impressed, price seems really low, I think once this game is finished price could double.
Cons - Ok so it is in Alpha/Beta atm and there are some bugs and they fixing them as well as adding new content, so my main gripes atm are to do with pregame bugs they will fix. If you build too many vehicles, it slows your game down, if you build too many tether lines same thing (though they have fixed that now, former is still a problem), you cannot presently unbuild something, so if you build too many vehicles and it slows game down then you prolly need to go back to an older save. There is less control over saves, I think it would be nice instead of just saving when you get in a vehicle or on a spaceship/base to be able to save with descriptive saves, so it is then possible to over save your good game with a laggy game.
Awesome Game though, playing this while waiting for Mass Effect 4, dig the whole exploration theme, build craft etc. :)
