While it lacks a lot of the polish from the previous games (especially Arkham City) Arkham Origins is very much an enjoyable game if you don't expect it to be what City was. Actually, the game did the mistake of trying to be another Arkham City, attempting to replicate open world aspects while failing to make them as enjoyable as they were.
Another thing that you surely heard about not being exactly on-point is the combat. It is not that is just bad, because the system is too good for that, but for all the nice new enemies that add additional variety, you will have a good few situations where the goons attack nonsensically fast or from too big distance, making you take hits you didn't expect.
The added system of challenges is hit-or-miss: often overly restrictive in where you can complete them, in some cases absolutely ridiculous with requirements (especially the combat-focused Shadow Vigilante tree, with a huge contribution of those unpolished elements that make you fail when you shouldn't).
So, why would I recommend it? Firstly, it is the good old Arkham formula, that works like a charm, especially thanks to a few new things thrown in (the enemies, a little bit of new gadgets, moves and upgrades).
Secondly, and most importantly, while the game feels a bit lacking as an open-world experience, it has possibly better direction of the story than any of the previous ones.
While it is true that Black Mask's potential was kind of wasted, bringing in Joker was, actually, mandatory. Arkham universe is very much about the dynamic between Batman and the Joker, and this one, as aprequel, was on a mission to establish this dynamic, which it did brilliantly! There is a lot of more and less subtle references to The Killing Joke, tying the actual canon with the one present in games.This is also very much a theme with everything that is done in the game: you will meet some more obscure character, have backgrounds of other finally used. Like Bane who has his origins acknowledged as well as sees motiffs from Knigthfall brought in. Which are then tied nicely to allow the very shallow approach to the character in the later timeline to be excused. There is a lot of little gems like that, and it is the story and usage of the universe that shines through here - a big achievement, considering the fact that Arkham City already did a very good job of it. But Origins beats it story-wise, taking you onto a nerdy ride that is sure to leave an impression, and will surprise you when it suddenly ends.
Because it makes one wish there was even more.

If you haven't played Spec Ops yet and know nothing about it, stop reading this review, buy it, play it when you have a day to spend.
Already heard some stuff about it?  Alright, the rest of this review is for you.
Spec Ops is a game where if you've heard about it, the cat is already out of the bag; it has an amazing story.  This is accurate, I went in expecting an excellent story, and I was still blown away.  It's not a long game (6 hours give or take), so you're not going to spend evenings falling in love with the characters like your favorite RPG, but it will be an intense ride that doesn't let up from beginning to end.  The story gives you no downtime in quality.  There is always something to take in.  If you should play this, it is for the story.
To elaborate on the above, the gameplay is average.  Very, very average.  Play on the normal difficulty setting, as any higher might take away from the cinematic experience.  The checkpoints aren't incredibly common, and the controls are far from perfect.  It's fine to play, and you won't get sick of the combat before you reach the end, but you won't be bragging about the basic combat by the time you finish.
Just play it.  I had high expectations of its story and I wasn't let down at any point.

I don't know where to start on Ori and the Blind Forest. Looking character-wise, Ori is one of the best in all of gaming. Ori symbolizes innocence and purity, along with being one of the most adorable characters of all time. I love this character to the bottom of my heart. The game itself is very good.  It's a procedurally generated arcade roguelike ala Rogue Legacy, where you use bling picked up during runs to unlock weapons/powers for future attempts.  You choose which stage/boss order to tackle Megaman Style.  You can take their powers after defeating them.
There's a melee character with unique weapons and movesets (huge plus for me) and a traditional Megaman shooter who can charge projectiles.
Controls are responsive and fun, moreso than Megaman itself.  You can chain wall jumps, dash, and do dash jumps.  You have a lot of air control with no momentum applied, so the movement feels responsive.  Jump height is controlled by how long you hold the jump button.  Everything is rebindable, even if you're playing with a controller.
There's also online coop and Spelunky daily challenges if you like to compete.

This is a
game... to pass the time. The concept is interesting, and it is implemented in a fun and easy to understand way. Gameplay feels very diverse, yet it still maintains balance. All in all it feels very well thought out.
That being said there are still a few areas I think this game lacks in. The main thing being replayability. There is only one game mode. In this game mode, you start off with a map/grid of sorts, and you complete waves. After completing a wave you unlock "tiles" from the map. There are different types of tiles, each of which do different things and interact with other tiles in different ways. When unlocked you have somewhat of a choice of which tiles go where.
Having such a range of different tiles that interact and do different things, and having the ability to choose which tile goes where is what gives this game such a diverse feeling. But after a certain wave, all the tiles are chosen, and that diversity slowly becomes a mundane and methodical "survival" game (albeit there are enemies that can destroy tiles which adds another level of depth to the game).
But there could be other game modes that add a level of replayability. A timed mode where you have a certain amount of time to get to the furthest wave possible. Or you have to reach a certain wave as fast as you can. And your scores are put up against other players. Or a gamemode where the tiles and enemies for each wave is predetermined and you have to find a way to survive, bringning out more of a puzzle-esque feel. Or some form of multiplayer gamemode. Even achievements or playercards would give it some sort of replayability.
But as it stands now, there is nothing about this games that shouts for me to come back and play it again, unless I have nothing else to do and am just biding my time with something else. Don't get me wrong, I do feel as though I got my money's worth so I will recommend it, but that doesn't mean this game couldn't be better.

I have gotten so much play out of Prison Architect since buying it. I was on the fence about buying it for a long time because I wasn't really connecting the graphic look I was seeing to a semi-serious game, and was kind of worried it would be too Roller Coaster Tycoon cutesy (which is GREAT for that setting but would be out of place here). But as a game it actually works pretty well and it's amazing how into it you can get watching your prison run. It's a really fascinating game that manages to be fun but also give the smallest odd insight into prison life. There's a good variety of settings. The escape mode is a laugh too, though I think it's better in a downloaded prison by someone else than using your own because you know your own prison's weaknesses TOO well.

There have been times I've found certain control elements slightly frustrating, or wondered "why is this happening", but there is basically always a logical explanation that makes sense once you find it. It's just that Prison Architect doesn't hold your hand as much as we've all become accustomed to in the last 15 years of mostly challenge-less gaming. Pretty much everything has a logical explanation, it's just not a game with flashing arrows saying WIN BUTTON HERE STUPID.

Also, it's nice to see a game that was actually in Early Access at one point that (1) wasn't a blatant scam or (2) was bought by 14 people and a dog in the Ukraine that has been abandonware for 14 months. A real, honest to goodness development success story that is still getting updates.
I've enjoyed games in the past like SimCity, Civilization, Tropico 4, Roller Coaster Tycoon 1 & 2, and I think if that's anywhere in your wheelhouse you really can get a lot out of this game. It's a unique setting executed well, and one of those games you'll go "well this is okay" then look up and realize it's 5 hours later.

This is Escape Mode, just one of the features added to Prison Architect [official site] for its final release. After four years in development and alpha the game is finally out. Is prison the absolute LOL sesh it is made out to be in popular television show Orange is the New Black? Or is it more like the Midnight Express? Come with me, into this dark corner of the holding cell, to find out Wot I Think. Please mind the vomit.
You may not have heard of Introversion’s prison sim, but only if you yourself have been in prison for the past half a decade. It is a game in which you lay down a prison piece by piece, from the armory and the cells, to the toilets in the cells, to the pipes that connect the toilets to the sewer, and so on. It plays a little bit like traditional management games and a little bit like PC gaming legend Dwarf Fortress. Thankfully, the creators have forgone the ASCII horror of the latter and given it a cutesy comic book art style. This sometimes clashes with the strangely serious tone of the introductory chapters, which see you execute a prisoner on death row by electric chair. These opening “missions” are called a campaign but they are more of a tutorial, easing you in and letting you play around with optional tasks at the close of each level.
And if ever a game needed a tutorial, it’s this. PA in its final form is complex, refreshing and sometimes frustrating. It will take you hours to get to a state of semi-comprehension and days to fully understand every little cog of the machine. In fact, I still can’t brave the use of logic switches or pressure plates, which can be used to micromanage every tiny movement of your prisoners and staff. I have just about got my head around installing a viable back-up generator and plumbing system, for when my primary power centre explodes and several janitors burn to death (this has happened twice).
That brings us to the core of what makes Prison Architect so appealing. Things can and do go wrong. A recently added events system throws disasters at you while you build. So you may be in the middle of scheduling a drugs programme to relieve addicts of their dependencies when suddenly the mayor calls you and tells you that a news story has broken about visitors smuggling heroin into a nearby prison, and we can’t be seen to be complacent. Shut down your visitation rooms or face fines, he will say. And you will look at your prisoners, trapped in their cells, shouting about their families, and wince.
Sometimes multiple things will go wrong at once. A fire broke out in the central power hub of my facility, knocking out both water and power to the maximum security wing. It was 2am in the morning and the firefighters I called in worked through the night to douse the flames. But at the same time, the mayor called me and told me casually that I was to remove all the weights benches from the prison because of public pressure. In my mind, I threw the phone to one side and thought: “I will do that later, for God’s sake, we are on fire here.” But as the dawn broke, power and water had still not been restored to the maximum security wing. The kitchen staff were unable to cook breakfast and as the prisoners woke up and roamed from the showers to the canteen, all they found were empty serving trays. The riot began almost at once. Five chefs were murdered.

Wow, currently my favourite game. The introduction says it is in Alpha, even pre Alpha, but they are doing beta testing. I think it is further along than many beta games I have played. Many people say it is similar to minecraft, I don't play minecraft so I wouldn't know. What I do know is that I quite often find myself playing till 2-3 am in the morning losing track of time and playing for 8 hours. While it is in alpha/beta, there are few bugs left and reporting them gets them fixed.
In reviewing this, I decided to describe the game, so you get a gist of what it is like.
So basically you start with a landing capsule on a planet and build your base up. At first you have to stay in range of your base because you need oxygen and energy, the latter is not essential. You need compounds (which you mine or trade for) to build tether lines which link you to the base and provide constant oxygen and energy, the latter provided you have built energy collectors. You can upgrade your character so you can carry more oxygen and more energy. Energy is produced in 3 ways, you can mine it, you can regenerate it with your suit by building mini solar collectors or a little wind turbine, or even carry a little generator around with you in your backpack or you can build vehicles and mount solar collectors on them. Your suit stores oxygen, but you cannot produce it in there. Vehicles have constant oxygen in them it seems, but without energy in them they won't run :), they can be used to weather out storms.
So basically you mine, explore, build in this game, mining is simplistic as you find the item called compound, mine it until you have enough to make one stack and then depending on the number of stacks you need of a particular mineral, you can build firstly the extension to your base (with resin) then build the work top for example, smelter to melt minerals - raw copper into stacks of copper etc., trade centre, vehicle station, research etc.
Uou power these buildings by building additional power generator/collectors in your base, these are different from your suit, but suit versions can be used in your base initially. It takes energy to mine, and you can basicallty dig minerals out and dig further under ground into whole cave structures with minerals and find hidden items, research items, crashes space ships with techniology you can then research.
There is a multiplayer option, I have not really encountered anyone.
You can build vehicles link them together so you have more space to carry things, build upgradews, cranes, winches, build additional storage, power etc.
So you build the main base, then you find the research for say, rover, truck, shuttle, spaceships :p Yes you can use a shuttle to land elsewhere start a second base, or you can find the research for a spaceship and build on a new planet.
So far things that have killed me, storms throwing rocks at me, poison underground, and falling off a cliff into an area underground.
No monsters thankfully, I hope they don't add any, Ossiris New Dawn is a similar game thopugh more realistic graphics it has monsters. this game uses anime style graphics, beautiful tundras, vibrant colours etc.
Pros - Explore, mine, research, build, craft, grow more advanced tech, use vehicles, build shuttles and ultimately a sapce ship, vibrant colours, beautiful landscapes, very impressed, price seems really low, I think once this game is finished price could double.
Cons - Ok so it is in Alpha/Beta atm and there are some bugs and they fixing them as well as adding new content, so my main gripes atm are to do with pregame bugs they will fix. If you build too many vehicles, it slows your game down, if you build too many tether lines same thing (though they have fixed that now, former is still a problem), you cannot presently unbuild something, so if you build too many vehicles and it slows game down then you prolly need to go back to an older save. There is less control over saves, I think it would be nice instead of just saving when you get in a vehicle or on a spaceship/base to be able to save with descriptive saves, so it is then possible to over save your good game with a laggy game.
Awesome Game though, playing this while waiting for Mass Effect 4, dig the whole exploration theme, build craft etc. :)

Also well colour coded enemies in this kind of game is a stupid idea, fighting a heavy enemy that only takes damage from the light damage weapon meant for crowd control just leads to you clearing out the rest of the encounter and then wailing on it for a minute while it never touches you and it just kills the pace of combat.

The game is pretty good for the first 9 levels, but when you hit the 10th you end up fighting game mechanics instead of enemies.  Just trying to get to the tower sees the camera getting fixed at a weird angle about midway through making falling highly likely requiring you to start over.  Fighting the boss sees more issues with screwed up camera angles that leave you fighting the mechanics to even get to the crystals you need to break instead of fighting the boss or evading his attacks.
You'll also never get full completion without going back to replay earlier missions over again once you have the right tools. The game isn't broken but its problems stem from the fact that ultimately the game is supposed to be a Devil May Cry game and the game decided to change some things about the formula in the stupidest ways.
Almost everyone knows about the character redesigns and personality differences. It's obvious the personality stuff was toned down to make Donte seem more likeable but ultimately all the characters still suck. They just don't suck as much.
The first issue is no lock on targeting. Want to focus the enemy over there, well better hope the game wants to target that enemy with your gun or grappling hook because you can't control it. Want to target the big guy to keep him in your line of sight nope can't do that either. Hope the camera pans to keep him in focus or he is just going to run off screen where you can't see him.
The second issue is the color coded enemies which are by far one of the dumbest enemy types to deal with in the game. Basically red weapons kill red enemies. Blue weapons kill blue ones. Rebellion and your guns, which are your main weapons can't touch either of these enemy types, so you are forced into this weapon kills this enemy. While this is dumb the game just gets flat out stupid when it decides to put a blue enemy and a red enemy in the same room. Attacking the blue enemy? Well here comes red and oops the enemy you weren’t targeting just interrupted your combo. "Man I’m killing this red guy you say." Then suddenly the blue enemy steps in from off screen and interrupts your combo. The stupid thing is this could have been avoided by either, 1 having rebellion be able to damage both types or by 2 making the enemy not interrupt your combo. Want it to do no damage fine but don’t make my weapon bounce off just because an off screen enemy decided to step into my combo.
The last issue is the rating system as a whole. Devil May Cry is a style fighter, so why the ♥♥♥♥ is the rating system based purely on damage. What a game, I mean.... What a Game!
This beautiful game is not only amazing to look at but full of intense moments where the wrong move can result in the demise of your cute, yet cool, character.
Everything from how the vibrant and lush world that Ori lives (and dies, and dies, and dies) in, to the mesmerizing movements of the enemies, the deep and rich ~nearly aromatic~ swells of orchestral music, and of course the tight, quick, and ultra responsive feeling while controlling your main character results in a fantastic experience where you never feel cheated when you die (and die, and die, and die), instead you feel a bit of disappointment in your own hand-eye coordination. I mean, you just watched it happen: you pressed left and you went left. You let go of left a bit late, and you died. The controls are so spot on that it is so absolutely obvious that wasn't "the controller" that did you in (although I suggest you lay the blame on it if others are watching), because Ori did exactly what your fingers told it to do.... and you died (and died, and died, and died) as a result. Which just makes you want to get better at it.
Well, I did. I got better, and better.. and it's still an absolute JOY to play this game (and die, and die, and die)!
Beautifully done! I can't give this game enough praise!

I am going to preface this with the fact that I really am not a big fan of platformers in general.  I am terrible at them, I get frustrated, and generally don't enjoy them as much as other types of games.  I play mostly FPS, so this game was pretty far out of my comfort zone.
And it's now in my top 10 favorite games of all time.
I laughed, I cried, I threw my controller.  It is a masterpiece work of art that will draw you in, make you cry, and then beat the living hell out of you over and over and over again as you try to get Ori through whatever hell-hole needed to progress.
The music, the visuals, it all comes together in such a masterful way with such lovable characters that you have no choice but to be engrossed in the world.
If you are thinking of picking this game up (which you will, of course.  How could you not?), there are two things that will make your experience much more positive:
1.) Use a controller.  I played the first hour or so with a keyboard and mouse, and I am pretty sure I never would have beaten the game if I had not switched over to my 360 controller.  It made it a much more pleasant experience.
2.) If you are a casual platformer like me and want to focus on the story, I would HIGHLY advise playing it on Easy mode.  This means you'll spend more time focusing on the plot and less time dying over and over and over again.  I played on Normal and I felt the difficulty kind of took away from the story line.  By the time you had died 100 times on the same spot and you FINALLY got past whatever you were stuck on, it detracted from the magic.
Overall, I really can't sing its praises loud enough.  If you're on the fence, take a walk through the review section.  It really is all that, and is certainly the best game I have played in recent memory.

Borderlands 2 is the weirdest game to judge. It's really dependent where you are at in the game. I don't play this game anymore just because I'm not in the mood most of the time. You probably heard that this game is amazing, full of guns and hilarious characters. Negative reviews commonly share the "too Grindy" aspect and tedious and boring gameplay. Completing the game on all the vault Hunter modes with 3 classes, I think I can explain where this game shines or falls flat.
Gameplay:
The game is designed to be a FPS RPG. Using elements from both genres such as sidequests and leveling from RPGs and Aiming down sights and shooting bad guys from FPS's. You can choose from a maximum of 6 classes, each with an ability, skill tree, cosmetics, and personality. Class skill trees usually favor a certain weapon type than others and of course favor a certain play style. However, at earlier levels this doesn't matter as much. You will find pistols all the time at low levels and it kind of seems as if your class doesn't really matter. You often find yourself trading out a gun just because it has a scope while the one you had is the exact same except without a scope. This is when some people quit as they think the guns should really all feel unique and not just a scope attachment. One thing I had a problem with was that the loot system doesn't connect with the classes or leveling system. You can find class modifications that are not even for your class. This becomes quite frustrating as you cannot build what you want to build because of your luck. On your first play through, you won't mind this as much. In fact, you probably won't notice. Starting a new character is when I started to notice this.

The game starts getting really good when you're around lvl 16ish. Side quests become abundant and reward you with weapons that feel very unique in terms of their feel, attributes, and cosmetics. Your skill tree actually starts building up and this is when your character feels different. Side quests also give shields, cosmetics, grenades, and class mods to diverse the rewards and again. These are unique as well. This is when I feel the game is in its prime and this IS the Borderlands 2 experience IMO. After completing the final main mission, you can restart the story with the same character fighting higher leveled enemies with more ways to kill you, this is also really a fun experience for me but again, it may be a little to early to go down memory lane for some.

If you wish to continue your character past lvl 50 and such, it becomes a questionable experience. Enemies gradually start to become overpowered and really hard to kill without legendary gear or slag. Classes such as the assassin start falling off without a perfect build. The balancing for this is questionable and the experience is completely dependent on your class and luck. To those who want a fun single player FPS, be warned that grinding is one aspect of this game. At times it gets repetitive and that's something you have to deal with in RPGs.

The co-op experience is completely different. The classes all have roles and although there isn't multiple loot drops, the combat gameplay really improves. I ultimately recommend you to go play with some friends. The experience is easily a 10/10.
So do I recommend this game? Yes, it has an interesting art style, interesting characters, a ton of guns (not as much as they say though), and a great co-op experience. After much deliberation I finally decided to try this game out, and I can honestly say that it was a great decision. As a long time Mega Man X fan, I have dreamed for a sequel of some sort to give me that action/platformer loving that I crave. From what time I have played, this game is definitely worth the buy in the sense that it already feels like a complete game; which is rather shocking considering its in EA and has a better quality than most 'launch' titles. The developers are also extremely active and helpful, which shows a lot of promise for this game's development.
As for gameplay, this is where it truly shines. The platforming is top-notch with many challenges for veterans and newbies to the genre, while also mixing in item drops to give it that Binding of Isaac feel. No one playthrough will ever be the same, and you can choose what order you would like to fight each boss. So if you completely hate one boss, you can skip it (most of the time), but that boss will get increasingly difficult as you put him off. So in some cases its best to just get it out of the way whenever possible, or you have the choice to tackle them when you have more upgrades. As seen in the intro vid, you can play as Nina (Mega Man) with the very familiar arm-gun to shoot enemies from afar, or Ace (Zero) with a beam saber for up close and personal balls-of-steel style gameplay. Each character can get weapon drops mid-game to completely change up how they use their current weapon as well, leading to multiple styles of gameplay within each character. If that's not enough, they added a daily challenge mode and a daily hardcore mode for players to sink their teeth into should they desire an extra bit of challenge. In the Challenge mode you can try to clear the game to make rankings on leaderboards, and in the daily hardcore you are faced with 3 skulls (or special scenarios) that change the way the game is played. These each reset once a day for your daily source of Mega Man action.
Last but not least, this game has multiplayer. Granted, all of my friends are naysayers and don't believe in this game, but if you have ever wanted to play a Mega Man game with a friend this is your chance. Having played a few multiplayer games with strangers you can just jump in and murder everything with little to no communication. Gotta love mindless mayhem, cuz I do. ^_^
Overall, I'm extremely pleased with this game. In fact, there really is not much to say about it negatively aside from one thing. The level 8 Sky Temple and go F*** itself. Having cleared the game multiple times, its the biggest nightmare of the game, and lasers will haunt your dreams.
Overall in its current state, I give this game a 9.5/10. I'll change the rating as EA progresses, but the tl;dr of this review is that this is probably one of the best roguelikes  on Steam currently, and wholeheartedly worth every penny.

I think I got addicted to it the moment I saw the art. The game is great and it is only in early access. On top of that, the controls are tight, the gameplay is phenomenal and the atmosphere feels just like a new Mega Man X game.

Overall, solid effort. It scratched that long-neglected itch I had for Mega Man platforming and put its own spin on things. Can't wait to see where this game goes in full release and what the devs do next.

This game is really great. I've never been a huge fan of Mega Man, but I do enjoy the games, and I've played them all. This is basically Roguelike CooP Mega Man, and that's great. It's pacing is super fun, and the enemy, item, upgrade and level variety is really quite expansive. Most of the enemies are just amped up versions of previous, weaker enemies, but that's fine. It still adds to the game quite a lot, in my opinion.
In the game there are two playable characters, one with a gun and one with a sword. Both do similar damage, but from what I saw the DPS of the melee character is higher, which makes sense considering he has to get in closer. There are also multiple weapons for each character that you can unlock and find within the game, which is really cool. Each weapon requires a different way of playing, and they all have their ups and downs. There are also powers which cost energy that you can acquire that equally change the battlefield, like a pack of fireballs that spin around you to block shots and hurt enemies, or a minigun that does decent damage over a good range. Lots of different powers.
Something I really like is the bonus timer: It incentivizes you to complete the level quickly, but it doesn't force you at all. The reward is an extra gold chest at the end, which contains an item or upgrade. Another thing is that each and every item and upgrade I've seen is actually substantial. I've never gotten something and thought, "Well this is kinda crap." Yes, some are better than others, but there are no useless upgrades, and no incredibly op ones as far as I can tell. The game is balanced quite well.
There are no real BS enemies. Some are frustrating to fight, but once you learn the patterns of each enemy you can dispatch them fairly easily, unless the level layout kinda cheeses you a bit, but that doesn't happen often. The bosses are plentiful (I believe I fought 6, but there may be more.), and each boss plays differently. I read some other reviews where bosses are spammy and cheap, but each attack that a boss does gives you a new opportunity to attack them. As far as I saw, there are no stupid instakill moves, no invincibility moves, nothing like that.
The graphics are okay, nothing to write home about but not terrible to look at. The design of things is really good, it's just the execution leaves a tiny bit to be desired, such as assymmetrical sprites simply flipping rather than being drawn from each side. Overall it doesn't detract from the game much, and it's still nice to look at, so no big deal. The sound and music are pretty good, sort of generic but not bad at all. The music is fast and upbeat and helps to set the mood and pace of the game, which is all it really needs to do.
In the end, if you like action platformers (Mega Man), and you like roguelikes, pick this one up. Bonus for coop! Have yet to play it with a friend but I have just the person in mind.  ;)  Great game for the price and for the fact that it's in early access. I encountered absolutely zero bugs, but the random generation can be a little strange, though that's a risk you run in every roguelike.

Full disclaimer: I recieved Morphblade as a gift from my girlfriend; not that that would stop me from giving my true opinion on the game (See: my Dead by Daylight review).
Morphblade is a procedurally generated bug-killing strategy game with difficulty that gets organically more difficult as you progress, and it is beautifully complex in its simplicity.  You start out on a hexed tile (hexed as in a description of the shape of the tile, not as in it has been cursed by a supernatural being) and your attack depends on which of the six different hexes you are standing on.  Some hex types allow you to damage enemies, while others let you heal, teleport, or strip enemies of armor.  As you gain kills with weapon hexes or kill enemies on top of “support” hexes, they level up and you can grant them abilities based upon the hexes adjacent to them.  Since the board grows between rounds, prompting you to select one new, random hex before progressing, you are encouraged to think about which hex type you choose and to prioritize types of hexes in certain places.  As you are forced to choose a new hex each round, the board gradually grows larger and larger, pulling you further and further away from your upgraded hexes; this forces you to be continually strategizing and smattering different types of hexes throughout the board, rather than just relying on your one maxed-out hex in the center.

is an amazing turn-based game about unlocking different tiles and defeating waves of enemies. At first glance it looks plain, but at its core is a well-designed strategy game that can last you between roughly 5 seconds or 15 minutes (depending on how much you think about it. I usually just speed through it).
As someone who is usually short on time and needs more games that are instant launch-and-play, this game is perfect for those 15 minute windows where I can do a few runs before I need to go somewhere else.
Addictive, original, fun and great for short breaks.

★★★☆☆
is a return to form, after the ugly, linear, action/shooter thriller that was Absolution.  Aside from social challenges, for optional replay value, and a decade worth of hardware upgrades, this entry does almost nothing better than Blood Money.  Its also not as good at "stealth sandbox" as MGSV, which released a year earlier.
+ Agent 47
+ Intuition vision
+ Hide bodies, then wear their pants
+ Difficulty option makes meaningful gameplay changes
+- Exploration is largely removed, due to "opportunities", basically quest tracking
+- Weapons and disguises are no longer collectibles, instead, linear score based unlocks, earned from challenges
+- Actual mission content is very short/limited, but there is a large amount of optional replay value, provided in challenges.
+- Loadouts are back, but not as good as Blood Money's.  With no currency system to reward you for playing well, and no equipment upgrades
+- Graphics look good, and run decently, but only ~30 FPS in large crowds on a 970, with vsync issues, and the game has hard crashed several times
+- Disguises somewhat work again, with only a handful of enemies who can spot you.  Less "hide in plain sight" than Blood Money, since you can too often be spotted in disguise.  This should simply be handled by getting too close to somebody in the same outfit.
- Clunky doors
- No FPS view mode
- No multi-takedowns
- Too much trial & error
- Poorly integrated "Demo"
- 47 never wears his iconic suit
- "Bonus" mission, that costs full price?
- Can't enable HDR, does it require DX12?
- Minimap should show trespassing zones
- Some challenges don't have descriptions?
- Always-online DRM, in a singleplayer game
- The episodic release of this game was idiotic
- Story barely exists, and then ends on a cliff hanger??
- Locations aren't as good as Blood Money, though much larger
- Shooting mechanics are rubbish, probably to encourage stealth
- Graphic settings seem to have almost no impact on quality or performance
- Clunky, near useless cover system, where you slide around corners into view
- The setup of the tutorial is a bit ridiculous.  Actors?  That you murder?  Fake murder?
- Map layouts, item locations, NPC locations and routines, are always exactly the same
- Escalations are incredibly lame content padding.  Expecting you to run the exact same scenario, 5 times in a row, with a stacking tweak to difficulty each time (like more cameras or targets)
- Button hold, instead of press, often required for actions.  Theoretically, this is used to fix
overlapping interactions, but it doesn't even accomplish that, and just makes all interactions clunky.
- Challenges are too often best completed by quickloading.  Too many require you to start in different places, exit in different places, or kill a target in different ways, forcing you to replay the level and/or quickload.  Some of them are even extra ridiculous, like:  Kill an enemy by electrocuting him, or, kill an enemy by getting his friend to electrocute him, but that second one doesn't complete the first.

Wuppo's a very free-roamy game with cutesy art along with a very easygoing soundtrack. There are a variety of bosses and challenges packed inside the game waiting for you to face them.

The enemies in the game aren't repetitive, and all the boss fights are pretty unique. You can tell the developers put a lot of hard work into this game.
You also have an insanely large inventory, so you'll most likely never run out of room during your adventures. With that, there are a good handful of hats to collect in the game to customize your character whenever you please.
The game's overall smooth controls make it very nice to move around in. (I often found myself jumping all over the place whenever I got the chance because it was honestly really satisfying seeing a little blob do sick backflips).
The game also pays attention to small details such as kicking rocks around as you walk past them, knocking over dishes if you jump around them, etc, so that's kind of a big deal.
One of my favorite parts of the game is Wonder Splenk. Its literally a theme park. You don't need to go there to progress through the story, however, there's no reason to pass it up. At Wonder Splenk, you can go on rides, get your fortune told, and play mini games. Be careful though; venture too far out into the sea and you'll be greeted by.. well, that's for you to find out. Do you like zany worlds, platforming while you puzzle, giant bosses
? Well, you might like Wuppo.
Full disclosure; I have been given a key before the time of writing this review. However I can confidently say I've enjoyed my time with the game thusfar. What starts off as a silly plot about a Wum dirtying a hallway, quickly throws you into a world and quest bigger than yourself. A very charming world, I might add. From the angry desk manager Carlos to elevator boy to loudmouthed Denksnavel, the first minutes set a great atmosphere. Don't let it's cartoony silliness fool you, however, when it comes to the gameplay. Wuppo asks you to pay attention and a lot of it.
Exploration is a big part of Wuppo and it rarely outright states where you have to go next. It's story is a puzzle as much as individual sequences and boss fights can be. Wuppo has little intention of holding your hand and it will let you know. Early, frustratingly and brutally. Fortunately there are save points a plenty and the reward of solving a puzzle, beating a platforming section or wooping some boss♥♥♥♥♥is all very satisfying. Don't get discouraged by some of the harder or more hidden bits, it pays off in the end.
What I liked most about Wuppo is how it marries it's world and gameplay with it's overlapping atmosphere. There's a boss somewhere midway that the further down you get his health, the more you feel like bullying him than vice versa. There's a boss whose projectiles you have to get hit by just to survive, instilling a feeling of desperation. There's a part in the game that tells you to
. It's filled with characters going about their lives, whose actions are just as important to the world as yours and individual NPCs their decisions are reflected in map and level design. All of this makes Wuppo, even with it's silly exterior, feel like a strongly immersive game. Just... Be ready to work for some of that experience.
Overall, if you like puzzle-platforming, possess the power of observation and enjoy a zany sense of humour, I think you'll enjoy getting lost in the world of Wuppo.

I acquired this game as part of the March 2017 Humble Monthly Bundle. Anyway, it's highly addicting. I had to learn that the tile options change after each wave, so if a tile is offering an arrow and you want that tile to be a heal, you just survive the wave and see if the next offering is a heal. I like to make super tiles, where it has one of each all around it. Then when it upgrades multiple times, it "inherets" qualities of the tiles around it. Eventually I can kill anything I teleport to from it, or anything that tries to attack me on that tile dies, etc. It will have several qualities besides it's own. I've played this game for 9 hours in the past few days. Definitely worth the $5 they are asking. No, I wouldn't wait to find it in another bundle. That's months you could be missing out! Maybe you have a friend who gets the Humble Monthly Bundle but doesn't claim all of the games? It's worth asking around. My best so far is surviving 25 waves. They said that is "Very Good". I look forward to making it even farther on a larger grid.
Hint: There are explosive bugs sometimes, and whatever tile you destroy them on destroys the tile. Putting an acid tile next to another acid tiles allows you to upgrade them both to neutralize explosive materials if the bug lands on that tile (if he is chasing you perhaps). Mind you, the bugs seem to take the most direct route to you (they don't avoid certain tiles) so make it chase you until it crosses over that tile. Then you won't lose any of your upgraded tiles. Another hint: Two heal tiles next to one another allows them both to be upgraded where if you cross over it, it grants you a shield and you can take 2 hits before dying instead of one. VERY USEFUL. Each game I try to quickly acquire 2 heal tiles next to one another and 2 acid tiles next to one another.
Enjoy the game to those of you who get it!!

I got this out of a humble bundle. I wouldn't buy it for 5$, but its good on sale. This is a point in click stratedgy game. You unlock hexagonal panels and kill a never ending hordes of sparning enemies that take a turn to spawn. Positioning is key. You can unlock panels that provide your ship/character "Morphblade" with different abilities when you are positioned on them. Enemies also very and strength and what is needed to kills them.

A fun little puzzle game, each game can be played through in about 5 minutes, depending on how long you think about each turn. There's an element of strategy involved, and I did get better over time. But it does have a limited shelf life before I got bored. I will go back to it after a while though!

Morphblade is a hex grid movement puzzle where you are trying to reach the the highest level of difficulty in the game. You are a bug killer and the objective is to survive until the highest possible level without getting killed by bugs. If you suffer 2 damage, you die.
There are 6 different type of hexes in the game.
a. Hammer Hex - Attacks directly in front of you.
b. Acid Hex - Removes enemy armor
c. Arrow Hex - Allows you to move and kill 2 hexes away
d. Heal Hex - Heals 1 damage
e. Blade Hex - Slices enemies to your sides when you move
f. Teleport Hex - Allows you to teleport anywhere
To win the game, you try to upgrade the hexes around you by moving into them every round. After 6 moves, you can give it a new ability on top of its basic ability.
Conclusion, do try it but it might be kind of a drag after a while.

I've played APB for about 2 years. I see alot of negative review concerning the game regarding poor matchmaking, bugs, hacking and most of all the community. To be honest I could not see APB nor could I enjoy playing it the same way if it weren't for those things. You are in a game where you can make yourself look however you want. Literally I've seen people walk around gunning people with what looked like underwear with a giant brown stain and a party hat. I've seen people paint masterpieces on the sides of cars and vans alike. I've seen people put so much detail in their characters they stand out no matter what. Everyone stands out somehow. You have your own personal touch that people will recognize. Your shirt, your car, your tie, your makeup or a tattoo. The customization on this game is endless and you can even make your own MIDI songs ingame. Sure they won't be pop quality songs but how many games can do that today in the MMO field?
Matchmaking is good the way it is simply because there are people who are on a higher tier than other players and pick on the newbies. This game is brutal concerning that one detail... Its f*** or die and granted that is sad but this is not a game that will spoon feed you skills nor will it hold your hand till you can walk by yourself. You can't just click a button or two to make your problems disappear. The more you play the more you will understand that it all comes down to two things. Skill and teamwork, with an emphasis on teamwork. The hardest, toughest mother*****r can be killed with teamwork that is guaranteed. However there will be times when its all you under the spotlight vs three other people and only 30 seconds left on the clock to finish the mission... You will probably fail but sometimes you will be able to shine. Once you put such a high bar in a game the satisfaction of winning is increased ten fold.
Now regarding the community... I want everyone for just a moment to understand something. This is a game where you either pretend to be a criminal or a vigilante (neither have a problem killing pedetrians at will). Its also an FPS game with things like "lootable" money. Also let us not forget this is the internet... Do you really think everyone is gona be nice or play nice? People will insult you, they will hate you, they will bother you, hell if they could they would perma crash all your cars, steal your money and leave you without clothes. However... Every world is the same town, there are good people and there are bad people. I've met decent human being on APB who were not hell bent on defecating on your gaming experience. The community of APB in my mind is exactly how San Pedro would be if such a situation ever existed. Besides I personal find satisfaction being s**t talked by the entire opposition for 30min after I win the game.
To conclude this game is not for everyone and it requires a bit getting used to. If you read this review and decide to give it a shot don't worry about sucking at this game. Even after you become the proest of them all, to someone (or a few people) you will always be a "noob" ;).

It's a nice game but after you played 2-3 mission it start to get very stale and repetitive... and there is mission to Agent 47 story at all. I literally completed the whole game in 10 hours.  All you do after the mission is keep doing challenges and I see no point doing meaningless challenges...

After the mildly disapointing Absolution, Hitman is a return to form. Big open levels, many ways to assasinate your targets.
The replay value is very high with dozens of challenges on every level that aren't mandatory for the storyline, but are fun enough that you'll want to do most if not all of them.
The inventory system isn't perfect (put it somewhere easier to access than just "i", I moved mine to tab) but it's a minor hiccup in an otherwise excellent game.
I know some people are put off by episodic content, but with all the episodes available now that shouldn't be an issue. Just get them all as a collection (or wait for them on sale). Honestly there was enough content in each to justify their release as episodes, the company was under financial pressure to get the game out. But rather than rush the game entirely they chose to polish each episode and release them one a time. The extra care that went into each is reflected in the final quality of the game overall.
Each episode is huge with a lot of replay value. The complete game could have been much worse off if they had been forced to put it all out earlier.
My only major complaint is the elusive target system: this was a set of bonus contracts released as one time events. But now those events have ended and there's a big glaring button that takes up 1/4 of the main menu that says "coming soon" for an event that is now over.
From a gameplay perspective you aren't missing anything. Elusive contracts don't offer anything more than what you can get from the "contracts" system that allows players to challenge each other. There are in fact 1000's of player created challenges above and beyond the official "elusive contracts", it just would have been a nice touch had they let new players have a crack at those. This is a single player game, it's a bit annoying to have a big part of the menu taken up by a  live event system that is no longer active. There are many ways they could have handled that better, but I digress.
The reality is with the contracts system that does exist you still have access to much more gameplay beyond the storyline.
If you enjoyed hitman bloodmoney or hitman contracts, you will likely enjoy this as well.
I've played every Hitman game, and while there's still room for improvment, this is overall the best one yet.
EDIT: As of November 27th 2017 the developers have decided to cycle through the Elusive Targets again. Each player can still only do them one-time (fair enough). But this allows new players their chance (though they still have expiration dates). This is a big plus that the developers at least listen a bit to their customers. IMO I'd like to see them cycle the ET's once a year so that each year anyone buying into the game for the first time will get their chance eventually.
Very much looking forward to Season 2 expantion of the game (still in development). In the mean time the GOTY update gave us a new mini campaign, a few more escalations (which I really enjoy) and some new toys to play with while we wait on the next full season. IMO this game is good and just keeps getting better.

I recieved this product in March 2017 via the Humble Bundle Monthly. This month had a myriad of great games but Morphblade really stood out as a great game for what it was. It is a trial-by-fire style strategy/puzzle game that gives you very little guidance. There are many different strategys you can follow and the game changes every single time you play it.
I managed to figure out a way to 'break' the game using a teleporter based strategy and was able to go 'infinite,' hitting level 300 before I gave up and died on purpose, as the strategy was the same from levels 50, to 300, and had no signs of ever needing to change due to the nature of the strategy.
For a 5 dollar game, most people will get 20-50 hours out of it depending on how much you enjoy replaying a game after you've solved it. People who aren't looking for the ultimate answer will likely get more time out of it than I did.
I'm rating this game based on the enjoyment you will get based on its price, genre, style, difficulty, and replayability.
My Rating: 8/10

Do you like puzzle games? The kind of wich you keep repeating trying to improve and get a better score? Well how procedurally generated elements? Well, this game has you covered
Morphblade is a weird mix between a simplistic puzzle game and a tactical battle game, you are a "white thing" in the middle and enemies try to kill you, after each round/turn the map gets bigger and you get to decide what kind of tile will appear, depending on wich tiles make the map and how they are positioned they can get different upgrades and effects, but those only work while you are on that tile, interesting game with lots of variation and complexity considering how simple the concept initially appears to be, you can try to play it fast and prioritize combat upgrades or you could try to lay poison trap tiles everywhere, or try to get upgrades that push enemies out of the map, neat.
Good for its price, perfect at a discount.

So...Spec Ops:The Line.
Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games.In this game we enter the boots of Martin Walker,a leader of Delta Squad with simple mission to recon of Dubai,which was hit with a lot of sandstorms and now 33rd american unit tries to save the city.This will end in very bad way.I mean everyone already knows that game have big amount of shocking moments but i won't spoil them.
Game in gameplay is typical TPS.Just go to cover,kill everything,and move on.Nothing special.But we can sometimes use enviroment to eliminate some tough choke points.That is very good and i enjoyed buring my enemies under sand.
To help,we have our 2 teammates.Lugo,using a sniper rifle to kill enemies from long distance,and Adams to mow down enemies with HMG and grenades.We can point enemies which they can kill,but you better don't do that.AI is ♥♥♥♥ing braindead.If you will use attack command there are 2 options:they kill him in some way,or they will push him,get every bullet they can and bleed out.Oh,right,if your teammates will die they will bleed out and you need to save them.
How many commands we have?ONE.You can only point an enemy.Sometimes they can use flash and kill(randomly and most of the time only flash,the rest you need to do) or when 1 of them will bleed,2nd one can help him.No flanking,no cover fire,no nothing.This is next problem because all your teammates do is just camping far away behind or push forward like idiots.Don't count on them mostly.
Graphics are great.From our character slowly losing armor and clothing in VERY detailed way as we get deeper into city to beautiful views of Dubai destroyed by sandstorms.
Sound is so epic.From radioman's songs which are used in fights then simple gun sounds to even just..simple wind which calms you down as you watch destroyed Dubai.
The main point in game is morality.We have like,4 choices in game which won't matter much at the end,but they will show who you are.And ending..oh god..even if you hate this game,getting to ending is worth so much,to just see that "The Line" in title means morality line. Even menu in game means that.When you 1st time open the game,there is a flag waving around Dubai,with American anthem of course.And after beating the game flag will be ripped and destroyed with pole,and anthem will be..poorly made.
Game is typical in gameplay but the story and ending itself make a new expierience.
Oh and you can play it in COOP.And there is MP.But who cares.
9/10.You think you are a hero?

This is a loving tribute to Mega Man, and a well-crafted Rogue-Like.
Even as early access, you can tell that this game has a solid core.  Randomly generated levels, fun enemy diversity and tight controls make for an excellent platformer.  The characters are analogues for Mega Man X and Zero, and both are fun to play as.  The randomly unlocked abilities and ever increasing difficulty make for a compelling game you can keep returning to.
I definitely recommend it to anyone who has enjoyed Mega Man games or games like Rogue Legacy.
I'm a Megaman and Megaman X junkie.  This game brings the best of both worlds.  If you like fast paced classic platform I would highly recommend this game.

20XX is an extremely polished cooperative platformer with rogue-like elements that are heavily inspired by the Mega Man X series.  You will play as characters that will remind you of X and Zero with similar challenges to those you remember from old-school Mega Man games, but now the consequences of death have been granted the pardons of the rogue-like genre.  I'm thoroughly impressed at how well this indie studio has put together such a wonderful homage that is fun enough to keep your attention.  The game continues to be regularly updated and it is clear that the developers listen to community feedback and want to make an enjoyable game that people want to play.

After the mildly disapointing Absolution, Hitman is a return to form. Big open levels, many ways to assasinate your targets.
The replay value is very high with dozens of challenges on every level that aren't mandatory for the storyline, but are fun enough that you'll want to do most if not all of them.
The inventory system isn't perfect (put it somewhere easier to access than just "i", I moved mine to tab) but it's a minor hiccup in an otherwise excellent game.
I know some people are put off by episodic content, but with all the episodes available now that shouldn't be an issue. Just get them all as a collection (or wait for them on sale). Honestly there was enough content in each to justify their release as episodes, the company was under financial pressure to get the game out. But rather than rush the game entirely they chose to polish each episode and release them one a time. The extra care that went into each is reflected in the final quality of the game overall.
Each episode is huge with a lot of replay value. The complete game could have been much worse off if they had been forced to put it all out earlier.
My only major complaint is the elusive target system: this was a set of bonus contracts released as one time events. But now those events have ended and there's a big glaring button that takes up 1/4 of the main menu that says "coming soon" for an event that is now over.
From a gameplay perspective you aren't missing anything. Elusive contracts don't offer anything more than what you can get from the "contracts" system that allows players to challenge each other. There are in fact 1000's of player created challenges above and beyond the official "elusive contracts", it just would have been a nice touch had they let new players have a crack at those. This is a single player game, it's a bit annoying to have a big part of the menu taken up by a  live event system that is no longer active. There are many ways they could have handled that better, but I digress.
The reality is with the contracts system that does exist you still have access to much more gameplay beyond the storyline.
If you enjoyed hitman bloodmoney or hitman contracts, you will likely enjoy this as well.
I've played every Hitman game, and while there's still room for improvment, this is overall the best one yet.
EDIT: As of November 27th 2017 the developers have decided to cycle through the Elusive Targets again. Each player can still only do them one-time (fair enough). But this allows new players their chance (though they still have expiration dates). This is a big plus that the developers at least listen a bit to their customers. IMO I'd like to see them cycle the ET's once a year so that each year anyone buying into the game for the first time will get their chance eventually.
Very much looking forward to Season 2 expantion of the game (still in development). In the mean time the GOTY update gave us a new mini campaign, a few more escalations (which I really enjoy) and some new toys to play with while we wait on the next full season. IMO this game is good and just keeps getting better.

Don't believe the haters. This is one of the best Devil May Cry games available. The criticism against it mostly centers on Capcom's decision to transform the iconic character of Dante. I promise, it's just a cosmetic change. No, he does not look like a gothic anime villain and he does not spend his time hunting demons in medieval castles. Aside from that, he's the same Dante he's been since DMC 3. Yes, he has attitude, but it's not as over-the-top as it used to be. DMC 3 let Dante perform ridiculous stunts like using a motorcycle to pulverize demons and wielding an electric, bat-shooting guitar, all while spouting off catchphrases straight from the Ninja Turtles. While that was campy and lots of fun, DMC shoots for a different tone. This is a serious game with a Dante that is more human than action hero. He's traded his anime garb for something along the lines of urban anarchist. But the game is GOOD. The combat is nearly flawless. Controls have been streamlined, so no more cycling through different fighting styles or trying to decide which weapon to take into battle. This isn't Resident Evil with swords anymore. It's a fully-fledged brawler and it can be legitimately challenging. The storyline is also a vast improvement over previous installments. The voice acting is no longer outrageous. Dante's demons don't haunt dark dungeons anymore. They live all around him: in the media, in junk food, in human lusts and appetites. These are the Seven Deadly Sins personified and Dante embodies them as much as he wants to destroy them. There is internal and external conflict going on, all blending seamlessly with brutal and satisfying combat. Dante's hits shake the earth. His enemies wield chainsaws and katanas. Fans of Nero will be happy to find that Dante's sword now has a grappling function to pull enemies close. Does it look like a Devil May Cry game? No. But all the familiar faces are there (including Vergil, whom you can control in the DLC); Dante's attitude hasn't changed, and there's a LOT to love here. Don't let the negative reviews discourage you. This is a truly phenomenal fighting game that pays homage to its predecessors. As someone who has played the heck out of every DMC game and even suffered through the terrible anime, I can say this is a worthy reboot of the franchise. 9/10.

I got this game as part of the March Humble Bundle and for around a month is sat in my library uninstalled. Finally I put on a podcast and played it. The game involves moving around a board where each tile transforms your piece into a certain variant. Each variant has a unique ability such as healing when you transform into it or being able to kill adjacent pieces instead of simply knocking them back. Much of the game's depth comes from its upgrade system, once you kill 6 enemies from the same tile you are allowed to upgrade it into a hybrid tile which adds an ability similar to another variant. For example upgrading a hammer tile (The one that lets you kill adjacent enemies) into a venom hybrid (Venom tiles remove enemy armor when they move over it) will allow you to kill armored units. It took me about 40 minutes of playing to fully understand the game mechanics and the goal of the game is to reach a highscore by surviving against enemies which gain new abilities with every wave. This game is simple yet complex at the same time and is very fun to pass some free time.

Morphblade, a recent abstract strategy game by Tom Francis, the creator of Gun Point. It is one of the games which looks simple, but hides complexity. In this game, you control a Morphblade, and all you need to do is to try to survive as many enemy attacks as possible. In itself, the game is a bit of an experiment in simplicity, as explained here:

The game takes place on a field consisting of hexagonal tiles. The core concept is that the Morphblade's abilities depends on the tile it is staying on. There are 6 different tiles. 3 attack tiles; The hammer (shoot one tile in any direction), the blade (move one tile and attack the tiles on the side) and the arrow (move two tiles in straight line, attack all in between). And 3 modifiers: Heal (heal the blade), Teleport (move to any tile on the grid) and poison (removes armor from armored enemies).. So far, so good. The complexity is introduced as the tiles can level up and combined with neighboring tiles. A tile can be leveled up when you have used it to kill 6 bugs. So a hammer tile can be combined with a poison tile, allowing you to shoot armored enemies, or two heal tiles can be combined into a shield tile. These tiles can be further leveled up again, adding more modifiers to them depending on surrounding tiles, resulting in over 700 tile combinations.
There are 5 different bugs - the normal bugs (takes away one life on hit, moves one square), flying bug (can move two tiles), pusher bug (can't hurt you, but pushes you one tile back, can push off the board), laser bugs (can fire a laser in straight line) and the elusive black level up bug (levels up the tile it is killed on). All bugs also comes in 3 'flavors' - red bugs (normal bugs), blue bugs (have armor, can not be killed) and green bugs (explodes when killed, removing the tile it is killed on).
The game is turn-based, and it is played in increasingly difficult waves (more and different bugs). The game starts with only 2 hexagonal tiles, and between each wave you can select a new tile to place from a selection of random tiles (though you can get "wild tiles" also). It sounds more complex here than it is to play, but it is one of those games that have the "i need to get to next wave" factor. It is relentless, but the turn-based nature makes it very fair, and when you loose it is always your fault for making the wrong move.

Fun, but it can get frustrating and old; and the main plot leaves you sort of hanging.   Ignoring the online debate, I would recommend the game for people who enjoy Hitman.  You get about ten missions (main story plus bonus missions) and also something called Escalation, which are missions in the various locations that have to be executed specific ways.  While the first few escalations were fun, doing more of them is where it got old, especially when the challenges within the escaltions got ridiculous  (e.g. keep your gun out the entire time!  make one person die in an accident, another in an explosion, within 30 seconds of each other! (same esclation event)).  While I enjoyed having more non-player-made contracts to fulfil with the escalations - and there are a lot of them - after the first few I got frustrated mainly because of the limitations and because many of those limitations did not make sense.  I prefer to do things my way, which is what Hitman is all about.
Still, I do recommend the game for people who like the Hitman games.  My quibbles are more to inform future buyers - of which I hope there are future buyers - of some of the things to expect.
P.S. Because I did not purchase and play this game when it was originally out, I missed all the Elusive Contracts.  They are not a part of the game, but special content available for a short period of time for players.  I'm a little miffed about it, because more targets = more game, but I suppose that's a price you (don't) pay for waiting for the full season to be out and on sale.

NOTE: I have not touched the Zombie portion of Black Ops 2, so this review will not cover that aspect.
As things stand today, Black Ops 2 is probably the last of the universally-acknowledged "good" Call of Duty games. While there are still things wrong with it (and in my opinion, it takes steps backwards from MW3 in some aspects, i.e. sound design), it remains more balanced and accessible than its successors.
The campaign is decent and sees you shifting forwards and backwards through time, following the perspectives of multiple characters to tell a story. While the story is nothing special, it does a fairly good job at being entertaining and keeps you playing until the end.
Multiplayer however is the meat of this game. While I cannot fathom why Treyarch introduced certain things into the game (shock charges, guardians, target finders, etc. - probably to cater for the console noobs) - as a package the multiplayer in Black Ops 2 is still fantastic today. The gun variety is good (although the weapons in my opinion feel a little too arcadey, and the sound design is rubbish in comparison to the Modern Warfare series), but it is the scorestreak/pick 10 system which really shines. The ability to mix and match with perks/guns/equipment is what really seperated this game from those before it; coupled with overall fantastic map design (Raid/Standoff <3), explains why this game was so popular at the time. There is still an active player base today -  while I would suggest caution if picking this up on that basis, you will likely still get many hours of enjoyment out of your purchase.
Highly recommended to FPS fans and anyone who has enjoyed Call of Duty in the past.

The most ultimate Hitman game? Probably. As a long-term fan of the franchise, simply can't jump to a conclusion like that espcially when I haven't played all the episodes. But I will say that it justifies its title HITMAN™.
Speaking of episodes, ever since I heard that its going to be episodic, I knew its a good idea (but a controversial one obviously). Since episodic structure allows the developers to perfect each mission by giving it a quality time. The Paris level "Showstopper" is a great example of what this structure can accomplish. Its easily one of the best Hitman levels. I've spent 10+ hours diging into everything that the level has to offer and yet there's definitely more left to find and try.
This game combines all the great elements of franchise and with a creative game desgin that works perfectly for a game like this. The gameplay is true to the classic Blood Money, nothing is toned down like in Absolution. Graphics are excellent with wide range of options to tweak. But its really the Level Design that stands out in the game. A lot of possiblities of accomplishing objectives. Like an Immersive-Sim, the game presents problems rather than puzzles. I'd reccomend turning off Oppurtunity Hints or keeping it on Minimal since you want the true Hitman experience. I think they are a nice addition especially for newcommers to the franchise.

If you've played Arkham Asylum or Arkham City before this game, then you already know what kind of game you're getting into. This follows closely to Arkham City, with a big open world, emphasis on introducing a good collection of classic villains and intuitive gameplay to a degree.
Arkham Origins shows laziness in design, compared to other Arkham games, which can break the immersion. Randomly poor textures in some areas, super glitchy physics and half dodgy cutscenes break the experience. Although this game is riddled with glitches, most hilarious, this is still not a bad game. It is still so much fun beating up gangs of thugs over and over again using multiple combos and gadgets. The combat system is arguably what defines the Arkham series, and so does the predator stealth gameplay, which is very apparent in this game still. There is a lot of gadgets to unlock and use to your advantage in combat and during stealth, which each work in different ways. For instance, my tactic to sneaking up on enemies was mainly to stalk them, throw a glue grenade at them (to freeze them in their tracks) then take them out quickly. Approaching enemies can be some differently almost every time, which is what makes this game fun and interesting.
The story is somewhat straightforward, but often decides to lose focus on the main plot and tries to pay attention to some other plot it wanted to tell, but had to squeze in to the plot. Initially, it is about the Joker, duh. Batman is new to Gotham, no one trusts him and Alfred wants to have Christmas dinner with Bruce. Yeah, this is also supposed to tell the introduction to the Joker, but is done somewhat poorly. Basically,Batman has a huge bounty on his head and a number of assassins now want batman's head for the money. They include some iconoc Batman villains. In the midst of this, Black Mask led a breakout at Black gate Prison, but there is a new murderer about in Gotham who proves to be more of a threat; The Joker. For some reason, the Joker's voice actor sounds weird. He sometimes turns British, and finds it hard to keep sounding like the Joker from other Arkham games, probably because of the change in voice actors. The story is ok, but is quite short and consists mainly of 3 things. 1. Batman being angry at everything 2. Alfred pestering Bruce to ahve Christmas dinner with him 3. The Joker having a crush on Batman, pushing the other villains aside. It's hit ad miss and kinda boring, but with some cool boss fights and fun levels.
Not to mention, this game doesn't expect you to be good at games. This game is very easy. Constant control hints and frequent cutscenes make the story feel driven for you a lot of the time, with you only really having full control in the open world and in predator sections. Even side missions hold your hand. The awesome looking detective mode had so much potential to make the player puzzle together a crime scene, but is incredibly linear and boring. Some side missions are really interesting and worth doing. Hunting down Deadshot is really cool and ends with a super good predator section that ahs you dealing with him looking through reflections that you have to monitor so he doesnt spot you. The Mad Hatter sends you into a mad dream inspired by landcapes and scenarios from Alice In Wonderland. Then, the Riddler keeps you hunting down his many collectibles and solving puzzles while he taunts you and fails to prove how clever he thinks he is. While gameplay is straight forward, it is still on the same level as every other Arkham game, and is stall damn fun to play, despite the multple set backs.
There's multiplayer, but I haven't bothered with that. No one is ever online to play it with. In the end, this is a good game. It has flaws, and is mainly showing off it's great graphics, but is still a fun Batman game to play. Gotham is interesting to explore, the standard Arkham gameplay is still there and works and there is plenty to do. This is not a bad game, but it is not a great game. This is essentially Arkham City, just in Gotham and with an angrier Batman.

Ori is one of the best games released in the last twenty years. It does almost everything right. It makes you want to be involved in videogames. The fact these games rarely come along in such a package might make you think twice though.
The artstyle, despite a lot of platformers using similar aesthetics, really does separate itself from the crowd. It's gorgeous, and I mean GORGEOUS. This thing is just a beautiful representation of pure art at its most worthwhile and engaging. But you probably already know that.
Instead, we'll get to the gameplay. And they pretty much hit it out of the park here. My only complaints are some slightly jerky movements now and then when on edges, but besides that this one plays like a dream. Ori's abilities are unlocked at about the right pace for anyone to learn and lock down the mechanics in a constructive way. The game can be hard at times, so if you are not used to platformers you really need to put the game on easy.
There are indeed sequences where you cannot save, and they will test your prowess and memorization. But in the end they are very much worth it to see the fruits of your labor.
Hard mode is where this one shines. It's a joy to play. The story isn't really the best thing ever written, but it does the job in a decent way, and the overall aesthetic matched with the designs of the characters says more in motion than it needs to say anywhere else. I'd say they probably could have written a couple more interesting tidbits along the way and made the story a tad less melodramatic, but it's not a big deal.
Top notch platforming with an old school vibe refined for a new age. Visuals that will blow your mind and make you wonder why no one else got it so right. And all from a Microsoft funded studio. Holy cow.

The best way to describe rust is that it is a pure sandbox game. You can play the game anyway you like, and this will definitely change your outlook on whether or not you enjoy it. You spawn in with nothing, and are left to explore an island left in shambles, to gather resources, meet other players, or more likely get killed by them if you're not careful. You can use the materials to build a base of any caliber, whether it be for the best defense, to be a shop, or to be a simple home. If it doesn't work out like you had planned, you can try a different approach on a different server or after the next wipe.
Over my time playing the game I have learned that if you are looking for a high risk environment and enjoy actively fearing for losing all of your stuff, servers with upwards of 50 players are what you should look for, but if you're looking for a more lenient game where you can get away with being a peaceful shop keep, or anything like that, a small server with a close community would be best for you.
I have really enjoyed rust over my 350 hours playing it at the time, and it has definitely grown a lot since I started. I would definitely reccomend it.
