- F2P FPS zombie action game mixing arcade/simulation
- Survival mode (freedom: loot supplies, defend safe zones, build barricades, kill X waves, get extracted; ratings: kill-based)
- Objective mode (direction: move through levels, loot what you can along the way, try avoiding zombies, handle key items to overcome obstacles, get extracted; ratings: extraction-based).
- Satisfying gunplay and melee (sounds, animations, power). Limited inventory size. Rather scarce ammo and medical supplies spawning when map loads partly randomly, partly in fixed locations and numbers. Supply drops via chopper after each 2-3 survival waves or when called with flaregun. Running/jumping/melee drain stamina/cause fatigue (melee depending on which melee weapon you use).
- Enemies: Slow walkers, fast runners (children, adults) moving directly towards you (not always because of sub-par pathfinding), taking swings or grabbing and biting you dealing direct damage and (random chances) bleeding/infection.
- Health restorable via medikits and health crates you find and carry to pre-defined spots in your safe zones. Bleeding drains health and slows you down. Pills delay (not cure) infection. Vision of infected turns dark/blurry, they drop dead or get killed by teammates (friendly fire is enabled for them) and rise again as A.I. controlled runners (players do not control zombies at any point).
- No levels/ranks, classes, XP system/skill trees/perks or microtransactions. Every player initially stands on equal ground in every regard. No "matchmaking" - utilizes the powerful Source/Steam server browser.
- Loose background lore and vaguely crafted characters/player models/voice sets. References to George A. Romero's movies. No visible story. Objective maps do not connect into campaigns.
Compared to L4D2: Less cinematic, less enemy types (slow walkers, fast adult and children runners), less humorous and characters/models with no visible background story or progression (perhaps there are references to Romero just as with some of the maps and prompts, but I don't know these older zombie movies).
NMRiH's is basically like Zombie: Panic Source, but co-op. It's strengths are the slower-paced gameplay, the rewarding melee and the survival aspects. It has a more simulative feeling than the arcade shooter that L4D2 is (it's not a simulation either, something inbetween). Unless you get a flaregun to call in supply drops (which need to be altered by the developers, you can call in infinite ones when using the flaregun properly) you have rather few ammo and medical supplies. Melee is your best friend in this game. Guns feel strong and good, I like their sounds, the reloading animations look neat too (different to L4D2 where the gunplay felt a bit shoddy and watered down). There are no crosshairs, guns you fire from the hip to the centre or down the sights, melee always strikes to the centre as well, feels and looks pretty good (your hands and weapons get bloddy, you hear the zombie heads bursting - neat details). Zombies walk/charge at you head-on - the pathfinding isn't perfect making them run back and forth at times, or they get stuck in greater numbers in front of certain doorways. Nothing too dramatic, it's just awkward and sometimes fun to look at, you can "abuse" certain map and object arrangements to fool them a bit even. Getting hit can cause bleeding and infection. There are bandages, medikits and pills (which delay - not cure - infection), not in too many great numbers, especially newbies are asking for this a lot. You can use hammers and wooden planks to spawn planks on pre-defined door and window spots (less useful in objective mode where you always want to keep moving, more useful in survival mode when zombies gather in front of them, allowing you to kill them efficiently with pre-positioned trap systems, grenades and molotov cocktails).
Once you get a hang of the game it isn't the most difficult one. The biggest "enemies" are sometimes your teammates even, wasting ammo and supplies too early for slow walkers a halfway skilled player could easily take down with melee and shoving moves, hording stuff they don't need, throwing empty guns and unneeded supplies into the zombie horde or into corners you won't find them in again, blocking you out with badly placed planks, hitting you intentionally or unintentionally when you are infected (infection enables friendly fire on you) while you could use your remaining time to gather supplies or (in survival mode) kill more zombies in order to get a respawn token.
The usability could be better, the game is rough and raw around some edges. Some people for example don't know they can call up a compass with "c" to guide them to safe zones (which you must protect in survival mode) or to items to advance with on objective maps (keys and propane tanks to blow doors, radios to call for extraction, keycodes and so on). The radial-shaped inventory arrangement may not be the most intuitive one, but one can get used to it. Where to use keys at isn't very obvious either, or how trap systems are refueled with propane tanks and gas canisters. If you look carefully you will notice and understand, but only few newbies seem to do. Not getting everything told directly supports communicating with others, just asking and talking with your teammates, but some may even be blind and deaf to that.
Some further polishement would also include better animations (they use the walking animations from Day of Defeat, which look awkward, and barricading leaves no visible animation to other players looking at you, to them you stand still holding a hammer with planks suddenly appearing in front of you).
There are too many server owners who don't understand the game, or who don't appreciate it as it is. They are running servers with infinite ammo, a gun spawning menu, an increased respawn token gain and all other sorts of stuff to make it easier to them. It makes the game easier than it already is (on vanilla servers you will still fail a lot, not because the game is brutally difficult but because of many newbies/noobs simply giving you no real support or hindering you even). Or they have alltalk and "ghosting" (listening to dead survivors giving you hints) enabled; ghosting is not possible by default, and there are walkie talkies items that would allow you alltalk once in your inventory, otherwise people only at some distance would hear you - a neat idea by the developers, but worthless if server owners decide to force alltalk right away. Then there are server owners who have decided to let you look at and listen to advertisements first before playing. That's not the developers fault, but still: I don't think I've ever added as many servers to a blacklist as I did in NMRiH. Thankfully there is still a moderate amount of vanilla(-ish) servers around.

Borderlands 2 is the weirdest game to judge. It's really dependent where you are at in the game. I don't play this game anymore just because I'm not in the mood most of the time. You probably heard that this game is amazing, full of guns and hilarious characters. Negative reviews commonly share the "too Grindy" aspect and tedious and boring gameplay. Completing the game on all the vault Hunter modes with 3 classes, I think I can explain where this game shines or falls flat.
Gameplay:
The game is designed to be a FPS RPG. Using elements from both genres such as sidequests and leveling from RPGs and Aiming down sights and shooting bad guys from FPS's. You can choose from a maximum of 6 classes, each with an ability, skill tree, cosmetics, and personality. Class skill trees usually favor a certain weapon type than others and of course favor a certain play style. However, at earlier levels this doesn't matter as much. You will find pistols all the time at low levels and it kind of seems as if your class doesn't really matter. You often find yourself trading out a gun just because it has a scope while the one you had is the exact same except without a scope. This is when some people quit as they think the guns should really all feel unique and not just a scope attachment. One thing I had a problem with was that the loot system doesn't connect with the classes or leveling system. You can find class modifications that are not even for your class. This becomes quite frustrating as you cannot build what you want to build because of your luck. On your first play through, you won't mind this as much. In fact, you probably won't notice. Starting a new character is when I started to notice this.

The game starts getting really good when you're around lvl 16ish. Side quests become abundant and reward you with weapons that feel very unique in terms of their feel, attributes, and cosmetics. Your skill tree actually starts building up and this is when your character feels different. Side quests also give shields, cosmetics, grenades, and class mods to diverse the rewards and again. These are unique as well. This is when I feel the game is in its prime and this IS the Borderlands 2 experience IMO. After completing the final main mission, you can restart the story with the same character fighting higher leveled enemies with more ways to kill you, this is also really a fun experience for me but again, it may be a little to early to go down memory lane for some.

If you wish to continue your character past lvl 50 and such, it becomes a questionable experience. Enemies gradually start to become overpowered and really hard to kill without legendary gear or slag. Classes such as the assassin start falling off without a perfect build. The balancing for this is questionable and the experience is completely dependent on your class and luck. To those who want a fun single player FPS, be warned that grinding is one aspect of this game. At times it gets repetitive and that's something you have to deal with in RPGs.

The co-op experience is completely different. The classes all have roles and although there isn't multiple loot drops, the combat gameplay really improves. I ultimately recommend you to go play with some friends. The experience is easily a 10/10.
So do I recommend this game? Yes, it has an interesting art style, interesting characters, a ton of guns (not as much as they say though), and a great co-op experience. But if you know anything about this game at all, you know you're not playing it for the shooting (although it is fun here) but for the story. It's a really good story. It made me feel things. :(
Many of the environments are absolutely beautiful and that makes the experience even sadder. Graphics are pretty good overall, and the voice acting is top-notch.

What makes this game so special? Simply put, the shock value. But here's the catcher. The whole story arc that envelops that very shocking moment of the game makes it memorable right to the ending. This is, I think, us gamer generation's Farewell to Arms.

If you've enjoyed games such as The Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon, yet also desired a new Mega Man game, I can certainly say this game is for you. 20XX is a roguelike action platformer that's
inspired by the Mega Man franchise, specifically the Classic and X series. It was inspired so much that the first cutscene has a nod to Mega Man 2's Title Screen. In fact, lots of the things in this game give little nods or references to other game franchises, which I do appreciate.
While there are only
10 levels in the game (with five/six locations being used total), you'd think the game could get stale rather quickly. That's where you would be wrong, as the levels are randomly generated (though with some common obsticles in between runs). While not extremely varied such as the likes of the Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon, I find this rather acceptable for a game such as this. The boss order of the first eight bosses are guarenteed to be different between runs. One thing to note is that in this game, the bosses get
the later you wait to fight them; such as having more health, more attacks, etc.
Besides the usual singleplayer, you can play local or online Co-Op with a friend if you so desire and tackle the
world of 20XX together. There's also daily challenges, leaderboards, various difficulties (such as easy mode granting three lives to the player instead of the usual one), and more. You can also buy perma upgrades, unlock new ones, or start with upgrades in your next run using a currency known as "Soul Nuts". Soul Nuts are mostly gained from killing off strong enemies, which usually have double the health and deal double damage. However they vanish upon starting a new run, so spend them wisely.
The only real gripe I have with the game is that the dash is used a bit too often, and is mandatory for tons of jumps, especially in the last few levels in the game. Of course, it's not a bad thing, it's just a personal distaste of mine.
Overall, I firmly believe 20XX was worth all the time and money I invested into it, even while the game was early in development. I
recommend giving this game a shot.

I'm of the opinion that this is worthy addition to the franchise. Some hardcore fans may hate the reboot, but I think it's best to go into it with an open mind. I intentionally avoided DmC for a while because I was under the impression it would have an overly emo, whiney vibe. I probably got that idea from the Angry Joe video review (if you've seen it then you know what I'm talking about). Thankfully, it's not at all as bad as Joe's video indicates in that regard and that terrible music video from his review is nowhere to be found (yet lol).
The main gripe people seem to have is the "new" Dante, both his look and his attitude. While he doesn't sport the classic Dante look, with the blonde hair and red jacket, his look is perfectly acceptable IMO. I don't really see the emo connection, except that I personally will never opt for that hairstyle. His attitude is that of a young man that can pull hot chicks. He goes to clubs and gets laid so his somewhat cocky attitude should be of no surprise. Take it or leave it...I myself don't care one way or the other.
The strong point of any Devil May Cry game has always been the combat and DmC definately delivers in that department. It's similar to previous games in the franchise but perhaps a bit more accessable. I like the camera a lot better here, more in line with your typical 3rd person perspective. The camera doesn't rotate all over, zooming in and out dynamically, which always bugged me about the previous games.
While it doesn't have a soundtrack with classic thrash metal ala the Big 4, it has a relatively exciting soundtrack with some nice chugging heavy metal riffage going on.
TBH I haven't played this very much yet, just thought I'd drop a quick note giving my initial impressions. Like me, if you were avoiding it thinking it'd be overly emo, give it a shot, I think you'll be pleasantly surprised.

I know I only have 3 and a half hours on this game at the time of writing, but I have to be honest here... this game is absolutely amazing! It's not trying to be something it's not, it's not showing off content that you can't find in the game and it's not trying to be anything more than what has been shown or released so far.
You're on a planet with some sort of machine that can harvest and terraform the planet as you see fit. You use the resources you find to initially build your settlement, then you start using those buildings to branch out and find other resources and explore more of the planet, whether it's underneath or on solid ground.
But it does it in a way that's fun and enjoyable and exploration is gradual, you can't explore freely immediately due to your limited amount of oxygen, so you have to build and you have to progress slowly in a natural feeling way.
At the end of the day, I can say this game is amazing! And half the price of No Man's Sky, I think I know what I'd rather play.

I don't know why this game didn't get more love.
I have had this game in my library for over a year and after reading so many negative reviews I was afraid to play it thinking that it must be super bad and not worth playing. After reading some reviews I expected it to even barely be recognizable as a Batman game.  However, having liked Arkham Asylum and absolutely loving Arkham City I figured I had to give it a try, especially if I plan on trying Arkham Knight. I was expecting a dog. Maybe it was because my expectations were so low, but I really enjoyed it a lot.
Granted, it didn't add a whole lot to the gameplay of Arkham City, but it was a great story in its own and having access to many of the gadgets and abilities right from the beginning, made it that much more enjoyable. There were a lot of varied things to do and for the first time I started playing in some of the challenge modes and I enjoyed the addition of the skill challenges during regular gameplay. I loved the Combat Challenges which helped train me as I went back into the game.
It might have lacked a bit of the polish that was in Arkham City and at times combat seemed a little bit clunkier, especially when trying to do a followup attack on a downed enemy, but I really feel that if this game had come out before Arkham City, it would be getting all of the praise and Arkham City would have been looked down on. It was a solid game and it stands on its own. Some say it was more like DLC for Arkham City, but I have never gotten this much time and enjoyment out of any DLC for any game. My current hours spent on this one surpass those I spent in Arkham City.
I don't consider myself a Batman fan or even a DC fan (I always liked Marvel and Spiderman). I am, however, a great fan of these Batman games and yes, that does include Arkham Origins.  If you enjoyed Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, you have to play this one. If you found Arkham City repetetive and not so good, don't play this one.
Please, if you did like the other Batman Arkham games, you owe it to yourself to try this one. Don't be influenced by all of the naysayers. This is a great game!!

I also enjoyed seeing some of the lesser known (less mainstream) villains like Copperhead and Electricutioner, though was dissapointed with the fact that there is no actual boss fight for the latter.
Another thing that I love is the addition of the Batcave as well. This is something that I have personally wanted to see in every Arkham game, and the small cave in Asylum just doesn't come close to the one here in Origins. It;s also a nice touch to add the Batwing as a form of transport (cut scene only) as it can help you rush around the map if you need to and the cut scenes look pretty awesome too.
I personally like the story in Origins too, much more than the story from Arkham City too. I know a lot of people dislike the fact that the Joker plays a pivotal role (This being the third game where he is the lead villain) but in all honesty, I think it works very well. It shows you the transition from the mainstream real life mafia crime family type thugs (sionis/falcone) to the much more twisted super-criminal breed like Joker and Harley Quinn. I think it is very well done in introducing Batman's arch-nemesis and showing the depths of his deviousness.
The game engine itself is basically the same as Arkham City. A few of the skills on the utility belt wheel have swapped around, but that has happened in every Arkham game so isn't a major change really. They have added one or two new gadgets as well (usually collected from an assassin once you have beaten them) and that does make the gadgets seem fresher than before which is a good thing.
The Cold, Cold Heart DLC is also masterfully done and it introduces you to Mr Freeze and shows you why he is the way he is. It also allows you to see a part of Wayne Manor, and you see one or two new toys that Batman has in his arsenal. Anarky also plays a small part in this DLC as there was a quest that was removed from the main game at the last minute and so was added to the DLC as an extra. Personally I feel that this is the best DLC to date, and whilst it can be completed in a matter of hours, it does feel like a game in itself.
I would say that this game get's far too much hate, and really doesn't deserve it. This is probably my second favourite in the series, and I would recommend this to anyone who has played any of the Arkham games and wants to see more.
Try it with an open mind, I can pretty much gaurentee that you will like it.

Great fun with a rewarding learning curve, it excels in value for what it is.
It runs better than expected, even on a low-end system with the appropriate adjustments to video settings. I've only encountered the most minor bugs, and nothing game breaking, but overall the experience is just what I'd been looking for. I think there are some cons, though, so a short list of pros vs cons might be helpful - all personal opinion, of course - but even with those I know this will continue to provide hours of enjoyment, and am happy to see a lot of developer feedback about improvements that will be coming in the near future. There isn't much of a tutorial (as in none at all), but plenty of helpful "how to" footage can be found on youtube, and once the basics are covered, it turns out that there's actually a ton of playstyle variety offered by this system with much more to be discovered as you go.
Pros: The maps are just large enough to offer depth in exploration, yet nothing is out of reach, and they are still tight enough to support faster, more intense gameplay. The settings are varied in a way that stays fresh, extremely detailed and interesting, and each map is as unique unto itself within this game as it is an homage to all things zombie horror. Plus, the description's correct in saying that every spawn offers a new set of weapons and enemy layouts, so you never know what you are going to get until you start looking around and fighting for your life. With deceptively simple game mode customization, there are many ways a player can enjoy every aspect whether alone or with a group; though it's clear the best way to be successful is with some teamwork focused cooperative play. I haven't beat an objective based map yet, but still, I've already had hours of fun on survival (defending "safe" areas from waves), learning how to use the environment to my advantage, healing, barricading, practicing my headshots, and of course, making some more room in hell so we can finally put an end to this crazy situation... with a shotgun.
Cons: The melee combat is slow. By that I mean, when running backwards and trying to swing, the player is slower than even the shambling zombies. It looks and feels slow, that is, often forcing the player to turn and run a short distance, then try to pull one enemy at a time, repeatedly. They all work at about the same speed, too, about one swing per second or less, and the cost/benefit difference between them really comes down to weight. The weight system is great, actually, regarding what you can carry, but a machete swings about as slow as a fireaxe or sledge hammer, and as much as this game does push for realism it loses some points there. In any game there can be reasonable limitations, I think, but a person who's not very strong could still probably swing even an axe a little faster than is portrayed here - especially in an adrenaline fueled corner - and the zombies grab on so quickly that by the time they are close, you are virtually dead meat no matter how skilled you are. Sadly, in order to be effective with melee you have to get a little cheap in your playstyle, or else they are pretty much useless. I think the issue could be addressed by accounting for speed versus weight so that the player can go nuts on multiple enemies with something like a machete or smaller axe, making more clear what is connecting where, and in some cases, giving impact/knockback to the zombie in addition to the shove technique all weapons have for heavier weapons. With something like the sledge, even two swings per second instead of one would make a huge difference to its fun factor as well as effectiveness and realism all around.
Luckily, especially in survival mode, there are guns and firebombs and all sorts of other goodies just about everywhere you look - sure the ammo can be scarce, but a replacement is just around every corner - and so melee is not quite as much of a factor as the game descrition covers... I'll be the first to admit, in fact, that every single gun I've handled in this game so far has been supremely satisfying to wield, and I can't wait to see the new additions they have coming on the horizon with the next patches. All things considered, and looking at its potential even if it needs the slightest bit of polish, I would have to rate this game as phenomenal and am so glad to have found it.

20xx does it right, and it does it right in so many ways. 20xx is an amazing action-platformer with a mix of roguelike. 20xx uses permanent death and the procedural level generation of a rogulike title and mixes it in with some fast paced Mega Man style gameplay, and then they throw in co-op on top of it.
I have always had a spot in my heart for platformers. Some of my most fond memories while growing up were stomping goombas in Mario, racing to stop Dr.Robotnik in Sonic, and playing Bonanza Bros with my brother in co-op.
20xx has a unique, compelling design. Because of the randomly generated levels, powerups, multiplayer, and permanent death. This game has so much to offer, one moment you will be flying across platforms hoping not to fall, the next moment you will be in a boss battle doing everything you can to survive and make it to the next level. Throw co-op into the mix and you have a recipie for success. The platforming genre was a thing of the past. Luckily, 20xx is bringing it all back, and doing so in a big way. The only complaint I have with this game is why I didn't find it sooner...

There is no such thing as hitboxes for body parts or headshots or any of that modern stuff, the whole player is one big hitbox (usualy bigger than the player model so they can kill you without even touching you. The servers run on a 40ms (ideal conditions - also never) tick rate that effects the gun play, and other aspects of the game. This means things only happen every 40ms, you can feel this delay the most when you are driving a car or pressing F to do an action, you can also see the shots you fired at lets say a car, hit it after some delay. This is kind of a problem to the gun play, you get the kill or not depends a lot not on your skill but on factors like if your shots are at the beginning or the end of that 40ms gap, witch is also greatly effected by crippling server side lag issues. It also seems that some people are favored by the server over others, they are so called lag armor users or people that kill you faster than the max fire rate of the weapon they are using. Its different from person to person, i guess the server somehow lines up people in a specific order when it processes information coming from them. There is also a big problem called ghost shots, its when you shoot but for whatever reason the server doesnt register any of your shots.
So yeah, this game is a really good idea, but the execution is terrible, dont waste your time unless you are a masochist like me.

After sinking alot of hours and money into this game I think I can review it. When I first started playing around 3 years ago it was great and I instantly fell in love with it, I spent money on G1C and made cars, clothing and bought guns and had fun designing different personas and because the customization is amazing you could make Miley Cyrus, make a tour van, get guns to suit her, make your theme when you kill someone her song and make your tour van blast out an entire song of hers. Or you could just make ♥♥♥♥♥ and hentai like 80% of people do there. The game in that sense is amazing but when it comes to combat it is still fun for the most part but has horrible matchmaking, hitboxes, ranking system. Lets say you are a Trainiee (The lowest rank and level 9) and you press K to ready up in a mission you will most likely get put against a Gold level 205 who has no fall damage, kevlar, fast car and a rocket launcher and that completely ruins the experience and they've even added a district with NO matchmaking so whoever presses K to enter a mission gets put with anyone and to me that seems like a cheap way to add stuff to the game without trying to fix anything and lets say you were to pull up next to your friend and run over his toe at 2mph he will die... INSTANTLY and that just makes the whole combat feel slow, broken and horrible.
There are three sets of money in this game, dollars, Joker Tickets and G1C, dollars are earned by selling on the ingame markey place, so cars and symbols, songs and themes and are earned by doing missions, killing people on bounty and such, its grindy to earn as a cop and ok to earn as a criminal as you can simply steal from stores on a low populated district and earn around 100k in a couple of hours but it gets broken by the fact that premium members who pay for membership get more money per mission and such and so the person whos talented at designing songs or symbols or who has the money to buy premium gets richer faster. Joker tickets are earned by completeling a set of objectives in Fight Club districts where its basically team deathmatch and you will get notifications like "Kill 5 people with granades" and you will get another after that and then you can earn Joker Tickets. These can be spent on getting temporary perks like car surfer to ride on cars or normally expensive weapons and cars, the next currency in the game is G1C this is real money in the Gamers First market place and its where the pay to win comes into play. You can either be like me and spend £350+ in the game and get 3 legendary weapons, alot and alot of cars, premium and symbols and stuff, or you can get lucky and buy a box for £4 and then get a legendary weapon worth millions in game but this marketplace is horrid, its all pay to win weapons and really makes the game not very fun to play when against someone with weapons from the store.
Customer Service from Gamers First is also horrible, I got banned about 2 years ago, maybe a year and a half ago for no reason, they said that I used an aimbot and such but i've never even downloaded one and after spending about £200 in the game at this point I was annoyed, I contacted them and explained my situation and even offered them to scan my PC using teamviewer or screenshots of my APB folders and game but they all said every time 'Theres nothing we can do, you are banned forever' and I gave up on the game and forgot about it for a month and tried to login and I was unbanned, so its very strange and I still dont have an explination for the ban to this day. Customer service hardly respond quickly and they always respond with an automated response, no real human so thats a massive dissapointment.
The missions consist of 'Capture this, deliver this, break this, steal this, deliver this, do this, go here' and you can do ALL of that, literally do ALL of that and then if your opposition has the better shot or gun you will lose the mission because at the end of EVERY mission it all comes down to who has the better car or gun. As a criminal you will most of the time be breaking into winwos and setting doors on fire to steal hard drives and deliver them, you can do ALL 5 set of missions before the end deathmatch and still lose the mission but if you are an enforcer and you stop the cirminal delivering the first hard drive congrats. You win. The missions you can for the most part live with but after a while they start repeating and get quickly boring so you'll find yourself in the Fight Club districts or the Asylum in team deathmatch just to spice things up or you'll find yourself in the very fun new dynamic missions that are present in the regular districts where they resemble the most recent Christmas event where you find a granade launcher and you need to kill 15 other players who try to kill you before delivering it to a contact, the granade launcher gives you buffed health and a buffed launcher.
Overall this game is very fun at parts but very very annoying at times so if you can put up with the Pay to win, the small amount of hackers, the bad combat, the boring missions and the horrible customer support to play a game that resembles a bad GTA with AMAZING customization then this game is great. I can put up with it so I love it, its my favorite game of all time so far and it still is even though it has its flaws and faults I love it and theres rumors going around that G1C are making a new game engine with updated graphics, physics and such so maybe, just maybe if its true and released before this game dies it will change the entire game for the better.
TL;DR: A very buggy game with awful combat, pay to win players, customer support, matchmaking, updates but its worth it if you like customization and want a game where you can make a million personas with cars, songs, symbols and clothes and if you can put up with the bad things you will fall in love with this game.

This is an amazing little turn-based strategy game, which in its heart most resembles chess. Except with hexes instead of squares.  Ahem...
Well, like chess, there there are six sorts of pieces which interact with each other in a myriad interesting ways.  And like chess, the pieces capture the enemy in different ways.  The most interesting thing about the game comes from learning about those interactions to survive as long as you can.
One match probably won't last more than 10 minutes (unless you have analysis paralysis), but to do well, you will have plan very carefully.  When you fail, it will be your own fault for not thinking things through. Nevertheless, the hardest part of this brain-taxing game is to stop yourself from starting a new game immediately upon finishing your last one.
The user interface is spare, but incredibly easy to understand.  If you look carefully, you will see that the developer has a nice understated sense of humor.
The only negative thing I can think to say about the game is that no attempt has been made to gamify the game.  There are no achievements.  There is no title screen. The graphics are utilitarian.  You can't save a match in mid progress, as best I can tell.  When you finally beat your previous best match score, the game does not make a big deal about it.  There is no Peggle-like "Ode to Joy" when you do something mildly cool. The game will give you a deep sense of satisfaction from seeing five moves ahead, but you'll have to seek your adrenaline rush from other sources.
This is my favorite new game of 2017, at least thus far.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the Prequel-Sequel to the previous 2 Arkham games. Developed and published by WB Montreal instead of Rocksteady, one might be turned off to the idea of this game and would be unwilling to give the game a try. I disagree. Here's why:
Arkham Origins takes place a few years before Arkham Asylum, 2 years after Bruce Wayne donned the cowl of Batman. One of the leading criminals, Black Mask, is tired of Batman ruining his plans and sends 10 elite mercenaries (some more elite than others) to kill Batman in one night, Christmas Eve, for 50 million dollars. The story mainly follows Batman evading and defeating the mercs, as well as chasing down the Black Mask. As with Arkham City, there are a few twists and turns along the way, bringing a good time to the game.
The "Origins" part of the game is very interesting, as it explores the origins of the Joker as the Red Hood (canon in the comics), if not only breifly. It also explores the stuggle Batman is having with himself and how he feels the need to protect gotham from itself and all the super-criminals.
Although the voice actors for Batman and the Joker are not the regular that we all know and love (Mark Hamill and Kevin Conroy), the replacements that WB Montreal found are absolutely a great substitute. While not the actors that made the characters what they are, the performances were far from sub-par, and should not be the factor that keeps you from playing the game. You can tell that the actors tried very hard to keep the roles what they were, in order to preserve the legacy. The actor who plays the Joker does a phenomenal job, and I did not even realize that the actor was not Mark Hamill until I heard his monologue around half-way through the game. The Batman actor is a bit more noticeable but nothing to complain about.
The map is bigger than Arkham City's, and feels as such. There are plenty of side activities to do when you are tired of (or done with) the main story. The most fun of all of these is definitely the Crime Scenes that you can come across, and pretty much "solve" murders and thefts. There are also radio towers that Enigma (The Riddler) has hacked. These can be restored through fighting through enemies and using your cryptographic sequencer. This is recommended to do as each tower you restore unlocks the district for fast travel, which signifigantly increases the speed of play.
The combat and gameplay is not very different from Arkham City or Asylum's, but this isn't a problem to me, as the combat does not need to be changed too much. There are 2 new enemies to fight, the martial arts expert, and Bane's super enforcers. While adding some diversity to the combat, it can feel repetitive at times, and I found myself avoiding combat situations and crime calls during the free roam parts of the game.
Overall, this game is a great addition to the Arkham series, even if not near close to the best game in the franchise, and if you plan to play through all of the games, do not forget Arkham Origins. Though nowhere near a perfect game, I personally find it a better game than Arkham City.

Some of the other reviews give this game a thumbs down for not being SimCity; I give this game a thumbs up primarily for not being SimCity.  It tries to do something different, and while it could use a TON more polish and mechanics that add a bit more depth and variety that keep it fresh for a longer period of time, the game is different enough that it scratches a managerial itch of mine I have trouble finding good ways to scratch.
Unlike a lot of trading games that demand you manually perform boring, routine transactions yourself, Spice Road automates nearly all the routine tasks.  That said, this is where it starts to run into problems, because it has the Final Fantasy XII problem of automating the simple, routine actions, but then not adding in anything else for you to actually do once you've set up the routine.
That said, to counter one of the complaints about the game made by some of the other reviewers, there's nothing particularly wrong with being able to hold TAB and speed the game up until things happen.  The game's base speed is a super-slow-motion, so that you can make tons of decisions in a relatively short span of time within the game, then, once all your orders are done, you just hold TAB until you're ready to take more actions (such as waiting for more money to come in to build the next building), and hitting F4 even explicitly exists as a "fast forward until the next building gets built" button, although I rarely bothered using that instead of TAB.
The interface in general is rather lacking, however.  It's great that things are automated, but at the same time, it's extremely hard to understand what's actually going on behind the scenes.  You can be told, for example, that a goods workshop consumes ore and tools, plus hires 10 workers and pays a salary to them, in order to craft goods... but then it doesn't say HOW MUCH ore is used to make how many goods.  Control over your city basically runs on seeing a HUD that has green lights when things are good, and which turns yellow, orange, or red when you need more of something, but beyond that, the game makes it very difficult to reverse-engineer anything about what's going on below the surface.  This often matters while playing, because you can have a city that produces tons of food or goods, but still have a yellow food or goods indicator because your city is trading away all the goods because some off-map trading node will pay more for your goods, and your merchants will trade away their own lunch and starve if it makes them an extra dollar of profit (then blame you for starving).
In most cases, it almost doesn't matter at all, however.  Outside of the "Isolation" mission, the only thing you really need to do is look at what's making profits, and look at the price indicator on the world map.  The only thing that actually seems to matter is the price of different commodities, so if something is expensive, you just try to build more of that thing.
I find the supply chain dissappointingly short.  Basically the only thing that you use to actually manufacture secondary goods is ore.  You need food, ore, one kind of "recreation" good (alcohol -which is for some bizarre reason not grown in the same place as food and vice versa in spite of anything you can brew almost definitionally being edible-, opium, and tea), and one luxury good (and one of the luxury goods can be manufactured through ore, so that's not even necessary).  This basically means that you need ore and food, and the rest is just fluff that you exploit solely to drive up profits.  Ore is used to make tools (needed to run almost everything), goods (needed in freakishly large quantities by your population), weapons (needed by soldiers for combat), and artisan (artificial luxury goods).  These make you all the money you will ever need, and beyond that, you just need access to food and a recreation resource.  (And you can easily trade for the latter, although you need enough food that there will be problems if you solely rely upon importing food.)
Likewise, there's a halfhearted attempt at having "inns" that allow for "tourism", but you basically just set down more churches and saloons and they generate money even if you have no other resources to exploit, which makes the other resources even more meaningless.
Beyond this, there are cities, where you invite nobles to your city to buy more things you can sell them for a profit, but which make increasing demands upon your city's infrastructure to the point that once you set down the palace and actually turn a town into a city, then unless you have leveled-up buildings, then you cannot build more infrastructure to meet needs fast enough.  (Build a palace, and it demands more security, so you build more barracks or a fortress, but then it needs more repair, so you build repair yards, then it needs more population, so you build apartments, but then you need more healthcare and recreation, so you build a hospital and casino, but then you need more population, so you build apartments, but then you need more religion, warehouse space, and water, so you build a cathedral, 3 more warehouses, and more wells, but then it needs more security and population...)  You can level up your buildings to make them more efficient, but the problem is that the high-tier buildings you get in cities require geometrically more experience to level up, and since you need to keep building more and more of everything, you never get the chance to level those things up.  Because of this, there's basically never any reason to have a city except to satisfy arbitrary mission objectives for one.  If you CAN build a city, then you're obviously making money hand-over-fist already, and therefore don't NEED a city to make any more money.  (Cities are generally just giant pits you throw money into, anyway...)
This brings us to the common failing of so many management games, which is that difficulty exists only in the earliest stages of a mission, and once you start making ANY profit at all, there's almost no reason outside of some catastrophically stupid self-inflicted blunder you would ever stop making money.  There is almost no way to feel a challenge in this game outside of finding out that the first town you blindly put on an unexplored map was placed near no resources, and you are forced to reset.  (Expect to make one blind guess-and-scout short session focused purely on exploring the map, then reset once you know where everything is for every mission.)  Combat does hypothetically exist, but it's a bit of a joke.  Build four barracks, set them to attack a town, and speed up time until you defeat everything.  Even if outnumbered, you can wear them down with attrition and replacing dead guards is cheap.
One other commodity is slaves.  Slaves are abysmally badly represented, and are basically just a "population recource" you find and exploit like ore mines or farms.  Slaves grow infinitely, and once in your slave huts, are just population that eat 45% as much and never cause any problems or change society in any visible way.
Graphics are also... bad.  Like N64 graphics bad.  I presume the developer bought them in some sort of medieval asset pack, because some of the graphics don't quite match the function of the building.  Apartments are clearly castle keeps, while slavers and silk weavers live in treehouses for some reason.  The world map is just made of colored semicircles and arrows gliding around.  I play management games that are practically just spreadsheet management games, however, so I don't particularly mind graphics, and the game has minimum specs low enough to run on a graphing calculator.  Just... don't expect to use it to wow your friends.
It's ultimately worth buying at least on sale for its novelty, but it desperately needs deeper mechanics to make it interesting for more than just grinding out the achievements.  It's a city manager where there's far too little to actually manage.

Dear reader,
Below please find my unenthusiastic recommendation for Spice Road:
The concept is interesting for about 7 hours.
What kills this game is the repetitive click-fest (even with the game on pause) to build several practically identical towns, as every building has to be built individually.  If you see screenshots of enormous towns for this game -- yeah.  Every single building has to be placed individually, and if you have 6 or more towns that becomes a new clicking game of itself, which I don't enjoy.
The game is not nearly as deep as I had hoped from some of the reviews.
Worst of all, the tutorial "storyline" is mandatory to access all the buildings in sandbox.  I would rather do away with the tutorial altogether, but forcing me to play it did show some interesting scenarios in the process.  It also guaranteed I would not have an adequate comprehension of the game BEFORE my 2 hour request Steam for a refund period.
So yeah -- the game is okay.  It could certainly be better.  It could certainly not force players through the tutorial and still allow for varied challenges if the developer had wanted to provide more options to the sandbox mode.  But instead, sandbox is inextricably tied to the amount of the tutorial the player has accomplished.
There is a technology tree, which allows access to buildings and building upgrades, but points for the technology tree only occur in the tutorial storyline as levels are completed.  Hence the tree is merely a means of blocking sandbox access to the full building menu until all the whole storyline is completed.
Once you start to win, once the wheel begins to turn, there's practically nothing to stop you.  But getting to that point can be an interesting challenge.
I would only recommend this to die-hard tycoon fans.

Well this game came as a surprise.  I love strategy games, and upon reading about this, and also seeing that it was inspired by Imbroglio, I knew I had to give it a try.  Glad I did, as strategy games like this are few and far between.
As you can gather from the game's description, the core mechanic of the game is that when you move onto a hex, your shape is changed into the shape shown on that hex.  And with these different shapes, comes different abilities.  So your attacks and powers are dependant on the hex you are standing on at the time... your actual "ship" has zero inherant powers of it's own.  None.  You are completely dependant on the grid itself to fight back against the unending bugs.
The true depth though, is where it then goes with that mechanic.  Each hex can gain experience.  For the three offensive hexes, they gain experience each time you make a kill when you started the turn on their position.  For the three special hexes, they gain experience whenever an enemy bug dies on top of them.  Hexes get one experience point at a time, and each time a hex gains 6, it can gain new abilities, however the abilities that you can add to that hex are entirely determined by which hex types are next to it.  For example, if a smasher hex (lets you attack an adjacent enemy without moving) is levelled up, and there is a healing hex next to it, one of the options available will be to give it the ability to heal you whenever you destroy an enemy with it.  However, these upgrades arent universal:  Upgrading a smasher hex only upgrades that one specific smasher... the others on the board are unaffected.  So each smasher hex could end up with different powers depending on what is next to it when it levels up.   This means that the board's structure is EVERYTHING.  All of the strategy is determined by it.  What's more, the strategy is deepened by the position of each individual hex in relation to other hexes, as the different powers each can gain really do make a huge difference.  And lastly, after each enemy "wave", a variety of possible new hexes appear on the edges of the board, and you can go and choose one, expanding the board further.  The bigger it gets, the more possibilities there are, but the complications multiply as the board keeps growing.
That of course isnt enough though:  the other half of the game is the different enemies.  At the start of each wave, enemies spawn in a group onto the board.  They take two turns to spawn:  for the first turn you'll see tiny versions of them on the space they are about to appear on (and they are invincible during this) and on the next, they fully spawn.  After that, they can act.  This means that you have a bit of time to look at the positioning of new monsters and can use that free turn to react to the situation.  This is good, because these enemies get pretty nasty.  Basic bugs are simple, just coming directly at you and dying in one hit, but things get really wonky when other abilities are added to them, such as armor, the ability to snipe, or explosiveness, which outright destroys the hex it's on when the enemy dies (losing a strong, upgraded hex to an explosive foe really sucks).  The good thing is, there are ways to counter everything in the game.  THose explosive jerks for instance.  Normally, they'll ALWAYS explode when killed.  But if you have an acid hex next to another acid hex, and level one of those up, selecting the acid-based power available to it, that acid hex will not only strip enemies that land on it of their armor (which is the acid hex's default ability), but it gains the additional ability to defuse explosive enemies.  There isnt really any all-powerful combination though; the enemy selection is designed as such that they can counter you as well.  Paying attention to enemy positions in relation to absolutely every other freaking thing is important.
The best thing though is that the game is very well balanced.  Of the 6 hexes, there arent any that are going to be rarely-used, all 6 are equally important.  The same goes for all the different abilities that can be gained by each type.  And there really isnt any single strategy that will always work.  One way or another, you absolutely will have to think your way through things anew every single time, and the situation just keeps changing througout each run.
The interface is nice too.  Everything is easy to read, easy to spot, easy to use... it's all very intuitive, clean, and efficient.  And you can right click on anything for more info.
The one disadvantage the game has:  There is NO other content than this basic mode.  None.  There's no unlockables, no "campaign", no other modes.... this even lacks a title screen, which I find moderately baffling.  This is effectively a game in it's absolute most purified form, and for some players, that could be an issue.  The game really is ENTIRELY about the core experience.  It reminds me of alot of older arcade games in that way:  those also had no seperate modes, no unlockables... it was just the absolute pure single experience and not a single thing else, with the goal being to score as high as you can (which is the goal here too).  So, this is something you need to keep in mind when deciding wether to buy this or not.
For me though, that's not even remotely an issue.  I play alot of games that have that aspect.  And one way or another, this is just a blast to play.  And with each run being not all that long yet still very deep, it has that "one more go" aspect to it, and I expect this one will keep me coming back over and over again.   It's fun, it's deep, it's challenging, it's the sort of strategy game I really like.
I do wish/hope that this can get released on mobile, too.  I'd absolutely love to have this on my iPad.  It would work just as well there as it does here.   But for now, this absolutely will do.   Highly recommended.

THAT Said... If you enjoyed Arkham Asylum, Arkham City, this is a reasonable continuation of that gameplay - with a larger map of new villians.

I love this game sooo much. I don't have much playtime on Steam, but on Xbox One and 360 I have a lot of time. Ironically, I've never beat this game. Some people may not like the art style. I think this is the only FPS/Shooter than will ever manage to do it right. Also, I love how funny this game is. It's an FPS that doesnt take itself way too seriously. Also, Handsome Jack and Claptrap will always be some of the funniest characters ever. I don't understand as to why this game had to be open world. I mean, yeah, and RPG isn't and RPG if it's not open world. but theres absolutley nothing to do but maybe kill some enemies or find easter eggs. Speaking of this game being an RPG, as an RPG, its not bad, and as a shooter, its awesome. I love the looting system in this game.  As a co-op game, it shines like gold. The hundreds of weapons you could find just makes this game more fun. Also, Borderlands 2's shield system is priceless. Theres almost as many shields as there are weapons, and each one is special in same way. Same goes for weapons. The boss battles arent anything to praise, but they're definitely fun. And the enemies are just so well done. There's got to be atleast 150-200 types of enemies. Psychos can be annoying at times, but are usually really easy to kill. Same enemies, I believe they're callled goliaths, can hold treasure chests on their back. Treasure chest hold loot, and how good the loot is depends on the color of it. Also, in an area on the map, there is a treasure chest, the best in the game, but this one must be opened with a special key. Sadly, the keys cannot be found on the map and must be obtained by making a SHIFT account then logging in in-game. The plot in Borderlands 2 isn't anything too special, but it doesnt matter as it doesnt really affect the game in any negative way. Even though Borderlands 2 is a great game, it has some flaws. I absolutely love and hate how the enemies level up as your character progresses in the game, but in a mission way, not a character level way. And yes, I know that made no sense. In other words, if you decide not kill everything you see, it will greatly affect the game. You'll end up being a wayy lower level than your enemies, who are ususally only one or two levels above, which adds a sense of difficulty to the game. As I mentioned, this game is and RPG. A very basic one. There are no choices in the game, and not really any sense on role-playing, only leveling up using skill trees and Bada** ranks, which can grow like vines if you go crazy and do like every side mission and kill every enemy you see. I've been rambling on way to long now, so I'm going to tell you my verdict.
Borderlands 2 is fun, humorous, FPS that doesn't take itself too seriously. While it has some RPG elements, I don't think it deserves to be called an RPG. The art style is beautiful and the game runs like Forrest Gump. The characters are well done, but the story doesn't entertain me as much as it might entertain others. I recommend Borderlands 2 if you like humor and FPS games with upt to 4 player co-op. It only costs 20 USD, and usually 5 USD when on sale. If you see this game on sale, buy it, and maybe get a friend to if you prefer co-op.
I'd also like to mention the DLC. There is already tons of missions to do, so DLC is pretty optional. I don't plan on buying any DLC, as I don't really think I'll finish this game any time soon. I hope you enjoy the game if you buy it!
EDIT: March 31, 2016: I've just completed the main storyline for Borderlands 2. Before this edit of the review I said that the story doesn't add much to the game. Oh, yes it does. Also, the game is even funnier as you go. I don't want to make this edit long, so I'll just end it by saying that the story is actually really good, and the comedy in Borderlands 2 gets better as you progress into the game.

A bit late to the party but I kept hearing about the outcry against this game.  Though this is my first DMC game I finished (I did play like the opening mission of 3 and a demo of 1.), I can't understand what all the hate was about outside maybe Dante's appearance. The game was superb. The art direction and enemies were creative and varied (Well, until about near the end of the game), The combat visceral and fun, and just using your hooks to whip around reminded me how fun Spiderman 2 was.
The problems I did have was a reoccurring problem in which the FPS would tank hard during random occasions. With my setup at the time of this review being a 970 and a 4790K, I greatly exceeded the recommended requirements so I wondered what was up. Whenever I would verify the game cache, the FPS drop would go away. It didn't happen frequently, but I did have to do it a couple of time, with definitely ruined game flow. Besides that though, this was a superb port. Don’t have any complaints. When the game ran smooth, it ran DAMN smooth.
The story is interesting, but not all that detailed (though I suppose it's one of the kind of games where story isn't the primary focus). Near the end, I did find that a few sections could have been cut and not much have been missed. The boss fights were spectacular, though the larger ones were pretty easy because they telegraph their attacks so readily. The fights with the smaller scale enemies like those Samurai enemies were harder than probably all the boss besides the last 2.
Besides my faults, I had a blast. It's a great game. Wouldn’t mind seeing a sequel.

Been playing this game on and off for years, and finally something somewhere was fixed and I can FINALLY play the game without server lag like I had all the time before. Now to get right into what I think and what you should/shouldn't expect.

If you're into a great balanced, and fair battle system, please stray as far away as possible from this game. APB has arguably the most back@ssed, unfair and poorly balanced gun mechanics I've ever seen in a game. I mean you could shoot the enemy in the face 10 times with a pistol and they won't die, I have literally hit people point black 100% accuracy with grenades and they took no damage and when they throw one in my general direction I went flying. The driving mechanics are also all miss, not even close to hitting but it gets the job done. Physics in this game do NOT EXIST. The missions get repetitive after a while, but you realize how much you need to do them to unlock everything so you'll have to bare with it. The matchmaking is also pretty terrible since there is no skill matching (at least that does its job) or level/rank system, so if you're starting out, have fun dying A LOT from people who have either been playing for a while and have better stuff than you or are hackers. That's another thing, this game is kinda old, and I feel like the developer just doesn't care much more about security so there are plenty of hackers.
Really, I'm sure by now you're probably going "wow this game sounds like it sucks bad" but let me give you my reasoning as to why this is still one of the most interesting and worthwhile (for a little while at least) MMO's around.

Customization. This game does it better than any game around, unless maybe you're playing Black Desert or Sims 4. Absolutely amazing customization options for detailed character creation, tattoos, cars, custom music, all kinds of armor options, and more. Honestly I would consider this more of a social simulator with guns and cars than an actual third-person shooter MMO, since the focus on the personal and social aspects seem to carry a bit more weight. Graphically the game has held up surprisingly really well. One of the more pretty games you'll see from the last generation of MMO's (obviously no match for something like ArcheAge, Black Desert or Dirty Bomb though (but who really cares)) Another maybe little but big to me thing that I love is that you can import your own music from your computer into your in-game radio to listen to in the car which adds a nice bit of immersion, and yes I know I could just open up Spotify, but I just like having it this way.
If you go into this game expecting GTA or Saints Row quality gameplay, you'll be surely disappointed. This isn't bad though. This game doesn't really try to BE either of the two. If you love having vast and unique customization tools and just trying something other than the typical cookie-cutter MMORPG/FPS give it a try. Don't just go in for 30 minutes, really give it a good few hours, learn the game, unlock some stuff and feel it out. It may or may not be for you.

Ori isn’t as much a game as it is a storybook come to life - its pages tell the tale of a colorful, lush world, where the dark underbelly of a volcano lies long dormant, the rivers run thick with pollution and the jagged insides of a mountain is home to only the ghost of a storm. It’s a tale of light and dark in the most obvious fashion - Ori is pure white, almost angelically so, whilst Kuro, whose name literally means black, rides under the cover of darkness, smoke bellowing from her feathered mane. Yet both have more in common than they know - and the story, though sparse, has a little more depth than its seemingly obvious conclusion might betray.
Mechanically, Ori is as about as standard a metroidvania as you can get - you move through different areas of the forest in a semi-linear fashion, picking up upgrades through the knowledge of ancestral spirits that teach you new moves to get to new areas so you can learn new moves and get to more new areas. Along the way you’ll find orbs that give you permanent upgrades in the form of ability points (which you use to unlock some useful, auxiliary skills), energy and life cells (MP/HP). There’s also some fun platforming escape sequences where you race against the clock, using all the moves at your disposal, but other than that, there’s nothing here that will floor you, no amazing gameplay gimmicks or unexpected plot twists - theres isn’t much to call Ori-ginal here (#sorrynotsorry), save for the great art and orchestral soundtrack. The music kind of has a Dreamworks vibe - every time I hear the title track, I think ‘this is how How To Train Your Dragon starts’. It’s not how it starts. Good movie, though.
A few gripes: you can’t remap keybindings without having to edit a text file outside of the game - I mean, come on guys, it’s 2016 - but this isn’t so bad up until you start having to use the Shift button a lot for the latter part of the game and you’re halfway through an escape sequence when Sticky Keys decides to pay a visit. Also you have to use W/A/S/D to move (and movement is super floaty), on top of a lot of Shifting, which means your fingers are gonna be doing some real tai chi♥♥♥♥♥♥to fit onto that cramped part of the keyboard - the platforming isn’t actually that hard, but coupled with the fiddly controls, it makes for a somewhat frustrating experience where you know exactly what to do but you just can’t do it. It also needs more performance optimizations - I’m running a pretty high-end rig, and I’ll still get random stuttering when there’s a lot going on in the screen.
I think Ori is one of those games where you can kind of guess if you’ll like it from the first half-hour - think of Pixar’s Up (and not How To Train Your Dragon), and how, in those first ten minutes, without a single word of dialogue, an entire lifetime passes by - Ori does something exactly like that in that time that sets up the rest of the game’s narrative arc. A creature brought into a suffering world, yet still chooses to help it - it’s exactly what a kid would do. Ori is a game that believes in that unyielding nature of goodness - and, through its convictions, manifests a goodness of its own.

20XX takes elements from Megaman X and combines them with roguelike elements to create an all-new experience. From what I've seen thus far it works really well, though the game itself is very clearly in alpha and can use many changes.
For one thing, I feel the physics engine could use a bit of tweaking. This game is obviously trying to emulate Megaman X's physics, but it doesn't feel quite as smooth and satisfying(ex. The dash isn't really as effective unless you have the powerup that increases the dash's power.). For the most part, it works pretty well, it's just kind of rough around the edges at the moment.
Another problem I have is how the levels are designed. I was incredibly interested in the idea of having randomly-generated levels, but the levels seem to give off more of a rage game vibe than anything else. The time limit really doesn't help either. Sure, it adds a bit of intensity to really beat the level, but it puts you in a state of stress that Megaman games generally do not have. The bosses, however, I have no problem with. I love how the bosses are designed.
All and all, I do like 20XX. It is a great concept and shows plenty of potential. I am excited to see what happens in the future.

[Original review:]
This is definitely Early Access. The game shows promise but is extremely rough around the edges. (E.g. I get sent to some debug mode that's full of bright red collision boxes whenever I press 'start' to pause the game and it'll randomly go away if I pause/unpause again a few times... Maybe... And my weapon charges while I hold 'right' on the d-pad — not on the analog stick though — making it very difficult to actually move right and shoot. However, I expect both of these problems to be relatively rare since there isn't a torrent of complaints about them in the forums.) Bosses aren't exactly super challenging but I can't imagine they'll stay like that forever. The platforming is pretty tight and controls are very responsive and feel good. 20XX basically has all the ingredients of a great platformer, it just needs to put them together in the right amounts using the right recipe.
If you are willing to buy a game on a promise and think this could become an interesting game, then you should definitely buy this. At this very moment there's not a whole lot to it and — since it's Early Access — there may never become anything of it, but if platforming and roguelikes (e.g. Spelunky and Rogue Legacy) is your thing, this could be your next favorite game ... when it's done.

Not going to spoil the story, basically it follows very young Dante who is uncovering his past and learning more about who he really is. Dante is same "old" yet younger self, still arrogant and hot headed like always. I found that for me, story in this game was much more enjoyable than in 4th DmC.

Non the less game looks good, with uniquely crazy DmC environments, a lot of low resolution textures, good motion capture and facial animation, great voice acting and challenging combat. Not much of eye candy in this one, than in DmC 4, but still great spectacle fighter with awesome yet evil story. Though who am I kidding, it's supposed to be evil. Enjoy.

Honestly, this review is very late to the party, and if you haven't already played Spec Ops: The Line, I don't know what more you need to be told to finally play it. This game is a rare example of a "Triple A" title that also manages to make a genuine artistic statement with its narrative, and is an overall phenomenal game.
The gameplay is simple enough, it's a third-person, cover-based shooter, a formula that had been perfected in the "Triple A" space for years even back when this game was first released, and that fact is reflected in tight, responsive controls. Of note is that there are a number of opportunities to make use of the environment to deal with enemies, and when giving commands to your squad, there are fully-voiced lines that will reference unique features about your current location, which is a nice touch. However, the gameplay, while technically competent and lacking any significant flaws, doesn't stand out, either. That said, Spec Ops: The Line's gameplay only exists as a means to deliver on the story, which is the real reason you want to buy this game right now. Oh, and there's a multiplayer mode, but it was clearly tacked-on to satisfy publisher demands, and I'm not factoring it into my review at all.
To go into too much detail about Spec Ops: The Line's story would give away the whole plot, but, the basic premise is that  Dubai has been hit with massive sandstorms, and the city's elite evacuated in secret, leaving thousands of innocent people to die. A Colonel John Konrad volunteered to help with relief efforts, and ultimately, his entire battalion defied orders to evacuate and effectively deserted. A number of troubling reports made their way out of the city regarding the actions of Konrad's battalion since then, and they were all disavowed as traitors.
When a radio message is received from Konrad declaring his attempt to evacuate the civilians of Dubai a complete failure, a covert team is sent in to retrieve him, by force if necessary, led by Captain Martin Walker (the player character), who always viewed Konrad with admiration. Now, the more well-read of you may have already noticed, but if this sounds suspiciously like Heart of Darkness (or Apocalypse Now!, its Vietnam-era adaptation), you're on the right track. However, that's just the starting point, the plot takes some very notable turns from there, at times even deliberately subverting one's familiarity with the works that inspired it.
Suffice it to say, the story is nothing short of brilliant, and while the game runs about five to eight hours total, the pacing makes that the perfect length. In fact, I would recommend you play through the game in a single sitting, to maximize its impact. This is a game that everybody should play through at least once, if you don't want to pay full price, put it on your wishlist and grab in during the next Steam sale. Either way, do NOT deny yourself this experience.

Pushing the boundaries of what fans have come to expect from the record-setting entertainment franchise, Call of Duty®: Black Ops II propels players into a near future Cold War. It's also pushing the boundaries of physics and common sense.
Everybody knows the Call of Duty formula by now, bombastic movie like experience. A shooter version of Telltale adventure game created by Michael Bay admirer. Which is ok. I'm not a fan of first person shooters but surprisingly enough I loved the first Black Ops, it was an engrossing thriller where you played the main role. Yes, interactions were limited and sometimes you could finish a mission just by running forward, but all in all the experience was great. And that's the campaign only, on top of that the multiplayer was great (as usual tho) and the zombie mode was fun enough.
Enter Black Ops 2. Well, where with the first BOps I completed mission after mission just to see what's going to happen next, here I was burned out after few missions. The plot was uninteresting, the missions boring and sometimes confusing. I finally managed to complete the game, a few years later while cleaning my backlog. And well. It's not good. But it has the worst plane sequence ever implemented in a video game, so that's something, right? The branching story would be interesting if it wasn't so forgettable. The game looks ok and plays ok, but it's like everything is mediocre here. Apart from the gun selection, which is quite good.
Multiplayer was probably fun if you liked CoD type multiplayer, but it's way after release date now and it's quite dead. All in all nowadays the game is not worth the admission price.

Spice Road reminds me of Railroad Tycoon -- optimizing finances and spending a good bit of time interpreting spread sheet data -- logistics. But where I got tired of Railroad Tycoon rather quickly, this game keeps my interest by having a bit of Civilization (the Sid Myers series) thrown in. The ability to train guard units and send them out alone or embedded in caravans really rounds out the game nicely. In the future, I hope there are more types of military units than simply "Guards," or some small expansion of combat. There are many types of buildings to put in your cities and choices to be made about when to level them up which also helps this game be more compelling than simply optimizing spread sheets.
The depth of game is quite good. Don't be fooled by early missions; there are like 20 missions for a good reaon -- it takes that long to learn the basic game. There is a lot of subtlety here which is key to keeping any game interesting after multiple play-throughs. After 2 missions you might think it is simple, but after 8 you realize it is anything but simple. After 12, the possibility of Buyer's Remorse begins to permanently fade.
I was hoping to learn a bit of history when I bought this game, and in that arena, I have been disappointed. I have not come away with a deeper understanding of who the major players of the area were nor what their cultures were like, but the game is still an enjoyable change of pace for thinking fans of strategy games. Adding a few sentences of historical context to each of the mission descriptions would go a long way for history buffs.
Still it is fun to engage in the virtual construction of opium dens, slave markets and monastaries with consequences for the choices you make. You can choose war or peace with NPC factions and pay protection money or fight NPC bandits. Limited finances will make you constantly choose carefully what to build next. Choices, choices!
Some complaints I have: When I start a new town and send out 4 scouts, I often leave 2 on auto-pilot and give 2 instructions on where to go. Later on, I can't easily tell which ones I'm controlling. I get the impression that if you ever take a scout out of auto-explore, it just patrols back and forth to the point you set, wasting time, not exploring after the first round trip. (Not sure if I fully understand its AI yet.)
Worse, the caravans and guards remove the fog of war, but don't fill in the resources, so I can't tell if a patch of ground has been explored for resources by scouts or not. Put it all together, and I feel quite out of control when it comes to exploring for resources. I need more information and more control. It is frustrating when resources are suddenly revealed long after you thought you had scouted out an area... long after you chose where to place your city in that area.
I'd like to see a path when I mouseover a scout -- his planned route of where to go next. Or maybe an icon showing whether he is on auto-pilot. I'd like the ability to return a patrolling scout back to auto-exploration. I'd like to see two different types of fog: one that lets me know if an area has been explored by scouts or not. Maybe a caravan can remove the fog of war, but the area still has a grey tinge until explored by a scout?
I'd like the scouts to look a little less like the caravans. A medium blue oval is sometimes hard to distinguish from a medium-small blue oval. How about adding some bumps to the caravan icon or something?
The list of commodities in the profit/loss view is not alphabetized, making you read the entire list every time you want to find "weapons" or "food" or "ore." On the other hand, at least there is a long enough list to make the game interesting.
Occasionally you will take out loans, but when you repay them, you must repay your largest loan first which can make it hard to get out of a hole once you get a little stuck.
All in all, Spice Road definitely has its charms. It is stable, smooth, coherent, and consistently entertaining. Despite discussing some specific short-comings, I expect to get a couple hundred hours out of this title. I got it on Steam sale for $11.99, and that price seems about right to me. I would hesitate at $20. I am hard to impress, but give it 6.8/10 in its current (Nov 2014) form -- a worthy entry in any Steam library of strategy games. New patches still coming out -- should improve over time.
