Imagine Anno, except not bad, or Children of the Nile, except released on Steam in 2014, and all about economy. You erect towns and make your lovable bumblebees happy (at least on the earlier levels, conjuring happiness involves building a few basic buildings and does not require careful balancing or come with trade-offs). In the meantime, you also try to maximise trade route efficiency and just make some good old fashioned dosh. No greenback no victory.
Every mission adds further jolly gameplay concepts, while finishing objectives gives you upgrade points to improve your buildings and unlock new ones.
Unfortunately no multiplayer and no sandbox mode.

I can highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys logistics & economical strategy games.
It reminds me a bit of some of my old favorites, such as Railroad Tycoon 3 or Capitalism 2.
To the people who say this is an easy game, they didn't give it enough time.
If you put it on hard, some of the scenarios in the first act even can be difficult. I'm sure it will increase the challenge in later acts as well.
It isn't just "put down some buildings and watch numbers change". That would be like saying the Civilization series is just building units and sending them to fight.
You have to think about:
- where to place camps
- when to upgrade
- which buildings to build RIGHT NOW, vs which to build later, vs which to never build.
- There are a variety of considerations to deal with: limited budgets (this is the main restriction), competing factions taking up good spaces if you aren't fast enogh, bandits taking out your caravans, etc.
With a limited budget, you really do have to think about what your next moves should be.
Cons:
- The campaign maps are static. Meaning if you have trouble and restart the mission, you know exactly where the resources are: you already found them in your last game. If you aren't exploring blind, you can get a big advantage by grabbing the best spots much earlier (since you know where they are now). To the dev: I'd suggest randomizing resource placement on the campaign maps to combat this.
- Once you get rolling and have a decent income, it isn't that difficult for the rest of the game. Maybe this changes in the later missions or sandbox mode. That said, there is still room for thought; you could just brute force build a bunch of stuff with your good income, but you'd maximize profits better by considering what to build when. (Perhaps later on when competition is more fierce this will be different.)
Review Caveats: I'm only through 6 campaign missions so far, will update if anything changes after playing through more.

After Absolution where we get to chase a redneck with a Frankenstein for a bodyguard, killing some broads in nun latex suits sent to kill us and all those absurd events, this feels like Hitman is back on track where it belongs. Which is not fantasy world, but a more realistic one with assassinations.
People are complaining about episodical releases and always DRM system but let us be honest if you do not have the ability or funding to maintain a stable connection in 2017, odds of you running this game is not really that great. Episodes? Meh, just wait for it and get the full release anyways.
Back to the game; visuals are stunning if you have a good system to run it. I encountered no bugs or crashes, nor silly AI scripts like in previous games. Some of the targets have random scripted take on some interactable objects in the world so possibilities to remove them are vast. Mechanics are also improved since now you can not choose a difficulty. There is only the based difficulty and after you finish an episode on it, game gives you the chance to replay it on "Silent Assassin" difficulty option with less odds in your favor let us say. This is good because now you can not shoot your way through the missions like in the old ones and stealth actually matters. AI still has that "extremely suspicious" approach to ordinary things that would go unnoticed in real life encounters but without it the game would be very easy I assume.
After playing all the games in the series I have realized that I did not used my fiber wire nor the silenced pistol even once in this one since throwable lethals (like scissors etc.) are less quiet and easier to use with discression. I am not sure how to feel about this but then again it is all about the approach. I bet there were opportunities and places you can do whatever and still get away with it.
All in all, it is worth the full price if you are a fan of the infamous Agent 47. If not, get it on a sale, enjoy your contracts.

Fantastic game.  I'm not sure if it's the game itself, the genre, or the nostalgia that got me - probably all of it.
MAJOR TECHNICAL NOTE: During the game setup (separate executable utility) choose software rendering under the video options.  If you don't, loading/saving will be super slow and the game itself will be choppy.  (At least this is the way it was for me in Windows 10.  You're probably fine in WinXP and earlier.  :P )
This is a Diablo-style game going by genre, view, and the single-character element.  But Divine Divinity is a much deeper RPG and allows for a ton of customization via skills and assignable attribute points.  The plot/story is decent, the mechanics are pretty simple, and the game offers plenty of hours of gameplay with many quests.  Even the grind (plenty of opponents out there) while exploring the land isn't bad since you're finding new places at the same time, although the final dungeon was definitely too grindy.
Some minor cons:
- There was a lot of dialogue that wasn't covered by audio and the voice acting wasn't the greatest.
- You can't use the automap to travel, so you have to keep clicking or holding the mouse button down to cover territory you've already explored.  There are teleporters that you can use to cover ground more quickly but....
- The weapons and armour in the game are randomly generated every time you identify the item.  Not the type (necessarily) but the specs.  This isn't so bad for generic stuff but when you find a "Sword of the Gods" and it's worse than something you picked up half the game ago, that ain't right.  To correct for this a lot of folks (myself included) saved before opening the containers that held special items, and kept reloading until the specs were decent.  Quick save and quick load features come in handy here.
Note that this is an older game, circa 2002.  I can't believe I missed this gem back then, and I heartily recommend it now.

Thanks to some top-notch customer service on the part of Aartform, I now have this on Steam! My play hours may not show it, but I've been playing this game for just under a year and have logged probably over 100 hours with it all-told. It was a great game to pass the time while I was commuting from my last job and it is surprisingly deep despite being a little rough around the edges visually. I'm absolutely overjoyed to be able to play it on Steam and start earning achievements!
First things first: This game mainly caters to the kind of player that is interested in logistics and supply chain economics and is only really a city-builder or Civ style game in the loosest sense. You are building a network of trade nodes and attempting to meet various scenario goals or self-created goals (in the sandbox mode) as opposed to fighting battles or growing population. The main challenge is building an efficient and profitable network of trade cities given the resources on the map.
One word of caution: The later scenarios are *hard*. You have to really know how the supply/demand model works and understand route efficiency. Route length and travel times are very important when trying to make the big bucks supplying a huge town. It can be very frustrating: I was stuck on one scenario for a long time because I didn't understand some concepts about the economic model. This game does *not* hold your hand and is for people looking for a mental challenge.
All told, this is well worth the price (I paid the full price and got more than my money's worth) if you are the kind of person that 1) loves classical economics and trade/logistics theory 2) are not afraid to step up to a challenge and 3) aren't too hung up on the dated graphics. BIG thumbs up!

Spice Road is an unique and interesing strategy game from Aartform Games that has a great deal of depth to it.
You start out on a grid based map and choose where you want to start a city/town. And then you build up the town with a huge focus on economy rather than supply management. This unique mechanic works really well thus distancing itself from other strategy games like Banished and Civ 5. (When I say economy, I'm talking about $ and trade routes) Aside from economy you'll be building your city/town from different categorries of buildings. (i.e. Housing, Administration, Resources, Trade, Recreation, Spiritual, Security, and Health) Each helping out the town in it's own way. For example: to keep people healthy you can build a well and to keep people spiritually active you can build a shrine, etc. Also, there are hardly any loading screens and the game can run on almost anything.
That being said, the game does suffer from poor graphics and poor audio quality. Also there is no combat and it's pretty easy. But overall, I can recommend this game to any strategy fan or gamer who wants to get into strategy games.
*Review copy was provided by Aartform Games; Thank you!*

I've played all of the Hitman games and this is arguably my favorite one yet. The numerous options, large levels, the story and how it's set years after the prior games, the graphics and voice acting, it just surpasses and improves upon all of the old Hitman games.
I really enjoyed the strength and mystery of the story. The shadow groups that work behind the ICA are intriguing as they try to outpower each other. I also enjoyed the amount of growing interest Diana has in Agent 47's origins, as she never really was keen on it all these years. I also enjoyed the fact that each contract/mission had seperate stories but were ultimitately intertwined in the Providence conspiracy. It felt perfect for the Hitman universe.
The level designs are amazing. The fact that they're so vast creates an incredible playground for Agent 47, there are so many opportunities for each assasination, opportunities to create distractions, etc. and so forth. I've only gone through each mission once, but there's so much room for replayability, as well as the featured contracts. I'm only disappointed that I didn't get to play the elusive target missions.
The best levels have to be Sapienza and Marrakesh. The sprawling markets and urban areas in both levels made them intense as well as full of life and atmosphere. I think they'll go down as some of the best levels in Hitman's history.
The sound editing and mixing in this game is also incredible. At time, the sound and background noise felt so real as if you were really there. This game is awesome really.

I'm going to go over my experience with this game during this review. When I first started playing and I was new to the game, I had the most fun I'd had in a long time. Just driving around town mowing down civilians (even though I was a cop) and losing all of my prestige was fun enough. I've always liked the idea of an open world city where players were free to do whatever they want and go into missions whenever you felt like it. The main thing that set this game apart from other shooters was that instead of a list of servers, you get a city and you're free to join a mission whenever you'd like.
The customization in this game is amazing. You can create your own decals to put on clothing and cars. The main issue that I have is the work and time you have to put into the game to unlock good cars, upgrades, guns, and clothing. An easier way to get these things would be to buy them with real money, which I find that many users do to have the advantage over new players. That brings me to my next point.
If you are just getting into the game, you're screwed. Simple as that. You will get your butt handed to you each time you play unless you gather a team of newbs or join more experienced players. After a while you will develop strategies and get better unlocks. If you don't have a high-end computer, you're also screwed.
To finish off this review, the game has potential. Does the game show that often? No. The game needs more updates and the missions get old. The NPCs all act basically the same and after a while, you get bored. The reason that I recommend this game is because I've spent countless hours playing this game and I've had a lot of fun with it for a free-to-play. I say it's worth checking out. I feel like there are better  updates to come.
Thanks for reading

Divine Divinity is a Hack&Slash RPG with a heavy focus on world building and immersion in a open world game.
The story itself tough is rather mediocre, evil demon threatens the world, the person you create is the chosen one who can raise in half-godhood to be able to defeat his demonspawn. It gets deeper with some side info on how the world has been created, many books you can read that help you immerse into the the ingame world.
The immersion is really great, especially with the soundtrack which is basically a couple of very good tracks that change when you get into new areas but there is always birds chirping or tree branches cracking in the background. Really good soundtrack, voice acting and fighting sounds tough are rather bland or even bad.
The fighting system is okay, many skills are really useless, dont work against many bosses/enemies and in the end its better to pick the fighter and mash some thief or /and mage abillities into him because money is in mid game no problem and you usually find better gear than you buy so you spend all your money mostly on enchantment tokens or potions for life, stamina or magic. But the game was very fun for me to play as a fighter and experiment with different kinds of abillities i seem to be working well with my build. There are lots of spells and other skills to choose from. The freedom of choice really saved the fighting system in my opinion.
The gameplay balance on the other hand isnt really that good in my opinion, as an example the game puts you into a village that is around orcs. You can only beat maximum around 2-3 alone, and if you go down the main path there are waiting 2 high level orcs with crossbows who instantly kill you before you can say "get rekt". Therefore you farm low level orcs, or skeletons in dungeons and run away from the higher level ones. The problem is also that you have no real chance against some of the enemies that are directly laid into your path because the numbers are totally against you. Only choice is abusing the game by using invisibillity potion and warrior special attack which makes you not invisible if you use it next to enemies. Due to this trick every boss is possible to beat by low level characters, but thats pretty broken in my opinion. Traps work aswell but dont give you xp. On the other hand the whole game is adventuring trough the world and testing out which quests are for you at the current level or should be left for later. But in the endgame you feel like a demi god reking trough all enemies and doing quests you couldnt do before. Balancing is the worst part in the game next to the bugs.
Game is full of bugs that can be gamebreaking, i didnt encounter any, but i experienced once that all of my teleporter checkpoints are gone and i had to re run the whole way. Save often/make backups because many experienced bugs that makes questlines broken, but it is not as frequent as many tell because i played trough the game twice already.
The open world is full of quests and dungeons to explore, the humor is great aswell. The quests are sometimes really good and well writen while others are just filler run to this and run to that point. Overall a good experience tough. Only part of the game i disliked was the endgame when you ascended to godhood . The last map is just a huge barren wasteland with nothing really to do there and the last boss is only reachable by beating all 5 bosses you already encountered in some part of the game. Yuck, i hate that.
I would give the game a 6.5/10. The whole game itself is really lacking a proper balance and is suffering from some bugs i still liked the freedom of the character development, very immersive world building and the good soundtrack that really saved for me the whole experience.

January 4th, 2016
Over a year later and the game is really starting to come into it's own. There's a lengthy initial startup time when you launch but gone is the lag at menus and start starts. Characters feel more fluid and it just feels good to control either blaster user Nina or sword user Ace. They've also added a choice at the end of the level, so you're less likely to get the same level sets in a row now. Boss health was reduced though as their life meters aren't as crazy as they use to be. Haven't had the chance to play co-op yet but the single player experience has very much improved and I still recommend the game to fans of the genre.
November 25th, 2014
Game is pretty bare bones at the moment, the levels are randomized but in the 45 minute co-op session I played we did see a level repeat. Bosses are tricky and can be a bit frustrating but the controls work well and a controller definately feels at home with the game. The gameplay feels very much like what you'd find in a Mega Man X game and it's fun to have it in a native PC game. The music is catchy and the levels are bright but have odd gaps in them and invisible walls. Some of the enemies blend in too well with the environment or match the background palette and feel bland.
For co-op, when players get spread out the camera zooms out to accomadate both players yet, this means you can rush off ahead if you want but it'll become difficult to navigate as some environmental hazards can be hard to discern and some of the enemies that palette match the background become near invisible. Still, Apart from having the screen turn split-screen or not allowing you to outpace your partnet it works well.
Also, for co-op, if your partnet dies you can stand at their "ghost" and shoot to give them half your life.
The game shows a lot of promise right now, I just hope they keep developing and continue to add features. Don't get it expecting a near complete game because it's not at that point, this might not be fair but right now it feels a stage or two above a prove of concept demo and doesn't seem to be entirely optimized as the game hangs (for me) when loading and becomes unresponsive for 1-2 minutes before opening, and even then it doesn't focus the window.
Tons of replayability, co-op, and difficulty.  What's not to like?

Morphblade is an endless, very simple puzzle game played on a hex grid. You change into a shape corresponding with the tile you move onto, and your goal is to survive for as long as possible against endlessly spawning enemies. It is a turn-based game, and you can level up the tiles you are on as well as add to the size of the hex grid.
Mechanically, the game is extraordinarily simple. There are six tile types in the game –hammer (shoot things in adjacent cells), arrow (jump 2 tiles forward, killing everything in your way – but if you only move one tile, you push them instead), blade (kill everything on either side of your line of attack), acid (strips armor from an enemy which moves onto it – armored enemies are otherwise invincible), repair (repairs you when you move onto it), and teleport (you can teleport to any point on the board from this hex).
Cells that can kill enemies gain one experience every time you kill an enemy from them. Cells that cannot kill enemies gain one experience every time an enemy dies on it. When a cell gains six experience, it levels, and allows you to choose a level benefit based on any hex adjacent to that tile. Acid cells can be made to kill enemies which are stripped by them if they choose the hammer benefit, for instance, or can repair you whenever an enemy moves onto them if the repair benefit is chosen. This adds more variety to the gameplay, and is really core to making it more than extremely simple (though it is still quite simple).
There are a handful of enemy types. All of them are called “bugs”, which move one hex towards you every turn (after spending one turn growing into adult forms), but they have various abilities – some just attack you if you’re next to them. Some can move two tiles at once. Some push you instead of hurting you. Some can attack from range in a straight line. Some are armored, being invincible until being stripped by an acid cell. And some are explosive – they destroy the cell they die on. These can all be mixed, so you can run into a flying, explosive, armored, pushing bug, for instance.
The longer the game goes on, the more (and more complicated) bugs spawn in each wave. If you get hit once, you turn red; if you get hit twice, you die. Between waves, you can move around freely, so it is easy to heal yourself up between waves; in waves, every move is at a premium, and if multiple bugs hit you on the same turn, you take damage for each. It is possible to gain one bonus hit point if you upgrade repair tiles with other repair tiles, giving you a maximum of three hit points, and as every wave ends you get to add another tile of a random type off a side of the grid of your choice (you can see which tile would be added in which spot, adding some strategy to the game). Sometimes you will also be able to add wild card tiles – blank tiles that you get to choose the type of.
So far, so simple. So, what’s the rub?
The problem is that this game is not only extremely simple, it is too simple. It just feels kind of pointless to play, like a throwaway mobile game or flash game, and after spending about 20 minutes or so with the game, you’ll understand how it works and there’s really nothing more after that. It is an endless game but in the end it is a rather boring one; there’s no goal, no greater purpose, no achievements, nothing to aim or strive for. It isn’t hard to get to wave 20+, and by that point, you will likely have fallen into a repetitive pattern which frankly just isn’t all that fun to do over and over again.
In the end, I got bored with this game within an hour of picking it up, and see no real reason to ever play it again.

DMC: Devil May Cry Review
I never had the pleasure to play the previous Devil May Cry games. They came out during a time when I was not allowed to not even touch an M-Rated game. Once I was older, I never sought them out and soon forgot about them. I regret that...slightly.
DMC is a prequel/reboot to the Devil May Cry series. It follows the spawn of an angel/demon relation as he tries to find out where he fits in this world and what a world it is! Ninja Theory may not be so subtle in their approach here, but it does go a long way to making DMC's world feel unique among its contemporaries. It's an entire satire on modern capitalism and political ideologies, but it's cool to see the developer have the guts to stick by its presentation and not skimp on it's more obvious satire of more popular people like the infamous Bill O' Reilly.
The gameplay is immensely visceral and very complex albeit I believe not as much as previous entries. Nonetheless it's a good starter point for anyone interested in the series. The combos, while there might be many, end up becoming quite simple to memorize after a while since every weapon has the same combos with some slight variations. Overall, it's very refreshing to play a melee combat game that has a bigger move-set than it's contemporaries. Be warned, while this game is easier than previous Devil May Cry iterations, those iterations were known to be pretty difficult. This leads to Devil May Cry being a tougher game than usual and a game that requires your full attention at all times. This might be one game that you should be able to start on Easy instead of Medium without making you feel like you suck. Thankfully the game makes it simple for you to remember combos and times to dodge by using creative visual cues. The gameplay is the main reason to play DMC and trust me it does not disappoint in that department.
As for the story of DMC, it ends up being kind of a mixed bag, but overall a much more compelling narrative than most titles released today. While sometimes you might wonder why the developers didn't just make a film, you'll quickly grow accustomed to the slick cinematography and intriguing story. Without giving any spoilers away, the game has some detours in the story that feel more like padding to artificially lengthen the game and ends up messing with the pacing of the story. The main bad guy is intriguing, but unfortunately is not given time to grow to feel like he is a menacing, credible threat. Towards the end a subplot is thrown in with very little flair and is never given enough time throughout the story to be believable. It makes the characters involved in this scene do things that are kind of uncharacteristic, and contradictory to their established personalities.  Overall the story is compelling, but is filled with many tropes and other maladies that bog it down a bit.
You may be wondering if I like this game? I’ll tell you this much. I love this game, and while my critical eye is quick to catch where it falls short, as a new fan I must say that I loved being in this world and following the characters on their respective journeys. So it pains me to say that it is a damn shame that we may not be getting a sequel to this game. Being the lowest sold in the series, it makes the prospects of a sequel highly unlikely, which is really unfortunate. From the slick presentation, intriguing story, compelling characters, to engaging combat; DMC will alway remain on my mind as a what if. A series with great potential held back by mediocre sales. One thing's for sure though...I’m going to go back and see if I can play all the old Devil May Cry games. I need more Devil May Cry!

Ori and the Blind Forest is a masterpiece, IMO. Why?
+ Compelling storytelling: I was already invested with the game within the first few minutes and it was done with minimal dialogue from the main characters. I found the plot powerful and intriguing, and the way it unfolded througout the game was great.
+ Beautiful visuals: "Beautiful" is  often used to describe Ori and the Blind Forest, and it's well-deserved. It's stylized art is something that left a remarkable impression to me.
+ Great music: I always played with my earphones on because of the music. It's something you have to experience.
+Solid gameplay: It had tight gameplay mechanics and outstanding level design. It's also good that you can change the difficulty to your liking, at any time. I played on normal difficulty the whole game, but I still found it to be a bit more on the hard side. It was rewarding nonetheless.
All in all, I recommend others to experience this wonderful game. I've played my fair share of platformers and metroidvania games, and I can confidently say that it's up there in terms of greatness.

Let me be open at the very beginning: I love this game to death, but it really isn't a good game. Now before you turn away, allow me to explain.
The premise of the game is that you and your squad are soldiers sent to recon the city of Dubai, which for unexplainable reasons has turned into a warzone and the last company of American military that went there have long since lost contact with command. Imagine Apocalypse Now, but a video game and set in the middle east instead of Vietnam.
No really, its almost the same thing.
If you liked Apocalypse Now or Apocalypse Now's source material (Heart of Darkness, good book btw), then you'll like the story of this game. If you're looking for something along the lines of Battlefield, CoD, etc, you should probably look somewhere else.
Now that that's outta the way, let's talk about gameplay.
Spec Ops The Line is a third person shooter that plays like Gears of War without the monsters and gore, or Uncharted without Nathan or parkour. It feels off, and I get that the devs were new and strapped for cash but the gameplay is not really a selling point. It feels more like a parody or even satire of video games that have done it better (which compliments the storyline, actually), and for that reason I would advise not going into this expecting great or even good gameplay. At best, this is an interactive movie that has controls but otherwise you won't care too much about the gameplay at all.
The story is the real selling point, and you can notice. Its dark, realistic, and I personally forgive the game's technical/gameplay shortcomings. I wholeheartedly recommend it for the storyline and music. This might not be an epiphany for you, but it'll definitely get you thinking about stuff.

"Do you feel like a hero yet?"
This line of dialogue has stuck with me for years after first playing The Line back upon release in 2012. The mediocre (yet solid) gameplay, is not this games main selling point.  It is instead the games haunting story and meta commentary on both the characters and audience that has etched this game into the memory of my friends and I for years.
The Line isn't really a game you "enjoy" playing, but it is a superlative representation of the artistic cabalities that are unqiue to gaming's interactive medium.
This is a game every person should play, nay... NEEDS to play.

Of course the game is based off the wonderful film Dawn of the Dead. As time goes on zombies go from slow staggering walks to all out sprinting. The zombies have decent variation, and I love the inclusion of child zombies. When you die in game your character becomes a sprinting zombie (sadly you can't play as it). The game includes a fair share of guns and melee weapons and there is a limit to the ammo (EXTREME LIMIT).
You are given the option of two gamemodes; survival and objective
In survival you, well survive, until rescue gets you. This is made difficult by the increasing number of zombies and their increasing speed. There are always supply crates laying around so you can heal, but they are all placed away from the main base so it's fair.
In objective you are to complete a series of tasks to get rescue to come and rescue you. The objectives usually include finding keyes or welding locks off of doors. The zombies seem to always be in the most convienient spots ever (for them).
Graphics wise, they aren't horrible. Animations are a little buggy sometimes and some of the NPC models could be updated but otherwise it's a good graphical experience.
Gameplay is smooth but requires a little getting used to, there are slight delays in reactions from NPC's but you can get over it because it is a good game. I do like how you board up windows, rather than having flying boards nail themselves to the wall (COD) you have to aim at where you want the board to go (in designated regions) and then you nail it in.
So yeah I give this game an 8/10 because it does become repetitive after a while.

I have played this game for little over a year now, with over 660 hours played and over £200 spend on ingame-items.
The game is fun when you first start. It is much like GTA but with factions added in. The gameplay can be very broken at times, and the server performance is very poor for EU servers. US servers are much better due to them having their hardware upgraded, so if you can, play on Joker (NA EAST) as it is the most stable server.
The community that resides around this game is like non-other. They will complain about anything and everything, but with good reason. It is only recently, that the game has made any progress in terms of quality of game-play, as the anti-cheat software was updated. The game went from using the free version of Punk Buster, to using Fair-fight, which saw a mass ban of cheaters for a short while. Due to the nature of this game, most cheaters will just create a new account and carry on the way they were. Major content updates are very rare, most updates are re-skinned guns, or clothing/car packs. Many features that we have been promised, such as a kill counter for events, are still yet to show their faces.
The support that is offered for transactions and other issues is not useful at all. It is dealt with by only 2-3 people, who will give you the same automated answer, even if it is not relevant to the ticket that you have made. The rest of the staff that you will com across throughout the game are all generally very pleasant people and good at what they do. Some of them are not so good, and often do controversial things which caused drama within the community, the latest of which is about many of the top tier NA players being accused of hacking and banned  hacking, or trash talking on the in-game VOIP software (Trash talking on VOIP is encouraged by in-game tips on loading screens).
In conclusion, if you want a semi-broken game to play with friends and dont have money to buy GTA, play this, but DO NOT spend any money on the game, otherwise you will end up like me (£200 out of pocket).

The goal is simple: survive
the mechanics are simple: each hex has one of 6 abilites you take on while standing on them
however, as each you kill you commit with one of the weapons (or ON on of the non weapons) gives that tile 1 out of 6 needed progress points to get an upgrade, the complexity starts to rise really quick. as each tile can only upgrade itself with tiles that are directly next to it, chosing your layout becomes very important. but upgrades ofcourse isn't the only thing you have to consider: On my first few tries i simply died because my layout just didn't have enough staying power against larger groups of enemies because i didn't build enough offense tiles in spots that i could actually use.
So trying to balance what you need from a tile and from it's upgrade and in which position exactly is a huge part of this game.
additionally: any enemy that you can't directly kill you can still push back (and of the map) if you are in a bind. and in some cases you are desperately trying to push a bomb bug off the map because you haven't upgraded your debuffing acid yet to destroy bombs... not to mention that there are also bugs that push you around.
I just wish the developer didn't go with a "angle and click" control scheme to move/attack, as that makes it very cumbersome to play on a touchscreen. a direct "click on tile" would be much more fluid.

A couple of tips to make this game more enjoyable:
Pros:

immersive music (no midis here)
Cons:
Childish / Hippie story line (the boss conflicts are all just the result of a misunderstanding)
ubiquitous insta-death
long sequences with no option to save (meaning you have to repeat the entire thing for one little mistake near the end)
Requires very precise movement and timing

lots of visual noise can make it hard to track the stuff that matters (your character, enemies, enemy projectiles, spikes created by enemy projectiles)
Ori is definitely at the Mario end of the platformer spectrum, with most difficulty and gameplay focusing on obstacles and pathfinding rather than combat.
It's combat system is downright minimalistic.  Your attacks will almost-always hit and you face only 1-3 enemies (most dying in 1-3 hits) at a time. The only fun part of combat is using your noncombat abilites (ground smash, rebounding off enemies/projectiles, etc.) to kill stuff.
Despite that, it's got a frustrating level of difficulty where you often die immediately because you overjumped by half your characters width.
The worst part, though, is the storyline. I don't know if it was written for preteens, by hippies, or just with a massive overdose of political correctness. Your quest is to revive the mystic forest you were born in (but left shortly after birth). All the NPC villains are more misunderstood than evil (one is just scared, another is trying to protect her child). It ends like a classic kids movie with everybody getting along and living happily together.

So here is the deal.  You can see how long I have played it.  Right now, at this time of the review, I have 75 hours in the game.  I have ONLY done the2 of the DLC.  I have beaten this game once through a torrent download, but I loved it so much I bought it.  I am trying to say, this game is HUGE and will take a long fricken time.  Now to the game.
BORDERLANDS 2:   Cue music.....
The STORY:
It is an action RPG basically.  You take the role of a guy that is on a newly terraformed planet.  Some stuff happens and you kill the bad guy.  I don't want to give up ANY of the story.  I don't want to ruin anything or any of the surprises this game will throw at you.  Just to clarify, I am one of the guys that told everyone that Han Solo dies, ugh, I did it again.  That is how much this game rocks.  The world is MASSIVE and immersive.  there is a story line which I assure you, is EXCELLENT writing.  Trust me, I am the most cynical critic of writing on the planet.  It makes Borderlands 1 feel like a tech demo.  If you want a definitive answer, then look at other reviews, or just play the game for gods sake.
The GRAPHICS:
60 FPS with an upscale to 1440 if need be.  It is very colorful and beautiful.  The game is cell shaded and yet it still looks realistic to a certain degree.  It is very fast paced.  There are ZERO lag spikes or fps spikes.  I first played this on a laptop from 2011 with the worstest of mobility cards and it was amazing, even at its lowest settings.
The CHARACTERS:
The voice acting is TOP NOTCH!  The villian is someone you truly want to hate.  The NPC's are believable and have decent voice acting.  You are a silent protagonist, which I understand many people dislike, but there is enough character interaction, that it isnt bothersome.  There are some new characters with the DLC.  I reccomend you get them.  Kreig, the psycho, is by far one of the best characters I have ever played in a first person shooter in my life.  Literally every skill is amazing.  Literally!
The Gameplay:
The elements of RPG are very good.  It plays just like a classic RPG.  If you go to an area at the wrong level, YOU WILL DIE 100% of the time everytime.  You will end up fighting creatures that are like 30 levels higher than you.  There is also a perk tree.  It gives you 3 main trees to choose from with 2 sub trees featuring a skill or perk you can level.  Things like, extra crit, extra gold, bonus reload speed ect.  With Krieg, the DLC character I just mentioned, he thrives on dying.  So his skills revolve around being killed and using your second wind to DESTROY everything.  Just get him, you will see. This game also has elemnts of an FPS.  It is very fast gameplay and requires aiming as well as the famous RPG element of percentage based attacks (like maybe a 20% crit for example).  There are tons of guns as you already know.  Millions.  You can get weapons with different elements or different firing styles or firing rates or whatever.  The possibilities are endless.   I am actually pretty amazed that the devs actually found a way to perfectly and flawlessly meld FPS and RPG.  Note: some grinding may be involved to proceed.
The VERDICT:
While the game is super fun to play, some grinding is involved.  But that is not a bad thing.  The gameplay is SUPER fun and not super repetitive.  You might need to grind for 30 minutes so you can access the next area so you don't immediatly die, but it only seems like 5 minutes went by.  Or you can just wing it and go to the next area and die a thousand times while killing an enemy here and there before you actually die, and level up that way.  Your call.  This game lets you explore at your pace and your free will.  You can say, "forget you" to the game and just go wing it and kill everyone and everything, or you can you proceed through the story and still kill everyone and everything.  Your call.  It is by far one of my favorite games with some of the best writing I have encountered in a long time.  It is highly addictive and exciting.  You WILL have those high anxiety fights.  You WILL have those times you die a million times.  You WILL have ultimate defeat, but you WILL have ultimate glory.  Just kill everything, collect everything, and f**k b*tches....

Ever since I was young I was fascinated by Trucks. I remember traveling a lot and seeing those huge cars on the road, imposing their presence on the other puny vehicles. They would carry equipment, containers, even other cars on their backs and their horns made such a powerful noise that was almost terrifying.
is one of the most relaxing experiences I've ever had in all my 20+ years of gaming. Nothing is more soothing, that driving a car from one place to another, delivering your goods, obeying the speed limit and the rules of the road (different on some countries!), having your radio on and enjoying the open road.
I know the game has developed sort of a cult status and in actuality there's a good reason for that. It promises you one thing and it delivers (HA!). A good approximation on how it feels to drive a truck. Gameplay wise the game has some depth with the ability to drive a truck and deliver good to your destination, all within the time limit and without you breaking or crashing into anything on the road/city. There are several European cities to travel from and to and DLCs which add even more. The driving is quite simple and easy if you choose it to be or you can opt into a more "realistic" approach.
You can buy your own truck and start your own company in a sort of career mode. Making money from deliveries, the more efficient you are, the more you earn. Some might argue that the novelty of the game wears off quickly but to each their own. For me, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a pretty solid game and quite a refreshing break from action games and I'm pretty sure you will find your own reasons to love the game. A definite recommendation for anyone who enjoys trucks, driving or just delivering things!

I can see from very extremely limited time with this game, that its going to be very deep, rewarding, and difficult..
You start by selectiong 1 of 3 classes Rogue, Warrior, Mage(2 of each class, of each gender, totalling 6).. Thats where the class system ends, and you can choose skills and stats however you like.. More akin to a classless system..
Combat is real time, ith a pause feature.. You can hotkey abilities, potions etc. but can only have one of them equipped at a time, and is used with the right mouse button.. Its actually visually appealing, even though its 15yrs old.. In all honesty, this IS my type of game... Im not sure if its because I have such a large unplayed backlog, if Im just not feeling this game, or if I just not in the mood because I know its going to take a serious investment learning, and playing throghj such a deep game.. But I am indeed having a hard time gett6ing started.. It doesnt help that theres no sense of direction, or help at the start.. Very much "heres your character.. GO!"  But its definitely going to be epic, if I can get myself over the initial hump!

In my opinion, Divine Divinity is a highly underrated action rpg. Although it has an incredibly cliché premise and setting, predictable story, and hilariously bad voice acting, all of these things almost work to the game's benefit. They make the characters surprisingly charming, funny  and memorable. Mechanically, it is derivative of both the Diablo and Ultima franchises, so it boasts some fast-paced combat and high amounts of environmental interactivity.
My recommendation here is somewhat tepid, however. I will warn players new to this game that the difficulty curve is all over the place. Some of the skills that your character can get are fairly useless while others can be enjoyment-shatteringly powerful under the right circumstances. Enemies which you can slaughter by the dozens with ease are sometimes mixed in with ones that can practically 1-shot you, which can be annoying if you want to do a melee-focused build. If unpredictable difficulty, frequent quick-saving and trial and error problem solving and character progression bother you, it may be best to avoid this title. Otherwise, there are plenty of helpful online resources, and this version comes with a digital copy of the manual in the game's files.

is even more action-oriented than HL itself. It feels like a HL episode condensed in the format of a
campaign and it doesn't last much longer.
You start right in the middle of the action and you'll feel compelled to fight your way until the end. Every fight is cleverly devised and there's not a single moment of boredom, even when the tension lowers.
There are no cutscenes or dialogues and, when it doesn't happen in front of your eyes, the story is told through the instructions that your mysterious employer sends you. Therefore, the action goes on basically without intermissions. That is not to say that the story isn't compelling and there's even room for a few unexpected twists.
Visually, the game is very well made; although the island's base where you start might not seem much, the further you go in and the more you'll appreciate the dirty, rusty human architectures of the underground bunkers and the coldness of the sinister Combine facilities. Again, even when you're not busy fighting, exploring the levels is interesting enough.
Finally, the game runs very smoothly and I've had zero issues of stability or bugs of any sort.
Absolutely recommended if you've finished all the episodes of HL2 and you feel you're not done fighting against the Combine.

Pretty large (free!) mod for HL2. It's a vast underground base similar to the citadel core (HL2-EP1), but unfortunately, quantity is not quality, and this one is more frustrating than fun, and difficult for the wrong reasons.
You'll likely get stuck miserably a couple of times because either the effect of buttons/levers is unclear, or -worse-, game progress (such as opening of doors) is triggered by clearing the area of enemies, so good luck finding that one last critter hiding in some corner while you walk around somewhere else wondering what to do or why a door is not opening. Extremely annoying. In other areas though, there are infinite enemy spawning points.
Your only communication with the outside world is an irritating text message system (plain text, no voice acting) which pops up to clog your screen at the most inconvenient moments and pester you with imbecile foul-mouthed rants ("what the ♥♥♥♥ are you doing, I don't have time all ♥♥♥♥ing day" etc).
The story/gameplay is very similar to the first half of HL2-EP1 (go down to the core, go back to the surface, confiscation fields, etc), which IMO was one of the weaker parts of the series. When I played EP1 and had to walk back into the citadel to stabilize it, and there was yet another elevator, yet another collapsing corridor, that feeling of "enough's enough, been there, done that" came up... Well, this mod feels like that almost the entire time, LOL.
I did finish it after all, but I was glad it was over when I reached the ending and, in hindsight, the whole ordeal felt like a goddamn waste of time.

Just list of most Game Mechanics and stuff in the game
##(Content "spoilers" not story)##
- Utilitys -
Electricity grid (Lights, Etc...).
Hot/Cold water pipes (Radiators, Showers, Sinks, Toilets, Sprinklers).
Electricity grid overload
Utility View mode
- Prisoners -
Prisoner Capacity.
Prisoner Mood (Health, Hunger, Environment, etc...).
Riots.
Gangs.
Prisoners can try to tunnel out over a certain period
Fights.
Low/Med/Max/Super Max prisoners.
Prisoner Programs(Education, Prison Labour, Drug Addiction, etc...)
- Building -
X 34 Rooms (Staff room, Cells, Canteens, Security, Showers, etc...)
Prebuilt rooms available.
Copy & Paste Rooms
Floor types (Metal, Wood, etc...).
Concrete/Brick wall type.
Logic circuits for opening/closing doors automatically(Not necessary but helpfull).
Security Systems (Hooked up via the Utility View Mode).
Each room has necessary objects available to place(Some are lacking)
- Other -
"Research" new staff and services.
Fire/Rain/Snow
Emergency Services.
Report Window (Prisoner intake, Meals, Loans, Grants).
Ability to toggle prison state (Shoot to kill, Lockdown, Shakedown(Prison search).

Janitors, Gardeners, Guards, Warden, Psychologist, Foreman, Lawyer, Sniper, Dog Units...
Guard Patrol Routes.
Staff needs (Available in BETA i've heard).
Able to assign guards to different section of prisons.

Dont build you prison with open routes available to edge of map, prisoners will escape and it can stop them from accesing the canteen and stuff (Use fences to seal off the prison and a large jail gate for the entrance).

Before I purchased this game, I had already owned the HD collection on my Xbox 360 and DMC4 on there too. I tried playing through DMC3 and it was quite enjoyable, however I feel like you can only enjoy the game truly by having some form of nostalgic value to it.
And this brings me to my review for DmC: Devil May Cry. This game enters a whole new realm of Devil May Cry, with a completely fresh storyline, new gameplay with how weapon switching was dealt with, and new ways to get around this amazingly designed world that is Limbo. There are 3 different guns to use, including the classic Ebony and Ivory, and 5 melee weapons, with Rebellion being one of them and the new idea of Angel and Devil weapons being implemented.
In terms of the combat I see mostly nothing wrong with it -- when you get your first SSS rank in combat it feels very rewarding with the voices that are said upon obtaining an S rank or above in Stylish rating. The weapons synergise very well, with "Deft" abilities being added to most weapons, meaning you can use a move on one weapon just by comboing with another weapon, e.g. using Rebellion then going into the Arbiter to do a Trinity Smash. The only problem with the combat is the gun called the Kablooey -- I feel it is too rewarding with the lack of effort you have to put in to use the weapon. I have reached SSS ranks just by blowing up a lot of enemies, which only requires me pressing X. Another problem is that Ebony and Ivory drop off very fast, with the shotgun being better to deal with most enemies, and the Kablooey being very overpowered.
The story is decent, being consistent all game and providing interesting and new ideas to the bosses in the Devil May Cry boss scene, the most intruiging one being the news reporter fight. Never in my life have I fought a giant digital head! The only thing with the story is that half the time you're not really focused on it and more on the fact that you're constantly being pulled into the world of Limbo, which I frankly care much more about -- the level design was practically perfect and the cutscenes were beautiful from start to end. The small flashbacks near the start of the game which sent you into quite peaceful broken worlds to unlock new abilities and weapons were extremely useful in helping me learn to play the game.
Now to address the start of my review. I am not an exprienced player in the Devil May Cry world, not having played the previous games when I was younger. From the perspective of someone who is new to the genre of Hack n' Slash or new to the Devil May Cry franchise, this game is probably your best bet into getting into the games as it will most likely pique your interest into the other games, as it did mine (I am going to finish DMC3 and play DMC4 now). However I feel like this DmC game is quite separated from all the other games, with just the characters' names and the idea of the brotherly story being the only part which links to Devil May Cry. A long-time DMC player will most likely tell you DMC3 and 4 are the best, however me being a fresh player I can say that you will probably only enjoy them more if you have a nostalgic link to them.

HITMAN is everything a Hitman game should be. After the massive dissapointment that was Absolution, IO decided to make an actual sequel and a worthy successor to Blood Money, and they pulled it off brilliantly. The level design is once again open and immersive, the objectives are interesting and fun to get to, and getting Silent Assassin is satisfying.
The disguise system is a clever mix of the systems of Blood Money and Absolution, meaning most people will be absolutely clueless to your presence, but some of them, named enforcers, will be able to see through your disguise, so you can't just go wherever you want once you get the right disguise like it was in Blood Money, but it's still nowhere near as obnoxious and boring as it was in Absolution.
The story is also exactly how it should be, interesting enough to get your attention while managing to stay out of the way of the gameplay. And I know a lot of people immediately disregard episodic releases, but if there's a game that deserves to adapt that model, it's Hitman, as it has always had an episodic structure that invites you to replay the same level over an over trying different routes and methods. The episodic release also allows the developers to maximize the polish in each level, and it shows.
TL/DR: Is good, buy.
This is just Season 1, but the game has enough content to justify the purchase. And in case the DRM was preventing you from getting the game, you should know that the Denuvo DRM has already been removed. That's because IO is now an independent studio, which means it's free from Square Enix's evil hands, but also that they need our support more than ever.

DAMN. Just finished playing. Let me start by saying that I'm a newbie for Hack n Slash games and the Devil May Cry franchise, so my review might end being highly subjective. 'Cause being an ignoramus on hack and slash games, it's a challenge to write a good and an objective review. But overall, this was just an awesome game, I enjoyed it very much, and I would reccomend it to someone who's completely new to the genre.
For me, the controls were a bit complex and it may have taken hours for me to get the hang of playing the game right.
But in the end, I think the controls were well designed and so were the combos that were difficult to execute at times because I'm an impatient person. The upgrade system didn't add much to the game for me, except for some essential combos and a few damage boosts. I think I wasn't looking enough for the variety the game would have offered. Probably because it was already complex enough and I kept on forgetting most of the combos constantly. So I played the game in a quite basic way, in the normal difficulty setting. Wasn't that hard, but a few bosses proved a satisfying challenge.
The atmosphere the game created was AMAZING. The game jumped immediately to a dark and intriguing cinematic experience. And after the first cutscene the action started right away, and with awesome music composed by Combichrist that just fit perfectly. The dialogues were cheesy and edgy on purpose but with some dark humor to lighten it up a bit. And one more thing I wanted to add about the music design is how well the transitions between running around, entering combat and finishing combat was made. The immersion never broke down.
The characters might have been a bit "one dimensional", except for Kat who you'll meet when you play the game :).
The story was mediocre, but the atmosphere revolving around the story and the setting made it feel better than it was.
I also liked the wide variety of enemy castes, and I saw how essential it was for the variety of combat itself. I bet half of the development time of this game went for the designing of these enemies.
The game had its usual average length of 9 hours but they tried to add some replayability by adding gameplay modes that remix the combat scenes and difficulty, which can be unlocked after completing the game.
Pros:
+Awesome music.
+Good bosses and gameplay overall.
+Immersion never broke down.
Cons:
-One dimensional story and characters.
TL;DR:
"being an ignoramus on hack and slash games, it's a challenge to write a good and an objective review. But overall, this was just an awesome game, I enjoyed it very much, and I would reccomend it to anyone who's completely new to the genre."
EDIT: For much easier and smoother gameplay, use a gamepad! In my case, an Xbox 360 controller.

I preordered the full version of this game and was extremely excited about its release... After the initial release my enthusiasm quickly turned into discust. At the time I couldn't even get the game to start and after I was able to fianlly get the game to start the whole experience was God awful. The optimization and game performance was horrindous, extremely glitchy, frame stuttering and unplayable. The specs of my gaming rig far surpassed the required specs for the game which could only mean that it was the game and not me... After several attempts to fix the situation I asked for a and recieved refund. About 5 months later, to my surprise I recieved a couple of episodes that were gifted to me be by one of my gamer friends that owed me a favor. Up until now (about a year after I recieved the gifted episodes) I have never played them for fear that the experience was going to be just as bad as the last. The other day I was bored and decided to go ahead and give them a try.
To my supprise everything had changed. The game loaded right up bug free! This is freaking great! Ever since Absolution I have enjoyed Hitmans extreme focus on detail oriented levels or maps. Everything and I mean EVERYTHING in a level is detailed in ways that aren't usually seen in other games. Cities are bustling with busy people and beutiful lanscapes. Although there are clones running around the Hitman team has made sure that these clones are far, few and inbetween. The "extras" as I cal them, are scattered around levels in a way that makes each busy lanscape seem totally real and immersive. There are times when I forget the target and just explore... Taking the time to look at every detail gives me a whole new appreciation for the Hitman team. They really want the gamers to feel like you are in Agent 47s world. I can't put into words just how detailed the enviornment of each level is. Its amazing how authentic everything seems. Absolution was the same way and Hitman: 2016 supprisingly does it better and I am loving every bit of it. The freedom that this games gives you to complete each assassination in your own way and playstyle is on the mark... You want to go in guns blazing then do it. You want to go in silent and deadly then do it. You want to mix things up and be the best of both worlds then you can do that as well. Without going into crazy details, just as in Absolution, there are so many different ways that you can complete your objective. Hitman: 2016 does this better as well... Not only are there more ways to dispose of your target but they are more creative. Beyond the common poisoning and random push off the balcony there are ways to kill your target that will inspire the most imaginative of assassins. Beyond everything that I just explained Hitman: 2016 goes above and beyond when you take it online. There is so much extra content offered online that I do not want to take the time to tell you about it. Not only would I be typing forever, but you would be reading forever as well. The best thing for me to do is tell you that the price for the full version (every episode) is 100% worth it just for everything that comes with Hitman: 2016 when you go online. It's unbelievable the extra bonus content you get with this game. To sweeten the deal, all of this is rolled up into a really engrossing and theatrical campaign with movie-star quality voice overs and a, award worthy musical soundtrack that puts a cherry on top of the whole thing.
When you factor in the crazy immersive and highly detailed levels and envioronments, the excellent replay value, the intuitive, responsive controlls, the ever changing online bonus content and the engaging storyline and campaign. You get an extremly wonderful and exciting game that is sure to keep you entertained for  100s of hours. I fell in love with Absolution and Hitman: 2016 has taken everything I loved about it and expanded on it 100 times and then some. If you enjoy the Hitman franchise then I am sure you will enjoy Hitman: 2016. If anything, you are more than able to purchase one episode just to give it a try. If you are going to go that route, in my opinion that makes Hitman: 2016 even better. Your not being forced into anything, but gently and gradually placed into it. If you don't like what your getting into then get out... It's a win win in my opinion, but then again all reviews are simply just that... An opinion. Its what you do with that opinion that really counts. All I have to say is that this game is great. You can either believe me ir not believe me. Its up to you. EIther way you still have my respect. That I can promise!

My first 150 hours of Rust have been incredibly enjoyable.
The gameplay isn't hard to get into once you know the basics, but there's always another way to do something better than before, and I really like that the PvP element pushes you to learn from your mistakes and improve your methods, whether it's constructing your base more efficiently or moving and dodging more effectively. What's more is that Rust continues to evolve with each update released. I'm always finding new ways to build bases and traps, and new tactics to outplay the people who live around me - and the updates just keep introducing new possibilities and styles of play. What makes Rust so good (in my opinion) is that it doesn't force you to play a certain way. Sure, you can go all-out with a big group and big guns, but if you'd rather trick your opponents and lure them into devious traps or ambush them while they're doing a recycling run, you can do that. The community continues to amaze me with unique tactics - you never know what to expect from another player.
While the visuals aren't exactly next-gen, they are VERY pretty and the sounds really match the ambience of the the overall game. Sitting in your base next to a barbeque while the sun sets and listening to the subtle crackling of the charcoal, or rustling through bushes in the pitch-black darkness of night and watching the moon-lit silhoutte of a deer on the horizon - it's beautiful.
I've heard many negative things about the recent twig and blueprint updates, and I too was sceptical at first, but after playing through it, I can wholeheartedly say that I support these changes and I think they really help the early-game stages stretch out - which is something that I feel is necessary for a survival game like Rust. I love that the team is still working hard on the game and producing regular updates with new and interesting content.
TL;DR: Great gameplay, great visuals, great fun.

I got this game about a week prior to this review and have spent a few hours each day after work to play it.  While it seems pretty solid at first it quickly becomes a serious test of patience.  after about 2 hours of gameplay, the cons list just quickly grew including problems such as: a bugged save system, bugged quests that prevent the completion of other unrelated quests, stuttering issues, sound erupting into bursts of static every so often, and exceptionally slow progression.  Other issues I had were with character development.  you get to choose from 3 classes: warrior, mage, rogue; but you're really shooting yerself in foot if you don't pick warrior from the beginning as anything else will have a REAL hard time surviving.  Granted, there is no limitation on skills you pick, i.e. just cus you roll warrior doesn't mean you don't have access to mage skills.  but if yer like me and wanted to roll pure-mage, well good luck and have fun teleporting to the one bed you can rest in every 2 minutes just to regen mana.  all this aside i figured i'd try and muscle thru but after reading that just one playthru can take upwards of 70 hours to complete, i can definitely say i don't have the patience for this. there are positives tho, while combat can be meticulous and infuriating at times (try not to mistakenly attack a cat or  else every cat in the known universe will come after you) the spells and skills can be a lot of fun (hell spikes and freeze were some personal favorites).  If you are a die hard ARPG fan or fan of the series (and it is a great series) and can muster the patience to play this game, go for it, I imagine it would be very rewarding as the story seems pretty dope with a good blend of humor.  keep in mind however, if you're playing this because you think you need it for some background to Divinity 2 or Original Sin well don't even sweat because you don't. both titles i just mentioned provide more than enough in-game lore to keep you up to snuff with what's going on.
In summary, I wish i could get into this game and recommend it but there are just too many bugs and design issues that keep me from getting immersed.  I know it's going for like $2.00 during summer sale, so if you absolutely need to try it, pick it up while it's on sale.
EDIT: Divine Divinity is $0.59 during summer sale, so go ahead and pick it up if you want to put the time into it, just don't get too attached.

This mod is a god dam masterpiece.
If you take the time to explore every single corner, one playthrough will keep you busy about as long as one of the episodes. I spent three hours playing it and I loved every single minute of it (that's a lie, but you get the idea).
This thing is outstanding in every single aspect. I almost quit during the first five minutes as the combat was rather hard on "Normal" difficulty, but once I switched to "Easy" it was pretty manageable and I found all following combat encounters to be set up in a rather good manner. Throughout the game, it is always pretty obvious which gun you are supposed to use and unless you want to be constantly out of ammo, you actually need to use most of them.
The maps are beautifully built and I'd give this thing 5 out of 5 stars for visuals alone. They're very well detailed and, I can't find another word to describe it, immersive. Whereas "average" maps always feel extremely artificial and linear, consisting of a series of rooms stringed together for gameplay purposes, this mod's maps feel extremely authentic and real, making you feel like you actually are in this place. Although in the end they are as linear as most Half-Life² maps, the whole thing feels extremely open-world-ish at times, since you have to explore, backtrack and move around a lot. I promise you'll have lots of "wait, THAT'S where I am?" moments when the brilliant map design leads you to re-visit a place seen earlier in the map. Also, the Combine parts of the map are way more Combine-ish than the citadel in Half-Life² ever was, and that's the highest praise I have to give.
Despite featuring plenty of gunfights, the mod also contains lots of puzzles, which are fun and rather challenging. A couple times, I had to google for solutions, only to realise afterwards that the puzzles were actually really obvious. The author makes it impossible for players to mess up in a way that renders the puzzle impossible - another proof of excellent design.
The soundtrack is very pleasant to listen to, if I understand correctly, it is a mixture between stock HL2 songs and custom ones. The story is very compelling and low-key reminiscent of that of Portal. Unlike with certain other mods, this story actually drives the game forward and makes the whole map come alive. Until right before the end, I was curious to find out what was going to happen next.
I've said it before, this thing is a masterpiece. It looks, feels and sounds as if it belongs right into the Half-Life universe, in fact, despite having nothing to do with Episode 3, this one feels like the most worthy successor to Half-Life² I have seen to day. The guy who created this was hired by Valve shortly after, and I dare say, he dam well earned it. Hats off.

I started on Minerva some number of years ago then dropped it because reasons. Recently I wanted to play something HL2ish, so I reinstalled and beat it this time.
, but I found myself getting frustrated or stuck more often than not:
A few of the rooms felt like playing "find-the-button" to progress, and I got turned around and confused in the first indoor area constantly. A couple of other areas weren't clear in what to do next, even after extensive exploring on my part. In fact, when I resorted to a video walkthrough for two specific places that I got hung up on, the author of the walkthrough had also gotten stuck at those same locations unsure of how to proceed.
The AI difficulty here seemed higher than in the original HL2; I swapped over to "easy" mode about halfway through because the baddies all felt like bullet sponges with more health than I recall them having in HL2 proper (although it's been even longer since I've played that, so maybe I'm just bad at video games these days). Their movements were very erratic and far from tactical, running down hallways and circling around for no apparent reason other than to never stop moving. It was like a goofy cartoon scene sometimes.
Minerva presents some fun twists on the HL2 formula, and there's some impressive level design displayed when revisiting previous areas after certain events take place. Overall I'm glad to have played through it, but I'm unsure of how to recommend it. I can't tell if most of my gripes stem from Minerva specifically or HL2 gameplay in general.
Minerva is worth a shot if you want to revisit HL2 with some fresh content, but unless you've really got that urge, you may want to pass.

Spec Ops: The Line is a very solid third-person shooter, with one of the most interesting takes on story of any modern day action game.
The gameplay is nothing to write home about. Stick to cover, order your squad mates around. Regenerating health, two weapons. Pop out, aim and shoot. It's mostly Gears of War without much reliance on chainsaws and such. There's nothing about this game's actual play to make it really stand out, other than the fact it is solid, entertaining, and quite challenging at times. The shooting is satisfying, and should keep you satisfied through the game's average running length.
The only real issues I ever faced were the usual annoyances with any third-person cover shooter. Running around like an idiot trying to stick to some object while you're being shot, instead of just being able to duck.
However, the reason you play this game is for the story, and the way it is presented. It's the kind of open-ended, interpretive narrative that people write their thesis about. It is as much an exploration on the nature of war and atrocity, human nature, and psychological trauma as it is a shooting game.
It's not the most interesting or profound experience you will ever have, but I think it's definitely worth going through at least once. Any vague hints will only spoil the experience, so I will only say that it's worth playing.
Great writing is something I feel should be rewarded these days, since it's seemingly more and more rare to come across it.

If you enjoy watching pros play this game on Youtube, then keep watching it on Youtube. Playing the game itself is a much different experience and I heavily regret dropping 33 bucks into this game. It's NOT READY. Not even close. It has a really long way to go before it's servicable and in its current state, 22$ CAD is way too much. This shouldn't be priced anywhere above 10$ because the value just isn't there. People are gonna call you salty if you get mad at this game. You will get mad, you will be salty and if you lose too many fights and lose too many bases you're gonna finally be humble enough to walk away from this game like I did. I have some bullet points explaing my issues with this game but I'll be less formal to start. The people on this game aren't "funny" like you've seen in youtube videos, they don't talk to eachother. They kill eachother. This game is not noob friendly. Everything and everyone is going to try to kill you and take everything you own and burn down what they can't take with them. And they will succeed. You will die, a lot. I have no problem with the developers of this game. They've made a decent game that is a little overpriced and visibly unfinished. It is the community that butchers any sense of enjoyment. I thought it was funny at first how toxic it was. But it is too toxic. And yes, I am salty.
1. Toxic Community (the sALT)
Players in Rust are hostile, offensive and above all else...SALTY. Some encounters with players can by pleasant but it's mostly people killing eachother over resources (which is a traumatic experience, given how hard it is to gather much of anything). Most conversations between players are people blasting music over their mic, players swearing and saying some pretty racist things and threats of real life violence. None of this is surprising apart from the racism and swearing since servers claim to have banned this behaviour. If they have then they've done a pretty terrible job so far.
2. PVP combat (slow, clunky, laggy)
The combat looks absolutely stupid. It's looks like gmod character models swinging rubber crowbars while jumping and strafing as best as the engine can handle it. Frame drops and lag issues tend to ruin fights and doesn't pair well with the slow, clunky movement controls. Most weapons lack any feeling of impact apart from some guns which actually control and handle pretty well. The issue with that is that guns are SO difficult to come by so you'll be getting shot with them more than you'll actually be holding one.
3. Resources gathering (Minecraft did it better)
Gathering wood and stone to make your first house takes RIDICULOUSLY long. Hatchets/Picks, foundations/walls/roofs and upgrading them to stone costs a LOT of resources. Actually mining all of it to make a solid base can potentially lead up to 1/2 an hour to a full hour of JUST grinding. For this reason, the stakes of fights with other players are just too high. If you lose a fight after grinding enough to build a house then you've lost a half hour at least. And if you couldn't find enough cloth to make a sleeping bag then you'll be respawned on the other side of the map. Good luck there.
4. Raids (offline raids, accesible to few)
ALL of the the raids I experienced happened offline. Around 2:00Am to 4:00Am was primetime for people to often blow open my front door and chop my body and sleeping bag and clear my house of all loot and furnishings. Raiding other people takes explosives or serious mining tools which, let's be honest. Unless you have a clan or a friend or two who are masters at this game and know where to look for the right components, you're not making these anytime soon, So raiding is only for the rich to grief the less fortunate.
5. No room for nakeds (noob killing, no tutorials)
This is actually a phenomenon that I don't see in a lot of other games. Sure enough call of duty/battlefield/any multiplayer game makes fun of noobs but usually there are a few people willing to teach someone the ropes. But Rust treats noobs horribly. People often camp the beaches and shoot new players who have just spawned in. There isn't a tutorial or any fellow players to teach nakeds how to even play the game so they're thrust into the game world where they're killed for sport over and over again. I understand the idea of "earning the right to be good" through player encounters and getting in fights but that doesn't work when people with guns are shooting you for your rock and torch.
If you havent heard of it yet, Ark is another survival game. It looks like clans are easier to join and that there is a little less player interaction since a large focus of the game is NPC dinosaurs that you can tame.It too seems overpriced at 80$ Canadian but it has some semblance of finish to it. It has many of the same problems from what I can tell but what I do know is that in terms of survival games, Rust still has a long way to go. Don't waste your time or money here, there are better games that can offer a much better expierience at a better price. Hopefully in a few years this game is finished but the community isn't going to be changing anytime soon. Stay salty.

As somebody who has owned every single Hitman game and has been a fan of the franchise since being a child, I 100% put my seal of approval on this title.
I always thought Blood Money was the strongest in the franchise, but after playing this I'm going to change that answer. Hitman improves on what made Blood Money so great. It keeps the general idea of doing individual contracts instead of some annoying story (looking at you there Absolution). I vastly improves on various mechanics, like the NPC AI. It feels so much more alive and realistic than any of the previous titles and adds a bunch of new features such as opportunities which are great. The disguise system is the best one implemented in the franchise and god rid of the awful system that Absolution used. Instead of anyone wearing the same outfit of you getting suspicious, now only people who it would make sense to be suspicious will be. Such as managers and team leaders who would know their staff.
I won't give too much away, I suggest giving it a go and finding out first hand how amazing this game is, whether you're a long time Hitman fan or a complete newbie to the franchise.
I should note that you need a pretty good PC to be able to run it though, with the huge maps and densely populated areas it can be quite demanding on your resources.

I haven't played the first 3 games of the HITMAN franchise but having played Hitman: Blood Money and Absolution, this game has been the best. First, I will have to appreciate the art and level design. It's just amazing. Each room looks hand-crafted and even a bathroom has so much work. It's truly appreciated.
The conversation from many individuals is so natural and syncs with the scene. I got caught at times because of popping of an unexpected civilian. Although it frustrated me, I actually find it interesting. It's not surprising when a normal civilian notices your crime but I have a feeling that their movement paths are pre-defined. You might think that the coast is clear and start subduing a guard or the target and there is a chance for a civilian to show up.
I'm glad they removed the instincts feature from Absolution where almost every crew of that respective disguise gets suspicious. Only the head crew or sometimes the target will get suspicious upon seeing you. Running doesn't get you to trouble so feel free. You can fool the AI quite easily at many places but that's in normal mode. Still haven't tried Professional mode.
We have this new feature called 'Opportunity'. There are quite many in a mission and you can use these to isolate the target and offer you a free kill. This is really convenient for players who are new to the HITMAN franchise.
I keep replaying each episode until I complete enough challenges and I'm only 2 episodes in. This game has a lot of replayability. It even has bonus missions. Go ahead and buy the game. It's totally worth the price.
