The only I remember about Spec Ops franchise back when my childhood days, its on Playstation X where the gameplay resembles and looks like Army Men franchise but with real soldiers as character you play in the realistic setting, after long years forgotten I found this game recommended as a game that every shooters and military genre fans should try. I played and finished this game twice when for the first time, I played it curiously because of the unconventional plot and great storyline about how bad the outcome of being in combat and military environment to question your morality as in the process to finish the game. And secondly, I re-played for fun and also make little bit different choices on the gameplay where SO:TL is basically third person shooter with linear plot but still give choices to its player to see what will we choose for better decisions on combat that later affects how we see the characters we play (that basically the player themselves) about the deed we have done every each chapter. One thing for war : Kill or be killed, or you dont have to?
Here is my review:
PLOT :
You are Martin, an idealistic soldier with high rank as captain. Along with your two partner and subordinate. You are deployed into a post-natural disaster state on Dubai, a city that was wiped by the standstorms. And here is your task, a simple task: Find survivors and mysterious radio signal that presumed as evacuation from inner city with civilian survivors and armies that you have to face in combat and later leads you into a journey of our main character mental state of mind choices where your partner question a lot about your decision into deep rabbit hole with the intense of inside city battles which you dont fight your enemy but also your sanity.
As a military shooter game, the plot will drag you into philosophical questions about choices and your realization (as player) to continue fighting and also SO:TL will deconstruct the whole thing of being what is right and what is wrong in military combat with realitic touch how are you the hero of this story when you have to fight what you tought is right as your duty.
CONTROL :
Grab your controller or simply use mouse+keyboard, the control is pretty responsive with stunning graphic and dynamic camera movement that shows third person perspective which makes this game easy to enjoy and not really hard when you are in combat, I personally use normal mode and found its challenging because as in combat you have to think on every single move you have to do.  As main character, you can bring two type of guns and explosives where you can find along the gameplay or you can simply grab your enemy weapons after being taken down. As a captain, you can order your two partners (as AI) to use their skills in order to solve the thightness in some combats where they can shoot specific enemies or doing distractions to move forward. The gameplay set some realitic tone when it comes to your health system, you wont see any healtbar or indicator, just avoid massive of gunfires from enemy or you instantly being killed, your character can survive if your partners maintain their distance in order to save you if you are taken down. Probably, the annoying side of control system is when the cover system in combat have false detection in deciding to take cover or moving forward.
VISUAL :
Enjoy stunning visual of post-disaster state of Dubai where sky scrappers are being torn and crushed buried among desert hills, walk and explore straight into miserable places of war casualties and what left that you will experience. Some parts are athmospheric and you may find some disturbing scenes (that involves with the plot) This game visual will touch your minds (literally) and your character mind when they face some odd strange situations where leads you into questioning, are you enjoying this kind of game, or you just feel something else. Moreover, this game have to offer interesting side of how music really influences how you perceive this game as serious but sometimes (in the early parts of games) it have the fun part of musical cues that can be enjoyed while you shoot everyone. The voice acting are top-notch and convincing that the characters you are playing have the situation as in the game.
FUN :
SO : TL have good tier storyline where I assumed eventhough the plot sounds cliche at the first time (about a soldier being a hero and typical American shooters where glorifies its greatness and you act like another Rambo in this game, eventually, I was wrong. This games have no fun when you really think of how it projects what is great being American soldier or simple being a soldier when facing the outcome what you did on the entire gameplay. Yes, you do mass killing people and blow some ♥♥♥♥♥ to progress, its fun on video game medium. But when SO : TL approaches of realistic tone of this kind of genre. It has the plus point where I stated this game deconstructs what is kind of type shooter genre looks like mostly, and this game prove us wrong.
If you like playing shooter game with great storyline and message, grab this game and experience your state of thought will be filled the consequences of various feeling on your main character decision and choice by the hand of yourself as the player in the challenging of combat system but still rewards you an thought-provolong experience.

Not played a decent 2D platformer since Yoshi's Island on my SNES back in the 90's!
This is an Ori-ginal platformer (surely someone's cracked that pun already!?) and I've had loads of fun playing it so far.
Beautiful environments, beautiful gameplay, beautiful audio, and a beautiful control system make this a pretty special game. If you're after a decent, modern, challenging 2D platformer, look no further.

+ Extremely good puzzle design
+ Different gimmicks for each main "dungeon" keep you on your toes
+ Beautiful character animations
+ Responsive controls (I used an XBox controller)
+ Fun, useful abilities and unlockable skills
- Quick travel ports too sparse
- Frustratingly hard even on easy mode
- No checkpoints, and saving isn't always accessible
- Not particularly original with the types of dungeons (Fire, ice, etc.)
- Sometimes hard to tell foreground objects from interactable objects. (Not fun when you leap onto a "platform" straight into lava.)
- Occasionally difficult to tell apart objects that will hurt you from safe ones
* Story was serviceable but not excellent
* Soundtrack has some great songs during cutscenes and chase sequences. It's forgettable but not distracting the rest of the time
Mixed feelings on this one. I wish Steam had the option to give a neutral review.
It was at the three-hour mark or so, inside the Ginso tree, that I realized I wasn't having fun. I hadn't been enjoying myself the entire game, actually. At that point I stopped and switched to easy mode, thinking it would let me relax and enjoy the story.
Easy mode only does two things for you: it makes enemies have lower health and attack power, and it gives you a handful of checkpoints during escape sequences. That's it. It doesn't stop you from having to use energy for each save, or let you save in places you normally can't. It doesn't turn insta-kill hazards into damaging ones, remove any of the spikes, add more platforms to difficult areas or make
of the obvious changes that would make the game more accessible. The unforgiving platforming mechanics are identical. Say what you like about unskilled players; when there's an "easy" version of the game, I believe it should respect the player's wish to play through the story without screaming in frustration.
As for the story itself...first it's worth mentioning that Ori's world is cleverly designed to be one giant puzzle, with rewards at the end of every difficult sequence of jumps. That's great from a gameplay perspective. Unfortunately, this prevented the world from actually feeling like a
to me. It's fun to explore because you're looking for power-ups, not because any of the areas are particularly interesting or memorable themselves. The five or so main characters appear to be the only ones living in the entire forest. Everything else tries to kill you. It's similar to the feeling that I got while playing Skyward Sword―the world's design is too calculated for it to seem like a real, tangible place.
Then comes the actual writing. The plot starts out promisingly enough. It pushes you through a sort of interactive cutscene, where reactions to certain parts of the story (as told by a narrative voiceover) are actually scripted into your movements. I can't recall anything quite like it. It's also helped along by some fantastic character animations, which really bring the adorable cast to life.
Unfortunately, from there it turns into a fairly typical videogame plot where your goal is to collect MacGuffins to restore the power of an ancient tree. Dialogue is limited to clunky exposition from your companion Sein. Often huge plot points are never fully explained. For instance,
The writing's decent, but the focus is definitely on gameplay.
TL;DR: I might have liked Ori more if it hadn't been so hyped up, particularly in the story department. I found the story pleasant but not as emotional as I expected. The main issue was that difficulty simply wasn't right for me, and easy mode did nothing to change that.  I'm glad I had the chance to experience this game and see what all the fuss was about, but by the end I was only playing because I wanted to finish it properly, not because I was enjoying the game itself; I can't imagine wanting to sit through the same frustration again.

Does it still hold up?
♥♥♥♥ yes, it does. Let me ramble real quick about it.
San Andreas improved literally everything from the previous games, from the better engine to the story, everything is top notch.
Ever since GTA III that the franchise gradually became more story focused but San Andreas is where Rockstar went all out. It features a really integrate plot that perfectly ties everything between the events in Vice CIty and III. You get the most memorable characters with real personalities in GTA along with the best protagonist in the franchise. The story finally deviates from cliche mafioso plot and is much longer and broken into multiple chapters that bring you to different places, you start in a guetto and suddenly you notice you own a casino in the big Las Venturas. Gladly the pace is flawless, it's just the right time and the story doesn't really contain any unecessary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The narrative and theme of the game is very unique and was pretty controversial when it came out.
The Special Edition of the game even contains a 20 minute cutscene with a ton of backstory and insight on the development of characters and events before the game starts:

This intro alone has more emotion and is better written than the entirety of GTA V. I wish that wasn't the case but sadly no other GTA game has surpassed San Andreas in terms of story and immersion.
The map in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, one of the best open world maps in my opinion. Rockstar didn't waste any space, everything is unique and has content and most of the time you get to explore cool places thanks to side missions. It features three very distinctive islands with big cities, countryside, a big mountain, a desert, loads of cool easter eggs. This was a big game changer for the franchise, the most we had before was 2 small islands with the same kind of aesthetics and you couldn't even swim or fly high. The map feels huge and I still prefer it to GTA V's take on San Andreas.
The refined engine really makes vehicule handling pretty ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, it brings tons of new mechanics to the game and prettier graphics. You have a much bigger selection of vehicules from sport cars to bikes, boats, planes and some very cool unique vehicules like the Vortex and the Kart.
Finally the soundtrack is very important to a GTA game, and this game simply has the best soundtrack in the franchise, only Vice City comes close but San Andreas has such a nice variety of genres that fit perfectly with the multiple settings. From listening to Radio Lost Santos in the hood to roaming endlessly listening to K-DUST in the desert. It's just too ♥♥♥♥ing good.
I probably forgot to mention a lot of things but I just finished it and wanted to get my thoughts out asap, I'll probably come back later and add more stuff.
Overall, It's still the best Grand Theft Auto game and I'm glad I replayed it again.

Minerva: Metastasis
Something has to be said for a game, especially a free one, that has me playing and beating it more than once on different difficulty settings.  It has to be something that is able to both catch and hold my attention, with an interesting story and great game play.  Few free single player mods capture this as much as Minerva does.
From start to finish it is a very well thought out and planed mod.  It is hard to believe a single person made all this, with the exception of the music I believe.  I do not want to spoil too much, but this island and it's beautiful beaches is certainly not a vacation hot spot in the tropics and there are dark secrets buried beneath all that pristine white sand...  From the moment you are dropped in you have to be on your guard and take down the nasty Combine and their Overwatch fiends.  Along the way you get coded messages sent to you by your employer and she (?) seems not too fond of you either.  After all, you are a traitor to both humanity and the Overwatch alike, being one of their own bio-engineered soldiers gone rogue.
There really is not much to complain about, maybe only suggest.  The computer voice in your head would of been much better done had it used a real voice, preferably a female's.  Surely the moder could have had a sister, a friend or another female they knew lend their voice for the role.  If not that, at least allow us to pause the game to read the text that pops up or allow us to view them later at our leisure.  In a lot of the examples you are in an intense fire fight and do not have time to seek cover and reload, much less to read the messages fully.  Then you will have to reload the last save to try and read it all again and fight the same battle you just fought.  And the little tidbits of information is worth it.
Also perhaps a co-op mode would have been the shinning jewel already on the golden crown, but perhaps that is asking for too much from one man.  Besides that though, there really is not cause to complain except perhaps you have to have HL2 Ep1 to play it.  Not every one in the community went out and bought that extra content.  (Although you should for it's own merits and Ep2 while you are at it!)  However with out it, it would not of looked as good as it did either.  I can see why Valve picked this person up to be on their team.  Do yourself a favor and pick this up!

Having never played the previous DMC games, I was worried if this game was worth the price during the summer sales. Despte some issues I was unfazed about, it was a satisfying experience as i was playing the game. The story mode started with a bang and you are thrown into action right away. From there, you will get to learn Dante's background and the ongoing violence around you. I would suggest those who have not played the previous series should set their difficulty to at least Devil Hunter as Human level is too easy and it may get too hard for newbies on nephilim. On Devil Hunter, you will encounter some deaths and face a satisfying number of challenges, something good for people who are trying to get into the series. Ok, now it is time for the pros and cons.
PROS:
- Great story. It got me engrossed for the most of it as I uncover theevents that apear in the upcoming missions
- Superb voice acting. The voice actors really did a great job, it really brought the characters alive
- Combat was fun. It is not your typical button-mashing game where you just blindly smash the buttons to defeat yur enemies, each enemy actually must be dealt differently which makes the combat more interesting and the players to have a great deal of tactical awareness and proficiency
CONS:
- DLC: Vergil's Downfall. Ok, I admit that I was not really keen on playing as Vergil. The DLC is pretty short with only a few missions and it would have been better if they have added more.To make matters worse, the DLC did not feature many CGI cutscenes and only the animated cutscenes were shown which made the game feel cartoonish
- 30 FPS in cutscenes. I am not sure why the in-game cutscenes are showing good FPS but not for this? Really disappointed after encountering these scenes
All in all, DMC is still a good game and I had fun playing this after 10 odd hours. I would recommend you to get this when there is a big discount on it as I thnk it is pretty pricey now.

Been a huge fan of the HITMAN series pretty much for as long as I can remember and I can safely say that this new iteration is the return of HITMAN that I have been waiting for. I was somewhat sceptical of the episodic release format deployed by the developers but for this particular game, it works well. To summarise:

They've taken everything you love from previous Hitman games and implemented each detail to form a pleasant world, offering a variety of ways to ply your trade and once again become 47.
This type of level design could enthrall any type of player:
The silent assassin type would benefit alot from planning. The proper execution of a plan on a level of this size would give anyone the satisfaction of an honest day's work.
The mass murderer has alot to mass murder.
The "I'm just walking around" type could very well enjoy the aesthetics without murdering anyone.
My point is, HITMAN appeals to every type of audience with ease and style.
Try some Opportunities. Those will help you learn the level fast. And trust me, there is quite alot to learn for each Destination.
Try featured contracts. I mean, the amount of content this game has to offer is almost endless, considering the Contracts system from Hitman Absolution, some bonus levels and perhaps the Elusive Target system.
Try walking up to them and chat them up, see what happens. Maybe offer them yoga lessons. That always ends well for them.
Also, as far as i understand, the original developer has gotten rid of their corporate overlords and now have complete control of the franchise. I can't wait to see where they're gonna go from here and I expect nothing but great games from them in the future.

This game was on my list for a long time because of the overwhelming praise that I heard about it. I went in expecting a deep story filled with tough choices relating to the horrors of war. After playing it, I feel like it was slightly over-hyped. What I got was a fun 3rd person shooter with an interesting war story, but one that lacked much choice or a shocking end that I was lead to believe it had.
The game is set in a sandstorm-decimated Dubai that was at its peak. A battalion of US soldiers were sent in to rescue the civilians but then contact is lost. Due to the constant sandstorms surrounding Dubai, only a squad of 3 is sent in to find out what happened, and this is their story. What you find in Dubai early on is that the battalion has gone rogue after abusing their power, and you are stuck between local rebel forces and the rogue battalion. Both of which want you dead.
If I ignore the expectations, this game is still a solid shooter. The graphics hold up ok from 2012 if you crank the hell out of the back-end settings, and the story is an interesting tale about war and the horrors that men are capable of.
Pros
- Solid shooter mechanics with basic squad command features
- Great voice acting
- Engaging team dynamics
- Interesting setting and story
- A good, short campaign at 5-6 hours
Cons
- Choices you make do not alter the story as much as hoped
- Ending fell a little flat on me

Divine Divinity is most likely one of the greatest isometric Hack-&Slay-RPGs of all time, including a well written story about demons, necromancers, heroes and cats. The land Rivellon is torn apart by war, civil unrest and greed...a group of fanatic villains and madmen created ways to bind a divinity for the sole reason of destroying the world. The tortured divinity managed to escape and blessed the upcoming hero with her divine light.
What will happen next is for the player to decide. Rivellon is a very large land that contains many side stories, quests and characters. The player is able to choose out of six different heroes - warrior, mage and thief, every class has a female and male counterpart - and can further customize the hero with several skills, lots of weapons and many clothes. The graphics did age well and the combat is simple but enjoyable.
I recommend Divine Divinity to everyone who likes Baldur's Gate, well written oldschool-RPGs and cats.

One of the best Half-Life 2 mods ever made-- so good, in fact, that Adam Foster was hired on by Valve because of it (and no, he wasn't arrested on the tarmac like the loser who leaked the HL2 beta.)
You play a reprogrammed Combine soldier tasked by a rogue AI with investigating a mysterious Combine controlled island. The level design and architecture is tight and very reminiscent of the Covenant ships in HALO. Enemy encounters are extremely challenging-- this is harder than vanilla HL2, but absolutely survivable on Hard difficulty if you keep your wits about you. It can be occasionally frustrating; It's not entirely clear when and if an enemy mob will continue to spawn endlessly, keeping you on your toes as to whether to camp or advance. The story is delightfully vague and actually rather spooky because of it, narrative being delivered to you through sudden environmental epiphanies or cryptic emails from your all-knowing, condescending heirarch.
I've been following this mod since back when it was a single, unfinished episode. There is a point toward the end where a lesser modder would have thrown in the towel and said, "The End" with a giant middle-finger, but with the support of Valve, Mr. Foster was kind enough to include a final, adrenaline-pumping episode to wrap things up with a happy ending.
If you enjoy this then I also highly recommend one of Adam's earlier pieces, "Someplace Else", a mod for the original Half-Life. It shares many of the same themes as Minerva.
Possibly the best mod for HL universe ever created. Hands down.

DmC: Devil May Cry exists in a really odd space.  On one hand, veterans of the DMC franchise are going to look down on it for it's simpler combat that doesn't offer fine control or complex, rewarding mechanics of games such as DMC 3 or DMC 4.  It is a significantly easier game and there is a lot less put into the fighting mechanics of the game itself.
On the other hand, DmC: Devil May Cry offers is a refined experience that I think most people will enjoy!  Despite it's flaws when held up to it's predicesors,  DmC offers smooth combat and top-notch presentation.  The major criticism I'd offer are that the boss fights are boring, QTE-ridden, forgettable snore-fests.
It's definitely not a bad game and as long as you are willing to remove expectations for DMC 5 from this title and accept it for what it is, it's a fine game by itself.

I had reviewed this game earlier, but deleted that review because, looking back at it, it seemed more like a "gripe session" as opposed to an actual, honest review. So, here we go again.
Which is actually a good place to start. Arkham Origins is the third game in the "Arkham" series, and has the distinction of being the only one NOT developed by Rocksteady. Rather, this game was developed by Warner Montreal, and that seems to be both a blessing and a curse.
It's a blessing because they're more willing to try new things, such as adding new gadgets or introducing new villains. Some of these ideas work and some don't, but it's refreshing to deal with something/someone we haven't seen before, rather than trying to find a new spin for a gadget/character we've already seen twice before.They've also "loosened" the combat system, allowing potential combos into the triple digit ranges.
The curse to come through in different ways, seemingly from a lack of understanding of either what made Arkham Asylum and Arkham City great, or through a seeming lack of knowledge regarding the source material itself. Here's an example: In Origins, you obtain a new gadget, the Remote Claw, where you aim, and hit the target, whereupon the claw  launches half of itself to a second target. You also encounter a new villain, the sinuously evil Copperhead. Both good, because it shows WB Montreal is trying to put their own mark on the series, but also disappointing, because the majority of the game, the remote claw serves the EXACT same function as the Line Launcher from the previous two games. Copperhead meanwhile, serves much the same function of poisoning Batman with a hallucinogenic venom, a la the absent Scarecrow's fear toxin. It would have made for a better mark, in my opinion, if the developers had focused instead on the flexibility of Copperhead, and required you to use the Remote Claw to lash her to the surroundings through multiple successful launche/hits.
The unfamiliarity that WB Montreal had with the source material, in this case both the comics AND the previous two games, manifested in other ways during the story. Arkham Origins is a story that itself replaces the absent Two-Face: It tries to tell a prequel to Arkham Asylum and explain what happened at Blackgate Prison that led to the inmates being sent to Arkham proper, but it also tries to tell an origin story of Batman encountering his enemies (Most notably the Joker) for the first time, and the two stories don't mesh well.
If it's an origin story for Batman, why does he have ALL of the same equipment that he uses in both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. Surely he would have upgraded SOME of his equipment (incorporating his Cryptographic Sequencer into the armor, instead of a separate gadget, comes to mind).
If ir's simply an origin story for the Arkham series, why introduce the majority of the villains as though Batman has never encountered them before, such as the aforementioned Joker. For much of the game, he's an unknown villain. Again, the "split-decision" doesn't really work.
Overall, I found Arkham Origins to be fairly satisfying, with the exceptions as noted above, but I DID encounter a MAJOR, MAJOR drawback. I don't know if I was experiencing a hardware glitch, or if it was a programming problem, but I frequently had active enemies just disappear from my screen (Killer Croc, in one play through), and had numerous "freeze-frames" while gliding from one section of town to another. These would last a minute or so on average, and were extremely frustrating. Consider yourself warned.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

This is my first serious review.
I'm not a huge fan of shooting games, but this one made at least my top 5 favorite ever. I've heard about this game before and even watched some playthrough, but basically, I went through blindly. I knew I was in for some dark stuff, such as war crimes and PTSD.
Pros :
- Nice graphics even good looking by today's standards.
- Engaging narrative that slowly builds up.
- Main character has good development (regression in his case).
- Illusion of choice well implemented with gameplay mechanics.
- Unique experience of exploring the hardship of PTSD.
- Conflicting themes of duty and grief enhance the world-building.
Cons :
- Repetitive and sometimes boring gameplay.
- SHORT, SHORT, SHORT!!!
- Have I said too short?
In the end of the day, I recommend this game to everyone who wish to have a better understanding on PTSD. The medium let you have an interactive experience and explore the issue in an new light. The repetitive gameplay actually makes sense in the context of PTSD. Mobs upon mobs run into you, soldiers or rebels, intentions or goals make no difference. You just shoot them without questions asked, but an uncomfortable feeling lingers in the back of your mind. This is where the illusion of choice comes in, shattering the gameplay's monotony. The mechanics incentivize a certain action, but you always have the option not to do so. Even if the results are the same, the choices always feel meaningful. Just like in real wars, there is always an alternative that will cause the lest pain, but most people won't notice it until it's too late, when their psyche rules over their consciousness. Ultimately, this game made me emotionally engaged and helped me grow into a better person.

Bought the game in its beginning (before Sapienza), and followed its evolution and updates to this day. A lot of people have issues with how the game was published and with some of IO Interactive's questionnable game design, especially with the always-on DRM, but those were never a problem to me. Even better, I truly think that the episodic development and publishing was a pretty neat idea, pushing the player to come back every now and then to discover new features, challenges and missions. I honestly don't think I would have played that much if the game came out in one piece, as I would have played levels after levels and wouldn't have had much interest in the secondary missions and objective. Whereas with this method of publishing, every ounce of content that came out was to be enjoyed when it came out. I still get how this could annoy people who would've expected a complete game from the start, but now that everything has been published, HITMAN is pretty well-rounded and fleshed out.
Though the game isn't that well optimised, it's still holds up on upper-middle ranges of computers such as mine, but it can become rapidly annoying to play it on lower-end PCs. If you manage to run it on your computer though, you'll discover a pretty neat game, graphically speaking. The different maps are full of details in every corners, and I found the lighting surprisingly well-done. A really good-looking game.
As for the music and voice-over, it's alright, but quite forgettable. The trailers, on the other hand, have incredible soundtracks. I'm thinking of the Sapienza trailer, which plays "Between Two Points" by the Glitch Mob, a masterpiece ! The voice-over is alright, they got David Bateson as 47, which is nice, but because he doesn't speak much, it's not a big selling point. The writting was pretty nice, though.
The gameplay mixes Blood Money and Absolution. Blood Money for the overall style and for the missions that are contract-based, and Absolution for some of its mechanics such as the ability to see through walls. The gameplay is close to perfect, it has so much things going on that it'll be difficult to me to make an exhaustive list of everything that you can do/use to accomplish your missions. You can:
And the list goes on, but just know that you'll have plenty to do if you want to get every achievments, or simply are afraid that the game as a bad replayability.
As for the story, the game being contract-based has an implicit and somewhat mysterious story, which is told right before and after completing a mission. Yet, this first season doesn't really go anywhere, exept the fact that we know there is an organization that want to take over the world or something. So if you are expecting a well-written story with complex characters, maybe you should avoid this game.
HITMAN truly shines with its gameplay, which is complex enough that you will want to replay each level at least once to discover everything that has to be discovered. It's well executed and you should consider buying it for everything that I've mentionned, whether it is on sale or not.

Simply saying that this game is a mind f*ck or that it has a plot twist isn't really doing it justice. There are so many layers and nuances to this story that I'm probably not even qualified to write about it. This is a game that (if you don't know the whole story yet) you really need to experience for yourself. On the other hand if you have already watched a bunch of youtube videos on it and read a bunch of stuff, I think you can skip the game seeing as how the gameplay itself isn't that good.

They've tried to make everything bigger and better in comparison to the previous games - open design, assassination options, multiple targets, guard numbers, excessive number of puzzle items - and it's had an unintended negative effect on the gameplay. I don't think they anticipated this.
Combined with the unfortunate change from a darker tone, unintelligible plot, and the over-utilised, cringeworthy attempt at NOLF style conversations - utilising the same 3 or 4 western voice actors - it becomes somewhat clinical and lifeless exercise.
The tone change is particularly worth mentioning - ICA doesn't know if it is a shadowy mercenary organisation, or a bunch of do-gooders. There is a moral quality. The cinematics looked quite expensive too. Could have been better spent on voice actors.
The locales are varied, but there appears to be an undersaturation in the colours, which is characteristic of the series I guess. It doesn't seem as vivid as it should be, considering the assets they have there.
It's dissapointing as so much effort has been poured into the design of the game. It appears to be a real labour of love, and a real desire to get back what to made their studio a great success.
It's almost as if they've overcooked it a bit. I can understand that from an episodic point of view, as they are under pressure to deliver a lot of content per episode to keep people interested. No doubt this is partly a result of the studio being gutted after Absolution and the publisher later selling IO. It is an unfortunate sales model, if only because it prevents them from returning to and touching up an area a bit later in development.
Still, it's Hitman game, and it's a minor miracle one is even being made today, let alone one that is overcomplicated rather than dumbed down.
The good things about this game are also the bad things - big maps, many choices etc.

An incredibly enthralling and rewarding experience. Very long to play through, but never feels repetitive or grindy (monsters don't respawn). Works great in Ultrawide HD (2560x1080), which is no small feat for a game this old.
There is a few things you should know before you start playing the game.
1. BUCK daggers. There is very low variety of dagger weapons, so if you want to rely on assassin's kiss you will be under-powered most of the time. Besides, you can't dual wield, and pairing a shield as high as your shoulder with a dinky dagger makes you look like a retard.
2. Craft magic potions to heal yourself. Using the Restoration skill is a lot more resource efficient and handy in combat than chugging healing potions. You will find enough of the latter to use in emergency when your health is too low.
3. Skills in the game can be raised three ways- points from leveling up, items (in the form of a skill book) and quest rewards. There are several quests that reward you Restoration, and a book of it you can find at an easy place, so don't waste points maxing it out (max level is 5).
4. If you want to reach ALL the loot, you will find the Telekinesis skill useful (I could only retrieve the aforementioned Restoration book with a level 2 Telekinesis skill).
5. Scorpion traps are absolutely OP.  Just throw a couple of them at any boss (by using the trap skill) and they will most likely kill it for you.
6. Gold will be plentiful. Ignore the Trading skill.
7. Save the game often, in different slots.
8. Regeneration is useless. Don't bother. It's too slow to be worth the points and you'll get plenty of potions anyway.

Minerva is like a stellar, even if low-budget, demo for the game Half Life 2 should have been.
For people who enjoyed the actual gameplay of the Halflife 2 games, this is not only an excellent sidestory, but also a fast paced and in depth run through a fairly challenging game with a good story. The balance between story and gameplay is excellent, with no long, game-stalling cutscenes, unnecessary and shallow character interactions, and no extended scenes with vehicals or gimmicks. Rather than boring the player with dialogue, narrative, character interaction, and exposition are delivered to the player through on-screen text which not only cuts down on the distractions of having someone constantly talking to the player, but also lends greatly to the game's aesthetic choices.
For the low price of "free", anyone who has exhausted the Halflife series and remotely enjoyed it should absolutely pick this up for a change of pace and excellent gameplay.
As a word of advice, if you have not played Halflife 2 or it episodic sequels, you should play them first, as Minerva may set the bar too high for the real thing.

DmC: Devil May Cry exists in a really odd space.  On one hand, veterans of the DMC franchise are going to look down on it for it's simpler combat that doesn't offer fine control or complex, rewarding mechanics of games such as DMC 3 or DMC 4.  It is a significantly easier game and there is a lot less put into the fighting mechanics of the game itself.
On the other hand, DmC: Devil May Cry offers is a refined experience that I think most people will enjoy!  Despite it's flaws when held up to it's predicesors,  DmC offers smooth combat and top-notch presentation.  The major criticism I'd offer are that the boss fights are boring, QTE-ridden, forgettable snore-fests.
It's definitely not a bad game and as long as you are willing to remove expectations for DMC 5 from this title and accept it for what it is, it's a fine game by itself.

I have just finished my playthrough of both the base game and the DLC Fall of Vergil gameplay on Devil Hunter difficulty. DMC has the humor and I feel they got Dante's cocky demeanor down to perfection. The story was pretty good, if not predictable at times but you don't really play games like these for stories, you play them to feel like a badass. In this case, the game delivers. The game is kind of short, as I have beaten the base game in 8 hours and the DLC in about 2.
Dante is given his trusty Ebony and Ivory, his sword Rebellion, and four other types of weapons. Two of them being more power based and the other two being more speed based. You can switch between the four extra weapons seamlessly for some pretty awesome combos. I found it pretty easy to get at least an S rating on combos once I got the controls down and I got them down really quickly. It's easy to understand how each weapon works and you're pretty much limited by your creativity when it comes down to putting combos together. Since I played the game on Devil Hunter (normal), it wasn't that hard to beat but still challenging enough to feel satisfied when you get an SSS combo score. No doubt the harder difficulties will provide some fun and frustration.
Fall of Vergil really pales in comparison. I know it's a DLC so it won't have as much content but will Vergil you're only given Yamato and his Illusion powers. Don't get me wrong, Vergil's a badass and it was rewarding to kick♥♥♥♥♥with him once I got used to him. The difference is that while Dante has an arsenal of weapons that allow him to handle multiple enemies at once allowing you to be a powerhouse, Vergil was more limited and I felt you have to be more evasive and strike more precisely. That said, his demon form is pretty cool and is a little more dynamic than Dante. Still it doesn't beat being able to switch multiple weapons and going to town on those demons.
The only way this game could have been better is a longer game and more interesting characters.
Do I recommend this game at full price? As cheap as I am, I would say no. But I feel I'm an outlier of the average consumer when it comes to assessing the worth of games. I'm incredibly cheap and I only ever really buy during sales. That said, I bought this game during the Summer Sale and by that I would absolutely recommend getting this game.
I say wait for a sale and then get it. But that's my personal opinion.
Don't knock it until you've tried it!  Just don't expect the same game as its predecessors...

This is a non-spoiler review, it is safe to read:
Batman: Arkham Origins is a third person action-adventure game, released on Octomber 25 2013, developed by WB Games Montréal and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. It serves as a prequel to Batman: Arkham Asylum, taking place around 5 years before Arkham Asylum. It follows a less experienced Batman on the quest to find Black Mask, a criminal kingpin, who started a bounty hunt for Batman's head with the price of $50.000.000 in the Christmas Eve. Eight of the best assassins in the DC Universe compete for the big price and Batman has to stop all of them. In this game, Batman confronts for the first time in his career many of the game's villains.
The game is highly criticised for the gameplay, beeing just a remake of Batman: Arkham City, just with the city covered in snow and Christman decorations. Well, I kinda agree, but in the same time, I don't really have a problem with this. Batman: Arkham Asylum and Arkham City were released in 2009 and 2011, both developed by Rocksteady Studios. In the program, one Arkham game was supposed to appear every two years, but as Rocksteady needed much more time to do the sequel to Arkham City (who will be called Arkham Knight), they didn't wanted to let the fans wait, so they allowed WB Games Montréal to make a prequel for Arkham Asylum using the Arkham City mechanics. Speaking of gameplay, Batman can free roam in a snowly Gotham City, gliding and climbing the buildings. Batman has many gadgets to help him fight the crime, the batarang beeing the best known out of all. Batman also has the Detective Mode, with it, you can see enemies through the walls and rooms. A new mechanic of Detective Mode that Arkham Origins made, was to solve a crime, murder or a robbery through evidence and 3D simulations that can explain and show the incident in detail. The combat is the best mechanic of the game. Same as Arkham Asylum/City, you can make combos, you can use gadgets and tricks and counter-attack enemies. Out of all Arkham games, Origins has the best story and the best boss-fights. Even after you finish the game's story, you still have more to do in the city. Solve crimes, find and capture the most wanted criminals and much more.
Overall, Batman: Arkham Origins is a great and fun game, it's indeed, an Arkham City re-released just as a place holder but it's really underrated, which is a shame.

Divine Divinity is described as a "2D Skyrim" in the advertisement video; however, I honestly think that's selling it a little short.  It's a much deeper game with much more customization available and a lot more hidden things to discover.  It's an ARPG in the sytles of Diablo but where Diablo focused on gameplay and had a tight/rushable grinding experience Divine Divinity spends much more time in the "Roleplaying" section of the ARPG namesake.  The pace is slower, you can customize your character in much greater ways to build one that's truly unique, and the narrative of the game is more story-centric and focused on taking you through various towns that you can explore that are populated with many different NPCs to interact with.  There are a lot of quests and many different hidden secrets and eastereggs to discover, so one of my favorite features is actually allowing you to place a personalized marker on the map to remind yourself of something you'll want to come back to at a later point in time.
I loved exploring the world and interacting with the characters.  The game is quite large, so there are several bugs and a few quests that break, but nothing that really detracted from the game for me.  Except the framerate.  I played the majority of the game on Direct 3D rendering mode and the framerate suffered.  Like, really suffered.  It's a testament to how much I enjoyed playing Divine Divinity that I continued along when every time poisoin clouds were being rendered or a lot of enemies were onscreen the engine slowed to a crawl.  When I switched to the Software renderer at about 50 hours of gametime in the framerate increased dramatically and I no longer experienced slowdowns.  It does break video cutscenes and doesn't look as nice but if you're aggravated by the framerate like I was give that a shot and swap back when you need to.
If you like ARPGs and would like to experience a living world around one don't pass on this game.

I love this game. The Divinity series is great in allowing true role playing and this was the progenitor of them all. It's world is huge and deep, with extensive lore and interesting characters. Fans of RPGs that look for something close to the table top games will really appreciate this one.
Books can be read, boxes moved, ingredients mashed together in your inventory. You can play as a virtuous hero that lives off hard earned food or a thief that nabs everything not nailed down (and even some things that are). Play as a naive young man that helps everyone he meets or a cunning rogue that beguiles her way through every encounter.
Every scenario has a myriad of outcomes. Why fought through a horde of enemies when you can just sneak past them and take their treasures? Can't get a guard to leave his post? Throw one of your teleporter pyramids behind him, drop the other outside, use it to get behind him, do what needs to be done, pick up the pyramid and teleport ball outside leaving no one the wiser.
The teleporter pyramids are a great addition that add a lot to game play. Throw them over traps or chasms, leave one outside a cave for a quick escape route, use them to quickly move between shops in a town when trying to game the economy (or sell one merchant's hidden stock to another).
This game provides so many interesting opportunities to play your way. Even the newer Divinity games don't quite match this one in terms of variety and options.
That said, it isn't perfect. It can be an extremely difficult game, often to the point of unfair, mostly because the combat isn't exactly stellar. This is one area that future games definitely improved upon. Don't come to this game for an extensive and complex combat system. You won't get much more than rudimentary fights.
Also, occasionally you will get bad outcomes to quests because you have to do very obscure things just to get given the option to work towards a different outcome. For Example:
**Minor Spoiler**
One quest involves collecting a magical tree branch for someone. You can find one in the very same town quite easily, but there is no indication that this is the wrong branch. If you hand in this branch you have to fight a very strong enemy to finish the quest. The "proper" way to end this quest is to go into a forest in the south, far from the quest giver and find the branch there. This isn't told to you at all and can only be found by stumbling upon it.
**End Spoiler**
Despite the difficulty and clunky combat, the game is awesome. The most fun you will have in this game is just from wandering around, taking in all the dialogue and flavour text. The stories are told excellently, allowing non-linearity and role-playing but never feeling like it's gone off the rails.
The sheer variety of options in this game is staggering, and most everything is open to you from the word go. This can be a bit overwhelming at times, but it really makes Rivellon feel like a real world.
In short, the game has its shortcomings, but all the other areas more than make up for them. The game hasn't aged super well, and it has a bit of a steep learning curve at the very beginning as you try to learn the controls, but it's still very playable.
Highly recommended, especially to fans of the newer Divinity games that want to see where the series came from. While the newer games are mechanically tighter and visually more impressive, you won't get quite the same experience as this anywhere else.

I wanted to share something really special for this milestone event. I have been pouring over different titles for almost two weeks now. I wanted to review something that really showcases the greatness and power of independant game developement. As many of you know, I have a strong passion for indie games, and their ability to really push video games forward as works of art.
This title should be a case study in any video game design course. Not only are the puzzles fantastically fun, but the artwork, music, and characters are outstanding. This is a must-have for anyone who wants to play from the couch, and even more so if you have a friend (or five! - yes this can get crazy).
Different colored totem sections can only go into like colors, which is where the puzzles begin. Your brain will twist, and you will struggle, and then you will rejoice when you succeed. In that order. The levels are devilishly difficult, but this is balanced by them being fairly short so you don't get too frustrated. I've mostly played local co-op with my wife and we have just had such a blast screaming at each other.
+Brilliantly done game mechanic of controlling multiple totem pole units to create a fantastic puzzle platformer
+Wonderful artwork, music, and character personalities
+Controller support is great
+Very difficult, yet do-able; puzzles are a nice length, and their are plenty of checkpoints
+I think the DLC is mandatory if you plan on buying the base game, but either way there is a ton of content
+Up to 6 local players at once!!!
-You will scream at your friends
That's the beauty of smaller scale games - they make risky decisions that often pay off with potent experiences that so often the AAA games lack.

There's a reason this game is regarded as the best of the three. It has great story-telling and fantastic action. The characters (especially Max) are great to watch and the plot is dark and tragic.
Now, don't get me wrong, I like to have fun and a laugh with my games, but the gameplay is great fun. Even if it doesn't have a lot of laughs (it is Max Payne after all).
With the Quick Save and Quick Load feature, replaying a part of the game over and over again didn't feel teidious or stressful. It's something MORE game need often, especially since the third game didn't have this.
The only downside to this game is that it is short. About the same length as your average Call of Duty game. But unlike Call of Duty, the story, plot and characters make this game worth seeing through and playing.
It's one of the best third person shooters today, even if it is short and the graphics might be a bit out of date for some, but it's still a fantastic game and one I highly recommend.

Max Payne 2 continues the tragic tale of Max Payne. The gameplay pretty much stayed the same. Gunplay is better and slow motion combat has been improved. Generally, the game also feels a bit easier, no more "enemies getting stronger, because you don't die" nonsense, but there's still a lot of trial and error in the game, which has always bugged me. You NEED to know where and when enemies spawn and where the ones already in the level are located to stand a chance even on the easiest of difficulty modes. On my Win 10 system the game also had some framerate hickups, which would cost you your life usually, but were at least random, so frequent quick saving is a must any way.
The story is still as cheesy and dark as it was, but overall the levels feel more complex and varied. You're still going to be done in roughly 5 to 6 hours though, but that's good, because just like its predecessor Max Payne 2 never introduces any new gameplay elements for you to experiment with. And some levels are just downright frustrating, for example when you have to cover some NPC and they get stuck or just die immediately. Then there are the times when you thought that saving now would be a good idea, but you actually just killed yourself by doing that. THAT's really annoying about only having 1 quick save file and it happened multiple times to me that I just saved and immediately after that a newly spawned enemy jumped through a window or sth like that.
Overall it's still a mostly enjoyable experience, but players averse to old gameplay and old graphics should just watch the comic style cutscenes online. I got this for about 3 bucks and I'm ok with that now.

Spec Ops is plays like your everyday run-of-the-mill military shooter. Shoot the bad guys, throw grenades, blow up helicopters, and take out that turret - all of which are common shooter tropes overused for a decade. For the first few chapters, there's not much to set Spec Ops apart from any other Call of Duty or Gears of War title.
Except it isn't one. Taking advantage of the thoughtlessness by which the game's mechanics seem to be built on, Spec Ops is a game that takes the player's thoughtlessness while completing the game and uses it to question as to why the military FPS even exists as a genre.
Whether you want to feel like an action hero or to have fun shooting targets, the game will make you wonder just what the hell are you doing.

Simply put, Spec Ops is one of the most underrated games of all time. The strength of it is in the way it tells its story, which is a way that you simply do not see in other games. It has a lot more in common with other mediums, such as movies, than The Last of Us ever has. It is truly phenomenal storytelling and direction. The cast did an amazing job. This game has a way of stirring your emotions and bringing out reactions in you, sometimes in ways that you didn't expect or even might disturb you.
The gameplay is solid, but not the strong point of this game. There were some frustrating elements in the gameplay, but I tend to forget what they were. Because the story is so engrossing that whatever flaws there are were soon forgiven and forgotten. The ways that the game tries to get reactions out of the player, through its storytelling, enhances the gameplay as well. It made the game more fun than it would otherwise be.
This is one of those games that you will play through then look for discussion on, or analysis videos on, after you've completed it. There is a lot of meaning behind this game that's enjoyable to explore even after you finish it. Have fun theorizing.
If you're a "story shmory" type, you won't see as much value in it. It's a pretty ordinary shooter on its own gameplay. But with the story telling, it's no ordinary shooter. Even if you're not into action shooters, if you are into story and like good storytelling in video games, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

I don't know what the developers were thinking but for me and a lot of other players (just google it) it ruined the game completely and rendered it virtually unplayable. Even on EASY Deathstroke is still super hard, I dread to think what he'd be like on the other difficulty settings. Two ways they could solve this - either patch it so Deathstroke adheres to the game difficulty setting, or patch it so after 3 or so defeats you have a skip/wimp out option, but I can't see them doing that so this game will sit on the shelf collecting dust.
My other gripe with this game is it doesn't improve upon Batman's sneak mechanic. More often than not you won't get the opportunity to do suprise attacks or silent take downs as the enemies always see you when you get within range, largely due to poor enemy placement (an example, two bad guys facing each other - you can't take them on as one is covering the other and they will see you even from the side), so most of the time it is a case of "rush in guns blazing" and beat the bad guys to a pulp before they have a chance to react properly (targeting the highest threat first such as an armed guy helps, but still not very sneaky and gives Batman the finesse of a brick through a window).
The long and the short of it is - I wouldn't reccomend this game to anyone unless they release a patch/fix for it at least for the Deathstroke problem (the other problem I can live with).
Pretty much the rest of the game is as you'd expect from tyhe Batman Arkham line, but with more refined graphics etc. I also noticed I could have the graphics settings higher on this one than on the first two without any lag, so there have been some significant improvements there, the game was far more fluid and spectacular looking. But looks mean nothing if the product fails like on the key elements above.
I'd give this game 4 stars out of ten, and those 4 are just for the graphics. If it wasn't for Deathstroke the game would have got 9/10 from me, but that one flaw is that annoying the game gets nothing but my utter contempt. *big thumbs down*

Am I allowed to say this game is too hard for me? I've played hard games and enjoyed them but in those games the impending failure at every turn was easily overlooked by loving the gameplay, a sensation I struggle to feel with Super Meat Boy.
Sacrilegious to say I’m sure but the platforming doesn’t compel me to retry over and over to get difficult sections right; let me explain. The controls are definitely tight, but for me too light as if lacking gravity and oomf with movements. Surely, the classic Super Mario Bros is too heavy for most tastes, thus why a more spunky, fluid and free move set was implemented in that series when Nintendo could. SMB takes that trend to far for me, giving you so much control in air it’s nerve racking. But isn't more control better? Surely that makes things easier! Well, that’s the problem, they design the levels to make use of the control in many threading-the-needle level of difficulty segments. I’m sure it’s exactly what I’m disliking here that many like; but I can’t help to think that if the difficulty was scaled in a different way I’d like it better. Let me explain it this way: have you ever played those “most impossible game ever” type flash games on an internet browser where you control a small colored pixel you have to navigate through impossible terrain, like ‘avoid all the other spinning pixels along a maze-like path’? It feels like that, and just as “not-fun” to me.
The aesthetics are a colorful and tight but a bit odd for my tastes. I could use a bit more Super Mario and a bit less Ren and Stimpy. The pacing of all the visuals from the cut scenes to the main menu fit into a perfect harmonious philosophy, it’s just that to me, it’s kinda an ugly one.
This game is for the hardcore platforming fan, someone I am clearly not. Like taking a date down to a roller-skating rink to find out it’s jammed packed with experts doing skating break-dancing, tricks, back flips etc, I’m forced to say “I’ll look elsewhere for fun, enjoy yourselves”.

If you like ARPGs, quests that can be long and hard to figure out sometimes, a bunch of freedom, and a huge open world to explore and develop your character in any way you can imagine, then this game is for you.  It's one of my all-time favorites.

I descend through the clouds of this strange new world that my astronaut has discovered. We touch down gently and I step out of my pod and take a look around. There’s many strange looking plants scattered around and some crystals protruding from the ground. I start walking around unsure what my purpose is and where I should be going. A wind storm hits and I’m dead. I respawn and begin my journey into the unknown again. My oxygen runs low and I die. Survival then is one of the aims in Astroneer because there are many ways in which this game will try to kill you.
Astroneer is a space exploration/survival sandbox adventure game which is being  developed by System Era Softworks, based in Seattle Washington. There is no story line and instead the player must mine resources in order to expand his/her colony by creating structures with the mined resources. The team working on Astroneers come from a background which involves work on games like Halo, Assassin’s Creed, Team Fortress, the Sims, amongst many others so they know what they are doing, something that becomes plain to see when you look at your watch 5 minutes after starting the game and realise an hour has passed.
So you start out by selecting your Astronaut who then detaches their pod from the orbiting station type structure. You head down into the atmosphere of the nearby planet admiring the beautiful looking clouds as you descend. You touch down and examine your immediate surroundings. You have nothing but your trusty suit and a mining tool that can deform the very ground you walk on and mine resources.
As you venture further out you’ll soon discover what resources are used for and how you can take advantage of their applications. You can extend your pod to include all sorts of useful applications from Printers to vehicle bays and machines that will research strange things you have discovered. I had no idea what I was doing to start with but I started to figure things out and I loved how things naturally start to make sense. Once you figure one piece of the puzzle the other pieces start to drop into place it’s a very satisfying experience and leaves you wanting more and more.
The control schemes are simple yet effective and do pretty much all you could want them to. it’s the polygon game world though that impresses. It’s simple yet looks gorgeous and all you want to do is explore. You can sculpt the world around you and even deform the ground right down to the planets core.
So what features do you get in this early access version of Astroneer? Well the developers have a hand list on their website so lets take a look.
Explore multitudes of procedural worlds.
Shape completely malleable terrain. Dig to the centre of the earth, or forge mountains.
Craft vehicles and discover resources to reach ever further in the galaxy.
Survive in ever more harsh and rewarding environments.
Play with friends in online or local multiplayer.
Astroneer is expected to be in early access for a year or two but it’s certainly something that you should be keeping tabs on because this game has all the hall marks of a classic in the making. I can’t wait to see what the developers have in store for the games future. So far they have done an astounding job, this is how early access games should be and what space exploration done right, looks like. This game is satisfying and beautiful to play.

When you look at other games in it's genre, Astroneer struggles to deliver enough content for it's $20 price tag. There are a handful of $20 early access survival games out there that offer far more content, Rust for instance. That being said, the game is pretty fun when playing with other people. We were able to get about 14 hours of gameplay in a co-op session knowing nothing about the games mechanics. However, it's pretty easy to figure everything out. Base building is quite simplistic, and requires very few resources to build. Finding the resources is where it might take a while depending on your location. There's really nothing you need to worry about in a survival sense either except for oxygen. Oxygen does not deplete as long as you are tehterd to a oxygen line. These lines can be made easily which basically negates this factor in your survival. On a whole, Astroneer isn't much of a survival game. You don't need to find food, you don't need to build a shelter, and theres maybe 1-2 hostile plant things that will injure you if you get close. Falling off from cliffs also will injure you. When you talk survival you're thinking I need to manage food, water, find shelter, sustainment, fend off predators - well theres no food, no water, no shelter unless you make yourself one for asthetic purposes, and no predatory creatures that will hunt you.
The fun right now in the game comes from the exploration, and for maybe 1-2 hours the researching mechanics. Researching artifacts is how you are able to build space ships and rovers etc. There aren't many things to research right now so this facet of the game quickly becomes obsolete. Exploring the randomly generated worlds is pretty cool though. I just wish there was more to the game. The good thing is - it looks promising, it's early access so theres more to come. The gameplay is smooth and has appealing visuals. The art style is neat too.  I'll still recommend this game if you have the $20 to blow on 14-15 hrs.

Batman: Arkham Origins is an open world action game developed by WB Games Montreal and Splash Damage and published by Warner Brothers. To my knowledge, it was also ported to PC by WB Montreal and Splash Damage. For some reason, Batman games just can't catch a solid break on PC, at least not at launch, but this game clearly suffers far worse than the rest of them. I personally didn't feel compelled to write this review until I went back to this game after completing Arkham Knight, the next game in the series, and realized many things about this game that I hadn't seen before. WB publicly announced, shortly after this game's launch, that they wouldn't be fixing any non-game-breaking bugs in order to develop more DLC for the product. As a result, the game remains bug-filled far after its launch.
The game uses the FreeFlow combat system, as in the previous Arkham games, but with a few new added features. A major gripe I have with this game in particular is the incredibly low time to counter given to counter some enemies attacks, sometimes less than a second. This would not be a problem necessarily on a rare, extremely difficult enemy, but this can appear even on the first enemies of the game. I talked about the stealth system in this game in
, but I'd like to talk about it in greater detail here. Dealing with armed enemies is
infuriating because, in most areas, the only avenues of efficient movement consist of the gargoyles mounted on the walls, usually one on each wall of a square/rectangular room. There are also floor grates placed under certain areas, but they are very restricting and often don't allow for many tactical takedown opportunities. The Disruptor, a weapon capable of disabling weapons and any enemy armaments, only has three charges (after one late-game upgrade), and the effect is lost after a few seconds. Enemies have very annoying AI in some areas, in that they will not give you any chance to enter or leave the floor grates. There are very few areas in which you can siphon away individual enemies, rendering most "takedown fodder" locations pointless. You get a total of one smoke pellet which recharges every 30 minutes; this is probably one of the only ways you can take down large groups of armed enemies.
The majority of the open world activities in Arkham Origins consist of, again, Riddler Trophies . My complaint with this system is that most of the 'extortion data packs' are locked behind some sort of gadget-wall, be it a generator that you have to power with the shock gloves, or a pipe bursting with hot steam that you have to seal with the glue grenade. The reason this is annoying is that this is often the only 'puzzle' element to these datapacks, and it's just there to make you go back to them later.
There are also the "most wanted" missions, in which you track down Gotham's most wanted criminals through a series of objectives. These are, more often than not, uninteresting chores that aren't very motivating. Also, I don't know if this was a bug or not, but I wasn't even aware of the
of Bird's most wanted until I happened upon the group of thugs that apparently starts the mission. Black Mask's most wanted also doesn't appear to be listed on the most wanted page for me, preventing me from tracking my progress.
The problem with Arkham Origin's open world in general is that all of the areas blend together and have no individuality whatsoever. I didn't feel motivated to explore the world, and I didn't feel rewarded for doing so as there's very little of import or interest to be found there. It's all so very empty, and you move so slowly across it as well.
This section is probably going to be where the review gets a little more positive, as graphics and performance is good overall for a 2013 title. It's not nearly as pretty as the Steam Store screenshots would have you believe, but it's not a bad looking game by any stretch of the word. I ran the game on max settings save Motion Blur (off) and Ambient Occlusion (very high), and had no significant frame rate drops on my system (i7 4790k, GTX 970). The quality of the lighting is probably the least strong point, and it's shamefully bad in the outdoor areas. Texture quality is relatively poor, as to be expected, along with general material/shader quality. The GameWorks snow, smoke, and paper effects are very good looking (I could probably live without the paper) and perform quite well, and the DX11 tessellation on ground snow is the best looking part of the game. Effects like fire and bloom can be somewhat dire; overall the game is better looking indoors than outdoors. Sound quality, surprisingly, can actually be horrible in some instances, especially in background sounds.
The graphics settings are acceptable, but the other settings are sadly not. Field of View is unchangeable, leaving some with a horribly narrow camera angle. There is no available Borderless Windowed mode, Anisotropic Filtering, and SMAA is not available. The game suffers a random stutter whenever you interact with most objects in the world, which will become annoying over time.
Also, what's the deal with the pre-rendered cutscenes in this game? I get pre-rendered cutscenes in games, I really do, but not when they're compressed at the same bitrate as my livestreams, run at thirty frames per second, and they even look worse than the in-engine ones, I have a hard time defending them. Especially considering that they're literally everywhere in this game,
The story consists of Batman being hunted by assassins sent by Black Mask
, and is a prequel to Arkham Asylum. The lack of a compelling story is a major problem with this game. It's all very cliche, and I even thought that it was over at some points until I consulted the most wanted screen. Most of the voice actors lack good delivery on their lines, and it's not particularly well-written either. Part of the problem is how little the most wanted missions tie-in with the main story, so you won't even realize that they're there until you play the next game and realize that there are side quests.
I have to give props to this game for introducing me to the Arkham series and Batman in general. I've never been a huge Batman fan, but I certainly appreciate the story of the Caped Crusader more after playing this game. It looks pretty good, it runs fairly well, but the world is lackluster and the story is too. Oh yeah, you'll also be pestered by a bug every few seconds, and Batman will somehow self-levitate 1/20 times you start flying.
If you can take the bugs, it's a fun game for running around as Batman and beating people up.

As far as sequels go, Max Payne 2 is pretty good. It definitely looks better than Max Payne 1; in fact it looks great for a 2003 game. It's a bit weird how Max Payne's appearance changed though - he looks kind of like Nicholas Cage. (I know I'd pay a lot of money for a game like this starring him, that's for sure.) The gunplay is better as well, with more satisfying weaponry and ragdoll physics added to the mix. Bullet time also doesn't slow you down anymore, which is a major factor in making the game easier than its predecessor, although not too easy.
It keeps with the dark noir theme of the first game, but it seems to lean more on the serious side - the 'love story' - than that game did. That's not a bad thing per se, given how smoothly executed it is and how good the gameplay is, but it doesn't quite have the desperate, blackly humorous essence the first game did. Payne's voice acting is more on the overwrought side when compared to the first game and its tone, at least. That's not quite to its detriment and more of a personal taste thing for me, though: the game deals more with Max's journey as a person this time around, a person struggling with the violent and tragic aftermath of what happened in the first game.
The story takes more twists and turns than in the first game as well, meaning you actually have to pay attention if you want context for the fighting you're doing. Mona Sax gets credit for having enough agency to capably fight alongside Max at times, even if she's ultimately Max's love interest.
If you're in the market for a good third-person shooter, you could do much worse than Max Payne 2, although the story won't make a whole lot of sense unless you've played the first game.

This game really does what a sequel needs to do. It adds a lot of improvements from the original Max Payne, while also fine tuning old things. For instance, the graphics are a lot better and the controls are smoother.
Overall the game itself is full of depth. There are many weapons to cycle through, from Molotov cocktails to grenades to sniper rifles to melee combat. You have many objectives in missions -- from peaceful ones without enemies where to need to simply figure out what to do, to oines where you'll have to guard someone or you'll need to take down a boss.
The story is the shining aspect of the game -- you follow a fully voiced adventure of Max Payne. There are noir style comics before each level, with each character voiced, while during gameplay Payne will comment about things you find and interact with other characters.
It's hard to describe how good the game is -- if you're there for the story and like a dark setting, get this. 89/100 for me, highly recommended.
