Massive, AAA games dominate the game industry. They're the biggest money-makers, require the most production time, and there can only be so many. They're pretty pricey, and the competition is pretty stiff. There's quite a bit at stake too. One flop can be enough to sink a company, with the amount of resources and work that goes into a game.
Wouldn't it be great if we could just, you know, not? Why can't we just NOT make massive AAA games? Why hasn't anyone thought of that? Make smaller, less AAA games. You know, maybe just a AA game. Or an A game. What's wrong with A's? A guy can like A's if he likes. It doesn't have to make you creepy. Why does there have to be this big stigma attached to liking A's? So what, they're just a little smaller. There's nothing wrong with that.
Let's just make a game like the way they used to make them. You know, one of those runny, jumpy, side to side games that don't have lots of guns and dubstep. You know what I mean? I'm sure no one has ever invented this. We can call it...
Indie game!
This is Indie Game.
Today, we're reviewing Indie Game. It's one of my favorite games. It's just like all of the old games we used to play, but it's new. Isn't that great?
Indie Game is about this little red square guy. He dies a lot.
Red Square Man needs to rescue his girlfriend from the bad guy, and it's up to you to help him by guiding him through all kinds of things to kill him. It's really hard.
Indie Game is a hard game. It's not an easy one. You'll literally die like, at least ten times per stage. If not more.
Indie Game is a very special game. It's genius in so many ways. Its level design is impeccable, and its mechanics are flawless. It takes everything that made retro games so good, adds a layer of modern design to it, and polishes it up nice and shiny for everyone to enjoy. They set the bar for indie developers incredibly high, and to be honest many still fail to reach that bar.
It might seem painfully simple at the first level. It's a game about running and jumping. But it's like a loving mother, holding your hand as you cross the street. Only to shove you into oncoming traffic, running and laughing as you panic and flail helplessly. Bragging about it to her friends from the book club over Jello shots and cocaine.
I HAD A TOUGH CHILDHOOD OKAY?
The difficulty is unforgiving, and the level design is brilliant in its constant sadistic punishment. Laying down the pain ruthlessly for your failures, and forcing you to take it like a good little ♥♥♥♥♥.
Whoever designed these levels really must have studied up or something. ♥♥♥♥ing nerd.
It's really just fantastic. The levels introduce new obstacles frequently, and yet introduce you slowly before ramming the entire girthy length up your♥♥♥♥♥with no more than a gentle tug of the hair to warn you of what's to come.
Deaths, while frequent, are quick and snappy. Splat. Respawn. Repeat. Endlessly if need be. The quickness of it all is perfect to hook you into the cycle of "♥♥♥♥, one more try.♥♥♥♥♥♥ one more try. SON OF A ♥♥♥♥♥, I'm done. ... Just one more try."
It relies on fast instincts and mastery of its physics, which are an obstacle in itself. You're particularly slippery and floaty, meaning getting the game to do what you want is part of the challenge. And yet it never feels unfair. The rules of the game are concrete. Victory and death are very clear, the level is static in its difficulty. It's equally a matter of memorization as it is skill and reflexes. The levels are never random, and there's a right way through every level.
Even more impressive, there's also usually a perfect straight path through every level. A subtly hidden straight path to the goal, requiring such perfect movements it's nearly an art itself. There's definitely an emphasis on speed, and the game will even reward you for reaching its par times. But existing in perfect parallel to each level's perfect speed route, there's collectibles and hidden secrets spread throughout the game's various levels. Meaning you'll often have to replay levels to collect everything for a true 100%. Unless you can somehow collect everything and reach the par time without dying in one try, but that's crazy talk.
And perfect gameplay design is one thing, but to have a game this incredibly polished that isn't an AAA game? It looks and feels amazing, the art style is cute and dripping with charm and other bodily fluids that are probably not sanitary, and the game has a killer soundtrack that makes being killed endlessly suddenly not so horrible after all. It's crammed with references, both subtle and incredibly obvious, to retro gaming and the indie game community.
It's a masterpiece of design, and a stellar title for any hardcore gaming fan. It's definitely not something you let grandma play, this isn't a casual game by far. Might give her 'Nam flashbacks or something.
Seriously, don't give this to grandma. Last time you tried to show her a game, you had to have a talk with your church about how you weren't really possessed by Satan. Do you really want that to happen again? I don't think so.

What's the deal with Super Meat Boy? It's one of the best indie games, and probably the best indie platformer game, ever. At least for me. Just when almost every dev trying to make games more casual, or more movie-like experiences, here comes super hard and super upsetting Super Meat Boy. It's starting as normal platformer and with every next chapter it shows how brutal this game is. Sometimes just to beat one level you will need to replay it dozens of times. Now imagine to get A+ grade on each super hard level for beating it under a predetermined time. And doing the same on Dark World, which levels are extra hard edition of super hard levels. And it's just get harder and harder until you will to die hundreds of times just to beat one level. Or not, because it will be too hard. Also, level editor - some levels made by players only left one thought: "Those levels were made to be impossible to beat... OH WOW, SOMEBODY BEAT IT BUT HOW!?". It's amazing how hard, frustrating and annoying game can bring so much fun. I'm not into S&M but this is really fun. Besides how difficult this game is, Super Meat Boy have simply but great looking graphics and amazing soundtrack - I'm not sure how much but I spent many hours listening to this OST outside the game. Especially music on levels of The Cotton Alley is relaxing and I will probably never get bored of it.
I completed already Super Meat Boy in 100% on X360, using original X360 controller - never broken one, never rage quited game. I'm not a very skilled gamer so I died for more than 25k times but hell, that was so much fun. Now, I will do the same but instead of controller I will use... keyboard. It's highly not recommended but still, it's not impossible to play on keyboard like almost everyone is saying. Also, more achievements for doing well on even more difficult things... yes, this game can be addictive. There is no other game like Super Meat Boy. Even if you might not like hard platform games, you must at least try Super Meat Boy. It's truly unforgettable experience.

Let me first say, I adore this game and if you haven't played it yet, you should. No one should miss this masterpiece of a game. If you are looking for a nearly-perfect platformer/exploration game similar to Rayman and Metroid, stop what you're doing now and get this game.
If you had asked me in the first few hours of playing what I'd rate it, I would give it a 10/10, no hesitation. The intro is beautiful and gives your mission purpose. As the world opens up, you're filled with wonder as you explore Nibel and start uncovering its secrets.
This game is not easy despite its calming aesthetic. It can at times prove to be extremely challenging and unfortunately at times it can also be very frustrating. Due to the escape sequences alone, I would really need to knock this game down to a 9/10, because they were just frustrating (and long) sequences of trial and error, and the margin for error is incredibly slim. One screw-up and you have to do the WHOLE thing over again. The worst part about them is that they'renot exactly the same every time, and you do have to rely on the enemy AI to work perfectly and hope you don't get screwed by the RNG. The rest of the game is so well-done and fun that it's hard to knock off too many points for these parts, but by comparison these parts of the game are just downright awful. Luckily, they are few and far between.
As far as the rest of the game is concerned, it's a blast. Just moving around as Ori is fun once you have all the powerups and abilities. At the start of the game you are weak and slow, and every enemy you come across is dangerous and scary. By the end, you are blasting through areas at the speed of light, doing complex maneuvers in the air and raining terror on all enemies in your path. When this game shines, it's a true joy.
The last thing I will say is that the presentation is just gorgeous. The music and the background art come together to elevate this game to the new standard for platformers.
I can't wait for the sequel, and I'll be extremely impressed if they manage to top this. Well done, Moon Studios. Well done.

The deck-builder that's not a deck-builder.
This game is crummy on several levels, not the least of which is the greed factor involved with the DLC approach that Handelbra, the publisher, decided to use. Naturally, this means that the core game is limited in options and selection, urging the player to spend more to get something that feels like a complete game. You do this by buying "mini-packs" or "packs" and/or subscribe to questionably priced season passes.
When you start a new game, you select a variable stable of heroes, a villain and an environment. Each of these selections comes with pre-made decks. While this makes it quick to jump into play, it's also a crude and uninteresting way to make a quasi-deck-builder. The art and appearance of all this is an amateur comic, with generic feeling heroes and villains fighting in trope-filled environments. Not terrible but not at all impressive. The interface and presentation is also clunky and unremarkable.
Nonetheless, because the core game comes with a small number of base decks--heroes, villains, environments--combined with the inability to customize those decks or the game play beyond meta-level selections, the game quickly feels repetitive and monotonous. (Unless you're willing to spend more money to buy diversity, of course!)
Luck also has a notable factor, meaning that a bad string of draws by the villain or environment can cause you to lose the game regardless of how strong you'd played to that point. Like it or not, you're going to lose a portion of games for no other reason than being unlucky. Given the sluggish pace of the game, this can be annoying.
That said, there is some strategy in what heroes you choose to bring against what villains, which is great. However, as you might surmise, this means that there are more or less optimal choices to bring against a villain or environment, further narrowing the variety and flavor of the game. (Unless you spend more!)
While I've dogged it here, I won't say it's a terrible game, but it is slow-paced, occasionally frustrating, and miserly. I would not recommend it over competing card-based games like Obsidian's Pathfinder Adventures, The Elder Scrolls: Legends or Card Hunter, all of which offer more robust and engaging games for more competitive cost.
The other reason to pick up this game is if you're a fan of the original physical game and can't help yourself.

+ Easy rules
+ Interesting setting
+ Fantastic music
+ Good UI
+ Very satisfying gameplay
+ Has multiplayer
- Multiplayer discourages playing with friends (more about it below)
- Pricey DLC
- Art can be a hit or miss
- Matches can be lengthy
I love this game. The best term I can come up with to describe it is "satisfying". It's very satisfying to finally beat the villain you thought is very hard at first, using new strategy. It's very satisfying to find out the hero you didn't like at first actually is amazing if used a bit differently or in different team composition.
The UI, while being stylized is perfectly functional, which is very important. And there's even a "rewind" button if you misclicked.
Combine it with a very easy set of rules that you'll easily understand after one tutorial match, fantastic music and that cheesy superhero setting that embodies all the genre tropes you can think of yet still stays unique... and you got yourself a fantastic game.
A fantastic game that still has a few flaws.
First one is entirely subjective - it's art. Some of it is great, detailed, fits the setting perfectly. And some of it is... well... It's very sloppy and at best looks like sketches. At worst - like a 3 year old has drawn it looking at the actual art in this game. And then there are 3D backgrounds that just look awkward in contrast with everything else being 2D.
Personally, I like most of it, it generally fits the overall theme of the game very well and gives it a very unique look. And with time it grew on me even more. But it's still a fair warning.
Second, the matches can take some time. If you are looking for quick, Hearthstone-like matches, you probably won't find them here. However. You can turn off most animations and transitions in this game to speed up the process. And the game saves automatically when you exit it, so you can stop and continue from whatever moment you want. So in all honesty, it's not a big deal. But if you are a kind of person that just MUST see the match from start to finish in one sitting, be aware that it can take 30 minutes or more (depending on how familiar you are with cards and UI).
Finally. The thing that actually bothers me most.
.
There are a lot of DLC and they are somewhat pricey, which is like... mostly ok. Many games do this. Whatever. Right?
Except in this game everybody in your multiplayer match MUST have the same DLC in order for any of you to use it.
Let me break it down. You can not use DLC you bought in a match with your friend if he does not have it. You still can play together, but the game will disable any DLC the other player does not have. Which is just ridiculous if you ask me. Why do I have to pester my friends to buy the exact same DLC that I own, just so I can play the characters I bought? Or, to put it differently, why can I not play the characters I bought if I want to play with my friends? That's one of the stupidest models I've seen in a while, to be honest, and I just can't get over it.
This issue may or may not be resolved in the future, since the developers stated that that is not the priority. Right now though things are what they are.
Thankfully, this game is still a lot of fun in single player, and the aforementioned DLC bring a lot of content - villains, environments, heroes with their unique decks... but if multiplayer is what you're primarily after, think twice before buying this game.
Otherwise, it is an astonishing game and I can not recommend it enough.

I'm the kind of guy who really likes co-op platformers.  So I'd been chomping at the bit since I heard about the game last December.  And Kalimba did not disappoint!  Some notes:
* stacking is harder than it looks... you need a ledge or a hole or something to do it
* more platform-y than puzzle-y
* difficult, but not extremely so (as some reviews implied)
* did not cause any existential marriage crises (as some reviews warned)
* got very exciting at some points
* similar feel to ibb&obb, but we liked Kalimba much better
* visual style is very nice
* lots of jokes that are ... somewhat funny
The scoring system is up to 70 points for getting all the goodies, minus 1 for each death.  The goodies are kept even when you die.  So you can get a pretty good score without being amazing, but it's quite hard to get all 70 points (and a golden totem).
The game is VERY short.  We completed all 20 co-op levels (so including dark void DLC) in 3 hours.  We didn't get 70 points in all the levels, and I'd say there's about a 50-50 chance that we care enough to go back.  Many of the levels introduced interesting gamplay mechanics, but by the end thing started to feel same-y.
So if you want to play a co-op puzzle platformer and you and your partner are both decent at platformers, then get this game!

This is a pretty simple action-platformer with a bunch of neat puzzles built into its unique movement mechanic. I didn't try improving my scores, but the ranking system that puts deaths and collectibles in a tug of war is really smart. Great art and audio. Hoe Bear as a story teller is a little out of place, but I still enjoy the silliness in the writing.
Overall it's a great game that ends before it outstays its welcome. The DLC adds some cool mechanics and is a little harder, but it made me sad to see what becomes of the characters that I enjoyed pre-DLC.

Kalimba is a great game that is really clever and provides the player with a nice mix of both action and puzzles. The sound, art and gameplay are all fantastic and really sets this game apart from other puzzle-platformers. The co-op is is a mix of coordination, frustration and fun which will test even the best of friendships. All in all well worth the $ albeit a bit short.

I descend through the clouds of this strange new world that my astronaut has discovered. We touch down gently and I step out of my pod and take a look around. There’s many strange looking plants scattered around and some crystals protruding from the ground. I start walking around unsure what my purpose is and where I should be going. A wind storm hits and I’m dead. I respawn and begin my journey into the unknown again. My oxygen runs low and I die. Survival then is one of the aims in Astroneer because there are many ways in which this game will try to kill you.
Astroneer is a space exploration/survival sandbox adventure game which is being  developed by System Era Softworks, based in Seattle Washington. There is no story line and instead the player must mine resources in order to expand his/her colony by creating structures with the mined resources. The team working on Astroneers come from a background which involves work on games like Halo, Assassin’s Creed, Team Fortress, the Sims, amongst many others so they know what they are doing, something that becomes plain to see when you look at your watch 5 minutes after starting the game and realise an hour has passed.
So you start out by selecting your Astronaut who then detaches their pod from the orbiting station type structure. You head down into the atmosphere of the nearby planet admiring the beautiful looking clouds as you descend. You touch down and examine your immediate surroundings. You have nothing but your trusty suit and a mining tool that can deform the very ground you walk on and mine resources.
As you venture further out you’ll soon discover what resources are used for and how you can take advantage of their applications. You can extend your pod to include all sorts of useful applications from Printers to vehicle bays and machines that will research strange things you have discovered. I had no idea what I was doing to start with but I started to figure things out and I loved how things naturally start to make sense. Once you figure one piece of the puzzle the other pieces start to drop into place it’s a very satisfying experience and leaves you wanting more and more.
The control schemes are simple yet effective and do pretty much all you could want them to. it’s the polygon game world though that impresses. It’s simple yet looks gorgeous and all you want to do is explore. You can sculpt the world around you and even deform the ground right down to the planets core.
So what features do you get in this early access version of Astroneer? Well the developers have a hand list on their website so lets take a look.
Explore multitudes of procedural worlds.
Shape completely malleable terrain. Dig to the centre of the earth, or forge mountains.
Craft vehicles and discover resources to reach ever further in the galaxy.
Survive in ever more harsh and rewarding environments.
Play with friends in online or local multiplayer.
Astroneer is expected to be in early access for a year or two but it’s certainly something that you should be keeping tabs on because this game has all the hall marks of a classic in the making. I can’t wait to see what the developers have in store for the games future. So far they have done an astounding job, this is how early access games should be and what space exploration done right, looks like. This game is satisfying and beautiful to play.

When you look at other games in it's genre, Astroneer struggles to deliver enough content for it's $20 price tag. There are a handful of $20 early access survival games out there that offer far more content, Rust for instance. That being said, the game is pretty fun when playing with other people. We were able to get about 14 hours of gameplay in a co-op session knowing nothing about the games mechanics. However, it's pretty easy to figure everything out. Base building is quite simplistic, and requires very few resources to build. Finding the resources is where it might take a while depending on your location. There's really nothing you need to worry about in a survival sense either except for oxygen. Oxygen does not deplete as long as you are tehterd to a oxygen line. These lines can be made easily which basically negates this factor in your survival. On a whole, Astroneer isn't much of a survival game. You don't need to find food, you don't need to build a shelter, and theres maybe 1-2 hostile plant things that will injure you if you get close. Falling off from cliffs also will injure you. When you talk survival you're thinking I need to manage food, water, find shelter, sustainment, fend off predators - well theres no food, no water, no shelter unless you make yourself one for asthetic purposes, and no predatory creatures that will hunt you.
The fun right now in the game comes from the exploration, and for maybe 1-2 hours the researching mechanics. Researching artifacts is how you are able to build space ships and rovers etc. There aren't many things to research right now so this facet of the game quickly becomes obsolete. Exploring the randomly generated worlds is pretty cool though. I just wish there was more to the game. The good thing is - it looks promising, it's early access so theres more to come. The gameplay is smooth and has appealing visuals. The art style is neat too.  I'll still recommend this game if you have the $20 to blow on 14-15 hrs.

I've played a bit more than what the Steam record says, and I do think this game has terrific atmosphere and heart. The world-building is superb. I only wish they'd figured out the game balance better. The grind wall is immediate, to the point where you have to start exploiting the game systems outside of what I'd consider normal or immersive gameplay. Past that, you're then over-leveled for everything except for certain creatures that will one-shot you unless you're essentially at end-game levels. I get (and like) having areas that are off-limits until you're a higher-level, but it's all so randomly mixed here and the starting quests already require you to grind - but where, since these are the starting areas? Compound this with skill and magic sets that range from exquisitely useful to worthless, and the balance is just massively off. I don't want to have to look at a guide to see what's useless or doesn't work in a game. For as much artistry as exists in the rest of the game, the gameplay itself is frustrating. It's a shame given the care that goes into the rest of the world.
The Diablo franchise never quite builds the world that Divine Divinity does, nor is it ever quite so open, but the gameplay is so much better balanced, so much more fun. Balance counts for a lot.
Some will still enjoy the grind elements as a price you have to pay to enter the world. They will enjoy it a lot more than I did. For me, the gameplay is an element to the story and if your gameplay is so ill-balanced, it can begin to amount to bad storytelling. That's what happens here. I can see why many consider it a classic, and I think it is. It acts like a classic, it feels like a classic, it oozes with mood. It just doesn't play like a classic, at least for me. If you don't like grind walls and OCD leveling, avoid this. If you don't mind them or that can be fun for you instead of infuriating, the story and world are richly rewarding.

The game is much less cheap than Max Payne 1 in terms of how enemies are placed and how they react to you, and the gunplay which was already great in the original game is honestly five times better, mostly due to improvements in physics. Enemies ragdoll in over-the-top ways when killed, and explosions make environmental objects fly into the air, which is just what Max Payne needed to perfect that stylish John Woo action. Everything feels much smoother, movement is less restrictive, and it's still an absolute blast to play today. The gameplay has hardly aged a day, unless you're someone who needs collectables and achievements to enjoy yourself. The story is more complex, has better writing, and is a little less cheesy, but still retains the humour and light parody of the original.
The graphics were improved a lot, and characters have real faces now that make better looking expressions than just "neutral" and "constipated". Obviously the visuals aren't great now in a technical sense, but it still looks fairly aesthetically pleasing, which I really can't say about the first game. The art style stayed the same in all the ways that matter; the graphic novel segments look better than ever, and are still the perfect way of telling this story. It's a little less dark and gritty than Max Payne 1 though.
One complaint: Though the first game is very difficult, this one actually went too far the other way, because it's a little too easy until you're nearing the end of the game, which is kind of a shame. Otherwise though, it improves on its predecessor in pretty much every way.

This game is very stylisticly simple, which makes it easy to understand, adding to the simulation/strategy goodness. I was immediately able to understand all of the menus and icons, and navigate it efficiently in a matter of minutes. I especially liked how in the female prisons they include the family cells and nurseries, understandably not in the male prisons because females are much more favored to have custody of children in the eyes of the law, which is a nice touch showing an understanding of law and order and biases inside of it. It also pays attention to the fact that rehabilitation over deturrance is what some people prefer, adding in the Pacifier warden and offering different schedualed rehabs like alcohol and substance abuse recoveries.
Now, the story is much different from this simplicity. The first one is very driving and shows lots of different emotions, displaying at least some of the psychology behind murderers and the spirituality touch just made it even better, even though I am not a very religious person. The reason is that those things already exist, and while I realize in actuality it would take at least some time to unlock those benefits, you must also understand that waiting in a game simply isn't fun. When amking one, you should assume your player is not playing any other game, while at the same time checking for things like alarming similarities with other famous games to prevent the online community from yelling at you. This prevents things like long wait times, but also overused game mechanics and carbon copy characters ripped from other games.

All the fun of a deck-builder, without all that annoying deck-building!
Sentinels of the Multiverse is the digital port of the co-op tabletop card game of the same name.  Using the motif of classic comic book archetypes, players use decks focused around a superhero and combine their efforts against a game-controlled supervillain using its own deck (scaled up in power compared to the heroes, of course).  It plays very much like a standard CCG:  Players play equipment and abilities from their hand to power up their hero and do damage to the villain and their minions, with the ultimate goal of reducing the villain to 0 HP before the villain does the same to all the heroes. Each deck has its own spread of cards, in varying amounts, which synergize together to form a cohesive strategy, such as no-nonsense damage, slow-building momentum, or complex combos.
One of the unique things about Sentinels is that, while it looks very much like a deck-building game or a CCG, all decks come pre-built and never change from game to game.  While this lack of customization may deter some deck-building fans, the ease of access pre-built decks offers is a clear net positive.  Ready-made decks means a player can be confident that a deck is going to “work” by design, as opposed to the randomness of a deck-builder, or the heavy level of strategic knowledge needed for a CCG.  Players can also more easily learn the intricacies of a deck from game to game, and pick the character that suits their interests the best, spending less time planning the game and more time PLAYING it.  This also holds for the villain decks as well:  winning a Sentinels game is not easy, but by learning a villain’s deck, players can prepare a strategy suitable to combat it in subsequent games.  And in all fairness to CCG veterans, while CCGs offer nigh-infinite combinations of cards to create the perfect deck, more often than not competitive decks will end up falling into the same few dozen “meta” configurations anyways.  Sentinels cuts out the middle man and has those solid meta-configurations at the ready from the word go, and with unified character-based flair to boot.
The base Sentinels game has a rather sparse choice in heroes and villains, but a vast quantity of expansions in accessible price ranges takes care of that problem quickly.  The variety of deck choices is a big part of the game, as different hero combinations can completely change the flow of a match, and each villain’s mechanics differ wildly; it’s rarely as easy as going hog wild on anything with a lifebar attached to it, and sometimes attacking the villain isn’t even the way to defeat them!  The wealth of different mechanics DOES mean that games of Sentinels can get complicated, with a lot of floating abilities and modifiers to keep track of, but that’s where the digital version of this game is a godsend.  Not only does the computer automate actions and conveniently display active effects, it even reminds the players of some conditional possibilities that could easily be forgotten (for example, stating which character will be the target of the villain’s impending doom next round, or how effective a player’s combo attack will be if used in the current situation).
The visual design of the game is a rather complex subject.  The character design and art is good enough, but not great, and characters adhere to comic book tropes perhaps a little TOO much; with a little effort it’s not hard to see the famous inspirations for many of the characters.  While it could be called uninspired design, or even satire, the truth is the creators have actually attempted to create an entire comic book universe as an homage to their childhood passions, complete with its own Gold, Silver, and Modern Age, and all the nuance that entails, but in the form of a card game, not comic books (for full details, listen to “The Letters Page” podcast).  Having listened to said podcast, I am fully-willing to forgive any deficiency or cliché in design I find and appreciate the sheer tenacity of the creators for building the world they’ve built.
Sentinels is perfect for the strategist gamers who enjoy card games and want to try something new.  Cooperative games also bring a lot more fun and friendship to the table than competitive ones, so if you’ve got a group of like-minded strategists at the ready, you’ll have a great time.

Of all the games I've played to date, three have nailed all three categories of storytelling. There was Morrowind, my favorite game; there was New Vegas, my second; and there was Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, my third favorite game of all time.
When I was younger, less open to new ideas, I was reluctant to pick this one up, even though I loved the series up to then--- the underlying reason being that it centered around a man with whose culture I never thought I could identify, and therefore not be able to become immersed.
I was wrong.
Carl Johnson is a subtle man as far as Rockstar characters go. He is thoughtful, careful, never impulsive. He is intelligent, not prone to being manipulated. A natural leader. He rarely shows passion when it comes to morals and can seem gray at times. He doesn't whine and complain like a spoiled preteen (you hear that, Niko?) It will take you deep into the game to see that he is a good man, if you ever come to that conclusion.
On his journey to the top, his downfall and journey back up, Carl sojourns through an odyssey of interesting characters who reach two different peaks: the neo conservative Mike Toreno, and the mad liberal known only as The Truth. Without either one of these men, who stand on opposite ends of the game's dynamic philosophical underlay, Carl would have been lost. Each presents his ideals and reasoning in a manner not hitting the player over the head, and stand out among the greatest and most memorable characters in gaming.
As for the villain--- Samuel L. Jackson never agreed to a better role.
The plot is presented in such a way that you feel every step Carl takes in his conquest of Los Santos; you feel the loss as he's betrayed when things are going so well and banished to the country; you feel his clawing back up, making new friends who help him build an empire across the state and back to where it all began.
As all that Carl has built steers toward the final battle, you feel the tension as his hometown descends into chaos reminiscent of the Los Angeles riots of '92. At the end of it all, you'll find yourself looking fondly on his accomplishments, his friends, even his trials and his enemies.
Finally, the atmosphere.
I remember looking out the window of a car dealership in GTA III (the one with the Banshee) and wishing that I was looking out into miles of farmland that I could actually explore. It amazes me to think that the devs of Rockstar were as inspired by imagination and wanderlust as I was. While San Andreas carried a lot of what Rockstar would later pejoratively label "empty space", I appreciated it (more than many fans, apparently). I loved it. It felt real, being stranded in the desert outside Las Venturas, a road trip through the green country on the other side of the map, flying over empty lands to find a magnificent dam and small community in the middle of nowhere. The graphics at the time were getting outdated, but the imagination and content (even the "empty space") made up for it a thousand times.
From my opening hour experiencing this world back on Playstation 2, Grove Street was my home. I was there. I laughed like a little girl at how real it felt when I helped hold up a fast food joint.
After each mission, when Carl would return home for the evening, I felt like I was headed home after a hard day's work. Dropping the friends home on the way was an especially nice touch. When I would return to Grove Street years later in GTA V, I got a little misty-eyed. Although the place had changed, it felt the same. A bitterness arose on seeing the cul-de-sac littered with Ballas.
Plot, characterization, setting. Each of these things were executed with power and precision by a company who to this day put their damnest into every thread of every tapestry they roll out to us. They are the masters of their craft and no one in the industry has deserved this level of success more than they.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game with standardized third-person shooter gameplay but with an aberrantly deep and powerful story with an unforgettable ending.
The game starts off with Captain Walker accompanied by Sergeant Lugo and Lieutenant Adams who begin as ordinary cliché characters who make cheesy remarks and below average quality humour jokes which is a usual formula for a game of this genre, however as the game progresses you encounter more and more horrific events which drastically deprives them of these characteristics and makes them cold-hearted soldiers. Instead of glorifying the image of being a soldier this game puts you through the relentless horrors and cruelty involved in a war zone. The conclusion is the absolute highlight of this game and features one of the best plot twists to date across all platforms of entertainment and that is what makes this game stand out from the rest of the other third-person shooters.
However despite how much I praise the storyline's uniqueness I can't exactly say the same for the gameplay. There is nothing wrong with it, but it certainly isn't anything special either; it's just average. If you've played another decent third-person shooter with a cover system this game will feel quite similar. You cover behind varying objects and peek your head to shoot when an enemy is exposed and when you have enough health to risk yourself being exposed. When you have taken damage you get back into cover until your health regenerates (kind of like Wolverine). Ammunition is scarce which makes the game more intense and makes it a requirement to determine whether a suitable weapon or a weapon with more ammo is a better idea in a situation.
You are accompanied with your allies for the majority of the game and them dying will result in a game over. This type of mechanic is usually detrimental to the enjoyment of the player because it becomes irritating and detracts from your ability to play the game and progress as you wish, however this is not the case in this instance. They help shoot enemies proficiently and you can even command them who to specifically kill and are able to use grenades even when you don't have any left, which can be used to kill people behind turrets, which adds a strategic component to combat. When a teammate is incapacitated you have a certain amount of time to heal him and get him back on his feet before he bleeds to death, but doing this isn't even necessary if another comrade is available who can heal the other comrade to health if you command him to do so. When your comrades are incapacitated it is usually due to your own incompetence rather than their idiocy since you have not been a helpful asset to the team, and are not killing enough enemy soldiers in time. (Unless you're playing on the "FUBAR difficulty" in which case your teammates will frequently fall in battle to add challenge to the most challenging difficulty setting in the game).
The game is set in Dhu Bai during a huge sandstorm which makes a great atmosphere for the game. Seeing and travelling from all the impressive skyscrapers in the middle of an intense sandstorm is spectacular.
Would I recommend this game? Well even though this is a "recommended review" I would exclusively recommend this to people who enjoy the third-person shooter genre. Lots of other reviewers on Steam claim this game to be an exception for third-person shooters however this game's main purpose is basically a big fat build up to the exceptional finale, so if you dislike third-person shooters in general this game will probably bore you.
The multiplayer segment of this game is an online service which involves you playing against other players with different types of modes which are unoriginal and monotonous. As I previously mentioned in the singleplayer section this game shines in terms of storyline, not gameplay, and the multiplayer option just feels like an inferior CS:GO or Call of Duty clone. Do not bother buying this game if the multiplayer aspect of games interests you.

→ interesting story, but not always presented quite as well (see below)
→ continuous and complete narrative with a solid pacing (no lazy game design that consists of running to the castle to save the girl just to fight every boss 3 times and eventually running back the exact same levels, just with another character *cough DMC4)
→ Character Development: Dante is no longer this likable, funny, easy going anime stock character with the obligatory white hair. Here he starts as a highly unlikable brat (imo), whose answer to everything seems to be 'F**k you', but takes responsibility eventually and learns some social skills.
Con
→ old and passionate fans should be able to stomach some design and story changes
→ caution: dialog writing may course spontaneous cringing at times (personally, I don't mind that much: bad dialog writing can be hilarious)
→ I'm under the impression that DmC takes itself too serious, especially after playing other DMCs
→ weapon balancing and combat rank system is kinda off (but I did not notice until I more or less knew what I was doing)
→ annoying side-kick
→ some enemies can only be hit with certain weapons (blue enemies with blue weapons, red with red) which can be annoying (→ if you own a ps4, you may consider buying the definite edition, which (from what I've heard) solves a lot of the original gameplay problems and adds more difficulty levels)
If you are interested in a brilliant over-the-top action title and you are willing to overlook some minor design flaws this game is for you.

I should start out by saying I am pretty new to games, so I am just going to explain how I enjoyed it from the perspective
Overall, the game was a lot of fun. It starts out pretty easy, explaining all the basics and letting you learn without much hand-holding, before it begins to get difficult. The most important part, is how fun the combat is. And I have to say, it was a lot of fun.
The controls were perfect, and it was a lot of fun trying new combos out on different baddies. All the demons are unique and fun to kill in their own way. It is stylish, enjoyable, and you want to get more and more points in hopes of hitting that SSS ranking. It took about 8 hours to play through all 20 missions, and I haven't even gotten into the famous NG+ content. I played through on Nephilim, or what would be hard. The graphics were pretty good, and the atmosphere was amazing. One of the best parts was the music. Ninja Theory did a great part on that, getting both Noisia and Combichrist to make some killer songs for it once again.
The only two complaints I have are the cutscenes and bosses. The cutscenes, while having great voice acting, were very stiff, and didn't really look up to date compared to the rest of the game. The second problem was that the bosses were really easy. At of all of them, only one really gave me trouble, and it wasn't even the final boss. They all seemed really easy to deal with, even for a beginner like me. Now, I know I wasn't on the hardest difficulty, but I doubt everyone will play through three more times to get the rest of the difficulties unlocked.
Either way, this was still a great game, and I would pick it up for the price it is at.

Spec Ops: The Line is somewhat unique title that ditches away with the savior hero figure and takes a more realistic approach to the horrors of war. I think that an appropriate description is Apocalypse Now 2: Modern Warfare. The story, the characters and the music hint towards a spiritual successor to the 1979 Vietnam themed movie. Be warned, this is no Shaving Ryan's Privates or anything like that; don't expect to play this game and dream at night that you're a hero.
The game startw with you leading a small team and proceed on a rescue mission in Dubai. Your main drive forward is the pursuit of your former superior and once life savior, Colonel John Konrad. As the story unfolds, you try to make sense of what happened and what is currently going on. I have played it only in the single player campaign, but the game menu list co-op and other forms of multiplayer. My run at a relaxed pace was a bit more that 7 hours, but your milage may vary by +-2 hours, depending on your skills and your desire to collect all the intelligence scattered across the game. The gameplay mechanics is a shoot from cover from 3rd person over the shoulder perspective. The run/sprint action is a bit awkward at first, but players should get used to it quite easily. There is no jumping, but you vault obstacles while running or from behind cover. What it lacks in freedom of movement and mechanics, it compensates by story, animation, voice acting and overall atmosphere. One thing worth remembering is that 33 is just the right-hand side of 88. Does that mean that it’s the right side, or that is just half the craziness? Well, play the game and find out!
Originally released in 2012, the graphics and sound hold very well in 2017. Maxed out with V-Sync on, the computer ran cool and quiet, sign that any proper recent GPU (I used an R9 390 8GB with a Ryzen 7, and back in the day an R9 270X with an FX-8350) will not shed a drop of sweat rendering it. In my case, compatibility with Windows 10 x64 was flawless, so I can only assume that the old problems reported on forums have already been dealt with.
Cons/missing:
- restricted freedom to move
- limited variety of orders that can be issued
- corridor type progression, even in a desert
- no vehicles to drive
- no night missions
Neutral:
* Gears of War type cover, shooting and movement
* some of the speech is cliche, but it is somewhat expected every time it happens
* the variety of environments and objectives in the missions is average
* AI has some highs in some instances when they try to flank you, but most of the time just rushes towards you; admittedly, from behind cover.
Plus:
+ the story is unusual and engaging
+ solid voice acting
+ the atmosphere is tense and recreates what the game story is trying to convey
+ weapons do solid damage, especially when used properly and you generally feel outnumbered, but not underpowered
+ graphics are good and framerate is smooth
+ character textures “evolve” as the game unfolds, further adding realism to the physical traumas and scars.
As a person who played the three newest Deus Ex games, and Dishonored 2 (I don’t remember what I did in Dishonored 1, did not get the Ghost achievement, but definitely no killing spree) without killing a single person, I totally recommend this game.

Never played this when it come out in 2002. Just finished it.
The game is very immersive. The graphics are isometric 3D, simply but they do the job. The music is weird. You can't called it good music, but in a way it is because it adds immensily to the immersiveness, with a lot of ambient music, and it sounds otherworldly. The characters and dialogue are pretty good, but not in a serious way. This game is not at all serious and you might be disappointed by the lore, the voice actors (very funny) and the discussions IF you take the game seriously. So you shouldn't in my oppinion. There is alot about Tolkien here, cause its high fantasy, but also some winks (like the dagger that shines when orcs are nearby) and some references to Terry Pratchett as well if I am correct. Also some insider stuff like the AA Gent scroll. The world map is quite large and pretty good, maybe a bit too much of the same though.
The battle system is relatively simple but basically like Diablo. I found to be challenging in the beginning but in accordance with the name of the game, you become godlike towards the end (health and resistances and stats begin to skyrocket with the use of gems). Also, frost is utterly broken, broken! Because of these things the game becomes too easy towards the end, even on the highest difficulties. So maybe it's not a bad idea to not use frost weapons and less gems. On the other hand, you can make so much potions that you can full heal like 99 times. In short, there are some balancing issues to this game, but they can be avoided if you so choose. There are quite alot of sequence bugs in quests as well and that kind of sucks.
Overall, I was happily surpriced by a game with Diable battle mechanics, a lot of questing and exploration and quite alot of humour, it is really a funny game.
So, I give a 7.5/10. I would have given a higher score if not for the bugs and overpowered stuff in the game.

A game that would've been great 15 years ago, and was surprisingly okay for nowadays.  The game play is a bit like the old Ultima games.  The world is pretty vast.  There are enough different abilities to keep it interesting.  And the plots and sidequests are intriguing.  It still has some of that old world adventuring - looking for hidden entrances and solving mysteries in addition to the more typical 'get me some herbs' adventuring that's overdone nowadays.  If you don't mind the older graphics and style, it'll be well worth playing.
Also, don't get too turned off at first.  I found the first 15-20% to be much less interesting than the last 80%.  Give it time to get going!
Additionally, if you love Divinity: Original Sin, you might enjoy this anyway: although neither is essential to the other, they are set in the same world, and you get loads of backstory here.  The only caveat: Beyond Divinity, the middle section of story, is much less playable.  I'd suggest playing Divine Divinity, then reading about what happens in Beyond Divinity, then playing (or replaying) Divinity: Original Sin.

It's kind of like Morrowind invaded Diablo II. It's a very open world ARPG without a terrible amount of guidance or quest markers. The only handholding this game will do is the occasional place mark of interest on automap if something is mentioned in dialogue thing. Quests are usually straightforward enough, but some require some critical thinking, exploring, and secret finding.
You can choose between 3 classes (Warrior, Mage, Survivor) with male and female variants, both starting with slightly different innate skills. You can also mix and match your character with other classes' abilities, and make a warrior-battlemage-paladin-thief if you so desire.
Combat:
You got your standard left click on enemy physical attack, character auto-attacks it until it dies. Your spells: Shove lightning bolts up enemies asses until they die. Then you got your Stealth: Lay traps, sneak around, backstab, and poison enemies until they die.
Exploration:
Being an open world game, there's a lot of land to cover, but what I didn't expect this game to have is some RTS elements, like fog of war, and being able to pan your camera anywhere in the current level by holding shift, and you can even pause the game to piddle about your inventory to take a potion or whatever. There's also several large overworlds connecting to the main one, and the way you enter them is you walk up to the black-wall-of-nothingness-end-of-level and it asks you whether to proceed to the next area or stay in the current one, reminds me of S.T.A.L.K.E.R, speaking of marked one...
Then there's the teleport stones and teleporters. Teleporters are much like waypoints in D2, in that you just find them and click on them to activate them. However, in this game its not that simple, you need specific teleporter activation scrolls to enable them. Like a couple of waypoints will require a human scroll, and some will require a dwarf scroll, etc. These scrolls don't expire and are simply needed to activate the teleporters, and can be found in various parts of the world, mainly from NPCs that will give them to you if they trust you enough.
The teleporter pyramid stones are much like a Farore's Wind, except they work anywhere. Lay one down one place, and lay the other one down another place to make a two way portal. You can also just use the one in your inventory to make a one way teleport. Ideally, you lay one down in an area with merchants (like a town), bring the other one with you, and use it to go back and forth to offload your loot and get supplies and the like. You can lose one or the other pretty easily if you don't remember to pick up the one you travel with back up after teleporting back. Man, talk about being anal about using a town portal. I love it.
Other: There's a metric ton of containers to loot, deposit items, and even put in your inventory to bring back with you to make a little home-made stash in your town of choice. As well as a lot of books and manuscripts to read, some being lore, or an illustration, a recipe, something completely random and silly, or something important to a quest.
There be tons of baddies everywhere to kill, and like a true RPG, some are incredibly overleveled and OP near the earlier areas, until you get swole and take revenge on their never respawning sorry asses. Yeah, it seems enemies never respawn, at least for the most part. This game remembers literally EVERYTHING. So if you're an elite OCD person, you could kill every enemy, merchant, guard, civilian, defenseless forest critter, loot every item, lift every rock (literally), and stuff every container down your trousers, and the game remembers it all. Save files got absolutely huge near the end of the game, somewhere around 50-70 MBs a save, that's pretty insane.
There's quite a lot of sidequests to take on, aside from the main quest, and at least most of them are pretty interesting and fun to solve.
Technical:
The game runs well enough on a modern OS (Windows 7), but it did crash a couple times, and then even worse, a large handful of times a random burst of static played, then after several seconds the game looped the last .3 seconds of sound over and over like it froze, but the game continued playing fine until several more seconds passed in which the game slowed to a crawl and held my CPU hostage constantly using 50% until I ctrl+alt+delete ♥♥♥♥♥smacked the process down. It's like the game's sound gets confused, and randomly holds my CPU at gunpoint. Quicksaving and quickloading after the burst of static seems to prevent it from hanging, preventing a reboot of the game.
Overall I give this an 8/10, an overlooked gem I wish I had discovered much earlier.

A worthy sequel to the original game, Max Payne 2 is pretty much on the same level. Better yet, there are some things that MP2 did to offer a more varied gameplay, such as:

It is still one of the best and most solid Third Person Shooters out there. The storytelling and the scenario itself reached a highter (and in my eyes even more mature) level than in the first game, the graphics were as good as they were possible back then (even current titles have a hard time creating as good character graphics as Max Payne 2 had) and the action itself is as exciting and cool as it can be. Right off the bat, the game is much harder than Max Payne, for better and for worse. Bullet time got a heavy nerf while remaining a strong tool for taking out enemies who don't come at you one by one. I've playing through all three difficulties, and at time the easiest one was the hardest thanks to the flexible difficulty. Moving up, the challenge remains the same, but as the game puts it: "This difficulty no longer adapts, YOU adapt." As for the worse, it's really unfortunate. I'm not sure why, but they decide to put enemies in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t locations where they can hit you before it's even possible to see them. In the first game, there was an occasional grenade down a staircase, but with this, it's just enemies running through a door pre-firing at your head that ONLY trigger when you get close to the door.
The boss fights this time around are much different. Most of them require something different aside from straight up killing them. It's a nice change of pace, but in the end, it results in you just killing them. One of the boss fights was completely reused from the first game, which is a shame given their budget and success of Max Payne.
It's as fun as ever. This is Max Payne. To compensate for the change to bullet time, you now have an in-combat reload that freezes time as you reload and keeps you in bullet time. It's very fun to play around with, but the speed at which you reload could have been increased. It's gets tedious the more you go into the game, but it's absolutely necessary to beat some of the clumps of enemies.
You get a few new weapons in this game, such as the MP5 with a scope, Dragonuv
which is an auto-sniper and Max finally learned how to hold two Desert Eagles. Other than that, you've got all of the classics back, with the exception of the Colt Commando being replaced with the Kalashnikov, which is the same thing. A problem solved from Max Payne is the weapon disparity towards the end of the game. Enemies finally get a mix of weapons that you can pick up without it being a run and gun with only the powerful AR.
Max cuts back on his edgy dialogue here, but not by much. He's still your dark brooding hero you know and love. In addition to playing as Max,
The overall quality of the voice acting to the visuals is an awesome improvement, which allows the story to be just as impactful as the original.
I love this game, I really do. After playing Max Payne 1 and 2 back to back though, Max Payne just has a certain charm to it. Both games are very fun, very though provoking and provide a decent challenge. Graphics and dialogue aside, I feel this game is a step down, but not by much. I gave the original a 9/10, this game is a solid 8.5/10. There's just something off about its gameplay that makes it different. With that said, there's been so many improvements from Max Payne that it's such a great game that just works out of the gate. It feels much less dated despite coming out just a few years after the first game. If you've made it this far, give both games a shot. Play them back to back, it makes everything that much better.

Since I have already posted a review of
, this review specifically covers the differences in the Definitive Edition and assumes the reader is already familiar with the game. If not, here’s the spoiler-free TLDR:
– it comes free with the Definitive Edition, and it will help you better appreciate the differences between the two versions, both the things that were added and the things that were lost.

I feel both versions deserve a 10/10 rating.
---
The “Definitive Edition” of this wonderful game represents a hard compromise between art and gameplay. Gameplay has been tweaked according to popular response to the original, but some aspects of art and game balance were sadly lost in the process.
The main differences include:
* An easier and a harder difficulty mode were added. These change how much damage you take when hit, and how much EXP is needed to purchase upgrades. Additionally, the Easy difficulty adds a checkpoint in the game’s notorious escape scenes.
* In the original game, it was possible to cheese the “Immortal” achievement for completing a game with no deaths with backups of your save file. While you can still do this in Definitive Edition, there’s a new “One Life” difficulty which takes a number of precautions against save-scumming in an attempt to force you to legitimately beat the game without dying, and a new “Unhinged” achievement for completing it.
* Two new optional areas were added, each a new power to learn. Black Root Burrows gives a new dash move, and Lost Grove gives an orb-throwing power. The new areas also have new music and cutscenes.
* Spirit wells can now be used for fast travel.
* Secret areas now count towards map completion percentage; getting 100% in an area now means it is truly finished.
*  Nothing is permanently missable anymore, and points of no return have been removed. You can now go back to any completed area at any time.
Many of these changes were made in response to criticism of the original game. People hated the escape sequences, so they had to be made easier. People hated missing secrets in the “lost forever” areas, so they are no longer lost forever. People hated crawling across the entire map repeatedly for missed collectibles, so fast travel was introduced. The cynic would say that the game has undergone a measure of “casualization”, and they wouldn’t be wrong. However, I don’t exactly disagree with any of the new changes from a gameplay perspective, and I think that the gameplay was improved because of them. In fact, I still consider the Definitive Edition to be a 10/10 game regardless of the criticisms I’m about to make, as the merit of the game far outweighs any of the flaws, but that won’t stop me from making note of the flaws.
My biggest gripe with Definitive Edition is the broken balance. The two new powers, the Dash and the Light Burst, absolutely break the game. The Light Burst in particular allows Ori to undermine almost every Bash puzzle in the game – both of the jumping puzzle variety, and of the variety which require you to kill far-off enemies. While the two new areas were built around the new powers, the rest of the game simply wasn’t built for them. To fix this, the designers did absolutely nothing except for adding about ten ugly doors to the game which require the use of the Light Burst to open, locking off various secret areas that could previously be reached early by skilled jumping or clever bashes. And this is perhaps the most disheartening part: although the light burst is “optional”, its mere existence now means you are punished for outside-the-box thinking. Whereas in the old game you were rewarded with an extra collectible for your innovative jumps and small sequence breaks, now you are met with a locked door and your collectible teasing you on the other side, mocking you for having not yet collected the most broken power in the game.
But in the end, while the Light Burst and Dash do break the game in a staggering number of ways, I can’t deny they are wickedly fun to use, so I begrudgingly approve of them… but really, they could have done without all those doors.
My second biggest gripe is a side-effect of the new fast travel system, and of the philosophy that nothing should be lost forever. In my review of the original game, I said “The game creates a sense that you are spreading your light everywhere you go, and every place you visit becomes better because you were there.” Putting it bluntly, this is no longer the case in Definitive Edition. In the old game, once you flooded the Ginso Tree to wash out all the tumors, it became locked forever so you could at least imagine it was now clean inside. In Definitive Edition, you can go back and see that, nope, the water isn’t there and the impurities haven’t been washed away! Or did you unleash the element of wind so powerful that it blew apart the entire Gumomon fortress? …Nope, you can go back and see that it’s all still there, just how you left it! Bring light to the cursed misty woods, dispelling the curse forever? Well, now you can go back into the darkness whenever you want (although, to the game’s credit, the light of the misty woods now functions as a “light switch” which you can turn off again if you wish to re-enter the cursed area. That was a nice little touch.)
The “lost forever” sections from the old game, I felt, fit perfectly with the game’s central themes of life, death, and mourning. It felt
when your path was blocked off, forcing you to accept it and just move on, just like how the characters had to accept the deaths of their loved ones and move on. It felt especially fitting when you entered Mt. Horu only to have a huge boulder block off the entrance behind you, sealing you in forever. That sense of fate and foreboding, that you have to keep moving forward and not look back, was emotionally gripping. Sadly, even that rock has been removed in Definitive Edition, and you can exit Mt. Horu whenever you want.
But in the end, after making the transition from engrossment in the game’s story to caring about 100% completion and achievements, the lost-forever sections are damn annoying when you miss just one thing and have to start a new file because of it. The Definitive Edition removes this frustration and makes the game better, so I begrudgingly approve of it.
Those are my two biggest problems with this re-release, and I can’t truly fault either of them since they are trade-offs for an overall better game experience. From here, all I have left to offer are some truly petty nitpicks:
* The gimmick of Black Root Burrows is darkness. We already had a world with this gimmick, did we really need two?
* The boulder escape in Black Root Burrows spoils the Lava Tsunami music too early in the game. For shame!
* My favorite piece of music in the game, “Completing the Circle”, plays when you acquire the Charge Jump. The “circle” refers to the ability circle on the pause menu, and since the Charge Jump is the final power, the circle becomes complete. In Definitive Edition, it’s possible to skip the Dash and Light Burst powers, so you can get “Completing the Circle” to play even when you don’t have a completed circle. FOR SHAME!!
Overall, Definitive Edition is
as good as the original game, still just as beautiful, just as unforgettable, just as replayable, and still one of my favorite games of the whole decade. The sequel has some big shoes to fill.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a Jump'n Run plattformer with Metroidvania elements. The gameplay is super tight and rewarding and finding collectables feels great rather than a chore. While the game is unforgiving in some instances you can circumvent frustration by collecting ability points to get an edge or just set your own save point right before the frustrating part. The save mechanic is genious in this game. You spend some energy to create a save point whereever you want. Depending on how much energy you have, you have to decide carefully where to save. An interesting challenge on its own. If you don't want that kind of tension you can collect energy cells and upgrade your saving skill. No problems there.
I loved the visuals and the soundtrack. There is an enourmous attention to detail - something I am very keen on. The areas are distinct but sometimes I felt they could use some more variety in enemy types or obstacles. You get your standard thorns pretty often. For me it didn't hinder my enjoyment and this is more nitpicking than real critique.
The only thing that frustrated me were some of the chasing sequences. The first one felt amazing and tense but after that the magic wears off quickly. These sections aren't well designed in my opinion. More often than not I died over and over again because I just had no idea where to go. If there is a timed event where you need to run and your reflexes get tested, the developers need to make sure the player knows where to go and what he or she has to do next. That wasn't always the case for me.
Other than that and the fiddly keyboard controls later in the game I can't say anything negative about this game. Use a gamepad instead because otherwise you'll have to do some QWOP-style keyboard inputs to get all the abilities right. Talk about jumping into dashing into bashing into using the feather into dashing again into throwing some light balls. Yes, you'll get an enormous moveset and it feels amazing to get around later in the game - if you can manage the controls :D.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes an exploration-based plattformer. You'll get between 8 and 10 hours of gameplay depending on your itch to collect stuff. For me it was one of the best plattformers I ever played and I tried a lot of them.

A TCG Board Game Turn based Superhero Game. Similar to the VS system Marvel tried for a few years with a slightly different game mechanic. Each player controls one or more heroes, while a villain and environment deck each run themselves. A given game includes 3 to 5 heroes, 1 villain and 1 environment, which can be mixed and matched to create a number of different scenarios. The core game comes with 10 heroes, 4 villains, and 4 environments. It has some wonderful pros and some cons.
A: If you love the comics, the look, and superheroes in general. Then you will enjoy this game at any age
B: The artwork and style is nicely executed. Though more serious comic fans may critisize the artwork as not graphic enough or of high grade. It gets the job done.
C: Each Hero and villain has a purpose and the game has a solid structure to expand from.
D: It has a narrative and a simple tutorial.
E: Pow! Biff! Wam!, Interesting Character powers, mechanics and combinations.
F; Alot of expansion potential, not just additional heroes and villains but adding some new mechanics to increase player choices in a turn.
CONS
A: It can be too distracting in its layout with too much going on. Not a modern version of comics layouts, more old style. The massive amount of colors can flatten its appearance than draw players eyes in.
B: The animation mechanics, HP tracker and HP visual hurt the overall concept. It comes across cheaply done. The game could use a player customization and UI to allow players to re size the main screen, Increase and decrease patterns to make it more pleasable to their tastes. Something to consider. For example a Black and White version or making the HP of each big, for the eye impaired.
C: If the game changable graphic and style wise in the future. Would vastly improve the game overall
D: There is a difficultly scale that can get frustating. Like most TCGs expansions, they can be a trap for the same type of gaming experience.
E; It's strength of simplisity is also its weakness. Heroes vs a Villain is nice, but after a while can get too redundant. You cannot just keep adding those two elements.
OVERALL: More of a company attacking a main stream than creating something new. Sentinels will have plenty of the same type expansions and the game needs work. If you love superheroes, card games and combination gaming, then Sentinels is for you. Preview the game in Discussion, then hit VIDEO, see the gameplay at hand before buying, and look for this game on sale.  It has great potential, but hopefully is not limited by its one style artwork or same gameply or players will go on to something else.  It has its place, even though it does not wow you will beautiful graphic comic book art, like Magic the Gathering or other great comic book art, but it is a game that is very addicting. A great start to build off of.

I write this review just about the multiplayer. I have spent hundreds of hours in this game and I am not done with it yet. At first I have to say that I am not a very picky player when it comes to the multiplayer shooters, thus I can tolerate some severe problems very easily - especially if the game offers something interisting for me. The question is, can you?
Pluses:
- well designed maps
- variety of the available weapons and their customization
- simple creation of your own classes
- killstreak and perk system
- good optimalization
- a lot of game modes
- theatre mode (in-game build function which records your matches and allows you to edit them)
Minuses:
- due to the actual amount of active players you can play just some game modes (you'll surely find team deathmatch, free for all, demolition and party games)
- interpolation (tool made to equal the difference between the strenght of internet connections and computers with the intention of bringing more stable gameplay, it may cause that you see your enemy on a little bit different spot from his actual position and opposite)
- unbalanced weapons
- occasional campers
Final verdict: Its worth it, just wait for big sale.

A marvelous gem among the RPG genre! The game, even though it's pretty old, boasts a number of features not commonly found back in the day when it came out. One of which has to be the insane amount of environment interactivity that enables you to pick up, take with you or move/throw pretty much anything that's not nailed to the floor.
Story-wise, it's a classic good vs. evil theme where you play a role of one of the chosen ones (yup, you're not a lone... well, not in the beginning at least :)) and you need to help a wizard stop the crazy Black ring cult from summoning the Lord of Chaos.
For all you Diablo fans out there - Divine Divinity pretty much takes whatever made Diablo II great and implements it perfectly within it's own concepts with a few extra tweaks to make the game unique. There are lots of armors and weapons and the vast palette of skills ensures you to craft the character to your liking. Wanna be a magic wielding warrior? Or a two-hander fighting mage? Not a problem in Divinity.
Steam version of this game is actually a re-release with enhanced graphics and fullHD resolution support (16:10 formats included!) so the game looks awesome, packed with details bursting out of your screen. I'm a sucker for 2D graphics but Divine Divinity really looks and feels warm'n'cousy all the time. Especially while visiting taverns with lots of NPCs to talk to, warm fire flickering in the corner while a local drunkard is trying to woo some poor waitress...
The game is packed with side quests and tiny details like NPC dialog that help you finish or find more quests which are never set in a way that holds your hand. Instead - You need to explore, ask around and find out for yourself everything that has to do with the current mission that you're on.
Unfortunately, the game has some bug issues most of which are patched or easily avoidable - but there are a few game breaking bugs you might run into. For example - looting an item way before gaining a quest that tells you that the same item belongs to a person and you need to return it. If you've sold it - you can't finish the quest. Or a specific NPC that's vital to the main story that bugs and disables you from teleporting further.
Luckily, the Divinity community is still very active and actually all bugs have a way of "un-bugging" them either by workarounds or simple "cheats".
As a huge RPG fan, this game is probably somewhere in my top 3 RPGs I've ever played.

Divine Divnity is a game that was lost under the massive shadow of Diablo 2's release. While the game is similar to Diablo in its isometric, hack-and-slash type mechanics, there's a lot more to the game than meets the eye. There's a lot of dialogue, RPG elements, quests and non-linear story progression that you can find in the game.
You can pick between three (technically six) classes: Warrior, Mage, and Survivor (aka thief). You can play as male or female, and each gender starts off with different abilities. Despite the class system, you can build your character any way you want through attribute and skill points. If you want to be a warrior that uses two-handed swords and casts spells, you can do that. If you want to be a character that's balanced in all three aspects, you can do that as well.
The story, for the most part, is told well and written well, but it's not particularly gripping. You play as an adventurer who wakes up in a basement in Aleroth, a village full of healers. The town's leader, Mardaneus, has been afflicted with Alzheimer's -- I mean, he's been possessed by an undead mage and he's gone crazy. After braving the village's catacombs to kill the jerk that bewitched Mardaneus, the player can explore outside of the village. The story has pretty cliche elements: an army of orcs is going to attack the human kingdom, dwarves don't get along with elves, evil wizards plotting in the background, etc. That being said, there's a lot of easter eggs in the world, and the game can at least be light-hearted and make fun of itself.
Combat is straightforward, but it can be exhausting at times; you'll be literally clearing through dozens and dozens of mobs in order to get to a single objective, and then you'll have to backtrack all the way through a dungeon to get to the next part of a quest (This is magnified tenfold in the final stages of the game). In addition, the game sometimes struggles with enemy balancing. For example, when you leave Aleroth, you will occasionally run into an orc that is at least ten levels higher than you. After a while, enemy level does not become an issue, but the problem is still prevalent early on in the game.
Despite a few quest-breaking bugs and sometimes repetitive gameplay, I liked Divine Divinity. It's a good game for a cheap price, and it's a refreshing change of pace from the AAA crap that is spewed out in 2016. Give it a try.
