This is difficult.
I've been playing Hitman games since 2002, with the release of 'Silent Assassin' and I have played through and beaten them all. Any game with a rating system for your missions, I would strive for dozens of hours to get the perfect and fastest Silent Assassin run one could get. This franchise stumbled heavily with Absolution, and cracked its skull on the pavement with this reboot. Where to begin?
The graphics, sound, voice acting, they are all absolutely fine. They got a very good VA to replace Diana, who sounds more like the original than the Absolution recast did. The level design is certainly a return to IO Interactive's clever origins. So if the game is graphically competant, the sound design is well implemented, and the voice acting is great, what is the issue?
I purchased this entire series for under $30, and for the amount of content, it was a somewhat justifiable purchase because I knew IO interactive was getting SOME of the money. IO Interactive is a great developer that has been held hostage by the horrible decisions of a corporate boardroom somewhere in Japan. I've yet to even finish the game, I feel it is just so over-developed in the levels and frankly boring. This was most likely done to try and justify purchasing individual levels. Some of the most memorable moments I've ever had in video games, nevermind in the Hitman franchise, were in levels developed by IO that were 1/20th the size of most HITMAN maps. Excess only succeeds if that excessiveness doesn't come at an excessive cost. I feel poor publishing decisions, anti-consumer practices, and bloated/artificial grind for particular play-styles ruins this. This is a great imitation of a Hitman game if marketed and published by a soulless, shifty demon.
A) Episodic Content. You will never be able to convince me this is a good idea. See, I remember Gabe and Valve's promise of Episodic Content. 11 years later, it's the biggest elephant in the room. Selling a game piecemeal will never be a good business practice. Spending $60-80 on a game and not knowing if 90% of its content will be good in the future is a shady practice whether the content ends up good or not.
B) Because of episodic content being one level at a time, too much is packed into a single map.
C) All of the clever ways to eliminate people, all the combinations of weapon use and situational awareness- all the potentially hilarious scenarios and funny stories you can tell your mates about your original kill... They've all been listed as achievements you can easily see. Worse, you need to go around and meticulously do these things in order to unlock the weapons you'd like to use in the first place- so by the time you have your W2000 rifle, you are bored of the map. This is one of the worst changes to me. I will never understand the artificial pursuit of unlocking corporate-guidelined 'achievements.' and HITMAN has been built entirely around this psychological mindgame of rewarding you with XP or items for unoriginality.
D) Always Online. Always connected to a corporate server. Anyone who thinks this is a good idea for a single player game needs to absolutely ♥♥♥♥ off. Anyone who thinks building a single player game around constant micro-updates of content and DLC packs in a game already sold piecemeal is a corporate drone of the highest order. I felt like I needed to do more while walking across the width of one screen, followed by the addition of a sidekick added into the story, hinting at more to come. Genius!
5 minutes was enough think: 'whoah, this is a proper classic game'.
I'm saving this for Saturday from 4 to 9.
I will recommend this for now, but I can't see it being thumbsed down by myself. It takes 5 minutes to know this is quality.
Edit: I've played a few more hours. BUY this great game!

Once upon a time, there was a Snorlax that befriended a glow monkey. They liked to chill and eat peaches in the forest. Then climate change came and caused ecological collapse. The Snorlax died of starvation due in part by its non-diversified diet. The glow monkey, initially broken by the loss of his friend, rises up and uses his glow monkey powers to crush the encroaching pathogenesis that is killing the forest, 'r nature 'r whatever...
This is a great game. I find it challenging and entertaining; when I play it I lose track of time which is a good sign for me that I am enjoying a game.

What I like about this game, is that it does well by the platformer genre: the controls, challenge level, the visuals, and the music fit together well for a enjoyable game. The controls of are crisp there is no feeling having the glow monkey character [Ori] floating about the screen.  As you progress in the game, Ori gets new powers and new platforming elements are added to the game such as double jumping, dashing, and ‘slingshotting’. (These mini RPG elements of the game are icing on the cake for me) As Ori gains new powers, the game gently progresses in difficulty. The game allows for
player generated check points as well; I really liked this feature because I could hold on to more of my game progress.
The aesthetics of the game are a nice touch and add to the to mood of the game. The game take place in a visually pleasing phosphorescent old growth forest. This is not an original concept, regardless the game developers did well in creating their own representation of it. The music is comprised of well composed soulful instrumentals and the narrator voice has a distinct paternal feel to contrast the game play through ‘mother nature.’ The audio-visual match up is a bit cheesy, but it is NOT done poorly.
I am really enjoying playing this game and I am pleased with my purchase. 8/10

Prison Architect
Genre: Strategy/Simulation - Real Time Strategy/Simulation
Rating: 9.5/10
Personal playing period: Few months
Is it worth a buy: Yes. Even at full price. This is a necessity for any strategy/sim players collection.
Girl vs Game: I think there may have been a few times that I did in fact pick the game.
Personal Comment:
This is really a great game with a lot of depth and immersion. I have 80 plus hours and still have not felt a need to play the campaign yet. This is that game where you say just 5 more minutes and then 3 hours later you have your girlfriend and the police knocking on your door thinking you died as you were supposed to pick her up for a date 2 hours ago. This is a great immersive game with a lot to do. It is so much fun trying to design the perfect prison. Just make sure you have a lot of time or just have no job or girlfriend;)
Short Summary:
This is a prison building simulation strategy game. You start off with some money and a few construction workers and a open piece of land. You then need to start planning and building a prison to house prisoners that will be dropped every 24 hours. You can set how many prisoners must be dropped, what danger level they can be, etc. You are in charge of building the prison, managing the money so you dont run out of it, managing the prisoners and ensuring that they get reformed and that  they are kept happy and maintaing staff and cashflow on a day to day basis. If you like strategy/simulation games then get this.
Online gaming:
Have not played online but you can via steam workshop play other peoples prisons and also use escape mode to escape from prisons created by fellow gamers.
Learning Curve and Gameplay:
The learning curve to this game is quite intense. There is a lot that needs to be learned and understood. The utilities must be very well managed in order to ensure the prison does not run out of power and secondly to ensure the power stations and their lines don't cross. Then you have the whole physical construction and layout of the prison that you need to design and build. And then there is the management of the prison, the finances and so many more elements. The game just offers so much that you will spend endless hours on this without batting an eye. Fortunately there is an "unlimited funds"game mode which I would recommend to start off with till you have the game play nailed. Then start a prison with limited funds and then the fun starts as budgeting and finance planning is added to the list of things to do.

If you're playing multiplayer, however, be aware that any DLC content you buy (and there's a lot of it) cannot be used unless every single person you play with also owns it.   That includes new heroes - if the other people don't own the hero you want to play, YOU don't get to play it.. even if nothing else in that particular game requires DLC in any way.   Your ability to use your purchased DLC is restricted by other players' willingness to also purchase it.
I could almost forgive it with Villains and Environments... but Heroes? Sentinels of the Multiverse is a cooperative comic book card game where you and your friends control between 3 and 5 heroes who team up to fight supervillain bosses and their minions.  I have never played the actual card game, so I do not know how well the experience translates into the video game realm.
Pros:
-Simplicity:  This is a living card game, not a collectible card game.  There is no deck building; customization comes in the form of building the most effective teams of heroes, and selecting which variant form of each hero to play.
-Cross Platform: The mac/pc version of the game functions flawlessly, and is completely compatible with ios/android versions.  You can sit at your computer and play cooperatively with a friend on his ipad, and another friend on samasung smartphone.
-Flexibility: There's a single player mode where you play all the heroes; or you and and a friend can each play multiple heroes; or five friends can each play one hero, or any other combination where between 3 and 5 heroes are controlled by one or more players.
-Variety: Each match consist of at least five decks of cards: a villain deack, a team of hero decks, and an environment deck, adding up to [[MATH!!!]] possible permutations for a fresh experience each time.
-Difficulty: The villains are ranked on a difficulty scale with higher numbers representing a greater challenge.  At the time of this review, the highest difficulty rating is 4.  Even at difficulty 1, the heroes are by no means guaranteed to win, and at diffulty 4 the heroes will need a solid team composition, smart plays, and a fair amount of lucky card draws to have any hope of victory.
Campiness:  Yes, this is a pro.  This game presents itself as a friendly and loving spoof of the comic book worlds we love.  It's filled with refences and inside jokes that are as much fun as the game itself.
Cons:
-Limited enjoyment to be had in single player.  This game does have a single player mode, as well as periodic "One-shots" and story challenges for the solo player controlling a team of heroes, and even a random matchmaking feature for online multi-player, but in general you need to have a group of friends to enjoy all that sentinels has to offer.
-All players in a multiplayer match need a particular DLC for anybody to use it.  If I owned an actual hero deck that you haven't bought yet, and I brought it to your house, I could play my new heroes, even if you only owned the basic set. In the video game, if I own the season one season pass, and you only own the basic set, then I have to be limited to the basic set as well if I want to join a mulitplayer game with you.
-Card Game:  In general, I do not like card games ported over to the digital realm.  My friends had to actually purchase the base set for me before I would try this game.  I'm glad they did, because it has proved an exception to the otherwise infallible rule.
-Sonic Damage:  I'm glad this company went through the effort to add visual and sound effects to the cards, as well as even some minimal voice acting.  But the sound effect of Sonic Damage, is a little too spot on, because it is literally painful.

As much as I wanted to be able to say I recommended Borderlands 2, I simply can't.  Recommending it would be lying for me.  When I bought Borderlands 2, I was expecting something closer to Borderlands 1.  I'm not saying that Borderlands 2 is a completely different genre, but it in no way lives up to the first game.  Let's take a look at some pros and cons shall we?
Pros:
Good enough graphics
Very diverse weapon array
Good Vehicle Gameplay
Cons:
Bad Story: Not that it wasn't interesting, but it doesn't really match up with vault hunting.  It's a little more of a Star Wars esque plot about a tyrannical entity ruling over a population with a rebellion that the player joins.
Terrible Singleplayer:  Borderlands 1's Singleplayer was excellent.  Though some missions would give a solo player some trouble, they were ALWAYS beatable.  In Borderlands 2, I spent a frustratingly large amount of time and ammo working through a maze of enemies to reach a boss, and said boss would just keep spawning more and more enemies to the point where I'd get overwhelmed.
Player Characters:  The playable characters in this game in no way lived up to the ones in the first game.  While they were fun and each had their own unique traits, I enjoyed playing as Mordecai WAY more than the people in this game.
In short, while Borderlands 2 is an okay game, I have to say that you're better off skipping this entry.  Hopefully they'll do a better job with Borderlands 3 than they did with this one, even Pre-Sequel was an improvment over this.

While not as recognized as the original classic, Max Payne 2 improves upon the original in almost every way. The graphics are better (Max in particular looks miles better than he did, especially in the face), the action and setpieces are cranked up and the gunplay is drastically improved. That last one is harder to explain, but it is immediately recognizeable once you start playing. The guns just feel better, and you can hit your target much more effectively in the sequel. They've also improved the use of bullet time, making it easier to simply turn it on, run into a room and gun people down. While you could do this in the first game, Max was much more likely to dive any time bullet time was activated, whereas he is less likely to do that in this game.
The story is also terrific, following up from the events of the first game, reintroducing characters and building upon them. The only thing that the original did better was the humour. While there is some in this game, I found myself laughing a lot less in this game. In essence, the took the "noir" out of film noir and ran with that, making for a very dark storytelling experience.
All that being said, if you didn't enjoy the first Max Payne, the sequel won't convince you, as the game is very much an iterative sequel. Not that there's anything wrong with that, as I loved the original. I highly recommend the sequel, as it is a phemomenal game that gets (unfairly) overshadowed by the original.

Max Payne 2 picks up where the original Max Payne left off, continuing the noir theme and wintry New York setting. The combat has been polished and refined slightly, with right clicking now activating bullet time without causing Max to dive through the air, which is still here, but tied to the shift key. While in bullet time, Max reloads faster, and obviously enemies are far easier to hit, but apart from the inclusion of this, gameplay largely remains the same as the first Max Payne, albeit with better physics.
The level design in Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is superb, with one rundown theme park being a highlight, and a locale returned to at multiple points in the game's story. Of course dream sequences return, though thankfully Max is no longer following trails of blood. The levels here are arguably superior to those in the original Max Payne, and the story is roughly on par with that of Max Payne's.
While Sam Lake, the writer of both Max Payne and Max Payne 2, no longer serves as the eponymous antihero's visage, a shame as his wacky faces were a joy to see in the original, this sequel is an incredible game, and well worth your time, though it would be better experienced after having played through the first Max Payne.

Now with that aside, it's time to get scathingly sarcastic and pessimistic.
I express my thanks to my good fellow friend who gifted me this game.
To him I exclaim with much gratitude:
.
Now, I have not played Borderlands 1 at all nor do I own my own copy of the Pre-Sequel (played a bit of it with a relative). I have heard Borderlands 2 was a large improvement over 1 and that it was Game of the Year (forgot which year). Having heard that, I had high hopes and expectations for something of such a high caliber. As I've played through it, however, I've come to think that I've been disappointed.
If you haven't known already this game is mostly balanced to multiplayer. Very heavily so. If you're new and are planning to play solo, you're going to get frustrated. From playing this game, I can very much tell from the enemies, loot system, mechanics and other aspects that multiplayer is a must. I'm okay when a game favors co-op, but when it punishes solo players with shafted mechanics I can't help but think it's rather unfair. One specific instance is that when you are downed to Fight For Your Life mode you have a small time window before bleeding out to get a kill to revive yourself (yeah, that's really how it works) or, in co-op, to wait for another player to revive you. The time in FFYL between solo and multiplayer is comparably different. For some reason, you have longer FFYL time in co-op than in solo. You would think solo would be more deserving for a longer time period as you don't have any means of being revived other than getting a kill, but no multiplayer has it. Oh yes, and some AIs are actually smart enough to where some enemies notice this mechanic and actually run away and/or stay behind cover when you are downed or ally npcs steal every kill in the vicinity, making having someone else there to revive you be more necessary. Fair, right?
I've beaten the game all the way up to the end of True Vaulter Hunter mode (that mode basically being a new game plus) on solo so it is very much possible, but I couldn't help but feel shafted then when I breezed through the same parts of the game with at least one other comrade at my side.
But you know what's one stinger out of all of this? Despite how all of this clearly makes the game meant for co-op, the story does not recognize multiplayer. By that, I mean that the npcs in the story still treat you as if there's only one player. Makes sense to make it heavily co-op balanced and have the story address players as singleplayer.
Oh, the story. Right, that's a thing. Corporation ravages planet in search for unobtainium and fabled Vault which grants powers, something like that. They also kill off others competing for such. You are of those others. You manage to live after a failed murder attempt and join the resistance in stopping
the corporation from total world domination all the while fighting off bandits and other life indigenous to the planet. That's the jist of the story. Oh and you meet people. Yeah. What are the specifics? Well... can't say at the top of my head. It's mainly because quite a bit of these story elements happen in the middle of heated action. Because I'm so focused on the action, I end up ignoring it. Most of that stuff is just jokes and character development anyways. It just ends up being fluff and nonsense amidst the heat of combat.
Enough about story, more about gameplay. It's an FPS RPG with loot. Blahblahblah
blahblah... Cool. Now specifics. You can level up your character and quests have a sort of recommendation on what level you should be before tackling them. What's cool is when you're on a level 14 quest at level 14 and enemies are 2 levels higher than you. Every time. There are other enemies that aren't as high, but come on. I realize there's gotta have challenge, but isn't there a better way than to solely rely on overleveled enemies? But hey, that's okay. Enemies not only simply overlevel you. Some of them can also one/two shot you. For instance, bandits with rocket launchers. One shot from them can instantly blast through your shields and put you on low health, leaving you open for others to finish you off. What do you do? Take cover. But sometimes they don't show until you step into their aggro area. The problem here is that sometimes the area is right in front of their spawn where they have a very clear line of sight. So you end up taking unavoidable damage. Or better yet you just get instantly downed.
Oh yes and how can I forget, the loot. You can be level 14 and fighting an enemy that's level 16. It drops a level 12 gun. A rather questionable design choice. I would rant about this, but I fear that I'm reaching the character limit that for some reason Steam refuses to display (another questionable design choice).
Now, you might be saying at this point, "Alright. This game has its flaws but it's not like any other game is flawless," or you could be yelling, "STFU GIT GUD SCURB." True, flaws are universal and unavoidable, but I can't exactly "git gud" when there are horribly irritating bugs that the developers just refuse to fix and that I'm getting shafted by these bugs. Let me just roll out some examples:
It's fun when enemies phase right through a closed door and instantly down you and then run away. I mean, surely you should've seen that coming. Shame on you for not expecting so.
It's fun when enemies get behind cover they rubber band as if there's multiplayer lag... in singleplayer. What, you can't aim at enemies glitching in and out of cover erraticly? Noob.
It's fun when legendary loot drops from a boss you have been painstakingly farming for and then the loot gets stuck somewhere or just falls through the ground. Since when is farming for long hours not fun anyways? Of course getting drops shouldn't be that easy. Just grab it before it glitches. Git gud.
It's fun when quests simply just don't work, and that you have to repeatedly restart the game until it does. Hey... it's...... I don't really have any sarcastic comebacks for this.
I could keep going on with this list, but I'll just end it on this:
It's fun when the devs simply refuse to fix horrible bugs that many people have brought up years before. Devs are people, too. Lay off. Not their fault they ignored all of that and just continued making expansions regardless and have eventually abandoned all attention to the game for another.
Sarcasm aside, for a "Game of the Year" this is pretty anticlimactic. Chances are, I will still play the game, but only if I'm bored and have nothing else to do.
With co-op being so heavily influenced on the game, I wouldn't recommend buying it if you plan to do only singeplayer. As a co-op game, it's fairly decent. As singleplayer, it's overall undeserving of its Game of the Year title. It's fun with friends mainly because it's with friends. People are fun. This game: not as much fun. If anything, co-op is there to basicly serve as a mask for these flaws.
Still want to play Borderlands? Buy Pre-Sequel. At least the devs are actually paying attention to that (maybe).
Going to play singleplayer? Hahaa~... good luck.

A decade after it was first released and the game is still enjoyable.
Divine Divinity is a classic isometric rpg with a perfect mix of Baldur's Gate's role play element, Diablo 2's action gameplay with big open world to explore ala Sacred Gold.
Unlike most rpg of it's kind you aren't locked to a certain class or skill trees.
The only difference between each characters that you can choose is their starting stats and skills.
So you can shape your character to be whatever you want.
A fighter with thieving skills or maybe an archer with arcane magic.
From graphical stand point it looks very similar to Diablo 2. Yeah it doesn't aged well.
Battles too are similar to Diablo 2. You can only control 1 character and you don't have companions following you everywhere you go. Sad.
You also have tactical pause too. Like in Baldur's Gate. In case you need some time to think and analyze the flow of battle.
The role playing aspect is pretty good with a lot of meaningful choices that you can make as you travel the world.
The world itself is pretty big with lots of secret and side quest in every nooks and cranny.
Overall the game is very enjoyable even though it's a decade old and has lots of bug.
FYI, most of the time i ended my playing session with the game forced close on me.
Though this can be remedied by playing the game wihtout steam (straight from the .exe file) and set the game to use only one core.
Personally i really recommend this game. It's very solid, fun and has decent replayability value.
If you are a fan of isometric rpg (and don't mind old graphics), you should play this game at least once in your lifetime.

MINERVA, or MINERVA: Metastasis are one and the same thing. Throughout the years I've heard people using both names and so I thought there was a sequel, but in truth it is not. This is the sole mod.
I enjoyed it. From a well-delivered story to outstanding level design, MINERVA is packed with non-stop action. It contains what made Half-Life 2 great, or shall I say...Episode One?
Now that I think about it each Half-Life game (aside from the first's expansions, mostly) has had its own, unique taste. Episode One, for example, had those creepy encounters and focus on Antilion/Zombie combat, but is at the same time hideous in pacing. You get the crowbar waaay later on.
This is another story, but even with that said I'd have to compare MINERVA to Episode One. It does not have the same horrible pacing, but it has the same familiarity. Half of the game is Combine combat, the other is mixed. You can feel the same vibes present.
I will not spoil the story more than I should, but the text-on-screen method of storytelling worked nicely, unlike most of the time you'd seen it fail. You are an ex-Combine soldier who's gone head-on into a Combine facility buried deep within an island. That's it for one, but it gets much more interesting along the way.
Now the only significant thing that has bothered me (no bugs/glitches encountered, guess I was lucky) was that our protagonist still wears the HEV suit model from the original game. Like, yes, it is a hazard suit, but why the same look? Wouldn't it be a little more fitting to have some black jumpsuit with armor pieces strapped on? I considered this to be a little immersion-breaking, but to be honest it's not something that will bother you a lot. The constant tension in between will make sure of that.
A great deal of work has been put into this map, and I'd like to congratulate the author. A must-try for Half-Life fans. Let's not even talk about the fact that it's free, but you still need to own Episode One.

Well I have to say I have never written a review for a game on steam so here goes.
I bought this game only a few days ago, and I have played for a few days now and there are limitless opportunities. Various planets and researchable items make this game all too fun! Having to generate enough power to do simple tasks and braving the sandstorms.
You will need patience to play this game, however you will be rewarded for your efforts. I may also add that the developers have certainly thought into the dynamics of this game and they are showing good early signs of communication with the ASTRONEER community which is always a BIG positive.
However; this is balanced with a few negatives:
I understand that this game is an EA game however optimisation is certainly required. For example, too many tethers placed will certainly affect your frames as you come towards the "End game" of that world save.
At the moment, you are not able to change the graphic quality settings; this may become an issue for lower end PC gamers as the game will be almost unplayable.
Edit: I have to add, the developers seem to be adding quite a few various updates and bug fixes these past few days, it certainly cements their dedication towards this game. This makes me even more so confident that this will turn into one of the best space sandbox games of this time!
Apart from that a good game!

I actually write reviews for a website, and the guy who runs it, RedHill, gave me the game for review purposes. Thanks to him for the game!
I'm not very vocal about this, but I'm actually a big fan of top-down shooters and bullet hell games. That being said, I don't play them very often. That's why I took the opportunity to review this game, to see if it would scratch an itch left untouched for years. After playing for a few hours with friends and myself, I think this game managed to scratch that itch.
You shouldn't be expecting much when it comes to graphics for a game in this genre. However, I will say that it does recreate the retro/arcade feeling well, and compared to other top-down shooters I've seen, it feels more authentic. However, one qualm I would say about the visuals is the fact I have trouble telling the robots apart from one another. I usually just view them as, "Okay, there's another guy to shoot." It would be nice to be able to distinguish the robots from each other. Did you expect a huge paragraph talking about this game's graphics? I didn't think so. It's still pretty nice though.
You're probably reading this to see if the overall gameplay is good or not. For a game like this, if the gameplay isn't good, then the game probably won't get much positive feedback. Now here's what I want you to do. Read that second sentence again. Now I want you to see if I gave this game a thumbs up or a thumbs down. Read that second sentence one more time. Get where I'm heading with this? Anyway, I loved the idea of the weapon upgrades, and it makes the game feel a lot more interesting. It makes the game feel more difficult (in a fun way) and also less "spammy", which could've killed the whole experience. Also, the game is much more enjoyable with friends. I haven't played too much of it with others, but from what I have played with them, the game is definitely more entertaining. My one issue with the gameplay is that I can't seem to find a use for the shield. Maybe it's just me, but after all, this is MY review. I'm supposed to tell the reader my thoughts and experience with the game. I couldn't find myself using the shield that much. I would recommend that the shield feels more "necessary" in some cases. For example, there could be a type of enemy with attacks that can't be avoided, so you'll need to use the shield. Aside from the bit with the shield, however, the gameplay is very enjoyable.
Go down to my verdict if you want me to elaborate. There's no overall story at the moment. However, it seems that the developers are trying to create a world of their own here.
Honestly, there's even less to say here than in the graphics department. There's no voice acting, and the audio overall is solid. Not great, not terrible. There's music, too, but I found it to be forgettable for the most part. I wish the soundtrack could've been a little more exciting.
The good thing about Circuit Breakers is that the replayability is surprisingly high. This game is an EXCELLENT time killer, and I wouldn't be shocked if you put a fair amount of time into it. With the fair and difficult gameplay. the fact that more content is on the way, and a few other things I don't feel like listing, you could put a lot of time into this. I'm going to have to keep this installed on my computer in case I'm ever bored. It's a great way to pass the time.
Overall, Circuit Breakers does have a few flaws, but the game is incredibly fun. There's even controller support, and although you may have a few problems with it at first, the bugs involving it are too minor for me. Add that with the fun co-op gameplay, the weapon upgrade concept, and high replayability, and you have yourself one of the best time wasters Steam has to offer.

This is another game that has a "Do Something" button.  In fact, it has SEVERAL "Do Something" buttons.  Almost every control the game has except for WASD has multiple context-dependent bindings, and you pray every time you use one that the game will decide to do what you intended.  This just adds to the confusion, especially when sometimes just nothing happens.  Or it LOOKS like the game has handed control back to you after a cut scene, but you can't actually do anything yet.  Oh, you blinked, or your attention was on a different spot on the screen?  Sorry, you just missed a control tutorial message you'll never get again.  Wait, did we forget to tell you how to use that?  Sucks to be you.  Q to throw a grenade?  Yeah, that makes ... um ... perfect sense.  NOT.
The main source of confusion, though, is that you start out on what seems to be a fairly straight-forward investigate-and-reconnoiter mission, that turns in short order into a rescue mission ... in which you can't actually rescue anyone.  Except for one guy, and then the next thing you know, within 20 minutes of beginning play, your rescue mission has turned into the game forcing you to fight and kill the people you set out to rescue in order to survive, you seem to be facing TWO enemy factions, both your own nation and both trying to kill you, and why the *@&$^@#^%$ am I here and what am I doing and why am I killing my own fellow soldiers and --
NOPE.  NOPE.  NOPE.  Enough.  Not doing this.  Too much crapsack, too much brain-hurts.
This game, at least in its opening phase, makes no sense.  Perhaps it'll all be explained further in, and the game will start to actually make sense, and perhaps you eventually acquire an understanding that there is some point to what you're doing, but ...  nope.  Too little, too late.  Spec Ops: The Line lost me in the first hour of undirected blind confusion and slaughtering everything that moves with no explanation of why I'm doing it.
Take Two had a generous beginning time window to gain my interest, get me invested and sell me on why I should play this game, and they blew it.

Great, albeit basic third-person duck and cover shooter. Spec Ops: The Line tries really hard to capture the gritty horrors of war and sometimes suffers from the occasional streak of corniness that detracts from the realism it hopes to convey. I had a blast with this though. Highly recommended on Suicide/Fubar difficulties for some really intense firefight challenges.
An occasional boss fight and a simple command ring for your squad mates would have made this game a bit better in my book, but what it lacks in variety and depth it makes up for in eye candy and subject matter. If you're into these kind of games,  it will be a fun ride from start to finish.  The amazing, Mad Max-esque apocalyptic setting of Dubai engulfed in sand makes for some wild level designs, but they did feel a little lackluster towards the very end of the campaign.
The plot is predicable but I couldn't help comparing it to recent stuff like MGSV: The Phantom Pain. This tale of revenge is way more effective and engaging in how it tells a story despite being linear and only a teeny tiny fraction of the open world stealth/action title.
The multiplayer seems dead but for a low price this game is a steal. I happened to snag this on a Humble Bundle sale and only paid a solid buck for it. Not much bad I can say about this game. I will definitely replay this again at some point when  the right mood hits. For a 10 hour romp this is a sure bet, check it out.

Gameplay-wise Spec Ops: The Line is basically a shooting gallery game with 3rd person controls implemented to get from gallery to gallery. And the shooting gallery mechanics can drive you mad at some points.
Story-wise; it is good. You have to finish the game all the way through to make sense of it, and if you're downright frustrated at the difficulty of the last few chapters (partly due to the clumsy mechanics) you can just watch the rest of the cutscenes on YouTube. Otherwise, the story will be a mess. When you finish it, it will make much more sense but I have to warn you, this is one of those stories that at the end, you have to backtrack every single key moment to understand what actually happened there. The game itself makes a very poor job of this. I'm not a huge fan of such storytelling. But overall, the story was good, yeah. I won't play it a second time though, because mechanics are bad.
My recommendation? If you have the resources (time & money), play through the game and see for yourself. You may or may not be disappointed, but the game will give you something.
If you don't want to pay a lot to a game that has clumsy gameplay, buy it on sale.

Mod: Minerva: Metastasis
For the game: Half-Life 2
Developer and publisher: Adam Foster
Released: 28 April, 2013
Genre: First-Person Shooter with Horror
Canon status: Non-canon
Setting: 15 October, 2009, an unnamed island, Baltic Sea, Europe, Earth
Spoiler-free plot summary: You play as an unnamed renegade Combine soldier only referred to as Perseus. After arriving on an island controlled by the Combine, a mysterious member of the Resistance, only referred to as Minerva, guides you via on-screen messages on your quest to destroy the facility built beneath the island.
Full review: Minerva is a short and mildly difficult mod for Half-Life 2: Episode 1. This mod is no doubt one of the best Half-Life mods ever created, and Valve must have thought so too because they ended up hiring Adam Foster to work with them!
Another Half-Life 2 mod, more typical Half-Life 2 gameplay of running-and-gunning and solving a few puzzles. No new game mechanics are introduced like several other Half-Life mods; instead, this mod is based on level design. Being set in an underground facility beneath a small island, the levels in Minerva are very vertical. You'll find that most of the combat sequences require shooting at enemies above and/or below you, and that navigating can be very maze-like, especially
.
Dialogue with Minerva can be quite awkward; if you proceed through levels too quickly, her messages will overlap, so you can miss out on crucial information, like how to solve a puzzle, and because the text is bright orange, you won't be able to read her messages in bright areas or against brightly-colored surfaces.
Do I recommend Minerva? Yes; it's higher in quality compared to other Half-Life mods, and it can entertain you for a couple of hours. If Half-Life 2 is a meal and its episodes are dessert, then this mod is a breath mint; small and sweet.

Vergil is there, Ebony and Ivory are there, and Rebellion is there, but this is no Devil May Cry. +Gameplay promises hours of fun, especially with a wheel
+The game structure is very mod friendly and open

Borderlands 2 is a first person looter shooter developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2K Games. It was ported to Mac & Linux by Aspyr. This is by far my favorite game ever; I love it wholeheartedly. It's crazy, but a perfect level to where it's not boring; it's comedic, but still manages to deliver a moving story. I definitely think that, if you haven't played this game, you should play it now and grab the DLC while you're at it.
The combat in Borderlands 2 is incredibly simple at first. Shoot everything without a green health bar. Or sometimes those too. It develops complexity, however, when you gain access to elemental weaponry; these come in the form of fire, shock, corrosive, and slag. The first three deal enhanced damage to a specific type of health (fire to flesh, shock to shields, and corrosive to armor), and slag causes enemies to take more damage from other elemental types. This system works because you can easily opt to use regular ballistic weaponry and not have to worry about it, or use elemental weaponry and deal vastly enhanced damage.
Each weapon has specific characteristics that make it unique. Rarity, level, parts, type, and manufacturer all play their part in making each weapon different. The Rarity influences the skin it will use, as well as enhancing all stats; the level will multiply all stats to make it applicable at high level; the parts will provide stat enhancements to specific stats, as well as visibly changing the weapon's model; the weapon type (assault rifle, SMG, sniper, pistol, shotgun, etc.); the manufacturer will add a special trait to the weapon (ex. Dahl weapons burst fire when zoomed). There's a whole lot of depth to be found here, but it's still very approachable if you don't want to mess with this stuff.
The amount of variety found in weapons greatly adds to the replayability of the game.
The story of Borderlands 2 is actually one of the high points of this game, something you wouldn't expect from one of these ultra-violent looter shooter games. It focuses on a Vault Hunter, your character, striving to find an ancient alien vault filled with loot hidden away on Pandora, a savage planet filled with vile creatures and vicious raiders. The Hyperion Corporation, led by maniacal antagonist Handsome Jack, is also searching for the vault, and seeks to harness its power to restore Pandora by killing everyone on it.
Borderlands 2 manages that perfect mix of comedy and seriousness that makes the story that much more immersive and believable. The characters, both returning from the first game and new to this one, are unforgettable, as is most of the rest of the game. There's fantastic writing paired with character depth and fantastic voice acting.
Another strong point of Borderlands 2 is how great the character customization is. You can pick between more heads and body colorings than you can count, and you have four weapon slots in which to equip guns simultaneously. Each class has their own head customizations, skill trees, and action skills. Each class has 3 skill trees (you aren't limited to one at a time) that each have their own focus. When playing in co-op, the classes work together really well, proving how much time and thought went into tailoring these skills.
Most of the levels look completely different from each other, and I could probably tell you which level you were showing me from a small screenshot of it. Almost every level has an easter egg of some sort, ranging from the whole Minecraft area filled with blocks and Creepers found in the Caustic Caverns to the "Rakkman Forever" or "R.O.U.S." enemies found in The Fridge. They aren't just "haha memes" easter eggs, they're incorporated into the world and used at just the right frequency to make them enjoyable instead of annoying. There'll always be one small detail that I notice every time I come back to a level. Some kind of secret treasure room or hidden vault symbol will always be there.
Each enemy faction feels unique, and you have to fight each one differently. For instance, Loaders will largely just charge you, but Rats and some Hyperion soldiers will try to use cover and distance wisely.
The Borderlands series has a unique visual style found in both lighting and textures. It's not the best lighting or the highest resolution textures to be found out there, but it's still visually pleasing because of its consistent art style. However, the PC version has a great options menu along with fantastic performance. One gripe is that PhysX seems to be a lot less optimized than the implementation found in
. Another is that the game only features SSAO and FXAA, but you can inject SMAA using ReShade or force MSAA from your graphics control panel. You can also implement HBAO+ as shown here,
something that is not usually possible. Part of the visual style, I think, is the lack of material shaders, making everything look like it was drawn on a piece of paper and then glued to the model. The comical cel shading effect makes this visual style work, where normally it would be atrocious.
Please buy this game. It's an amazing looting experience backed up by a fantastic story and great character customization, making it enjoyable even by your fifth playthrough. Even the DLC is good! It's well optimized, it's not the most graphically advanced game but it still looks great, and the menus are well designed. Even if you don't play the co-op game in co-op mode, it's still very enjoyable and well-balanced.

If you enjoyed Marten Jonsson's Star Sky, you will enjoy Star Sky 2 even more.  As with all his games each one improves on the walking simulator/puzzle concept.  This game is no exception.
In Star Sky 2 the player interacts with two different characters the woman (the gardener) and the man (the dreamwalker) separately.  The woman walks to the left, the man to the right, each with their own encounters, adventures, and mysteries (puzzles) to solve.  However, both can "interact" or change the circumstances/environments of the other.  This is where the layered mystery is and were the puzzles become more complex.
An added feature to this game (taken from a previous game called Meadowland) is the hint/clue boxes which occur just before an event.  The hint/clue boxes not only tell the player what to do, and how many events there are, but also what circumstances/conditions need to be present just by looking at the clue picture.  Match the picture and watch the event unfold.  Now just exactly how does one match the picture is the puzzle part and quite often requires the other walker's involvement.  (There are four circumstances/condition variables the walkers effect but I am not saying what since that would spoil the discovery.)
The main "painting" of both the gardener (woman) and the dreamwalker (man) that occurs at the end of each "adventure" is also a huge clue to where events are located.  Also if the player looks closely at the main painting, three different types of pictures occur on the far left under the window showing the type of ending the player recieved: sadness (gravestone), loneliness (torch in hand), or happiness (child in hand)
Another feature of the game is the ability to "circle" through areas more then once which can be quite helpful when trying to trigger certain events.
Same light relaxing type of soft music as Star Sky with the same no-stress gameplay.  Relatively short gameplay, I finished in 2 1/2 hours, which is fine with me.  Something light, soothing and positive at the end of a long day is something I do appreciate. Star Sky 2 like Jonsson's other games is a love story.
I very much recommend this game, even at full price.
P.S.  Quick hint for my achievement hunting friends DO NOT skip the ending.

I never played Star Sky 1 so this was all new to me.  Star Sky 2 is like no other game I've played or seen before. Its concept of the player choosing their own path is wonderful and its story is so vague you can interpret it many different ways or at least that's what I got out of it. During my playthrough, I checked more than once whether it was windy or pouring rain outside my window because the ingame sounds are so well done I couldn't tell the difference. Overall, I had a blast playing Star Sky 2 and highly recommend this to anyone who wants a short relaxing experience. Seriously, it's really relaxing. It only has 3 controls; Up, Right, and Left on the arrow keys so you can lean back in your chair or lie down in bed with a laptop.

The soothing night-time walking simulator is back, with more places to stroll through, more events to wait around and observe, and now you can play a left-walking lady in addition to Right-walking Reggy. Visual cues and hints have been added (and can be turned off for the hardcore night-walkers who don't need hints of where to stand), it's possible to return to the same place during the same session, and there is even a map which will highlight which paths you've already taken and what's still waiting for you. Some may think it's odd that I was giddy to play Star Sky 2 after the first one, but others will appreciate a very serene walking simulator like this, which is great for relaxing or a change of scenery.

Welcome to Dubai, you are Captain Walker and everything is your fault. ^_^
The basic premis is that you and two Delta Force buddies arrive in Dubai in the mids of the worst sandstorm ever to help evacuate any remaining locals. What do you get? A city torn by a war of epic proportions.
The story unfolds slowly at first, in the guise of being a pretty average and meh basic plot for plot sake but it kind of turns the table on you. The gameplay is what is the average here and not the plot. The plot was quite frankly what kept me going as the fights where kind of grindy and frustrating at times as it is quite easy to die. (The game even had the audacity to ask me if I wanted to turn the difficulty down.)
As the plot progresses you are put in a few situations where the choises are really between horrible and worse and the game has no qualms about rubbing it in your face. While the gameplay is lacking the game delivers some very powerful imagry that still sticks with me. And the choises made me think about what I would do in a war situation and I honestly think I wouldn't do much better.
So I complained a few times about the average gameplay, so what about it?
In short the coversystem, while useful, could work better. Turning around outside corners means leaving cover, walking around the bend and then going into cover again, leaving you exposed. Switching from cover to cover was also poorly explained but I got the hang of it later in the game. (I'm not very proficient at cover-based shooters.)
Another thing was the weapons. The game has a load of different weapons availible and while very fun to use the downside is that the sound effects from them are quite lacking. Am I firing an automatic shotgun or a cork rifle? I couldn't tell you from the sound alone.
So I bought the game for the reputation and stayed for the story. If you don't care about story and only gameplay I'm sure there are other games that would play better for you. :)

Circuit Breakers is an arcade retro shooter, developed by Triverske, releasing in November 2015. There isn’t really a story to this game, it’s completely focused on the gameplay, as I would expect from an arcade title, so don’t go into this expecting a deep thriller backstory.
The gameplay concept is very simple; you pick which character you want to play as at the start of the game, these are based on what weapon you use, such as machine gun, shotgun, rocket launcher and laser, these classes have their own strength and weaknesses, but are not apparent from the start.  The objective in the game is to kill all the enemies in a room and then progress to the next, every ten rooms you complete you will have to take on a boss.  Probably my favourite feature in Circuit Breakers, is that you are able to upgrade your weapon to a stronger one of the same type, simply by killing enemies and finding more “ammo” pickups, and once you run out of ammo, you just drop down to the previous gun you were using, it sounds complicated but it actually plays out very smoothly and adds a nice level of excitement to your runs.  The game play is very fast paced as you can sometimes get hundreds of enemies on the screen at once, the enemies are for the most part very easy to mow through but some can take a good pounding before finally being beaten.
The art style on show in Circuit Breakers has a very retro arcade feel to it. I really liked this art style and it is not very often you see it done as well as this. It takes a very Metal Slug vibe very strongly, and I salute the developers for pulling this off. All of the rooms and backdrops in which you fight in throughout the game are really nicely designed too, with lots of different textures and layouts to keep you on your toes.
Circuit Breakers is a very hard game. I only managed to get past the first 10 rooms on a handful of occasions, purely because the latter stages of the rooms you just get absolutely swarmed with enemies and you have to be very quick on your feet to keep ahead of them. Where you can get an advantage is playing with more than one person in the local co-op side of the game; this is where you will probably get the most enjoyment as well. If you have someone to play with that isn’t the best at video games, maybe a partner or younger sibling, I would still recommend they try it with you, since the controls and gameplay is very simple to pick up, only difficult to master.
I have been playing Circuit Breakers for an hour here and there over the past two weeks and managed to rack up just over 20 hours of time in it. I haven’t come close to getting even one of the achievements, let a long completing the game.  On top of the game’s arcade mode which is where you will probably spend a lot of your time, the game also has a challenge mode. You unlock challenges by progressing in the arcade mode; I really liked this way of unlocking new challenges as it gives you incentive to better yourself to unlock more content. The replay ability factor and addictiveness nature of this game stands it in good stead to be a game I will keep installed on my PC allowing me to drop in for an hour here every now and again.
The only technical issue I ran into when playing is, that if you don’t launch the game when you have your controller plugged in, it won’t recognise it unless you reload. It’s not a major problem, just a little issue that I found annoying. Other than that, it runs well on all resolutions without any issues.
To sum up, Circuit Breakers is a really good game to play in short bursts with a very fast paced action based game play to keep you coming back for more. Definitely one that gets better the more people you play with, and has a really high difficulty ceiling to. With online leader boards with your friends, it will also bring out your competitive nature as well.  I can highly recommend Circuit Breakers, especially for its low retail price of £6,99.

Circuit Breakers is an excellent game with addicting gameplay.  I highly recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of top-down shooters or someone that is starting to get into shooters of this type.
There is no story, you pretty much go from level to level defeating enemies while fighting bosses along the way.  You keep fighting until you lose then you start the whole process over again.
The gameplay is what makes it fun, watching the enemies explode is quite amusing.  There are different characters with their own special wepons that you can use to wreak havoc onto your enemies.
Also, this game can shoot in 8 directions only, but most of the time you mainly shoot in the 4 directions.  This isn't really a problem and I kind of enjoy it this way for the game.
One downside that I am not quite fond of which others might not like either is the power up system.  As you kill enemies they drop these blue crystals, you collect them to power up your weapon, and the more crystals you collect the stronger your weapon becomes.  But as you shoot or take damage you weapon starts to lose power and actually downgrades to a weaker weapon.  I know this system is a bit lame and kind of a downer, but it is really not that bad.
There are many opportunities to gain crystals to power up your weapon, the lowest I have dropped is weapon lvl 2, I don't think I have ever downgraded to my basic weapon (lvl 1) and I shoot quite a bit, but not spamming though.  Also, I have deliberately downgraded my weapon to 1 throughout the levels, you can still kill enemies but it'll just take you a bit longer.  So you're not really dead in the water, thank goodness, although I would like to see a buff in weapon lvl 1 damage eventually.
Overall this is a very fun game, it is great to pick up and play whenever you want to shoot some enemies.

Circuit Breakers is actually* a recruitment tool developed in the 25th century. In the future, rapid advances in Artifical Intelligence will lead to robots declaring humanity "an obsolete by-product of a forgotten age" and also "really disgusting". If left un-checked, this menace will wipe out all that we hold dear. Don't be surprised if some guy named Centauri comes to your house, ranting and raving about your hi-score in a twin-stick shooter. Just be aware that this man will have you enter his car - which is actually a time machine - and before you know it, you'll be fighting for the future of Neo-Earth.
Now I know what you're thinking: If time-travel is possible. Why not simply go back in time to prevent the robots from being created? First off, don't sweat the minor details. Secondly, all roads in time eventually lead to genocide via robots. Face it, if we're not eaten by zombies, we'll be stabbed, splatted, and vaporized by robots. If that doesn't happen, then I can only assume
will be what destroys us once and for all. So my advice is to do your part, and check out Circuit Breakers.
These days it takes more than running and shooting to make a worthwhile twin-stick shooter. This genre has seen countless game releases, and it probably will be the 25th century by the time we've played them all. Aside from being a quality title in terms of the basic fundamentals, Circuit Breakers also has some depth to it. Each playable character has their own weapon. What might be effective in some situations, won't cut it in others. For example: Samson's rocket launcher is powerful, but its low fire-rate and high ammo costs mean that you have to be selective in your shots. Also, you just caught the part about ammo, right? Robots and artillery alike run on energium. By destroying robots you collect their energy, and your level of fire-power can increase. While you can't run out of ammo, your weapon can become so puny and ineffective, that you'll be no match for the horde of mechs. Your ammo can also be expended to put up an emergency shield. By holding down the button you can push through crowds, and by tapping it you can reflect enemy-fire.
While you can and should shoot everything that moves, you also have to consider the scoring system. Yep, even when surrounded by hundreds of dangerous robots, your first thought is going to be on profiting from the chaos. By destroying multiple robots in a short time, you build up a combo chain. Taking damage, or simply taking too long to wreck bots, will result in the chain being broken. To further complicate matters, each robot is worth a varying amount of points. What you'll want to do is destroy the weak and plentiful bots, before moving on to the bigger and badder creations. As with any other arcade game, you have milliseconds to develop your scoring strategy, and apply it to the situation at hand.
Circuit Breakers uses a retro-aesthetic, and relies on tried and true game-design elements such as audio cues and color-coded enemies. This makes the action easier to follow, because you'll always have some awareness of what's going on around you. Robots with guns always make a distinct noise before they fire, same with the floating mines that explode, or the droids unleashing their homing missiles. While it seems odd that I would applaud the fundamentals, all too often developers forget or ignore these imperative aspects, and their games suffer as a result. Other essentials such as controls and enemy behavior are also solid.
This game features a nice set of modes and variables. The arcade mode consists of 50 rooms, five boss-fights, and a plethora of bots and mini-bosses to contend with. Apparently it also loops indefinitely, so you can play as long as you have lives remaining. The score-attack mode is much more focused, since each level consists of a handful of rooms. Not only do you have to master the scoring system, but you also have to take advantage of modifiers. Before starting the game, you can increase your scoring potential by making things more difficult. I don't have all of the settings unlocked, but to give you an idea, these modifiers can include: raising enemy health, spawning more "elite" mechs, and decreasing the amount of energium recovery. Each game is further differentiated by your character of choice, and anyone you decide to partner up with. Multiplayer is a big part of this game. There's always a party, if you can convince up to three friends to join in on the action.
However, it should be mentioned that there's no leveling of any kind. These days it seems like every arcade-style shooter offers players methods for strengthening their characters through grinding. This isn't the case here, as your survival is determined entirely by the experience
acquire. That said, unlocking some of the content - such as hidden characters and modifiers - can feel like a grind. Completing all of the challenges will require an absurd number of hours, but if you're having fun, then this isn't much of a complaint.
There are some aspects of the game that could use some tuning. For one, some characters are underpowered for critical situations. Payne is one of the hidden playable characters, and he uses a flame-thrower. This is a fantastic weapon for handling large crowds of weak mechs, but it's too ineffective for tougher bots and bosses. This problem can be addressed by playing co-op, as Tay with her laser can make for a powerful team. These and other more minor issues have been mentioned in the discussion forums, and the developer is very open to all of the feedback.
All that said, Circuit Breakers is an exceptional addition to any gamer's library. There's a sizable amount of content, and more importantly, the game-design is fully realized. You have to carefully manage your firepower, due to the energium system. When coupled with the smart scoring techniques, this makes for a shooter that's far more strategic than most. In a way, these limitations make the game more satisfying and visceral. Usually when I play, I tap the right-stick to fire, so as not to waste ammo. When I hold the right-stick in the direction of robots, that commitment to destruction feels pretty good. Basically, this game is worth your time.

The quick pace of the game is what makes it so addicting; being able to run at, run away from, and shoot at the robots in a swift manner creates a rush of adrenaline that makes you want to keep pressing the start button. The game does a great job of keeping the player actually focused by employing a system of crystals used to upgrade characters' weapons and double as ammunition. Instead of mindless shooting, you have to constantly pick up more crystals as you shoot so your weapon doesn't downgrade.
One of my favorite things about this game is how oddly soothing it is to shoot at the robots. Playing as Aldo and letting loose a cascade of bullets is just plain fun.

I am obsessed with this game right now!  I bought it irl, then shortly thereafter on Steam.  The more I play the game, the more I feel like what they managed to do is created a classic RPG (in the video game sense) in card format.  This is like a co-op, cardboard version of old-school Final Fantasy:  you have heros, enemies, hit points, attack points, you use abilities each turn, you get stronger over time, and you work together to defeat the boss.  The different characters are great, each one is unique and fun and each one has different play mechanics and cards that combo in different ways.  No matter what your play style, you will find multiple characters that are fun.  The heros, villains, and environments combine to create literally hundreds of variations so that it doens't get old.  You can adjust the relative difficulty by playing with fewer heros, and then there is Advanced Mode if you really want to challenge yourself (die).
Don't let the comic book theme scare you away.  I am not a comic book or super hero fan, in fact I'm pretty sick of super heroes in the media at this point.  This led me to avoid Sentinels for a long time despite hearing good things about the game.  But the super hero thing is only for artistic and thematic purposes, as I said this plays like a classic RPG, and to my surprise, the character and the artwork have grown on me the more I've played.
Don't pay full price on Steam, you can buy a key for the base game very cheaply online, I paid $1 for the base game then immediately bought Season Pass 1 which is the purchase I would recommend.  So grab the base game for cheap and if you like it, it's well worth $25 for all the stuff you get in the Season 1 expansion, I paid ~$70 for the first two double-expansions in real life and got less stuff than I got in the Season 1 pass.  Oh and if you're the type that likes acheivements, there are plenty of variants to chase (a variant is a different version of your character card that gives you a different base power) and some of them are quite difficult to unlock.  Although there's no campaign mode per se, chasing variants makes it really fun to play in single player.
One thing that really makes me mad, though, is that the expansions you buy here don't carry over to other platforms.  If you buy this on Android, they expect you to pay AGAIN for all the expansions on Android.  Seriously?  Most games nowadays, you get the game for all platforms when you buy it.  At the very least it should recognize the content you've already purchased.

As a big fan of things like TCGs, board games, and whatnot, there's always tons of awesome-looking "geeky" sorts of games out there that I find (you know, the sort that tend to look really complicated and detailed), and that look like lots of fun... and that I'll never get to try, because they all require multiple players, and everyone I know is too busy playing Dark Souls over and over and over again.  So I was pleasantly surprised to find this game, which is that sort yet can be played solo.
Sentinels of the Multiverse is a card game with many similarities to a TCG, except that you do not build decks here.  The idea is pretty simple:  Your team of heroes, VS a single supervillain, in a battle to save the world or whatever.  Your team consists of 3-5 heroes of your choosing, and each one of them has their own specific deck that they'll bring with them.  Likewise, each of the game's villains also has their own deck.  There are also "environment" decks, which are filled with cards that tend to just screw with things.  Unlike villain cards, environmental decks arent specifically aligned against you, so you can often find screwy ways to use them against your opponent.
In addition, each character also has a special card representing them.  For heroes, their core card will have a special power that they can call on at the end of each of their turns.  For villains, there's typically a lengthy set of special rules and effects that they bring to the table; in addition, villains can switch "modes" by flipping over their card, revealing new and often crazier powers to make your existence miserable, all of which have different things that trigger them.  For example, Baron Blade is nasty enough to begin with, starting out with a shielded defense platform that makes him immune to everything, and having a sort of countdown: If there's too many cards in his deck's discard pile, he smashes the moon into the Earth and insta-wins.  Because of course he does.  Drain all of his HP though, and he switches to a power-suit mode, where he gets a massive refill of HP and just starts getting to freely chop chunks of health off of your heroes at the end of every turn.   Or there's Citizen Dawn, who starts with a giant pile of minions in play (all with complicated effects), and when you take out 5 of them, she goes berserk, flipping her card over and becoming invincible until she has a certain number of minions back on the table.  Fortunately she can only do this once, but it's a nasty move nonetheless, and of course she's got loads of other tricks too.
And villain cards in general tend to be like that:  Huge effects that hit your team like a freight train.  It makes sense, as it's your entire team against just ONE supervillain.... so of course they've got huge power to back them up.  And loads of HP.
The overall rules of the game are pretty simple to understand:  Hero turns start with you playing a card, followed by using one of your hero's currently available powers, and then drawing a card, and onto the next hero.  After your overall turn (as in, all of your heroes are done), the environment deck goes, playing the top card and resolving any effects.  Villain decks work the same way, simply playing the top card, and resolving things.  A simple and easy to understand overall flow to the game.
Not that the game as a whole is simple, though.  It can get very complicated, with all sorts of effects in play at once, and many different card types to keep track of.  Each hero is good at different things, but they also have varying levels of complexity.  Haka for instance is pretty easy to understand:  He's mostly about beating the cheese out of things, with a ton of ways to directly strike opponents.  Whereas Absolute Zero is complicated as hell, and when you first try him out, he seems mostly good at shoving exploding fireballs up his own nose.  In addition, the different combinations of all of these decks can drastically change the way the game plays out.  You can have one game with a specific set of heroes, and specific environment and villain decks, and then in the next game switch out just ONE hero, and you'll likely find that it plays out very differently indeed.  Which means that even the base game has massive replay value.   And lots of challenge, too:  This is not an easy game, and it'll frequently throw you into situations that make you say "Okay, how in the heck do I get out of THIS one?!?"   Finding solutions to each situation, and defeating your enemies is very satisfying though... it tends to make for a very rewarding game overall... but it's one that wont hesitate to stomp your head in.
The one downside though:  This is NOT a cheap game.   Like the physical card game it's based on, Sentinels is divided into about a squillion expansions and add-ons.  You certainly dont NEED these to enjoy the game, but each new one that you decide to get just multiplies the already vast possibilities that the game has for you.  But yeah, it'll cost ya.  You can pick and choose the ones that seem most interesting to you, adding new villains/heroes/mechanics/environments/whatever to make things that much more interesting.  This means though that if you're on a budget, you're likely stuck with just the base set.  Though you still get quite alot even in just that.
Overall, this is a complicated, engaging, deep and challenging game that is very rewarding and enjoyable to play, with loads of replay value.  And I have to say the music is pretty darned good, as is the art, and there's a ton of lore here if you like that sort of thing (seriously, there's a LOT of it).  I'm impressed by the obvious effort and love that clearly went into this.  I can see why this game is popular and why it's received so many expanisons, and I can definitely recommend it to anyone.
And it probably just gets even better when played with friends (co-op against the villain), but I wouldnt know anything about THAT, now would I...

HITMAN™ is a fun experience in the franchise itself and in stealth games generally.
For newcomers and casual players the game offers interesting choices to choose your own style to approach the assasination objectives and offers guidance with opportunity tracking, which is sort of a "mini-quest" system in the game.
Story isn't exactly forced to the player and serves a background stage settings for the maps and missions, but for those who want to focus the story more can find bits and pieces between the lines that are carefully placed in the gameplay sections themselves. You can't hear or see everything in one go, but eventually with multiple different approaches you'll understand the bigger picture. It's up to the players themselves then to decide whether the story is a good one, or just trash (personally I find it quite decent and interesting.)
Gameplay is smooth in most parts of the game with good hardware, but everyone who has played video games should know that eventually you'll start to see the weaker points. One for AI being sometimes too fast to make conclusions what it just saw when it comes to illegal/crime actions, and sometimes they even see things trough walls, doors, covered windows or even stairs. This is somewhat annoying especially on higher difficulties and challenges, when you usually wait longer periods of time to strike and then a random guy in the other room watching TV suddenly realizes from a bare shadow that some other poor fellow was just struck by world class assassin (and who else it could be than the one and only Agent 47 that no one has ever seen or heard about? :p) This is something that has been done better IMO in a games like MGS5 example.
Stronger points of the game are the maps and what they offer. A small sandboxes that feels alive most of the time, making it fun to explore and to beat. And for more challenge looking players all the maps can offer good amount of difficulty with professional stage and even secrets that are very hard to figure out alone (don't be afraid to look help from the community.)
Lastly, humour value of the game is worth alone for all those who enjoy modern day espionage themes.

Finally Hitman is back. I was disappointed by Absolution, it was a very dumbed down Hitman game, with only couple of good levels first being the best one. The new Hitman game gave everything I desired and more.
It is a completely different game. You’re being thrown into huge levels and must eliminate your targets. But unlike in Absolution you can choose countless ways to do that. You can explore the maps, find disguises and walk almost freely everywhere or you can sneak. You can kill innocent people or just knock them out. Shooting everyone will not work here like it worked in Absolution. You can make your game easy or hard depending on your playstyle. Sneaking while wearing suit might be very hard. If you get appropriate disguise you’re safe to walk around. So it’s up to you how to play. Disguise works differently now and has logic to it. If lets say you knock out a security guard and get his uniform, some security guards will get suspicious but most of them will not notice there's something wrong with you. Same goes for all other disguises, so while you can move freely you must avoid some people.
You can simply follow your targets and kill them, you can lure them into a bathroom by poisoning their drink and drown them in a toilet, you can set up an accident and electrocute or blow up your target. If you have a required tool you can disguise as mechanic for example and drop the lamp on your poor target. You can infiltrate the most secure zone, make your target think that you’re someone else, talk to him and then kill him. There are countless ways to achieve your goal. This game has really good replayability value, it has challenges and various timed events, so every playthrough can be totally different.
Graphics are really nice, can’t say anything bad about it. Game runs well, there’s many object on the screen and many things happening on the map, fps stays steady most of the time. Game looks brilliant, so much detail, so much going on.
Many people disliked episodic format. I personally liked it. There are couple of reasons why. First is that releasing episode after episode developers always can improve the next episode depending on user feedback. Another thing is, if you want to buy it day one you don’t need to spend 60€ on it, you buy one episode, save some money, buy another one, so it works better for people who can’t pay full price. It’s a shame if this was the reason why the game sold poorly. But I think there’s another reason to it which contributed to poor sales. Absolution…well…it wasn’t good, people were disappointed and were afraid to buy this one, especially when it’s released by Square Enix, I love them, own most of their games, but sometimes they make stupid decisions. But to my surprise this game has only one DLC and no pre-order ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I hope the second season will follow the same formula – no DLC and pre-order bonuses.
Another thing people disliked is always online. I personally have no problems with that, but I can understand those who has. But hey it's 2017, who doesn't have internet these days?
So if you like absolute freedom, sandbox style gameplay, want many hours of enjoyment  get this, you’ll not be disappointed.

Mårten Jonsson has a wonderfully creative mind. His games tend to be polarizing as the Steam reviews on the original Star Sky attest. You either love the artistic flair that the games present or you feel as though you’re wasting your time because you simply cannot appreciate his art form for the beauty that it is. I am still developing my taste for art and as such part of the splendor that is Star Sky 2 is lost upon me. I think that it’s unfortunate because I know that it is there. To me a quarter of an hour spent within the game is an achievement fest. Let’s see how many I can unlock in the shortest time possible. The answer  was 7 in about 11 minutes. That’s great for my Steam profile but sadly a lost opportunity to appreciate something beautiful. Ainslie, however, is a big fan of art. She’s also gifted enough to be able to press the left or right arrow key while appreciating the art that is on the screen and deft of hearing enough to listen out for music to tell her to stop a moment while the magic unfolds in front of her very eyes. Therefore because I know that she’ll be able to put into words her appreciation for Jonsson’s beautiful sequel to the original Star Sky I’ll present her another opportunity to share some little pearls.
AINSLIE’S LITTLE PEARLS
Like Warwick said I have a greater appreciation for art than what he does. With that being said I guess I did appreciate Star Sky 2 a little bit more than what he did. I don’t think that games as art generally sticks as being one game genre over another. I think all games can be viewed as art. What I liked about the game was the tranquility of the game. It is the type of game that I could come home and play a few minutes of after a rough day at work – I’m a nurse – and chill out with. That would be the greatest ambition for this game. It’s not really a game as much as it is a meditation simulator. The player doesn’t have to do too much just press one key and try out different sequences than what they have done in prior attempts with each sequence leading to a different achievement. I quite liked the the artwork but I preferred the soothing music that goes along with it.
If you’re wanting to play something that will help in your relaxation you should get Star Sky 2.
