Well, what is Divine Divinity?
It is the prove that a hack&slay-style gameplay doesn't mean that you can't have a deep and long story with true roleplaying. It is the prove that choosing a class for your character in an rpg doesn't need to limit your further character development. It is the prove that you can have story, the freedom of choice, open world AND action in one game. And it is the prove that mad magicians can invent words even imps can't pronounce properly...
Well, Divine Divinity is a 2D game with isometric view where you controll a single character. The game lets you interact with almost any object in the game, has some kind of crafting system, a story, hack&slay-like battles, a character system where your class only defines your starting skills but everything else is completely open to you. You have moral choices, influence on other characters depending on your choices, different possibilities to solve (or not solve) quests, guilds that you can join, conflicts to solve and a world to save from a great plot of ancient evil powers.
It is a game from 2003, so don't expect too much from the graphics, but everything else can compete against most recent games. Divine Divinity was the first part of the Divinity-series (followed by Beyond Divinity, Divinity II (which was obviously the third part) and Divinity: Original Sin and the Spin-Off Divinity: Dragon Commander) and still I think it was the best part of the series.
What you can await from this game? Well, at least around 30 hours of gameplay if you only go for the main story. Some very hard and frustrating fights in the beginning of the game, a lot possibilities to break quests or even the game by doing stupid things you are not supposed to do (so keep some different save-files...) and some mad humor when you are least awaiting it. The game requires a bit of skill and intelligent planning. If you have difficulties, it is no shame to rely on a guide on for example which are the skills that are worth upgrading or which things you definitly should not do to not break important quests, but it is also much fun strolling around and experiment.
Do I recommend the game? Yes, if you have some frustration tolerance. The price tag is always worth it.

Interested in Circuit Breakers?  Better hope your buddies are too, 'cuz you're gonna need 'em.
Circuit Breakers is a fun little Smash TV-inspired blastemup that puts one to four players in rooms loaded with aggressive robots, with every 10 stages ending in a challenging boss battle.  The four characters available each have their own weapon:  Aldo uses machine gun, Shelby's a shotgunner, Tay fires lasers, and Samson's got the rocket launcher.  I'm sure Circuit Breakers is a great time with pals, but what if you prefer to go it alone?  Well...
You see, I've been spoiled by one of my favorite games, Assault Android Cactus, so I went into Circuit Breakers in hopes of getting the same thrill of blasting through hordes of enemies while also getting overwhelmed by them.  However, the robots aren't the only opposition in this game, as one will discover just how strict this game is when it comes to simply shooting them.  Much like with Assault Android Cactus, there is a weapon level system that allows you to collect "energium" crystals from downed enemies to level up your weapon.  However, unlike with the other game, shooting your weapon here uses that precious energium, and at an alarming rate.  Level down your weapon, and it's not gonna do a great deal, yo.  So, aside from gobbling up them-there crystals, you need to keep your gun from weakening by avoiding damage and using short, controlled bursts if you want to survive.  Otherwise, it's "GAME OVER, MAN, GAME OVER!"  Don't fret though!  If those enemy bullets enter the fray, you can use your Shield to reflect them back at your opponents -- at the cost of energium.  Well, at least you're allowed to rush to the next room when prompted, with no need to kill every single baddie.
Sure, the energium gimmick is a unique idea, and I eventually adjusted my mindset to play by the game's rules.  Unfortunately with Circuit Breakers, those rules grew more annoying session after session, as I already had enough on my plate.  There is a good variety of enemies you'll face, and you'll grow to really hate some of them as you dance around the cybernetic swarms -- any dash-attacking droids and "bullet-sploders" are at the top of my list.  After defeating a boss and advancing to the next area, the enemies and their attacks become faster, making life more difficult for you and your gun as you grow desperate in staving off the aggressive A.I..  I ultimately realized that being a lone wolf here was foolish when I saw myself barely chipping away at the third boss' health bar during its berserk mode.
Oh, and Circuit Breakers doesn't believe in Continues.
I really want to fully embrace Circuit Breakers, with its charming 2D graphics and lovely sound and music.  However, like I said, I've been spoiled by another similar shooter that provides a good challenge that happens to be more sensible.  If all of this is still appealing to you though, I would like to recommend this game.  For best results -- bring friends, and "use short, controlled bursts."  Have fun, space marines! ;)

Although this game is very hard and the majority of its players are now lying in padded cells, it is actually an incredibly addictive and fun masterpiece by the makers of The Binding Of Isaac, Team Meat. The games replayability is surprisingly prominent with its dark levels and secret hidden easter eggs and warp worlds.
In short, Super Meat Boy is about a small boy made of meat (pretty super if you ask me) on a journey to rescue his girlfriend, bandage girl, from the evil super villan, doctor fetus. His journey takes him on an adventure through such worlds as "rapture" and "woods" filled with conveniently placed walls (and inconveniently placed spinning blades) for fast paced and difficult 2D parkour. This game's blend of dark humour and impossible to complete final levels will leave you laughing whilst also crying in fear and rage.
This N-esque game (most amazing flash game ever) targets your nostalgia whilst also inviting new game mechanics and much harder levels. Some of the bosses are quite reminiscent of The Binding of Isaac, not in gameplay, but in it's spooky, speechless personality.
This game is notoriously challenging yet its sense of achievement is found in few other games on steam. This game deserves a strong 9.5/10 with the only downside being its floatyness (sorry, personable opinion) however this game will always have a place in my heart.

Well I have to say I have never written a review for a game on steam so here goes.
I bought this game only a few days ago, and I have played for a few days now and there are limitless opportunities. Various planets and researchable items make this game all too fun! Having to generate enough power to do simple tasks and braving the sandstorms.

However; this is balanced with a few negatives:
I understand that this game is an EA game however optimisation is certainly required. For example, too many tethers placed will certainly affect your frames as you come towards the "End game" of that world save.

Spec Ops: The Line is not only a fantastic game in its own right but acts as a perfect time capsule for a generation in gaming.
The seventh generation of gaming was certainly one where the medium started experiencing some major growing pains, especially in regards to the kind of content it wanted to cover. Many development studios decided that they were done with the fun animal mascot characters and wanted to move in on telling gritty stories with human characters in more realistic environments but not being too sure on how to go about it. Given the large success of titles like Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare it became very common to see gruff military men in many games that took themselves way too seriously which made many titles come off as extremely generic and caused the industry as a whole feel like it was somewhat stagnating. Towards the later end of this came Spec Ops: The Line, a game to hold up a mirror to it all.
Story is absolutely one of Spec Op's strongest points. Set in Dubai after it's been hit by a massive storm Delta team is sent in to make contact with the locals and the previously stationed 33rd Infantry Battalion. As Walker and his team go deeper down the rabbit hole they begin to see the extremes both the 33rd and the populace were pushed to and endured along with the impacts it's had on them mentally, facing their own conflicts as they proceed. It's a game that manages to capture that more real, gritty feeling no other games did which is quite an accomplishment especially as it doesn't then glorify it. The game dabbles in many themes as you go along and offers a few different options to the player as they progress that help shape the narrative. With a multiple choices and many little details you might not have noticed the first time the game is extremely fascinating to replay.
The story is given even more weight by the absolutely flawless voice acting in this game. You might be sick of hearing the default voice of Nolan North in plenty of titles but I assure this game will show you what a little bit of solid directing can achieve. The rest of the cast all pull off equally incredible performances adding a much more real and raw feel to the dialogue. As the game also capitalises on its setting with excellent camera work and scenery design you'll get some truly fantastic shots as you make your way through the fallen Dubai, this accompanied by the voice acting create some incredibly powerful scenes.
Gameplay is where people tend to have issues with Spec Ops due to it being very run-of-the-mill. While it is true that this title doesn't really bring anything new to the table mechanically and is a fairly clunky third person shooter I feel like people do not appreciate how the gameplay is used. It takes that gameplay and weaves it perfectly into the narrative itself. A simple example of this would be letting you control characters when making story decisions instead of just pressing A or B, which means there are more options than you may realise if you're willing to think outside the box. It truly is a game that takes total advantage of the medium in many ways that because of that I find it hard to knock the gameplay aspect of it even if the moment to moment of it is somewhat generic. It's worth noting that game is not worth picking up if you are in it for the multiplayer. Adding to it being a time capsule is the fact it includes a tacked on multiplayer that is completely throw away which even lead designer Cory Davis referred to as "cancerous".
In closing if you're a player who wants a good story, engaging use of gameplay, or wants to see the kind of game that many in the seventh generation was always trying to be and then some, pick up Spec Ops: The Line.

Spec Ops, 100% completion in 5-6 hours.
Very small stutter when saving, otherwise no techincal issues at maximum settings. No crashes other. Handles being alt-tabbed well, but only once you get to the main menu.
Features a multiplayer, singleplayer, and a co-op. Variety of gamemodes for multiplayer, four difficulty levels for singleplayer (last one needs to be unlocked), multiple endings, haven't done the coop. Singleplayer has 15 (16?) chapters, longest are maybe 30 minutes.
Achievements are entirely singelplayer. Many are for getting X number of kills with a certain weapon category (shotguns, grenades, squad commands, etc), many are choices, several are one-offs like killing an enemy under certain conditions or doing something with the environment (guess the deer hunter achievement). Chapter select unlocked at the end allow you to go back to specific chapters (including the ending) and choosing alternate actions. You can also get achievement for the difficulties in this manner instead of doing the campagin.
Spec Ops presents itself as a third person shooter where you're leading a small team to Dubai on a recon mission. No doubt you've read or heard about this game and about it being "subversive" and the mundane controls and gameplay being intentional so as to illustrate this. While I agree that the game's story is unique, I think  that in a number of big "moral" moments, choices are forced upon you. I will say there were several great moments were I felt genuine discomfort, not because I was doing something new so much as the context. There was one great moment where all the years of shooter conditioning made me pull the trigger, and it was only when as I was pulling that I actually recoginzed what I was aiming at.
Texture work is looks like last gen, animations look like last gen, controls feel subpar for a third person shooter. Game runs fine though. Cutscenes are a combination of pre-recorded footage (mostly skippable), and in-engine (mostly skippable). There are sequences where you are slowed down, to listen to the comms or some other reason. Gameplay is very simple. Go from cover to cover, peak out and pop heads. You navigate both outdoor and indoor environemnts in a highly linear manner.
Not sure it's really worth it at anything beyond $15-$20 would recommend on sale. I will say that It's definitely one of the few, if not the only, modern miilitary shooters with this kind of narrative.

Finally Hitman is back. I was disappointed by Absolution, it was a very dumbed down Hitman game, with only couple of good levels first being the best one. The new Hitman game gave everything I desired and more.
It is a completely different game. You’re being thrown into huge levels and must eliminate your targets. But unlike in Absolution you can choose countless ways to do that. You can explore the maps, find disguises and walk almost freely everywhere or you can sneak. You can kill innocent people or just knock them out. Shooting everyone will not work here like it worked in Absolution. You can make your game easy or hard depending on your playstyle. Sneaking while wearing suit might be very hard. If you get appropriate disguise you’re safe to walk around. So it’s up to you how to play. Disguise works differently now and has logic to it. If lets say you knock out a security guard and get his uniform, some security guards will get suspicious but most of them will not notice there's something wrong with you. Same goes for all other disguises, so while you can move freely you must avoid some people.
You can simply follow your targets and kill them, you can lure them into a bathroom by poisoning their drink and drown them in a toilet, you can set up an accident and electrocute or blow up your target. If you have a required tool you can disguise as mechanic for example and drop the lamp on your poor target. You can infiltrate the most secure zone, make your target think that you’re someone else, talk to him and then kill him. There are countless ways to achieve your goal. This game has really good replayability value, it has challenges and various timed events, so every playthrough can be totally different.
Graphics are really nice, can’t say anything bad about it. Game runs well, there’s many object on the screen and many things happening on the map, fps stays steady most of the time. Game looks brilliant, so much detail, so much going on.
Many people disliked episodic format. I personally liked it. There are couple of reasons why. First is that releasing episode after episode developers always can improve the next episode depending on user feedback. Another thing is, if you want to buy it day one you don’t need to spend 60€ on it, you buy one episode, save some money, buy another one, so it works better for people who can’t pay full price. It’s a shame if this was the reason why the game sold poorly. But I think there’s another reason to it which contributed to poor sales. Absolution…well…it wasn’t good, people were disappointed and were afraid to buy this one, especially when it’s released by Square Enix, I love them, own most of their games, but sometimes they make stupid decisions. But to my surprise this game has only one DLC and no pre-order ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I hope the second season will follow the same formula – no DLC and pre-order bonuses.
Another thing people disliked is always online. I personally have no problems with that, but I can understand those who has. But hey it's 2017, who doesn't have internet these days?
So if you like absolute freedom, sandbox style gameplay, want many hours of enjoyment  get this, you’ll not be disappointed.

This game is great. Although it lacks a defining villain, one which was seen in both Blood Money and Absolution, the game has followed some sort of narrative. However, unlike Absolution and like Blood Money, innovative and open level design has returned, and the much more classic feel of Hitman has as well, which is identifiable through the rating system, the loadouts, the levels, and the other gameplay mechanics. Instinct no longer shows the path of targets, or allows for 'bullet time', and instead is used to highlight interactions, objects, and targets in the world. The gameplay is fun and interesting, as the different locations you visit have massive replay value with escalation contracts, bonus objectives and kill variations, multiple paths and opportunities, story, elusive targets, player-made contracts and now professional level versions of the missions. The episodic release, although quite annoying and controversial, made each new scenario seem more diverse and interesting, and did well in expanding the longevity of the game's lifespan. The classic feel of Hitman returns with updated graphics, and it would be amiss of me not to mention how beautiful the game looks sometimes (especially Hokkaido). The positioning of the 3rd person camera is wider, gone from the cramped view from Absolution, traditional stealth gameplay feels revived (where blunt objects such as bricks and bottles don't kill, only knock-out, unlike Absolution), and the work of the developers to improve and update aspects of the game through new contracts and such is awesome. For those who enjoy a run-and-gun approach, silenced and non-silenced shotguns, pistols, assault rifles, SMGs, and snipers are all in the game, along with a variety of disguises, lethal and non-lethal melee weapons, poisons for killing, sedating, or for forcing trips to the nearest restroom, gadgets, distractions, explosives, and more. The level of personalisation in the game is phenomenal, and allows any situation to be faced in a variety of ways. However, the game has some issues. The forced online means that rewards will not be earned if you play offline, and there are still some glitches and bugs in the game. Even with the entire first season being released, there still seems to be not a huge amount of content, and if a planned release for a second and maybe even third season is true, then the nature of the release of that future content (in terms of episodic/non-episodic nature and the pricing) may come under scrutiny. The soundtrack is the same for different phases (one for combat, one for suspicious, one for target killed, one for hidden, etc.) and the voice actors of NPCs such as guards, civilians, personnel and more doesn't alter hugely, even when in different locations (American and British sounding guards in Hokkaido). However, some of the background conversations and interactions between NPCs and 47 can be quite funny, and many different comments will link in to different stories you hear about and from others.
Anyway, this review, although spur of the moment, has gone on for quite long, so I will end it here. HITMAN is a great game, which not only revives the classic feeling from Blood Money, but also changes and updates old systems, while adding in new content and new levels of customisation. Although required online connectivity may be a pain, and the episodic nature of the game is not the most popular method of releasing content, I hope that a second season is released, and possibly even more after that, because the gameplay value that this game holds is massive. Seriously consider picking this game up if you're a big fan of stealth or you enjoy the Hitman series.
Also, on an unrelated side note, can we have the dual silenced silverballers added into the game as new content? Because nothing felt more badass in Blood Money and in Absolution as storming into a room with a target and a bunch of guards and shooting them all down with 47's trademark dual pistols. Please make this happen.

I've been a Hitman fan for almost a decade and a half now. I remember playing Hitman 2: Silent Assassin with my friend at his house after school. We were rampaging through the levels and, afterwards, trying to find the stealth approach. Good times. Over the years I've played every single Hitman game and I even (kind of) liked Absolution.
Hitman 2016 is a dream come true. It's Blood Money, but with quality over quantity i.e. instead of many small to medium sized levels, you have a few large to huge levels (with 3 smaller bonus levels) with a dozen or so ways to complete each objective. Player freedom was obviously on the mind of the developers and they delivered in spades. The atmosphere is more akin to Silent Assassin (i.e. James Bond-ish) instead of the rather grim feeling of Blood Money or the almost horror presentation of Contracts.
I have a few nitpicks though. Professional difficulty (which was added in a free patch) adds a lot of forced, contrived ways of increasing the difficulty of the levels e.g. by adding guards in places most used by the players (which includes such ridiculous ideas as bodyguards in empty bathrooms because reasons), cameras up the a-ss and only one save per level. Limited saves are arguably the most damning "feature" of this mode - with some levels having as many as four targets, no safe places (I'm looking at you Colorado) this is a total trial and error affair which will make you tear your hair out of frustration. Fortunately, the unlocks for Pro are just reskins of the equipment you can get through normal difficulty playthroughs.
Escalation contracts. Optional contracts which have 5 levels with additional objectives being added with each level. For the most part they are tedious (since they require you to replay the same objectives several times) and attaining Silent Assassin rank is extremely obnoxious. Thankfully, SA is not needed for any unlocks or achievements or even completion. Most players will rush through 10 escalations (out of a couple dozen) to complete a challenge and get achievements and never touch them again. IMO they are the worst part of the game.
My other nitpick is the music. It's not Jesper Kyd. It's generic. It's not bad or good, it's just... there. You'll only remember it because of replaying the levels so many times.
Anyway, if you are a Hitman fan, this is a no-brainer. If you like stealth games, the first part of the season (training levels) are for free, so you can try it out.

Basically this game, as many have noticed after a few minutes, is just a bad imitation of the Devil May Cry saga. Combos, controls, Devil Tigger, characters, story, level design are all different.
Defining it as a bad imitation is not, however, a way of telling that it is, also, a bad game. Despite differences, some gameplay approaches are enjoyable, like the possibility of using the entire arsenal at Dante's disposal. Let's just say it's a decent action game that expected to be dragged to the success through the use of a popular franchise, or at least for the most part. If we pass above all of this we have in our hands a pretty funny 10 hours action game. I enjoy this reboot more than the original series - it plays a lot like Bayonetta, although I personally prefer Bayonetta.
Basically the game is about performing stylish combos. In this way it is a lot like a rhythm game or even an extreme sports game like Tony Hawk's Pro Skater in the sense that your main goal (other than beating levels and not dying) is to link together seamless combos.
Don't be disheartened if you suck at this game at first - I really did. It makes great use of all of the buttons on the controller (I played with an Xbox 360 controller). You must be constantly messing with the shoulder buttons and using them in tandem with ABXY as the shoulder buttons change your weapons on the fly when you're holding them. It's a system that was difficult for me to get used to, but after about four hours I was handling it pretty well.
The main game doesn't take very long to beat, but the fun of it is being able to play the game again on harder difficulties. The main difficulty is not very hard, and I rarely died. But as you get into the higher difficulties that are unlocked as you beat previous difficulties the game tests your ability to quickly think up smart combos and understand how to deal with each enemy.
Aside from the gameplay, the game has a fantastic presentation and a decent story. The story is predictable and bland, but it serves the game and it is satisfying when you finally get to take down the games main bad dude.
The presentation is wonderful - really cool colors, especially when you take the contrast between the "real world" and "limbo" into consideration, which I think was intentional. The real world is really depressing and bland, but limbo is ridiculous and colorful.
Very cool game and I highly recommend it now that it's cheaper.

Spec Ops, 100% completion in 5-6 hours.
Very small stutter when saving, otherwise no techincal issues at maximum settings. No crashes other. Handles being alt-tabbed well, but only once you get to the main menu.
Features a multiplayer, singleplayer, and a co-op. Variety of gamemodes for multiplayer, four difficulty levels for singleplayer (last one needs to be unlocked), multiple endings, haven't done the coop. Singleplayer has 15 (16?) chapters, longest are maybe 30 minutes.
Achievements are entirely singelplayer. Many are for getting X number of kills with a certain weapon category (shotguns, grenades, squad commands, etc), many are choices, several are one-offs like killing an enemy under certain conditions or doing something with the environment (guess the deer hunter achievement). Chapter select unlocked at the end allow you to go back to specific chapters (including the ending) and choosing alternate actions. You can also get achievement for the difficulties in this manner instead of doing the campagin.
Spec Ops presents itself as a third person shooter where you're leading a small team to Dubai on a recon mission. No doubt you've read or heard about this game and about it being "subversive" and the mundane controls and gameplay being intentional so as to illustrate this. While I agree that the game's story is unique, I think  that in a number of big "moral" moments, choices are forced upon you. I will say there were several great moments were I felt genuine discomfort, not because I was doing something new so much as the context. There was one great moment where all the years of shooter conditioning made me pull the trigger, and it was only when as I was pulling that I actually recoginzed what I was aiming at.
Texture work is looks like last gen, animations look like last gen, controls feel subpar for a third person shooter. Game runs fine though. Cutscenes are a combination of pre-recorded footage (mostly skippable), and in-engine (mostly skippable). There are sequences where you are slowed down, to listen to the comms or some other reason. Gameplay is very simple. Go from cover to cover, peak out and pop heads. You navigate both outdoor and indoor environemnts in a highly linear manner.
Not sure it's really worth it at anything beyond $15-$20 would recommend on sale. I will say that It's definitely one of the few, if not the only, modern miilitary shooters with this kind of narrative.

First of all, Spec Ops: The Line has become one of my favorite games.
Note: I have played the through the campaign in normal, suicide and FUBAR modes.
Story - Didn't have very much depth to it. It certainly had its ideas and thoughts it wanted to convey and did, but in regards to the story itself it was lacking. Also, you didn't really have a chance to develop feelings for your teammates through communication, which also partially impacted the story's depth negatively. Playthrough experience - I loved every second of the 3 campaign playthroughs i did. Although there isn't potential for tens of hours of gameplay, there is still approximately 20 hours, depending on the person. Although there were some locations where I died several times in one area, it just made me more interested in finding out the right way to complete it (applies mostly only in FUBAR difficulty).
Music - absolutely fantastic. *minor spoiler alert* Every time the ingame music in the background started while a gunfight was going on it just pumped me up. The choice of music fit very well with each chapter and the game itself..
Guns - There is quite a variety of guns actually, although most of them only appear in the chapters towards the end.
Any cons?
- You can die in a certain area several times before you understand what you did wrong xd
- I died 105 times total in FUBAR difficulty. Yes, I actually counted every death.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who loves third person shooters.

The biggest and longest instalment of the GTA 3D trilogy offers the most complex and serious storyline that spans three cities and a never-ending series of optional challenges. But it’s probably too big for its own good, with so many things to do that it eventually feels empty.
GTA: San Andreas is
GTA game for many, and with good reason: unlike any other titles in the franchise, it has a whole miniature state with three cities (GTA versions of Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Las Vegas) and several towns. These all offer a variety of activities from collectibles to minigames and side-missions, on top of the already lengthy story.
This time you play as a black gangbanger who returns home after several years of self-imposed exile, only to find his old gang reduced to three members, the neighbourhood trashed, and a corrupt cop running half of the city. Just like how Vice City was a nod to the 80s shows like Miami Vice, San Andreas tries to capture the essence of early 90s blaxploitation movies like New Jack City, down to the obscene amount of profanity in every dialogue.
The plot is split to several chapters and moves around a huge cast of great characters, but maybe it is a tad too large for its own good. Missions try to be interesting, but eventually start repeating themselves, especially around the third city, where the story loses most of the steam, just like the additional content.
The large map also has drawbacks. There are lots of optional things to, but it often feels empty, especially when driving back and forth between the cities. Also, the rampages were removed from the PC version, taking away one of the most crucial elements of this era of GTAs, the random mindless violence.
These drawbacks only put a small dent into the shiny finish of the 3D era GTAs, and by all means, San Andreas was the perfect way to say farewell to this game engine and one of the best trilogies of action games.

Pros:
- It tries to replicate Arkham City, which is a great game.
- The shock gloves are fun to use. This is only a temporary buff so it doesn’t make combat completely trivial.
- Some boss fights are interesting and different from what we've seen.
Cons:
- Just a recycle of Arkham City, with little new and lots of flaws.
- Grapple boosting is clunky. Many building have edges that look like you should be able to grapple to… but you actually can’t. So you’ll often glide and desperately wriggle around trying to find something else to boost off of. This often leads to boosting to some random location, or falling to the ground. Grapple boosting was so seamless in AC.
- Combat is a mess that is glitchy and clunky. Enemies attack faster than they did in AC, which is not a good thing. For example, if you're in the middle of a long attack animation and a shielded enemy comes to bash you, you can't avoid it. Especially in hard mode, you often don't have time to react to even regular attacks. When performining special moves (double button presses), you have to press both buttons almost exactly at the same time with almost no buffer window. This isn't easily doable so you'll often mess up and end up doing an unnecessary counter or something, messing up your combo. In AC (and a lot of games, in general), there is a buffer window so that your special move registers even if you press the two buttons in quick succession.
- The upgrade system forces you to get upgrades in specific orders. This means it’ll take a while before you can get the upgrades you want. In AC, multiple takedowns and blade dodge takedown were some of the earliest upgrades I got since they made combat fun. The armor upgrades were some of the last upgrades I got since they did nothing to enhance combat. In AO, you have to upgrade the combat armor 3 times before you can obtain the blade dodge takedown, the ballistic armor 3 times before you can get the multiple takedowns, etc. It took hours of upgrading about a dozen pre-requisites before I could get some of the upgrades I wanted.
- Some upgrades require you to perform specific side quests or complete certain tasks to unlock. This sounds pretty cool on paper, but the execution is poorly done. One of the predator requirements is to get a vent take down, weak wall explosion takedown, ledge takedown, and a corner takedown in one predator room. The problem is that there are very few instances in the story this can be done. If you miss these few opportunities, you are screwed until new game plus. They can’t be done in challenge modes.
- AO’s equivalent of AC’s Riddler trophies aren’t cleverly designed and are not fun to collect.
- The voice acting for some of the characters is terrible.
- Dialogue is uninteresting, and the story is a bit random and seems to lose direction at times.
- Boss fights are repetitive, repeating the same QTE’s over and over and over and over…
- Open world feels dead.
- Too many more issues and random bugs to list.
AO is not a bad game, by any means. However, after AC, it’s hard to enjoy AO with all its annoying flaws. I personally had much more fun replaying through AC for the 5th time, and since AO’s story isn’t important to the series, it’s hard to recommend this title.

In short - it's probably the best single player HL2 mod out there. It's creator was famously (and deservedly) hired by Valve after working on this.
It's a mod that masterfully uses a lot of the available game assets (up to Ep. 1) to add to the original game - it does this somewhat in story but mostly in gameplay style. The result is a short cohesive experience that almost stands up there with Valve's single player campaigns (well almost - this is still just a little mod).
+ detailed production, good pacing
+ unique vertical/layered level design
+ occasional puzzles and HL style set pieces
+ surprisingly good soundtrack (partially new)
+ challenging combat (compared to HL2)
+ decent self contained story set in the HL universe
- constant backtracking can get tedious and/or confusing at times
- combat challenge mostly stems from endlessly respawning enemies
- the character that should serve as a guide in the game world actually ends up being quite annoying
- also the vague greek symbolism within the story is kind of forced and pretentious (but that can all be thankfully ignored)
- frankly the pacing is so good (for a mod) that you inevitably forget you're playing a mod, and that means that sometimes the campaign can feel a bit lacking in polish (at least compared to HL2, one of the greatest games ever, mind you)

The fact that I sank, with one of my mates, 160ish hours into this game is a testament to its quality.
While the original Borderlands was enjoyable, it lacked... a certain something. Perhaps the characters weren't engaging enough, or the enemies too repetitious, who knows. But Borderlands 2 managed to fix that and wind up better than the original.
Engaging, unique characters abound, the storyline is thoroughly enjoyable and even throws some slight curveballs that, while not earth-shattering, are welcome and a little surprising. The gunplay is fantastic and though it sometimes slides dangerously close to "numbers comparison simulator" at certain points, they've largely done a good job at making weapon comparison easy and organic. The enemies have appropriate AI and are equal parts challenging, colorful, and fun to fight.
But this game isn't without flaws. If you don't have a group of people to 'raid' with, the replayability diminishes noticeably, and the DLC is, in a word, garbage. The base game itself is loads of fun with a lot to explore and do. The DLC, though, is unnecessary. Don't buy it, you'll waste your money. If you want certain guns, either console command them in or resign yourself to endless hours of killing the same boss over and over again. Some people like that, I'll admit, but given the format it just doesn't seem appealing.
The characters all have a number of unique, interesting skill-trees to spec into, and it's easy enough to re-spec that you can experiment pretty well with different trees. I'm not sure if this is a side effect, but some of those trees are useless if you're playing with other people. Zer0's melee skill tree? Absolute garbage against just about any boss, and so I found myself useless until I respecced. It's a tricky balance, though; if everyone could do everything, what's the point? But getting punished so hard for playing the way "I want" seems a tad unfair.
Summary
Borderlands 2 is definitely superior to its predecessor. Colorful, engaging characters, great gunplay, engrossing storyline, and pleasing aesthetic are sure to draw players in for at least a few play-throughs. The game can get a bit grindy if you want certain guns, and depending on what you're doing the skill tree you selected might turn out worthless. Also the DLC is a total waste of time, which is really a shame.

I don't like this game, I love this game. I discovered it randomly while searching for boardgame adaptation, I bought it and the season 1 pass and enjoyed it.
I didn't intend to write review about it. The game has a fair amount of positive one, but after reading some negative review I wanted to adress two points often brought by people not recommending this game.
1) It's an adaptation of a boardgame and its expansions. The game uses a lot of different deck and sometimes you know you have lost just because you got crappy cards and the villain(s) got a wonderful start.
So, it's random, it's chaotic, and sometimes it's hopeless. And i enjoy this kind of game. But I know it's a real turn off for other player.
So I would NEVER recommend you to buy the game and all the expansion at once.
But if you enjoy boardgame, wait for the base game to be on reduced price (it happens regulary) and give it a shot. Do the tutorial, then have a go at the four villains. Best case, you'll get a game you enjoy. Worst case, you'll have just lost 1 to 3 dollars. Even if you can't afford to spent that amount of money on a game you may not like, just go on Youtube and watch some let's play and ask yourself, do I want to play this ?
Then, and only then, if you enjoy the base game, you may give some tought on the expansions ... which leads me to the second point negative reviews make :
2) This game is NOT a paywall. I hate DLC, I stayed away of Mass Effect and Dragon Age because I refuse to spend 5.99 to have that 'extra super hyper character whose code is in the base game but that we refuse to let you use if you don't give you more money'. This kind of thing is pure thievery.
As I said, this game is a copy of a real boardgame and its expansion. Handelabra develloped the base game exactly like it is when you bough it in real life : 10 Heroes, 4 villains and 4 environments. Then they spend time develloping each expansion (They are working on 'Villains of the Multiverse as I wrote this). I hate DLC, but for me I think paying for expansion is fair. In video game, I bought the Neverwinter Nights and all expansions, in the board game I bought Arkham Horror and all their expansion. Paying full price for each.
So yeah, I can understand why people just discovering this game are upset because they just found a game with 5 or 6 expansion and three more to come in the future ... And each one of them 'just' add cards. Duh, just like a boardgame then !
Again, try the base game, even with this you can play with people owning everything. Then like people do with boardgame, if you enjoy it and want to have different experience with this game, buy expansions.
One small details that is important for me too : The Handelabra really loves their game. They are reactive, discuss with their fan, and the community is great. They even twitch every week and discuss with fans.
I played a lot of games, I play a game, then move on another and another ... SotM is the game I never stopped playing since I bought it, and I don't intend to stop anytime soon.
So yes, it's chaotic and random, but NO it isn't a paywall.

This game makes me very
sad. I didn't know about this game until late 2015 when I saw a friend playing it. I bought it and all its available DLC at the time during a Steam sale and never got around to firing it up. Fast forward to this year and my wife just gave birth to my second child. I needed a game I could play with just the mouse while I hold the sleeping baby on my other arm, and through semi-random chance I chose this one from my library. The original card game came out in 2011 with this digital version following in 2014.
I love RPG's, I love cards, I love things that make me think, and I love the superhero setting. This game hits on all of these. Each hero deck is its own character whose role(s) you will play in the conflict. Each environment is a character in and of itself that will help or hinder you...usually it's both. Each villain deck is a unique entity that really has its theme and character come to life through the mechanics of its deck and card plays. You won't play against Baron Blade the same way you will against The Dreamer. Well...you might...unsuccessfully.
Now, if you play games as much as I have (30+ years of gaming at this point) you eventually come to terms that a lot of games out there have their own set of rules and that once you're familiar with those rules the game itself becomes a formality. You know exactly what to do at any given moment and you can just autopilot your way through the game if you've spent enough time with it.
. By giving you set characters to play, but making their abilities based on a card deck that you shuffle and draw from, there is always an element of randomness in how you'll play your hero. You might have all your favorite abilities in your hand; you might have none of them. You'll have to adapt to the circumstances of each game with whichever abilities you have in hand. The environment deck in play adds another element of randomness. The villain deck you're trying to defeat adds yet a third layer, and then the number of and order in which you choose to play the heroes will also have its effect on how the game turns out. Once you factor in just how many villains, heroes, and environments are available you see how no game is every truly identical due to all the possible permutations.
I chose to play this game out of utility and absolutely fell in love with the gameplay, the art, and the lore. I ended up grabbing myself a copy on my PC and my phone, grabbing my son a PC and phone copy, as well as ordering "The Entire Multiverse" (Tabletop Sentinels players know what that means).
TL;DR:
. I can't recommend it enough; and the season passes are a STEAL for the replayability they offer, especially when measured against the cost of their physical counterparts.

The game is a card superhero game.  You pick your heroes and villain and an environment to battle in.  Each hero and villain has their own deck to use.  You do not need to collect cards or tweak decks.  You play the powers your hero has and work with the other heroes in your team to defeat villains, who have their own decks against you.  Best part is the environment also has it's own deck and plays against both heroes and villains.  It takes strategy and teamwork to beat ANY of the villains in this game, or you will lose.  This game will push you..
I'm over 100 hrs of play at time of this review, and I really couldn't enjoy this game as much without the season passes.  I love the new heroes and villains.  (Shout out to the Vengeance pack!  Adding team battles was a great move!)  There are still ALOT of villains I cannot beat, but so fun trying...
America's Newest Legacy, The Super Scientific Tachyon and Fanatic are my fav together (now add the Sentinels!).  Get enough cards in Tachyon's grave, buffed by Legacy and suddenly your doing over 20pts of dmg...  It's all how you play your heroes together.. and even then the environment can ruin your day when you don't expect it.
I recommend it... try the basic pack, then get the season passes if you like it.  Not much in the basic pack, but enough to see how the game plays.  The real fun is in the variety of heroes and villains and environments (THANK YOU for the Freedom Tower environment devs!!).
Just remember it's not a TCG or CCG.  It is multiplayer online as well.

This game is a great representation of the card game, and allows for cross platform multiplayer.  This game has become my "go-to" game when my group of friends need a quick game to play.  The impressive ongoing development and the Weekly One-Shot challenges keep me coming back for more.
Some people complain about the DLC price, but there is a lot of development and effort that goes into creating and automating the complex system which is the Sentinels card game.  Given how inexpensive this game is compared to the gross DLC-grabs from other companies, you get what you pay for, and you are buying an enjoyable video game adapation of a fun boardgame.

Spec Ops: The Line provides a much different experience to other modern shooters in that the protaganist is far from the war hero that he thinks he is becoming, saving a doomed Dubai from an old military corps gone evil.
We are thrown in as you and your team of two embark on a scouting mission to gain intel on the progress of the evacuation of Dubai civilians under supervision by a military division who defied orders in favour of helping the people escape. However as the story progresses. This division is under the command of a general you once served with and state that you owe your life to, after being wounded and dragged from battle by this what is seen as a god like figure by our main protaganist. The perceived events that are taking place by our main character are called in to serious question as you willingly make decisions that truly prove that some of the worst things can be done with the best intentions.
Aesthetically the game is your run of the mill military style graphics with a slightly washed out colour pallette, however the ambience created by level building sets the game apart in terms of details and keeping in with the idea that you're in a city succumbed to anarchy and panic amidst a catastrophic natural disaster. Transitions between checkpoints and key changes in pace are executed flawlessly to suit the ebb and flow of realistic modern combat.
Combat feels similar to that of the Gears of War games, third person with an interactive cover/move system that allows for tactical movement without prolonged exposure to enemy fire, however is most useful for those who seek a challenge and try the game at higher difficulty.
Your two squadmates can be commanded to attack specific enemies to cover your movements or to concentrate fire to free up and area of the map for you to then flank the enemy yourself, a much welcome feature even though they seem to hit next to nothing (Assuming this is to increase difficulty and reduce you letting the squad deal the damage for you)
As mentioned previously the level design is a step above the standard lesser known shooter titles and allows for both tactical movements and easy concealment of secrets/collectables.
Overall, Spec Ops: The Line is a true independant game in terms of story and environment in which you as the player are left confused at how what you have just done was possibly misinterpreted and the effects it has had on the wider city of Dubai, it's inhabitants and the entire physche of a soldier just doing his 'duty'
.... The emotional horror of war visualized

This review is a real shame to have to write.  The game itself has a very fun mechanic, it could genuinely have been a pleasant game and for £6.99 would be a reasonable price for the game too.  The problem is that the vast majority of the game is hidden behind a paywall meaning that you either pay £30.00+ for all the DLC or have a basically worthless demo for the money you have paid.
I feel pretty tricked by this purchase and hope that this review will help others to avoid the same fate.
RESPONSE TO DEV RESPONSE:
Having come online I have noted the dev response to my review and feel I need to clarify some points to ensure people have the full picture of my review before deciding to purchase.
I agree that the base game has 10 heroes, 4 villains and 4 environments.  Its worth noting that the point of the game is to defeat the villains using a card mechanic.  As I mentioned in my previous review the mechanic of the game is not at fault, it is well programed, nice art work and a decent basic game idea.
To explain my downvote, the point of this game is to defeat the villains, you get 4... out of the 47 available villains.  Thats less than 10% of the primary goal mechanic of the game.  The rest of the villains are found in DLC.  I call this hiding basic game mechanics behind a paywall the dev considers this an expansion.  I will leave it to you to decide for yourself if you feel this is reasonable.
I have had two fans post very rude and disrespectful comments on this review (though one has deleted his comments now and I have removed my responses).  They and the dev below has mentioned that this is the same as the physical board game.  Bluntly I do not personally consider this a reasonable comparison.  To elaborate a board game revolves around the creation of, shipping of and storage in shops etc of the physical board game.  I can understand that this pay structure is arguable in such a medium so that cards can be sold seperately which make for easier shipping etc.  Such considerations are not comparable in a digital scenario.  Should the devs have sold the game with most or all of the villains for a higher price (say 14.99) I would say having additional environments /heroes would be reasonable DLC but as it stands I still feel this was an inappropriate pay structure for the medium.
It is up to you to decide for yourself which of these opinions most agrees with your own.  If you disagree please desist from leaving offensive comments in reply.

The biggest and longest instalment of the GTA 3D trilogy offers the most complex and serious storyline that spans three cities and a never-ending series of optional challenges. But it’s probably too big for its own good, with so many things to do that it eventually feels empty.
GTA: San Andreas is
GTA game for many, and with good reason: unlike any other titles in the franchise, it has a whole miniature state with three cities (GTA versions of Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Las Vegas) and several towns. These all offer a variety of activities from collectibles to minigames and side-missions, on top of the already lengthy story.
This time you play as a black gangbanger who returns home after several years of self-imposed exile, only to find his old gang reduced to three members, the neighbourhood trashed, and a corrupt cop running half of the city. Just like how Vice City was a nod to the 80s shows like Miami Vice, San Andreas tries to capture the essence of early 90s blaxploitation movies like New Jack City, down to the obscene amount of profanity in every dialogue.
The plot is split to several chapters and moves around a huge cast of great characters, but maybe it is a tad too large for its own good. Missions try to be interesting, but eventually start repeating themselves, especially around the third city, where the story loses most of the steam, just like the additional content.
The large map also has drawbacks. There are lots of optional things to, but it often feels empty, especially when driving back and forth between the cities. Also, the rampages were removed from the PC version, taking away one of the most crucial elements of this era of GTAs, the random mindless violence.
These drawbacks only put a small dent into the shiny finish of the 3D era GTAs, and by all means, San Andreas was the perfect way to say farewell to this game engine and one of the best trilogies of action games.

There is no denying for the fact that the new Dante was not a well established protagonist. Although the developer Ninja Theory might slightly missed their aim for the moon, they definitely landed themselves among the stars. DMC : Devil May Cry is without doubt a game that has been well thought of from its mechanics, all the way to its overall design. This is a reboot done right.
DMC : Devil May Cry lets you play as Dante, an angel and demon hybrid that lost his memories from early childhood and possesses the ability to travel in-between worlds called Limbo, a twisted alternatives of the real world. In this world, every secrets, lies and deceit of the powerful, evil (literally) bank CEO that controls the economy are exposed, but only Dante are able to see them. Experience as Dante teams up with a splinter group as they tries to send the devil back into corporate hell (literally. okay I should stop saying that).
If the summary of the story sounds somewhat ridiculous to you, trust me when I say that the story was delivered flawlessly in the game. I do not know how the developers able to achieve it, but they did it.
Review Summary -
You should forgive this game for its :
- Majority of the characters in the game are not likeable to some degree, but at least their motives are deep enough to give them a bit of character.
- If you ended up hated listening to the new Dante when he is talking, you could always mute the sound. No big deal, come on.
- PC controls can be difficult to master, but god bless the option to be able to remap the keys. So you could find the control sets that suits you.
You should LOVE this game for its :
- EXCELLENT FULL BODY MOCAP. The in game cinematics was well made, and the excellent mocap contributes a lot for its delivery in storytelling. Their facial expressions is extremely lifelike.
- EXCELLENT GAMEPLAY AND COMBAT ANIMATIONS - Good job for Ninja Theory that chooses fully keyframed animations  just like the old DMC. Keyframed animations (compared to dynamic animations like Euphoria) allows for a very well translated moves, seeing Dante in combat has never been so realistic and believable. Every swing of Rebellion (the name of the sword) looks realistic and carries inertia with them.
- WIDE RANGE OF ENEMY TYPES offers new challenges as you progressing further in the game, so there is no such thing as repetitive combat playstyles.
- TRUE DIFFICULTY. Did you know, on higher difficulties, enemies and bosses not only react more quickly, but the also possesses new combat moves when attacking. This ultimately creates new experiences and rewards huge replay value for the players. Cool, right? Some developers went lazy in higher difficulty by raising ONLY the hit points and damage dealt upon the player. So job well done Ninja Theory.
- A REBOOT DONE RIGHT. Ninja Theory is daring and strong enough to take this franchise to new directions. Without taking too much from the old material but only the amazing combat play, the developers has made a game worthy for a reboot. Ninja Theory does not rely on the power of nostalgia, but they believed that some originality will still appeal to most gamers out there, and they are right.
The unforgiving thing about this :
-The final boss fight is a huge disappointment. Enjoy the fight with regular enemies and early bosses as much as you can. Its a damn shame, the combat mechanics can be used exponentially, but they ended up as some gigantic fat♥♥♥♥♥blob for the final boss. urghh.
- No DMC sequel. Are you kidding me capcom? Canned the sequel for a reboot? Because the sales did not met expectations? Thats a ♥♥♥♥♥ slap to the fans of the new reboot. Sorry boys.
-The only bad thing about this game is only the characters. Thats unfortunate, but If you think you are going to dislike the reboot, there is always the old franchise for you to play. They're not yet extinct, people. There is a franchise for almost everybody out there.
Final Verdict
"DMC is a game that remains true to the core of classic hack and slash games, while offering new directions in storytelling and dynamic level designs. A game worthy for a reboot. 9/10."

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne - a noir love story.
The ingredients list, the texture, the flavour, even the ending. What you get couldn't be more written on the tin if it tried. Which is both its selling point and its main detractor.
As a game, it's excellent. The pacing is seamless, the mechanics responsive, the direction flawless. Where the first game gave you a tenuous dripfeed of bullettime, the sequel drowns you in it - each encounter usually ending in an invincible assault on wolves rendered sitting ducks as the sands of time become a suggestion and not a command - where even the default pistols quickly down the single enemy type, putting enough bullets in brains to say you're sharpening lead.
On top of the quickly-recharging "I Win" meter, you have your spammable bullet-time dodge that doesn't use meter, but is balanced by the recovery frames meaning that you will die using it. It doesn't get used often.
Weapons themselves are bog-standard. Pistols, rifles, shotguns, just about everything you could expect. It's never in danger of getting too inventive.
A trait that plagues the game. The noir love story is fine, it's okay, it drives the game. But this was the sequel to Max Payne, the meta-deconstruction deliberate trainwreck that balanced insanity with quotable lines. Just about everything memorable about Max Payne 2's setting, details and dialogue is a direct reference to the permanent constipated grimace writing of the first game.
It brings its own comparatively muted flavour to the table - you have optional TV shows that parody the game itself, along with a slurry of easter eggs and interactable objects. But every vestige of interest is shunted to the side like an unwanted child, a quality applicable to much of The Fall of Max Payne.
The OST is fantastic, but only spikes up when it feels like it and tends to feel totally out of place, a trippy mix of tunes blasting while you're idly checking dead bodies for painkillers. The periods of calm between the firefights, where you're just wandering around interacting with stuff, don't wear out their welcome (especially compared to some of these recent games that slow you down to a crawl to compensate for that being their sole gameplay) but honestly there's not enough of them compared to the samey-looking construction rooms full of goons they're happy to throw at you.
On the flipside, there's no real bossfights either. The one at the end is a physics puzzle. Combine the two and you have a game where neither the climactic moments nor the downtime manage to satisfy.
There's a couple of points that are straight improvement over the first game. Especially in regards to compatibility - these days, Max Payne 1 is a bit of a chore to get running. Max Payne 2 looks better, runs better, and works straight out of the box. It's even compatible with the Steam Overlay, you don't see that often with games from the same era. Even difficulty-wise it's an absolute improvement - while the first game was all about abusing the coded accuracy drop while roll-strafing, the sequel lets you handle enemies with a whole lot more grace and style.
Even if it does tend to come down to "whoever lands a shot first wins". Get used to savescumming if your reflexes are as bad as mine.
Max Payne 2 is a great game worth playing. A noir love story that rides on the adrenaline-bloodlines of New York. Even if it does lose quite a bit of the magic from the first.

A direct sequel for the tragedy of Max Payne.
Back as a cop once again thanks to Senator Alfred Woden's influence, Max is following a case about a criminal gang disguised as cleaners. This new epsode will take us to old places, old friends and will uncover some dirty secrets. Gameplay follows the first max payne, a 3rd person view action with bullet time, and the story is told by Max with comic pages, as already happened before. One again the game is divided in 3 acts with chapters preceded by some prologue dream sessions.
The dark noir atmosphere is always strong, with urban ambiences, old known locations such as the RagnaRock, and other new locations. Now levels are more articulated, details rich and filled with Sam Lake... I mean side stories disguised as Sam La... I mean, TV series. This might sound dumb or useless, but creating a world in a world helps in making it more real and credible.
The engine is an improved and updated version of Max Payne's MaxFX, so now, besides a general graphic update, we can have real 3d face expressions in place of the old 2d flat faces. Too bad they're way less expressive now. Now the story isn't being told with comics alone but there are more scenes in-game, especially action scenes rendered and studied with a great direction as usual.
Truth be told everything in this chapter is well done and studied, the story, plot twists, engine and gameplay. The problem is it doesn't innovate much the game as much as expected, as we'll mostly see characters and places from the previous title, and facts in the story will essentially be the same, or follow the same structure established in the first title. The only innovation lies in the fact we won't be playing as Max in a bunch of chapters, where we'll move a characters moving along with Max and catching up with him.
Considering the age of this game it might give some minor troubles when you launch it, mainly incompatibilities with modern OSs (Such as Windows 10), which can be easily solved with compatibility mode. Another issue could be with integrated GPUs, it recognized my laptop's intel GPU but not my nVidia GPU. Luckily my Intel GPU was performing enough to handle MP2 maxed out at 90 FPS or more, so I didn't even had to try to force it to run with my nVidia.
It won't work for me, but it's still great!

This game has been sitting in my Steam library gathering dust for months. I received it in a survival-themed bundle, and had little interest in it then. I had never played it when the alpha was first released, and all of my impressions about the game were based on brief comments from friends who had played it years ago, and a Dunkey video I watched a long time ago. Needless to say, while I thought I knew what the game was about, I knew next to nothing about how it felt to actually play it.
Then, last Saturday (October 28, 2017) I found myself bored wondering what game I should play. I saw Rust, and installed it. "What the heck, why not," I thought to myself.
A couple minutes later it had installed. I fired it up, and I liked the look of the main menu and matte background of the loading screen. I waited while the game loaded up a server, completely unaware as to how awesome the next few hours would be.
I expected a potato. My fuzzy half-memory of the one snippet of gameplay I had seen was from 2013 or something, and the game looks CONSIDERABLY different now. It is simply beautiful. I genuinely felt a sense of wonder as I looked around the beach around me. I opened up my inventory and was jolted awake by the fact that my character was naked, legitmately, 100% naked with no censoring. I realized this game had much in store, and wasn't holding back any punches.
The server I was on was mostly chill - it was a 100 person server, but only 29 people were on. I ran around exploring, picking crops from gardens and staring in intimidated trepidation at the stone castles other players had built. I, meanwhile, had only just managed to put shoes on my feet.
After twenty minutes of skulking around, rough-hewn spear in hand and my hunger satiated from eating wild mushrooms, I told my brother to buy the game immediately so we could play together.
I cannot overstate how much fun it was to experience awakening on the beach for the first time, naked and defenseless. Especially since it was on a server where the other players were already so advanced. It very authentically simulated the feeling of being outnumbered, outgunned, and in a constant state of danger. I thorougnly enjoyed it.
The next twelve hours were a blast. I am enjoying myself more than I have with a game in probably six months. It's given me that sense of childlike wonder again. I thoroughly underappreciated how awesome this game was going to be.
I followed some basic advice when I first played, that I think is worth relaying here: don't jump into a 350 person server immediately.  Don't even bother with the official servers. Hop into a community server, and just don't be toxic. There are chill people playing this game - not all of them are toxic griefers and kill-on-sight trolls.
Pros:
- Beautiful, massive world maps
- Extremely deliberate, pretty animations: you can really tell how much love is being poured into this project. The devs are great.
- Extremely frequent updates. The devs are committed and responsive.
- A lively community that is still thriving.
- Immersive gameplay.
- Fun with friends.
- Server wipes ensure that the game doesn't get stale.
- It's inexpensive for the amount of hours you'll get out of it
Cons:
- Some players are toxic
- as with all survival games, there is no real objective other than survive and explore, so players who tend to get bogged down by too much freedom will feel aimless and bored pretty soon.
(That being said, those kinds of things are par for the course for survival games, so it's not REALLY a con, just something to be aware of.)

This game annoys me for many reasons. Mainly it is down to consistency.
They managed to screw up the brilliant combat system. While it is still fun, it is inferior to the previous two games. Sometimes you can free flow to an opponent, sometimes you'll punch the air and sometimes you'll favour hitting a guy already on the floor instead of the one who is standing next to him. The upshot is that you will lose your combo and this is annoying. You also have to be careful with quickfire gadgets, you can fire a batclaw at the only standing enemy and before you're finished slamming him another guy can stand up slide to you and break your combo with no chance of countering him. Same goes for any move which takes longer than a single beat (cape stun, mine laying etc). I like the idea that you have to be careful when to use these multi beat moves but the lack of consistency and apparent psychic/superhuman powers of your enemies means that it is less about skill and more luck.
The linear nature of this game is very obvious. There will be doors which look like other doors you can use but which are nothing other than scenery, no interaction, no trying to budge a blocked door or funny little animations of henchmen surprised that Batman is knocking on their door. The line launcher only works on rare and obvious anchor points. The grappler will sometimes let you grapple, but sometimes you will just hit the side of the building you're trying to glide to.
There seems to be one way to approach situations and any other idea you may have will be blocked by scenery (Batman is defeated by a single strand of police tape.. don't tell Joker), bad grapple mechanics or doors which mysteriously lock themselves after you've walked through them. I think it's a cheek to call this an open world game. The ability to hang from a ledge you are perched on has been removed, one can only assume because the developers were drunk or suffered head injuries.
The Deathstroke fight was little more than a button mashing interactive movie, ensuring you get to see all the animations the devs have made for you. Speaking of animations, a great improvement on AA by AC was the death animations. You know, where the bad guy would taunt Batman as he lay dying. They're great, but you don't want to be forced to watch them 20 times while you learn how to beat whatever stage you're on. Arkham City allowed you to skip these and get back to the game, Arkham Origins has gone back to the philosophy of Arkham Asylum (i.e. watch this animation, then wait for a reload).
The new detective mode is nice except it also suffers the linearity problems. You'll need to scan various aspects of the scene to build up a picture of what happened but you can't progress to the next peice of evidence until Batman has finished musing to himself about the previous one and forcing you, again, to watch animations.
I was going to finish this one before starting Arkham Knight but I think I'll skip it for now, though I will probably return to it when I want some more Batman. All in all, I wont recommend the game because the problems are too numerous. It isn't terrible overall, but it does leave a sour taste. If the other games didn't exist, I probably wouldn't mind so much. Get it on sale or something.

I want to say that I enjoyed Borderlands 2 to the fullest. But to be quite honest, I have a hard time looking past the flaws of this game. First flaw I found is that the gameplay gets boring and tedious very quickly. Even after getting to level 50 and higher (Which you can only do if you buy DLC) , you'll find that you'll be shooting the same enemies over and over again with the same amount of bullets in the same enemies, despite the amount of damage your gun says you're doing. You start off with very little inventory space so the constant trek back and forth to sell worthless items becomes tedious, and towards the end, money stops mattering as there's nothing to really spend it on. Now here's where it really starts to get bad. You beat the game with your first character around level 29-32. A pop-up says that you can now raise the difficulty. Don't be fooled. If you want to leave the game with a positive opinion, do not replay it. Changing the difficulty sends you back to the beginning of the game and forces you to watch the same cutscenes and do the same quests.(as it stands, I remember almost every bit of dialog with claptrap in the beginning) And if you want to try all the characters at least once, you'll be doing the same intro over and over. While this is decent design for making you get used to the character, its dull for the people who just want to play. (If you do end up buying this game with its DLC, for the most truly difficult and fun experience, play Krieg) Another problem with the combat is there are certain creatures that can simply run up to you and start taking off chunks of your shield/health. Even worse are the ones that pull you towards them. My point being is that there are very few ways to avoid taking damage. I would appreciate the game a lot more if there were options to evade attacks such as dodging or rolling, something that allows the player to respond to certain situations rather than simply tanking. My last gripe with the series is how minor characters are introduced in a spectacular cutscene and then never interact with the player in a meaningful way aside from being a plot devise. They may talk about their past or add some sort of joke or reference but aside from the main characters in the previous game, they do not aid you in combat. They're just quest givers with a backstory. And as far as characters go, they can be entertaining to listen to, but it doesn't feel like they have much meaning.
Go play Max Payne first if you haven't.
