Criminally underrated and an often unrecognised milestone for the third-person shooter and gaming as a whole,
was quite the contrast to everything that had preceded it. While gritty and dark level design was apparent in the likes of
,
and
, the concept of film noir had yet to be truly tested within the format of a video game.
During a time in which the first-person shooter reigned supreme and the so-called “golden age” neared its end, a small Finnish studio decided to try something bold and new.
Enter Remedy Entertainment and the landmark that is
Armed with a turned-up leather jacket, a weapon in each hand and a tonne of pills, you return as everyone’s favourite anti-hero detective and are unleashed once again upon the filthy underbelly of New York City. Caught within the throes of a rapidly deteriorating gang war and still gripped by grief of his young family’s death, your journey to break the cycle of crime will only lead Max further into the darkness and confrontation he has tried to avoid for so long.
As both friend and foe make their play from the shadows and the stakes continue to be raised however, how far you are willing to push both the man and the city towards redemption is no longer for you to decide. Prepare for unforeseen consequences.
Best described as the equivalent of AC/DC’s Hells Bells, the core gameplay of the
series is some of the best yet seen in a shooter and, without a doubt, as stylish as the influences it wears so well. From leaping through the air with specks of debris trailing in your path as you clear out a room of enemies, to running and gunning your way through an entire building of psyched-up addicts, ‘satisfying’ doesn’t even begin to capture how incredible the mayhem is to experience. John Woo would be proud.
With their only prior release in the form of a charming little DOS-based racer called
, the low-budget origins of Remedy’s classic continues to demonstrate just how inspired and creative a small team can be. Depicting such a dreary and seemingly hopeless world that often veers from poetic self-reflection to the downright comical is a testament to the love put into crafting the world and the developer’s skill as a whole.
The series’ iconic cutscenes, (once home to Remedy’s friends and even Sam Lake himself), have taken more of a backseat this time around, favouring in-game rendering for most of the set pieces on offer. Admittedly, the transition between the two can be more jarring than usual when the graphic novel style is forced to cover through implication what the engine is unable to handle, but visually the game has held up admirably after all these years.
Thanks to the higher production value,
certainly isn’t bland and being transported into the depths of a dream sequence and Max’s tortured mind will quickly remind you of this, if the brilliantly moody soundtrack and fluid animation hasn't done so already.
Alongside the character of the city itself, Mona Sax is definitely the standout, with her well established femme fatale dynamic with Max carrying over from the first game. The excellent performances by Timothy Gibbs, Kathy Tong, James McCaffrey and Wendy Hoopes respectively deliver the top-notch voice acting alongside the equally stellar cast of both the new and returning characters. (Who could forget
?)
As one of the most fascinating and tragic relationships in gaming, the ultimately
attraction between the two characters is incredibly well-written, with the nuance stealing the show. Here’s looking at you, kid.
The few complaints that I could make generally come down to uneven difficulty and some hilarious physics moments, but these are mostly negligible. The changes to bullet time might be considered sacrilege by some, but electing for a more fast-paced than methodical approach hasn't hurt combat in the slightest, with the sheer power of the many weapons on offer providing some of the best action of its time.
is still quite short, but the clear and concise direction that it takes throughout redeems the amount of hours, particularly if you throw in some mods or a 'Dead on Arrival' run too.
is a remarkable achievement in nearly all aspects of its design and a worthy follow-up to the original, even more so when compared to the countless pale imitations or lifeless big budget titles that have emerged since. As masters of their craft, Remedy have more than fulfilled the series' goal of translating film noir alongside the impressive technical action and produced an enduring icon of the gaming industry.
While not exactly a “joy” to experience, wake yourself up from the American Dream and embrace one of the best third-person shooters ever made. Thumbs up.

Max Payne 2 suitably uses the tagline, "A Film-Noir Love Story", and I think that accurately describes the game. While gameplay doesn't actually consist of anything in a noir film, the theme and style of one are both there. Once again you are playing as Max Payne, who is back as a detective for the NYPD. Most of the story will have you running around with Mona Sax, and eventually, falling for her.
Gameplay is just like the first game, with small but much appreciated enhancements. It would make any John Woo fan proud, the fluidity and fun of combat is stunning, to the point where you'd be hard pressed to something similar in other games. Supported by a wide arsenal, Max will be vaulting, jumping, rolling, sliding, running, and flipping around enemies while he fires at them in slow mo. This is one of the few games that really encaptures how badass and cool looking action sequences look in movies, and fully recreates it. On combat alone, this game is a 10.
The story mainly relies on characters from the first game, so if you haven't played it, you should (that too is an amazing game). The game creates a new narrative for them to fall into, and includes a few revelations about the events of the first game. Where this game shines in story however, is not in the sometimes cliche story about a rogue government agency, but with Max and Mona. Mona serves as a conduit of self discovery for Max, and the love story between the two is really stellar. You feel for them, and you're at the edge of your seat each time one of them is put in danger. While the story as itself is doable, the sprinling of Max's depressed nature and of his kindling romance with Mona really supports it; it makes you care and put emotional investment into it. The love story essentially carries the plot, which is alright, because it's damn good.
All in all, i feel like this game markets itself as a noir film a bit too much, while it has the styling of one, not much else could attribute to it. The story is weak in certain parts, but incredibly strong in others. The main highlight of the story is Max's introspection and struggle to go on, as well as his relationship with Mona Sax, the rest of the plot is somewhat dull and more akin to an average action movie than anything else. The gameplay is addictive and fun, and makes killing repetitive waves of enemies fun and stylish, in ways few other games have accomplished. While it is a bit short, and lacks anything other than the main quest, the higher difficulties add a little bit or replay value and alternate (if not canon) endings. Max Payne 2 is the highlight of the trilogy, mixing fun John Woo-inspired combat, with a noir narative, MP2 solidifies itself as a classic game, and is worth anybody's time.

So I heard good things about this game, really good things. (from like 1 person) so I decided to buy it, I wasn't disapointed, I've been looking for a game that allows me to drive realistically, But then I realised "What about Euro Truck Simulator?" Turns out driving a lorry (truck) is really hard, even in games, but it's realistic and I get so mad at myself when I crash, especially this morning where I kept dozing off and ending up waking myself up by crashing, so there's that...
So what this game is about is you start off driving lorries around short distances, then you start going long distances and all around Europe, I myself want to find every place in the UK before going to Europe, but the game has great controls, especially if you use a controller or a steering wheel, it's quite accurate and to be honest really doesn't need explaining much, it's really spot on with the controls.
But the game itself is mainly driving on motorways, which may not be for everyone, but the thing is it's got the realistic driving mechanic to it, which makes it way more fun, I'm scared half the time that I'm going to crash and lose most of the profit from the job I do.
To be honest, this game is only for you if you like realistic driving physics and/or trucks, I certainly had no interest in trucks but I still love this game.
This game gets a 9.8/10
Also make sure to constantly check on the speed limit as sometimes it goes down from 60 to 50 next to a camera and you get fined, also, Used a gamepad or wheel controller, works WAYY better. (or just use the mouse if you have neither)
STEAM CONTROLLER REVIEW:
I set the steam controller's Gyro controls to drive, and honestly it's better than what you'd think it would be like, it doesn't work like it does in motion controlled racing games, it works better, as you're not going 90mph in this game and you're not doing huge turns at said speed, it's pretty accurate and I would recommend using the Gyro controls for anyone who wants to simulate using a wheel by turning the controller.

Though most of the puzzle segments only served to bog down the otherwise upbeat tone, and turned it into a stressful nightmare at times, when you were asked to think critically under a barrage of enemy fire and an uncontrolled setting, though sometimes it offered a significant feeling of reward after completion. The challenge is certainly greater than what you may be used to, throwing you right into the deep end from the get go, but it works out well as it asks you to use your environment and prowess to defeat your enemies. It's not unfair, at least towards the beginning, but unfortunately it gets a little too hectic towards the end. The final payoff makes up for it in the end. The levels made for some memorable scenes and there were a lot of great "this is really cool" moments. Oppurtunities and challenges you could learn from as a level designer, and a thinker. A surprising and magnificent feat for one man, definitely deserves the praise it received.

Some have problems running it on never operating systems, but there are fixes for most on the forum.
Then there are the countless bugs, a few gamebreaking, but you'll learn about them soon enough.
That aside, it's a pretty damn swell game. Not too serious but also not too goofy, and yet it is brutal and lets you fail if you don't pay attention.

As someone who doesn't really go out of my way to try new games, especially if I'm under the misconception that I'll be frustrated by it, I'm so, so, SO happy I tried out this game. The music is great, the sound effects just pop out at you, and though I occasionally get a weird static sound because I'm on Windows 7, that one little thing doesn't keep the game from running great on my trash laptop. Loot is one of my favorite things in RPGs, and it is freaking glorious in this game, and you can get skills like enchanting, identifying, and repair that makes it so much more fun and rewarding. Speaking of skills, if you were perhaps a bit more "casual", as in you haven't played older RPGs, and feel intimidated by this, or maybe you like games like Skyrim that let you use any weapon and use magic as a big buff axe-wielding barbarian, this game is for you - any class can use any skill - a pickpocketing wizard, a lightning-slinging warrior, a thief in heavy plate. It's easy to pick up, and ridonculous amounts of fun to master.

Divine Divinity is Diablo II made into an actual RPG, but with significantly less polish, more broken skills and writing done by people whose native language obviously is not English. But it's so much better than it sounds.
The world is huge and full of quests and weirdos and choices and consequences. There are multiple ways to solve nearly every quest, most of the dialogues have good snarky options and the whole game drips with enthusiasm. It may be flawed, it may be ugly in places, it may be silly beyond all get out, but it was obviously made by people who wanted to make it. Larian are probably my favorite developer; I don't know that anyone else is as passionate about the games they make as those guys.
Their games aren't the best. They're often uneven. Sometimes they're even complete messes. Divine Divinity is no different. But it's got a lot of character. It's got a lot of soul, and it set the stage for all the fun stuff Larian's made since.
There are games with better combat, with more coherent worlds, with more fleshed-out characters, with more memorable plots, but few games exude the joy and excitement that Larian games do. I recommend all of them.
...Except Beyond Divinity. That one ain't very good.

If you're anything like me and you've played the other Arkham games but overlooked this game as it wasn't made by Rocksteady and got mediocre reviews, but are still itching for some more Batman fun then this game is worth a try.
I can't really say too much bad about this game, it's alright really. Nothing special, but worth a play through. It's very similar to Arkham City and even reuses a lot of the same assets, but it differentiates itself enough for it to feel like it has its own thing going on.
The story is a bit routine and mundane but it does have its fun moments, and it does a decent job of providing the Arkham series with a starting point in its narrative, not that I necessarily feel like that was actually needed. I particularly liked the boss battles. I won't spoil it by naming names, but there is one boss battle in particular which makes this game worth playing.
There is some slight oddness with the free-flow combos for me, like they just don't quite work nicely, and I often dropped out of a combo when I feel like I shouldn't have. It's like the timing on pressing the buttons at the right time is a little too slow. I had a few slight glitches and I had one hard crash towards the start, but generally speaking the game works quite well. I got a pretty consistent framerate and the graphics are fairly pleasing if unremarkable.
I would say this game is better than a lot of the initial reviews may have made it seem. That being said I understand the game was reported to have had a lot of bugs and issues at release, but I didn't play it until recently. I got the game for free with all the DLC from WB after the whole Arkham Knight debacle. I'm not so sure I would have been too impressed with the game had I paid full price, but I would say it's definitely worth buying if you can get it on sale for a decent price.

Max Payne 2 is a direct sequel to the original and picks up after the events of that game. Max, now a detective and wearier than ever of the world, once again has his hands full as he finds himself hopelessly attached to the lovely Mona Sax, a murder suspect and part of a bigger plot that ties in to Max's own dark past. There are tons of references and parallels to the original story. Fans will undoubtedly be pleased by some of the nudging and winking, though someone starting off with Max Payne 2 would probably feel rather left out, despite the presence of an optional cutscene that summarizes what happened leading up to Max Payne 2. Still, this is a surprisingly complex narrative for a game, irrespective of the genre.
The storyline unfolds in much the same fashion as the original. It uses some very slick, graphic novel-style storyboards--complete with melodramatic dialogue straight out of a pulp detective novel--and good voice-over to go with it. These graphic novel sequences are unmistakably similar to those of the first game, though they are, in some cases, even more artistic this time around. Max Payne 2 certainly isn't lacking in its presentation. Even the game's special edition DVD-style packaging is slick, and all of the game's between-level loading screens and graphic novel sequences are impressive-looking and often very cool. The plot itself features a number of twists but is rather convoluted the first go-round. Play through the game a second time (perhaps on the higher difficulty setting that's unlocked after you finish it the first time) and you'll likely get a much clearer sense of what's happening.

"Gentlemen....welcome to Dubai."
This is the quote that I find myself repeating as the end credits roll in Spec Ops: The Line. Since the game's release in 2012, I have spent small amounts of time dabbling within the game's demo that was released for the Xbox 360 as well the full release for when I purchased it here on Steam, but the game never captured my attention enough to commit to finishing it and I often found myself lost behind the confines of chapter 3 upon attempting to replay it and properly asserting myself back within the story. Yet, the other day I chose to gamble once more on the prospect that is Spec Ops: The Line and I am glad that I did, for this time I finished it. Many believe that The Line is its own entity, despite having the Spec Ops title tacked onto it. Spec Ops is a long running franchise that had its start on the original Playstation as a semi realistic tactical shooter that served to immerse players within the various different roles of the military. As the franchise grew, each installment grew more formulaic than its predecessor, as the last Spec Ops title to release was Spec Ops: Airborne Commando in 2002, which was a top down shooter. Fast forward a decade and here we have The Line. The shell of Spec Ops: The Line is a generic, third person, cover shooter with bare bones squad mechanics. Ever since its inception the Spec Ops franchise has attempted to set itself apart from the rest of the cannon fodder military shooters on the market and The Line upholds that creed. While the game's shooting mechanics are generic as can be, the differentiation comes in the form of its story, the horrific yet realistic imagery that it portrays, as well as the effect that this hell has on protaganist Martin Walker's mental state. Throughout the game, the player is taken on a journey as Delta Squad attempts to do good by the people they were ordered to rescue. Upon the opening of the first chapter, the game's credits list each of the developer's names as one would expect, but at the end, the subtitle "Special Guest: *insert player's name*" displays on screen. That is where the heart of The Line lies, within the choices you as the player make. For the choices are not Walker's or even that of his squadmates, but of yours and the player must suffer the consequences of those choices and actions because of it. Spec Ops: The Line is a meticulously crafted piece of media and deserves to be played by hardcore audiences, avid gamers, and even bro dudes racking up killstreaks. Well done.

No More Room in Hell, or NMRiH, is a recently released free-to-play FPS in which you select from a small assortment of characters to survive in a post-apocalyptic zombie-infested world and try to survive with friends to aid you online. You could complete tasks in objective mode in order to be rescued or hold off huge hordes of zombies in survival mode as you await salvation. Some of the fun of this game are the modded servers, such as infinite ammo, health bars, and the ability to change your character to other fan made player models, such as the Joker from Batman, or Mario from Nintendo (which I thought was pretty hilarious). It's surprising that this game was given for free, because Steam really outdid themselves by adding it to the libraries of many people. This is one realistic survival horror you don't want to miss out on. If you're still reading this, then I suggest you STOP reading and go get this game from the store. Remember, it's free! But how could she get it when she had no money available? Well, let me tell you, she searched hard and somewhere, one day, she found a way to play the beautiful game, thanks to a wonderful person who helped her.
After opening the game, she was welcomed with a story about a cute white shiny creature and the forest in which it lived. As the story progressed, it became more and more intriguing, taking her on a rollercoaster of emotions, from absolute happiness to absolute sadness.
The sounds of the forest and the music in the background were magical and made her fall in love with the soundtrack. Absolutely beautiful and magical.
The controls were smooth and the game had no problems running, even on her not-so-good laptop. The platforming of the game was good, sometimes easy, sometimes it made her want to rip her hairs out, one by one. It required her skills and a lot (and I mean, A LOT) of patience and deaths to pass.
Now here is that girl, 2 years later, writing a review for her favourite game of all time, still thinking how it made her cry so much, so often, yet it filled her with happiness. And writing this review, she asked herself: WHAT THE HELL ARE YOU STILL WAITING FOR? GET THE GAME, GET ANGRY, CRY, SMILE, ENJOY IT.

Astroneer is an open-world interplanetary space exploration game with focuses on survival and crafting. Launched in its current Pre-Alpha Early Access state, the folks over at System Era have done a phenomenal job at setting a good example of how the Early Access platform should be used. With only a few bug issues and fairly rare performance drops this debut title has some massive potential. With its charming aesthetic and beautiful art-style, it's hard not to immediately be drawn in. Currently, the game has a decent amount of content be that solo or drop-in co-op (with up to 4-players) and a pretty wide variety of equipment to make, resources to gather, and places to explore. It's safe to say that Astroneer has made a great first impression and definitely a game to keep your eye on.
Note: It definitely seems like a passion project to the developers and already it's beginning to show. They've kept active on steam and their forums with patches coming in daily and constantly asking for community feedback. I hope they get the continued support they need so long as they keep taking the right steps.

Some would argue that once you complete Astroneer, there is nothing left to keep you playing, but the beauty of Astroneer is not in the completion of the game, it is but the process in which you go through, to not only to complete the game, but the exploration of the beautifully crafted worlds of Astroneer.
With little instructions on what to do and how to get started in Astroneer, the game often leaves you thinking, even after you have stopped playing. Prepare for sleepless nights as you think of the many beautiful worlds you have explored and the many mysteries will discover and solve; the wreckages of other space craft; the weird and wonderful plants; that odd shaped structure in the distance....
One of the wonderful game mechanics of Astroneer is that even in the death of your character, you can still appreciate the beauty and design of the game. Enjoy discovering death, is all I can say.
Overall Astroneer offers a beautiful and simplistic experience that is both challenging and enjoyable, a combination that is often difficult to find in these types of games. System Era has created not just a game, but an impacting experience that you are assure to enjoy.

This game is NOT without its shortcomings and annoyances, but there is nothing major that I felt made this game not deserve my recommendation. First off; the save system is bad, and there were points in the game where I felt the game should have automatically saved but it didn't. There's nothing more annoying than dying and having to replay the last 15 minutes of the game, that being said if you get into the habit of saving this stops being an issue. Secondly, the cutscenes that you can't skip are a pain to sit through on the second playthrough and I feel like there should be an option to disable them along with the little tooltip helper things that pop up every single time you collect a health/energy orb or ability orb. Lastly, there are a few parts in this game where the object you're trying to jump to, usually something really skinny like the top of a hanging log, feels kind of sticky. It's a weird thing to describe but it makes menuevering on these obstacles a bit tedious unless you figure out the distance you have to jump away from the object before ori stops trying to CLIMB it rather than jump ONTO it, I only encountered this maybe 3 - 4 times in the game but it did trip me up a bit.
All in all I'd have to say this was a very difficult but equally rewarding experience and I presonally feel this game is a modern classic that I'll probably play through many times over the years.

Atmosphere:  The atmosphere is true to Half-life games of old. The island gives you plenty of areas to explore, like the usual old buildings, worn down docks on beachfronts, and combine infrastructures. Overall: Excellent game! If you're suffering from Half-life withdrawal and need a lifeline, this is the game for you! It's a free mod, that's about a 4 hour playthrough and the quality is certainly there.

I have reached level 5 as a female Survivor. Trudging through the farm fields, I get a nostalgic feeling. This game is a vastly improved Faery Tale Adventure. The game was first released in 1986 and I played it on the Sega Genesis in the early 90's. It was a large expanse to travel through, and you hacked and slashed to treasure and experience points. The genre of action RPGs has come a long way, and Divine Divinity shines in the amount of depth and interactivity you can have with the environment. It's a mixture of Record of Lodoss War(Dreamcast version), Ultima VII, and Baldur's Gate.

An early 2000's RPG, Divine Divinity appears to be trying to capture the success of the Diablo games. As a top-down action roleplaying game it is along the same lines as Diablo; However, it seems to have a more comprehensive conversation system in place, allowing for branched conversation trees. You can also develop your character according to your own personal play style regardless of the class you choose. This is actually not a concept found in many earlier RPG's, which gives Divine Divinity an added layer of appeal. All in All I thought it was fairly well done. It is an older game, so the visuals are not what you have probably come to expect, but the game still has charm and is still interesting and has a well thought out storyline. The background ambience is a nice touch, as is the changing music depending on where you go. I think if you are a fan of old school RPG's you will like Divine Divinity. Good choice for the RPG fan out there.

Though it shows its age at times, this game is engrossing and challenging, and sports a wicked sense of humor. The only real complaints that I can level at this game are that some of the skills are buggy, and there is a strange audio glitch sometimes. Other than that, this game is a 10/10, with an excellent soundtrack, to boot.

The story:
You are a Combine Soldier who was set free from the Combine bondage and retasked to explore this peculiar island, were the Combine forces have set a base for operations. You are left off at its shores with only your weapons and a mysterious voice guiding you along your path. The adventure begins!
Pros:
This mod pushes the Source engine to its limits, with its fantastic artwork and level design on each map. The settings remind pretty much, many parts of Half Life, Half Life 2 and Half Life 2 Episode One. The story is consistent with many elements that a decent cyberpunk production must feature. The gameplay is action packed, always giving you enemies to fight and objectives to complete. Finally, the music fits the settings, story and gameplay perfectly, enhancing the overall game experience.
Cons:
Swarm of enemies at times, may make you feel depressed about your next move or how to counter. Objectives are given only through text and sometimes during battle times, thus ignoring them and literally spending a few seconds untill you get back on track on how to complete them or what to do next (May I suggest a voice actor for providing the voice of the AI text?). Several "Node graph out of date. Rebuilding..." messages, that seem to affect the load times of several maps. 5
Overall, I would give this mod a 11/10, for delivering such an amazing gameplay experience.

First thing's first, I got this game recently and the first thing I can say is that it does require a few hours to get into and to understand. I've experienced constant crashes and the game is extremely glitchy. I highly doubt it is because of my PC as my other friends with better specs have had the same issues. The game does not respect your time and if you really wanna get somewhere early after the wipe, you're gonna be spending 6-10 hours a day playing. Over the past 3 weekends, I've been staying up until 3/4 a.m. to raid bases(Not because I want to offline raid, but because it takes me all day to gather the resources). It is the most satisfying feeling running away from a raid with good loot, but the most dreadful feeling dying on the way back. The reward system in this game is incredible and really creates satisfaction that is insatiable in other games. I recommend it if you're willing to spend the time and don't mind losing all your progress after hours and hours of work.

-----DISCLAIMER FOR WIN8/WIN8.1/WIN10 USERS------
I had several Problems with this game on Windows 10, but after some research, it runs fine on Windows 10.
1. Run in Compatibility mode (Windows XP)
2. Rename the install Folder to smth without spaces like: "MaxPayne2"
3. Then in your steamapps folder find appmanifest_12150 and edit the install dir line to match your renamed folder (you might have to close Steam to do this or restart Steam)
4. Disable Steam Overlay for this game
5. Make sure everything stays the same after Steam restart -> sometimes Steam changes stuff back
After this steps (and propably 2 Hours looking throug forums -> which is why i decided to post this review) it runs great.
-----GAMEPLAY------
-The game itself is a masterpiece, equaly in storytelling as well as in gameplay.
-I really enjoy the fact that you die very quickly, especially on harder difficulties, which makes this game challening.
-The developers designed the gun fights to be realistic -> Bullet to the head enemy dies (same for you) -> no real bosses like in the first game.
-This game is really skill rewarding and the more you play it the easier it will get, to a point at which you switch fluently through bullet time, bullet time jumps and real time shooting.
-Great arsenal of weapons -> all feel and play different
-Overall it's a great fast paced third person shooter, that gets better everytime you play it.
-----STORY------
-Great Story (dont want to spoiler anything) but if you are into the story I would recommend playing Max Payne 1 first.
-I recommend finishing it on hardest difficulty for a suprise ending;)
-NOIR comic strips to tell the story is just AWESOME
-Funny dialogs between enemys
-----SOUND-----
-Awesome music -> gives me goosebumps everytime I'm in the main menu
-Good weapon sounds -> you can tell weapons apart just by hearing them shoot (helps to decide how to fight)
-Good voiceacting -> Max's voice is super badass
-----GRAPHICS-----
-This game still looks amazing for it's age and still has some graphical parts that even newer games can't get right (talking about mirrors -> just try it yourself and you know what i mean;) )
-Overall this game aged amazingly well.
-Nightmare levels and NOIRE comics have an oustanding artwork.
-----CONCLUSION-----

Spectacular game!  I'd never played the card game before playing the digital version and I probably never would have.  It's a game that would require a tremendous amount of book-keeping and tracking various effects.  Luckily, this developer packed all that up into a tidy, fluid UI that does the heavy lifting and lets me just have fun.
I highly recommend buying the DLC as it dramatically increases the replay value.  You'll get much more playtime for your dollar with the DLC than without it.  That makes it worth it to me!
The multiplayer is pretty well done - however I rarely use it.  It makes for longer games and the activity seems rather low during the hours I play (evening in Europe).  There's almost always some people playing, though.
That being said, playing solo takes nothing away from the game and it's worth the buy even if you don't ever use the multi-player feature.

Computerized, online version of the excellent deckbuilding card game. Now you can save the universe with friends around the globe!
Not exactly a TOTAL replacement for the real deal, even once they get all the expansions added, but a lot easier to set up and play a game than busting out the tabletop version.
The Season passes might seem expensive but are TOTALLY worth it. If you're not sure, just grab the base game and if you want more, you won't be disappointed with season pass 1.
As of the writing of this review, Season Pass 2 is still mostly unreleased but will be adding new game modes and tons of new heroes and villains.
If you like superheroes and tabletop games or if this looks up your alley, give it a shot.
ADDITIONAL NOTE: At least one negative review seems to be under the misapprehension that this is a collectible card game. It is not, except in the fact that you can buy new decks. The decks are fully built and fixed (cannot be altered, beyond variant hero character cards). This might share a few similar concepts with Magic: The Gathering but it isn't about building a stupidly broken deck to crush opponents, it's about using fixed hero decks to co-operatively defeat a villain. To me, far more interesting than getting squashed by a guy who beat you because he has six ultra-rare thousand-dollar cards in his deck, but that's just me.

A 100% faithful reproduction of the physical SotM card game (WHICH IS AMAZING BTW), at less than 1/5 the price. One might even say Sentinels Digital is the "definitive" version of the game, since it includes errata and official rulings on ambiguous situations that spawned endless debates on the physical game's forum. Gameplay is further enhanced by Jean-Marc's amazing soundtrack. Sentinels Digital also tends to play faster than the tabletop game, since the engine automatically tracks HP, start-and-end-of-turn effects, conditional effects, and other bookkeeping headaches (so you don't have to).
Absolutely do get one or both Season Passes. Unlike most games where the DLC adds little to the core gameplay (maybe a different item to use, or a few hours of side missions that have little bearing on the main game), each Sentinels DLC you pick up adds exponentially more possible setups to the game, increasing the replay value immensely. The base game has 9312 hero vs. villain setups (ignoring turn order and unlockable hero variants), though admittedly they'll start to feel stale after you've seen all 16 combinations of "Villain X in Environment Y." With SP1, that expands to a whopping 9544080 setups (again ignoring turn order and variants), with 345 Villain/Environment pairs.
How much do I love this game? I'm one of the 61 crazies who shelled out $500 for EVERYTHING EVERER in the tabletop version's Spring 2016 Kickstarter, and I STILL bought Sentinels Digital and both season passes, and have everything else that the season passes don't cover on preorder.

I originally played this on the PS2 when I was 8 years old. I didn't know how to really play it but my human nature was able to figure out how to jack a car and blow an old womens face off in the street. Now that i'm older I can truly experience Grand Theft Auto San Andreas, I will tell you the good and the bad about this game, first I will start with the good
The good
Right off the bat you're able to roam around the giant city of Los Santos and do whatever you want free of any real life reprecution, and once you start to play through the story missions of Grand Theft Auto San Andreas you will be able to unlock more of the map and explore neighboring cities Los Ventures and San Fiero with the wilderness around it if you really want to explore. This game is set in the early 90's with the earlier rap music and gang activity being a very real concept in the game with you actually being part of the Grove Street Families and doing missions for Big Smoke, Ryder, OG Loc, and Sweet Carls brother. The map is still huge and has so many side activities when you complete the main story. I really enjoy this games music, gun play, and story much more than say Grand Theft Auto IV.
The bad
The game looks very dated even in the HD release on PC, 360, and Mobile. The physics get a little jacked up when you take the annoying frame limiter off, I was trying to swim with the frame limiter off and I swam slower than a turtle with a missing leg, I couldn't even go underwater correctly with that annoying frame limiter off. It's story has been done before and has even been done better in some games like Saints Row and Saints Row 2.
That's it for my review, i'm gonna give the game a 9/10 because it's not perfect but it's still one of the best Grand Theft Auto games to date period.

Spec Ops: The Line is a highly underrated, greatly overlooked third-person shooter with a primary focus on the Campaign.
The Campaign is intriguingly-crafted with an unconventional story usually not found in shooters. It depicts the story of a regular soldier relieving various brutal scenes of war, such as the mass slaughtering of American soldiers simply trying to follow orders, the burning of civilians with a scene centered on the charred corpses of a mother clutching her baby, and the mass shooting of a civilian mob. Subtle hints to the game's true story is hidden in the Campaign. For example, at the start of the Campaign, the protagonist's uniform is tidy and clean, whereas towards the end of the story it becomes tattered. Also, the protagonist's voice commands are professional and calm at the beginning, whereas towards the end of the story they become erratic and reveals the reality that the protagonist is simply a psychotic killing machine. The plot twist at the end blew my mind, and when the game puts you into moral dilemmas, it's really hard to decide. This shooter is centred around showing the brutality of war, the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder soldiers suffer when going home after war, and to question the player's moral integrity on whether war should really be portraited as video games in the style of Call of Duty and related games. This is truly a memorable shooter. For those of you looking for a straight-up run-and-gun CoD-style shooter, this isn't for you. This game is for the people who truly take a moment to take it all in and think about the actual situations happening in-game. However, the cover system used in-game has a few problems here and there, and the controls are slightly weird and a little unfamiliar. The graphics are mediocre for its generation, but I'd still give the Campaign a solid 9/10.
As for the Multiplayer it's not really worth playing, it's dead for a long time. The controls are unfamiliar, the gameplay is not really as smooth as the Campaign. It's really just a generic shooter in the Multiplayer aspect that has none of the charm in the Campaign.
I have not played the Cooperative Mode, so I do not have the right to comment on it. But I'll assume it's just as dull and generic as the Multiplayer.
Overall, the game itself is worth full price just for the Campaign experience alone.

Prepare to run around for 45 minutes wondering why you need 100 rocks but you can't pick any up. There are trees and loose branches *everywhere,* but can you pick up any wood? Nope. It's probably for show. Wait, what if you- nope, you were murdered by some guy with an AK-47.
Okay, turns out you have a rock in your inventory and you can use it to smash trees/other rocks. Okay, weird, but whatever. Why does a sleeping bag need 3 marijuana plants and 100 pieces of wood? Who cares? In my experience, you won't spawn there anyway. (I had two. Ended up on the beach.) Now I have some wood and stone- I'm going to make a house (or I would, except I can only build a door.)
Wait, you need to make paper, then a blueprint from that, and *then* start building? And you need the blueprint to build? Okay, sure. Why do my walls have 5 health? I guess I should upgrade... the blueprint won't let me upgrade. *back to Google* Dangit, there's Mr. AK-47 again. Hello, starting from scratch. Nice to see you again.
Now I need to gather all that wood and stone again, plus another 100 wood to make a hammer. Sure, why not.
I'm also starving, but it's easier to just get killed and respawn with food in my belly than it is to find any animals at all, much less ones that a) can't outrun me, and b) won't kill me. Are these mushrooms poisonous? Doesn't matter, because you won't survive long enough for the poison to kill you. Oh great, NOW Mr. AK doesn't want to show up.
TL;DR: Takes some getting used to and DESPERATELY needs a single player mode. Instructions are non-existent. Animals, and thus food, are hard to find. Prepare to die. A lot. Don't hold your good stuff because you'll get murdered by some nudist with a big rock for your wood.

I made the decision to pick this game up and play it through today. I'm surprised to say that this game has undoubtedly made it's way into my memory forever.
Everything about this game is magical: the visuals, the story, the gameplay. Easily has slipped its way (in 6 hours of gameplay), to my top-favorites list.
The Visuals: Are you kidding me? The details, effects, and environment in this game are beautiful. I can't wait until I pick up my 4k monitor come Christmas time so I can play this through again in even more splendor.
The Story: It feels weird to say, but the story manages to be subtle and powerful at the same time. It feels distant, yet ever-so-close. I've never found myself getting attached to a set of characters so fast in a game.
The Gameplay: I played this with an Xbox One controller, so cannot speak on behalf of mouse & keyboard players for this one. The control schema is easy to understand and master. The game starts off a bit slow, and at first I worried it would be too simple. As I progressed, the challenges I faced became more difficult and margins of error narrowed. I was pleased to find myself groaning after dying for the 12th time in the same spot on several different occasions.
I've heard rumors of a sequel: best believe I'll be buying that day 1. I would recommend this to ANY gamer without a second guess. Do yourself a favor, take a break from your go-to-games (we all have em) and give this one a go.

I've been playing APB since original RTW Beta/EarlyAccess. It has remained one of my all time favorite games.
There are a number of issues with the game (repetitive at times, some hackers here and there, not a very friendly community) but in my opinion it still has a lot to offer when it comes to being a fun game.
For the most part, the game is F2P, but there is a marketplace (microtransactions) that allows purchasing of in-game guns and vehicles, clothing, etc. Though, please take to mind that this game is in no way Pay2Win. The guns/vehicles offered in the marketplace are mostly permanent/re-meshed(re-skinned) versions of the same weapons obtainable in-game. The one exception is the legendary reward from their Joker Mystery Boxes which offers a unique gun in both aesthetics and functionality, but the weapons are still not P2W and just offer a different play style.
If you find your place in the community, you can easily find yourself playing this game for years, I know I have. I've also spent hundreds of dollars on the marketplace (Buying many of the permanent versions of the weapons, but mostly "gambling" with the Joker Mystery Boxes for a chance at the legendary weapons.) It's also a lot of fun when you play with IRL friends, family or your girlfriend/fiancee/wife (as I do).
Overall, I'd rate this game a 4.7/5. It's not perfect, but it's a damn good game. If you ever find yourself on Joker (NA East), look me up if you'd like to chat or play around (Enforcer is Neonis, Criminals are Rozial and Sorley). I'm not the best (still Gold threat though ^-^;), but I can help out any new players with advice and guidance.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the sort of prequel to the other Arkham games, that of Rocksteady's Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. I have played both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City through my physical copies of the games. Arkham Origins is not developed by the folks at Rocksteady Studios instead it is developed by WB Games Montreal, and you can tell as a majority of the voice actors from the previous Arkham games are not featured in this one
The story basically shows Batman starting out his life of saving innocent people and combating crime in the city of Gotham, a city filled with crime, drugs, violence and corruption. The snowy city returns once again in the open world style that the previous game (Arkham City) offered and that is the problem that Arkham Origins has... its more of just the same game, only it tells a different story with the same characters and new ones
The graphics are very pretty and I played it at the right time of December as Arkham Origins takes place in the one night of Christmas Eve. I noticed that the game did stutter whilst it was saving and nearing the end of the game, in one of the boss battles, the frame rate did dip drastically, due to the amount of baddies there were
Apparently this game had a lot of techincal issues, which thankfully, by the time I bought it I experienced no technical issues, just the stutter and frame rate drop here and there
The gameplay mechanics are the same as the previous Arkham games, nothing to write home about. You have to bash the left mouse button as much as you can, then press the right mouse button to counter and press a few buttons here and there to counter attack, it gets pretty boring after a while. The thing to write home about, is the boss battles, and it is not something nice to write home about. The boss battles are... bad, on the level of Arkham Asylum's boss battle and worse, what on earth were they thinking... some boss battles you have to just press one button, whereas some other boss battles you have to do the same attack pattern over and over again...
The voice acting, although I did not really like Batman's voice actor (Roger Craig Smith) as opposed to Batman's voice actor (Kevin Conroy) in the previous Arkham games, however I did like Joker's voice actor (Troy Baker) but nobody beats Mark Hamill as the Joker
Overall, Arkham Origins is not a bad game but not as good as its predecessors. If I had the choice of paying 60.00EUR or the price I had to pay for it which was cheaper that what WB Games is squashing out of its consumers with its ridiculous full pricing options. I would pay the cheaper price, if I had to pay full price and with all the problems it had when it came out, then I would not have been satisfied...

Max Payne 2 is so far the best Max Payne in the series: It is technolocially more advanced than the first one and it doesn't take itself as seriously as the third one. For such a low low price, I can recommend it to anyone who enjoys 3rd person shooters with strong story.
The story of Max Payne 2 is nothing special: a detective who plays by his own rules and has nothing to lose has to undercover another conspiracy against him and the people of NYC.
Very serious stuff but what makes this story-line bearable compared to the 3rd ones whinetastic borefest is that everything around our main characters (enemies, tv-shows and other npcs) are not taking themselfs seriously.
for example: The tv-shows we see throughout the game are recapping the story in a extremely corny way and the enemies are bumbling doofuses.
The gameplay is somewhat showing its age: combat usually happens withing 10 meter radius.
This is partly because weapons have randomized spread but mostly because the maps are VERY small on todays standards (altough back in the PS2 era they were AMAZING).
The main positive of the randomized spread is that cutscenes are something pure comical gold (for example the scene where the police-chief Bravura gets shot multible times he sometimes won't get hit once but he still gets bullet-holes in his chest)
An addiditon to the absurdity of gun-fights is the early ragdoll-physics that cause bodies to fly all over the place (this is especially funny dring the "dramatic slowmo" scenes that pop up in specific parts of the game)
My advice?
Go to slowmo (or "bullet-time" as the game calls it) when enemies appear (preferably after they have spouted their funny dialoge), get within touching distance and start sircle strafing: nothing can survive that.
This migth be a cheap tactic but so is the game: enemies are way accurate than you and there is more of 'em.
Then again: you can heal yourself and use basic tactics against an enemy that mostly just runs at you.
Only negative that I can really point out is that when you do the John Woo style jump, Max will stand up immediately after releasing the shoot-button (no matter how amny enemies are aiming him down) and you can't fire during the stand-up animation but this can be countered by using basic tactics.
The guns that the game offers you are mostly pea-shooters but the game ie VERY generous with its ammo so it evens out in the end (exept the shotguns which all suck nards).
In conclusion: This game does show it's age but it is still a solid game experience with goor replayability.
It was good in 2003 and it still holds up in 2016.

So pros and cons
Pros -
-The gameplay mechanics are fantastic.
- The art is comic book style and even at the change of turns, its like the page flips to show more of the battle ensue.
- 16 hours of gameplay for $10 is top notch.
- There is a lot of strategy to the game.

Figure out how they play, READ THE ADVANCED OPTIONS FOR EACH CARD!!, and attack their weaknesses and you will win every single game. -I'm still not sayings its anywhere close to easy. Plan to be oblitherated for at least the first match.
Cons -
- Although I really like the gameplay mechanics, they may scare off players if they can't get through at least 2 fights.
- $50 for the expansions. (Though this may increase gameplay hours to the hundreds)
- Wish there was a bit more variety of villains and environments in the base game.
This one will depend on the player-

If the developers could figure out a way to increase the online community for this game, it would make it a lot better for the expansions, but if you and your friends want a new card game to try, buy the base game and play online with each other.
If you like card games where you must strategize, it's definitely worth a look.

I am well aware of the stigma that follows this game. In the beginning I was one of the many naysayers. However, after giving this game a shot I was very pleasantly surprised. It took some time. It wasn't until about a quarter to halfway through the story that this game, and its protagonist began to grow on me. This is not the Devil May Cry you grew up with. At all. And to some that's a  deal breaker. But shunning this game on preconceived notions of what the character looks or acts like is shortsighted. While the very eastern feel of the originals still clicks with me in a fun, sort of campy way, this game can  be taken more seriously from a narrative standpoint. And while the new Dante is somewhat abrasive at the beginning, this serves to show his characters transition by the end.
Obviously first and foremost this is a game, and many have valid concerns about a change in gameplay. The gameplay is different. It's more fluid. Some say it's easier, but ultimately it's just more playable. No clumsy D-Pad style changes or awkward random hits from enemies that simply flail unavoidable attacks. when you're hit you deserve it. It's not senselessly punshing. You don't feel cheated. It helps you learn and improve. The adjustments made to combat are very intuitive and easy to remember. And if you find the game too easy try some of the higher difficulties. There are PLENTY to choose from.
To summarize it, the gameplay is fluid and stylish as ever. Bright colors; terrific animations. Challenging but fair. The story is more fleshed out that any previous installments. As are the characters. If you give the game its fair chance, and go in with the understanding that while it's not the same, it is quality, you'll enjoy yourself. You'll be hard pressed to find many hack'n'slashes of this caliber, and I hope dearly that its lukewarm reception hasn't eliminated the chance for a sequel.

If you simply would like a recommendation as to whether or not you should buy this game... then yes, go ahead. Now.
If you enjoy beautifully realised platform games then you won't be disappointed. It's a truly fantastic game that delights on so many levels. So much so that this quickly became one of my favourite games of all time; quite an achievement considering the number of games I've played over the last three and a half decades. I originally purchased the game on Xbox One - the 'regular' version of the game - and played through that many times. I then purchased the 'Definitive Version', on Xbox One, and played through several times yet again. The additional areas / content and tweaks were certainly worth the additional cost. However, as PC is where my greater passion for gaming lies, I just had to buy Ori and the Blind Forest yet again - hence the decision to purchase via Steam. I now sit here having played through the game yet again and I honestly enjoyed it as much as the first play-through.
Simply put, it's a beautiful game. In an age where gaming systems are capable of rendering impressive imagery, Ori and the Blind Forest still manages to be a real stand-out title. The artwork and animation is a real credit to the art team; from the stunning backdrops against which the action takes place to the incedible animation that adds such life and character to Ori. It's a pleasure to see and the changing colour palettes and aesthetics suit the various areas of the game world perfectly.
Of course, a game needs to play well if it is to be successful and I feel that the developers nailed the game mechanics pretty much perfectly. The way in which Ori leaps and navigates the levels is nicely pitched. It's easy to establish a solid feeling of control and, as the power-ups start to accumulate, you soon find yourself traversing areas almost effortlesssly. Of course, there may be puzzles and creatures to defeat along the way but the level of control over Ori is just right. Even  the trickier sections of the game (that may initially feel impossible to many!) can soon be overcome with a little patience and perseverence. And, believe me, it's worth the effort so as to be able to enjoy the game to its fullest.
It's not really possible to review this game without highlighting the emotional response that the game can impart on the player. To quote modern lingo, it can get you right in the "feels" (I think that's the right word). I won't disclose the story here but it is a story that may well bring a smile, possibly bittersweet, and maybe a lump to the throat, too. The music helps set the scene and feeling for the story wonderfully.
In fact, the soundtrack for the game is incredible. Coker has produced a musical masterpiece that is equally as captivating as the game itself. The way the music tantalisingly compliments the storytelling and the way in which it drives the player through the game is absolute perfection.
I can't wait for Ori and the Will of the Wisps!

Amazing. How best to sell cognitive dissonance than by making me reject the plotline. They made a violent action game anti-violence. They brought color, life and depth to a theme you never wanted to see it in. This is a mature game by all standards, and a must-play for anybody who thinks games are childish. It does help to know a bit about what you're getting into - I would remind you that when your UserName appears in the opening credits, they mean it - you're playing an active part in the world as any character in the game. This game may not get a sequel, but all action games could learn so many things from how to tell a linear story.
Apart from that, enjoy a challenging cover shooter experience. Expertly handled squad and enemy AI versus amazing character animation and handling, and an amazing weapon toolset with some of the best level design in the business. The helicopter scene, as well as some tricky situation battles, require a LOT of patience. Stick with it, watch some videos, and don't get discouraged by the beautiful but hacky opening - it's not a generic war shooter game.

I won this game in a giveaway and was excited to try it out because I've always loved isometric action RPGs (aRPGs). I was satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like isometric aRPGs, exploring a lore- and loot-heavy world, and fantasy elements, then you will enjoy this game. It reminded me a lot of the Diablo franchise (1 and 2), 2 being the game that I still have played for the longest in my entire life (2 entire summers).
The aesthetics are good - the amount of detail in the massive game world is very nice. The different effects for spells and skills is numerous enough to keep things interesting. Extra lore is provided in the form of readable text like books and pages, adding to the well-written story. I liked that the characters in the selection screen actually speak out their bios (and that they were actually different for each hero, even though they were simple male/female variants of the mage, warrior, and rogue/survivor). The music and sounds are good, adding to the fantasy atmosphere.
Controls are easy to familiarize yourself with, but may take some time if you are not experienced with aRPGs. There is no tutorial, so a new player's start may progress slowly at first. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your familiarity with aRPGs - because the skill tree allows you to select from all three heroes' routes, it is possible to roll/develop a character that is horribly underlevelled/underpowered. I strongly recommend you save often, and in multiple slots.
Gameplay consists of you moving around the game world, with attacks hotkeyed to your left- and right-mouse click. For example, I can have a weapon (dagger) assigned to my left-click and a spell (fireball) assigned to my right-click when using my mage. Before you begin your game, you will be able to select a character from 6 options - male or female mage, warrior, or rogue. You cannot customize how they look, but you can change the character portrait. Each character starts with different stats (ex: warrior is combat oriented and has more health than the other heroes), however, you have access to the entire skill network, so it is possible to select abilities from the mage and rogue trees when you level up and are playing a warrior. This allows you to experiment with different character combinations to suit your playstyle. The heroes also have different special attacks (ex: mage can teleport a short distance). When you level up, you can also allocate skill points to your base stats like constitution and strength.
The game world is fairly expansive, and there are plenty of opportunities to explore hidden areas and dungeons if you are thorough enough. These extra locations are great for farming levels and loot, however, be sure to bring a lot of potions. There is a minimap that you can toggle to help with navigation.
Combat is typical of your standard aRPG - spam your attacks and spells/abilities until your opponents are dead. Enemies will sometimes drop loot like gold and weapons. Feedback is given whenever you hit or are hit, indicating how much damage is traded; experience gain is also shown.
Overall, the game is a very good aRPG, and anyone interested in the genre should definitely give it a try.
Recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

I bought the original game when it came out - got about 2/3 of the way through it.
I bought the definitive edition on sale and played it to completion.
Total playing time (both games)  32 hours...
...but I don't think it is a particularly good game.
Pros and cons first:
*Played on 'Normal' difficulty*
Pros
====
Cons
====

Discussion
========
Ori and the Blind Forest is a game about getting insta-killed on spikes and other scenery.  The game has a "health bar" system where you have a number of health orbs (can be increased with colletibles) and can therefore take a number of hits... except you can't.  If you fall among spikes then you will either be insta-killed or you will be killed two seconds later when the health orbs are gone.  Enemies can often take off three or four health orbs which means you're either dead on the first hit or compromised to the point that you go back to the last save.  Might as well have made everything insta-kill and got rid of a pointless mechanic.
The save system is also annoying.  You have energy orbs (can carry more with collectibles) so you can only save if you have at least one orb.  BUT!  You can also only save in certain places and under certain conditions.  With the latter limitations to saving WHY BOTHER WITH ORBS??  Like the health orbs, it seems to be a mechanic that was just added for the sake of it.
There are some nice puzzle elements to the game but there is also a "progression" mechanic where many places aren't accessible until Ori has developed a certain skill.  Unfortunately there is no hint to this when exploring areas and I found myself wasting a few minutes over and over again trying to get to something that looked like it
be accessible (sloppy controls - maybe it takes 10 tries to actually achieve a very difficult jump) only to find later that I needed a certain skill.  Over the course of the game those minutes add up and it felt like wasted time rather than fun time.
The game looks and sounds beautiful and whilst the game is fairly difficult on "normal" setting, the main difficulty comes from the sloppiness in Ori's response to the controls.  Added to this is the fact that many sequences will involve dealing with enemies and enemy projectiles at the same time as navigating the obstacles.  These combined mean that many sequences will need to be played dozens of times before success.  This would be OK but with the controls and the semi-randomness of when an enemy fires a projectile - and sometimes you will need to use those projectiles to jump further - the result was more annoying for me than challenging.  The repetition increases the length of the game but doesn't necessarily make the extra time enjoyable.  I only completed the game so that I had closure on it.
I know this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews.  In many ways it is a masterclass in presentation but I found the gameplay was far more irritating than it was rewarding.  For me this game wasn't enjoyable enough to recommend.

One of the best card game I ever played. This is not a deck-building card game, it's a board game for 1 to 5 players that get transferred as a PC game. There is also the tablet ann phone version.
Basically, you play a team of Super-Heros 3 to 5 and go against a Villain in a specific environment until the heroes get incapacitated or that you manage to do the winning conditions. Every turns, the villain play, then the heroes and at last is the environment.
Each hero in the game has its own deck, depending on the kind of hero you play, some have differents power, others are war machine that uses differents equipment. Every hero has it,s own unique playstyle. The cards you draw lead the way on how you react or the attribute you can use with that hero. Very detailed and well-balanced deck with a lot of work on it. There is 3 phase to the hero turns. First, the hero plays a card from the cards in hand. Then there is the power phase, where the hero can use a power or an equipment. Then the hero draws a card. Sometimes there is some specific rules that can change the order or the number of cards a hero can play in a turn, the number of power a hero can use in a turn and also the number f cards a hero can draw in a turn.
On the other end, the villain you face also have its own unique deck depending on the villain you face. Some have different winning conditions, they all have their unique abilities and use differents powers, equipment, devices or even henchmen or creatures to fight against the heroes. The villain deck is shuffled at the start and every turn unless there are some special rules for that specific villain, a card is played from the villain deck and act as the villain action for this turn. Depending on the villain cards, there may be some other events that happen or special rules that may vary the gameplay.
There is also another variable to take into consideration, where the heroes fight the villain. This is determined by an environment deck. Every environment has it's own deck of 15 cards. Usually, 1 environment card is played from the environment deck per turn unless there is some special rules or events. Some environment is nasty and have creatures fighting the heroes and also the villain. There is also some event that can happen, as for example, a volcano erupts and deals damage to everyone or some paparazzi on the scene that forbid the heroes to use their power for a turn.
This game is really awesome, if you like strategy and cards game, this is a unique game with so much to offer. The community isn't huge, but this is a small community of people who really like this game. You can find the online game most evening from American Time zone. Usually, this is when there are the most players online.

For example, when a large group of targets needs to be damaged/healed, it will ask for every instance, unless it is affecting all instances.  A precise example is one of the cards for the Argent Adept. It states 5 targets gain 1 hp. In this case you need to individually choose each target, whereas in the card game you can easliy just call it out and each person manages their own targets.  Small gripe, but it bothered me at first.
This is only managed this way to have complete control over anything that happens in the game. This stiffness can easliy be overlooked due to how well this adaptation handles how the game is governed. We actually use most of the unusual rulings of the physical game as the video game would handle it.
Finally I would say that my favorite part about this game is how easy it is to play by yourself. It is very difficult to annoying to manage everything that each match has going on in card form. However, this is all handled by the game automatically making the only thing required to do is make the decisions of the heroes.
If you are a fan of the original card game or are unfamilar with this franchise as a whole, I would recommend at least trying this game out.

After finally finishing this gem of a game I can only but recommend this game to any RPG lover out there. Beneath the now dated graphics lies a sound game with a complex world, rich lore and funny little gameplay gimmicks that made me smile a lot.
The good:
- Rich lore, decent story (if a bit cliché by now)
- Plenty of content (Took me appr. 70 hours to finish)
- Pretty extensive and flexible RPG elements (create whatever character you like as you go)
- Easy to get into, but challenges along the way
- Lot's of little tricks and secrets hidden in the world
The bad:
- A couple of the dungeons look mostly the same
- Some rare and random game crashes
- No tutorial in the beginning (some actions in the game could use explanation)
- Addicitive
- Rare side-quest breaking bugs (hint: keep a walkthrough at hand)
Divine Divinity is a RPG that is focussed around hack-and-slashing and that is something you do a lot.
The world is littered with all kinds of different enemies and dungeons and all have something special. That is mostly because of the lore and quests that even challenges you in small ways you could easily miss. For example: there are many books to find and read, some of them contain hints for quests and how to complete them.
In roleplaying terms the modern gamer will find various ways to develop his or her character. The game starts with the choice of three classes: Warrior (Fighter), Survivor (Rogue) and Mage (Wizard). But don't worry, once the game is underway, all skills are available for the choosing so you can create any character you wish. For example, I created a powerful mage with great bow skills because I like to keep my distance in combat.
In terms of loot and interactivity in the world this game surprised me. Pretty much every object that is not stuck to something can be picked up or interacted with. Haven't got lockpicks with you? Just drag the closed container to your inventory and open it later. Found a closed door you can't pick? There could be a switch hidden behind some stacked boxes. Looking for a hidden dungeon? Try under some barrels. Are you out of potions? Use your alchemy skills to create a potion from a plant, etc, etc. There is also plenty of loot. There are the usual magical weapons and armor, but also item-upgrade runes, may different potions, spellbooks, and countless miscellaneous items.
The game's difficulty level was okay. If you stick to the story, especially in the beginning, you get balanced combat situations and will have plenty of opportunity to find your own style. Enemies don't scale with your level, but have fixed levels and are found in fixed places in the world. If you stray from the path as a level 10 character, get ready to be insta-killed. But don't worry, as you develop your character you get to kick more and more♥♥♥♥♥
Note: most of the game you are a lone wolf. The only companions you get are the ones you magicaly spawn yourself. In many a situation I found that some tactical thinking is required to get through combat as a wave of 10 or more enemies at once is not that rare.
Lastly I would like to mention the technical aspects of this game. What surprised me is that I was able to play this game instantly after installing it. Older games often have trouble on a powerful 64bit machine.
I found the graphics to be charming and 'oldschool' and the sound decent for it's age. I also liked the voicework that was both fitting and refreshing at times (you have to read a lot).
I only had a few crashes but when you save often that is only a minor problem.
Warning: this game requires manual saving! No automatic checkpoint system that holds your hand as you play!
I hope you found this review helpful. Have fun with this awesome game!

This game is hands down, the best RPG I have ever played. When I saw the trailers I thought it looked terrible: abysmal voice acting, dated graphics, reviews had told me it was buggy as hell, and I didn't like the top down aspect of the game. But I still bought it, and I'm so glad I did.
The quests are interesting and fun, even the fetch quests feel like an adventure. The fighting style and skills system is ingenius, any class can have any skills and stats, and this means that as well as being able to fully customise your abilities, that you get a choice between generic hack and slash or more tactical spell casting. The game world is large and incredibly immersive, every decision feels like it matters. The plot is fairly generic, but it still feels like an epic journey, and you actually get to feel for the characters, despite the fact that they sound almost entirely uninterested in anything that's happening, (The voice acting really is terrible). This game feels like it should be one of the worst in gaming history, but it truly gives you the feeling that all other RPG's are aiming for.
