This game is *amazing*.  Every hero plays different, and plays as you'd expect them to.  The Batman-esque hero pulls gadgets out of her utility belt and has one for nearly any situation.  The Superman/Captain America hero leads from the front, inspiring people and taking hits for them.  The Punisher just blasts people with guns.
The *villains* all fight differently.  From the mad scientist trying to smash the moon into the earth to the creepy,  but innocent little girl who can't help that her nightmares become real and attack people, to the drugged-up serial killer who eventually overdoses when the heroes track him down and brawls with them for the remainder of the game, none of them (or at least, very few of them) are just big buckets of hitpoints for the heroes to whittle down.
It perfectly captures the feel of a comic book crossover, and even features fun variant intro quotes when heroes fight their "nemeses."  And the lore is actually pretty good, if you get into it, though I do wish the game had a bit more of the information availible on online wikis.
And, as a video game adaptation, it works very well.  The art and dialogue are all crisp and clean, the card art is usually big enough to read without sacrificing the fun flavor text and art that help bring the title to life, and the controls are generally intuitive and easy to use.  It even offers unique, non-microtransaction-based means of unlocking "variants" for the heroes.  Plus, many people have commented that having a computer to do all the math and run all the mechanics for them allows them to better-understand the paper game!
Also, the devs support the game fairly frequently, and allow people who don't care about achievements to just unlock the variant cards that are just unfairly difficult to acquire.
I only have three major words of warning, and one criticism, for potential customers to heed.
First, the game is rather chopped-up, with a lot of content partitioned off into DLC.  If you're going to buy the title, you might want to wait for a sale on the season pass to get ahold of it.  Second, the game is a fixed-deck experience, not a trading card one.  If you want the same kind of customizability or Skinner-box hits as those kinds of games, this one will not provide.  Third, this is almost-completely an adaptation of the card game, with little attempt made to "video-game" it out with story modes and things.  (Which, though I'd love a story mode, is just as well.  The game is already pretty "narrative" via its mechanics.)
And, as a critique, it is, thus far, *incomplete*.  But, since the devs are a smaller team and programming Sky-Scraper, Setback, the alternate fight system from Vengeance would all be difficult, I get why.
This is a superb adaptation of a superb game, and I cannot recommend it enough.

DMC: Devil May Cry is an action hack and slash. It introduces a young Dante, whom some of you may know from previous iterations of the game, with a solid background story.
The protagonist is Dante, son of Sparda - a Nephilim born of angel and demon. Through a rough upbringing, Dante is arrogant and narcissistic. This is quickly apparent from the opening scene of the game.
The story is quite well written, albeit there are a fair amount of admittedly unavoidable cliche moments. A strong connection is built between characters and the protagonist is interested and terrifying.
While the story is solid, the game mechanics force players into focusing more on combat and therefore skill level rather than the story going on around them. While combat is an extremely important part of this game genre - it should not subtract from story elements by forcing the player to fight as efficiently and quickly as possible in order to maintain a higher skill rating. This is due to the game having a time based skill rating modifier. While you can of course replay through the levels to achieve a high skill rating, no one aims for “average” the first time around.
Combat in this game is extremely fun and rewarding. Combat is extremely fluid, with the player linking combo after combo. I thought that targeting may have been an issue when fighting large groups of enemies or singling out flying enemies from ground enemies but I can honestly say I never really had an issue. Now and then I’d grapple the wrong enemy, but it wasn’t frequent enough to cause any real issue. Personally I found some of the gunplay lacking and underpowered but it did serve excellent purpose when it came to making an enemy flinch or by eroding health from a safe distance.
Abilities and weaponry in DMC feel extremely rewarding. By this I mean that the earlier combos, while fun, have absolutely nothing on the more complex and devastating combos unlocked later on. Running through crowds of enemies with incredible juggles and AoE attack was extremely enjoyable - and somehow the developers were able to maintain this joy with more pronounced combos for Boss fight scenarios. Usually a character has either strong single target attacks or strong AoE, in DMC I felt as if these attack damages were purely based on skill.
There are some issues later on with certain combo inputs, particularly ones with more than one button press at the same time. Input seemed delayed and the user has to time it much too specifically than what the developer was aiming for.
The broad array of weapons only serves to keep combat fresh and entertaining. The balancing in great on each weapon, with each serving a different purpose. I never found myself using one weapon too much more than another. That being said, ranged attacks did feel a little bit weak in comparison.
If you are a fan of action and fast-paced hack and slashes, this game is for you. If you are a returning DMC fan, don’t expect this to be like the previous iterations of the series. While it shares some similarity with combat and other core mechanics / characters - it feels alien. This is why I feel as if returning players should attribute this game to a new branch of the series or avoid it if you are unable to do so.
For those who do buy it, you can expect your money’s worth. I enjoyed the story and loved the combat and movement abilities. It took up a great money to gameplay ratio and continued to keep the combat refreshing as Dante learned new abilities and unlocked new weapons.

I've played every DMC game and was kind of skeptical playing this one, especially considering the level or rebootification the series has gone through. Ninja Theory makes some great games, and this is no exception.
The combat is fun, though simpler than some of the previous entries. The level design is colorful, loud and enjoyable to explore. There is a lot of replay value, especially in trying to find all the secret keys/missions. The music is perfect for the aesthetic, and the world is about as believable and consistent as a DMC game can be.
Some people will criticize this game for the new Dante, the "mature teen" storyline and sometimes childish dialogue, but given that DMC has never been a truly serious game, I can't fault it at all. I hope there's a sequel in this style, bridging the stylistic differences between the last two games.

Max Payne 2 continues the same formula of its predecessor. That is, heavy focus on storytelling, dark/adult themes and of course action packed gameplay. Sadly, it does not reach the success of MP1.
The story just as expected is about crime, mafia infiltration, vengeance, violence and guild. In my opinion, the storytelling of MP2 feels a bit forced and overall just shallow compared to that of MP1. Maybe that is because MP1's story was so much richer with more characters, while MP2 focuses mainly on Max Payne character's inner struggle. Another thing I disliked is the addition of the love story of MP with a female character from the first game. It basically becomes the main theme of the game and I think that was unnecessary. At least it provides some enjoyable parts of gameplay in the later stages of the game, as you have to control both of the characters at some point which was maybe the highlight of the game.
No big additions were made on the gameplay and the mechanics of the game. A couple more guns and some fancy slow motion maneuver and that is all. I was hoping they had fixed the trial and error aspect of the previous game but it’s still there. This is the biggest drawback of the Max Payne series in my opinion. You basically are forced to abuse the save/load option in order to stand a chance, as it is impossible to complete the game without mapping out all your opponents.
The overall sound and graphics are an improvement from MP1 and especially the music. The soundtrack is a killer. Also, the game feels more polished and detailed.
All in all while MP2 does a decent job you really have to be an old school player to enjoy this one. It is brutally unforgiving punishing your every mistake. I am sure the newer generations of players would probably brake their monitor out of frustration playing the Max Payne series.
To be fair however, MP2 was released in 2003 and was quite ahead of its time. Even now I would rate it as a good action shooter with a unique story presentation.

Let's start with why I bought Spec Ops; The Line in the first place. Well, it was for the story, because it was the only thing I heard about this game- "Story! Story! Story!". So I had to try this game out. And after completing it I can say that there is two major assets this game is made out of- story and gameplay. But the problem is that one those assets is compelling, interesting and sometimes breathtaking, while the other sucks major dic*. I can first talk about the good part.
The story of this game is about a group of three soldiers that are sent to half-destroyed Dubaii as a rescue mission. Their mission is to save civillians and find out what shady business is taking place in the sandy ruins of Dubaii. And then everything spuns out of control. First there is only the physical conflict that drives Spec Ops, but then you understand that the main conflict is actually mental, but nearly everything about it is a spoiler. And it is that mental conflict that makes everyone love this game's story, because the physical conflict is the thing that always gets in the way of the "real" conflict. And that leads into the pinnacle of all the physical conflicts in this game- gameplay. And oh boy, the gameplay surely is something in this game.
Boring, repetitive, frustrating. You can choose any of those words- all of them are perfect in describing the gameplay of Spec Ops: The Line. I personally played the game on what the game presents as "Normal" difficulty, but it felt like I was playing on at least "Hard". I alway felt like I was pushed into a corner and had to peak and kill enemies one by one. And it always and I mean ALWAYS felt repetitive to be in all firefights. Every area felt the same, only some of the Areas had more holes that enemies could crawl out of than the others. The thing that bothered me the most about Spec Ops was the cover system- it was bad. I mean really bad. I played with controller because I thought that if it was originally made for controllers then it would not be that bad. But it was. You use A/X to go into cover, the same button you use to run(btw- If you press A/X while walking you will start running and the only way to make your character walk again is to stop completely and then start walking again, which was frustrating, escpacially in firefights). The cover system itself is close to non-existant. You have no quick button that you can press to move to the next cover- you have to do it all manually, which can get really hard when there are enemies shooting at you from all the sides. To go behind a 90 degree corner while in cover is also imposible without getting out of cover and moving behind the cover manually. At least in some areas you could change side of the cover by pressing A/X, but I used that option only a couple of time throughout the whole game, because there were so little sposts where you could perform that action. The last thing I want to say before wrapping up is the granades from enemies- they always make you run out of your cover, but there is not always a place to run to, especially while having the bad coversystem I talked about earlier. There are probably more problems with the gameplay of Spec Ops, but I think I covered the things I hated most about it.
To wrap it up I want to say that you should probably check out Spec Ops: The Line. Yes, there is the bad gameplay, but at the end you get a great story with, by the way, multiple endings. So I think it will be worth your trouble. Enjoy the game!

I think Spec Ops is a very special case for a game.  It's a fantastic game, but it's also a pretty typical game for the gameplay.  However the story of Spec Ops is the make or break point.  If you watch all the cutscenes, and really think about the game, you'll get a fantastic and interesting narrative that is quite unique.
The first time I played the game I thought the game was good, the second time I played through it, I was like "yeah this is way better now."  Then I played it a third time and I was blow away yet again by how brilliant the story is.
But at the same time, I feel like a LOT of people oversell the story, or get the wrong message, or read too far into it.  This isn't Citizen Kane, and while it's based on the Heart of Darkness, it's not Apocalypse Now.  It's a average shooter, with a great story for a video game, and that last part is key.   It's not a exceptional story, but it's a pretty damn good story for modern shooters.
It's a shame, because with a few more tweaks, with a little more summery at the end, the game could have been really exceptional. but it's story lacks that full impact it seems to think it has.
The other downside is that in my opinion the game really only kicks into gear in the second half of the game, and that's a real shame too because the story is what is driving the game.  If you play 5 levels and think it's mostly an average shooter, you'd be right.
Hell if you play 14 levels and think it's an average shooter, you're mostly right, and that's the game's downfall.  It's a game where someone has to tell you "You need to play this all the way through."  and if you do that, it's really great.   But the beginning is definitely lacking something.
But still.  "You need to play this all the way through."

DmC was a game that had a whole lot of attention around it when it first came out... as well as a whole lot of hate and hurt feelings. After all, this was the next in a series of (mostly) great action games put out by Capcom, games known for their hype stylish combat, likable, over the top characters, and visceral difficulty, and yet the new developers Ninja Theory were changing things up a bit, with a complete make over of the characters, looks and personality-wise. Some people didn't mind the change. Others were... much less accepting, to say the least. So the game was released to some vitriol, with major fans of the previous games vowing never to sully themselves by even glancing at it. But does DmC deserve the scorn it got from the more rabid fans?
Honestly... no. DmC is actually a pretty fun and well done action game, one of the better ones I've played. It has just about everything you'd want; tight controls, fun moves to perform, crazy combos to pull off, fun (if somewhat cliche) characters, fantastic graphics, and a decent enough story. As a fan of the past Devil May Cry games (the 3rd being my personal favorite), I enjoyed it... as long as I pretended that it has just about nothing to do with the others. Frankly, it kind of doesn't anyway.
DmC is basically a re-imagining of the Devil May Cry series and its characters, and it does this in a big way. The main protagonist, Dante, is no longer sporting the neck length white hair he used to, nor does he seem as devil may care (though that part of his personality is still there). Now he looks more like a 90's grunge rocker, with short black hair, and more rumpled clothing (though he still has a long, red, overcoat). He also seems to act more like a "magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" than a wisea$$ in this game, though the wisea$$ antics still come out at times. This change was pretty much the focus of the rage people had with the game, but to be fair, when one looks at the story and the world this game has, it works. The old Dante would not have fit into this darker, more cynical world that Ninja Theory crafted, and the game would have suffered for it. Basically, the story is a retelling and renewed origin story for Dante and his twin brother Vergil, and their place in the world they happen to inhabit; it's a somewhat darker, more cynical tale, with some rather sharp commentary on current American society (complete with a Pat O'Reilly stand in), but told with some the over the top camp that one tends to see in a decent late night b movie on HBO. There is still a lot of the zany antics and insane moments that one comes to expect from the Devil May Cry series (complete with Dante just going along with the demon invasions and high level property damage like it's just another day in the park for him, as well as the casual way he jumps around and dodges damage in cut scenes), just done with a different style than some might be used to.
Let's get into why the game is good: the gameplay itself, and the presentation. Ninja Theory has proven before that they know how to do action, and this game continues that tend. They pretty much streamlined the combat from past games, and it works VERY well here. The controls are tight and responsive, with all your attacks ready to go at a moments notice. You basically have up to 5 different weapons ready to go during combat (your sword, your guns, a quick "angelic" weapon, a heavy "demonic" weapon, and a grapple hook type tool that can either pull enemies towards you, or you to them), and you can switch between them while wreaking havoc on the demonic abominations in your way. You can combine attacks pretty much any way you want, so combos are pretty much limited to your imagination. The better your combos, the more points you get to level up your weapons and attacks, as well as giving you the ability to buy new ones to use. You also find new weapons to use along the way that can also be leveled up with new attacks, so you'll always have a large variety of techniques at your disposal.
All this is wrapped in a rather pretty package: the graphics are well done, with vibrant colors and well imagined designs. Honestly, I think some of the designs here are better than things I've seen in the older games (such as Dante's sword and pistols... I really do think they look better than the old ones). The limbo that Dante gets pulled in is always very interesting to look at, with some rather wild looking locals that show a level of imagination I don't really see in a lot of AAA titles... that, and the fact that vibrant colors were used in the first place.
The story itself was decent, though somewhat cliche... we've pretty much seen this tale told before (the world and humans are secretly being ruled by hidden masters, the hero is a special "half-breed" destined to overthrow the evil masters, but has to come to grips with who he is). It's told competently enough however, so I have no real complaints... other than one pet peeve I have about what what Dante and Vergil are supposed to be. In this game, they are half angel, half demon, and are called nephalim. That was really the only thing in the game that made me grind my teeth, since that's NOT what a nephalim is. A nephalim is actually the offspring of an angel and a HUMAN, not an angel and a demon, Yes, I know, a minor thing, but it still annoyed the hell out of me. If you're going to use old mythic terms, Ninja Theory, do it right!
Overall, I found DmC to be very enjoyable, and I'm glad I picked it up when I did. The gameplay is tight, the action is great, the graphics are pretty damn good, and the story, while not completely original, is still pretty entertaining, and even funny at times. The Dante in this game may not be the Dante of old, but as long as you come to terms with that and take him for what he is in this game (or just pretend he's someone else altogether, just some other dude with the same name), you'll find this game is certainly worth your time. Definitely recommended.

So, I have to say I was worried about this one based on the initial reaction when "hipster Dante" was unveiled, and a couple early play-throughs attacked the campy tone. If those are your concerns, don't worry about it.
I can't say "hipster Dante" was much of an issue for me in terms of enjoying the game goes, and the campiness was pitch-perfect for a game about a half-demon, half-angel who takes on an "immortal" demon that killed his mother and imprisoned his father. Seriously, if people were expecting fine literature, they were the problem, not the game. There were a few times where I got annoyed with the camera, and I can't say the color-coded enemies were my thing, but overall it was well worth my discounted summer-sale money. It's not $50 of game in my opinion, and I'm not going to stay up pondering the story, or what it all means, but with 10+ hours of gameplay, and the main storyline completed, I can actually see myself coming back and playing at higher difficulties just for kicks, and I haven't done that since DMC1. So that's saying something.
Buy it on sale, and just embrace it for what it is—a silly romp through a "hellish" city, driven by a wisecracking lead with a heart of gold, and a tendancy to be vulgar.

I'm not sure why I didn't get my hands on this game until now. And I probably wouldn't have played it still for years to come if I hadn't received it as a gift from a dear friend of mine. The best way to describe Divine Divinity is that it's a mix between Baldur's Gate, Diablo and Skyrim. Chances are that you'll love this game if you've played any of them, or better yet, all of them. However, one thing that you should know before diving into this game, is that it's pretty hard and requires quite a bit of dedication and perseverance. There will definitely be moments when you might want to give up and ragequit but try to hang in there and give it a chance because otherwise you'll miss out on a fantastic RPG experience.
You can play as either a male or a female human and there are three classes - survivor, warrior and wizard - that you can choose from. Depending on which gender you pick, you receive certain starting attribute bonuses, for example, the male character has more strength and the female character is more agile.
At the beginning of the game, your character wakes up in the cellar of a house in the small town called Aleroth that's home to several healers. Before long, s/he finds out that the leader of the healers has gone insane and s/he is, as might be expected, asked to find a solution to this problem. The story begins to unfold from there.
- Divine Divinity has definitely aged well, although I believe that the art style that's been used in the game is pretty much ageless anyway. Furthermore, various patches have enabled DD to be played in widescreen and higher resolutions. The textures are crisp and spell effects still look pretty damn cool. All in all, as far as graphics go, I believe that DD could easily measure up to any point & click action RPG that's been released in recent years.
- The soundtrack fits the eerie atmosphere of the game down to a tee.
- The storyline is gripping and cohesive. It sure kept me glued to my screen for several hours at a time!
- Odd, yet welcome, comical bits that pop up here and there. When I first encountered one of these random humorous encounters I felt slightly confused because up to that point I'd been under the impression that the game was very dark and serious. As I progressed through the game and started seeing these goofy bits more often I just got used to it and dealt with it, so to speak.
- Lots and lots of sidequests. Some of them are pretty straightforward, others require you to do a bit of thinking, solve some puzzles or do a bit of research.
- Familiar fantasy setting with various races like elves, dwarves, orcs, etc., that makes it easy for any RPG fan to immerse themselves in the world and maybe even grow to care about the characters that they meet.
- Although the game has three classes to choose from, you can learn almost any skill that you want. For example, if you've picked the wizard class because you love to use magic but you really want to use a bow as your main weapon, then you can totally do that!
- Overdramatic and cringeworthy voice acting.
- Some very difficult boss fights that might seem impossible to win if you haven't levelled your character properly.
- The font becomes very small with bigger resolutions and it's hard to read books, manuscripts, etc., unless you're sitting very close to the screen. To fix this, download a font enlargement patch.
- The interface isn't very player friendly and it's quite awkward to use until you grow used to it. I think that it could have probably been handled a bit better. You can only map spells/skills/potions to the F-keys which means that you've only got 12 keys for all the stuff that you wish to map, and it isn't exactly natural to press those instead of the usual 1 to 0 buttons.
- There's no button to make your character stand and attack on the spot during combat, so if you prefer to use ranged attacks and you misclick, then you can accidentally run into a horde of enemies and get yourself killed.
In conclusion I'd say that if you're an RPG fan who hasn't played Divine Divinity yet, you should definitely give this game a go. Perseverance will be rewarded!

Great game. Got this from bundle sale for about 5€, and consider my self lucky for getting it for that price. (4 game bundle @ 90% discount being actually cheaper then the game itself (that also was in sale for about 7€..)
Would have bought ages ago, if I knew it's this deep and addicting. I remember I considered buying this on the dev stage, I have a recollection that when I first saw this, it was on a stage where if you bought it then, you could have your own name to the game as one of the prisoners, and now thinking back I really wish I had bought that back then.
There are many ways to go in the game. You can take in low-sec prisoners only, make them work and keep them happy, try to rehibilate them, or maybe go just the other way and rule with armed guards, tiny cells, tought punishment, with an iron fist, and get lots of money from max security prisoners (-who in turn are violent, and if you don't handle security right things can get out of hand very quickly).
Or anywhere in between.
Game seems to be also very well balanced, if you penalize the prisoners, they aren't happy and might turn more violent - then again if you don't, then you get minus poins for letting them off too easy. So it's very much balancing things out, and there is a learning curve to get the hang of it.
For example, when you get a bit more things unlocked while you play, you can later use things like CCTV, logic gates, logic bridges, door automation and timers, gather intel with phone taps, use metal detectors around your prison if you can afford it, hire K9 guards to sniff out drugs and contraband, train guards to use tazers and whatnot.
With logic gates you can do pretty much anything, like build a doorway with three doors for example, from which only one can be open at a time. Or maybe build one-way-only corridor with similar multiple door setup using logic gates (OR, NOR, NOT, AND, NAND, XOR, =).
I'd imagine that the replayability value is good also, you might not play this every day, but rather like a civ game where you can come in anytime after months of break, and spend long hours again, just enjoying the game.
I would want to try and describe this more - don't know if I would get it for ~30€, but definitely grab it if you see it on 50% sale or cheaper.
Have to warn though that if you get into this, you might find your self spending countless hours perfecting your vision of the perfect prison - maybe only to see it getting destroyed by some factor that you overlooked - or maybe not.
Tutorial is awesome, as it's build in as a story with progressing chapters where you have to manage different prison scenarios (riots, fire etc..)
There are also variables you can pick when you start building your prison, like weather changes, different warden type bonuses, which are all a nice addition to the game.
Definitely did not expect this much all though have thought many times before getting this, but always would up buying something else. Glad I got this one finally, was very positively suprised.
Props for the designers and programmers for this one. (y)

Syberia is better.
- mostly okay but some puzzles are fairly dumb. For example, use "object that reacts to light" on *that very specific*, extremely generic lamp for a clue that the kidnapped professor left because he knew his daughter would be looking at this extremely generic lamp with this special contraption; or give *that very specific* paper to the mute person in order to communicate, but none of the other papers around. Or, get the keycode from your diary which has a unique screenshot of a taped scene – instead of getting it from the tape / in-game monitor itself: which feels unintuitive and makes no sense whatsoever.
- dumb puzzles like these are the reason why you're using brute-force combinations of items and objects in the end.
- the "show interactive objects in this room" feature (that was made to get rid of "pixelhunting") felt like cheating at first, but in hindsight, I like it. It's super optional and you don't get penalized for using it. If the feature hadn't been there, I would have spent more time with the game, though with frustration rather than enjoyment.
- I played it in English (I guess I shouldn't have) and not a single voice actor was able to correctly pronounce the French name Nicole Charlesroi. Ugh. An effort like this would take less than 5 minute, but no, they didn't feel like it was worth it.
- cringe-worthy dialog and – which is why I don't think it's a translation issue – reasoning. The plot isn't that sound (or interesting) either.
- some of the animations are a bit too stiff for my taste.
- the "rooms" look alright and sometimes even somewhat beautiful, fitting for a point-n-clicker; though, definitely not breath-taking.
- occasionally, there's an abstract mini-puzzle challenging you. They were kind of fun.
- halfway through the game, players are introduced to a "Maniac Mansion"-similar character-switching mechanic. I didn't like the voice actor performance of the secondary character at all, but still, I think the game would have felt much more interesting if that mechanic would have been used more often, and sooner.
EDIT: Just replayed it in German and – wow! A difference of night and day!
The flawed reasoning is still there, but there is significantly less cringe and much more professionalism (*so* much more) due to the experienced voice actors. As a result, the whole game feels much more enjoyable. They even properly pronounced Ms. Charlesroi, 1oo% of the time.
It's alright. Not highly, but quite recommendable to point-n-click afficionados. However, stay away from the English voice over. That's an entirely different story …

This is an amazing port, of a (presumably) amazing cooperative card/board game!
I've never played the original card game it's based on (though I'm fairly sure I will with my regular gaming group, once I get a chance). It's similar to a game like Magic: The Gathering in a way, however, it's also very different. It's not a "CCG" (because it contains expansions with cards, you don't buy "packs" and try to get cards or build decks). This is true in both the card and video game versions. The game is strictly cooperative, 1 to 5 players versus the Villain, the base game (the video game at least) has 4 villains and about 10 heroes. Cards are dealt out, you play various ongoing, one-shot, and other types of cards to get an effect or deal damage to the villain or it's minions or devices, it in turn, tries to kill you all (Grand Lord Voss is a PitA).
What really impresses me is how well it plays, both single and multiplayer (multiplayer has some weird hitches and people don't see cards at the same time, depending on how fast they click or have their animation speed set) and you do a lot of "voting" and "suggesting" what the other players do or can do, that's handy for text, but a bit less-so for voice (the game does not support voice natively, you'll need your own client), though I understand why it's set up this way) it's ages beyond how well the various versions of Magic play on Steam (though they're nice, they don't work as well and seamlessly as this game). It's extremely addicting if you love comics, superheroes, cooperative card games, board games, or just doing stuff with your friends, (though it plays perfectly fine solo also).
Check it out; you'll be glad you did!

Sentinels of the Multiverse is a computer card game. In it, you control a group of heroes, and you combat a villain. The game is represented by cards – each character is a card, with their own power and hit points, and their own unique deck. The game proceeds by having the villain (controlled by an AI) play, then the heroes play, with each hero having their own hand of cards, and then having the environment (again controlled by an AI) play.
The gameplay is about what you’d expect out of something like this, and all in all, the decks of the various characters are reasonably interesting. The villain throws something at the heroes every turn, be it some sort of attack, a minion, something which blocks their progress, ect. Sometimes, the villain card itself will attack as well on top of whatever the card they drew doing.
Likewise, each of the player characters in their own turn gets to play a card, then use a power, and finally draw a card. This power can either be the power on their card, or a power on a card they played. Some cards give passive bonuses, some are powers which have to be activated during the power turn, and some just are a one-shot ability which does something.
The environment basically does stuff to help or impair the heroes and villains. Some of the cards are really disadvantageous for the heroes, some hurt the villains, some do very little, some are easily gotten rid of, and some are very deadly.
While all of this is reasonable enough, it becomes clear very quickly that the game is short on content. The game comes with ten heroes, four villains, and four environments. Given you can play with up to 5 heroes every round, you’re really looking at only a handful of games before you run out of new content. There is an “advanced” mode for the villains, but it is really ultimately just a minor tweak which ups the villains’ difficulty rather than giving a real burst of new content.
But there are packs of heroes and villains which can be purchased as DLC…
And that’s really what this is – the base game is basically a demo for the “full game”. You can buy the season 1 DLC pack for as much as the base price of the game ($20 right now) which greatly increases the content – overall adding 8 new heroes, 14 new villains, and 8 new environments. The base game experience just isn’t very varied, and you will likely quickly become bored with fighting the villains after one or two times.
There isn’t really a story or anything else – while there are character background pages, expecting any story beyond that will leave you disappointed. And while there is a new weekly challenge every week, most of them require the DLC, and in any case, they’re just the standard scenarios, just with preset villains and hero sets – and as far as I can tell, none of them really incorporate stories or anything special like that.
Really, then, this isn’t a complete game without the DLC – so expect to spend as much as the base game + the DLC, meaning this is basically a $40 game, not $20. At the sort of price range they’re asking for, I don’t think this game is really worth it – frankly, I got about three hours of vague interest out of it, followed by about five hours of achievement hunting and the realization that I wasn’t really having fun anymore.
Overall, I don’t think that spending the extra money is really going to make it all that much more fun – just increase the amount of time you spend on it being vaguely amused at best. There are just so many more games out there which try so much more to make you happy, I just can’t really say that you’d be justified spending your time on this one. It isn’t awful, and it is an okay-designed card game, but there’s just nothing special about it.

I picked up Ori and the Blind Forest recently via the Steam Summer Sale. After putting a few hours into it, I have to say it is a blast. Not since Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night have I so enjoyed an open world 2D platformer.
The art direction and music are both excellent. The characters are lovable and the story, while not entirely original, is well told. The Developers did a fine job of being creative with Ori's character abilities and the game does a fairly good job on guiding you through the gameplay with areas designed specifically for said skills.
Even though I haven't played this game all the way through, I already see myself giving it a sold 9/10. Why not a 10 you ask?
The Ginso Tree, the M****R F*****G Ginso Tree! I have never so much wanted to simultaneously save and destroy something in a game before. As soon as you help the  heartless demon plant it tries to drown you in tears of frustrated gamers. Why can't Ori just charge up an energy burst and blow a hole in the side of the D**N thing?!?!
For an otherwise excellent game, that sequence is a miserable experience. Is it difficult? It's rediculous! It's worse than "Nintendo Hard." If the NES sat up all night eating oysters and snorting lines of Viagra it couldn't get this hard! What makes it difficult you may ask?
First off you must make precise jumps with very few mistakes. Some jumps require enemy projectiles, which enemies don't always fire on time. Why would they? They are the enemy! I guess they know they are going to die so they are doing a great job by not letting Ori use her abilities. Second the water escape is timed so that you always have the pressure of churning waters rising from underneath your character, threatening to drown her. This would be fine if the waters rose at a steady level but no...it rubber bands based on your progress. You get a few good jumps in? You think you will be rewarded by a little more time? Nope, it is instantly on Ori's butt like white on rice...or neon white on a glowing cat-monkey-mouse creature. Lastly, there are NO save points along the way. I died so many damn times right near the end from a very, very, very slightly misplaced jump.
I got Ori killed a lot during this Ginso Tree water escape sequence. I died maybe a hundred times, maybe more? I keep thinking PETA might show up at my place for cruelty to animals with how many times I drowned this poor cat-monkey-mouse. If they do, I'm sending them straight to the Developers!
Whew...rant over. I did complete the Ginso Tree water escape. The game is great, everything else feels like it's a leisurely downhill slide. If the Developers ever make Ori 2, don't ever include a section in a game like that again please? Or at least let me blow up the F*****G Ginso Tree! Burn it down...die Ginso Tree die!

FIrst off, you can't play this game without crashing after every campaign level if you have more than 50 people in your Steam Friends list. Second, this game will wreak havoc on lower-end computers and laptops. Lowering the quality is highly advised if your system isn't optimized unless you want to play at a constant 10 frames for the whole campaign.
And third, you might want to check the keybinds when you first start up the game. It's weird having to press Mouse3 when you want to throw a tactical grenade, so you might want to rebind some of those controls.
All in all, I like the campaign. It's arguably the best out of any Call of Duty game I've played on PC and console. Playing in the past and future brings a new feel to the gameplay as the story unravels. I give it an 8 out of 10.

Or anywhere in between.
Game seems to be also very well balanced, if you penalize the prisoners, they aren't happy and might turn more violent - then again if you don't, then you get minus poins for letting them off too easy. So it's very much balancing things out, and there is a learning curve to get the hang of it.
For example, when you get a bit more things unlocked while you play, you can later use things like CCTV, logic gates, logic bridges, door automation and timers, gather intel with phone taps, use metal detectors around your prison if you can afford it, hire K9 guards to sniff out drugs and contraband, train guards to use tazers and whatnot.
With logic gates you can do pretty much anything, like build a doorway with three doors for example, from which only one can be open at a time. Or maybe build one-way-only corridor with similar multiple door setup using logic gates (OR, NOR, NOT, AND, NAND, XOR, =).
I'd imagine that the replayability value is good also, you might not play this every day, but rather like a civ game where you can come in anytime after months of break, and spend long hours again, just enjoying the game.
I would want to try and describe this more - don't know if I would get it for ~30€, but definitely grab it if you see it on 50% sale or cheaper.
Have to warn though that if you get into this, you might find your self spending countless hours perfecting your vision of the perfect prison - maybe only to see it getting destroyed by some factor that you overlooked - or maybe not.
Tutorial is awesome, as it's build in as a story with progressing chapters where you have to manage different prison scenarios (riots, fire etc..)
There are also variables you can pick when you start building your prison, like weather changes, different warden type bonuses, which are all a nice addition to the game.
Definitely did not expect this much all though have thought many times before getting this, but always would up buying something else. Glad I got this one finally, was very positively suprised.
Props for the designers and programmers for this one. (y)

Board game come video game with card battling superheroes and villains.
----
+ Hero deck designs are interesting
+ Card interactions are interesting
- Clunky presentation
- Slow paced
- No multiplayer community
- Seems far too expensive for what it is, especially when DLC is taken into account
- No story
- No stakes
- Not fun
----
I've never played or heard of the associated board game, but I can compare it to other card battling video games without too much bias. To that end - this sucks.
I'll break it down with some choice arguments;
- The game begins with a tutorial that basically plays the game for you for 15 minutes whilst explaining very little in a lot of words.
- The meat of the gameplay involves playing various combinations of heroes on a choice of stages against a choice of villains with no overarching purpose or story to speak of at all.
- You cannot customise any of the decks in any way.
- The interface is clunky to use and confusing to look at.
- The pace of the game is monumentally slow, particularly if you have to read a lot of card text (which you most definitely will).
- A lot of the game is locked behind the DLC paywall, which to my mind is priced quite high considering most of it just adds more heroes, villains and stages to choose from and does nothing for the directionless gameplay.
- As of this writing, there is basically no online community to speak of.
It's not all doom and gloom though, the decks that are in play are quite interesting and each hero has a unique theme, feel and playstyle. The villains do pose quite a threat and the addition of the environment having a deck is interesting, although it often seems to screw you in seemingly unfair ways. I expect these aspects probably make for a great board game, so it's a shame that as a functional video game this is kind of a failure.
Overall? There are a lot of vastly superior options if you want to play a card game. The only reason I can think of to get this is if you really enjoy the board game, but even then - just play the board game. Then you can threaten your friends with physical violence and liven the whole thing up a bit.

This game does not respect your time. It took one hour and fifteen minutes for me to finish the tutorial fight, and by "finish" I mean lose.  I never even landed a hit on the first enemy's second form. While I can see a lot of work went into this game, it takes a painfully long time to make any progress. Anyone who finds turn-based strategy games slow would beg for the pace those move at, because this is far, far slower. I -could- try to do the tutorial again, but when I have to spend over an hour trying to do it, why would I? And if the tutorial is that rough, I know better than to try to take on the rest of the game, even if I did manage to get past the tutorial battle.
If you're looking for something difficult to play that wants to to waste far more time than most other types of single player games can manage to waste in the first fight of the game, then look no further! You've found your match in Sentinels of the Multiverse.

I don't really like comics, but I make an exception for this game. Sentinels of the Multiverse is basically one big love letter to comics, and it makes for a fun co-op superhero card game whether or not you're into comics in the first place. It normally involves a lot of number crunching, which the video game version takes care of so you can strategize and listen to that sweet, sweet music. A number of other little touches make the game pretty special, although the interface is a little stiff.
While this game does all the complex computations for you, it also requires you to confirm every little choice that requires player input. Those are things you'd normally handwave in the physical game with stuff like 'villain does 4 damage to all heroes, but Hero X played Damage Negating Card Y, your turn Hero Z'. Be prepared for some clicking once a game really heats up.
Multiplayer isn't exactly bursting at the seams - this is very much a game to pick up with a friend or two - but the existing community is actually pretty friendly. Just make sure to pick up some of the DLC; the content in the base game is kind of sparse.

TL,DR:
Like others have said, this feels like a demo...that you paid $15 for.  Despite a couple interesting mechanics, there are so many other card-battle games that provide more for the money (MTG, infinity war, hearthstone, scrolls, etc).  Don't pay $15 for it unless you really want an asymetric and/or super-hero themed card-battle game.
Pros:
- The comic/card based combat is a cool idea, and I like the asymetric gameplay.
- The environment being a force that can help or hurt either side makes you stay on your toes.
- Simple gameplay, if you have played any card battle game, this will make sense immediately.  If you haven't, you should be able to pick it up in 5-10 min.
- Some of the villians (Citizen Dawn) are pretty interesting and unique.  Others not so much...and there are only 4.
Cons:
- Very few villians/heros/environments to start with.
- The hero options you have are mostly pretty derivative (a tank that looks kind of like a tank, a psychic, a theif, an alien version of storm, an angel, etc).
- Similarly, the art direction is totally servicable but equally forgettable.
- No customization of any of the decks.  Want to tweak a hero's playstyle?  Too bad.
- Many of the decks' playstyles are not particularly flexible, you will have the play the character the way it was designed to be played.  Basically, creativity seems to have limited usefulness here.
- The few heros who are somewhat unique (such as absolute zero) are interesting at first...but once you figure out how they work you realize there isn't that much to them after all.
- Multiplayer, if you can find a game at all, is pretty lackluster.
- Again, really only enough content to dip your toes in, this should have been a free demo.  I would not pay any amount of money for this amount of content.

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is the second game in the Max Payne trilogy developed by Remedy Entertainment, the same people behind the Alan Wake game and published by none other than Rockstar Games, makers of such games as Bully, Manhunt, L.A. Noire and the Grand Theft Auto series
The story continues right after Max Payne, I won't spoil anything from either the previous game or this sequel's story, however the story is action packed to the brim, just the same as Max Payne
Thankfully Max Payne 2 ran much better than Max Payne, however, you will need a widescreen modification for widescreen monitors, but on the whole, Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne ran much better than Max Payne, obviously Max Payne was developed much more before Max Payne 2 so it is understandable
The graphics, for what they were at the time have aged pretty well. The environments are well designed and the attention to detail is really there, and the character models too have been greatly improved
The music and sound effects are good and the voice acting is good too. However, the game does suffer with volume level issues, sometimes the voice actors sound loud then at some points they sound low. Sometimes the cutscenes volume is good and at some points I can't hear a thing and have to riase the volume from my speakers to hear what they are saying, this is due to it being an old game so I don't blame the game per sei. Thankfully, it wasn't as bad as Max Payne
The cutscenes are told through a mixture of a form of a graphic novel and in-game custcenes and although Max Payne did suffer with the graphic novel custcenes (see Max Payne review for more details), they have been greatly improved in the sequel
The gameplay is a mixed bag. The famous bullet time is fun and will save you a lot of health as Max Payne dies easily, even on medium and easy difficulty. And the game is hard, you will die constantly, so much so, that I had to replay the game from medium difficulty to easy difficulty and still the game was hard
You will die constantly, and this is where my main complaint comes in. There is no auto save! If you get shot and die, you will reset to the latest save you or the game has done which is normally in the beginning of a chapter, so if you did not save manually (either by pressing F5 or by saving in the main menu), then expect to be teleported back to the latest save either you or the game did for you. This can be extremely annoying!
However, Max Payne 2 is a fantastic sequel to the trilogy and I can't wait to play Rockstar's take in; Max Payne 3
Max Payne 2 runs very well on modern systems, just be sure to download a mod that makes the game playable on widescreen monitors and you should be fine! Just be wary of the game's difficulty at some points...
If you liked the first one, you'll like the second one. It is shorter though. Would still recommend.

Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter centered on the catastrophic collapse of Dubai amid raging sandstorms that decimated the cities infrastructure and communications to the outside world. You play as Captain Martin Walker, who leads a three-man reconnaissance team to survey and assess the situation; errant communication and the discovery of slain US soldiers leads Captain Walker’s men into the heart of the unknown.
There’s a lot that can be said about Spec Ops, but to avoid spoilers it’s tough to delve into some of the symbolic themes and subtle ques the game throws at you. Having played through the game multiple times, you really start to see the game’s strengths in story-telling, character develop and dialogue. On the other side of the coin, you also feel the gameplay becomes a begrudgingly stagnant towards the third act of the game, especially during heavy combat.
When you begin your journey, you’ll be trekking through the desert on a standard recon mission when things turn sideways near instantly and you’re in the middle of a treasonous bloodbath with no clear virtuous side in sight. The chaotic nature of the story, mixed with clever dialogue really sets the tone for something exciting. Captain Walker, Lt. Adams and Sgt. Lugo all have very diverse personalities from the start, mixing a symbiotic relationship between dark comedy and the serious overtones of war.
Spec Ops offers some of the same when it comes to your modern shooter; it offers a cover system much akin to things like Gears of War and Call of Duty, an array of small arms, long guns and explosives to defeat your enemies which can be found or recovered from the corpses of various enemies, and a melee option. Melee is all but useless in the game, though, with firefights being too hectic to properly utilize.
Enemy AI is average at best, even at higher difficulties. The highest difficulties being “Suicide” and “FUBAR” [the hardest difficulty] you’ll often notice enemies stopping in the open, face the wrong direction or have detection issues where they won’t even notice you, which is especially noticeable in Chapter 14. That being said, enemies do have some positives to help level the playing field. They’ll provide cover fire for their troops, blind fire, throw grenades if you stay entrenched in cover, flank your position and call for backup when applicable.
The game itself is a linear story progression with several instances of heavy-handed decision making that slowly splinters the atmosphere of the game depending on what you decide. Interestingly enough, your partner AI will react and respond differently depending on the choices you make. Again, these changes are subtle, but if you notice them it makes the game a bit more satisfying to play.
Probably the most creative aspect of Spec Ops is the dialogue; it truly sets it apart from other shooters. As Captain Walker and company progress the storyline, your relationship with your Lt. and Sgt. become strained and significantly more volatile while the commands you give become hostile and blunt. Your uniforms become haggard, torn and bloodied, and Captain Walker’s reaction to killing enemies loses its cool and becomes more psychotic. It’s easily my favorite part of the whole game.
The main game aside, Spec Ops does have a co-op option which follows specific missions and not the storyline and an all but dead multiplayer ability. Neither were the main focus of the developer due to them distracting from the harsh reality of war the main campaign explores. If you don't have a partner to play with or bought it too late to try the multiplayer, you were never missing much.


Overall, Spec Ops isn’t going to blow you away, nor reinvent the wheel when it comes to modern shooters. It provides a game of adequate length, plenty of curve balls, some great character development and plenty of twists to keep it interesting. I don’t feel it merits the stellar reviews some have given it, but it does try to break the mold of the modern day shooter and for that I can appreciate it.

For all the games I’ve played throughout my lifetime, Spec Ops: The Line has to be up there when it comes to being one of the weirdest that I’ve encountered. I don’t mean that it’s weird in the traditional sense, either – what I mean is that’s there’s so much going on, and so much the game tries to achieve and stir within you, that it’s honestly hard to know where to start talking about it.
Since that’s the case, let’s start with the basics; the gameplay and graphics, actual solid and concrete features that are easily observable. Unfortunately, as becomes rapidly apparent as you start playing, these are features the game is deeply lacking an abundance of in the quality department. This is very much a generic cover based shooter that you’ve probably played a thousand times before, and it’s not even a good example of that genre. It doesn’t feel engaging or enjoyable to play, and in fact pretty lacks anything that make it special in any way. Indeed, the only lasting memory of the gameplay I have is how the fiddly controls (especially regarding cover) are what killed me more than anything else.
This is a problem that is then only exasperated more by the dismal visuals on display. While I accept this came out five years ago, the actual graphics are merely tolerable when compared to other titles from the same time period. I’m also aware that considering the game's tone, the dull looking nature of every landscape you encounter is clearly a deliberate design choice. The real problem is just that everything’s so... Forgettable. You’ll pass through area after area completely passively, retaining no information as to what they may have ever looked like. There’s simply nothing engaging to grasp on to; no dramatic vistas or battlefields, and no compelling gameplay to try and counter this defect. It’s the purest definition of bland.

Yet – and here’s where things start getting weird – it’s clear Spec Ops: The Line never really cared for these matters in the first place. What it really wants to focus on, and the whole purpose for it existing in the first place, is how it’s a brutal deconstruction of the military shooter genre as a whole. This is a title that rips apart so many ideas and beliefs common to all the other similar titles around it that it’s honestly difficult to keep up. The idea that America is always there to save the day, the glorification of the army and war in general, even the idea that you could put violence into the form of a video game and call it entertainment... All these topics and more are picked up, scrutinised, and then torn to shreds.
It’s startling to see, and effective for the most part, but it’s not perfect. There’s a deep problem ingrained in the message that's trying to be conveyed here, and to demonstrate this, you only have to take a look at the pivotal moment that occurs around the halfway point. Its dark, presented to you without compromise, and will make you feel incredibly miserable for a good while afterwards. It’s also the stepping stone by which the second half of the game really ramps the story and its moral message into high gear, with practically everything setting you down a emotionally dark path – loading screens and all.
The problem is this, however – you’re forced to do it. There’s no alternative way out, much as you might like to find one; the only way forward is to commit the atrocities set out in front of you. Yet since you’re so railroaded into doing this, the game telling you you’re an awful person afterwards feels a big hypocritical; you were never given a say in the matter, after all. To commit to a terrible analogy, it’s like me making you a delicious sandwich, placing it in front of you, and then criticising you when you actually decide to eat it – considering the way everything has been presented before the outcome, the outcome itself simply doesn't make sense.
The developers have argued in interviews that there is another option to take; simply turn it off. Yet that feels completely at odds to the way every other video game in existence works -  you’ve paid money and invested your time into this product, so you’re naturally going to wish to proceed and not just give up halfway. Besides, if the developers are stating that the best course of action is to stop playing – why create anything after this point? Why develop it at all? The fact this experience takes the form of a video game is both its greatest asset and its greatest curse – it needs to force you to do things to proceed forwards, but by doing so it fundamentally weakens their impact.
There are other smaller moments throughout which provide some form of actual choice, and it’s actually these that fare a great deal better. One in particular saw an intense situation physically panic me, pushing me into making a terrible decision. It was only after the event that I realised there was a better solution I could have taken, the realisation of which made me feel terrible in a distinctly more organic way.  This isn’t really a critique of the other emotional moments the game places in front of you – far from it - it’s just a shame that these moments of true choice aren’t a little more prevalent.
Spec Ops: The Line, therefore, is a lot to take in. As a piece of entertainment, something to actually have fun with, it’s a complete and utter failure. Whether it’s actually a good game is hard to answer as well, because I’m not sure how you define “good” in the context of something that’s as dark as this.  As a think piece, however - something to look at, examine and discuss – it’s a sterling success. It’s made me question things long after I put the controller down, and you only have to glance at the internet to see how much discussion this has created. That’s why it’s so weird and so much in a class of its own – and something that is, despite its many faults, well worth your time.

My, where to begin...
For starters, this is what an Early Access title should feel like. The game as it currently stands feels more complete than other Early Access games ever were when they 'pulled the plug'. I fell like I can enjoy this game as it stands for hours on end and play with my friends.

Maybe even supporting up to 16 different players at a time. Also, if you're not the host machine, expect to crash a bit. If my high specced machine (64 GB RAM, GTX 1080, i7-6850K) can crash on an AMD FX based host machine that seems to be impervious to the crashes then there needs to be some work done in the processing department.
THE BEST PART IS THAT WHEN YOU CRASH YOU CAN RESTART THE GAME AND END UP BACK IN THE MULTIPLAYER WORLD YOU CRASHED IN!
The bad news is you lose everything when that happens. Were you on a different planet with rare metals and some solar panels? Ooops! not anymore!
Just being thrust out there with no tutorials is a fun way to just die. I remember the first time I suffocated, I got killed by a red dust storm, I fell from a great height, got killed by some interesting plants, etc. I think it should stay that way. You do get some basic help with the controls in the menu and when you first start the game, and honestly thats enough.
I wish the technology was tiered so that you don't get the fuel condenser and trade platform when you barely have anything at all. You can exploit this and then all of a sudden you don't need to go digging anymore unless you want to do more research. If the research was tiered then you would have to dive deep into caves.
On the subject, these caves are very impressive, somewhat scary pieces of darkness. Without a tether, you're basically on a timer. And remember those plants? They're down there too. Soon you get lost, scared, suffocate and die (just like normal life). The music adds to this spookyness as well as some of the sounds you come across in the game.
If I had one major critique, the one thing that would ruin the game for me, it's the mining tool. It's a bit wonky. Not so much the add and subtract part (they do need a bit of work), but rather the flattening. It's hard to judge what level you're flattening to, and sometimes it just feels like all I'm doing is adding more material rather than trying to create a nice, flat bridge over a chasam for my rover(s).
On a scale of non-powered Ice Box to 0 degrees K, I would rate this a Samsung refrigerator because it is very good, but has the ability to explode on occasion.

The story is based on the real life Tunguska event in which a massive explosion, thought to have resulted from a meteor crash, rocked Siberia in 1908. It's a great idea to base an adventure game around investigating a real life mystery, but unfortunately it is executed horribly here. Everything is cliched, the story moves at a snails pace, and all the characters are totally unlikable. This extends to the protagonist, Nina, who is extremely unkind to everyone she interacts with and even goes as far as regularly insulting the player's actions. There's a large variety of backdrops, characters, and even a love story thrown in, but it's all incredibly uninteresting.
Secret Files is a pretty typical point and click adventure game. Click on things to observe or interact with them. Collect, combine, and use items to solve puzzles and advance. The game allows you to press a button to show everything on screen that can be interacted with, which prevents "pixel hunting" and circumvents a lot of frustration. Unfortunately, the puzzles are generally either extremely simple or incredibly convoluted and illogical. I ended up using guides for large parts of this game because I simply didn't want to take the time trying to interact every item with every object in the game in order to advance.
Like it's other bargain bin adventure game brethren, Secret Files is an ugly game, even without taking its age into account. The game features simple 2D backgrounds and stiffly animated 3D characters. Despite the variety of locals, its all very boring.
Possibly the worst part of the game. The music is fine but the voice acting is truly atrocious, especially from the actress playing Nina. If you want to get a sample of it, jump to 27:55 in the episode. I think part of this is that the game was originally in German and a lot got lost in translation so the actors have no idea how to deliver the bizarre lines that they have to. Also, despite traveling the globe in this game, everyone speaks in an American accent.
Overall, I do not recommend that anyone plays this game under any circumstances. It's just plain bad.

Simply put, the best true platforming game to come out in YEARS. As you can immediately notice, the user scores are quite polarized, and I believe this is true to the nature of the game. If you find joy in surmounting difficult (But FAIR) platforming challenges, this game is the PERFECT game for you. Let me also state that the 10 I assigned this game was not some knee-jerk reaction to a merely clever indie game. This game is fantastic by ANY standard, it is perfectly executed. There is nothing in the game where I have ever said, man, I wish X existed. In a time where games like Fallout New Vegas and Civ 5 release with the swath of glitches and bugs in the game, it is refreshing to have a game ship out that is immensely bug free, it is absolutely precise. You may even grow to treat this precision as a foe, as there is a razor thin edge between success and death in each level, there is no "give", if you touch a deadly obstacle with any part of your hit-box, you can count on dying. However, this consistency gives rise to the games greatest achievement, the overall fairness of the game. I am astounded that I read other user reviews that actually complained about the controls, they are absolutely astounding. To be fair, I do use a Xbox360 controller, I could see that without one it may take longer to "pick up" but the controls are nevertheless, precise. The character becomes an extension of your will, you'll find sometimes that when an unexpected hazard appears, you react quickly and ably within fractions of a second, as if you were acting out of instinct. I am also disturbed to read some people claiming that this game's difficulty is just a mechanism to lengthen the game. I find it hard to believe we even played the same game. The levels are difficult to be sure, but they are absolutely fair, if you die, it is your fault, there are no invisible traps, your character will not move if you don't tell him to. And even if you die, the levels each can be completed in under a minute, so if you do die (and you will die, often) almost no progress is lost. You will not be spending 5 minutes just to get a chance to practice the spot you died at last time. The other reason I find this explanation difficult to believe is that there are over 300 levels. The game is already massive, it wouldn't need to be lengthened by unnecessary difficulty.
In short: A difficult platformer, but an absolute masterpiece if you are willing to take up the challenge.

Where to begin? It's a decent game, but not one that belongs in the Devil May Cry universe. it has anice aesthetic but that's about it. The story is somewhat of a carbon coby from DCM3, which is imo a much much better game.
The combatd is flawed, too slow, and you can't combo because there are color coded enemies on which only 1 of your weapons will work, so a scoring a long combo to get points is out of the question, not that it matters anyway.
The combat "style" meter you see, is tied to how much damage you do and really easy to maintain. There's no challenge in it what so ever and makes the game uber easy. Alsotaking hints from GoW, your weapons range goes accros the screen. This is not how DMC should be.
Devil trigger is absolutely useless because for some reason it launches all your enemies in the air. It's forcing you to go aerial, which is neat, but in other DMC games you had the CHOICE to do that and i was not a thing forcibly pushing mechanics.
ALso where other DMC guys are riddled which exceptionally well designed boss battles, this one has only ONE memorable one, the bob bardas fight, and even that is way too easy.
Conclusion: the levels and general aestethic look really nice, but it's gameplay that this game is lacking, a game needs more then just eyecandy to be good. It's like all other Ninja Theory games: they show promise but it's that "Almost good, but not quite there yet" why their games are so mediocre.

I really wanted to like this game. But the controls, interface, and funfactor isn't polished enough for me. I feel like there's way more micromanaging than needed. For instance, if I want to build a cell, I'll literally have to supply everything from the furniture to the door to the possible recreation items. I thought I wanted this type of micromanagement in other similar types of games. However, I'd rather just have the already supplied "room" tool with different levels (cheap, economy, pricey) of cost to build out the prison rooms. It'd be faster and more enjoyable to build out a prison in no time. Yes the customization wouldn't be as intricate, but do I really care how many serving tables really go into the canteen? If I literally have hundreds of cells do I really want to build each one? Not one bit. There's a difference between customization and funfactor.
The controls and user interface are muddled. For some items I expect in one dialog box, they are organized in another. Some prompts don't really educate me on what's really going on. The campaign is supposed to act like a tutorial, yet it exposed all the wrinkles the game designers missed. I think the game designers were supposed to create an atmosphere of overwhelming proportions except they forgot to stop somewhere along the line.
Instead of putting everything on their brainstorming whiteboard into the game they should have left some things out in order to fully polish the core mechanics. Games like City Skylines can be overwhelming, but it never feels daunting. Starting out a fresh new game in Prison Architect and I'm pretty lost. I don't feel like a game should force me to learn from the community and walkthroughs in order to get a basic handling of controls and bugs. There is a great game in here somewhere. It just needs a lot of retooling and reorganization.

This is true cooperative survival-horror. The atmosphere is dark and grim and gritty. If you don't find a flashlight, you'll be blind in quite a few areas. The zombies are so much more threatening, so much more frightening. Most move slow, relentlessly, and dangerously, which gives the few rare ones that sprint or run so much more of a terrifying presence. The zombies here differ so much from those in Left 4 Dead, where they are little more than nuisances to be blown away with a heavy machinegun. These undead will grab you and eat you alive. If you are lucky enough to escape with only a bite or two, you most likely have been infected, and will die soon to join the ranks of the living dead anyway. The zombies are not so easily killed by a single bullet or one swing of a bat. Putting a single zombie down is always a risk, and could result in your quick and unforgiving death. Just finding a weapon with which to do so may be a challenge in itself. If that weapon happens to be a gun, you'll need to find the ammo for it. Perhaps a friend picked up a couple 12 gauge shells on his way out of the previous house. If you are injured, you may bleed to death. Bandages must be found to wrap your wound. The pharmacy you've found is closed up with a padlock. Luckily, one of your teammates found a welding tool earlier and can burn the lock off. The pharmacy looks like an easily-defendable area, so you board the entry ways up with planks and bunk down for a while. Soon you are overrun, and there is no escape. This game is a fantastic and realistic experience, and best of all... IT'S FREE!

I love the diversity of the hero decks and how they alter gameplay to make you hero feel like it's specific type (for example Tachyon who is similar to 'the flash' is designed to draw, play, and discard multiple cards to make it feel like you're playing 'fast'). Since my introduction to this game in physical card form two years ago, I've opened up the eyes of people who would consider my gaming tendencies to be "weird" or "complicated" to the wonder that is the gaming world.
While at first I was a bit reticent to purchase simply a (currently) more incomplete digital version of the game, I'm incredibly pleased that I did - the creators successfully captured the essence of the game and perhaps intensified it with appropriate (and nostalgic) sound effects, and amazing tracks of music and ambient sounds customized for each individual villain and each featured environment.
And everything is automated.
For those who have never played the card game - it's big. At times, there's so many resolutions that must take place from any given effect that something might be missed or not taken into account. But everything is automated - damage, effects, draws, plays, with options during multiplayer for your teammates to make suggestions as to which to target to select, etc...
On that note... Multiplayer in this game is a treat. I love having only the knowledge of the cards in my possession, rather than those of my teammates' being visible ( I know this isn't mandatory, but that always seems to be the way it's played in my circle ); as a result, it creates for a more social experience to the game, where it's not only about working with a group of teammates, but talking about what everyone's possibilities are.
Which makes actual game knowledge quite, quite useful.
And speaking of possibilities: Character variants are unlockable... which makes for even more... variance... >.>; Seriously, though, it's awesome to play as some of the variants in a way I consider "legitimate". And while I don't normally like achievements... those that are ... achieveable through Steam make for fun and challenging scenarios.
Anyway... TLDR? If you enjoy the physical game, I can't imagine how you'll not enjoy the digital version.

This game recieves a bit of hate because of the reboot of the DmC Series. Being my first DmC game, I wasn't sure what to expect. I can safely say that is a good game. Graphically, it is good and runs quite smoothly. The style and great was and the stages are nicely done. The voice acting is fair and the music helps put you in the mood to slash things.  But what's really the fun part is the ability to chain endless combo's if you have the skills to.  The twist is that a rating is given to you based on how stylish you fought at the end of each battle. This motivates you to add different moves in order to achieve a higher rating and prevents the game from just being a button mashing feast. Dante (the protagonist) has guns and melee weapons at his disposal. New weapons will come along as you progress through the story, while slightly differing from the previous ones, they still serve the same purpose. The game is divided into fighting and platforming which isn't bad at all.
Many old school fans hate on the series because it is "easier" and think the knew Dante suck. New to the series, I think he's just fine.  As for the "easier" gameplay, it is just simply for accessible for new people to get into. You can unlock more difficulties after beating the game if you want more of a challenge.
In the end, this is a good game that brings some fast paced action that is fun and easy to learn.  I recommend you pick it up if you're in the mood for some hack n slash that has a good setting/style to it.

So DmC: Devil May Cry is a hark back to the old slash'em-ups of old. This one has a delightfully agressive modern twist, which I loved! The style, and the execution of the combat and environments were done perfectly and whilst I found the story lacking I did enjoy the characters.
Shame the mobs were a bit generic, but all in all a decent game. (Oh yeah, controller is a MUST).
