I honestly can't remember playing a single game that has kept me as consistently engaged, challenged, and enthralled as
has done. The game is paced very well, if a tiny bit hurriedly, but I'd take that over a repetitive slog any day. Progression feels consistent and earned, with each new ability meshing very well with both new and already-seen areas, and opening up lots of fun options to approach and deal with enemies. Combat is quite simple, with the basic attack targeting and damaging the nearest enemy at a button press. The challenge comes from the game’s biggest strength: Movement. Moving through the world is fun and flowing; I spent a lot of time just jumping around empty areas because I wanted to take a weird and unorthodox route for the hell of it. Many enemies shoot projectiles, requiring you to dance around them or find a safe position to attack from.

The interaction between the (hand-painted!) visuals and gameplay make the world feel deep and alive. The way the grass waves in Ori's wake, and trees shake and shudder after using a powerful attack grounds you in the world and accentuates your interactions with it. The sound design is equally stunning - Dashes and stomps have you ripping through air with effort and vigor, while Ori's scurried movement sounds light and efficient. My favorite bit of soundwork on this game is actually of Ori himself: He sounds young, naive, and innocent - not obnoxious, stupid, and arrogant, being the issue I take with many child-like characters. His pained cries upon taking damage are very indicative and hard to ignore, but sound genuine and restrained.

The weakest part of the game is its story, in my opinion. It's simple and predictable, but certainly not bad or cringeworthy. It takes enough of a backseat to not be intrusive, and cutscenes get short and sparse enough after the introductory areas. That said, the characters were likable enough to retain my interest.

's titular blind forest, Nibel, is a joy to navigate and explore. I only got stuck once, left to wander for about 45 minutes until I realised a certain boulder could be moved to access an area (i.e. I'm a dumb idiot.) After that, it was pretty much smooth sailing throughout. Nibel's various environmental puzzles usually aren't super complex, and put more focus onto utilizing the game's excellent movement mechanics to avoid traps, enemies, and other forms of death, which CAN often present quite a challenge.

Thankfully,
uses an exceptionally elegant save system: You can save just about anywhere, anytime, at the cost of the same resource you use to perform powerful attacks and open certain areas. This provides an interesting conflict: Do I save here, risking an inability to open the next door or kill a particularly powerful enemy, or do I push forward, possibly resulting in me having to redo the last 10 minutes of play? Normally, I feel I'd be against such a system, but every death really did feel like it was my fault. Not once did I honestly think, 'stupid broken game, I totally made that jump!' It's a wonderful system that can only work because of the game's tactile and reliable mechanics.

Although this game has lots of potential, I myself have found a few things wrong with it:
Firstly, the game is simply too resource-demanding. I myself have an Alienware 14 with a NVIDIA GeForce GT 750M, and 8GB of memory. To start with, this $1,000 laptop barely even runs this game on moderate graphics settings, forcing me to switch to low-end graphics just so the game can have a smooth, playable framerate. MAYBE this is something wrong with my laptop, but I think not.
Even playing on the lowest graphics settings possible, the game still manages to lag and otherwise have random FPS drops that would often result in instant death in the middle of a firefight. The vehicle control feels a little too arcade-y for my liking. In addition, there is a rather alarming population of cheaters on servers. Utilizing a mathematical formula—100 missions played, averaging 4 players to each faction for each mission—I found that over the course of those 100 missions that a total of 89 people were hacking in some way, shape, or form. If we conclude that in 100 missions that you will encounter 700 people (800 minus yourself in each mission), there is an average hacker ratio of 0.127 (12.7%). While Reloaded Production's newest Fair Fight Anti-Cheat Technology should help reduce this number, I still can see a large population of hackers managing to bypass this.
Regarding the servers, their software is outdated and faulty at best. Only the dedicated servers seem to run anywhere near smoothly, but even then their calculation systems and arithmatic formulas often result in a laggy experience.
Pros:
Decent graphics
Dynamic gameplay
ENDLESS character customization
Cons:
Requires a high-end gaming laptop in order to run smoothly
Arcade-esque vehicle handling
Combat utilizes hit-scans, which often bugs
Outdated servers
High hacker population
Overall score: 5.1/10.

Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.
Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years :)
For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.
Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.
Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.
Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.
If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.
Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.
Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. Whether you're a longtime fan (with an open mind) or a total newcomer just looking for a solid character action game, it's hard to imagine anyone feeling overly dissatisfied with this new game. A reboot is a chance to revitalize a flagging series, and Ninja Theory has done that with a striking vision for the DMC universe and top-notch combat. It should be noted, with a certain severity, that the 360 version is clearly superior in this pair. Its PS3 counterpart struggles to keep a steady framerate which is sadly characteristic of PS3 games running on the Unreal Engine. When you turn off your brain and let your intuition take over, you become one with Dante in a wild and seductive game you just want to play over when it finally ends. Ninja Theory are calling the DMC shots now and they're doing it well. The fighting mechanics are a little bit easier to master and perhaps not as deep as before, but on the other hand the storytelling is improved with skillfully crafted cutscenes. Put up with a rather dull introduction and you're in for a great game. This is a title that gets most of the important parts right when it comes to an action game. It makes you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥♥ thanks to the cool-looking combat and easy-to-produce combos, but remains deep to allow people to delve into the system and pull off some wild moves.

More Devil May Cry is always a bonus, in this case the trick is to pretend its not actually DMC but a clone using the same game mechanics, and then the whole reboot is less of an issue.

This is my first time playing a Devil May Cry game, with this being what introduced me to the series. Having never played any of the previous games in the series, all I knew was this being a hack and slash game and that it was a reboot of the series. I know this game received a lot of hate when it was initially released, because of it being a reboot, having a brand new Dante, and that sort of stuff. My review can't really speak on that as I haven't played any of the other games in the series. So my review will be based solely on this game itself and my experience with it. That said, I can definitely say I really enjoyed this game and had a lot of fun with it. The soundtrack is a pretty wild one, with some crazy music, but it definitely suits the atmosphere of the game and makes the battles and fights rather exciting. The atmosphere of the game was really great, as it didn't take long for me to be immersed into the world of Devil May Cry. From the level designs to the art style of the game, Devil May Cry's visuals definitely impressed me and just added to the amount of fun I was already having with the game. It also further impressed me as well. The fights themselves are smooth and fast-paced, with the music just really adding a lot to the fights. It definitely got me really into the fights. There's also a lot of stuff to do in the game as well. The main game consists of 20 missions, but it's more than that. There's lots of collectibles, side missions, and more. With storyline, I thought it was pretty good for a hack and slash adventure-action game, It definitely kept me interested until the end, and even wanting more. Fingers crossed that this game does get a sequel. But yeah, adding onto the game's content, there's definitely a lot of replay value, with the various difficulty modes of the game, which can be unlocked by completing other modes. Or going back through levels to collect missed items, find hidden secrets, and more. As I said, a lot of replay value. To be honest, I think at the beginning of the game, Dante was someone you could have mixed feelings for, but I think he had some great character development as the game progressed, developing into a hero that made me proud to have played.
Overall, I found DmC: Devil May Cry to be a great game that I had a lot of fun with until the very end, and yet still wanting more. From an awesome soundtrack to interesting storyline to impressive visuals and atmosphere, this game impressed me in many areas. I had my doubts about this game before going into it, however after giving it a chance and playing it fully through, I can definitely say my initial doubts where proven wrong. I'm glad I took the chance on this game, as I had a lot of fun with it. I've got no problem recommending this game to any of my friends. It's well worth two thumbs up from me.

(This is more of a journal of thoughts than a review, sorry if I'm not too clear on some things).
I completed my first playthrough in a little over 2.5 hours on normal difficulty, probably half an hour of which was being stuck (three specific areas, one of which I feel incredibly stupid for being stuck on). Minerva is a challenging game, compared to Half-Life 2 and it's episodes, at least. Level design is interesting and gorgeous, albeit a couple of parts that aren't too clear on how to proceed, and some issues w/ framerate. There's four loading screens throughout the entire game, and each level is fairly huge, so I experienced quite a few frame drops... big ones: 300 fps - below 40 fps at times, and hovering around 60-120 while looking in some directions (I'm running a GTX 770 and an AMD 8 core, and I tried lowering the graphics settings to no avail).
Combat is challenging and on occasion relentless, but you're given plenty of opportunity and supplies to restock and fight on (the pacing of this mod reminds me a bit of another HL2 mod, Station 51, only that was shorter). I dont know if it's just me, but the enemies seem tougher on normal than in the other hl2 games.
I just finished the game at the time of writing this, so these are first impressions. The game left enough of an impression on me to make me write something on it. For a free mod, I'd say it's worth your time, especially if you're into Half-Life 2 inspired settings and challenging gameplay.
My personal score: 7 out of 10 - was a bit frustrating, especially with staggering frame drops here and there hindering combat (nobody else I've seen mentioned this problem, so you might be good), but aside from that I enjoyed it. Maps are beautiful and for the most part straight forward, and I had a challenge in a Half-Life game that I havent had in years.

A nice quick and fun point-and-click adventure game.
Pros:
- Engaging storyline.  I personally liked the plot and the flow of the story
- Well-designed background graphics.  Each location was very well done in my opinion.
- Quick-travel to adjacent "scene".  Many of the other adventure games I've played have to wait for the character to completely transition to the edge of the map to get to the next scene.  The double-click fast travel was a welcome addition
Neutral:
- Voice acting.  Many of the voice actors' lines felt bland and uninspiring with only a few lines that really stood out.  And those that did stand out could have done with a little more "emotion" applicable to the scene.  Thankfully they don't detract from the gameplay but would have been a nice to have.
- No "map" travel.  A lot of the puzzles require you to travel back and forth between locations, some separated by several screens.  Being able to easily jump from location to location would have been welcome.
- FMV character models / animations could have been done better.  Several have a lack of facial expressions that made the scene feel out of place but the FMVs are short enough that they don't really impact the storyline or gameplay.
Overall a good game and worth adding to your collection.  It's no Telltale as far as acting goes but it's good enough given how short it took me to finish it. Even more highly recommended if you can get it on sale.

''Take Origins with a grain of salt, but play online.''
Having played Arkham Asylum and Arkham City from pre-order purchases, I can say with an honest opinion that I understand the negative reviews and comments that come aimed at Arkham Origins from players who played through the first two games. different developer who jumped into an already successful series and tried to make it theirs. Points for effort.
It captures the heart of arkham series to be sure, but its feeling is different. that said, it’s not bad, just not the same, though oddly repetitive.
gameplay remains very much the same as Asylum and City, the biggest issue I personally have is with the story and visuals. Yes, it’s a different company and the game is beautiful, but it’s the character models I’m referring to. Being a 'prequel' therefore origins, it’s understandable that people may be younger. However, adults don’t change that much in a few years typically, and Joker, if anything looks older not younger. Killer Croc looks completely different in form and size, apparently explained in the bio, that he changes as he ages.. ok.. same with everyone else by that logic I suppose.
Take Origins with a grain of salt, but play online.
Online play, though having drawbacks, could have really pushed origins into the streamline of games like Teamfortress2 or Dirty Bomb. Though no chat feature, it has custom character layouts, achieved through play / play credits earned from matches or even as p2w dlc content.
You can pre-select your faction, if you only ever want to be Team-Joker/Team-Bain. and you can customize your batman/robin costumes if you are selected to be a caped-crusader during roulette (or opt-out if you don’t want to be a hero). Unfortunately, not enough people play online, so you sometimes have to wait a long while to find players as it REQUIRES 8 to start a match. and unfortunately people’s voice-over (mic) usage is annoyingly unfiltered, luckily you can turn off reception of players’ individual mics in the pre-game lobby.
Luckily for those who haven’t played any Arkham games, they are often on sale these days for less than $5 or found in bundles. Currently you can get all the Arkham games if you pre-purchase Arkham Knight (due to their pc-release fail, as an apology, which matters not for those of us who already own the series contents).

My hands-down favorite memory from college was sitting around a table with people in my hall, acting out fictional comic book scenarios. This game brought complete strangers together and gave us a common goal: To save the multiverse. While it sounded cheesy at first, playing a turn-based cooperative superhero card game turned out to be the best time I ever spent away from studies. It was very easy to pick up the rules, each hero felt different from the rest, there were hilarious homages to real comics spanning numerous companies, and we would find ourselves immersed after hours planning, laughing, dreading, and cheering for the results of a simple card game. We weren't students escaping from engineering studies; we were superheroes fighting for mankind.
Four years later, the strangers are now great friends, expansion packs have been collected, and we still come together over the internet to save the multiverse every week.

Divine Divinity is a game that I discovered after playing another excellent game developed by Larian called Divinity: Dragon Commander.  At first I thought it looked like a Diablo clone, but it differentiates itself from Diablo in many areas.  My playtime clocked in at 40 hours. I ended up skipping a lot of content not because I wanted to but because my character had become practically invincible by Act 3 and that the game simply does not care whether you fail a side quest.
I played the game on a 1024x768 resolution that was stretched to fit my monitor with black borders in the left and right.  Text does not scale well to a 1920x1080 resolution.  This is an artifact from the time the game was created.  The text for dialogue and item descriptions on higher resolutions was not unreadable or blurry, but it was annoyingly small.  Another reason for using the smaller resolution is that the game uses a sight range statistic. This mechanic means that enemies out side of your sight range are not visible even if you can 'see' that area of the map around yourself. Enemies pop up practically next to you when your sight range is low.  This was jarring for me and the problem was fixed with the lower resolution.
Why would you play a game like this? Because it offers so many different ways to play.  Abilities are not set to any particular class. Every ability can be used by any class and can be leveled up five times.  You gain one skill point per level and every five level you gain an additional skill point.  This system  forces one to make deliberate choices in what skills to acquire and upgrade to create a powerful and versatile character, but there are many successful paths to take.  A lot of the fun in playing an RPG is discovering skill sets and items that work well together.  Divine Divinity succeeds in providing customization.
There are mechanics in the game that are not explained well.  I highly suggest reading the manual before playing because I stumbled a few times. Items in the environment can be moved by left clicking and dragging it away from its initial position.  I believe that there is check against the strength statistic and the weight of the item to see if you can move it. There are many secret passages and items that are found behind piles of crates, barrels, rocks and haystacks so keep an eye out.  In order to equip runes to gear that has 'charm x' quality, you need to skill up an enchant weapon skill in the warrior tree.  Runes are key to improving resistances and stats your character is deficient in.
Combat is simple hack and slash and provides ample opportunity to kite tougher enemies.  Left click on an enemy and auto attacks happen until it either it dies or you die. Abilities and spells are performed with right clicks.  The game lets you hotkey spells, items, and potions to the function keys F1, F2, etc.  I used these to toggle between melee weapons and ranged weapons and to change my spells.  Selecting a spell through a hotkey sets it for use on a right click.  The game also has a pause function that allows you to change your spell at your leisure.  There is a lot of combat and it is mediocre at best.  The game throws different enemies at you that require different strategies to be effective against and some of the bosses are brutal without preparation.
The graphics for outdoor environments are highly detailed a nice to look at.  As you explore the musical score fades in an out so you can traverse the wilderness listening to background noises of the forest, fields and cities.  Dungeons are darker and blander.  There are four large overland maps that are littered with quests, monsters and new places to discover.  A few multilevel dungeons give the game its Diablo like feel.  It is a good mix of overland exploration and dungeoneering.
Voice acting is limited  and what exists is woefully terrible.  Despite that, I could not get enough of my character yelling “Fantastic!” every time she leveled up. I think this game is better than classic DMC fanboys give it credit for. Is it easier than the other games? Yes, but that doesm't mean it isn't hard, especially as you reach Dante must Die difficulty and higher. The specifics are down below, but to keep it simple the game is amazing. While short, it has a good story, beautiful graphics, great music, and ever so stylish combat.
This game has a lot more going for it. The music is phenomenal, and it fits the overall feel of the game perfectly. However, sometimes that same track is used over, and over, and over again, to the point that it gets kind of dull (once you beat the game you'll know which one I'm talking about...). Still, it's a pretty balling soundtrack. The graphics are great as well. The game looks beautiful, especially on the outdoor segments, or some of the cutscenes. Everything looks really good over the course of the game, and I don't think at one point I ever went "gah, this game is hideous."
But, the most important factor is gameplay. Fighting in this game is great. Combat is tight, and in the ongoing quest to be "SSSensational!", this is a huge plus. Switching between weapons in the middle of long combos is easy and quick, and you have so much freedom both in-air and on-ground that you can clean up a whole room of enemies without taking one hit or ever ending your combo. The variety of weapons (the default/neutral sword and firearm, and then 2 demon side weapons, 2 angel side weapons, and 2 more firearms) is beautifully integrated into the game, as each enemy requires varying techniques. When a bundle of different enemies with different strengths and weaknesses comes your way, you can easily switch to whatever weapon you need by having all weapon assignments mapped on to the mouse (scroll up on the wheel to switch angel weapons, down on the wheel to switch demon weapons, and click to change firearms).
The only complaint I have related to combat is that it's harder to use demon or angel side weapons (in my opinion) since they are mapped to the "E" and "Q" keys respectively. Since you have to hold the key to use its respective side, this assignment limits movement and makes it hard to switch between the two easily or use either for prolonged periods of time without letting go of the keys. Even though it's doable, in this regard I would recommended using a controller, since you can map the demon and angel keys to triggers, instead of any other buttons on the face of the controller.
The only other complaints I have are related specifically to the story. While good, this game is short, which means that a lot of crucial plot points are kind of glossed over, or not even talked about at all. I for one am really interested in background information on characters and their relation to the story, and unfortunately, it's just not there. You do learn a little about some of the characters over the course of the game, but there's not that much past base level.
Other than that, there's some side missions, exploration (the levels are linear, but to get more goodies and what not you have to explore every crook and nanny, which is a nice change of pace from whacking demons), minimal customization (there's more if you buy the dlc, which I recommend), and an extra mode called the Bloody Palace which puts all of your skills to the test.
9/10, would play again, and again, and again until I can beat Hell or Hell mode.

This game is an excellent adaptation of the physical card game.  The mechanics are solid, and it's a fun game.  Alone, you can play as a team of super-heroes, trying to stop a villain by playing cards & using 'powers' on the cards you've got in play.  In multiplayer, you can take control of one or more heroes in games with friends, or whoever happens to be online.
Every hero gets a character card that always stays in play, and a deck to draw from.  Some of the cards are one-shots that have an effect and go away, others are ongoing & stay in play until something gets rid of them.  Heroes and villains have hit-points, and if a hero runs out, their card flips, they can't play any new cards, but they still get a turn, and a few powers to choose from that can help  the rest of the team.
The developer is still putting in a good deal of work on this title, having weekly challenges set up with comic book cover style images to represent each, and a 'collection' going back, showing which ones you've done, and an opportunity to re-play any of them.  They've been doing these for over a year now!  Most heroes also have a variant (or two) to their base card that can greatly change the way they play.  These variants are unlocked by accomplishing certain conditions in game, some of which are quite easy, and you're likely to stumble across in normal play, and others are devilishly hard, requiring a bit of luck, or some careful planning to make them happen.  The community is always quite active when new variants come available, creating long discussions to figure out the unlock conditions.  If you don't enjoy that kind of thing, though, there's always a button to unlock them without the work.  When Season 2 finishes, the video game will have everything the physical card game has, so every hero will have at least one variant.
The DLC corresponds to the expansion releases for the physical games, and greatly expands the setup options for the game.  Adding online multi-player brought in some of the social element that's great in the tabletop version, and while there's a bit of a learning curve, the in-game chat usually yields a friendly community, willing to help new players.
There's a free demo version put out by the game makers.  If you want to get a feel for the game before you buy, give it a try.

I don't quite know what it is about this game. I bought it upon release, since an old friend of mine had introduced me to the tabletop version of it, and I was enjoying it. I bought the season passs, but I had one bad game and then set it aside, not playing it for months. Now we're in January 2016 and I've put almost 20 hours into it in the last two weeks.
So if you buy this and don't get into it right away, step back for a bit (not four months obviously) and then come back to it again. You won't regret it.
But what *is* this game you might ask? It is a co-operative digital card game, which you can play solo or online as a group of unique superheroes, against any one of a number of unique villians, in various environments. I haven't played online so my review is based on my single player experiences.
The graphics are limited to drawing of the various heroes and villians, with some slight changes as they take damage and become incapacitated, as well as damage animations. The music however is pretty badass. But what about the gameplay?
The tutorial is recommended when you start to get the basics down; the villian has a turn where they play cards, and then the heroes go. Each hero can play a card, use a special power, and then draw a card. Certain things may cause you to skip one or more phases, and if you skip the first two on your own you draw two cards. After all the heroes go, the environment you are on has a turn, and this can be good or bad depending on what environment you pick.
The goal is to defeat the villian, but each one is different, and this is where the meat of the game comes in; the strategy. A fight against the same villian can be different depending on which environment you have; you can also have your team  be anywhere from 3 heroes up to 5, which can cause differences in the battle as well, and each heros deck and powers make them distinct from one another. Also, each villian also has an advanced mode if you're looking for a more sizeable challenge. So the number of various scenarios you can have is very large.
The game has no story or campaign of the sort at the moment of this writing. They have introduced what is called a 'weekly one shot' where the community gets a specific challenge based on a certain group of heroes versus a certain villian in a certain environment, and then are encouraged to discuss it on the forums. There are also "variants" on the existing cards you can unlock, but the condiitions for doing so are very convoluted in some cases so it is best to refer to the well written community guides to determine how to do so.
Outside of unlocking the variants and the 'one shots' then the game is basically setting up your own matches by yourself and with friends to see how you do. You can let the game randomize a match for you, or set one up yourself. As I said, there are numerous combinations in the base game, but to get the best experience it is recommended you try to get the DLC for the additional heroes and villians to increase the replayability of the game.
It is expensive, what with the main game at $17 and the Season Pass at $21, but for the fun you will have it is worth it. Absolute 10/10 recommendation.

Max Payne 2 is such a perfect sequel that I almost find it difficult to recommend it without playing May Payne 1 directly before it. Both games offer complete stories, but Remedy has filled the game with details that link back to the first game in such a way that the two games feel like one single package. Max Payne 2 improves arguably every aspect of the game, bringing the graphics to more modern standards and refining the gameplay by making Max more responsive and improving his bullet time abilities. If you're only going to play one game in the series I would break my vow of playing every series in order and say to go with this one because it's just such a great game, but even if you can't get into Max Payne 1's older gameplay it's worth seeing it through just to be able to appreciate this game even a little bit more.

I don't quite know what it is about this game. I bought it upon release, since an old friend of mine had introduced me to the tabletop version of it, and I was enjoying it. I bought the season passs, but I had one bad game and then set it aside, not playing it for months. Now we're in January 2016 and I've put almost 20 hours into it in the last two weeks.
So if you buy this and don't get into it right away, step back for a bit (not four months obviously) and then come back to it again. You won't regret it.
But what *is* this game you might ask? It is a co-operative digital card game, which you can play solo or online as a group of unique superheroes, against any one of a number of unique villians, in various environments. I haven't played online so my review is based on my single player experiences.
The graphics are limited to drawing of the various heroes and villians, with some slight changes as they take damage and become incapacitated, as well as damage animations. The music however is pretty badass. But what about the gameplay?
The tutorial is recommended when you start to get the basics down; the villian has a turn where they play cards, and then the heroes go. Each hero can play a card, use a special power, and then draw a card. Certain things may cause you to skip one or more phases, and if you skip the first two on your own you draw two cards. After all the heroes go, the environment you are on has a turn, and this can be good or bad depending on what environment you pick.
The goal is to defeat the villian, but each one is different, and this is where the meat of the game comes in; the strategy. A fight against the same villian can be different depending on which environment you have; you can also have your team  be anywhere from 3 heroes up to 5, which can cause differences in the battle as well, and each heros deck and powers make them distinct from one another. Also, each villian also has an advanced mode if you're looking for a more sizeable challenge. So the number of various scenarios you can have is very large.
The game has no story or campaign of the sort at the moment of this writing. They have introduced what is called a 'weekly one shot' where the community gets a specific challenge based on a certain group of heroes versus a certain villian in a certain environment, and then are encouraged to discuss it on the forums. There are also "variants" on the existing cards you can unlock, but the condiitions for doing so are very convoluted in some cases so it is best to refer to the well written community guides to determine how to do so.
Outside of unlocking the variants and the 'one shots' then the game is basically setting up your own matches by yourself and with friends to see how you do. You can let the game randomize a match for you, or set one up yourself. As I said, there are numerous combinations in the base game, but to get the best experience it is recommended you try to get the DLC for the additional heroes and villians to increase the replayability of the game.
It is expensive, what with the main game at $17 and the Season Pass at $21, but for the fun you will have it is worth it. Absolute 10/10 recommendation.

Where it isn't original, it offers variant versions of certain character decks. The UI is helpful, colorful. and loyal to the original game's art. Again, where it isn't totally faithful to the art, it adds more by depicting characters at different amounts of damage.
For people who own the card game, this will really let you explore the game fully, because the computer takes away all the fiddly counters. Less time spent with setup, and book keeping, means more time spent playing. Due to this, I have gained a better understanding of the game, and enjoy it more.
You should know this: The various combinations of heroes, environments, and villains can make the game nearly impossible to win, or ridiculously easy to win. Experience with the various decks will eventually guide you to the difficulty that you would like.
On that note, Sentinels currently provides weekly scenarios for you to beat. It's nothing more than different combinations of decks, but like I said, that's what makes the game challenging.

This card game is simple to learn, yet incredibly rich and complex, You can make 10 matches with the same villain and the same heroes without ever getting the same outcome twice, and the big variety of characters gives you an infinite replayability, especially in multiplayer.
The characters are "copies" of Marvel/DC comic books characters, yet they're charismatic and their personality and lore are very detailed, which makes them as endearing as their counterparts - sometimes even more. I care a lot more about Legacy's story and struggles than I could care about Superman.
If you are into card games and/or co-op multiplayer games, I strongly recommend Sentinels of the Multiverse.

Divine Divinity has intuitive controls, a clear user interface (although this does not apply for the inventory) and offers some comfort features like hotkeys, a minimap and a great quest log. The battles are simple, but can get a little bit confusing when you're surrounded by many enemies or have to fight behind obstacles. Also, there's not much tactic needed (and possible) - you either end up clicking opponent after opponent to smash them to bits or do the same thing from the distance with arrows or spells. The game's pretty challenging especially at the beginning though, when you're low on health and don't deal much damage, but gets a lot easier once you've got good armor and a powerful weapon (or spells, if you're playing as a mage). Divine Divinity perfectly evokes your drive for more and better items and constantly satisfies it, since enemies often drop useful things and there are chests full of great loot around every corner.
The huge downside of this game is that it's got a pretty weak technology. I experienced regular crashes or hang-ups - sometimes without an accountable reason, sometimes when I tried to open a book or pick up an item. That's annoying, but can be compensated by saving often and on different savegames. What's worse is that some core mechanics are either buggy or completely inoperative. There are some skills that don't have an effect on battles even if they're expected to, others are extremely overpowered and you can break several quests by entering certain areas earlier than intended by the developers or using the (unapparantly) wrong speech options. This worsens the overall impression and tempers the gaming experience constantly.
The storyline is key to every good role-playing game, and while you certainly cannot expect Divine Divinity to have the greatest plot ever seen in the gaming industry, its golden thread is enjoyable and sometimes even a bit exciting. The presentation isn't always perfectly well-made, however - some dialogs seem clumsy, some core parts of the story are treated too hasty and the last (and fortunately short) part of the game is pretty boring and doesn't match up to the rest of the game.
A huge strong point of Divine Divinity are its quests. They are almost always specific in one way or the other - be it because of an unexpected turn, very bizarre characters or a good portion of humour. The game keeps the typical "Bring me 25 red flowers" or "Kill 20 orcs" quests within a limit, but provides lots of side quests to stop you from following the main quest nevertheless.
While the game's general atmosphere is quite nice and consistent, particularly in certain areas like Aleroth, the village in which you get started, or a huge forest in the south of the game's main region, there are a few things that sometimes take you out of the illusion to be a part of an authentic and comprehensible world. The bettermost example for this issue are the elves, one of Rivellon's most important races, who can get very old, and therefore could be expected to reach wisdom and calmness in the process, but instead mostly act like pubescent humans. Things like these may be dependent on personal preferences, but are one reason why Divine Divinity can not quite match up to the real RPG greats.
If the graphics are the or at least one of the most important parts of a game for you, you definitely should beware of even thinking about playing Divine Divinity. I mostly liked its style and wasn't bothered about that it doesn't even look exceptionally good for a twelve years old game, but that's something every player has to decide for himself by looking at screenshots or watching videos.
The situation is different with the sound, which is some kind of a two-edged sword. On the one hand, the effects aren't anything to speak of and I experienced a very disturbing and loud noise interference on some rare occasions. The music, however, is always enjoyable and the score has got some outstanding pieces that are capable of adding a lot more atmosphere to the situations they accompany.
Divine Divinity might not be one of the greatest games in history, but it offers many hours of an unfeigend and nostalgic adventure that will make you want to come back to the lands of Rivellon whenever possible and stay as long as you can. The game offers a good mix of story elements and battles to make sure that both Hack and Slay as well as RPG fans will get their money worth and will entertain you with around 60 hours of fun (given you take your time to discover every corner of the world and solve all the side quests). There are some flaws, and some of them aren't negligible, but if you aren't addicted to amazing graphics and don't get frustrated by games with some rough edges, you certainly should not miss out on an exciting journes to this fantastic world.

First of all when I first saw the trailer I was... what is the meaning of this? It had my eyebrows raised in disbelief. I couldn't believe that the one before me was the cheesy classy white haired guy I was so familiar with. At first I was enraged but then it hit me, the play style and the trailer where I must say intriguing. I always imagined and wished in the back of my mind to have this sort of heavy dark psychotic game involving DMC series as they were demons and to me it would make sense to have in it.
Well then the game came as I was once again disappointed since in the end due to mass people whining (so I heard) they changed the direction totally. What a pity I said to myself and I forgot about it for a while.
And here I am, one day, a while after everything, I was surfing YouTube I ran into one of the DMC soundtracks. To be completely honest, it's what made me think to give this game another chance.
I pick it up and started playing it and oh boy I'm glad I did. Now I want to kick myself in the mouth for not playing it a lot sooner.
It's very fun to play, the action combat is really great, very fluid, very natural. The number of combinations that you can do are simply mind blowing. Fighting never looked so good before this. It feels very natural and you can emerge yourself and be one with the character. I was really rusty so I started with HUMAN difficulty and I have to say for the first time in all my DMC series I truly felt it was the way it should have been. Easy, noob friendly with a little bit of challenge now and then.
I don't know about you, but to be honest, there were 3 things I actually hated in the previous DMC versions and 1 are the weird crappy camera angles, 2 the jumping missions and parts of the game (mostly due to the weird camera angles) and crappy hotkeys or optimizations.
Now let me tell you about camera angles in this version: if you get a weird camera angle it means you are on the wrong path. The rest I think I've met only once or twice in the entire game.
Now to the jumping part: it is really, really enjoyable and the difficulty progresses as you advance in the story.
The game controls for PC aka keyboard is flawlessly set up. Very easy, very intuitive, very user friendly. DMC really blew my mind on this aspect.
Some argued with the colored specific monsters and being a bad decision, but I personally enjoyed it. It added something extra to the mix.
For the story itself now, since I was and I will always be a sucker for stories. I felt that they could have explored so much more even with the current story. It had a proper foundation for a really deep story and which allowed several ways to develop it. I would have loved an ANGELIC trigger... now seriously..
Dante's turn: Some may argue how crude and bad the jokes are but I enjoyed it a lot. This Dante is standing alone with no connections whatsoever with the series so why would he be anything alike? Hmm, yeah.. he doesn't have to be. I think it went well with his overall personality, style and everything else about him, including the hairstyle which at first I was kind of.. o.O about it.
Vergil's turn: Everything makes sense about him and mostly his story and where you put that you get to even play him. Oh man how much I have enjoyed doing that (oops, maybe spoiler?) I seriously need more of that style in my life. I have to say I have enjoyed playing him more than I liked playing  Dante.
The story between Dante and Vergil was decently developed to. Overall the story was really well told even if it was insufficient and with a logical line and efficient at it. It added a lot more dynamic into the mix.
now the TLDR part:
Pro:
Awesome fighting style, very fluid, awesome optimization for PC, no weird camera angles, very new player friendly, great story and very fun play overall. Fighting with great style has met the benchmark for DMC with great combos and 'infinite' choices to make. PS: awesome soundtrack
Cons:
Story too short, I feel that it could have been developed more, not enough Vergil I want more in my life, I wish it had more bosses. The game mechanics are a bit easy once you learn it. You no longer have fighting styles, but you get a ton of weapons to switch in between.
Final note: I give this game a 8/10 MUST PLAY (mostly due story shortness and not enough Vergil)

DmC: Devil May Cry is a reboot of the famous Devil May Cry series. It stars Dante, son of Sparda, who is the son of a demonic father and an angelic mother. You will see how demons and angels merge as the story progresses. Dante’s lifestyle is that of a playboy, living a life of booze, parties, and sex. The story centers around two other characters: Kat, the psychic, and Vergil, Dante’s brother. The story truly evolves when Kat and Vergil meet up with Dante in place called Limbo.
The combat in the game is generally about the use of melee weapons and your ability to use combos against the various demons. The combat is entertaining enough that it makes DmC: Devil May Cry a fun reboot in the aggregate. You begin to learn the basics of melee combat with the Rebellion sword. Melee turns into learning so many different moves so that you can score style points under the game’s scoring system. Eventually, other melee weapons come into play and they are demon based as wells as angel based. This is when combat becomes even more important since some demons are vulnerable only to demonic weapons and other demons are vulnerable only to angelic weapons.
The story includes world domination, evil, love and conspiracy theories. The characters are pretty good because their voiceovers are excellent. The cutscenes display drama and the characters tend to walk a fine line between good and evil as the plot is well detailed.
The missions are quite linear, but they are never boring since they are diverse enough and lack tedium. In one mission you are fighting demon hordes in a city that appears to be crumbling. In another mission you are inside the offices of a TV network where you must face groups of demons as you go from one office to another. The melee weapons eventually include a Rebellion and Osiris. The Rebellion is a demonic axe with plenty of power, but at the expense of speed. The Osiris is an angelic weapon with plenty of speed. Both weapons can be used to lift demons in the air and you can jump into the air to score major chain combos for the most style points. The idea of the scoring system is to vary your attacks, chain your combos, and finish off the demons in short order. The style points are displayed on the screen while you are in the heat of battle with SSS being the highest possible grade for your combat performance. I used the mouse/keyboard controls throughout the game and they were smooth. I got used to the controls pretty quickly, but it takes time to master the moves, including platforming. There is a lot of jumping from platform to platform and that includes angel lifts and angel boosts. Angel lifting is the jumping from platform to platform using Dante’s grappling hook on blue circles. Angel boosting is jumping and flying/boosting above large gaps to reach a faraway platform. One interesting weapon that Dante acquires later in the game is the Aquila, an angelic weapon that can be used for melee and can be thrown to cut through vines.
Completionists will always find something to do in each mission. To complete 100% of each mission you will have to return to a mission to collect keys that will open doors to secret missions and free lost souls waiting to be liberated. The secret missions require keys that reflect the difficulty of each secret mission. Copper keys are keys that open doors to the easiest secret missions. Argent keys open doors to more challenging secret missions. Gold keys are for the hardest secret missions. The secret missions are short and can help you practice your moves. I learned from the secret missions that Dante’s combat moves are easy to learn, hard to master. Some challenges include killing all demons without taking a hit and scoring hits only by using demon evade, a well-timed way of evading demon attacks while armed only with a demonic weapon such as the Arbiter.
The boss fights are entertaining in their own right, although they are formulaic. You fight bosses while learning their moves so that you figure out how to defeat them. One boss near the end of the story, Mundus, is quite convincing as a mean monster since the voiceover is superb. The one minor problem with combat against either bosses or other demons is that sometimes the camera angles can get in the way, preventing you from seeing everything in the spur of the moment. However, this problem is so minor it doesn’t take much away from the entertainment value of the combat.
I think DmC: Devil May Cry is worth your time since the combat is well choreographed and the controls are excellent. If there are problems with combat it is usually because the timing of the combos is not right. It takes plenty of practice to master the different combos. The varied missions are entertaining and will never bore you. The game has more replay value if you decide to play Vergil’s Downfall DLC, which stars Dante’s brother Vergil.

*NOTICE* I just finished playing this mod and here is my final verdict.
MINERVA: Metastasis, what may appear as a generic, fanmade Half-Life 2 mod on the outside actually appears more on the inside. I have played many Half-Life 2 mods and this one definetely goes on my list of one of the most interesting if not one of the best Half-Life 2 mods I have ever played. The mod is mysterious which really fits into the Half-Life universe, the story is told via text which may seem horrible on paper with many flaws, which it does don't get me wrong, but it gets the job done and in a way gives MINERVA its character.
The level design in MINERVA is very similar to Half-Life 2's level design yet also has some variation with the mod being more maze-like than Half-Life 2's which in my honest opinion gives the mod more variation and gives an immersion factor to it. The mod is also surprisingly challenging compared to Half-Life 2 and I was playing on Normal difficulty! I mean its not rage inducing hard but the beginning levels do stir up a challenge with the mod throwing enemies at you in tight corridor-like locations. It the kind of hard difficulty which does test you, makes you think and makes you aware of your surroundings and makes you think of plans to take on the many Combine foot soldiers and aliens head crabs and zombies that you will encounter.
There is a lot more to say about MINERVA, the design of the levels and the detail that the mod developer placed are truly amazing, the gameplay and pacing is spot on and the mod just truly feels interesting to play. Many things in MINERVA are also interesting with the themes of Greek Mythology being in the game with the Narrator telling you your mission objectives via text.
The story in MINERVA like I said is mysterious with a lot of what is going on is confusing but atleast there's forums to explain whats going on. A lot with MINERVA also fits in with the Half-Life universe that I feel that someday Valve should incorporate into that next Half-Life game that we are all waiting for. When you get to a certain part involving a portal you'll see what I mean, not spoiling it that is.
In the end MINERVA is a must play, it really makes you happy to play a good Half-Life 2 mod, its short yet sweet, and plus it makes you think more as to what Half-Life 3 could be.

If you enjoy the card game, you'll enjoy this. But you absolutely don't need to know the card game to be able to pick this up. It is a well done port of the card game; it does all the fiddly math bits that can bog down the tabletop version. The developer video casts of games can help you learn how to better utilize the cards in unfamiliar decks. The variant unlock system is fun, providing a challenge for those who want it. The added multiplayer option allows you to play with your friends online. And the new weekly one-shot games will keep you coming back to replay. There's plenty more expansion content in the pipeline to keep it fresh and exciting.

This is the best job I habe ever seen of turning a board/card game into a video game.  The interface is well designed and responsive and the layout manages to show you everythjng you need without getting overly cluttered.
It should be noted that, unlike most multiplayer card games, SotM is actually also fun to play by yourself, and the steam version makes this really convenient.

With the addition of the weekly one-shot there's a separate reason to play this game, which finally edges it into the "thumbs up" camp.
It's still the boardgame, aptly converted into electronic form, so if you can get multiplayer going it should be way fun, it was just that the single player option was somewhat lacking in reason to why you should keep playing. (The "unlocking variants" is occasionally a bit too far-fetched to be fun. Plus it's a bit too secret about what you should do - especially for the more esoteric solutions.)

MINERVA is a beautiful, well paced mod for Half Life 2. Taking place on an island occupied by the combine, it features fantastic level design that rivals that of vanilla Half Life 2. The areas weave together in a very believable way and every area is shrouded by an air of mystery. Also noteworthy is the expert use of verticality. I often found I was able to use this to my advantage against the numerous, well placed enemies in MINERVA. Not only are the areas well designed, but each is also visibly distinct. Because of this, I never found myself lost for long. I even stopped once to admire the setting sun reflecting off the ocean's waves. The Story is engaging enough. It does a good job of adding to the mystery of the island, although it would have benefited from proper voice acting as it is sometimes difficult to read during intense gunfights.
Over all, MINERVA provides some of the best Half Life 2 content I have experienced. Anyone with a copy of Half Life 2 owes it to themselves to give this a try.

When you start Secret Files: Tunguska, you will notice several things, but what stands out immediately is the voice acting, being at the best of times, tiresome, somewhat embarrassing and even downright abysmal. To be fair, a few good actors do a good job, but between the unusual “never use contractions” thing, the odd phrasing and peculiar word choice, the “breaking of the fourth-wall” and the main characters voice choice being all over the place in terms of quality, you’d have a hard time bringing yourself to finishing the game.
Puzzles were regularly the “combine some items” types which are generally a staple for any self-proclaimed adventure game, but they were about as contrived as “puzzle” of this type can get. Before long, you would be sick to death of guessing which inane impromptu tool you are supposed to make from the items in your inventory.
So by finally finishing the game, you would see the extent of its dull, inane, meandering story; hear your fair share of sub-standard voice acting; you’d enjoy plenty of robotic animations; you’d play your fair share of 'hunt for the pixels that you can click on to find an item as you would assume was there more times than you’d liked; and you had gone through puzzles that, had if you had played the game organically, probably would have meant resorting to systematically trying to combine everything in my inventory until you stumbled across the right pairing.
I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone unless they'd run out of other adventure games to play and needed one that would probably would have taken them a long time to get through.

This is a pretty good game! It has a single plot line so it plays kinda like an interactive graphic novel, but it's pretty cool anyway. It has some humor and the plot was enough to keep me on the edge of my seat. I actually stayed up all night (accidentally, I swear!) because I wanted to know what was going to happen next. The speech is a little odd here and there but not bad considering the era the game was made and the graphics are really good.
The game has no tutorial, so it took me a little while to figure out that you click to move and right click to examine things and left click to interact. That sounds simple but it isn't so much so, as you'll see, because of the inventory items and needing to combine them. You have to select the item, then move the cursor over the other item or spot until it lights up for interaction. One beef I had was that the game has her (or Max) speak something whenever you examine something, but you don't always know what spot will go to what, so they may repeat something several times. Luckily you can fast-forward what they say or it could get REALLY irritating. I think most of the length of the game comes from listening to the characters talk; it's a pretty long game (much longer than I was expecting). It felt like around 26 hours? but it might vary depending on how fast you play and what you do.
Also, there's a magnifying glass you can click on in every scene to see everything you can look at or interact with and the location of movement arrows to go to new locations (so you don't have to guess where to click.) Periodically you'll hear the sound of an old-fashioned typewriter, signifying that you have another journal entry. A lot of them merely chronicle your adventures but some contain useful information that you need to solve puzzles, so it's helpful to look at them.
The puzzles aren't always intuitive, but they are varied and interesting. Avid puzzle gamers will enjoy this game! There's also some beautiful scenery to enjoy as you solve your way through the story. I was pretty amazed by some of the graphics. Overall, great game, and I'd recommend it for puzzle lovers.

So Spec Ops; The Line, is the darkest third person shooter single player campaign I've ever played. But I will say this, it's a very affecting one. The game follows three men in Delta Force out in a post-apocalyptic Dubai to rescue civilians, but things go south very fast. The story begins to question you almost like this "Are you really a hero?" The game is directly based on the novel Heart of Darkness (Joseph Conrad), which gives the force to get it's messages on heroism across in effective and powerful ways. One of the chatacters is even a nod to the author of the book. I say to give it a try for the single player experience. The multiplayer is just tacked on and unless your willing to screw around with your friends in a private lobby, it's dead. Also, the gameplay mechanics are just good old run, aim, and cover shooter mechanics. If your okay with this, then this is disturbing, sometimes beautifully constructed story, using it's Dubai setting to create a hellish atmoshpere that builds with tension and fear.
Amazing. Spec Ops: The Line is a brilliantly executed deconstruction of its genre.

DmC tries too hard. "Dante is cool in this one," it says, "see these girls? He totally had sex with her last night. Sex is cool, right?"
"And look at the bad guys," it gushes, "they're metaphors for corporate sleazebags who try to keep society dumb and obedient. Enslavement through faux (Fox?) news and sugary drinks! Get it?"
"You're the Resistance. You're standing up to the demons (corporate overlords) and insulting them in their faces! Ever wanted to say '♥♥♥♥ you' to the Man? Dude, we have you covered, there's so many '♥♥♥♥ you' lines in this game that you're going to feel empowered as all♥♥♥♥♥♥"
There's the seed for a good plot in there somewhere, buried beneath piles of awkward dialogue, oversimple characterization and the promotion of social-commentary-that-should-be-subtext into neon-lettered, 50-foot high signage. Dante isn't really likeable, the storytelling is awkward and I was embarrassed several times watching really badly-written dialogue exchanges. Worse, I found myself cheering for Virgil, the more put-together brother who bothers thinking ahead to what's going to happen after he and Dante bring down the Evil Overlord. What's wrong with being the guy in charge of picking up the pieces after the world is turned upside down, again? I guess it's bad because DmC has a very marked punk ideology and becoming the authorities goes against that?
So why do I recommend DmC? The gameplay is pretty good, and that should be the main reason for you to buy this. Not as good as Devil May Cry 3, but then what is?

Level design perfection.
I have not played a single game with such deep level design in my life. The map will function without you. The NPCs have schedules and triggers and you have some minor control over that. The level is a beautifully deep clockwork machine running on many levels.
You are the wrench that breaks the clock.
Agent 47 is the one part of the level that can change everything. Fashion Show? Cancelled. Boat Party? Cancelled. I have never seen before the amount that a single action can derail everything so that you, the master assassin, can swoop in on your unfortunate victim to kill them in a miriad of ways.
Shoot them, drown them, shank them, choke them, snap their necks, drop a chandelier on them, snipe them, bomb them, poison them, clobber them, it is your choice.
The maps have near endless replayability because of the Escalation contracts and other modes. I enjoyed the Challenges not because of achievements or as a completionist but as a tool to learn the huge maps. I learned disguise locations, object locations, NPC schedules, the triggers they react to, escape routes and such all through playing the challenges. This meant that when the time came to play an escalation contract I was a master of the map!
Highly recommended, easily the best sandbox assassination game on the market.

I first played this game when it was in a Games Magazine in October 2005. I've I first played this game when it was in a Games Magazine in October 2005. I've loved it ever since, and It's still my favourite game. Being released in 2002, it obviously can't hold a candle to any new game in terms of graphics, but I STILL love it's looks. I've played it through 4 times before, and just had the urge to play it again, and thought "I might as well get it on steam" and am now writing this review while it downloads ^^
There are two main aspects that make Divinity to my favourite Game of all times:
The First is the incredibly deep World and characters it provides, the quests you receive tell you about their lives, be it the soldier who asks you for a feign death potion, to go home to his fiancé, the Orc who tries to right his people's wrongs, or the ♥♥♥♥ing Brat who asks you to do whatever♥♥♥♥♥♥he can't be bothered to. All of these define the characters more than Skyrim for example did. Also the two Skeletons that explode upon Philosophizing about how they're held together without any flesh or muscles.
The second aspect is the Music. In Divine Divinity, as well as Divinity 2: Ego Draconis, the music (composed by Kirill Pokrovsky)  fills you with excitement and tension, always fitting the Area you're in. In fact, my most played song on Itunes it "On the Brink of Defeat" from Divine Divinity.
I can only say that Divine Divinity is a game you HAVE to play, if you're a fan of RPGs in which the focus lies in the story and characters.

Can't believe I never took the time to play this sooner.  As far as RPGs go it's in the big leagues.  It starts off slow, and the 1st major challenge is a little much, but the freaking thing sucks you in like crack.  It's smooth cracksmoke sailing from there on out as far as I can tell.  The closest thing I can think of to describe it is Diablo 1 with a much much much bigger world and combat a hair behind it (not much, just minor stuff).  Half of the problem is missing convenience controls like a stand-still-while♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥button, and not-so-much-ease in other combat controls like switching weapons (lots of things you can hotkey, some things seem like you can't though).  The other half is the engine itself: it doesn't schedule work well, so when it gets enough on the screen at once it starts ignoring control input, which engine design should never allow.  It happens *rarely* though (so far only with lots of projectiles in flight), and it may have been fine at release (coulda just been DX6- approaches to drawing that weren't properly dealt with in the update), so it's not a big deal for me.  The issue shows itself in lack of Steam overlay support too, by the way.  Aggravating, but the game is way way worth it.  The story is as big and seemingly non-linear as the world, and the number of quests and quest complexity matches it.  Alongside that is significant ability customization, and different layouts do seem to matter in most ways you'd expect.  It's got the cheeziest humor, so bad it's good, and speaking of that the voice acting is freaking horrrrrific.  The next one in the series better be as bad, I'm looking forward to the (un)intended humor.  Best of all, it's one of those games where you can tell how much the dev team loved it--there's attention to detail all around, and it wasn't rushed out so fast it didn't get needed polish.  All in all, 94/100 for me.

Like leaves on the trees when the autumn comes, I peered into the prodigious ravine they call the Steam Store and found this diamond in the rough layed out before me. "$2.00" it whispered into my ears and I was sold - I knew I had to get this; boy was I delighted with the treat I found in stored for me.
Many claim they can see the end of times upon them with this coming era but I stayed vigilant. I gave hope to the fallen kings of men and entered a realm unknownst to any before me. It was this day that I found out what it meant to be the Chosen.
My journey started like any other - I was weak, heedful of my surroundings, aware that any danger I find may soon be my very last. Destiny called however, and I knew my place was among the Gods. I stepped forward into a brave new world and accepted the very fate thrusted on me.
Orcs struck, evil mages lashed out with their foul magicks, knights that knew no loyalty saw fit to bring me to their knees; yet I stood firmed. I slayed everyone and everything - from friends to tyrants. None shall stand before my blade and see the light of day again.
"Monster!", they yelled at me. "♥♥♥♥  you", I said in return as I stuck the tip end of my weapon up their haughty buttocks. Tyrants and dragons alike would fall to my sleight of hand as I became the all-powerful, omniscient being the prophets themselves had called to pass.
In my final hour I would lay waste to the Lord of Chaos. His reign was over and my destiny, fulfilled. Men shall not know the end times again as long as I breathe. With one final sigh I gazed back behind me...
What have I done.
In my wake, nothing was left. I had saved the world but at the cost of the world itself. I was but a lone God overseeing a world with no one - how could I ever be the Chosen when there's nothing left to protect? I fell to my knees and cried; there was only one thing left to do. I pulled out my trusted blade that had been by my side this entire time and made some potions out of the nearby red mushrooms.

Good developers, good game, good price.
You can easily sink dozens of hours working on a single prison, or trying to escape one you built.
It is a simulator, of sorts. You build a prison, take in prisoners, meet grants, take in prisoners, expand your prison, take in prisoners, hire more security, take in more prisoners, have to deal with assassination and escape attempts, take in more prisoners, and have fun while doing it.
It is fairly simple, but has dozens of mechanics which game the game unique and worthwhile. Riots, random events, failure conditions (all toggleable), fires, prisoners attempting to tunnel out, stab guards, stir up trouble, even expand their gangs.
It also features some powerful, yet subtle AOI logic gates and mechanics.
A strong modding community also helps a great deal, especially with the workshop. There isn't much more I can say without repeating myself or others. Play it, and realize you've spent 30 hours playing.

The story is weaved together nicely. It starts off very gently, just giving you a few clues and then you get the bigger picture. Even though there's a lot of supernatural elements in the game, it was done in such a way it didn't make the characters feel out of place. Nina is as a young woman who has no superpowers, but is pulled into a mystery where she must confront these strange things. It makes you relate to her and her own worries.
I found the story very good. It kept me interested and wanted me to really finish the game. The game makes you travel to many different areas in the world. I liked the change of environment and due to the complicated story, it also makes sense as to why Nina would travel all these areas without it feeling out of place. The new places allows for lots of exploring on it's own and are not confined to a few areas.
Finding out the clues are mostly not that difficult. There are some very clever clues, like needing to look at paintings and see what it represents in numbers to open up a safe. There are some objects in the game which are annoyingly tiny on the screen, as you see each area and room from quite a distance. It can be quite annoying when you have to click on an itty bitty edge of a carpet, as the pointer doesn't register unless you are close enough to the specific area. Thankfully there aren't a lot of these.
The game is good at providing ideas of what to do next. Nina will make comments about her environment and gives good clues about how to solve things. It doesn't spoil anything or leave it too easy, just enough to make you think things through. At one point, Nina reads a poem which indicates what items she needs, masked though the words. At some points in the game, you have two characters to control. This is a great idea which works out very well, you swap between them in the same area, so that they can complete things in different parts of the building. Clever use of mechanics and storytelling.
I admit, sometimes I got very frustrated as I knew what I wanted to do, yet the characters kept complaning they couldn't, despite needing the item. Sometimes you have to prepare a lot of other things before you can use the idea first at hand. At one part, Nina needs to climb an area which she does awfully slow, then if you forget an item or need to go back and try something else, she will slowly get back the same way. Going back and forth between these two could be very tedious, but thankfully they shorten the time you have to watch it, to not waste time.
The mini-games weren't annoyingly complicated, they were difficult enough to manage on my own without having to look at some guide. One of them is pushing lighted buttons until all lights are out, and certain buttons only turn off or light certain lights. There aren't a lot of these, thankfully,
There is some funny dialogue at times, which lightens the mood when you're stuck for a while figuring things out. Nina will usually make quirky or sarcastic comments about the items she tries using or the situations she has been in.
The english voicework isn't really that enjoyable, so I wish they could have had an option for the original german voice acting. Nina's voice is in particular very straining for the ears. I can tolerate her voice due to the dialogue being fun at times. I don't know what it is about her voice that bothers me, but I think it is the fact that I couldn't honestly tell how old Nina is supposed to be. She sounds like she is 10, but she looks like she's about 17. Her voice just sounds really childish.
Overall, I enjoyed this game and piecing the story together. Even though the ending is a bit over the top. There are some nice cutscenes in the game and the ending credits features what happened to all the characters after the game ends. Some are very funny to read.

A difficult, time consuming, fun game.
Super Meat Boy is a platformer, similar to Super Mario Bros., but a LOT more difficult.
There are no checkpoints: no chances: and the requirement of skill.
There are 8 worlds to this game.
But when you complete them all, you still haven't completed the game!
You now must face the ultimate challenge.
The Dark Worlds.
A Dark World is a certain version of a particular level in the light world/normal world. It is very similar to the level in the light world, except one thing: it is a lot harder.
To complete World 5-8 in the Dark World without dying, is absolutely near-impossible, and if you have done-so: I congratulate you, as these levels are near impossible, let alone to do them all in 1 shot without even dying.
I reccomend this game, for the default price, and most certainly if it is on sale.

Sentinels is a very fun, very well-made game. You control a team of 3-5 comic book heroes and battle a comic book villain in a combat system that uses cards. The game is fun in single-player, local multi-player, and online multi-player modes.
Pros:
+ Each hero and villain has a unique deck, giving each combination of heroes and villains a pretty unique feeling. In fact, each hero has a kind of "theme" that makes their gameplay style unique. Likewise for the villains.
+ UI is very well-designed. All the information you need is right there. You even have the option to rewind the game if you accidentally play a wrong card, or your action has unintended consequences.
+ Good level of challenge and balance. Some ability to customize the difficulty by changing the heroes, villain, environment, or switching to "advanced" mode.
Cons:
- The base game doesn't include very much content. The base game was almost a demo in my mind. However, I ended up liking it enough to buy the expansion packs, which vastly expand the number of heroes, villains, and environments to choose from.
