Ori is a really well-controlling metroidvania with an emphasis on platforming. It is a fairly challenging game that occasionally veers into frustrating territory, but is compelling enough that I wanted to come back to it - even if I had to stop playing for a bit when the game was kicking my [proverbial]. With great gameplay and stunning visuals, Ori could have been something truly special, but problems with the story combined with a couple of minor annoyances mean that it is 'merely' a very good game.
Despite my problems with the game, I did enjoy it enough to continue playing post-credits, in order to get 100%. Didn't seem to get any special 'true ending' for collecting everything, so I recommend just playing the game until you finish it. A very good game indeed.
These things annoyed me enough to want to talk about them, because it is clear that this game wants to be a strong, emotional story despite not really providing a compelling narrative to support this. I got legitimately frustrated at points, but the quality of the rest of the game means that they didn't stop the game from being enjoyable in general.

Good developers, good game, good price.
You can easily sink dozens of hours working on a single prison, or trying to escape one you built.
It is a simulator, of sorts. You build a prison, take in prisoners, meet grants, take in prisoners, expand your prison, take in prisoners, hire more security, take in more prisoners, have to deal with assassination and escape attempts, take in more prisoners, and have fun while doing it.
It is fairly simple, but has dozens of mechanics which game the game unique and worthwhile. Riots, random events, failure conditions (all toggleable), fires, prisoners attempting to tunnel out, stab guards, stir up trouble, even expand their gangs.
It also features some powerful, yet subtle AOI logic gates and mechanics.
A strong modding community also helps a great deal, especially with the workshop. There isn't much more I can say without repeating myself or others. Play it, and realize you've spent 30 hours playing.

A return to Blood Money form tarnished by terrible progression and always online.
Hitman games live or die on their levels, and this entry has the most expansive and detailed levels yet.
They may even be too expansive, twice as many levels at half the size would still give plenty of different paths while significantly increasing variety.
Unfortunately its dragged down by the progression and always online model.
Unlocking gear, even playing on "professional" difficulty requires grinding the same level over and over again to earn experience points from challenges.
This means you can't use something as simple as a sniper rifle, triggered explosives, electronic lockpicks, or certain poisons until you've reached the right level by replaying missions over and over again.
Professional difficulty is the only right way to play a Hitman game, yet to unlock it here you need to play each level 10+ times. There's no way to play the real difficulty without wasting tens of hours grinding the same levels over and over.
All of this progression is locked off in the offline version. Although you can use items you already unlocked, you can't earn any experience to unlock more without being online.
There isn't a single feature in this game which requires an always online connection. The few pieces of content which do require connecting to the internet could easily be designed to only connect when necessary (scoreboards and player made contracts).
Many IO made contracts outside of the main story are also locked to online-only.

Being a nephilim with the destiny of killing the Demon King is a dangerous way to live storywise, but gameplaywise it’s fun, brutal and stylish. Fans of the original series should look at this game as a prequel, after all, the main characters are different at first, but in the end they are the characters old fans loved or loved to hate. That said, this game is a good way to introduce new fans to the franchise, even though some things won’t be the same, like some plot details and the gameplay.
This is the story of the rise of Dante, from being a junkie that has supernatural potential but decides to use it to fool around to the demon hunter, protector of humanity. He fights in a world where a Demon King controls humans through debt, who controls the mass media and has a line of products that gets its consumers docile. Dante is introduced to the truth, by his brother, Vergil, the leader of an organization that seeks to free the world by killing the demons that enthrall it and by merging the human world with Limbo, the surreal place where you’ll face your opponents and whatever the environment changes.
The gameplay is what makes the game shine. There is a variety of moves to take down a variety of monsters. Combining heavy with light attacks followed by ranged attack, then pulling some other poor victim with a red chain to do your personal pattern on him is your fun and their bane. Three ranged weapons and three swords, along with the characters abilities is enough to make you love killing demons and enough to make you replay the game just to get all the moves.  Aside from the standard powers, the angelic and demonic ones are what make you feel most in control, by using the former to get to the enemies and for crowd control, and the later to pull them to you and deliver them heavy blows.  There are many types of difficulties; while the typical three are present(easy, normal, hard), after completing the game you’ll have a harder mode that serves as a new game plus, followed by one where everyone(including you) dies from one hit and the last one, where only you die from one hit, difficulties that present another reason to replay the game for those who enjoy the combat or hunt for achievments.
There are keys in secret places that open specific doors in the game, doors that lead you to secret levels, which can be challenging, depending on their tier. Aside from keys, there are lost souls that need to be killed for the sake of being a completitionist.
This is one of those games I wished I’d bought earlier, because it was definitely worth the price. It’s entertaining, stylish and the story, although it seems to be made for the teen audience, is engaging and by the end of the game, you’ll know it’s a memorable game

If you are the type who likes to unravel story, conquer enemies and levels, upgrading and powering up and unlocking achievements and abilities and cosmetics along the way...this won't be for you.
Interaction at times can be stiff or finnicky.
Would be nice if the starting dialogue was tailored based on villain, heroes present, and environment. For example, maybe rivals skip the small talk and just diss each other.
For example, with multiple card discards, it seems odd to go one at a time with confirmation, instead of batch selecting with a highlight and then confirming.
You will probably have to do a little research to learn to play well early on. Stick to low difficulty stuff until you learn your interactions.
Sentinels of the Multiverse is an adaption of a physical board/card game. It offers an accessible, challenging, and varied experience to anyone willing to put in a little time to learn the intricacies. It is a faithful reproduction, balanced, satisfying, and the developers seem solid with a lot of community interaction and involvement. The comic styled theme is deftly executed, which adds a lot to the experience and charm of this title.
Your gameplay will consist mostly of strategizing: you pick what heroes to use, villain to face, and environment to do so in; by carefully choosing what cards to play, what cards to use, and the order certain events happen in, you can have a large degree of impact on how well or poorly you perform in your fights against evil. The tutorial covers the basics and is comprehensive, but can leave you lost as to how you are supposed to properly utilize heroes, or what heroes may be good for specific tasks. My advice in this regard is that no matter how you approach this game, if you are new to it, stick with the same heroes and an easy villian initially, and you'll learn soon enough.
The expansions massively increase the size of the roster, but even with the base game, there is a large variety of options for villains and heroes of which all feel unique; offering you the ability to adapt or to play the way you want with a large degree of freedom. While certain heroes are definitely more suited to certain villains, you don't ultimately have to use them to be successful.
In Sentinals of the Multiverse, you put a card into play at the start of your turn; this card may be a one off, a piece of equipment that stays on the field, or an on-going effect/power that can be utilized every turn. After you play a card, you can use one of many powers, of which each hero has a unique variety, as well as their own inbuilt power. Normally, you can use one power per turn; these powers can be anything from drawing one or two cards, healing your team, damaging the enemy or yourself, dealing low damage to many (or all) targets, or buffing your fellow teammates. Equipment and powers tend to fuel your cards--in turn fueling your hero--and be where most heroes derive the bulk of their strength or utility. After you have run out of powers you can use, you will draw a card, and then your turn will end. Pretty simple, right? It's really the interactions that make up the intracacy of this game, which is beautiful, because the actual act of playing is simple and easy, but the ability to do so well is entirely about your knowledge and cunning. This makes for satisfying defeats and triumphs.
The art could certainly be better in some respects, but the style is consistent and very well executed. There could stand to be more animations and effects. The comic style lends itself to nice and quick transitions and creative menu graphics. Everything is bright, colorful, and vivid, so you really get that saturday morning hero vibe at all times.
Well, being that this isn't exactly a AAA 3D game, I can't comment on lighting, shaders, the quality of the models and animations, etc. so that's about all you'd want to keep in mind.
The music in SotM is very pleasing. I almost don't want to start games because I really like the main menu track especially. The sounds utilized for the various damage type are actually quite fitting and have their own charm. I really like the sound of the cards. Sound seems underutilized in SotM, and I feel like it could desperately use some subtle sounds when highlighting menu options and especially when clicking them. Well, the good news is, you don't really need much sound in a title like this, so it doesn't have as much impact as it would in a 3D adventure FPS.
Sentinels of the Multiverse is a great card game for those familiar or unfamiliar with the physical game. It offers a lot of pros, with almost no significant cons. It's easy to pick up, but it might take you a bit to learn how to utilize heroes to their fullest. The graphics and music will keep you pleased while you are sitting there trying to think your way through anything, or waiting on a friend in the newly implemented multiplayer.

This is easily one of the best Half Life 2 mods. It offers a comfortably similar mission style to compliment Half Life 2. Minerva may be short in overall game hours, but if you enjoyed Half Life 2 you will definitely enjoy this reminiscent detour.
Minerva offers exactly what you would expect from what is a mod side story that is intent on delivering a unique and enjoyable experience with purposely simlar gameplay to Half Life 2.
I would highly reccomend Minerva to anyone that enjoyed the Half life 2 singleplayer experience, but is still craving more of what made Half Life 2 one of the most atmospheric as well as story driven FPS games ever made. You will not be dissapointed.

I dare say this is damn near a masterpiece. On more than one occasion, this phenomenal game is better than Half-Life 2 itself. The level design is some of the smartest I've ever played. Its pacing is also a great mix of suspense and tension, never leaving me bored the way some sections of HL2 did. Minerva's use of the HL universe is also fantastic. It cleverly builds on the existing material and pushes to delve deeper into the Combine's sinister plots.
The game isn't without its problems however. I found myself lost twice, having to look up the solution in a walkthrough. The problem would have easily been caught by a larger QA team, so it's hard to hold that against the creator. I also would really have preferred a voiced narration instead of blocks of text. What a dissonant experience this game is! At first, it excites you with the production and the set pieces. Then it gets quite repetitive and a bit boring cover shooter. Then the story takes a very dark and twisted turn. The game is still a repetitive cover shooter all the way through and its gameplay mechanics get old really fast. It is not a long game, but the gameplay overstays its welcome in the first few hours. The cutscenes and the dialogues during the game are what drives you forward to find out more and then it grips you so much - you are willing to "suffer" through the uninspired shooting and covering.
A couple of scenes work really well. A few, punch you in a gut and make you feel miserable. The second half of the game is not fun, narrative-wise. This is a one dark story. Despite a few endings - none is a happy one and the game won't leave you feel satisfied and pleased with yourself. Good stuff!
If you love shooting and blowing stuff up, if you enjoy war violence - the game is for you and is a great fit in all but the story. If you are not into those things - the gameplay is worth your patience for the plot and the characters.
Also, the twist at the end might send you playing the game again, so there's a bit of a replayability factor there.
So in summary, good graphics, quite a few great set pieces and scenes, derivative shooting and covering and a one great story you will remember long after you've finished the game.

I would highly reccomend Spec Ops: The Line to anyone. The main draw of the game is its narrative, as you explore an essentially post-apocalyptic Dubai that is tearing itself apart in Civil War. The themes of the narrative focus on war and its destructive power. Spec Ops: The Line really tries to convey how destructive war can be. Your character is often forced to make several moral choices where there is no good outcome, no matter what you do.
There are very few games that can make me actually learn something or feel something new through the power of their narrative. If a shooter that actually tells a compelling story sounds like something that would interest you, then I highly reccomend playing Spec Ops: The Line.

DMC Devil May Cry has certainly been the victim to a bunch of hate, some of it warranted, but most of it just nitpicky and unnecessary. If you go into this game with an open mind and are aware that is a reboot and a reimagining of the tale of Dante then you will be more than able to thoroughly enjoy yourself, However if you go into it expecting Devil May Cry 5 then you will be sadly disappointed.
The game still focuses on the stringing together fast paced, brutal combos in an action-oriented combat that system that were so prominent in the previous entries. And the game still offers the style ranking system based on how well you perform in combat. But while the game still focuses heavily on the two key components that made the franchise famous…It does make them incredibly more “accessible” to players who have never played any of the previous entries, which wouldn’t be a bad thing seeing as the game offers seven different difficulty levels, However only three are unlocked from the start of the game and all three are simple enough where you can easily breeze through and get “Savage” or better on most levels. So unless you truly want to get some form of challenge from the game you’ll have to do a few play-throughs of the game before you really find yourself struggling to chain together a good enough combo to actually feel proud of yourself when you hear the omnipresent announcer proclaim “Savage!”. The oversimplification isn’t all bad, the game does offer incredibly streamlined controls that allow for lengthy combos to be chained together while swapping through all 8 weapons and both grappling hooks on the fly without any obstructive interface or item swapping. The natural feel provided from the streamlined controls is easily one of the game’s greatest features.
Besides the dumbed down difficulty and scoring system the game is also hindered by its generic level and enemy design. None of the design in the game feels new or fresh; it’s just a bunch of dark, glum, narrow corridors with hordes of the same bland enemies with some fairly enjoyable platforming elements sprinkled in between. Not only are the designs of both the enemies and levels bland, but the main characters themselves are also both predictable, and flat. This isn’t the bias hate rambling of a fan-boy who’s♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥they changed Dante’s hair color, I’m honestly fine with the appearance of all the characters, even the new Emo Dante, but the game does offer plenty of alternative skins for those who are too turned off by the emo vibe.
The visuals of the game are another one of the games strong points, offering easily some of the best visual graphics to come out of a Capcom game to date. And the game is certainly a solid PC port, during my playthroughs of the game I managed to stay well over 100fps without any dips that could potentially interfere with the fast paced combo chaining combat.  The soundtrack of the game is honestly a hit or miss based on your view of how you feel about Electronic Body Music, as the soundtrack consists primarily of the band Combichrist, I personally enjoy it however to each their own.
After hearing the review thus far you would probably expect me to poorly rate the game, but its actually quite the opposite. Despite all of the complaints and flaws that this game has, it somehow manages to get passed all of that and provide an experience that is genuinely fun. If you look at the game you can easily pick apart the design flaws and nerfed difficulty, but even with all the flaws, DMC Devil May Cry proves to be an excellent game with strong enough legs to stand on its own and not be judged based on the previous entries in the franchise….because that’s the whole point of a reboot, to break away from the past and become something new. So don’t let the look of the game turn you off, pick up a controller and play through the game on the hardest difficulty you can and experience the beauty of the fast paced, stylish, streamlined, chaotic fun that you will have.

The game looks a bit like Diablo 2 (isometric) but plays different, instead of holding the mouse to attack you can just click once to keep attacking. You can pause the whole game (with spacebar) to relax and take a look at your potions and equipment. Health (and stats in general) doesn’t increase so dramatically on higher levels. Also the whole world is not infested by demons (like in diablo) and you will meet a lot of friendly NPC's in the world.
It's a lot bigger than you would think judging by first glance, there are caves and underground areas and there are always people around to talk with that can give you something to do, despite some of them having trivial problems. I'm level 23 for god sake and slaughter orcs in almost two hits, I don't care about your lost kitty little girl! But then again some of these quests do have a more suprising outcome.
The game does not give you any visual hints of where to go and what to do regarding quests, you should just read the note in the quest-log. The main plot also gets a little bit lost when you are running around trying to get quests and level up. So you might end up not really knowing where to go and just wander into uncharted territory hoping to get something useful. At least that is how I go about it.
Do however note that the game gets a little cryptic at the end you might just wander past stuff you were supposed to be doing something and by pressing alt (to see items etc.) you can't find everything you need all the time. It had me search stuff in the internet otherwise I would've just been stuck a whole lot more times, maybe old fashioned game design is to blame here.
Overall it's a really fun game despite the flaws, worth the price if you like to play isometric RPGs. I also have to say that I find the combat in this more satisfying than for example titan quest. Though it does sometimes send enemies at you that are way too strong but which you could just defeat later on.

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne looks, plays, and feels like it's what the first entry in the series  would have been if they'd spent a few more years and a few more dollars on it. Detective Payne has traded his ridiculous, frozen smirk of the past game for a fully-rendered face with lips that actually move in the rare occurrence that he utters something out loud. The TV shows that can be watched on scattered TV sets have been similarly flesh out. Not only do they tell longer, more complete stories, but those stories tie into the game's plot thematically. Even the platforming elements that made the original Max Payne seem overall less professional have been toned down to the point of unobtrusiveness. And of course, there's still a full shooting gallery worth of mooks to mow down in bullet-time, all of which is still broken up by graphic novel-styled cutscenes. This sequel is simply a second helping of Payne with a few improvements thrown into the mix - almost a continuation. Loose ends left by its predecessor are tied up along the way and this distinct tale finishes up a little neater than the last. It feels like the punctuation on Max's story, and though more of this good thing would be welcome, it feels complete.

The game requires DirectX 9 to run, and the installer doesn't install DirectX 9 at all, so you're left with a game you can't run. The DirectX installer offered on Microsoft's website says it works on Windows 8, but it actually doesn't.

Just like the conversion of books into movies and TV shows, card or board games into digital formats can often miss crucial features or ruin things with horrible AI.  I've fallen prey to this before with my digital board/card game collection on my phone.  Handelabra however, man, they've done it just perfectly.
This game was made with constant communication between the digital creators and the original creators, and it reflects so well.  The rules are faithful, and any uncertainties that crop up in the physical game are ironed out here by the original creators (Greater Than Games).  As a result, not only does this play smoothly and faithfully to the game as one would hope for, but it also serves as a definitive FAQ on rules.  Fantastic!
The concept of the game and the mechanics behind it are incredibly simple; A group of heroes need to take down a villain in an over-the-top comic book boss fight.  That's it.  The rules are equally simple, essentially boiling down to "Do what each step of the cards say, in conjunction with the turn order".  It's simple enough in the physical form, but the digital version handles all that for you and ensure you can literally sit down and play, especially with their short and sweet tutorial that explains the interface and base concepts to achieve this.  In case something works a little differently than you'd anticipated, there's even a rewind button (albeit with a reasonable limit on just how far back you can go), allowing you to reassess what you were trying to accomplish.
The theme has the potential to be very rich, and this digital format really brings that out, with some music and small graphical displays to highlight this.  I would recommend that those wanting to truly embrace the feel of it to read the flavour text on each card, as it really helps bring it to life with the narrative.
With the new multiplayer update, the largest feature lacking from the game is now rectified, making this the most faithful and enjoyable digital rendition of a board/card game I've played, a spot previously owned by Talisman, for those not able to play these games in person, or instead preferring to just have a digital game handle the rules and turn orders on their behalf.
The only other feature I'd like to see is an integrated story mode, as I find this helps to make up for the lack of direct human interaction that these games are supposed to have.  However, the fanbase for this game is creative and always in pursuit of new challenges, meaning that such a thing can be found around the forums without too much difficulty.  These range from general storylines to increasingly more difficult challenge modes, in addition to the integrated achievements the game has for unlocking extra cards (promo cards, minor variants of original hero or villain cards - given out to those who pre-ordered the physical boxes of the game and its expansions, truly minimising content variation between the digital and physical variants of the game).

Sentinels of the Multiverse ts a card driven co-op combat game where you do boss fight after boss fight. The game has simple rules and is easy to pickup and play. Each hero has an unique deck and style of play to give them flavor. Heroes fits a variety of themes with a wealth of powers and abilities to cater to many different strategies and styles of play. For Example Legacy excels at buffing team damage, healing, and with the right setup can tank damage for the entire team, Tachyon is a flexible utility character who is all about burning through her deck with rapid card draw and multiple card plays, she gets more powerful as her discard pile grows.
One of the joys of the game is finding and discovering how powers can interact with other heroes to compliment and feed off of each other and make devastating combinations. Example: Legacy does "Heroic Interception" an "ongoing" type power to make the team immune to damage or "Take Down" an "ongoing" type power to lock the villain deck, then the Visionary uses "Mental Divergence" (Take an ongoing out of the trash and put on top of the deck) to make those Legacy powers a retrievable resource. Ra uses some fire damage to hit Absolute Zero which helps Absolute Zero fuel "Thermal Shockwave" (Fire damage he takes can be converted into a Cold area of effect attack) to wipe the board of minions.
Villains have their own decks full of powerful detriments, damage, and minions to make battles challenging. Villains have a normal mode (or form) but also a mode where they "flip" when they meet a certain condition (think of it as a final "desperation" form) where they will have empowered effects that often raise the stakes and accelerate the battle.
The Environment is another factor and is like another entity onto itself. The environment has its own complete deck and place in the turn order. Most environment effects are minor detriments or boons for the heroes, but some can be brutal and game ending if you aren't prepared. With clever play you can use the environment to great effect against the villain. For example: In "Insula Primalis" (Think of Xmen's Savage Land) There is a card "Velociraptor Pack" that attacks the target with the lowest HP, So you can weaken enemies for velociraptors to gang up and kill for you. Or at "Wagner Mars Base," there is a card "Oxygen Leak" that causes MASSIVE "Toxic" damage to everything if you don't deal with it for a full turn (effectively venting the atmosphere into the vacuum of space), but if you can find a way to make your team immune to "Toxic" damage you can have "Oxygen Leak" trash the enemy while you remain unscratched.
The game has a few unlocks which give you alternative versions of the heroes with different innate powers, but the game has no true persistence, The characters have all of their powers and features right from the get go. The replay and variety comes from all of different characters, bosses, and environments playing off of each other in unique ways help keep the game fresh, it is rare to see two battles play out in the same way. Something that was a minor nuisance in the first game can be a devastating game changer in the next game.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun, and chat works great to help communication, but it could still use a few more features: more keyboard shortcuts, tool tips, and some minor improvements like an indicator for lag/sin, a method to view player status, and a way to alert/ping players. Regardless the game itself rises well above any of those minor scruples. The game is just fun, and is enhanced tremendously with more people to share the experience with.
The game really shines in its wealth of clever hero combinations you discover and ways you manipulate the villain and environment to your own ends.The challenge is figuring out the best way to go about mitigating the damage the boss will continue to throw at you, while managing the growing amount of minions (crowd control), being wary of the environment, and finally actually developing a strategy to wear down the boss so you can defeat them before you become overwhelmed. When you succeed in pulling out a near impossible comeback or clever reversal it's one of the best feelings this game has to offer. However there are plenty of frustrating moments where the environment will completely nullify your team, or the villain will chain together some brutal combo the wipes you out.
The UI is simple but functional, most things are clear and easy to understand. However having more tool tips on the small versions of the cards, and clearer card labeling could really aid to speed up the game and make gameplay feel smoother. Some key things like if card will attack ALL heroes or just a couple heroes isn't clearly indicated through labeling or tool tips. So often you will find yourself in a situation where a card is forcing you to chose the order of how your heroes recieve damage and you need to go back and re-read the card itself, or click on the "meanwhile" button to get out of the choice window to look at the broader picture and view all of the modifiers before you go back to smart choices with all of the info. This situation comes up A LOT and is my biggest gripe with the game. Sure, eventually you will memorize the card with repeated play, but it would be nice if there was a quick way to glean the info quickly without having to go back and re-read, particularly when you are learning a new villain or environment.
Some other minor things can sometimes be fiddly, but thankful the devs have updated and made right clicking cards to expand them much more consistent. However would be nice if you can see a re-creation of the modifiers leading up the choice more visually. For instance if an enemy is immune to a certain damage or will retaliate if you fulfill a certain condition you have to memorize that info or hunt for it since it isn't clearly indicated visually in UI.
The go back/undo feature is handy to fix blunders and silly mistakes, but it would be nice to have the UI help with a little more information to aid in getting the summary of the info from any said card quickly for faster (but smart) decision-making.
Despite some minor gripes with lack of UI features, the game is faithful to the table top and adds much to the theme and atmosphere. It is great solitaire card combat game, and is great co-op too.
In Summary:
Players control heroes in a co-operative team to take down the villain or boss in a hostile environment.If you enjoy managing your resources as a group, optimizing an effective strategy, all while improvising through challenges the deck, villain, and environment will throw at you to squash your plans then this game will give you A LOT of bang for your buck.
You know that feeling in a traditional RPG where you have a party of adventurers and you are against the final dungeon boss and you have to use all of your abilities and resources to peel through the enemy defensive layers and overcome the puzzle and tempo of a boss fight to win the battle? Now imagine a game where the whole game is that. RPG boss fight after boss fight. That is what this game is in comic book form!

Yet another early access sandbox space game? Yes. While these appear to be the next trend, I have to say Astroneer is a very strong candidate in the category to become something amazing and excel. I'd rate it higher than I did Osiris: New Dawn, which I really enjoy as well. Upon starting your first game, you are welcomed to a beautiful landscape of a foreign alien planet. Honestly, beautiful doesn't even describe how the game looks and feels. The colors, the weather, the ambiance, all come together perfectly and really immerses you in this game. It feels like a trip and you're suddenly peaking, wanting to experience this vibrant and vast world. Just watching the stars and planets rise on the horizon will keep you entertained by just how well done it looks.
So aside from the graphics, what sets this game apart from the plethora of other early access space sandbox games? The actual sandbox. You are able to shape and mold the landscape to your will in almost any way you want. The terraform tool is something that puts Minecraft to shame, it left me awestruck multiple times with how good it feels to dig just a simple hole. The cave generation is absolutely stunning. You will travel for miles in caves, and thankfully with the tether system, you will always have a line to get back home. You will lose hours without realizing it playing this. The survival is not a constant nag, expect for oxygen which you will lose rather quick without the tether system. Honestly though, the tether system is a great thing and takes the concept of putting torches down in Minecraft to mark your way back, and just amplifies that by ten.
Astroneer has a very unusual tranquil feeling to it, at least for me, even with the constant danger of sandstorms hurling huge rocks that instantly kill you and oxygen demands, I never felt pressured. Playing this felt the same as Minecraft back in Indev before anyone knew about the game and talked about all the secrets. Just a beautiful serene experience, and it's almost impossible to think the developers think this is a pre-alpha. The developers might have lofty goals, but they've already hit gold.

The first mission after the two tutorial ones takes place in a big ol Paris mansion that's fully realized; there are no fake doors, you can go into every room on every floor. This scale and detail and challenges bring with it so much content and replayablity it'll make your head spin.
Infact you can also play alternative targets on these maps. And they don't just make you kill another NPC, the map will actually be re-organized and re-decorated. For example, the normal Italy mission takes place during the day and the targets are usually around this villa. But there's an alternate mission which takes place in the same Italian town, but during the night and the target is a movie star on a film set that is now set up in the town's square.
Each level is kind of it's own short game, I actually understand why they went the episodic route.
The music is no Jesper Kyd, but it's nice and dynamic, when you'll be doing something risky or violent it'll instantly react to your actions. And the 'escape' theme song once you've completed your objectives is great.
I have some complaints, like some of the strange control mappings and for some reason you cant throw guns, while you can throw everything else. Maybe some fans will also miss the dark and sexual themes the series has often had, but I like sleek stylish feel of the game. And I miss taking hostages too.
All in all I think this is the most beautiful and grand Hitman game, and I've been playing since Silent Assassin.
You can argue with the episodic structure and the DRM, but at the end of the day this is a SOLID Hitman game.

First off I just want to say I had zero technical issues, bugs, etc. with this game. It is pretty well polished.
Although I enjoyed the narrative gameplay of Absolution and all the new challanges it put on me, the return to the open environment style of gameplay we saw in Blood Money, were you can decide how to tackle your objective in a non linear approach, was wonderful. However I felt some of the changes to the core mechanics of the game made some things, well, a little easier and other things not so much challenging but tedious. The main reason for this is the simple fact that 47 ditched his tranquilizers and now has the ability to knock out anyone with a sleeper hold. I do admit that I appreciate the realism of this but I wish they added some mechanic so that the people knocked out with the sleeper hold might wake up or something and you got to keep the two tranquilizers as a sure thing and could use the sleeper hold as a back up. To counter this there usually is not a "magic disguise" that is near foolproof and grants unlimited access to the whole level like in some of the other games. Some enemies will realize that although you wear the uniform, the face just doesn't match. A smart player will be able to work this on most levels by avoiding eye contact and waiting for the right moment to move, which is the tedious part. That perfect Silent Assassin rating just became so much easier yet so much more annoying to achieve.
To compensate for this it seems the developers chose to focus more on replaying the same level over and over again to perform the same assassination in different ways, each way presented by various challenges which need to be completed to unlock new gear. I did like this as it forced me to think outside the box and created lots of replayability. My tried and true assassination technique that has carried me since Blood Money will no longer always cut it. I had to get creative to achieve my goals just like in Absolution but I also had the freedom of movement found in Blood Money. However I find the hard earned, near impossible method that is more or less the only way to get Silent Assassin in previous titles preferable. Most of the methods presented in the challanges were easy to achieve for a veteren Hitman player like me and the gear they unlocked was not necessary as I am more than capable of getting a Silent Assassin rating with the gear provided the first time you do each contract. I simply didn't do many of them in the later levels as I had no need to and they were not that much fun after a while. As such, I have less gameplay hours on this than any other Hitman game I have played to date. This one was short and sweet for me.
This does not mean this is a bad game though. It was a blast to play and I look forward to the next installment. Trust me, you will spend plenty of hours trying to figure out the best way to achieve the perfect assassination. The only other complaint I can give is no Silver Ballers! You get one but its pretty much a reskin of your standard pistol, no akimbo hand cannons of death like in previous titles. Of course the true assassin has no need for such weapons, but I always liked having the option ;)
Conclusion: Although it is not perfect and lacks some of the challenge of previous titles, HITMAN is fun to play and provides plenty of new ways to assassinate your targets, forcing Hitman fans out of their comfort zone sometimes but not so much it makes a bad game. Thumbs Up!!!

I'm glad I finally pulled this game out of my backlog; it is an overlooked gem.

Everything works beautifully -- the art, level design, and music. Each map has a different theme, challenges, and sometimes a new ability to learn. Exploration and the unexpected are the main thrills of the game.
Gameplay is casual, low-challenge and easily accessible for all ages. All movement is done with the mouse. Abilities are a few key presses. Full controller support is one puzzling omission as the game is perfect for it. Players with a Steam controller could easily create a profile that works. All this for a very reasonable price that offers about 8-10 hours of engagement depending on how fast you work.

What a dissonant experience this game is! At first, it excites you with the production and the set pieces. Then it gets quite repetitive and a bit boring cover shooter. Then the story takes a very dark and twisted turn. The game is still a repetitive cover shooter all the way through and its gameplay mechanics get old really fast. It is not a long game, but the gameplay overstays its welcome in the first few hours. The cutscenes and the dialogues during the game are what drives you forward to find out more and then it grips you so much - you are willing to "suffer" through the uninspired shooting and covering.
A couple of scenes work really well. A few, punch you in a gut and make you feel miserable. The second half of the game is not fun, narrative-wise. This is a one dark story. Despite a few endings - none is a happy one and the game won't leave you feel satisfied and pleased with yourself. Good stuff!
If you love shooting and blowing stuff up, if you enjoy war violence - the game is for you and is a great fit in all but the story. If you are not into those things - the gameplay is worth your patience for the plot and the characters.
Also, the twist at the end might send you playing the game again, so there's a bit of a replayability factor there.
So in summary, good graphics, quite a few great set pieces and scenes, derivative shooting and covering and a one great story you will remember long after you've finished the game.

There are very few games that can make me actually learn something or feel something new through the power of their narrative. If a shooter that actually tells a compelling story sounds like something that would interest you, then I highly reccomend playing Spec Ops: The Line.

A free mod for Half-Life 2: Episode 1. MINERVA places you in the Half-Life world, taking the role of a mute protagonist (NOT Gordon Freeman, mind you) undergoing an investigative operation to a remote island which the Combine seemingly have great interest in protecting. Following the instructions of a somewhat foul-mouthed guide via text messages on your HUD you partake in a mission that goes deeper than you initially thought.
My ultimate opinion about MINERVA is that yes, it's short with only four levels. But it's a free Source mod so that is so easily forgiven. The gameplay is the same as Half-Life 2, so there isn't much to mention there. The maps however are extremely well made, with obvious passion in their design and are very fun and satisfying to move through.
For the gripes, the previously mentioned  texts acting as your instruction are often long-winded and distracting to read, especially in the heat of combat, and often I have found that I didn't know what to do or where to go because I missed the message, and there isn't an option to re-read them anywhere (so I recommend taking a screen-shot of each message then read them over when you've got the time to do so).
Ulimately: MINERVA is a very well made mod, with lots of heart and passion put into it's design. The story is pretty darn good, there's a very intense challenge keeping it from being too lightweighted like most other Source mods I've seen in the past and as I've said, the mapmaking is very impressive.
So yes, I'd definitely recommend you give MINERVA a go.
Possibly one of my favorite Half-Life 2 Mods.

When it came out, like most people, I didn’t care. Another cover-based TPS following the Modern Warfare hype train. Not my cup of tea, so I passed on it. Then, a lot of people started to praise the game and it gained sort of a cult following. I wanted to see for myself, so I picked it up for dirt cheap while on sale.
As I said above, it’s a rather basic cover-based TPS with squad command elements and a few gameplay elements related to sand, like sandstorms. The gameplay itself isn’t brilliant - not bad but rather generic and sometimes clunky. As for the graphics department, the design is really cool but the execution is, again, generic.
But what really shines is the story and the narrative. I never felt that much involved in a narrative with a TPS game before. Without going into spoiler territory
, Spec Ops is very psychological. Every choice is a burden to carry further on; everything you experience has a meaning. And as the story progresses, it gets you into a very uncomfortable side of warfare which is always toned down in favor of heroism in this kind of games.
I also consider SOTL as a proof that a game can be very deep and emotional without going the “Quantic Dream” way, where the story and player’s involvement is top notch but the gameplay is lacking, weird, or even almost absent (like Heavy Rain). I love those games too but they’re more interactive movies than games while SOTL is a game first and foremost.
I really,
recommend this game. Its psychological and philosophical aspects are very well done to the point where it becomes more of an experience than just a game. If you like Silent Hill, Jacob’s Ladder and things like that, you’ll love Spec Ops: The Line.

It has a lot of good going for it but falls short due to repetitive gameplay, probably because it's so much on rails. There's nothing wrong with the gameplay mechanics, it's just that it becomes a bit boring after a while. In a way, the story outshines the gameplay.
Although the game isn't long, I think they could have made the game shorter without really leaving out anything of what makes this game good. It's not a bad game, but it would've been better as a movie, IMHO.
+ Very good story
+ Interesting setting
+ Bruce Boxleitner!
+ Graphics are still pretty good for such an "old" game
- Repetitive gameplay
- Annoying controls at times (same buttons do different things depending on context, invisible walls when attempting to drop down or vault on the right places, but not the exact right position)
Final verdict: I dunno... Pick it up on a sale, but only if you're into on-rails shooters with a console:y feel. If you're mostly interested in the story, watch the cut scenes on YT or something. :]

I tend to be hot and cold with platformers. I either love them or hate them. This one, however is a LOVE. Capital letters for emphasis. I'm playing on normal mode and I'm not even halfway through the game, but this is the most beautiful platformer I've ever played and I'm thorougly enjoying the ride through the game for the first time. The visuals are incredible. The story gives you just enough information to be satisfied with what has already happened and leave you with questions that make you want to continue forward with the game. The more skills I unlock the more shocked I am with how they came up with the concept. The different parts of the game remind me of Super Mario, where the levels are so well thought out that they're just hard enough to make you frustrated but not so hard to make you give up. This game also has a bit of a puzzle aspect to it. There are some places where you really need to think about exactly what you are doing instead of trying to just stomp everything in front of you. There are parts of the game that you have to go back to because you can't complete them until you move forward with the game, which gives me a reason to head back into the first parts of the game and find new things I couldn't get to before. This game is brilliant, I can't wait to finish it and then play the sequel!

The oringinal Sentinels of the Multiverse is a co-operative card game in which each player is given a superhero character and a deck of cards representing that character's powers. You spend the game trying to defeat a dastardly supervillain. All characters and villains have a difficulty rating based on the complexity of the decks so that you can start out with the more direct style heroes and move up in level of difficulty as you feel confident in your understanding of the rules.
The Sentinels characters themselves have an introductory online comic and interesting background stories you can look up. Aside from helping you identify expys, this also highlights one of the strengths of the Sentinel's characters: diversity. You want a black Iron Man character? How about a female Asian Batman? Or a lesbian Flash?
In terms of a computer port, this is a beautiful game. There's different music to enhance the feeling of each environment option. You get a tutorial mode to help you learn. And the computer tracks all of the damage details. Additionally, you can control the fine details of the play, or tell the computer to take care of minor details for you (like who draws cards first or is damaged first).
Sentinels also has a pile of varient cards that were ported to the computer game as unlockables to provide additional challenges.
Whether you want to play by yourself or with friends on line, I definitely recommend Sentinels. And, if you're going to buy it, I'd also recommend the Season 1 pass. Not all of the expansions are out at this moment, but I have played with physical copies of all of the items that will be included, and they are all good.

I've played a lot of Sentinels... the actual physical card/chit game.

It really clairified a lot of rules that I was not fully understanding in the RL Cardgame, which is great... in the card game you have to calculate everything yourself with the help of chits and cardboard flags "+1 Attack"...
It ends up a little quirky when you dont know what abilities "stack"... the computerized version pulls together all the info as it plays out to say where these stacking bonuses or penalties are coming from which helps you play the RL card game much better.
So this computerized version is a great "tutor" as well. Confused on how Omnitron works in the card game? try it in the computer game!
Though (the computer game) is cool and applies some effort in simple animations, it may not be for everyone. If you are a card-game player, you will like this, and if you haven't, you might pick up the card-game for real... because there is nothing like sitting down with friends and playing for real on the table, with chits, cardboard flags and socializing the game.

I probably love Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne as much as the first game in series. To keep it short, everything that was already god-tier, remained as good as possible or is even better. Every encounter with enemies is fun, killing them while using slowmo, or without it, is Max of fun. Characters, story and music stays for very long time in memory. Heck, even after playing it again for the first time in 10+ years I haven't forget many stuff. Maybe after so many time I started to think that story in this game is much darker than in previous one.
Comics like always are interesting but for some reason, I really missed style used in first game. But for this little Payne, we got something much more amazing - MONA SAX. How fun it is to play here, to move her beatiful body. Probably one of my first gaming loves that never ended. Many years ago there was also special mod... who played Max Payne 2 back then will know what kind of mod I'm talking about. Wasn't dissapointed when I got my hands on this mod, even tho you could call this The Fall nowadays, I didn't regret anything.
There is also this amazing game mode where you fight waves of enemies - I remember how many times I played this together with a friend of mine. To show-off who really is better, who reached the 5th minute for the first time, who managed to kill more enemies (yes, while one was playing the other one was counting dead bodies). Really great times and memories.
It's not only nostalgia, Max Payne 2 is really great game. Some people will prefer the first one, some this one, but I really love both of Max Payne games and can't really think which one is better. If you enjoyed the previous one, if you want more, get it and play it. Few difficulty modes, additional game mode and beating each of chapters of game as fast as you can will bring you many hours of fun. I'm sure that there will be time when I will once again play this masterpiece.

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne improves on everything which made the first game great and even surpasses it in some aspects. The gameplay isn't as awkward as before thanks to improved hitboxes and bullet trajectories, a sense of realism surrounds the game because of physics simulations like ragdoll effects, and the identity of the series has been given a new facelift thanks to higher production values. Overall, an excellent action game that's worthy of the Max Payne name and fans will be happy with this installment. However, if you're new to the series or have only played the Rockstar-made entry, you won't get as much from this game and everything will just look like a confusing mess. Max Payne 2 is a story-centric game and it builds on what fans and players of the first game already knows. This time around, the true intentions of the first game's major players are shown and reveals a new side to them, making them more believable rather than being a one-sided cliche of a character. The story focuses on Max after the events of the first title as he reflects on his past choices and how he copes up with the decisions that he's made. I highly suggest that new players play the first game or watch a recap video because without knowledge of the characters' background and the events leading up to this game, the story becomes much less impactful and you won't get much out of it because of its focus on the cast rather than plot.
And there you have it.

One of the best RPG I have ever played, it's a real gem that every RPG lover MUST play.
In my opinion it's a 10/10, you have to consider this is a 12 years old game (it came out in 2002) so I'm basing my judgement on that, but if you want to compare it to a more recent game, I guess we all agree if I say it's a 2D Skyrim.
The main quest is quite short if you just rush it to the end, but you can't, the game sidetracks you from everything you are doing with sidequests, exploration and fights. Don't be mislead by my playing time, it says 16 hrs but I played a lot in offline mode and it doesn't show, I think it's 70hrs more or less and I havent finished all sidequests.
Let's now talk about specific stuff, shall we?
***Graphics -  9/10 Considering the game age I'd say. Your character's equipment is pretty detailed and so is the environment, you almost never have the feeling of visiting a place already seen, not a single room is like the other, the only exception is for cave dungeons, these have always the same dark rock tiles and walls, and it gets boring after 15 mins, also it's so dark that you have trouble finding levers to open the doors.
***Sound - 10/10 The music is just perfect, calm and sweet when you're travelling the forest but dark and deep when you're facing demons in the depths of the earth. Voice acting reminds me of theatre plays and maybe someone could dislike it, however it's really good. I had just one problem with sound, which I couldn't get rid of, it was like a scratch sound that played randomly at times, hopefully not too often, I guess it's some conflict due to the game being played on modern machines, but still, nothing to worry about.
***Story - 10/10 Main quests and sidequests are pretty awesome, there is everything, from monster slaying to the only-talking quests. Some of them are very VERY long and sometimes you find out that completing a quest helps you in another one. There is even room for humor which is quite nice, and this is everywhere in the game, from dialogue answers to stats description, try reading then when values are low. Just once or twice I found myself baffled by the deus ex machina that comes at the right moment to save your skin without a serious explanation.
***Gameplay & mechanics - 10/10 (unless you break it on purpose) Apart from the chaos of the menus, which is scary at the beginning, everything is just fine, you can build your character the way you like, pick up one of the classes (rogue, mage, warrior) and do whatever you want. The only problem is that there are 2 skill that are game breaking, one is frost and the other one is trap: steel scorpion. The first one makes you godlike by freezing your enemies for a lot of time and the latter one lets you summon minions that inflict an amount of damage that is simply unbelievable, if you also have the ability to charm them so that the scorpions follow you, then you can sit down and let them kill everything. So, don't do that and enjoy the game without these 2 skills, you have many others.
***Replayable -YES. First playthrough I built a rougue-warrior, but I'm curious to see what a mage looks like. So this is a plus in the overall score.
*** BONUS *** Steam version allows you to modify the resolution, otherwise you end up losing your eyes.
TL, DR  it's 1,69€ on sale and 5€  full price. Just buy it and shut up.

One of my favourite RPGs of all time, it has beautiful isometric artwork, fun combat and an intriguing plot with good characters.
The artwork is great in my opinion, coming at the end of an era of great iosmetric games and utilising the available technology post-millenium, making me sad that this genre was all but dropped for a decade.
Combat is a kind of Diablo-like with left clicking to melee and right clicking to fling spells and a button to lock on to enemies if you need the extra accuracy. I found it a lot of fun, although some abilities are quite unbalanced. There is certainly plenty of scope for roleplaying and building custom classes (there are starting classes but no restrictions on gear or abilities) but you might find yourself using some abilities and skills simply because they're very effective.
The plot is interesting, with plenty of intrigue and wonder and it takes you to many interesting places, varied environments and great characters abound. It also has a good sense of humour, without overdoing it, something that Larian are usually quite good at.
In summary, this game feels like Diablo got a shot of Baldur's Gate and a taste of Elder Scrolls and I feel it is highly underrated. If you enjoy RPGs you shouldn't miss out on this gem.

Spec Ops: The Line is the playable Apocalypse Now in present day Dubai. Gameplay is banal yet fun in contrast to its story which is thrilling but uncomfortable.
Featuring average linear shooter mechanics, the game lulls the player into a sense of traversing in known realms. The premise of Spec Ops: The Line wouldn't work with an all new innovative gameplay because it requires knowledge of the genre in order to build on expected player behaviour. It's a pleasant cover shooter, despite its finicky controls.
Initially, Spec Ops: The Line is rewarding to play. The beautiful scenery is second to none and the music is reminiscent of almost every anti-war film about the Vietnam War. Even if mostly destroyed, the pomp of Dubai is as colourful and impressive as the vegetation of the tropics. Mundane effects such as the shaky camera in cutscenes, the death animations and particularly the slow motion headshots give the impression of playing an action-packed Hollywood movie.
Slight spoiler ahead.
It's fun to play, it feels good landing headshots in a row hearing Walker scream “Kill is ♥♥♥♥ing confirmed!” but over time, the player sees more and more of the horror that stems from the actions of him and his kind. Spec Ops: The Line is a unique and invigorating experience.

This game is pretty good. It's an action platformer.
Controls are responsive enough for the purposes of the game. I don't think it's really hard enough to be considered a Metroid clone although the map/leveling up/new powers to explore more elements are there. I haven't really run into difficult platforming though as I've pretty much been able to one or two shot every area of the map. I've been using a ps4 controller so your experience on a keyboard might vary. I died a lot more in Symphony of the Night than I have here.
The art and soundtrack fit the theme very well and are beautiful (reminds me a little of Okami but not nearly as open world). I don't think I can overstate this point. I've had roommates walk into my room while I'm playing this to ask about the soundtrack, then just sit and watch me play for 2 hours straight. The only reason they stopped is because I ended my play session. I've had friends of my roommates end up doing this instead of watching sports with my roommates. I can guarantee you that, asides from progressing the story, I'm not doing anything extra to hold their interest.
The story is decent. I mostly say that because I've run into a number of bugs where I've been forced to exit the game and replay long cutscenes. It doesn't have the same impact when you're forced to watch something 3 times in a row. In a similar vein I also haven't been able to trigger certain scenes consistently (stupid light orb in misty forest counts for nearly 20 minutes of gametime, not counting the 5 or 6 restarts of steam I had to do to finally trigger it and breaking down and looking at a guide to see if I missed a required step). I might just be really unlucky though as I'm not seeing that complaint pop up in other reviews.
As a note, be prepared that the intro takes 10 or so minutes before you can actually play. I thought it was well done but I know my brother would have probably quit as it went on long enough to think the rest of the game would be that pace. He hated the gameplay in Journey enough to not play until I unlocked the white robe.
With the above said, I'd still highly recommend this game. My main issue is that this isn't a game I can drop into and play for 30 minutes. I need to block out at least 4 hours.

“Hero of Many” is a very clever game, and that’s a word rarely used these days. Seemingly a metaphorical game of light versus dark, with no gray areas. You play as a small blob of light, and it’s that blob that the player controls with the mouse.
But you don’t play against the forces of darkness unassisted. Nor will you stay a small blob. As you travel through what is apparently an underwater world, you come across stationary small blobs, and close proximity causes you both to merge, increasing your size. You will also encounter fish-looking characters: bright ones will join you, dark ones will attack you and your “swarm”. Perhaps you can sneak past the dark ones, or attract some away, keeping battles small and manageable. But there seem to be some larger dark creatures that cannot be defeated, and your swarm cannot protect you against them for long….
“Hero of Many” seems simple, and to some degree it is. But you are given almost no instructions, which adds to the game’s complexity. The world you inhabit is large, with many small and intertwining passages. Lights go on along the edges to show where you’ve been, and large crystals act as highly visible save points. The goal is to advance to a sort of “drain”, leading to the next level, with as many swarm members as possible.
Others things will be encountered in the game. As your swarm progress in the game it will encounter food, dangerous plants (or not, how to tell?) and large swarms of dark enemies. Also, they will constantly lose small bits of light, weakening steadily. Individual swarm members aren’t smart, and will easily get separated or lost from the main swarm. The larger the swarm, the harder to lead or control, and the more likely lost to the dangers they will encounter. But, the greater the protection offered by larger swarms.
“Hero of Many” is a surprisingly endearing game, and rapidly develops a sense of personality. The swarm is so dedicated to providing protection that the desire to return that protection is very strong. The save point are logical and reasonable, and I can only imagine that further levels become more challenging and interesting. At this low (discount) price, I would give “Hero of Many” my strongest recommendation.

It's a good adaptation of the card game: a cooperative superhero game.
Each player has one or more heroes, and there's one villain and one environment. Each of these has its own deck, so there's a strong theme for each. Eg. Ra is a straightforward hero who burns things, gets certain cards into play, then helps everyone burn everything. Legacy mostly buffs other characters, Tempest is good at crowd control, and so on. No character is totally locked into one role, though. The villains and environment play automatically (play top card of deck, follow rules on villain card) and each has its own theme. The villains have two modes with special conditions for flipping, so each battle has distinct phases like Baron Blade giving up on his superweapon to attack you directly. You're racing to get hero cards into play while fighting the villain and his minions and averting some location-based disasters like angry T-rexes or a Martian self-destruct device. So, there's a constant struggle to cope with threats as they arise and there are tough decisions to make about what to focus on. Expect to lose sometimes, especially against the nastier villains and environments. As in the original, there are ratings to warn you about each hero's complexity and each villain's difficulty, though not about the locations. (Try Insula Primalis first.) Difficulty is usually somewhat lower with more heroes.
The bad: it can be frustrating when certain card orders come out, especially the "lose all your stuff" cards. Some heroes are crippled by effects like that, making them feel useless against those villains. On the other hand, there are some effects so useful they can seem abusive in your favor. (Volcanic Eruption + Flesh of the Sun God = everyone bathes in lava, only bad guys take damage.) Those are just excessive cases in a game where finding powerful combinations is very important and fun; teamwork is key.
About this online version: you're getting a straight copy of the card game, with 10 heroes, 4 villains, and 4 environments. Currently $20 will get you all of the expansions through "Cosmos" besides "Vengeance", the "Tactics" spinoff (and maybe unimportant promo cards like the Prime Wardens, I think), though some aren't released yet. The digital format can make it a bit hard to read the cards without clicking on them to magnify, so players unfamiliar with the cards may be annoyed at first. Note also that online multiplayer is still in beta as of this writing (15.8.26) but is easy to opt into. Expect to treat this as a solo game at first, but it's fun even in that solitaire format.

Of the first three Batman games in this series, this is my least favorite.  Note:  I have not played nor do I intend to play Arkahm Knight.
I've been playing games longer than I care to remember.  I find myself using the walkthrough for this game more than any game I can recall.  The story is very linear, so if you decide to go "open" and roam about to do random things, it's sometimes hard to get back on track.  In some parts of the side missions, you can find yourself in a dead end with no obvious way to proceed, thus the need for the walkthroughs.
Combat has been made noticably harder, and it's not uncommon to get into situations where you can do little more than wait for enemy attacks and repeatedly counter until numbers get to a manageable number.  Note I'm playing on "normal" and am not great at "button masher" combat, but had no issues with Arkham Asylum or Arkham City.
Other than some of the villians, this game really brings nothing new to the series.  You're just as well to go back and play either Arkham Asylum or Arkham City again, to be honest.  The "year zero" approach just doesn't work for me.  Revealing Joker as if Batman didn't know who he was?  I understand what the makers are trying to do, but this approach is lame for anyone other than those who are truly noobs to the character.  If this approach had been used in the first game, it would not have been any more effective, but would have at least been a logical progression.
I will say that the Cold, Cold Heart campaign is the one exception to my comments above.  I don't want to spoil it for anyone that is considering a purchase and wants surprises, but this part of the game was original and broke the mold (as much as you can) compared to AA and AC.  I find myself wondering why this wasn't rolled into the overall game as the starting point for the "real" campaign... oh, well.
If you've read some of my other posts -- I hate the "up" or "down" voting system on Steam.
If you're looking for something fresh and original in the Batman Arkham series, this really isn't it.  <thumbs down>
If you're ok with something that's largely a replay of AA and AC, with a little freshness from Cold, Cold Heart?  <thumbs up>
Overall, I find this game more frustrating from getting stuck than fun from the limited freshness.  Since I have to pick up or down, I pick down because I don't like games that make me (a reasonably intelligent and long-time gamer) get angry.  Hopefully my comments have given you enough context that you can make you're own decision.
If you get a good deal and REALLY like Batman, you probably won't be disappointed.  Even though I get angry at times, I'm "pushing through the pain" for now to see how the rest of the story unfolds.  That said, if you were here in my house you would hear far more cussing at the computer screen than is normally the case with games I choose to invest time in.

Sentinels of the Multiverse is a computer adaptation of the tabletop card game of the same name. It is very faithful to the original and really captures the essence and feel of fielding a team of superheroes against a villain (and their minions) in a unique environment. One of reasons that I enjoy the game is that it does a good job of keeping track of all of the on-going abilities, pluses, minuses, impacts and conditions which are easy to forget or overlook when playing the card game. I *believe* that there are a few minor bugs in logic to still hammer out, but for the most part I think that the game is very enjoyable.
There are also Variants of the heroes and villains, so you have some desire to go back and keep playing in order to unlock another aspect of your favorites. If you prefer Handalabra gives you a code when you click on More Info, so you can simply unlock the varients quickly and easily.
This is a terrific game to get a quick skirmish in. These battles last 30 minutes or so, so they are not too long. I found the music compelling and sometimes find myself humming the theme. I wish there was a little more variety in the sound effects. All melee attacks sound the same; all projectile attacks sound the same, etc. It would be very cool if Expatriette’s Tactical shotgun sounded differently than Wraith’s Throwing Knives. For better or worse there is no character speech at all in the game.
The artwork on the cards is good, effective for the style. I enjoy it, although some may find it underwhelming. I also laugh at the subtle humor in their characters.
I find myself really looking forward to the next DLC to add to the list of villains and environments. As of this writing Multiplayers is approaching testing, but I saw people enjoying it at Gen Con.
If you enjoy Superheroes, or non-stress card games, this game is a sure hit.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to Rocksteady's Batman Arkham Asylum. It is, once again, being developed in the Unreal Engine, however, this time, by different developers.
The story in Arkham Origins takes place during Christmas at night, where Batman is being hunted down by several hired assassins. The story starts out slow and gradually starts getting more interesting, as well as giving a satisfying conclusion for the game. It constantly introduces new villians (to Batman, but not to the player, at least) and helps fill in the gaps before Arkham Asylum. It provides its own unique take on Batman's formal introduction to all the villians we know and love and does not disappoint. The story is fairly long and is about the length of any Arkham's game main story, not counting the side missions for either.
Gameplay-wise, Batman Arkham Origins plays extremely similar to its previous games, with barely any new gameplay features introduced. There are new gadgets with different purposes gradually introduced throughout the game, some of which can be extremely helpful in combat. Boss battles in Arkham Origins, however, are by far (in my opinion) the best out of all the Arkham games, including Arkham Knight. With each boss battle, there is always a unique take on it and you will have to find out different ways to defeat the bosses as the game tries its best to not be repetitive with boss fights. Instead of generic "punch the boss and dodge" fighting, you get much more intense boss fights which require you to think as they all have a unique mechanic. Therefore, gameplay style is the same, with the addition of better boss battles and new gadgets.
Graphics-wise, Arkham Origins does a fine job and the graphics look better than Arkham City's. However, it is nothing amazing or a huge improvement that it is noticable, and therefore, will not play a major part.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Story: 9/10
Graphics: 8.5/10
Total: 8.5/10
If you have the money to spare or you are a Batman fan, this certainly won't disappoint you nor will it impress you. It is basically as good as a DLC for Arkham City with a new story, slightly better graphics and new gadgets and better boss fights. If you loved Arkham City, you will love this. If you're looking for a huge improvement, such as from Asylum to City, go for Arkham Knight.

Dungeon-crawling RPG, along the same lines as the original Diablo but quite a bit bigger.  You will do some "fetch" quests and some monster-slaying quests for the local people, who will reward you with experience points, cash, and equipment.  You will spend a lot of time fighting monster mobs looking for experience to level-up, and you will be checking corpses and containers for health potions and bigger/badder weapons.  You have a choice of male or female from the classic character archetypes (rogue, fighter, wizard) and each of them has some utility.  The fighter can carry high weight and do big damage from swords and axes... makes the beginning of the game easier.  The mage obviously can cast some devastating spells to wipe out the enemy, but has low survivability and really is harder in the beginning and easier in the late stages of the game.  The rogue uses lighter weapons and armor, combined with speed... good with a bow.  I have not yet played as the rogue though so I won't say anything about how easy or hard it is.  One thing I don't like about this one and its sequel is that once you kill something or open a box it stays dead or opened.  So you are very limited in opportunities to get experience/level-ups and items.  Other than that, this game is lots of fun if you're into dungeon-crawler RPG.
Unlike Diablo, you actually travel considerably in this game.  You start in a small village, which has a "baby dungeon" below it.  From there, you travel through a forest (inhabited by a bunch of Orcs) and across a bridge (which of course is guarded by Trolls) to reach the part of the world where you will do most of your adventuring.  You have to survive in the wilderness as you travel between several towns and castles, as well as into the sewers and a few other types of dungeons below them.  The story behind the game is pretty interesting, although it's not really great... typical plot for RPG's of the time:  you are "the chosen one" and you have to bring the various races together (elf, orc, dwarf, human) to fight against a greater evil.  You'll be aided by a crazy wizard named Zandalor among other characters.  The side-quests are actually more interesting than the main story, although several of them have you running halfway around the world two or three times in order to complete them.
It is a great game, however at times it can feel like a maze.

Easily one of the best games I have ever played.
If you are even considering buying this game, I strongly encouage you to do so.
It is an absolutely stunning experience.
Pros:
-The art style: I am certain you can tell by the images and trailer above, but this game looks incredible. There are some people who would pay $20 for the art alone.
-The music: The best soundtrack I have ever heard in a video game. I listen to the soundtrack for this game while playing other games and I have 0 regrets.
-The story: This game was a very touching story that is likely to change you by the time you finish it. The characters are all deep and were clearly well thought out.
-The gameplay: Many people I know have called this game a "plotformer" a game that sort of plays itself with you merely being there for the story. Thosepeople are DEAD wrong. Ori has incredible gameplay mainly due to the tight controls and how agile Ori actually is. By the end of this game you will feel awesome as you fly through the air expertly gliding over obstacles and enemies.
-The world: The map itself is relatively expansive and, as the rest of the game is, a work of art. Each area feels different with a distinct cast of enemies and obstacles. Naturally, as with all Metroidvannia games, new abilities are needed to access certain areas of the map so the player will need to do some back tracking. In other Metroidvannias this can be annoying, but in Ori, it is a pleasure. It means you get to spend more time in the stunning world blessed with the incredible music and visuals.
-The optimization: I have had no problem running this game, save a few stutters during some of the more graphic intensive scenes. I run this game on a laptop, that can barely take a game like Overwatch, almost perfectly. This means that just about everybody could run it, which means just about everybody can enjoy this work of art.
Cons:
-The difficulty: Many people will get incredibly anrgy with this games. Most of the game is rather easy and intuitive. There are, however, incredibly difficult segments in the game.
If you rage easily this game may require a bit of patience.
In Conclusion:
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the greatest games ever made. It is a pleasure for both the eyes and the ears and the gameplay is tight and fast. The game may get difficult at times, but the incredible music and artstyle will make it difficult to get angry even after you die 10 times in a row. This game is a masterpiece of the platforming genre and should be what all platformers aspire to be.
