The reviews don't lie. This game is a masterpiece. I usually like to lay out a list of pros and cons for the games that I review, but I can't do that with Ori and the Blind Forest. I'll just leave some comments below, and you can decide if it's for you.
+The art is spectacular; I spend several minutes at a time just staring at the ladnscapes.
+The story is beautiful... One of the best I've ever played in a video game, and I play a lot of story driven games.
+The soundtrack brings a full grown man to tears. Seriously, I would leave the main menu open just to listen to the song.
+The sound design is well-crafted. Each sound in this game was well-thought out and it shows.
+The characters are so lovable; I wish I could jump through the screen and hug them all, but that might be creepy.
+The game plays so fluidly. I don't typically enjoy this type of gameplay, but Ori nails everything good about this genre.
+This game is what AAA studios should aim to create.
Am I overhyping? Maybe, but this game touched me in a way few do. I was bawling in the first 10 minutes. If you want an amazing experience combined with excellent gameplay and breathtaking art, then Ori is for you. You won't regret it.

Max Payne 2 is a direct sequel, continuing the titular character's grim tale. Now a police detective, Max is thrust into a conspiracy involving a group of hitmen known as the "Cleaners." In the process of digging up their identity, he comes across Mona Sax, a femme fatale he assumed had been dead for two years. Making an unlikely duo, they work together to uncover dark secrets and create new ones.
The first game set the bar with its bullet time mechanics, and the sequel works to apply a fine polish. Now, during slowdown, you can quickly reload with a stylish spin, allowing you to pull of some impressive clears. All the guns handle well and the controls are precise. There wasn't a bad action sequence in this game.
Max and Mona's complex relationship adds a layer of intrigue to the mystery. Given their nature--one a cop, one a criminal--the story chooses to test how far they will go to aid each other. Like all good noir stories, there is romance, betrayal, violence, and overwhelming darkness. It's a short story, but the plot is solid, an improvement from the previous title. This time to graphic novel style looks a little better in appearance, and isn't as overwhelmed with tiresome metaphors.
Contrary to the last game, Max Payne 2 has some wonderful environments. Back alleys, drug dens, funhouses, police stations; it's much more varied this time. While it remains a linear game, there is plenty to explore and uncover. Every stage has television sets that you can interact with. Each features a handful of shows that will reoccur throughout the game. They are very campy in nature and tend to have parallels with Max's own situation, revealing how silly the plot can sound without the dark overtones. It's clear that the game isn't afraid to make fun of itself, and that makes the experience easy to appreciate.
It only took about five hours to beat the game. At 9.99 this is no issue. It's well worth the money. But at the same time, this game was once sold at full retail price. There are plenty of modes to replay the game with, but I'm not sure if it would have warranted a full purchase. I don't want to undersell how much I loved the game (it has to be one of the best games I've ever played), but it was almost too short. The first game had a good length, and this one was about three hours short of that. That said, nothing in the game feels like a waste of time. There is no padding to be found. Everything that occurs moves the plot along efficiently. It's unfortunate that such a good experience only lasts for such a short time, but I understand the reasoning.
There was one level, an escort mission, that I had issues with due to a glitch. The character I was protecting would not go through a doorway, and continued to get stuck even when I restarted the mission. It took a bit of fiddling around to manage to get him through (I basically had to use the door to smash him through the doorway). This was the only part of the game I had issues with, but it did dampen my experience. Without this moment of annoyance, Max Payne 2 could've been an entirely perfect game. It's strange to witness, as the rest of the game seems technically astounding.
It puts most current-gen shooters to shame and has a story that is enjoyable from start to finish. The short length is a bit jarring, but the end result is a game that feels like a full experience. There is no useless filler to pad out the experience. Instead, Max Payne 2 leaves you feeling very satisfied by the end.
It's one of the best shooting games out there.

DmC has easily become one of my favorite games of all-time. Despite the opinion of the naysayers that appear to be stuck in their roots and decided to hate on the game because it wasn't an exact replica of the older games in the series.. DmC has a ton of personality, charm, and atmosphere.
The combat system isn't as in depth as previous games, but the combat remains satisfying and rewarding, nonetheless. The difficulty IS there, if you decide to play on some of the harder modes.
As far as Dante's new look, I'm happy with it. It brings a fresh new perspective to what Dante would have looked like back in his younger origin years. With older Dante's personality, I don't have a hard time "believing" this representation of him. Also, the idea that the stronger his powers become, the whiter his hair starts to turn, makes sense in the longrun and sets up the previous games.
The story leaves a bit to be desired, but it felt fresh and new and it didn't keep me from having a good time during my playthrough.
I think people are just so stuck in the past and can't handle change of any kind when it comes to their favorite franchises, which is a shame, because it only holds them back from an otherwise enjoyable experience.
As a huge fan of the franchise myself, and having played all previous games, I came into this game with an open-mind and was pleasantly surprised, considering all the negative opinions I had heard prior to playing DmC.
It's saddening that the game wasn't better received, otherwise we probably would have ended up with an interesting sequel in which to build upon the origin story and characters. I honestly feel that if this game had been marketed as another title altogether, fans of the series wouldn't have judged and dismissed so quickly.
tld;r All in all, despite the closed-minded fans of the franchise, this game is incredibly enjoyable and I highly recommend it for anyone that enjoys the hack-n-slash action genre.

First and foremost let me mention that I don't like the release module used for this game, I don't think that a Hitman game should be released in an episodic format especially considering that it breaks immersion and pacing, and also that the consumer would be paying for an unfinished product is something that I personally tend to not support. As a result I refused to purchase the game until it was complete and I would only puchase it during a very reasonable sale, with all of this out of the way let me say what I actually think of the game.
I liked Hitman, there isnt any two ways to go about it. The game is very enjoyable and overall pretty well put toghether (not flawless though), there are a ton of different ways that you can complete a mission which adds to replayability and that is good however it doesn't justify an episodic release since replaying the same level over and over again without going through the entire game first can be pretty boring. This leads to a big issue caused by the episodic style release, that is that after every mission I have to go back to the main screen in order to go to the next mission and I feel that by doing that it breaks my immersion a bit.
Voice acting is top notch and the soundtrack although to me not memorable blends well with the game's environment. The gameplay is pretty solid although when you knock out a character and want to drag him and if there are a few items lying around the KO'd character it can be a pain to get the drag prompt to appear, this becomes annoying especially if you are in a hurry because a NPC is coming towards the room you are in and you need to desperately hide the body.
I would of liked Agent 47 to have a bit more of variattion in his moveset, for example if you takedown an enemy next to a container he could chuck him inside it as part of the takedown, it would be a pretty cool way to use the enviornment to hide away bodies in a quick and efficient manner. It would of been nice if you could walk up to a character while concealing your gun behind your back since it is something I picture an assassin doing. Looking at current game technology it does feel like the combat mechanics weren't as refinned as they could of been.
I feel like levels are a bit too small in scale, at times I would of liked to have a slighly larger environment to play around in and be a bit more constructive with how I could take out my target. Although not really that big of an issue but with only 6 levels the game left me wishing for a bit more at the end.
In my opinion the weakest part of the game is the story, it doesn't connect too well with the gameplay part and feels very disjointed and feels more like padding than something necessary. You could remove the entire plot from the game and get the exact same experience, which is a shame since I like a good narrative in a game, also story doen't answer any questions at it's conclusion and only raises even more. The game is obviously following a TV season style of storytelling but here is something the game does wrong, a season finale normally answers most if not all of the season's questions while raising new important ones and Hitman fails terribly at that.
Overall it's a fun although slightly flawed game, I would recommend it to anyone but not as a full priced game since it does feel a little bit lacking so I would recommend to pick it up during a sale.
If I had to give it a score I would say it's a solid 7/10

No More Room in Hell is a very interesting game. It takes a lot of elements from classic zombie films and blends them into a multiplayer shooter with survival horror elements. The objective of the game is varied, but most maps require you to either defend a point or get to a certain area. Zombies are slow and relatively weak, despite a few who are speedier than the others. However, the most compelling mechanic is that YOU, the player, can get infected. If a zombie bites you, you'll begin to turn. If you can't find medicine, your friends may need to neutralize you before you become a threat. Supplies are limited and you'll engage in melee combat with zombies frequently. If I had a complaint, it's that some of the parts of the game need polish. When a zombie grabs you, sometimes it looks awkward and the graphics are a bit ugly in some areas. However, it's solid overall and it's free. I'd recommend it.

Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is a great game, having played it for many years I got excited when I saw that it was on steam. It is quite an old game (2003, I believe. I am a fan of old games, for some reason) however it is still one of the best games that I have ever played. The storyline of Max Payne is complex but as you begin to play the game you will understand a bit of what it going on, the characters are well thought out and the missions can be quite fun, reading through the graphic novel function is interesting as instead of having cutscenes, the plot is shown through a graphic novel. You also encounter things like TVs and you can view the ingame TV shows.
However, there are some downsides to the game also such as,
Sometimes a bit of it can be hard to follow and you don't know what is happening/why the mission relates to the game.
Despite the graphic novel being entertaining, it can be a bit slow and you can get bored of it however there is a skip button if you aren't interested in the game.
The last downside is minor but in my opinion the game is quite short, it only took me 7 hours to finish and it would have been a bit better if there were a few more missions.
Overall I rate this game an 9/10, it is a great game to play and I would recommend it to anyone.

Do you like somewhat accurate betrayals of guns in video games? Do you like having the ability to aim down your gun like anyone with two ♥♥♥♥ing arms? Finally, do you not like getting killed for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reasons? Well, if you agreed with any of the above, CSGO might not be for you.
This game can be very frustrating at times, times where nothing seems to make sense. The bullet spreads of the guns in this game are very strange, along with not being able to use the sights of a gun (besides snipers and acogs). There are some guns, *cough* negev *cough*, that have the weirdest way to shoot accurately. Some do crazy amounts of damage, while others are there for decoration.
There is basically only one game mode, which is competitive. You can play casual or one of the party games, but there is little point. The casual and party games don’t give you the same XP, and you will have to search for someone with a mic.
But if you love spending money, this game is for you. The whole game is centered on the skins(like camos) of the guns you use. So, for the low price of around $2, you unlock a case to win a skin. They say you can get drops at the end of a round, but the drops are the worst skins you can get. There are many cash grabbers in this game, such as having to pay to name your guns.
Overall, it's an alright game, especially for being only $15. The game is much too focused on the gambling part of it, shoving crates and the need for skins down your throat. But if you are looking for some fun with friends, this game will do.

For anyone who enjoys PvE, card games, board games, superheroes, turn based games, or strategy game, I would highly recommend this game. It is a true adaptation of a well recieved indy card game wherein a team of 3-5 heroes duke it out with one villain in a setting.
There are plenty of heroes to choose from, 4 villains in the base set (more with expansions) and 4 settings (more with expansions) which makes for a large number of unique combinations and possibilities. Expansions only add to those combinations.
Each hero, villain, and setting has an entirely unique deck that provides them with their own "feel". I won't detail them all here, but there are a number of parallels to popular fictional characters, even so the game keeps its characters very unique.
Settings provide random events that happen every turn, one or two cards in a setting deck may actually help the players, but most of the time the deck provides chaos that must be dealt with during the battle (a volcano errupts, there is a hostage situation, water is flooding the battleground, etc...)
The original card game was co-op, unfortunately the video game isn't co-op unless you all want to get together and pass a mouse around (I won't judge). This game is a fantastic solitaire game, but it would benefit most from a multiplayer online upgrade. The Steam page says it is local co-op, near as I can tell that means playing on the same PC (it would work well if your PC is hooked up to a TV and could be tonnes of fun with friends).
Anyway, the game is great, pick it up and enjoy it.

As a fan of both collectible trading card games and superheroes, Sentinels of the Multiverse hits a special sweet spot for me.
The graphics are colorful and pretty. The style is authentically superhero in nature, feeling like panels lifted from a comic book. I appreciate the page turn wipe mechanic to illustrate the rotation of turns from character to character; though, this effect slows the game down, so I eventually did turn it off. Also, the animations for damage infliction have been improved since launch, which demonstrates the developers dedication to refining and expanding the game, though these quickly become tedious.
The characters are diverse, as are the cards that you play to simulate their superpowers and manuevers on the battlefield. In general, the cards are well-illustrated and have great flavor text. Combining the abilities of different heroes often results in synergies that mirror a team of superpowered beings working together to defeat one arch-villain, as well as containing that random element that can make CCGs addicting by their ability to reveal combinations and pitfalls over time.
I did find the characters to be wildly out of balance, with some being useful against virtually every foe and in every circumstance. While other characters require very particular draws or circumstances, or the understanding and exploitation of a self-damage mechanic to make them effective. I tended to avoid these, focusing instead on looking at the pool of abilities that the team possessed, which may well have been the focus the developers had in mind.
Similarly, most of the villains are interesting puzzles to solve that present different challenges depending on your chosen cast of characters and the environment in which you do battle. However, some villains operate under a broad rule-breaking mechanic that renders a particular character almost useless, or they have one particular trick around which you have to orient and time your strategy. I felt those villains had less replay value than the more broadly accessible and understandable villains. Others may appreciate these asymmetric enemies more than I do.
Fortunately, the season pass has, thus far, yielded fun additions of heroes, arch-villains and environments. If I had a criticism, I'd like to see more playable hero characters in relation to the number of arch-villains, but the mix might be sweeter to someone else's taste.
The music is upbeat from the main screen and varies appropriately with the various environments; though, like the comic book page turn wipes, I did eventually turn it off. Much more quickly, I turned off the sound effects: those become repetitive almost immediately (especially the projectile damage sound effect, which gets played frequently).
A major shortfall of the game is the lack of customization of individual hero decks. While variants on the various heroes and villains in the game can be opened up by meeting very specific gameplay requirements, they amount to having a single different core power. Being able to unlock and select different cards in an attempt to kit out a particular hero to face a specific enemy would have added another layer of strategic depth and might have made the more narrow villains more interesting to me.
Taking into account the fast game play, the colorful illustrations, the great writing on the color text and myriad combinations of heroes, arch-villains and environment (with many more coming down the pipe) that play out in many different ways, I can't help but to give this game a total thumbs-up.

I got this game in a bundle besides other games that I wanted more, but I must say, I absolutely adore this game. This is a very polished, very beautiful game, that has perfectly crafted aesthetic. It has a very deep story line of growth and death, redemption and vengeance, and got me to connect with little faceless /things/ on a much deeper level than some blockbuster rpgs out there. There is no dialogue here, the story is fleshed out purely through gameplay, and unobtrusive "cutscenes" where you give up control for a couple of seconds of scripted actions that don't really stop the pace. The music also serves as a sort of exposition on what you're supposed to feel, and the soundtrack is great. I'm not finished with the game yet, but even so far it has been totally worth it. There are puzzles that don't feel like puzzles. The game teaches you the quirks without a word, yet it does not feel like it's holding your hand.
In the game, you guide a silver circle-thing through a maze-like world with other critters. You get flagellated creatures (referred to as 'friends' in the achievements) to follow you. The conflict is brought out by a race of equivalent creatures, only they are black. You find that they attack you on sight, and, as you have no defences against them, you need your friends to save you.
There are sections of the game where you have very few friends (if at all), and the game plays very much like a stealth game, with you trying to make sure enemies don't see you. It plays like an RTS/RPG when you are up against the other side (black friends? enemies?) with a similar forces. It has amusing puzzles that will make you go "ahhh!!" when you realize the mechanics behind them. It will have you feeling triumphant after you've first beat the higher class enemies. It will have you feel scared for your life whilst you're being chased. It will make you feel sorrowful and self-loathing when the one friend that stuck by you gets impaled on a spike, or eaten by hanging flagella because you led him there.
The only thing that can count as a con here is the minimalistic UI. Though it works great aesthetically, it will take you a couple of seconds to realize what the few buttons that there are do, but once you do, you intuit it quite well. During the actual game, there are no UI elements unless you pause the game., which is just another way this game reaches the level of immersion it does. Writing this review has been hard as none of the creatures are really given in-game names.
TL;DR: Beautifully crafted, excellent use of color and sound to create a story. Like a Japanese garden, Hero of Many has attained a level of aesthetic perfection where nothing can be taken out or added without detracting from its experience.

Spec Ops has developed a cult following due to it's story, and twists and although i'd agree that the these factors are well done, the game itself is entirely forgettable. This negativity stems from it's repetitive, monontomous uninsprired gameplay housed in a poor UI and a fairly ugly looking game graphically. To think this game came out 6 years later than Gears of War which revived and arguably perfected the 3rd person cover-based shooter, is a bit of a shock. The games weapons arnt really fun to use aside from the AA12 which you only ever find twice in the game.
I played through the game on Sucidial and then FUBAR difficulty, and by lord the harder difficulties really shine to light a lot of the issues the game. Your squadmates are inherently stupid, they will frequently get themsevles downed nowhere near cover (which on FUBAR difficullty frequently meant a restart as youre going to die in the animation to pick them up). Additionally the continious deaths you'll inevitably experience on these difficulties will mean that you get to discover just how stupid the locations for some of the checkpoints are. It's not the frequency that is the issue - but rather you'll reload a checkpoint which requires you to rewatch an entire unskipable little in-game cutscene type segment. Coupled with this you'll notice that a lot of the time the shoulderhigh cover doesnt seem to work, the controls are clunky and youll find yourself not running into cover when you told your game to.
I'm not saying the game is awful, because it isnt, it's very playable and even for the story you could easily do it once and enjoy it. My issue is that the game doesnt last anymore past that. Treat it like a big blockbuster movie, watch it once, have some fun and be done with it. Because the more you look at Spec Ops the less pretty it is.

There are always games and shows where a character searches for that perfect enemy to defeat. Trying to stay alive enough to do their mission. This is a different situation for Die With Glory. You play as Sigurd, an old Viking warrior, looking for a battle that will give him a glorious death and a ticket to Valhalla. It also helps your love is a valkyrie willing to bring you back when Valhalla rejects you.
Interestingly this is set up as storytime, each section of Hack and Slash Tavern is a new area you can play. As Sigurd remembers the event, you decide what happens to others before going in. Each area has it's own puzzles and tasks you have to do. This is honestly easy as wandering through the level, but some are more difficult to get through. By the end of the level you would be weapon ready for your opponent.
There are a lot of jokes and easter eggs. From what you and other characters say to how the level is designed. These jokes can easily not hit and can seem a little pointless. Also if you are looking to get to know a lot of the characters, you won't. As most of them either say jokes, has an item you need, or is a device to decide your path. The only people you really need to remember is Sigurd and his companions as they do get a little voice acting in this (I do wish this happened more often).
There are limitations of what you can do. You can not go off of what you said in the beginning, so if you said this person did not die, you have to make sure they did not die. This decision can carry over to at least another area and can change it up a bit. Nothing too drastic, but it can block off other alternate verisons of the story unless you go back and choose differently. The puzzles can differ, but it mostly ends the same way. This can be especially tedious towards the end as it turns into doing the same thing. By just play through it without going back, excluding when it forces you to, Die WIth Glory gives a two hour experience.
The point and click aspect can be awkward at times. Many actions you need to do works fine, but the platforming can cause you to do multiple clicks to move. I'm sure this is better in the mobile app as you work with your fingers rather than a mouse. With this in mind, having controller support would of actually helped with smoothing the platforming out. Of course this takes away the point of a point and click game but sometimes it doesn't fit.
I do like both art styles they decided to go for, the rough black and white style cutscene and the cartoonish style the gameplay takes place. Sadly, they are disconnected from each other. If you had a different weapon other than a sword, it will still be a sword in the cutscene. Also, the battle happens in the cutscene than happens again in the cartoon style. Making Sigurd awkwardly hold his weapon most of the time in the air before the sequence of events happen again. So either taking out the sequence after the cutscene or just doing everything in a cartoon style would of been better.
This only contains one chapter of Sigurd's tale. I do wish this was advertised as an episodic game as it is very disappointing when you find out. I can't help to also wonder how the other chapters will be added. If it's just going to be a free update or paid DLC and if so how much.
+ Art work
+ Love the voice work
- Can be awkward with the platforming
- Disconnection between both art styles
Die With Glory brings you the goal of being accepting into Valhalla as you play as Sigurd, the unreliable Viking story teller. Each of his adventures framed in a way that you can decide what alternate version you want to do in each section of Hack and Slash Tavern. But with this only container one chapter, and hinting that the tavern will be built upon, does Sigurd actually achieve his death? He can't already be in Valhalla as people who you said died is not there and one person makes a small line about how Valhalla might not be what Sigurd thinks it is. So either this eventually goes away from this framing, never dies at the end, or just everyone at the tavern attacks him. Despite the flaws I do find it fun and recommend this, but I might be leaning more towards the mobile app (IOS and Android for $2.99) rather than the steam release. Hopefully Sigurd does go to Valhalla eventually.

First and foremost let me mention that I don't like the release module used for this game, I don't think that a Hitman game should be released in an episodic format especially considering that it breaks immersion and pacing, and also that the consumer would be paying for an unfinished product is something that I personally tend to not support. As a result I refused to purchase the game until it was complete and I would only puchase it during a very reasonable sale, with all of this out of the way let me say what I actually think of the game.
I liked Hitman, there isnt any two ways to go about it. The game is very enjoyable and overall pretty well put toghether (not flawless though), there are a ton of different ways that you can complete a mission which adds to replayability and that is good however it doesn't justify an episodic release since replaying the same level over and over again without going through the entire game first can be pretty boring. This leads to a big issue caused by the episodic style release, that is that after every mission I have to go back to the main screen in order to go to the next mission and I feel that by doing that it breaks my immersion a bit.
Voice acting is top notch and the soundtrack although to me not memorable blends well with the game's environment. The gameplay is pretty solid although when you knock out a character and want to drag him and if there are a few items lying around the KO'd character it can be a pain to get the drag prompt to appear, this becomes annoying especially if you are in a hurry because a NPC is coming towards the room you are in and you need to desperately hide the body.
I would of liked Agent 47 to have a bit more of variattion in his moveset, for example if you takedown an enemy next to a container he could chuck him inside it as part of the takedown, it would be a pretty cool way to use the enviornment to hide away bodies in a quick and efficient manner. It would of been nice if you could walk up to a character while concealing your gun behind your back since it is something I picture an assassin doing. Looking at current game technology it does feel like the combat mechanics weren't as refinned as they could of been.
I feel like levels are a bit too small in scale, at times I would of liked to have a slighly larger environment to play around in and be a bit more constructive with how I could take out my target. Although not really that big of an issue but with only 6 levels the game left me wishing for a bit more at the end.
In my opinion the weakest part of the game is the story, it doesn't connect too well with the gameplay part and feels very disjointed and feels more like padding than something necessary. You could remove the entire plot from the game and get the exact same experience, which is a shame since I like a good narrative in a game, also story doen't answer any questions at it's conclusion and only raises even more. The game is obviously following a TV season style of storytelling but here is something the game does wrong, a season finale normally answers most if not all of the season's questions while raising new important ones and Hitman fails terribly at that.
Overall it's a fun although slightly flawed game, I would recommend it to anyone but not as a full priced game since it does feel a little bit lacking so I would recommend to pick it up during a sale.
If I had to give it a score I would say it's a solid 7/10

Honestly pretty upset about that Flaw and yes it is a flaw). The Music was great as well capturing the tone and depression of the Crime noir feel (The two best examples:
and
The gameplay improvements were small but still ironed of the little faults of the original nicely (And to be fair having the best bulet time mechanics of the series). But oppose to 3 the improved Gameplay didnt come at the cost of the story as it still had the classic Max Payne charm and character with writing and film noir presentation.
The only problem being the length. A 4-6 hour game (Possibly even shorter if very comofortable with the gameplay) but games have been shorter before like Uncharted. However unlike something as Uncharted MP2 Didnt feel as well fleshed out as it couldve been for the deeper analytical view it tried to have of Max's crumbling mind instead having to rush scenes. Say what you want about MP3 but every moment felt important to the plot and fleshed out enough for both the story and the gameplay perfectly to leave an impact. While MP2 Instead feels very disconnected instead jumping from piece to piece.
Despite that its still a very good game even if not as fleshed out as it could be. In case it dosent seem to want to work though:

Basically adapting the gameplay of MP3 into 2 and adding a lot more content into the game from Time trials to neat arcade modes designed by the fans which add a lot more to the game although not tampering with the main campaign length so not quite ficing the larger issue. Still a mod defitnely worth checking out.

Several times I thought a cutscene meant the end, only to be put in a very similar level only with different background color. If you want to invest the time for an at times very lovely and meditative experience, it's well worth it , even though it gets long-winded.

What to say about Heroes of Scene? Simple. Don't play it!
No-one provides anything for free, and this is a perfect example. You play cards to summon units, but unsurprsingly, the best units are locked behind microtransactions. Every player online seems to have the best units, and you don't stand a chance against them. A microtransaction model in itself means that you have to be able to unlock the units through natural progression, though this aspect of the game is *broken*. You only are awarded cards when you win a battle against a human opponent, and you can only realistically win when you have *already* forked out for better cards!
I was thinking that because it advertises itself as a 'single-player' game, maybe I could just play against the AI, and rack up some wins there? Well, you sure can play against an AI! ...Only for the tutorial level though. To play any proper matches, you need to play with other players. You're not getting out of their payment scheme *that* easily!
You can buy new cards in the shop right? Well, I actually had enough tokens for a single pack, so I thought I'd check that out. You get three heroes or spells... or so you think. The screen after opening the pack shows that you got three cards... though if you check your library, you'll see you only actually got one of them! A heavily microtransaction-driven game that actually *scams* its purchasers!? Wow!
The gameplay itself is actually quite fun, and could make for a decent game if it was implemented properly. Sadly, it is not. It is incredibly glitchy. I tried to adjust the game to windowed mode, and found it odd that the toggle was set to windowed mode already, though the game had loaded fullscreen. I had to toggle it to fullscreen and back to get it to window properly. After doing this, it locked my mouse to the top two-thirds of the screen, so in order to fix that, I had to adjust the screen resolution twice as well.
The developers seem to have cut a lot of corners everywhere. I checked the official achievements to try and get an idea of what exactly the game has to offer, and got more confused than I was after trying to adjust the settings! The developers are clearly non-native English speakers, but they didn't even *attempt* to make the instructions in English. Seriously, a Google Translation would have done a far better job. That's a nitpick, but just goes to show how little the developers actually care about their game.
Ignore the fact that this game is "free", and avoid this game like the plague.

The level design is done very well, but the sameness of the levels gets
very repetitive.  There are a few elements that change, but overall they don't vary
the levels enough to inspire the player.
The combat is sound, but is nothing special.  If you don't mind casual games
that are very repetitive, this might be a game to get, if on sale.  It's not horrible,
but I don't see myself playing this game again, or buying this game knowing what I
know now.

Spec Ops: The Line is an anti war war-game with a story very rich with character development and moral choices. The game has around 12 chapters, and would probably take you around 6 hours to finish(I took 8 because I played it at the hardest difficulty and I died A LOT, AI is fairly decent in this game). The game features generic 3rd person shooter combat, ala gears of war, but that's not really a bad thing in my opinion. AI is also worth mentioning in this game as they will try their best in combat, the AI also understands the concept of higher ground, flanking, and many more squad tactics. The use of environmental objects during combat also adds a twist of action to the combat, shooting glass to bury your enemies in sand never gets old, though I wish I could've used these more in non-scripted situations. One major flaw in the game though is the awkward controls, getting to cover can sometimes feel like a total chore as your character struggles to hide behind the proper object at the proper angle, the controls during combat also feel a bit clunky due to this. Overall The decent challenge offered by the game wrapped up in its deep and engrossing story is an experience you shouldn't miss.

IO interactive deserve praise for the Hitman series, which with each entry have been trying a new take. The 1:st entry
(Hitman codename 47) was a load of boring assignments and is sadly unplayable today, mostly due to gameplay mechanical issues. The music was quite good though.
The Second game (Hitman 2: Silent Assasin) intruduced better mechanics, graphics and even better music scores! The story was somewhat stereotypical and wasn´t that good.
The Third entry (if you can call it that) Hitman Contracts was more like a reboot or "BEST OF" Classic Hitman Codename 47, it was a bit buggy but played more like Silent Assasin. They tried a different narrative in this game, with hitman remembering the different assasinations, making you play them.
Hitman Bloody Money amped up graphics, music, story and it was insanely silly and goregous at the same time. They also had an interesting review system that changed the difficulty depending on how bad you played. It also let you buy upgrades for your weapons before each mission.
Hitman Absolution felt to me like they tried to mix Hitman with a grindhouse movie, and they streamlined to formula to a degree that it failed to deliver anything. They focused more on the story here. And let´s be honest...Hitman never had a great story to begin with!?
With HITMAN (why the name?) they went back to blood money formula, but episodical. The Result? Well it´s good, plays well, feels great and it does what it does.
However, personally I didn´t enjoy it as much as I enjoyed Blood Money. I can´t tell why though.
It´s not a bad game at all! It great! Plays well and has multiple axcess points for taking out your targets and such. But something is missing. Maybe it´s the music? Could it be something as simple as cutting out Jesper Kyd´s music since Absolution has made Hitman less enjoyable?
I don´t know. But something is missing and it shows.
I will still recommend the game though, cuz it IS a good game which offer a lot of value for it´s money!

In my opinion this game is in most aspects an improvement over the original. But be warned: Steam version is as bad as Max Payne 1. If you have an OS that is newer than Windows XP, you will need to find and install some fixes for the game to even run, and then some more to fix the sounds issues and give it proper widescreen support.
After you get it up and running properly, expect the following:
- This game is much, much easier than the original Max Payne. Probably not too easy, but at least you will suffer much less cheap deaths, especially instant ones. Aiming is still hindered by forced vSync, but feels significantly more fluid than in previous game. There are harder modes for more challenge, but you need to beat it on default difficulty first.
- Combat feels less luck-based and more dependent on player's actual skill. Enemies, however, are not as mobile as in MP1, but still move around quite a bit. Weapons are rebalanced and are more diverse and shooting feels, for a lack of better term, just better. However, in most situations the player is stocked with enormous amount of weapons and ammo, which is nice from the variety perspective, but it also means that there is only a handful of instances where ammo conservation is a thing. The boss battle is also much more interesting.
- Physics are improved and expanded. There is semi-decent ragdoll in place now, and there's a lot of reactive clutter all over the levels, which adds quite a bit to the spectacle, especially when there are explosions going off. Speaking of spectacle - it looks just phenomenal for its age. Only human models are somewhat sub-par, but still huge improvement over the original.
- There is a metric ton of side content - TV shows, conversations, environmental storytelling, and thankfully you can skip it all very easily.
- The tone is entirely different now. MP1 was gritty, its humor was dark. MP2 is still a blood-soaked tragedy, but much lighter and cheesier, shifting from noir to alsmot being kitsch. It is both serious and deconstructive at the same time, hard-hitting the player with tangible drama, and then outright mocking events that predated the sequel - just watch a couple of 'episodes' of♥♥♥♥♥♥Justice on MP2's TVs. MP1 was suffering of both character and player, and MP2 leaves the pain to Payne(see what I did there?). But despite being somewhat bipolar, it delivers the 'feels' when it has the intent to do so.
- Bullet time is revamped. It regenerates now and is easier to use. Whether you'll like it or not is up to a personal preference.
If you enjoy story-rich third-person shooters this is one of the better ones. Buy it and play it. Just maybe try to buy it elsewhere first.

DMC: Devil May Cry is not its predecessors.
It shares the same basic edge, the "Devil may care" attitude and wordplay, the completely ridiculous slash-em-down combat we've all come to know and love, but it is not just a continuation or re-coloring of the past four games. In my opinion, this is not necessarily a bad thing.
Ninja Theory has come a long way in their game developement, from a sword-heavy Resident Evil clone all the way to the dynamic smash of DMC4. This is simply a further step in their evolution, and it shows that, while storyline can still be lacking with these guys, they're keeping all the things they love about the series and trying to shine a new light on it.
Mind you, I'm playing on a laptop -- a laptop I bought for school purposes, at that. Sometimes it gets laggy, or the controls aren't quite perfect on my system, something I've seen is not nearly as much of an issue on a console or better computer. Even with the technical downgrades I suffer through, though, this game was a visual and finger-flying f***fest, and I adore it.
Too bad it looks like the last they'll be doing with Dante.....

DmC is not a bad game. Its got great graphics, good music, well done voice acting, and smooth gameplay. So why am I not recommending it? For a couple reasons.
1. Super repetitive. Everything from the areas you are in, to the challenges you must do, to the fights, and overall graphics. Oh look, its another part of the city thats getting mutated into a chaos realm. Joy. Hardly any variation. Levels in this game are what those special "Artistic" levels in other games do as that one time side mission. Only, these are EVERY part of the game. The gameplay in each is always the same too, with the game going through the same sets of scripted events over and over again. "Oh, think you made it to the end of the level, NOPE, here are more enemies, or here's a roadblock that suddenly forms causing you to find another way." Rinse, repeat. I kept hoping for even one level that didnt have that "you've done way too many drugs" look to it, and it hasnt yet happened. Overall, just playing through these levels and the gameplay, is dull.
2. Too many combos. Sounds silly right? There comes a point when the 8+ buttons your fingers have to manage on a controller have surpassed the insane when it comes to various combinations they must learn and use. Its good for a game to have combos. Games like God of War showed this, Combos gives you that extra bit of exciting "oomph" to combat beyond bland button mashing. However, this game goes to the extreme with the amount of buton combinations you have to use, enough to tie your fingers in knots. It then scores you based on how many of these seemingly infinite combos you can do. The irony is, many of the enemies DIE before you can manage to do enough combos to often get a good combo rating.  This game is litterally like "Twister" for your fingers.

This game will probably make you cry.
The graphics and music are beautiful enough to move you to tears.
The story might make you bawl like a little girl; The first 10-15 minutes of this game has a lot in common with the first part of Up, and it doesn't let up from there.
But most of all, you *will* almost certainly cry tears of frustration, because those graphics, music, and story hide a ball-breaking hard metroidvania platformer that gives you maybe 10 minutes of hand-holding before putting you through jumps and challenges you might have seen in the final stages of a Mega Man game or in one of those Super Mario world hacks. This game tracks your deaths, and don't be surpised if you hit triple digits you first time through, even if you've been playing these types of games for years. There is a reason the achievement for the 1-life mode is called "Unhinged."
That being said, there are very few (though a couple do exist) places where the game does anything bs, it's always something you did and can improve on. So if you like crying, or consider this sort of game the kind of challenge that drives you, it is a great buy. Just make sure to bring tissues.

The story is really good. But, the gameplay not so much.
Generally speaking it's good. The guns are nice, the ammo (or rather lack there of) is pretty good considering it actually makes you have to conserve some of it and choose your weapons carefully. You can't just carry a rocket launcher for the lol's you have to carry two automatic weapons otherwise you don't have enough ammo to get through the level.
But the controls are awful. The controls for: Sprint, Take cover, and heal team mates. Are all bound to the same key: Spacebar! Which is all sorts of stupid. Normal games would put shift on run, space on take cover, and put interaction kets on something like F or E or even V. Unfortunately, the shift button is used as the interaction key for (Some reason?)
So if you're in a hectic firefight trying to fight off 30 enemies at once while healing a team mate and dodging the many many grenades that always get thrown non stop, you'll end up having a control issue and dying.
I'm one of those people who like playing games on the hardest difficulty they have to offer, and I started off that way too. But after half way through the game (literally at the half way point) I just go so tired of the controls ♥♥♥♥ing me over, and the A.I team mates not being good enough to kill anything fast enough (Though they only died like 3 times so that's a plus) that I just ripped it all the way down to easy and tried to enjoy the story instead.
It was worth the money, and the 7-8 hours I spent going through the campaign the first time. It's also worth the immersion factor. Mostly because the main character is how you want him to be, he's as cruel or forgiving as you make him.
I think it's worth it for the story. But if you're here for a COD type single player/cooperative shooter, you might want to look somewhere else. This game is here for the story, not the gunplay. It's more like a story book that happens to have a gun ducktaped to the side.

Sentinels of the Multiverse is a fully co-operative card game with a heavy comic book theme. You pick a villain, a group of heroes, and an environment to battle in, and then fight it out. The game plays mechanically simply... each hero gets to play a card, use a power, then draw a card... But there is a lot of depth and complexity here, and you'll need to come up with clever strategies to keep ahead of the game.
Variety and replayability are key here, and that's expressed well in the cards. Picking a character doesn't just change a couple of variables; everyone has their own completely unique deck with their own gimmicks that come in to play. Bunker is a guy in a transforming mech suit, with different modes that improve some of his traits at the cost of others. Tachyon is a speedster who blasts through her deck, being able to launch absurdly powerful attacks the bigger her discard pile is. The Visionary is a precognitive psychic who specialises is controlling the flow of the game over direct damage, and so on. Unlockable variants take this a step further, giving characters alternate base powers that can substantially change how they play.
As someone who's a big fan of the physical card game, this is my preferred way to play; there can be a lot to keep track of and it's great to have the game do this for you, especially with any special information only a click away. They've also added weekly challenges to take on, Steam achievements, and a lot of other additional elements.
Basically, if you have any love for these types of games, you can't afford to pass Sentinels by. I recommend not just getting this game, but also the DLC season pass; the amount of extra content already out is *absurd*, with new heroes, environments, and villains, and more on the way, and the game gets exponentially better as you can try out new combinations. For the price, the DLC is a steal.

I only recently got in to SotM, the physical card game.. and swiftly bought everything there is available for it, and have been playing the hell out of it. I absolutely adore the game. It's super quick to learn and every hero and villain plays differently. It's even a ton of fun to play solo- but it takes up so much space!
This version is pretty much perfect for me. It's the same game.. Same mechanics, same rules, same characters, but takes up a hell of a lot less space and does the calculations for me (which those who've played the card game know there's a lot of calculations).
The one issue I have is I'm having to rebuy things I already have. I mean, I'll buy all the DLC for it for certain, but I already spent nearly $200 on this game... but I enjoy it enough on the PC to drop the $35 (plus the next sets of DLC, I look forward to Vengeance!) on it.
I also would love to see remote multiplayer.
But what about someone who's never played the card game? That's the big thing for this.. how is it for someone who doesn't play it already?
Well!
Sentinels of the Multiverse, just the base game has a ton of potential options for play with 10 heroes, 4 villains and 4 environments (and so many more to come).
Each hero plays differently, and often not just in terms of "their cards do different things", there are actually different playstyles for each hero. The same goes for the villains and environments. Every set up of heroes, villain and environment you play will play a bit differently.
The mechanics are simple, which is because this isn not a digital card game but a digital reproduction of a physical card game, so the mechanics are all ones that a human mind can track. This doesn't mean they're weak though, they function very well for the idea of the game.
The strategies are fairly in depth in how you stack your team, including the order you play them in, and the more you play it the more you'll come to understand which strategies work well against which villains, and which characters go best in the 'first player' position.
The game plays like a comic book. All it needs is pithy dialogue between the heroes and villains in combat- Though there are little quotes on ever card. If comics books and super heroes are your thing, it's definitely up your alley.
The super heroes in Sentinels of the Multiverse feel like.. somewhere between knockoffs of and hommages to archetypal heroes such as Batman, Superman, etc. Each one even has a bio, if you feel like getting more immersed in the world. If you played City of Heroes back in the day, you'll find the characters and world have a similar feel. I still think the folks over at >Games played it.
Over all?
If you've played SotM and want an easier way to play solo: Instabuy.
If you've played SotM and don't like it: Pass.
If you've never played SotM, and like digital card games: Buy it.

I played this back when it was first released but couldn't remember much about it so I decided to replay it.  It still holds up surprisingly well for being an older game.  The gunplay feels good (with better hit detection than the original Max Payne), the graphics are improved, and it seems to take itself a little more seriously by dropping all the goofy cartoon faces that Max Payne would make in the original (there's even an audio clip in the game where they kind of make fun of themselves for doing that).
The same old comic-style noir cut scenes are still here and as good as ever.  The story seemed a little less interesting this time and was more about Max chasing Mona Sax around and shooting up all kinds of baddies in the process.  There's a tag team section where Mona covers Max with a sniper rifle while he traverses a construction yard that is probably the pinnacle of the game's ingenuity.  The "All Ghillied Up" mission in Call of Duty 4 gets a lot of praise for this idea but Max Payne 2 really thought of it first even if they didn't execute it quite as stylistically.
Lots of interesting locales though and the way you defeat the final boss was a means of thinking outside the box before it was cool to make games that think outside the box.

As the silence gradually gets filled by creeping and submerged ambient sounds, and as a bright divine-like light slowly emerges in a atmospheric monochrome world surrounded by black silhouettes, you know Hero of Many by Czech-developer Trickster Arts isn’t your ordinary action-adventure game. The simplicity of the game experienced in the first few minutes of gameplay is stunning – yet genius and immersive.
The player takes the role as a nameless and thus anonymous orb-like microorganism on a quest to defeat lethal black counterparts whilst rescuing as many friends as possible. In good accordance with the wordless story, there is no way of telling which way is the correct way through any of the 26 different maze-like maps. Players may only navigate using their memory, or by the guidance of carefully placed lanterns which gets activated once passed. However, as there is no time limit, exploration immediately becomes the natural first priority. By exploring all caves and corridors the player furthermore ensures to find close-to-all friends – the more friends you collect, the stronger (and exposed) you become.
Hero of Many is an atmospheric-action adventure set in a deep undersea and monochrome world with an immersive design. Packed with friends and foes, exploration and survival becomes a natural aspect of the game, and without words or back-story, the player is allowed and encouraged to create their own story and follow their own paths.

This game, though it uses no speech or text, conveys a surprisingly emotional plot as you follow your water creatures through their journey.  The visuals are deeply artistic, and the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal.  This is the perfect game for a road trip or simply a free afternoon.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful game in every facet of its being. As should be evident from the PV, the visuals are vibrant, detailed, and create a dreamlike atmosphere. Visually, this game is truly a work of art.
The story is simple and touching, though somewhat vague at times. The classic theme of light and darkness is pervasive throughout and is woven in more of a yin and yang type fashion rather than good vs evil.
The music is gentle and unobtrusive without betraying a sense of urgency when appropriate. I wouldn't say the musical score is all that memorable, but its ephemeral charm matches the visuals well.
The movement and combat mechanics are fluid and polished. The controls are mapped well and I seldom found myself frustrated by anything other than operator error. There is a variety of abilities to learn, but not so many as to become confusing.
The developers did an impressive job of giving the player lots of mobility. Many of the abilities you unlock are movement enhancements that allow you to access new areas of the map and traverse the world more gracefully. There are several parts of the game where speed and timing are critical and your mastery of these skills is tested.
There are plenty of secrets and achievements to keep you busy for a little while after completing the game. They don't make it too tedious to explore and find all of the secret areas.
This is a very comfy and well-designed game that I think just about anyone could enjoy.

While the ideas of demons running the world's companies and media outlets, etc. is intrigueing, the game is often crass and tasteless for no reason at all.  The death metal soundtrack, while appropriate, becomes grating after awhile also.  In short, it's fun until about halfway through when you say "enough is enough".

Hey do you want a game that makes you feel like rotten slime all the time but is oddly super enguaging? Are you curious for what video games can be as a medium other than just cheap fun entertainment? Then this is a game for you. This game is great.
But first off lets go with the negatives and why i don't think they are that bad:
The campaign which is the only thing that matters in this game (there is a crummy stock multiplayer tacked on but you can safely ignore it), is relatively short. I completed it in around 6 hours and a not insignificant amount of that time was spent dying. With a price tag of 30 smackums this may seem a little short but a couple thing. 1. This is one of the few campaign experiences I might actually play again so probably bump that time up a little bit. 2. This is probably the most important to me, considering the other forms of entertainment we spend our money on, dollars per gaming hour is normally incredibly cheap. Even with this price tag you are probably breaking even with a movie theater experience and this game is no batman vs. superman, it is incredibly compelling and worth it. That being said I'm a cheapo and grabbed this game during the steam summer sale.
It's next biggest shortfall is the clunkyness of the combat system. A lot of its weaknesses actually play to the advantage that the atmosphere is trying to project however the cover system in a cover shooting game is inexcusable. A lot of my aformentioned dying occured do to my inability to predictably go into and out of cover and or jump over cover to progress at key moments. That being said  this is not a shoot em up. It is an interactive drama disguised as a shoot em up. So its shortfalls in this area doesn't impact the experience of the game as much as it would in a battlefield clone.
One last thing is that if you look closely enough especially at earlier events in the game once you understand a little better what is happening you might find some things that seem like plot holes. That being said if you are looking that hard you will be enguaged enough to not really care about them.
Now for the positives:
The narrative is compelling, the story pacing is spot on, the character development is good, and the ability for the game to make you feel like you should just quit and uninstal life is a calculated science. This last part is the most impressive thing to me. The game uses every little trick it can to make you enguage and feel culpable with every bad thing the main character ends up doing. The music, the visuals, the dialog, everything, all synergizes to make the "choices" you make feel like your own.
In summary, the shooter mechanics aren't great, the story is great, and you will feel bad when you finish it and probably end up writing a review on steam for the first time recommending it to complete strangers.
*Also, and this is important the M rating is not for show, GTA doesn't hold a candle on how disturbing this game is so keep that in mind when playing it and probably don't play it around people you wouldn't want to watch apocalypse now.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter developed by "Yager" and was released on the 26th of June in 2012.
You're playing as Martin Walker, he is part of the United States Army's "Delta Force".
Walker and his squad are on a recon mission in Dubai which has been hit by a disastrous sandstorm turning it into a broken and apocalyptic city.
I really had no expectations when I bought this game so I didn't really know if it was gonna be another military shooter or not.
Well it turned out that it wasn't your typical military shooter.
Right from the beginning you're put in a helicopter behind a minigun shooting at incoming attack choppers.
After that you're introduced to your squad and they are surprisingly well designed.
It took me some time to get used to the controls which are really "odd" in my opinion since spacebar is used for sprinting, taking cover and interacting with doors or something.
Another thing what I really disliked was the checkpoint system, it's not uncommon to get a checkpoint at the beginning of a cut scene which wouldn't be a problem if you didn't have to skip it every time you have to restart.
I also had the issue that whenever you tried to run from one place to another your character would sometimes sit behind cover because sprinting and taking cover is bound to the same button.
I also had an issue with scoped rifle's that whenever I used the scope that aiming would become a real pain because the aiming feels like it's jittering as in it skips pixels or barely reacts to my mouse movement at all, I have no clue if this is a bug or just an dreadful design choice.
The character design and character development however is really good, throughout the game your squad members will start behaving differently the further you get into the game, Lugo was by far my favorite character in the game.
The guns feel solid and balanced as well I didn't really feel like a certain weapon was overpowered even though I mainly used the ak trough at least sixty percent of the game.
and you really don't get your hands on some of the more powerful guns until you're further in the game.
You can also command your squad to take down a certain enemy or trow a flashbang when you're in trouble this worked fine for the most part but you can only use the flash command whenever you're pinned down but the problem is that sometimes you could really use the flash command and the game didn't allow you to.
The game puts you into really tough situations where you have to make choices where you have to pick between one horrible thing and another, some of these decisions where really hard to make and these decisions had often shocking results.

A military combat game that puts the spotlight on the value of life and decisions.
STORY
This is a short one. But it shouldn't be long anyway. The story is presented in the grittiest manner possible. It is filled with characters that evolve as you move forward, characters that feel real, characters that respond to the situations in front of you. This game's tale begins as one thing and ends as another.
Plenty of cut scenes to ensure that you feel the story, your objectives and your men's mental and emotional conditions. I believe that the story IS the core of the game. Yes, the shooting is fun and everything, but staying true to the message of the game which is the story is the primary concern while playing this game.
So much emotions are packed into each sector of the game, after 4 hours I already felt the weight and burden of the protagonist, and truth be told - I started to feel tired. "Tired but having to move forward" is what the game is about, so it is a joy that the developers were able to make its gamer feel what the heros' feel.
CONTROLS and MECHANICS
The controls are a little quirky at times. Sometimes, I'd initiate cover and nothing would happen, thus I'd get shot - a lot. Other times, the game would insist that I move cover to cover or stick to cover needlessly, which is annoying. I found myself dying over and over because of the issue I had with the control system. It was ruining my immersion with the story. Thus, I had to turn down the difficulty. Like what I said earlier, the story and immersion is the main concern of the game.
Shooting rifles feel nice, the recoil is good. The sound, complements the gameplay very well. What  tops these, are the satisfaction I got from landing head shots down to blasting a bad guy with a big old shotgun.
One bad thing I can say is the gameplay feels repetitive: bad guys shooting at you, you hide and shoot back until they are dead. I did enjoy the area where you had to stealth-snipe your way through a well guarded building. Apart from that, everything is repeated. Since the game is acceptably short, its repetitive nature is not that big of an issue.
VERDICT
A must play! Bare with the repetitive game play and you will be rewarded with a story worthy of your time.

SO:TL sacrifices inventive gameplay to show the player the horrors of war, where "just following orders" can lead, and what happens when you go "too far".

Story - 6.75/10 - Interesting, but, nothing I haven't seen before. Maybe it had more of an edge when it was first released. Also, none of your choices effect the game in any way.
Overall - 6.5/10 - Play through on Easy, the story is what you're here for.

Everyone knows the big-name role playing games: Dragon Age, Oblivion, Final Fantasy, etc. And believe me, I've played them all.
However, one of the greatest role playing games I've ever played isn't one of them. In fact, I'll bet you've never heard of it. Even if you did hear about it, you probably never bothered to look at it due to the game's wacky title: Divine Divinity. Divinity is a PC role playing game developed by Larian Studios, released in 2002. The game has everything you could want in an epic RPG: solid graphics (at least for the time), excellent storytelling, engaging gameplay & combat, and incredible immersion. A sequel was released in 2009 which I have yet to try, though I am very much looking forward to doing so.
The story of the game is probably one of its greatest assets; never have I played a game so deep and involving. Divine Divinity takes on a relatively dark tone, in which the world is experiencing a lot of instability and turmoil. It's typical fantasy fare, but it contains a lot of twists, epic adventures, and dangerous enemies. You'll really start to invest yourself in the characters and the setting.
The game world is absolutely massive, spanning many thousands of screens. Traveling through the world is also very exciting -- there is no simple "fast travel" system like their is in Oblivion so you actually feel like you're journeying through the lands. There are teleporter scrolls and stones you can unlock, but you'll have to complete some hefty side quests to obtain them. I actually like this design, since it forces you to earn any form of fast travel (I didn't enjoy fast travel in Oblivion since it kind of spoiled me and brought me out of the world in a way).
But the main appeal of this game is that the world it takes place in simply feels alive. Not only is it large, there is so much going on in it, too, and Divinity does an excellent job of creating one hell of an immersive atmosphere that you can almost feel like a part of. One of the ways the game accomplishes this is by sprinkling little events throughout the game world. For example, in the middle of one of the forests there is a series of gold coins laid out in a "trail" that leads off the main path; if you choose to follow the trail of gold, you'll eventually end up into a clearing where a large group of orcs will ambush (and likely kill) you. Another example -- there is a random human army outpost in the middle of the woods that seems friendly enough -- that is, until you enter. Once you enter, a mage from the Black Ring cult (your chief antagonists in the game) magically appears and casts a mind control spell on everyone, turning them all against you. Little things like this really serve to immerse you in the instability and danger that permeates the land. Immersion and narrative are the chief things I value in a video game, and Divinity delivers in spades.
There is SO much to see, do, and explore in this game -- I barely scratched the surface of this game...you can easily put 300 hours into this game on a single playthrough if you are thorough. There are tons and tons of side quests, and the game almost requires you to do several of them (since they give you much needed experience points). But do not fear - side quests in Divine Divinity are rarely menial, like the typical fetch quests of other RPGs (gather 10 pieces of wood, kill 20 wolves, etc.). Instead, side quests are like mini storylines with several chapters, and they tell compelling narratives on their own. For example, one side quest involved finding the source of a poison that was infecting a town's population; another had me investigating political corruption within another town. These side quests are meaningful and important, and increase your stake in the game world and its inhabitants. Also, most side quests also have multiple endings, meaning that your choices actually impact the game world. This is another example of how immersive the game world is.
Adding to this is the game's "population"; there are hundreds of NPC's populating the game world, and each one of them has a unique personality to match. They all go about their lives in an organic way, waking up in the morning and going to bed at night (yes, the game has a realistic day/night cycle) Dialogue in the game is more free-form (a la Mass Effect), meaning you can interact with them in many ways.
Probably one of the only issues with the design of Divine Divinity is that the pacing is a bit off, especially in the beginning of the game. This is partly because, since the entire game world is open to exploration right from the start (save for a few areas) and this world is so enthralling, it gives you the itch to start exploring right away despite the fact that you start the game ill equipped to handle some of the game's tougher foes. I remember the first time I played the game, I opted to leave the village of Aleroth (the game's starting point) since I wanted to see the game's vast sights; however, outside the walls of town, I kept dying easily at the hands of any and all enemies I encountered.
Finally, the music score of the game is absolutely awesome; it does an incredible job of setting the darker mood of the game and adds a lot to the immersion factor.
Overall, if you are a fan of games similar to Diablo/Diablo II, you will feel right at home with Divine Divinity.

Yes, I own the tabletop game and I really enjoy it.  I bought the digital version to play alone, since my board game group only meets once a week, and we don't want to play Sentinels every time.  It's a different kind of experience playing alone, where strategy takes precedence over socialization.
It's great that all the fluctuating bonuses and immunities get calculated for you, and the rewind feature is nice if you want a "do over" without having to backtrack through everything that just happened.  Expect a game against easy villains to be 30 minutes or less.  Grand Warlord Voss takes about an hour.  So far I've played against every villain with no bugs or glitches (which is quite an accomplishment, given the sheer variety of card interactivity).
Sentinels Digital is a really good tactical stretegic solitaire experience.  Much better than say, Elder Sign Omens, which is solitaire Cthulu Yahtzee.  If you are on the fence about buying the tabletop game, this is the best tutorial you can get, for less than half the price.  The artwork is vibrant and colorful, befitting the comic book superhero theme.  Even if it never gets online multiplayer, I will still enjoy this one as a solo challenge.

Caution: this game is a trap. You play a game, or two, and suddenly it's four in the morning and you have to get up at six to go to work. In the evening you play another game, and then you feel compelled to buy the tabletop version... and then all the expansions... Developers, have mercy: my board game shelf cannot fit anything else!
In all seriousness, this is a great port of a wonderful game. If you like cooperative board games (it reminds me a bit of how Ghost Stories plays, not in pure mechanics, but in the mood and brain usage), or semi-cooperative games like Legendary, Sentinels should be a no-brainer. The graphics are very stylized and comic-book like, which was slightly distracting at first, but after a couple games, I grew used to it. Luckily, the music is a great recompense; I even found myself leaving the game running once or twice in the background to listen to the soundtrack.
Recommended!

Cannot but agree with all of the comments below. This game is first and foremost an emotional, story driven experience, even though the story is abstract and metaphorical. Anyone who likes to play games that are immersive in mood will surely enjoy this tadpole adventure. Also, the audio is a must - without it, you loose a great deal of what this game has to offer. (PS: I played it on a tablet)

Hero Of Many tells the story of an orb-like creature who’s on a quest to defeat ‘black’ (evil) and at the same time save as many of its friends as possible. It draws inspiration from several games, including Journey, Limbo and even a bit of Pikmin. ‘Three awesome games ? This must be awesome too then’, I hear you say ? Well, yes and no.
Let me start by saying why I think it draws inspiration from the aforementioned games:
Journey because it tells a story without saying or showing any words; you start the game and you can pretty much immediately control the main character. Limbo because of its silhouette art style, even if it uses some background colors later on and Pikmin because you’ll be guiding your friends through obstacles, while avoiding and killing enemies.
But you don’t directly control your tadpole-like creatures. You can send them into a certain direction but you don’t control their actions. They’ll do the best they can, so if they see something edible they will consume it and if they need to break something they’ll break it. Maybe not all of them, but some of them, at least. Still, it’s all mostly an automatic process.
You’ll guide your character and the rest of the creatures through 26 levels. Except for a few of them, these levels are built in largely the same way. Navigate through maze-like levels while saving your friends and killing/avoiding enemies and get to the exit. This is fun and interesting at first, and like I said, the game does throw a few other challenges your way later in the game, but you’ll be doing mostly the same stuff for the entire duration of the game.
This isn’t a long game with just a few hours of gameplay but halfway through I grew a bit bored by it. There wasn’t much of a challenge and you’d rarely die. Was the entire game going to be this easy ? The answer is no. Because halfway through you’ll also start earning new powers. These don’t seem like much, but they’re actually quite handy once you realize the game would’ve been so much easier if you’d have started with them. So, they’re a good addition to your character and they fit the game; nothing over-the-top. You’ll earn a power to attract your buddies, you’ll earn a power to bounce off enemies/open doors and you’ll earn a power to destroy things. And yes, during the course of the game you will eventually die. Probably several times. At times it won’t always be exactly clear what’s expected of you and it might take you a few tries more than it officially should take you. This is one of the shortcomings of trying to let people experience the story instead of actually telling it. You’ll probably learn it after a while anyway, but I made me feel bitter about the game, especially because things should feel natural if you do it this way.
As I already mentioned the game’s graphics reminded me of those of Limbo, but with some much needed colors. Your creature will have a bit of color inside of it, and the backgrounds, but the rest of it is all black and white. It’s a good contrast and the use of colors give you an idea of progression.
It all looks beautiful in motion, though there is a bit of stutter every now and then. Note that the framerate doesn’t drop, not even for a second, but somehow the game does slow down from time to time. Really weird and this shouldn’t happen in a 2D game.
The interface is clearly made with mobile phones in mind and it’s one of the things that could’ve used a bit of extra work. Don’t get me wrong, it all works very nicely. It’s just shown in such a way that I was frequently reminded that I’m dealing with a port here.
The music is beautifully orchestrated and has a good, bombastic atmosphere. I’m not sure if a band was really used here, or that it was all manufactured but I was absolutely impressed by it. Excellent work, really.
Hero Of Many isn’t a long game and it should take you roughly 5-6 hours to complete. After that there’s no real reason to go through it again, but that’s okay. I think it’s a game meant to be played just once, or at least once every (couple of) year(s). For me personally it was long enough, I actually would’ve enjoyed it a bit more if it was shorter, but most of you will enjoy it regardless.
Hero Of Many isn’t my hero, but it might just be for the rest of you. In that case its title
carefully chosen. It’s an enjoyable game that drags on for a bit too long but it’s not in the least boring or bad enough to not play it. So give it a try if you can.
[Rating: 77/100]
