TL;DR. Ori focuses heavily on platforming through beautiful environments with an outstanding soundtrack. If you’re looking for a similar style game with more emphasis on combat and boss battles, then I suggest Hollow Knight. Both are great games and worth checking out if you enjoy Metroidvania style games.

Pros:
+Story and characters
+Artwork and environment
+Soundtrack
These points might vary depending on your taste but most seem to agree these are the strongest aspects of the game. They manage to tell the story wonderfully in a few short cutscenes throughout the game.
+Skill Tree: It features a straightforward linear skill tree that’s accessible to all types of gamers without feeling overwhelmed. This might be a negative for some that favor complexity; but keeping it simple helps keep the focus on the gameplay rather than optimizing your skill points.
+Map: Areas stay revealed as you explore and objectives are clearly marked. Later you can unlock skills that mark upgrades. This isn’t something I would have even thought of putting as a pro until I played Hollow Knight.
+Progression/Completion Tracking: Don’t grind enemies in this game to level up. Instead spend that time exploring and finding secrets. The progression is made so that you complete your entire skill tree just playing through normally. You will know your completion rate and total number of upgrades left at all times since it keeps track of each area.
+Difficulty Settings: They added difficulty settings to cater to players of all skill levels. You can lower the difficulty to ‘Easy’ so that it saves during escape sequences that you may have trouble on. There’s also a ‘One Life’ difficulty where you have to start from the beginning if you die.
Cons:
-Enemy Variety: There are only a handful of enemy types in this game that just get reskinned to fit the environment. I don’t mind reusing enemies but there was very little variety in their attacks in new areas. However, if you consider environmental hazards as enemies then you may not consider this an issue.

-Lack of Boss Battles: There aren’t any true boss battles in this game. Instead, the dungeons will end in escape sequences with a time limit, in the form of environmental hazards. However, there are mini-boss areas where you have to defeat multiple enemies or a common enemy with more hit points.
Neutral:
~Gameplay: For me the gameplay was a pro since I really enjoy platforming. But some people may go into this game expecting more combat and end up feeling disappointed. This only gets worse as they reach the more difficult platforming sections leaving them frustrated. Even though this is a Metroidvania style game, I have to say most of the gameplay feels more like Mario or Donkey Kong Country.
~Length: For me it was a little shorter than I expected but in no way did it affect my enjoyment of the game. I appreciate not having to grind enemies to artificially increase the length of the game. In 31 hours I was able to beat the game in every difficulty and finish all achievements. My first playthrough was just under 10 hours for 100% on Hard difficulty. Subsequent 100% playthroughs on all other difficulties were roughly 3 hours. The rest of the time was spent doing run throughs planning the route for One Life difficulty. If you don’t care about 100% then I would imagine it would be roughly 5-7 hours on first playthrough depending on your skill level.

I mention this because I know some people put a lot of value on game length. I really hope it doesn’t deter you from purchasing the game. Although I got it on sale, I would still be satisfied with my purchase if I paid full price.
Overall I think it’s a must play and I really look forward to the sequel. Those seasoned in platforming games will absolutely enjoy this game but newcomers will find this game too frustrating. Thanks for reading my review and I hope it helps in your purchasing decision.

If what you're looking for is more Half-Life--and you don't think you can wait on Valve to satisfy--then MINERVA gives you a bit of what you want. As much high praise as this game has received, though, I feel obligated to make a few criticisms.
The first is obvious: this is MORE Half-Life. Nothing here hasn't been done already, or better. It has a few problems of its own, though. Some encounters seemed almost designed to annoy. In several places the direction the player should take is not at all obvious. Of course, MINVERVA (the character) is always there to berate you for not seeing what should be, but isn't, clear. Speaking of which, what's worse than poorly-written monologue? Why, poorly-written monologue that's supposed to sound clever but comes off as ham-fisted.
Of course, these criticisms somewhat overlook the fact that, in the end, this is a mod. And as mods go, it's pretty good. It's also free. So if you've already finished Half-Life 2, might as well give it a whirl.

My all time favorite isometric RPG.
Divine Divinity is a classic 2D open-world RPG game. The freedom to do everything you please makes this game feels like a classic Skyrim. You can ignore quest and kill everyone, or be the hero and save the world. Everything is yours to decide.
One of the best thing in this game is the ability pick any object that can be dragged into your inventory window. Let say you want some chest or barrel to store your item, you can drag it on your inventory window and when you arrive at your house, you can drop it and store your items or gears. The chest/barrel will stay in that place for the rest of the game so it's safe to use.
Did I mentioned house? Well what a surprise! You can actually customize your house by picking objects on your travels such as plants, chests, decorations, chairs, foods, fruits, gardening tools even small objects like knife and seasoning salt and drop them in your house to make it livelier.
And when you're done decorating your house maybe you need a quick nap? Well you can do that in this game. You can drop the teleportation item for quick access to your house so you can sleep in your bed to recover your mana and when you wake up you'll be ready to kill skeleton warriors again.

A single-player fantasy RPG with top-down view, the 1st title of Divinity series by Belgian developer Larian Studios. Player can make their characters learn any skill regardless of their initial class. It's up to player to when & where to go, what to do. Sadly the latter 1/3 part is somehow tedious because player's character becomes too strong or enemies too weak, but overall quality is high, especially its graphics and music are impressive. With plenty of sub-quests, at least 40 to 60 hours playing is guaranteed. Getting "Divinity Anthology" which includes 3 titles of the series (this game and its spin-off "Beyond Divinity" and ultimate edition of sequel "Divinity 2 Developer's Cut") during sale on Steam saves some money.
Some tips: Manual (dd_manual.pdf) and story (story.pdf) are inside the installed folder. 1 sub quest requires some reputation so always try to commit good deeds, there's no merit of committing bad ones. (You'll be arrested by guards or executed instantly!) Some skills make the game too easy, "Aura of Command" allows to manipulate all summoned creatures including enemy's, "Deadly Gift" allows to use "Scorpion Trap", which even tears the final boss apart.

This is a faithful recreation of the rules of the tabletop game. Tracking minutiae of when various effects start and end is all taken care of. Given the potentially complex interactions between abilities that is an achievement. It allows players to experiment with the different heroes and try out strategies much more quickly than with a physical set.
However, it is better viewed as a sentinels solitaire game or a sentinels puzzle.
Because there are no other human players (and hence all cards in all hands are known) there is none of the cooperative aspect from the physical game. Multilayer would have significantly improved matters. The variant unlocks require playing in counter intuitive and sub-optimal ways waiting for combinations of cards to randomly come out of the villain deck in the correct order. This moves in the direction of puzzle rather than trying to win the game itself. But frustratingly, a puzzle with a high degree of randomness in it.
The other aspect is the user interface. There is a strong case of tablet-itess with this one.
Dragging cards up to play them with the mouse often triggers the "you must be meaning to swipe on your touch screen to scroll through your hand" action. When multiple cards are to be selected (e.g. for discard) they must be chosen one at a time rather than for example, click three and push a "do it" button.  When a card is to be played on a villain card, why can I not drag it to the card I wish to target?
Events are not collected together as they perhaps could have been. Cards which have effects like - do one damage then do another one damage - could have been collected together where there is no possibility of other effects interfering between them.
There is a lack of animations to help the player understand the context in which actions are occurring. Why did this card just appear in the middle of the screen? Whose deck did it come from? If you are familiar with the game you can probably work this out, but more animation would help? Why was it drawn? Sequences like The Visionary's one player draws a card and plays a card make visual aids to keep track of game state (e.g. whose turn is it really) important.
In summary: it might be an interesting additional experimental tool for existing players, but it is not a good introduction for new players and not a substitute for the interaction of the physical game.
Needed more work on the interface to make a good PC port.

Amazing! Absolutely amazing!
I love card strategy games and Sentinels of the Multiverse is no exception. The world of Sentinels that is brought to us through the games wonderfully expresses the creators' love for their favorite comic book settings while at the same time offering interesting characters and stories that are all their own.
The game holds great depth and variability between the multiple heroes, villains and environments which can comprise a game: each of them is well designed, both mechanically and thematically, to the point where I have a blast playing as any heroes in any environment against any villain. Comboes and synchronicity are everywhere: two heroes you may not like individually may have a combo together that you love, or a villain that you trounced easily in the city might be a completely different challenge when facing her in the ruins of Atlantis. It is an adventure just to explore the full space of possibilities which the game holds.
I'd say the Steam version of the game is well worth it, even if you are planning on acquiring (or already own) the tabletop version: the Steam version lets you get in some intensive play in which you control the entire team of heroes and have the opportunity to experiment with extreme plays and risky, involved combos before suggesting them at the game table. Better to try it out in this setting, where the computer keeps track of all those stacking effects and lets you trace back (in a limited capacity) through a sequence of plays back to a precise phase you want to re-examine or retry.
I was disappointed at first that the Steam version doesn't have multiplayer, but I am sure that it is in our future.
If you are a fan of card strategy games, cooperative games, superheroes or comic books, you owe it to yourself to give Sentinels of the Multiverse a look!

As has been said in other reviews, this is a very fun game with a huge variety of options that allow for unique playthrough each time.
Because each deck (Villain, Environment, and Heroes) is shuffled before the game, and sometimes during from card effects no two games play out the same way, even if you choose the same combination the order in which you receive powers will change, as well as how dangerous the villain starts out.  This is one of my favorite things about the game.  That and figuring out which hero combinations work well agaainst which villains.
Also, this game is an INCREDIBLE deal.  I own all of the core expansions and the game in physical form and it cost me upwards of $150 dollars.  You will get all of this content for the price of the game and season 1 pass, $14.99 and $19.99, although at this time you will be waiting  for each expansion to be coded in, over the course of this next year.  Also, some cards that were only available as Promos and which are a little more difficult to find in physical form have and will continue to become available as unlockable variants within the game.  With the next expansion they have also done a brilliant option, instead of paying to unlock them, those who don't want to face the challenge of mastering the variant unlock strategies can wait 30 days and unlock it with a code released at that time.
Note, I think you will find it highly worthwhile to purchase the core physical game as well, and perhaps some expansions with heroes you enjoy from the physical game.  Although this game does lend itself extremely well to local multiplayer, there is something about sitting around the table with some friends cards laid out on the table.. WARNING WARNING, DANGER WILL ROBINSON.  One of the greatest thing this game accomplished is the de-clutterifying of the game.  On the table you have various hitpoint counters in 1/5/10/25 cardboard tokens, as well as tokens indicating damage boosts, immunities, and other types.  A game with 5 players and certain heroes who have a lot of ongoing cards and equipment out can take up a lot of table space.  Then there is cleanup.  With this game, all of those items are secured in the computers memory, and calculations are made for you and presented with all of your options.
If there is one thing I don't like about this game it is minor elements of the UX (User interface), overall it's great... but because some options have multiple possible effects, there is a lot of confirming of your actions.  One of the neat things about the card game is that the order damage is assigned can be very significant, for example if a villain minion would deal 3 fire damage to each hero and one hero has an effect that attacks back when they receive damage, and their return attack would kill that minion choosing to damage that hero first kills the minion and prevents damage to other heroes.  Likewise, a hero may have an ability out that can change a damage type (fire), and another power that provides immunity to that type, while the environment has still another type that changes all damage to melee.  In this case you would want to have the environment change it to melee first, then the power change it to fire, and no damage is done.
Normally when I play the physical game I already know what I want done and so I make all the adjustments in my head.  But on the computer you have to communicate those decisions to the game.  And so the amount of confirming decisions you have already made can add a little bit of a delay to actions you would normally nearly instantaneously take in your head.  GOOD NEWS though, the developer is very proactive in adding increased and improved functionality in this game, and judging by their solution to the Variant unlocking debate (pretty big debate) they will continue to come up with clever ways to make the game better.
Note: The variant unlock debate, some players wanted to be able to pay to unlock the variants while others wanted to keep the challenge of figuring it out.  Handleabra solved both by offering the variant unlocks at no price after a unlock period, so those who want to can figure out and share how to unlock the variants early.  Once a method has been confirmed Handleabra will post on a special forum the unlock conditions for each variant.  That way you still have the option of trying to complete those conditions, and if the frustration becomes too much, you will still be able to unlock them with a "cheat" code.

I still remember the initial feeling of anger and disgust when the first trailers and news bits about this game came out. The unnecessary reboot, the new developer and of course all that EMO. Or, if everyone was honest - mainly the emo. And to a certain degree, the fears were justified - but who cares, the game is freaking awsome.
Sure, there are some bad points. It's too short and too easy, especially if you're used to the brutality of previous games. I recommend  starting at the hardest available difficulty and playiong with one hand. I made the mistake of playing on medium first, and I literally never died (compared to DMC3, which made me cry on the first sub-boss, which was the second level).
And the story... Oh boy, the story. DMC3 is one of my favorite games precisely because of its story, and this reboot... All the elements are there - Dante, Vergil, Mundus, amulets, hell gates, Sparda... And the story isn't bad, per say; it just feels like it's been written by a 16-yo d*ck with severe angst issues. It has strong "no one understands me so I cut myself to get attention" and "I'm not that good at social situations, so down with society, go anarchy" vibes or some bullsh*t like that; it's predictable and most of the characters are unlikable d*cks (though most 16yo teens might find them relateable). I suppose it's better than a game just about Nero and Kyrie, but it's just super lame.
The saving grace is the gameplay. It's simply superb. I'd even say it's the best game in the series, easy difficulty nonwithstanding. The combat is fluid, engaging and (once you unlock harder game modes) brutal. True, they simplified the combat style system from DMC3/4 into oblivion, but in this case, simple is better. Now you can glide through all your swords faster that blinking, all while dodging and shooting and giggling at that awesome combo you just made. And it's not like they removed anything - well, except for Royal Guard, but come on, who really used THAT? - everything's just been reworked so you have access to all your moves all the time, without having to switch from Trickster to Swordmaster or whatever. It's really amazing.
The level design also gets 5 stars. Platforming bits are neat, and the design look very good. And the techno soundtrack's been replaced mostly by metalcore and by something that Wikipedia tells me is called "aggrotech". Yeah. Not everyone's piece ot candy, I suppose, but it goes well with the new style and more importantly - with the gameplay.
So yeah, the reboot is unnecessary and the game is waay too emo. But you'll be having too much fun to notice, really.

Well, lets summarize the pros and cons after 2 and a half hours of playing:
Lets start with the negatives:
- there is a basic tutorial, but it is REALLY basic. It doesn't explain all the different things you can build and it doesn't tell you you should try things out in training mode.
- matchmaking is a little wonky, probably due to low amounts of online players. It can match you with people from the top of the rankings even in your first match.
- it takes time to get enough ingame currency to buy anything at all. Highest amount I got from a battle was around 250 whereas you need about 1k for a simple card upgrade from level 1 to 2 or 10k for 3 new random cards.
Up to the pros:
- The game is free to play and got the payment system implemented in a nice way. you can buy gold (rather low price compared to other F2P games) to get cards quicker or to buy avatars. Except for those Avatars everything else you need can be aquired by the ingame currency (the silver coins).
- The game really is a real time strategy game. It is fun once you understand it and there are multiple strategies that work out fine - well, if your opponent doesn't counter them that is ^^
- While grinding silver coins for upgrades and unlocks, you randomly get cards for battles. This makes it quite attractive to battle - also, battles are the best way to learn the game except:
- the chat - there are quite some players who'll help you if you have questions or need advice - well, there are also those who just scream how they can't get a grip on the game or how they get steamrolled. If that happens to you, just ask how you could improve and most players will answer - noobbashing is no fun anyhow ;)
- the graphics are easy on the eye .
- Ediths comment: As you can see in the comments here, the devs are quite active and take players seriously. THAT is a definite plus.
I'd recommend it for everyone. As a single battle doesn't take long you can't go wrong trying it - and don't get frustrated by the "tutorial" - and don't worry about the cards you start with - atm my strategy is pumping out hedgehogs (one of the starters) while upgrading the smithy to give my creatures one more damage for each other creature I got. Hedgehogs give +2 damage to every other hedgehog in battle =3

feels like it’s more or less abandoned (and I say that as I’m trying the game out on the day that ‘big’ patch 1.2 has been released). There’s only 2-3 people playing (the game is multiplayer only), game content is extremely basic and the Steam forums are dead.
The game is almost like a proof of concept, vertical slice, early access build. The graphics are charming, and the foundation is reasonably solid, but other than that it’s hard to justify spending more than 30 minutes here. At least it’s free?
I’ll admit that I’ve played for a bit more than 30 minutes. This is largely because I picked up ‘Koshey’ in the one starter pack I was able to purchase with my ounce of free newbie gold. Koshey is known to be over powered and, what can I say, I do like winning so that’s kept me going. I have only lost one game rushing straight to level 10 and 2000 shields. (Shields are what passes for the game’s ranking system with a 2000 shield max (highest) rank.)
The game itself is extremely simple. Build some basic resource producing buildings (‘rooms’ in a house), ramp up production to build units, then send these units one by one towards the centre of the 2D, single-plane map.  The front unit from each player then proceeds to beat the snot out of the front unit of the other player until one player is ground back to their base and defeat.
Of note, the game desperately wants you to spend money, but seriously, on what? I can’t say, personally, because despite my winning streak I still haven’t earned enough in-game coinage to splurge on a single extra pack.
There are occasional card drops after winning a game but these are pretty stingy too – perhaps one card drop per five games or so, most of which were duplicates of cards I already had. This shouldn’t be surprising since the card pool seems tiny. Well, I guess, how much diversity can there be in lining up creatures @rse to toe in a conga line?
In a sense, there’s nothing wrong with giving this game a whirl for a few minutes. It’s free to play, after all. But there isn’t enough content, strategic diversity, other players or any significant sense of progression that might justify making an in-game purchase or medium-term time investment here.

I know there are several games like this, but in my opinion. It seems like it's a merge of several games in one. Of course it has the whole Left 4 Dead style of campaign; however, ammo is scarce and you have to deal with types of situations. The fact that infection is something that can only be delayed is something I have not seen with many games from this generation of games. I give this game more credit than some of the zombie survival games because. In other zombie games, you only sit in a room crouching over a window facing your gun over the wooden platform to shoot the zombies. It doesn't add to the immersion of "human ability." What I am trying to get at, is that it requires more than just your basic game style. It requires you to literally depend on your team and if your team is "shy" or REALLY! immersed in the game, panic. I've played with groups of people who stayed together, they were having fun and all, but you can tell what was happening. At this point I try to break it and go on an axe-spree to see if anyone is alright. I adore that part of this game. Even the mechanics of it seem a bit polished to me. They give you stuff, but nothing that would let you rush in. Unless it's your first time you think you can, but it really does lead down to strategic ways to get around a map.
The only thing I would consider bad for this game is the few glitches I come across, like grabbing specific ammo for your gun. It won't let you grab it all the time oddly. Also I had several times happen when I got infected by air. I know a zombie did hit me, but he was really out of distance and somehow smacked a kiss to me.
The immerson, the gameplay, the style is why I am rating this as a game to play. The mechanics, the physics, they are good and all, they just need a bit of tweaking. Like I got slingshoted in the air by trying to grab an item that fell into a invisible barrier and took fall damage. Was a great scene, nonetheless, was a glitch/bug.

Minerva is a two hour FPS set in the universe of HL2.
It has probably the most beautiful maps and design I have seen in a source game or mod since playing through Shadgrimgrvy's Paranoia map series. It has decent sound design, and an overall above average story (that I'd rather not spoil). However, it simply is far too difficult to be fun. The majority of encounters in this mod consist of seemingly buffed enemies, with numerous units. Generally, you are armed with weapons that are inneffective, and twice in the story, you are forced to lose all of your weapons. These are followed by encounters that are frequently annoying or cause you to die more than you really should half to.
In fact, the very ending of the game is the easiest encounter, which is strange considering that it's a battle with a gunship.
Overall, the difficulty of this game is almost to the level of being heinous, and it never stops forcing you through encounters, no respites or times to really admire the rather beautiful scenery, or just take in the sounds of the world. The game is just poorly balanced combat- and the difficulty settings hardly seem to work. I know the difficulty is the only thing I'm talking about, but it honestly is just that bad.
If you want to learn how not to balance a game, or see what you can really do with the source Hammer editor, then I'd really suggest giving it a shot. Otherwise, just look at the screenshots section. I do have to repeat that it is a really pretty game, and that if you are an aspiring source mapper, then you should spend the two hours with it.

A very mediocre military, third-person, cover shooter guided by a crazy good story (emphasis on crazy). There's a few cool mechanics like shooting glass and drowning your enemies in sand, or using a grenade to kick up sand to distract your enemies, but let's be honest: no one gave this game a thumbs up for the shooting. The level design is also INCREDIBLY linear, but there are a number of cool set pieces that would feel right at home in a Call of Duty campaign in terms of scope and sheer destruction.
The story wears it's influences on it's sleeve. If you like Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now, you'll really love this. Just be warned: this is some morbid, gut-wrenching stuff, and not just in terms of blood 'n' guts. It's emotionally draining, to say the least. The twist at the end is done well, but I can see why people might be put off by it. And do try to find all of the intel scattered around each level. The writing makes it worth it.
The game is as long as it needs to be; about five hours.

I wanted to give this game a thumbs-up, but the poor level design, clunky shooting and awkward cover system made it the opposite.
The game deserves a lot of credit for trying to do something interesting with a "standard shooter", but it just isn't all that compelling.
The story is too vague, shallow and short to really be compelling. It is definitely a cut above its peers, but the gameplay will leave you frustrated out of the experience. Opportunities for emergent gameplay and imaginative solutions to problems using sand and destructible glass are ignored by the developers except for in certain situations where you are prompted to do so. That aspect of the game was an outright fabrication.
You die -way- too easily, and many of the enemies are respawning bullet sponges. A lot of the level design is very, very poor, which is odd considering how pretty the game can be at times. For all its big open vistas, though, the game is a corridor railroad, both in story and gameplay. A corridor through a bunch of sandy buildings in the middle east. You've done this before.
The cover system seems unfinished, with actions that are common in other games being locked off or remapped to strange button choices.
I found all the main characters completely unlikeable, and all of the choices felt empty and contrived by the end. The story only gets interesting after the game has already slogged through several hours of nothing, by which point are the majority of players have either quit or lost interest. A watched pot never boils, but this game's stove isn't even on. The pace is excruciatingly slow.
Ultimately this is a 6-7/10 action game with an 8/10 action game story. If you really need something to shoot, pick it up for under $10USD at absolute maximum.

In short, if you’re a fan of the Capcom games or hack n slash in general, go and pick this baby up.  Don’t let the stylistic new design or the fact that Dante looks a bit emo keep you away from this great title.  You’re missing the MOST INSANE combat system ever produced if you do.
The good:  It’s all about the combat here.  DMC is the most fluid, responsive and dynamically creative combat system I’ve ever played.  The game gives you a whole bunch of tools, including 4 different melee weapons, 3 different guns, bizzilions of combos, two grappling hooks, and it lets you combine them all, on the fly, to give the player a breath-taking free form combat system with endless possibilities.  Seriously, this is the best combat I have ever played in 20 years of gaming.  Also, the cut scenes and story are pretty nice, and graphically, for a console game, it looks pretty sweet with a kinda post-modern urban feel to things.  The way the levels change and morph before your eyes is a joy to behold.  Generally, it’s just a cool game.
The bad:  Well, although the levels looks as sweet as pie, very little thought was put into their design.  Strip away all the fancy graphics and all you have are long corridors to walk down and fight things in.  Ok ok, there’s a wee bit of simple platforming to do, but generally you might as well be playing Streets of Rage.  Aside from the factory level, there’s very little vertical scope in the game, and next to no environmental puzzles.   Also, the bosses are far too simple, even on the harder mode.  They look cool, but follow the same predictable attack patterns.  In fact, on the harder modes, the normal enemies are more of a challenge.
Listen, give this game a change. Despite my critisicms, and the fact that I’m a huge fan of the Capcom originals, I loved me some DMC and played through it twice already.  It’s a good story, it looks slick, and the combat is the best I’ve ever played.  More interesting level design, environmental puzzles and better bosses might have made this a classic, but as it stands it’s still a worthy hack n slash affair.
Also, let it be known that this thankfully does not feature any stupid quick-time events, which is a blessing for a console action game.

Orginal Review
After much internal debate I came to the assement that the developers managed to digitized a GREAT tabletop game...however I still have to give this the thumb downs. So to be clear...I enjoyed the mechanics, the game runs smoothly, and there seems to have a very good developer to community relationship (at least in my experience) yet I still would not recomend purchasing this game.
I was disappointed to find this talbletop/card game that fails to add any compeling elements despite the fact that it has ascended into the digital world. This is a sin I cannot overlook and makes me regret not buying the tabletop version. I would say being given the keys to go anywhere and do anything at Disneyworld and then refusing to leave the parking lot does not make a bad person but it does make me wonder what end of the autism spectrum you sit. This is not a bad "game" just an unnecessarily limited "video game" and a complete waste of potential.
To clarify the game itself is FUN and well designed with the different combinations of decks (heros, villians, environment) providing a good deal of variety in terms of playstyle from game to game. However there are no animations past the static comic book pieces of art (though well done at from what I can tell on par with the carboard box takehome) and very little else to help color the experience after multiple playthroughs. It may be that every game is different but it honestly does not feel much different to me. There are some very obscure conditions that allow you to unlock "variants" of particular decks (heros and villains no location unlocks) but most of that satisfaction feeling I usually get after succesfully beating a game or fufilling a condition of an unlock is absent.
There is an overall lack of content here. I understand and believe that the developers where trying to be as faithful as possible to the tabletop version and they succeed in doing so here. In the end the human element that is lost by playing this game solo (no multiplayer option to attempt to replace human contact either) makes it a failure. Again this a true shame as their really is a ton of potential here. There is no progression or advancment that I can see and it lacks window dressing.
All that being said I am going to purchase the tabletop game and give it a go at game night with my friends this week. Again this is a great "GAME" but a poor "VIDEO GAME" I would recommend you support the game in it's original form but skip on this version.

(Despite not having the game in my library, I have the physical card game with expansions. Recently, my brother bought the PC version and we've been playing it often)
So, if you know the real one and also consider it the best cooperative game ever, you don't need to know anything else - it's the same awesomeness but with everything more automatic...the tokens, the effects, the math...same fun, less work! Honestly, you'll love this version!
Now, if you don't know what Sentinels of the Multiverse is, just imagine that you and your friends are superheroes and you need to group together and fight a supervillain, in a scenario that constantly keeps throwing modifiers.
You have to act as a team, studying what cards to play, keeping in mind what the other players will do. It really involves a lot of strategy, but the comic book look and supeheroes theme, makes it very fun to play.
After two or three games, you can easily understand the game mechanics, and you'll start to notice that some heroes match better with others...or you can just hit randomize and go for it! Like I said above, the computer version makes it easier to keep track of all the stats and modifiers, so the gameplay is much smoother.
There are different heroes, villains and scenarios, with more to come in future DLCs, but for now there are enough for many hours of fun, alone (but playing at least 3 heroes, to have a chance at winning) or with friends and family, in couch co-op (you only need one game).
I really recommend this game, if you love comic books and cooperative games!

A friend once casually mentioned to me that he had bought this game and enjoyed it.  "Just check it out," he said.  "It's pretty interesting," he said.  So, I did.
In the future, I will look back and will be able to pinpoint my purchase of Prison Architect as the exact moment that I first ruined my chances of ever having a social life again.
Every time I load it up now I flip flop between elated and horrified at what I am spending countless hours building: do I feel like being a fierce and supremely hard-handed dictator who controls every movement, or a benevolent leader who encourages personal growth and education towards a better society?  Thankfully this game allows you to play this game however you want on the scale of Worst-Person-Ever to Basically-an-Angel (sometimes even both in the same prison), and still considers you playing the game properly.
Playing a sandbox game gives you the absolute freedom of doing basically whatever you want but it is in the campaign that the game really shines.  The story is harrowing, emotion-driven and, for the first time in a long time, I have actually felt guilty about accidently killing an NPC.
I cannot recommend this game enough and if you haven't played it yet, well... just check it out.  It's pretty interesting.

I don't know why the steam version doesn't have a proper ESRB rating (like GTA) but the console version is rated M for Blood, Drug Reference, Partial Nudity, Sexual Content, Strong Language, Violence. The tutorial campaign has scenes of sex & violence. Regular game has avatar nudity for showers and avatar fights/death though you often miss them unless you stop playing the game to look for it.
It's a prison building simulator with a short campaign, free/sandbox mode, and a basic escape mode.
The campaign serves as a tutorial that teaches only the basics. It's only 5 episodes so story is compact, like a framework to a more epic story, showing only the key/best parts. There are several mini-storylines where characters drop out of the story and you never hear from them again.
Grants make a nice quest system to give you objectives you aim for when developing your prison. The money rewards make improving/expanding go smoothly but when the grants run out it's up to you to make your own goals. The end game is up to you to make fun for yourself.
In escape mode, you control one prisoner and try to escape via foot or tunnel, quietly or armed. You can choose any prison (one you make or one from the workshop). It's a very basic mode. You don't need to follow the schedule with other prisoners. Don't need to fulfill any needs. The guards ignore you unless you do something blatantly wrong so you can just fight for more than 2 skill points, get arrested, then use one point to automatically skip the punishment wait and repeat until you max out skills.
Edit: A proper escape mode is like the game 'The Escapist' which has that but no architect simulator.
One thing missing here that I remember in other simulation games (like RollerCoaster Tycoon and Big Pharma) are scenario challenges where you clear a target objective within a certain time (or have other specified goals).
Worth a try if you enjoy simulation/tycoon games.

I thought the game did an excellent job of empowering the player to implement policies of positive or negative reinforcement to guarantee prisoner cooperation.  As I played the game, I started to think about the way my choices would influence the prisoners under my control to learn from their mistakes, or simply to survive long enough to escape the confines of my walls.
After seeing countless attempts at simulation games ruin their subject matter, I was concerned at first that this was just another attempt at a "hardcore" prison simulator that would highlight all of the violence and punishment that takes place in prision systems around the world - particularly in the United States.  Instead, I played a game that managed to be enjoyable at the same time it exposed the difficult decisions we must face as socities with regard to the correct way to correct errant behavior.

Using only assets and mechanics from
and its episodes - minus a few minors additions -,
still manages to deliver a gaming experience far different from Valve's game.
From the nagging text monologues of the titular Minerva, strongly reminescent of
's SHODAN and
's Durandal, to the eldritch-ness, vastness and level of detail of the underground structure, the ambience is tense, cryptic and sometimes contemplative. The game is also challenging, both in its riddles and its combat, thanks to its unusual level design.
Indeed, what really sets this mods apart from its progenitor, and from most FPS, is its level design. Instead of providing the player a world, Adam Foster provided his world a player. Don't expect strategically located chest-high walls, or conveniently located ammo crates. Every element is placed somewhere it would belong if the Combine's installation was a real-world place and not a videogame level. You will therefore often find yourself back-tracking or realizing several ways lead to the same location.
This mod is truly a gem of game design and videoludic storytelling - no wonder its creator was hired by Valve afterwards.

I'll focus more on the gameplay instead of the story here:
Actual fighting is barely more than repeatedly hammering the attack button near the target and letting the auto-aiming bullets whittle it down. Later on there are stomps and dashes, but both relate more to the what the gameplay truly heavily focuses on: Movement.
And it looks beautiful. Ori has such a vast amount of animations that transition from one movement to another, going up and down cliffs and traveling through the corridors just feels very satisfying. The downside is that, as you unlock more and more ways to move around, the controls get very overloaded. Every button has at least one function and you constantly vary between all of them. It just gets extremely busy as you dash, triple jump, climb, float, repel. It also comes at the price of being so precise that even a few pixels too far away from a wall ends with you falling down instead of pushing yourself off.
And the game isn't very kind about you falling down from things. It constantly teases you to make a leap of faith but most of the time you are just greeted with instant-death spikes at the bottom. Until you just carefully slide down walls instead of further enjoying the fluent and exhilarating rush of movement.
The save-system is helping with that, but it is as flexible as it is restricting. You can create your own save-points almost anywhere but it will cost you energy from which you have very little in the beginning. Energy is also used to unlock various doors, perform more powerful attacks and later enhance your freedom for movement, so it can end up being a bottleneck and you have to look for energy crystals to harvest. Especially in the beginning, these crystals barely amount to more than "Save your game now"-prompts, you save in front of the crystal and harvest it to fill up your energy again, because you are so limited.
There are a few frustrating sections, especially those where you have to make a ton of precise, varied and fast movements in succession for an extended period of time and failure means starting over. In the worst cases, it hinges on RNG if you depend on enemy AI to behave a certain way for you to make progress.
The world is pretty big and a blast to explore. A lot of sections are sealed off until you have the skill necessary to pass them. However, some minor roadblocks aren't quite impossible enough and can be completed without the intended upgrade. Of course this involves a lot of struggling and makes you wonder "I THINK I can do that. Or can I? Am I making this unnecessarily hard for myself?". Backtracking is necessary but it gets rather quick once you unlock more movement options and there are a few fast-travel points. I wouldn't mind more of those but the amount is alright.
Overall, I really enjoyed the great fast-paced movement-focused gameplay, it is a lot of fun if it doesn't happen to be under heavy pressure where a slightly off jump can set you back a great deal. Don't forget to save frequently!

When I've heard about All Points Bulletin for the first time... God, I was excited. It was a fresh formula combining typical 'GTA sandbox' with MMO elements. I followed every pre-release video, trailer and so on. When It finally came out on the market (Funny thing, APB was meant to be free-to-play from the beginning. As we can see now - the chance for everyone to play was only for fabricating the hype) It wasn't really THAT bad...
I think that creators of the game condemned their game for failure just from the beginning. They didn't mentioned anything about the REAL formula of APB - 'cause APB isn't a GTA MMO - it's an online shooter with a really big arena and cars. Media and gamers called this game a 'GTA Online'. Back then, the developers didn't deny it.
APB had mostly technical issues, bugs and strange gameplay solutions. But it still offered much fun through customizing your car, your own character and shooting other people with this char. The game was fun to play, but had some unforgivable issues.
Now, about so called 'Reloaded' version. ABANDON ALL HOPE, YE WHO ENTER HERE. After so many years the new developers didn't removed 4 YEARS OLD bugs and technical issues. Seriously. What's more - practically, they have created more. The game may not even work on some PC configurations. I managed to launch original 2010 APB on Intel Core 2 Duo + GeForce 8600GTX, but for some reason, after many hours of fixing up the problem, APB:Reloaded won't last played for 0,5h on Intel i5 + Radeon HD7870. Because f*ck the player.
The game is fun to play itself, but after slow progress it can get bored for a while. Especially when you fight those Premium players. The disbalance of Premium and non-Premium characters is very big - in cash, in weapons, in experience and so on. There is even a limit on a graphics that you can put on clothes or cars. Seriously. Because f*ck the player.
Customization is still good, even after 4 years. What a shame, that it's so limited for a regular player. But you can still create something similar to your character of a dreams. You can slowly earn up for a car and car's modifications, but it is much longer process.
Driving a car is not very good because of server's delay. When you turn left, you send a signal to the servers of APB to make you drive left, and that causes some lags if you don't have a really good internet connection. This delay may be a bit similar to 'Hollywood car chase', but it's still a technical issue. Still not removed. Because f*ck the player.
Shooting is k, most of the time, sometimes your character will not shoot to your crosshair location, because s*it happens. It still fun, and that's an advantage of APB:R's gameplay.
There is a good variety of missions, as well as arenas, so you won't get bored in ~15 hours, at least I was still interested to play even, when I get to know all the game's missions.
If you get APB:Reloaded to work properly - it may be a fun and interesting experience, depends on your liking of 'GTA like' games. Otherwise, you will get upset many times, for sure.
tl;dr
Still fun to play, but with tons of technical issues and bugs, much disproportions between premium players and non premium players, try it out, 'cause it's free, darling, my final rating is 3-/6.

*Possible Spoliers* I played through almost the entire game thinking about how much I hated it.  After a little cooldown, I understand that this game really wasn't that bad.  I find the character scripts to be pretty awful most of the time, especially the Joker.  I absolutely loooooovveeed his scene with Harley where he gives an almost romantic description of the bat, but most of his script was garbage, especially the hotel scene (I visibly cringed at the whole "Fruitcake" thing).  Overall though the game was fun to play, here I will give a little bit of a description of some of the most important aspects of the game
Playability: I had very little trouble playing this game.  There were spots where I had some frame rate drops, but mostly I stayed around 60fps with medium-high settings
Graphics:  Nothing majorly stand-out, but very nice graphics overall
Story:  More than anything I was just dissapointed at the lack of focus on Black-mask, as I was looking forward to taking a break from the Joker (although the Joker is my #1 favorite comic book character, I think that batman has some really brilliant villians that get overshadowed by him).  I also found the lack of involvement of the assassins to be a little dissapointing, as the trailer put a lot of focus on them.  Overall I think that this game just suffers from that lack of a strong main plot that we got a little of in Arkham City (Arkham city story is amazing, but has a hard time finding focus) and It doesn't give a lot of the characters a good look.
Combat: As with all of the Arkham games, this game has some of the best combat around, but at the same time the removal of the ability to cancel a punch to block was very annoying, and the combos and special moves were much less straightforward than City.
Stealth:  Aside from the occasional glitch keeping me from getting that apex predator rating, I Thouroghly enjoyed the stealth.
Boss Fights:  I probably wouldn't have included this section but I feel that the boss fights really fell short in this game.  They were very similar to the boss fights that you find in a lot of rushed games that come out, with straightforward mechanics and laughable difficulty.
Overall:  The only real reason I don't recommend this game is just because instead I would recommend either buying City and Asylum if you haven't already, and playing them again if you have.  I do really wish that I had just gone back and played City again instead of playing this.  If you are just looking for a little more of the genius fighting and stealth mechanics and are tired of playing City and Asylum over and over again, then I would recommend this game for you as it definitley serves that purpose.

Spec Ops: The Line had one of the best single player campaigns I have played in any shooter. It is a real shame we never got any follow ups or spinoffs. Excellent story telling more than makes up for average gameplay in my book.

Do I recommend this game?
, very much. But only if you're prepared to slug through it a little bit - the combat isn't exactly the most rewarding you have ever seen in a video game. But believe me when I say this,
. I must warn people going into this game that it is an amazing experience, but not to mindlessy shoot things, but rather to immerse yourself in a game that can be brought up in a discourse about video games as art.
This game's story is on par with that of Bioshock: Infinite and its moral choice mechanics are very similar to that of Undertale. The setting reminds people of Call of Duty and that is 100% intentional to give people expectations just to mercilessly crush them in a brilliant manner.
Spec Ops: The Line is not perfect, but it deserves a playthrough by every gamer who considers the medium fascinating, because this game makes great use of almost all tools a developer has to deliver a very unique experience.

It starts simple, with a simple task, and them escalates to something surprisingly bigger.
If Half-Life 2 Lost Cost is a extra short chapter to Half-Life 2, Minerva is worth saying it's 4 full new chapters, presenting the player to the familiar gameplay, but with a completely new scenario. It's really worth playing while waiting for the next Half-Life game. And, hey, it's free.

MINERVA is a highly recommendable Half-Life 2 mod, set during the Combine occupation of Earth in the Half-Life saga. With some great map design, including large scenarios and interconnected rooms, it provides plenty of options for ambushing your enemies, and it also allows the AI to shine, giving them plenty of places to take cover and flank the player.
It's a great experience, in my opinion, and it really seems to fit within the Half-Life canon, although nobody at Valve has confirmed that. Even then, the fact that its creator, Adam Foster, ended up working at Valve, says something about the quality of this mod.

has veeeeery good level design. Great pacing, very challenging. The Combine Soldier's AI feels much smarter here than it did in
, but I'm not sure if it was modified, or if it just works better with these maps.
This is the best missionpack mod for HL2, imo. Adam Foster truly does deserve his place at Valve. Don't know what more should be said, it's free HL2 goodness.

This problem is made worse by the fact that 2 of the 4 villains - Baron Blade and Omnitron - are  pitifully easy (I have never lost to either of them yet) while the other 2 are frustratingly hard and not that much fun to fight because of it (and they work disappointingly similarly to each other to boot!).
Now that I have beaten the 2 hard villains once each, I NEVER want to fight them again. So that's half the enemy content persona non grata already, and the other half making for a somewhat boring game because you know you will win.
It's a game crying out for expansions, in fact you could say the game is almost DESIGNED to make you want expansions, as the central mechanic is fun and works really well! As I said, the game particularly needs more Villains (more Environments wouldn't hurt either).
Either way, I highly recommend it. 7.5/10

A completely different change of pace from the recent slew of fast-paced zombie shooters. Realistic almost to a fault and follows Max Brook's Zombie Survival Guide's core rules of what to do during a zombie apocalypse almost down to a T.
Melee is less like Half-Life/L4D and more akin to Chivalry, where headshots are especially important, with most weapons being able to OHKO with the right hit.
Ammo and supplies are usually extremely scarce, as it should be during a real outbreak. You even have to find your own flashlight, which is usually a given in any other game.
Overall, I'd reccomend people to play this, but only with a group of friends. Playing alone with a bunch of pubs is asking to be griefed, either by trolls or by shit♥♥♥♥ers.

Divine Divinity is in essence a fleshed out version of  Diablo 1 & 2, with a mixture of Baldur's Gate thrown in for good measure. The game boasts an amazing soundtrack, gorgeous visuals, (for it's time), and an indepth and interactive item system. Nearly anything and everything in the game can be used, sold, bartered for, or combined. That goes for jugs, barrels, mushrooms, and so forth. The game, sadly, only makes use of about 3 classes, but makes up for that loss with an impressive array of skills. Any skill found in the game can be used by any class of character, (although as a Warrior a Fireball skill isn't necessarily that useful). All in all, Divine Divinity will provide a lengthy and interesting gaming experience for a low sum of 6 dollars.

There are a lot of side-quests, epic loot, a large world with lore and magic, and more.  I have maybe seen a 3rd of the game world and it's environs, and I enjoyed it enough to recommend this game, dispite not completing it.

Just two years after the first Max Payne (2001) was released, Remedy came up with their second creation of the series, Max Payne 2 (2003). This time they developed a game which had a whole lot of better graphics, upgraded game mechanics, more interesting level design, a bunch of new guns and an enhanced level of voice acting as well as an enhanced level of enemy AI.
Anyhow, like it's predecessor, Max Payne 2 is also quite a fast-paced game. The guns introduced in the game have a good feel on them and while bullet time or shoot dodge is being used at the same time, it will double the enjoyment. Also, the enemies are not able to take a ridiculous amount of bullets anymore before they die, which is a huge improvement on its own over what could be seen on the first Max Payne game. Gradually slowing bullet time is an awesome invention as it is easier for the player to handle several opponents at the same time by using it. The controllability of Max's moves along with the level of voice acting is still great and because there is some improvements on the enemy AI, Max Payne 2 is a very enjoyable game at its best.
Now, not only the game mechanics has been proven to be better in Max Payne 2, but also the graphics have taken a big leap forward. Overall the environmental texturing has gotten to a higher level. Max can see his own reflection and the faces seen in the game are more natural than they used to be in the previous Max Payne game. Cars are a bit more than just boxes on the wheels and the whole level design is much more interesting. The miserable storyline is what makes you feeling positively anxious again, and the dreams and illusions, though not being quite as gloomy and exciting as they were on the Max Payne 1, keep telling you that this game has definitely earned it's place as a successor.
Unfortunately, despite all the enhancements, the game is still all about running and shooting with no considerable variation between the firefights you encounter. The overall amount of usable weapons is still quite low and the game will not last for too long, as an average person could easily beat it in about 5 hours. Additional game modes seem to be quite useless to try as you can't really achieve anything by trying them out.
After all there is a huge amount of improvements in Max Payne 2, even though the run and shoot part still leaves much to be desired along with some other downsides described above. Throughout the game you can still find some easter eggs, and the mods made for this game can offer you a lot of additional fun, just like before. To this date I've had six separate playthroughs: three times before I had the game on Steam and three times after that, with every given difficulty option. Because the game is quite short, I ended up spending only about 30 hours by playing it and could maybe give it a one more try. In short, this game is definitely worth a try. If you liked the predecessor of Max Payne 2, without a doubt you will fall in love with this one too.

Now this is the Hitman experience you have been waiting for.
I have played all the Hitman games all the way through (yes, even contracts... *shudders*) and there is no denying that this game is the best one, and that's by a lot too.
First of all the story has never been too important in Hitman games, but somehow they managed to make it interesting this time around. Almost made me feel like I wanted a movie out of this or something. Weird!
Of course the most important part about Hitman games is the gameplay. You are an assassin and your goal is to take down your target with any means you see fit. You are rewarded for handling your task quietly, but a little bit of mayhem every now and then can't be too bad now can it?
Everything just feels right. They nailed it. I like playing silently myself, trying to figure out this puzzle of a mission each time. Taking my time, observing the situation. Characters move predictably, but you must discreetly follow them around to figure out where they will be and at what time... and then make your plan.
Biggest problem the game had was its episodic release, where they sold a couple of maps at a time during the course of a year. It didn't quite work and people lost interest. This ended up in SE dropping the company - lets hope someone picks them up so we get more of the same we have here, because all of it is actually good stuff.
It is the definitive Hitman experience.

Sentinels of the Multiverse is, as you may have figured out by taking even a simple look at the cover, a cooperative super-hero comic-book themed board game where each player controls a costumed-crusader to work together and fight the super-villain. Each turn, the players play a card, use a power, and draw a card. Most of the time, it works together quite well; even without the option to have multiple players, this Steam port works quite well, and produces quite a lot of fun, even. However, it is not without flaws.
Chief among these is that Greater Than Games does not appear to understand how Combo decks work, or why people want to play them. While they have gotten better at it over the years, there is still the problem where the combo-centric heroes like Absolute Zero (the local Ice-manipulator) and Bunker (NotIronman) have huge, convoluted six-card combos that, when finally assembled, accomplish some big numbers, certainly, but never big enough numbers to compensate for not having a hero doing things for most of the game. You'll throw out a burst of ten damage, in a game where the absolute highest HP an enemy can have is two-hundred and most flutter somewhere around ninety, and then you'll do the math and realize that NotBatman has dealt far, far more damage in the time it took you to assemble that. Oh, and if the villain casually drops a card that nukes the field of everything? Well, you're screwed, have fun.
Speaking of which, the board wipes. Now, this is something GtG has learned from since then, as evidenced by most newer villains lacking a straight-up "Destroy all X and beat the crap out of everyone" card and instead having "Destroy a sizable amount of X, and maybe deal a small amount of damage to everyone" cards, but this is their earlier work, so the villains have a much higher amount of nukage then ought ever have been the case. If they drop one of their board wipes, you have nothing. You flounder a bit because the action economy hates you, and you maybe get back up ten-hp lesser. Or you just outright die because there's nothing you can really do about a board-wipe. Worse, due to the nature of the beast, when the wipes come out is utterly random, so you can't really plan ahead for them, and they're all on villains you can't afford to hold back for, so you can't even strategize for them.
In spite of all that, however, the game is still a fun romp through magical-superhero-land, and the nigh-infinite combinations it affords make it a long-lasting one at that. Just keep in mind that it is far from perfect, and you'll have plenty of fun.

Based on the excellent card game of the same name, this is a very good game.  When I feel that my biggest complaint is I want more more more of exactly the same, a game is generally in good shape.
The player takes the role of 3 to 5 heroes (out of 10) in the fight against 1 of 4 supervillians in 1 of 4 different locations.  All decks are non-customizable at this time, and there is an "advanced" mode for those that are actually good at the game.  Each hero, villian, and environment play significantly differently, leading to the usual discussion of which heroes are stronger, and which villains/environments are tougher.  Heroes are generally intended to play specific roles, so the hero comparison may not always be fair.  Some of the hero/villain cards have unlockable "variants" which change how they play.
The villain plays first (often, the villain's initial play and win conditions vary due to the number of heroes arrayed against them), then each of the heroes (play hero cards, then use powers), and then the environment.  After the environment, the villain plays again.
Pros:
Interesting tactical possibilities with mixing and matching heroes, villains, and environments
Variant cards provide additional depth for heroes and villains
Each match against a villain, even with the same heroes in the same environment, feels different due to the randomized nature of the card play
Good music
Cons:
Artwork is not bad, but not particularly good.  To me, it looks more like an 80s Saturday morning cartoon than a modern comic book.
Waiting for the expansions for the game to be released is going to be annoying

Spec-Ops The line is, at first glance, a generic military shooter with fun gameplay. The story however is some of the best writing I've seen in a video game and has so many little details in it one of which you have to turn around and glance again to see. That may sound cyptic but I don't want to put any spoilers in this review.  It's a very cerebral game that has five endings and when you finish the game you should check out some of the fan theories on it because they are great. I would love to tell you which two theories combined I agree with but again, spoilers so I can't.
Now for the one single thing I didn't like about this game. During the (spoiler) scene it FORCES you to use the (spoiler) or you can't progress. Like I was fully loaded up on M4A1 ammo with an RPG that had like 5 rockets and I was ready and fully capable of taking on all the soldiers but shortly after I shot one I noticed another would spawn out of view then run and stand in the dead one's place. They do this infinitely and I found it personally insulting that the game didn't let me shoot them all as an alternate solution. This was especially apparent with the snipers on the roof. I COULD have played cover peekaboo for like 10 minutes and shot them all but the game had to push me into the story. There should have been at least a secret 6th ending right there after that part was completed without using (spoiler.)﻿
That being said, buy this game and play it. I was surprised by how great it was and I don't remember how much I got it on sale for but it's worth $10-15 easily. I would say $20 but it only took me 6 hours to complete and get all five endings and my friend did it in like 3.5 hours.

is a third-person action shooter made by Rockstar Games, the developers of Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption, Bully and many more. You follow the story of Max Payne, a former DEA agent for the New York City Police Department who has trouble keeping up with his life. You will need to fight trough loads of enemies using many available weapons and skills such as slow motion. The game features 3 difficulties; Detective - Enemies and health spawns adapt you, Hard Boiled - Enemies are harder and painkillers spawn rarely, Dead On Arrival - Same as Hard Boiled but with limited saves. There are also 2 bonus difficulties; New York Minute where you need to complete the level as fast as possible and Dead Man Walking where you fight enemies in arena until you die. The game takes around 8 hours to beat depending on what difficulty you took. I really recommend buying this game, you can get it for 2.49€ or for 2.99€ in a great Max Payne 1+2 pack on sale.

Spawn system/level design is one of the best I've seen. There's a set number of enemies per "event" (like opening a door, there's a lot of these), meaning you can clear it out entirely and feel somewhat safe. But the "events" put spawns far away at times, making the enemies then run towards the sound of fire but only arrive after most things are dead, surprising you without feeling random and making the experience harder and more lifelike at the same time. Never coming at you alone, always from several angles. At times scaring me to screams, panicing against what seemed like impossible odds in the moment. Fast paced, fluid, brutal. Excellent.
If you have Episode One and like combat more than running around looking at the view then you should play it. That's not to say it's not a beautiful game, it's probably the best looking game in the entire franchise... and it's a mod.

Starting off, I don't consider this game pay to win like a lot of people are saying. The people saying this probably got matched into a couple of bad games and thought that the cards that other people had were unlocked through in game transactions. I got all of necessary cards by simply playing the game.
In terms of gameplay, the game is extremely unbalanced and can be hard for new players who don't understand how the level scaling works. When starting off, only having 3 cards and not having a solid strategy, the game can seem boring and unfair (not saying it isn't, but maybe not as much as the first impression might suggest). It generally consists of throwing out your robot and reaper in the lvl 1-2 range, beating your opponent in 30 seconds if they put their resources into production and didn't plan to counter your attack. Until lvl 7ish the game will consist of these cheesy strats, from my experience it seems you get random cards from matchmaking and so you might have a bad experience between these lvls, but by the time you get to around lvl 7ish you should have enough of the cards to make a solid deck. The problem I have at this point is that the "Sabotage" card is way too strong and completely controls the game. Whoever uses this card effectively, stopping your opponents resources and research will win. There are not enough cards in the game to allow varied decks, and the Sabotage card has to be in your deck at the higher levels or you lose. This is the main problem I have with the game, there is no where near enough variety in cards making the game boring after you get to this point.
I will give the game some credit, it can be fun for those who hate the large amount of micro-management in modern rts games but like the idea behind it. Getting a strategy together with different cards and finding the best way to manage your resources can be fun, but it still doesn't help the fact that there isn't enough variation in the games mechanics for it to be fun for over 10hrs.
So what about how the game runs? Does it have noticable bugs? What about the community?
Well I can't say there is much positivity here. The game runs fine which is somewhat expected from what is essentially a mobile port. The big problem comes with the random crashes and some weird bugs that will force you to restart the game. Can't say much about the crashes except that they are random and somewhat frequent, never found a cause, never found a pattern as to when they happen. Adding to this, me and some friends who played the game encountered a bug in which the game would stick on a loading screen after a battle. The only way to get past this as far as I know is to restart the game. This bug seemed very frequent when I first started playing the game, though it seemed to happen less and less the more I played the game.
So onto the main bugs I encountered in the game. The bugs are mostly just annoying, but annoying is still taking away from the game experience and I think its important to point them out. First up is a wierd bug in which your heroes will just teleport back and forth as they are going along. This can be a problem when using spells on your heroes, but its not a huge problem outside of just being really annoying. Somewhat similar to the first bug is the strange way that rooms work. Resources seem to update very slowly, clicking to build a room can be slow with the building appearing a second after clicking to build the room. Probably doesn't seem like a big problem, but it just makes the game seem so out of sync and awkward. Final bug I've encountered a few times is a bug when searching for a match. So you want to play a game against another player, click play and wait... and wait.... and then you get impatient so you try to cancel the matchmaking and it does nothing. Turns out it was glitched and it was probably not searching for a match anyway. So you have to restart the game and click play again, takes 10-30 seconds and you are in a game. Again, its mostly just annoying but when annoying is so frequent in a game its hard to start liking it.
So I'll quickly mention the global chat and move on. Most of it is russian which is fine because you are not very likely to make friends on this game anyway. The problem comes with the random spam and racism that appears in the global chat. There is no community for this game so don't expect to find other people willing to make friends.
So if you want to pass the time with a fun little game I would say go play another indie title like binding of isaac or FTL. But if you don't have the money to get those titles and you happen to come across this game, give it a try. I enjoyed what I played then got bored really quickly. It has bugs to fix and needs to sort out its balancing, but its free to play and has a very small file size, so just try it out. If you can get past the bugs then you might just have fun playing this simple strategy game about pitting toys against eachother in a staged base race.

As the whole package (First season... and the last) it's a great Hitman game and even when taking the advantages of modern technology into consideration, it's an impressive game and possibly the greatest Hitman... well, i don't compare games anymore, but it's definitely a wonderful addition to the series.
But, from the perspective of a customer who piece by piece bought the game's episodes (I actually even played the very early leaked alpha from 2015? and they removed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of features) and downloaded the huge patches. It's been a very rocky road and a messy one too. Due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ episodic format this game was made in mind with, i constantly had my skills rusty between the episodes and i always had lost the hype and excitement for the game so every time a new map came out, i wasn't really too thrilled about it even though i bought and played them all on release.
Also, a huuuuuge flaw in this one that absolutely NONE of the previous entries had (Especially Contracts and Absolution) is the complete lack of atmosphere... i don't know if they were going for a dead and utterly soulless ''feel'' on purpose... as a reference to our main character Agent 47's personality, but this game has a very distinct LACK of theme and atmosphere. C47 had a mysterious and a ''stranger to this world'' feel to it. SA had a much more emotional and humane feel due to the plot. Contracts probably had a creepy and eery atmosphere to it since it was taking a place in a sociopath's (47) disturbed mind. While Blood Money had that cold and professional theme to it and the lighting mixed with Kyd's OST gave the game a very dynamic ''emotion'' to it. Absolution went for the grindhouse feel as stated by the devs back in the day and it worked very well.
There's simply no atmosphere in this new game and it's probably my biggest problem with it. Hitman 6 plainly put, feels dead and unfinished in the atmosphere department, especially when compared to the previous games.
Anyway... since IOI's doing really badly and refuses to admit it... Hitman is now dead and i won't be writing anymore.. because i'm gonna take a hot shower once again and my fingers are tired as ♥♥♥♥!
Summed up - A great sequel, but the release format (Episodic) ruined it and it shows since now Hitman is basically deader than Elvis...

Seeing it in ultra high resolution with the settings kicked up was incredible. Rocksteady kind of lost their Batman cred when they made Bane into a growling baboon. They made what is truly the first epic comic book to video game adaptation, but didn't necessarily stay true to the source material. This world feels like Tim Burtonesque Batman Returns with the snow and Christmas lights. Also stayed true to the comics with the accurate portrayal of super-villains. This leads to more of a Batman "feel" and I absolutely love it. It immerses you from the start into it's world, and it carries it on for the length of the campaign.
I almost wish I paid more for this game. I know people have made jokes about the AI and what not, but this looks incredible in UHD and as a fan of Batman through all his mediums, this is the closest to what I remember from reading the comics as a kid. And that is a gift that I truly appreciate. It is art masquerading as entertainment. To feel like a kid visiting Gotham again is priceless. Please make another Batman game, WB Games Montreal. If you enjoyed Batman the comic book, then Batman the animated series, and to a lesser extent the films, then this is highly recommended.

Batman Arkham Origins is a game made by Warner Bros. Montreal and not by Rocksteady, but it inherits the same amazing gameplay and quality story-telling. This is a very good game, that seems exactly the same as any other Batman Arkham game, which in my opinion, is in no way a bad thing. Firstly, one of the best things about the game are the boss fights, which are many and all fun. The worst one is definitely Shocker, since (spoiler alert) you hit him once and he's down - lazyness or did they try to make Batman more epic? I don't know, maybe both.
The city is pretty big, and the snow is gorgeous. If you liked any other Batman game you'll either love this or at least appreciate what there is here.
Some bad things about the game include the fact that the ending comes without you even expecting it unfortunately, and the ending isn't particularly great and I felt the story was sorta unresolved. Also, Batman is a bit too angry for my likes, and not in a good way - especially towards Alfred, who took care of him since he was a small boy. Also, if you are a bit bad at navigating you might get lost at one point when you're on a ship, since it is so linear and Bats always takes the long way around. The game is also awfully short too, clocking at 11 hours with beating all the bosses. Either way, it is a good game, and you need to buy it on, at least, a sale.
I would give Batman Arkham Origins a 7.5/10.

I rate the game Max Payne 2 2.5/5. OK. Well, not really ok. Actually it's kind of crappy.
Max Payne is a DRAMA QUEEN. Sure a lot of bad stuff happens to him and he has difficult situations to survive. However, what Max Payne goes through is as nothing when compared to what the average character has to go through during the course of any given Fallout game and you don't hear them whining about it so continuously. Look at what happens to Adam Jensen in Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Sure he complains but he does so nowhere near as much as Max Payne does. Remember all the crap that happened to Gordon Freeman from the Half Life games? Max Payne wouldn't have survived any of it because he would have been too busy feeling sorry for himself, wrapped up in his own melodrama. Sometimes Max Payne's attitude is funny but more often it just gets annoying.
This game's overdone, hard-boiled graphic novel style spoofs the original Max Payne's style except that game didn't even need spoofing. To make matters worse, the story feels disjointed and haphazardly slapped together. By today's standards the graphics have not aged well either as many of the environments now seem a little bland. The Lords and Lady's fake TV show is nice to see though and wandering around the police station was fun also. Overall though this third-person perspective action game is too linear and its plot is, to be frank, boring. The AI is good though (except for their terrible tendency to accidentally kill themselves with their own grenades). The ending feels a bit abrupt as well. The controls are good and the few bugs which occur are not too serious. The sound is excellent but only the menu theme song is any good and its merely a re-orchestrated version of the main theme from the first game. This game really should allow you to make choices which actually affect the plot (which would have made it much more fun and replayable) instead of forcing us to listen to the main character whine incessantly about how he doesn't have any choice and wax philosophical about moral-intellectual stuff of which he, and the game's developers and writers for that matter, clearly have absolutely no understanding. Worst of all (or perhaps best of all if you're sick of hearing Max Payne moan and groan) is that this is a very short game.
