Wow. In just 2 years Remedy was able to make a sequel that made the combat even more engaging, have the dream sequences feel even more ominous, have more depth into it's main character and have some great development in-general. The atmosphere of the world is so thick you can shoot bullets through it. This game also acts as a staple of "past generation game design" with some solutions to problems being left for you to figure it out and some non-linear paths to events of the gameplay just from the player mucking about or listening to NPCs. One moment has Payne going through an apartment complex with a couple civillians that can tag along with you, helping you out in gunfights and even giving you cover when you reach a certain point. Or you can simply shoot them right away, there's no penalty for it. As long as you have a gun in your had at the time you can shoot anyone and everyone you like.
There's simple touches to the gameplay that don't do much other than making Payne look even cooler (slo-mo reloading). Another one of these is TV, yes you can just sit back (stand) and watch some telly. Being honest, I spent 10 minutes watching different things on the TV until it started repeating, damn. One of the things on the TV leads into the great and not very obvious or in your face symbolism. 2 of the recurring shows on the TV give some nice symbolism to the events of the story at the moment that you watch it, or into Payne's own mindset. Sometimes even teasing future events yet to happen. And by the last level you can watch both series finale's. It's this great dream-like state that the game has that I particularly loved and that the games use to great effect. There's some nice cameo's that, if you're paying attention, you'll notice right away as well. A few points give you control of a second character for story purposes, and it's a little weird when you discover that she has the same bullet-time abilities as Payne.
Just like the last one, Max's VA is just brilliant at his lines. While everyone else is either "eergh", okay or inconsistant with  their performance. Unlike the last one the game works like a charm, with absolutely no bugs or technical problems. By the end the game's world feels just as lonely and cold as Payne is feeling from what's happened during the game, the way the story unravels is great and some moment are pretty heavy *-*. Unfortuately it doesn't have the visual scope of the original and a lot of the locations you are in are just the same places you were in the last game. There are a couple great set pieces though that allow opportunities for the level design to be more creative and one being a theme park of sorts for one of the TV shows in the game, which is mainly for the psychological themes to kick in. But that unfortunately get old by the 2nd and 3rd visit there. You should already be playing/ have finished this if you enjoyed the first one, and the ending gives some great mystery to where Max's life is going to head to next. I ONLY wish it was longer.

As the whole package (First season... and the last) it's a great Hitman game and even when taking the advantages of modern technology into consideration, it's an impressive game and possibly the greatest Hitman... well, i don't compare games anymore, but it's definitely a wonderful addition to the series.
But, from the perspective of a customer who piece by piece bought the game's episodes (I actually even played the very early leaked alpha from 2015? and they removed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of features) and downloaded the huge patches. It's been a very rocky road and a messy one too. Due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ episodic format this game was made in mind with, i constantly had my skills rusty between the episodes and i always had lost the hype and excitement for the game so every time a new map came out, i wasn't really too thrilled about it even though i bought and played them all on release.
Also, a huuuuuge flaw in this one that absolutely NONE of the previous entries had (Especially Contracts and Absolution) is the complete lack of atmosphere... i don't know if they were going for a dead and utterly soulless ''feel'' on purpose... as a reference to our main character Agent 47's personality, but this game has a very distinct LACK of theme and atmosphere. C47 had a mysterious and a ''stranger to this world'' feel to it. SA had a much more emotional and humane feel due to the plot. Contracts probably had a creepy and eery atmosphere to it since it was taking a place in a sociopath's (47) disturbed mind. While Blood Money had that cold and professional theme to it and the lighting mixed with Kyd's OST gave the game a very dynamic ''emotion'' to it. Absolution went for the grindhouse feel as stated by the devs back in the day and it worked very well.
There's simply no atmosphere in this new game and it's probably my biggest problem with it. Hitman 6 plainly put, feels dead and unfinished in the atmosphere department, especially when compared to the previous games.
Anyway... since IOI's doing really badly and refuses to admit it... Hitman is now dead and i won't be writing anymore.. because i'm gonna take a hot shower once again and my fingers are tired as ♥♥♥♥!
Summed up - A great sequel, but the release format (Episodic) ruined it and it shows since now Hitman is basically deader than Elvis...

Spec Ops the Line
At first Spec ops the line is a normal modern 3rd and first person shooter like Call of Duty and or Battlefield, you play as Captain Martin Walker who has been sent into Dubai some months after a series of horrific sands storms have totalled the city. We hear that the military was involved in evacuating the city but it turned sour for reasons not clear at first.
When you start this game it seems like any common garden shooter complete with wise creaking companions and an ‘America is so great’ vibe that constitutes most modern 3rd person shooter. However, over the course of the campaign that vibe melts away to show a truly disturbing story of the horrors of war, PTSD and how even the best of intensions can lead to the worst possible outcomes.
I want to call it horror as it does have its fill of really heart wrenching, visually distressing sequences that would classify it as horror 3rdPS. The game play is bog standard and nothing special, it is kind of clever in that respect as it allows the player to focus on the story aspects but it does not excuse it entirely as even games with the best of stories should have great game play to back it up (Dark souls, Undertale and Blood borne to name a few).
I cannot really say much more about Spec ops the line. I wish I could, I really wish I could but I don’t want to spoil it for you. If you are prepared to experience a terrific story that is going to make you feel really depressed and shocked at what happens then please pick it up. This game is something special and must be supported.
Just as a side note to anyone who picks this up. Watch the main menu.

Dont let the admittedly strange title put you off. This RPG from Belgian developer Larian Studios combines the open-endedness of an Elder Scrolls game with combat reminiscent of Diablo II, and does it very well. Very lengthy and challenging.

Much better than the junk the big companies try to pass as games. An epic, fun to play, and challenging RPG that is actually playable and doesn't crash  (unlike every bethesda game).

In the sea of Diablo clones in the early 2000s, Larian's Divinity series stands out. Not only do they hold true to the genre, hack and slash gameplay in grimdark settings, but they also innovated. Witty and campy dialogue combine in side quests throughout the largely open world. A free form class system ensures you won't be stuck with the same boring archetypes. Puzzles and movable objects break up the grind. A lot of people dismissed this as just another clone when it came up, but it's so much more. If you're burnt out on Diablo 3 and looking for something a little more old school, look no further. Divine Divinity is a fantastic game in a genre largely flooded with lackluster copy-pastes.

Absolutely excellent game. Very good story, good graphics and physics (they have aged a little bit), and good game/level design. I highly recommend this game, but only if you've played Max Payne 1 (which introduced Bullet Time to video games) as the story in this game is a direct continuation. The ending is also badass, Max Payne endings are always very cool. The selection of weapons you have in this game are actually more limited in variety than in the prequel, there are no melee weapons and the M79 grenade launcher is gone from the original game. However, new weapons have been introduced to make up for this. These include the MP5, AK-47, M4 Carbine, Striker (obviously based on the real life DAO-12), and the Dragunov. Bullet Time and its role has been expanded upon. You can now reload weapons while in bullet time, via a stylish spin maneuver, and shootdodging no longer requires Adrenaline. In terms of replayability, there really isn't much. I still like to go back and replay Max Payne games sometimes, but that's just me. There is a new arcade mode called "Dead Man Walking," but all it is about is surviving for as long as possible in small maps and trying to beat your score from last time. No multiplayer unfortunately. So to reiterate, Max Payne 2 is definitely worth your time, but only if you've played Max Payne 1 and you're fine with a game with little replay value (if you're not like me).
It's not the best Max Payne game, but a great action game nonetheless with a decent story and acting. Personal all time favorite classic.

"The Fall of Max Payne". Funny, I don't remember there ever being a "Rise of Max Payne". These games are about a man who lost everything, there was never a rise...was there? Sometime in-between completing Max Payne 1 and the sequel, I finally watched John Woo's
. While a classic in its own right due to the intense shoot-outs, I was especially impressed by its usage of tragedy. Ah Jong is an assassin, but he has morals and a sense of honor. Early on in the film, he accidentally blinds Jennie - a nightclub singer - during a hired hit. Thus, he takes on one last job. The reward would be used for Jennie's vision-saving operation. However, Jong is betrayed by his superiors.
(SPOILERS)
Over the course of the movie, Ah Jong befriends and eventually partners with Inspector Li Ying. Before the climatic battle, Jong asks Ying to promise that if/when he dies, his corneas be used to save Jennie's eyesight. So even if worst came to worst, Jennie could hopefully return to a normal life.  Unfortunately, in the last minutes of the movie, he's shot in the eyes by the villain. Before Jong succumbs to his wounds, he can hear Jennie's cries. Due to their blindness, neither of them can find one another, despite being just a few feet apart. Not only does Jong die, but his noble sacrifice is denied. Everything he worked (and killed) for over the course of the movie was for naught. Although Ying survives, he has lost good friends, and becomes disillusioned with the concept of justice.
Shortly after starting a new game in Max Payne 1, you're treated to the horrifying deaths of Max's wife and child. As time passes, he is framed for murder, wipes out half the criminal underworld, and develops an addiction to painkillers. However, if you've played through the game, then you can recall the final lines: "Woden grinned smugly. It was the grin of a winner. That made two of us." Max Payne is a winner. He succeeded in his mission of vengeance. For us, the audience, that's a satisfying end. So in its own way, Max Payne 1 chronicled the rise, so now we must witness the fall. Tragedy isn't just when a person dies, it's also when their hopes, dreams, and emotions are extinguished.
All that said, there is a lot of joy to be found in Max Payne 2. It's a twisted game, one that isn't afraid to poke fun at itself. This sense of humor keeps the game from coming off as overly dour. It feels especially rewarding to fans of the first title, because they'll pick up on all of the references. It's the kind of humor that fits the tone of the story. It's dark and depressing, but it also has a very distinct noir quality to it. Everything is interconnected, and you get the sense that Max might just be a small part of a much larger story. The "TV shows" that can be seen in various points of the game are a reflection of this. MP2 is a little shorter than its predecessor, but there's more imagery to absorb in every scene.
As for the actual videogame, I believe the combat mechanics are a marked improvement over the first entry. The concept hasn't changed much. You run through every level shooting all of the bad guys. Where this game differs is it showcases a bit more nuance, and a higher level of confidence. One of the first notable changes is that Max takes less damage. This brings it more in-line with the John Woo movies, where good guys shrug off bullets. A couple shot-gun blasts are still usually enough to bring Max from very healthy to dead, but occasional stray shots don't take large chunks of life either. This change gives Remedy a little more freedom when designing encounters. They're more involved, and there tends to be more memorable situations. Max Payne 1 was compelling enough even when combat was just "room full of thugs". The sequel changes things up, and it works very well. I don't even hate the escort missions, well...maybe I still hate them a little. These sections run parallel with some interesting and amusing ideas, so I guess I'll let them slide.
While I'm not sure if I can attribute this to experience with the prequel, or actual changes, the "bullet-time" system also feels substantially better. When Max slows everything down, his heightened reflexes really come into their own. It's really fun running into an area, triggering the bullet-time, and wasting everyone. The first enemy is still flying through the air from Max's shotgun blast as he kills two more men in rapid succession. Occurences such as this are always welcome. Max also pulls off some sweet reloads while in bullet-time. One other minor but welcome change is that when diving and shooting, Max can continue firing while lying on the ground, until his clip is empty. This game uses Havok physics, but the enemies are properly weighted. This makes it so that kills carry some semblance of realism to them, but the few times where enemies soar, or get knocked around in massive explosions, are still very amusing.
On the surface, MP2 comes off as the easier game, but it's balanced out by more thoughtful encounters and harrowing situations. There's a bit more creativity to throw around, and hopefully it keeps players from hitting F5/F9 so much (no guarantees though). Unlike the first game, there is a distinct lack of "boss enemies" aka "thugs who take a lot more bullets to kill". I consider this another positive. Also, just when you really think you've got it down, there are still more difficulties and extra modes to explore. Don't forget to look for the minor details, like people complaining when you stand in-front of them, while they're trying to watch TV.
Basically, if you played through the first Max Payne, you're required to check out the sequel. It's a phenomenal game, and features some of the best third-person shooting action around. The story is fantastic as well, and MP2's usage of various interactive elements really sells the "games-as-art" idea. Oh and don't forget the wide-screen fix.

Maybe it was the crude humor,cheasy action sequences (the opening one is kicka**), or the story that i was actually interested by. I usually have trouble completing games, because i lose interest, take a brake for an evening and then never really feel in the mood to play a game for awhile, or a multitude of other reasons. However, I had no trouble spending a good chunk of my Saturday marathoning this game.
Positive:
- Gameplay. As i said above I am not a huge fan of combo based H&S games, but the fluidness of this game made it very enjoyable.
- Story. I came into this game with little more info than I was playing as a guy named Dante, despite owning a ps2 i never played the originals, so I was very pleased to be drawn into a great story.
- Characters. It is possible to make a good story with no characters (except usually your own) being a bunch of bland morons. The characters in DmC are colorful, and full of life.
- Map. The areas in which you fight in are incredibly detailed, and provide a great amount of variety and fun.
- Music. Personally I loved the heavy metal that plays during all the fights. Makes me feel like a bada**

Spec Ops the Line
At first Spec ops the line is a normal modern 3rd and first person shooter like Call of Duty and or Battlefield, you play as Captain Martin Walker who has been sent into Dubai some months after a series of horrific sands storms have totalled the city. We hear that the military was involved in evacuating the city but it turned sour for reasons not clear at first.
When you start this game it seems like any common garden shooter complete with wise creaking companions and an ‘America is so great’ vibe that constitutes most modern 3rd person shooter. However, over the course of the campaign that vibe melts away to show a truly disturbing story of the horrors of war, PTSD and how even the best of intensions can lead to the worst possible outcomes.
I want to call it horror as it does have its fill of really heart wrenching, visually distressing sequences that would classify it as horror 3rdPS. The game play is bog standard and nothing special, it is kind of clever in that respect as it allows the player to focus on the story aspects but it does not excuse it entirely as even games with the best of stories should have great game play to back it up (Dark souls, Undertale and Blood borne to name a few).
I cannot really say much more about Spec ops the line. I wish I could, I really wish I could but I don’t want to spoil it for you. If you are prepared to experience a terrific story that is going to make you feel really depressed and shocked at what happens then please pick it up. This game is something special and must be supported.
Just as a side note to anyone who picks this up. Watch the main menu.

I wouldn't say this game is amazing but it's decent and worth the buy at a lower price. There's a powerful message throughout and the story does well to compliment that. The strongest reason for me to recommend this is the story.
What the game does right:
The timing and progression is well done and not many games out there make you doubt what you're doing is right. This is very emotionally driven and shows something people usually don't think about. The ai in the story is pretty decent but sometimes prone to running out in the open, albeit rarely. The gunplay is mediocre and fairly standard of what you'd expect.
The problems i came across:
Bad/Poorly made controls are something I personally can't stand so you can ignore this part if it doesn't bother you. Control while running is quite awful. It feels incredibly clunky and difficult to move in the direction you want to if it's not forward. The overuse of space and left shift is also problematic. There's nothing wrong with using a key for multiple functions but space is used for both sprinting and getting behind cover and there's issues with timing which makes them alternate when it doesn't seem appropriate. The function switch detection is poorly made and is detrimental to the gameplay. You also can't jump down ledges without the use of the space key and in some areas, it makes it more difficult to position yourself.
Overall, I'd say this is certainly worth the buy at a $20 or lower price. The game is fairly short (around 6 hours average) and the bulk of the good rating comes from the story..

This game is *amazing*, don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
Sure, people complain and talk smack about it because of redesigned characters, but that's really nitpicking, considering how the other DMCs have almost zero story or character development in the first place.
So we'll start there. The story of DMC is great. Very interesting how instead of half-human, Dante and Vergil are "Nephilim", which is an angel/demon hybrid. Don't wanna say much more about the story, except that I feel they drew heavily upon the reality of our existence on this planet (Media, banking etc. controlled by sinister forces).
The story affects the combat in that Dante has Angel weapons (Left trigger) and Demon weapons (Right trigger). They're all very stylish, although most will probably stick to the demon weapons since the angelic ones are very weak (although they look awesome -- a scythe and a giant shuriken).
The game consists of ~20 missions, and within those missions are hidden items and secret missions with specific combat or platforming goals. I'd wager it's about a 15 hour adventure, although between this version and the 360 version, I've got about 50 hours into it. This is made possible due to the many difficulty levels. About seven, I believe. I recommend starting on Nephilim, unless you're entirely new to this franchise or action games in general.
This game looks amazing, especially in Limbo. Limbo (purgatory) is where you'll spend the vast majority of the game. It's always twisting and turning to some effect, whether it be to block your progress, trying to trap you, or throwing enemies at you. You can move the camera as you wish, although you probably won't have to often, as the auto focus is very well done.
Honestly, there's not much to complain about in DMC. Devil Trigger is almost useless and nowhere near as cool as it could be, which was a disappointment. As mentioned before, the Angel weapons are overshadowed by the Demon weapons due to weak power. This ties into my biggest issue with the game, which is the enemies. There's not a whole lot of enemy variety, and the color-coded ones force you to use either all-angel or all-demon weapons.
The Style ranking system is perhaps a little too easy, whereas previous games required a LOT of practice to achieve S rank or higher. I think this was a design choice to enable more casual play (you feel like a total badass without having to dedicate many hours to the game), but this could easily be fixed by having the Style system fluctuate with the difficulty level. Other complaints are the way Vergil is handled (can't spoil it), and the lack of a lock-on...both of which I actually enjoy. Yes, sometimes you'll attack a different enemy than you wanted, but it's kind of rare, and I personally only encountered it when dealing with the flying enemies, and even then it was easily remedied by closing some distance.
Ultimately, DMC is my favorite Devil May Cry game. I loved the others (minus 2), but this reboot, DMC, is by far the edgiest, most stylish game I've ever played. The way Dante's coat flows through combat, the way his sword sheans with each slice, enemies gibbing and shredding when killed...the list goes on with ways of making each battle make you're killing these demons with extreme prejudice. And although the boss battles are certainly too easy, their presentation, along with the rest of the game, is phenomenal.

Two years after the events of the previous game, Max Payne is an NYPD. + One of the few occasions, in which the story of the sequel is better than the original's. The concept might be more mainstream, but it is unraveled way better.

+ Bullet time

Neutral

Concluding, i absolutely recommend this game, even on full price since it has replayability and you dont buy it only for one use.

Max Payne 2 is more of the same, and that's not really a bad thing.  If you're not familiar with the game series, it's a third person shooter with bullet time effects and a noir style story.
There are slight improvements over the first game, such as being able to equip grenades / molotovs as a "secondary weapon" instead of having to switch from a gun to use them.  The graphics are much easier on the eyes too.  Probably the most novel part of MP2 is the levels where you have to work alongside or play as Max's love interest / femme fatale, Mona Sax.  It's interesting to play through the same timespan from both characters' point of view.
The story is fairly predictable, and the gunplay is fun as always.  The writers have played it safe with a formula that works (with a few tweaks), and as a result have made another solid game in the series.  Recommended.

Unfortunately, this game does have problems.  No matter what OS you use, you will have to do something to make the game run correctly.  In the case of windows 7 and beyond, you will have to shut one or more of your core processors off in order to make the game run.  If you update the game, you won't be able to play it.  If you play on XP, you will have sound issues.
Despite all of this, this is a game that I am sure you will love.  Come for the gameplay, and stay for the humor that's still present.

I really, really, really like this game, but I'm not recommending it.
I was a fan of the tabletop card game before playing this digital version. This is an incredibly faithful recreation of that experience. The only reason I'm not recommending the game is because of a lack of content and features for the $15.00 price point.
PROS:
+ Faithful recreation of the tabletop gameplay.
+ Faithful recreation of the tabletop art.
+ Hero and Villain variants provide something to work towards, and a variance on standard gameplay.
+ Amazingly corny music is amazingly appropriate. I catch myself humming it in the shower or while doing dishes.
+ Trading card support!
CONS:
+ No achievements.
+ No campaign or story mode.
+ No situational challenge mode (i.e. beat this villain at location with these heroes).
+ Not enough variants to unlock.
+ Variant unlock requirements are somewhat obscure. You'll probably have to look them up.
+ Absolute Zero is still Absolute Zero.
+ Lack of beer and pretzels experience.
Because of the above, the game is just not something I can recommend to a general audience. This game is only really good for new players to Sentinels who want to practice by themselves, or veterans who want to experiment with different hero combinations before their next board game group gathering. And people who can't ever get a group together to play the tabletop game due to work, school, or other life obligations.
I hope that one day this game is updated with a lot of the missing content. I'll gladly change my recommendation when that day comes.

Not your standard FPS take on the Zombie Apocalypse theme, NMRIH drops its players into the open, rotting arms of the slow, shambling zombie masses of 'Night of the Living Dead' fame. The game provides thrilling gameplay with inventory management, strategy and team co-operation as integral elements to success. Currently there are two game modes: survival & objection-based. Survival mode may seem familiar to Left 4 Dead veterans. In both games players are set in a given area which is fortified and stockpiled with supplies, things like ammunition, weapons and medical items. Waves of ever increasing numbers of 'Zekes' pound on the shores of the survivor's holdfast, and the situation can soon become dire as supplies run low, players become infected and start dropping like flies. The major difference between both games survival modes is that in NMRIH, if they make it far enough, eventually the survivors can be extracted to safety and win the round.
On Objective-Based maps, players embark on a mini-campaign together where they must journey through the usually shadowy, labyrinthian zombie infested alleyways of places such as New York's China Town, a cemetary and a lonely cabin in the woods. The players must stick close together and systematically proceed through the objetions of the map. Find a gas can and fill up a generator here, enter in a code to a locked room on a keypad there, all the while double-tapping Zombies and scavenging for new weapons and ammunition.
NMRIH may be unforgiving to newbies, even those familiar with survival-horror first-person shooters and the HL2 Source game engine. Give the game a try, listen to the veteran players and read gameplay guides on the Steam Community page. There are many little tips and tricks out there which will start you on your path to becoming a veritable Zombie killing-machine! If I can offer you one word of advice before we part ways: Never forget to always keep moving and to check where you've been. You never know when there may be a zombie coming up behind y ...

Thank you guys for doing a game right, for the morons ♥♥♥♥♥ing about a broken game this game is PRE-ALPHA meaning its a work in progress, hell there is even a big blue box that says "early access game" that you have to scroll by to even get to the purchase button, instead of QQing for refunds, submit HELPFUL bug report "its broken" isnt a bug report, for those who have never done a bug report here is a helpful format. also opinions have no place in a bug report so leave the trash talk out of it, help these guys improve an already great game.
Impotant terms,
Crash - this means the game exits with or without a dump/error screen
Softlock - this means the game is still running and the player has some interaction, but progress is is not able to be made
Harlock - this means the game is frozen and will not exit or continue (audio can still play but may be distorted or be hung on a single tone, this can be an important detail so include it in your video and in your description)
Dump file - this is where details are stored about program errors/crashes and is important in narrowing where bugs occur if your able to include it  do so
Check to make sure your bug hasnt already reported, if there is a missing detail take note of the bug number and add "Bug refrance #(what ever the previously reported bug number was) to your description so the dev can look at that bug and know they are related. the bug tracker does provide a bug number. you  want to be as concise and breif as possible the devs have to read literally thousands of these so the less time they are reading the more time they are fixing (and inevitbly breaking, sorry worked in the industry for awhile inside joke) the game.
Brief descritption: (Ex. Truck strarted flying through the air after adding research item to the vehicle storage socket)
Where were you when it broke? (Ex. near my base)
how did it break? (Ex. the physics went crazy)
Did you do somthing when it broke? (Ex. Added research item to a vehicle storage unit)
Did this make the game unplayable? (Ex. no)
Is this bug easy to duplicate? (Ex. yes)
Additional notes (include special circumstances here such as "i morphed terrain using flat tool"): (ex. this happens to any vehicle storage on the rover and truck, i havent tested it on spaceship)

(Minor gameplay spoilers ahead) I purchased Astroneer last night and immediately felt drawn into the experience. I launched from space and landed on a planet with colorful environments and a simple yet pleasing aesthetic. A nearby mountain invited me to explore the mysteries of its dark caves and a crashed spaceship at its peak, but alas, I didn't have the means to venture there safely because Oxygen is at a premium and staying tethered to my tiny ship was the only thing keeping me alive. This is what makes this type of game so rewarding; They give you an inviting world to explore but start you off with a short leash that only gets longer with baby steps and a little "hard" work. Astroneer does not disappoint in this regard and had a very solid base for an early access game.
After some resource gathering and research I could get to that mountain and explore to my heart's content. After a little more research and exploration I could expand my horizons even further. I crafted vehicles, travelled far, discovered new biomes and tech, built my tiny habitat into a respectable base, and had a tense five minutes of being hopelessly lost in a cave while oxygen resources dried up. Fun! So far so good!
After several hours of gameplay I exhausted what this planet could teach me and plotted a course for the next planet. It was just as exciting as it was the first time but it only took me ten minutes to realize this new planet had nothing offer me other than a slightly different environment. I had already discovered the dozen or so items available for research and there were no other boundaries or limitations to overcome, and so after less than a day's play there’s no reason for me to continue playing until we get some hefty future updates.
I don’t regret paying my $20 because I hope it will go towards further development on this very promising game, but at present there’s not enough here for me to recommend Astroneer to a friend at a $20 price point when there are similar early access games you can buy for $20 or less that offer so much more as of writing this review.

DmC Devil May Cry may not have lived up to the hopes from a lot of long time fans of the series but the reboot in my honest opinion is still a fantastic game. There are some problems with the gameplay but overall the game is fantastic and is a must own in anyone's library.
DmC is a combo based Hack and Slash, Action Adventure game that is a reboot of the long running series Devil May Cry. In this game you play as Dante, a half demon/half angel Nephilim that while learning about his origins fights his way through demons to get to the demon king. As stated since DmC is a hack and slash combo game you must master combos of various weapons in order to kill waves of demons and get a higher combo score. This Combo score is scored on a lettering system which is in the order of Dirty, Cruel, Brutal, Anarchic, Savage!, SSadistic!! and SSSensational!!!. The higher the combo score the more XP you get in order to upgrade Dante's weapons which include his sword, Rebellion, his demon weapons Arbiter (Axe) and Eryx (Gloves), his angel weapons Osiris (Scythe) and Aquila (Shuriken) and his ranged weapons Ebony & Ivory, Revenant and Kablooey. Along with upgrading these weapons you have the ability to unlock new combos that you can use to more effectively kill demons and get a higher combo score.

In order to get a higher combo score you must mix up combos and weapons without getting hit by an enemy. Despite it being a bit complex it is nowhere near the complexity of the original Devil May Cry games which is a big reason a lot of long time fans were not happy about the reboot. Along with the dumbing down of the combat it is also a lot easier to get a SSS rank which takes a lot of the challenge out of a hack and slash combo game. Another quirk that was a problem with this game was the color coded enemies. This severely limited your options of what weapons you could use against an enemy. Though it added a little layer of complexity to the combat it was more of an irritant that something enjoyable. Otherwise the combat was a lot of fun and I got a huge satisfaction of killing enemies and using various combos while fighting.
One more thing to add is that in the original Devil May Cry series, the player was forced to go through very monotonous jumping puzzles that really served no purpose being in the game. DmC improved on this greatly and despite it still having the jumping puzzles they are a lot more satisfying. For example, at one point you are in limbo mode while Vergil and Kat are in the real world. All during this time the world around you is falling apart and while jumping around and fighting enemies you have to help them avoid obstructions that would kill them. Just seeing the world crumble and try to defeat you itself is fascinating and a lot more fun than the puzzles in the original series.

As I mentioned before you play as Dante, a half demon/half angel Nephilim, who was pulled into a Limbo one day after he met Kat. Limbo is a parallel world to the real world where the demons live. This is the only place that Dante can actively fight the demons and use his powers to stop them. After his initial fight he is brought before Vergil who informs him that he is a Nephilim and that Vergil is his twin brother who runs an organization called "The Order". Vergil explains that their ultimate goal is to bring down the demons ore more specifically the Demon King Mundus who has been searching for Dante because he knew Dante was a Nephilim.
The reboot did a great job of bringing back the characters and giving them a whole different spin. In the original series Dante was an egocentric maniac that was overconfident and used to fighting demons. In the reboot, they show him in his younger more naive state that is just learning about his origins and what it means to him to be a Nephilim. I found the story absolutely fascinating and was quite engaging especially the character development of Dante himself. He started out as someone who only cared about himself, drank and partied all the time and changed into someone that began to find compassion for his friends and for others.

Now this game being a couple years old doesn't have the best graphics but they are still very good. On top of that, Ninja Theory did an absolutely fantastic job differentiating between the living world and Limbo. When you are out in the living world, it is very dull, dark, grey and boring. It represents how many in the living world are stuck doing the same monotonous tasks over and over again because they have been under control the entire time. When you play in Limbo the world is colorful, unique, full of amazing looking scenery and level designs.  You can really feel the passion that went into making Limbo as great looking as they can.
On top of that the soundtrack is absolutely fantastic. It has a great mix of electronic, rock, classical and many other genres that just compliment each level and scenario you are playing in. A soundtrack can absolutely make or break a game/movie. You watch Star Wars without any of the background music from John Williams and you lose a lot of emotional appeal of what is going on, especially that scene where Luke finds his Aunt and Uncle dead.  It just complimented the scene so well and the soundtrack in DmC does the same. Along with the music the voice acting is also superb. They really made it sound like their characters were engaged and made them more believable.

Overall, DmC is one of my favorite games and a must play in my opinion. The gameplay may have been dumbed down from the original series but that isn't to say it isn't still a lot of fun to just destroy the various demons. It helps that Ninja Theory wrote a great story and did a fantastic job with differentiating between the two worlds. The game may be a single player game however it isn't without a bit of replay value thanks to unlocking new game+ and being able to go back and get all the collectables.

"You are dead to me." This quote came from a friend at work when I informed him I was playing Devil May Cry 2013. Why did he feel so strongly? Because he, like many others, thought the new look of Dante was somehow sacriligious to past Devil May Cry games. Well after finishing the game, all I can say is he and the others are missing out. DMC is everything that is great about the series only with a fresh coat of paint. Let's examine what this game is. This is a reboot of an origin story for a very bad♥♥♥♥♥character.
I won't lie and say I am a die hard fan. I have only played DMC 1 and 4.DMC 1 was good but did not have a lasting impact on me. DMC 4 was the first game I purchased for my PS3 years ago and I thouroughly enjoyed the (at the time) stunning visuals and breakneck gameplay. The opening sequence was what hooked me and the gameplay was spectacular. Thanks to the many amazing games on the PS3 (and so little time), DMC 2013 came and past without a purchase and I thought it would be just one more DMC game I would never play.
Fast forward to October 2014 steam sale in which I purchased my first gaming laptop and saw DMC 2013 for $17.00. DMC 4 had been a worthwhile purchase back on the PS3 so I bought DMC 2013 and I am very pleased that I did. Let's talk about that fresh coat of paint. This is a modern twist on the DMC formula. The story gives us a look at a young Dante and his transformation from a selfish punk to the world's hope amongst the demons. This story will not apeal to everyone, but it is well writtenand I laughed a few times at Dante's sense of humor. The characters are very likeable (a special nod to Virgil) including Dante by the end of the tale.
What about the gameplay you ask? After all this is the real reason someone would play any game. I am happy to report this is the DMC action we all know and love. The gameplay is fun and chaotic. The levels are beautiful and makes exploring a pleasure. Keep in mind this is DMC so don't use too much time exploring unless you want a lower rating. On the default normal difficulty, the game is challenging but not cheap. Every time I died it was my own fault for getting carried away hacking at an enemy. The enemies get re-used but in different configurations over the course of the game. Two minor gripes would be the camera angle sometimes gets in the way and how deep the combo system can be. The problem I have with the combo system is that it can be difficult in the heat of battle to remember all the diffirent attacks you can do. This is not a deal breaker though because it also makes for some very exciting battles. I will finally also mention one of the most underrated aspects of gaming these days and that is the excellent checkpoint system. Again this is my own opinion, but a good checkpoint system is really important (losing loads of progress when you have so little time to play is not ideal).
So in conclusion, despite my untimely death in the eyes of my co-worker, this game is completely worth your attention. Despite the reboot menatlity (Dante's new look, the modern setting, the backstory) and the few flaws (wonky camera at times, overwhelming combo system) this game is amazing. I would highly recommend that any action game or Devil May Cry enthusiast check it out. I had such a good time with this game and I am happy that it was my first game I purchased and beat on my new laptop.

Just finished my first playthrough of MINERVA: Metastasis. What an excellent, excellent mod. It is all the more impressive when you know it's been made by one guy, who went on to be hired by Valve.
And no wonder: the level design is excellent. None of those frequent loading screens that plague Source games. In fact, I only remembering one loading screen in a 4-hour playthrough of massive proportions. It makes great use of space, compressing game areas, using verticality, sending you back and forth sometimes - never tediously.
Another excellent bit is the pacing. This is a brutal fight from start to finish, with intermittent calm stretches. The rhythm is perfect. The modder manages to craft action sequences within HL2's trademark limited perspective. Unlike modern games where you feel like you are watching your character do all the cool stuff, here you get to do them yourself.
At one point, you are stripped of all your weapons & ammo, and soon an avalanche of enemies is unleashed on you and you must scramble down foreign corridors, frantically searching for an armory, solving puzzles at lightning speed with your pursuers hot on your heels.
Even though the game is linear, in true HL fashion, I often found myself stuck, only to finally go "of course!" notice and solve a mini-puzzle, and proceed to the next bit. It's refreshing to once again play a game that doesn't hold your hand - I can't help but be used to that by now, with modern games going out of their way to nudge you in the right direction at all times.
So yes, breathtaking difficulty - of the thrilling kind, not the frustrating kind - and no hand holding. Although if you stay stuck for a long long time, there is a subtle and plot-appropriate hint system.
The plot is very basic, but very intriguing. It doesn't get in the way, and it's not an afterthought by any means - but it leaves you with questions, and that's very cool.
One last thing - the mod uses some HL2 musical tracks, but there's an additional musical score that's awesome, and I must acquire it.
Could have been a missing chapter of half life 2. Really well made and put together mod.

I have the actual board game version of the game, including the expansions, and I'm very happy with the digital one. As the "bad guy" deck is made to play itself, it fits really well with the digital version, no need for an AI. Playing by yourself is essentially solitaire, since there's no multiplayer. If you get people together at your place, it'll play just like the card game (it's a coop, so you can show your hand to each other), only it'll be tracking all the effects for you!
It also comes with undo, letting you rewind back several steps. A bit cheaty if you go back to previous turns, but it's a good touch if you grab the wrong card, or misread the text.
All in all it's polished and bug-free. Only ran into one occassion when the calculations didn't seem to agree with the cards in play, out of a dozen games or so. Hard to tell if that's common or not yet.

Sentinels of the Multiverse is one of those games that is great to play whenever someone comes over. While the current version doesn't support online play, it is much more user friendly to new players in comparison to the tabletop, allowing for a much quicker tutorial or first play. While you may not play against each other in Sentinels, the tension is extremely real and you'll easily find yourself anticipating or dreading the card flips as they come up. What's funny is that each game will never feel the same due to the number of variables of what does or doesn't happen for both the heroes, villains and environment.
In addition to the gameplay, the game has in depth bios of characters and bits of their evolving story on the flavor text of cards. The universe that the game exists in is expansive beyond just the tabletop experience, and you'll notice that the way how the character plays in the game is very representative of how their character bios describe them. There's also a lot of story that isn't just rubbed in your face, which will become a lot more relevant once they release the expansion material that exists right now for the tabletop game.
With Handelbra and GtG games both working hard to continually develop the digital version after it's release, this game is definitely a must buy for anyone who loves tabletop, card, or cooperative games.
EDIT: After nearly 2 years, this game has received a constant stream of support in terms of bug fixes and new content. It's to the point where the game is massively different from when I first reviewed it, which begs the need for me to return to this topic.
- So far they've added a whole season of new DLC along with the second season already done with production and about to start flowing out.
- Variants to hero and villan cards come in the form of community challenges where players have to seek out the means to unlock them with only the character's story and the name of the variant to go off of. For those of you either late to the race or don't want to deal with the challenges in order to play with the variants, there is a button to unlock them about a month down the line.
- Weekly challenges which puts you in a specific scenario with locked rules, forcing you to try and complete the game with heroes you wouldn't normally use or environments you don't normally play in. There's even a ranking system depending on how many tries it takes you to complete them.
- Online Multiplayer, while open rooms are kind of dead now, it does allow you to play with your friends without having to be in the same room with them. There are also settings which allow you to modify how many alerts players need to go through to progress through an action, suiting the speed you want to play the game at.
- Foil Card DLC can probably be seen as a bit of a cash grab by some, but it was something given through those who gave to kickstarter, and the price didn't go up when they made it available for purchase as DLC. The range of new art is pretty fantastic, and any updates to it will be given to any player who purchased it for free instead of releasing them in packs (This only pertains to the "Hero" version since the "Villain" version was seperate even in the Kickstarter and will have it's own updates).
Once again, I fully recommend this game to anyone who is an avid fan of tabletop games, and anyone who is already a fan of Sentinels of the Multiverse. The depth of it's strategic gameplay, story and mechanics have only grown more elaborate with time and its still probably the best transfer of a tabletop game into digital format to date.

TLDR; 8/10, 10/10 when multiplayer realeases
Preface: I am very much a fan of the table top game SoTM
Sentinels of the Multiverse is a Co-optional card based game, where you and your fellow friends play as super heros battling against a villain and the enviroments. The play structure is simple which allows for anyone to pick up the game. Yet, for how simple the rules are, the game has incredible depth and replayability. Every hero, villain, and enviroment deck has different mechanics that really give you the feel of an epic comicbook battle.
For those who are already a fan of the tabletop game, you'll be happy to find that all of the math and book keeping that kind of brings down the physical game is now just process for you. This means you won't be missing any card triggers or buffs you might look over in regular play. I know that this is integral part of a digital version, but it is worth mentioning
Anyone who has no experience with the table top format, you will find an excellent co-op game that you and your company will enjoy multiple times.
Issues I have with the game; the ui is chunky and confusing the first time around. This isn't a deal breaker but something that should and probably be remedied with patches. Also the lack of multiplayer on realease was slightly disappointing, although, will also be included in furture patches or DLC. (hopefully not DLC)

So I want to make the pros and cons short, sweet, and to the point. Because it's late and I'm too tired to write a lengthy review.
Pros:
Beautiful game. For being a Desert city, it's very colorful and unique.
Story is different for its genre. I mean it is predictible if you've seen this kind of story before, or even if you've seen Apocalypse Now. However it is nice to see a deeper meaning to the bloodshed, no matter how shallow it might be.
The transition of your protagonist and your comrades. I won't say more for fear of spoilers.
Cons:
Garbage ai. The game as a false sense as to what constitutes difficulty. The game thinks that difficulty = pinpoint accurate enemies that bum rush you. I played it on suicide, and I thought it was easy when the ai acted more... human... and impossible when the enemy snipes you from 500 km with one shot with a bloody smg.
Limited enemies. I'd like variety to the people I kill. Names, faces, and some sort of intelligence. The game is meant to make every bullet you fire seem significant, but in the end it's just you and your mates mowing down ai.
Horrible PC controls. I guess the ones who ported the controls have never played an FPS or TPS on a keyboard+mouse before.
Bland, generic characters. The main protagonist is great. Same with the people you meet in Dubai. But your comrades are so cringy sometimes.
Neutral:
Linear story telling. I mean that's also a pro in my opinion since I hate these modern shooters that are like "dur dur open world" when in actuality they're linear too. Just with less strict rules. At least when you "make decisions", it's to further the plot and not because "lol dead people".
Political messages about video games. There seems to be some sort of message about violent video games and how they make us numb to the realities of war. Ugh. Same♥♥♥♥♥♥different day. At least for the most part it's tasteful. Unlike a certain COD MW 2 mission we all know and love.
Short game time. It's neutral cause the scenery does get old, and so does the messages, and so do the samey enemies. It ends right before I completely lost interest.
Bottom Line (heh)
Buy it on sale. Play it for the aesthetics and solid shooting gameplay. And enjoy a game rightfully rated 76% of metacritic (at the time of this review).

A great game, possibly the best of the Call of duty series(in my opinion). The maps are fun and always fun to replay. The guns and equipment, apart from the SCAR-H,AN-94 and C4, are mostly well-balanced. Movement is medium-fast paced, which is a good thing, compared to newer CoD titles, like Advanced and Infinite Warfare. Cheaters and bad connection happen rarely to never. The game runs surprisingly well, even on lower end systems(close to minimal system requirements).

Everybody's second-favourite Call of Duty sub-franchise returns, picking through the carnage of the preceding game's CIA conspiracy while simultaneously barrelling onward into the cyber-enhanced future-war of 2025.
The game flits between control of David Mason, son of the first Blops' protagonist, and flashbacks to (not terribly) covert missions taking place during the conflicts of the late 20th century. For the most part, it follows familiar Call of Duty rote: enemies swarm out and you pop their heads and push forward. Like Whack-a-mole, but with foreigners. You shoot men in 1980s Afghanistan. You shoot men and robots in future-LA. Hither and thither, men are shot, their demise serving a globe-trotting anti-terrorism yarn that would be amusingly ludicrous if it weren't laser-targeted to evoke actual middle-American paranoia.
But before we get to that: let me tell you about my horse. My horse keeps on falling through the ground. It doesn't fall far – just up to its flanks – but it's very hard to fend off a Russian assault on a half-buried horse. I can't get off my horse because I haven't quite reached the horse-dismounting checkpoint. I am stuck. I reload and reload and reload and eventually make it through.
I mention this because my problem with Blops 2 and CoD in general is not that they are cinematic shooters of little mechanical imagination or meaningful interactivity – I'm completely cool with that. CoD is essentially Duck Hunt with multidirectional movement and a hysterically self-pitying, bellicose view of global politics. That's OK. That's allowed. But I take issue when I repeatedly crash through its flimsy world into the unglamorous workings behind.
It's not even that Blops 2 is buggy: it's just so inflexible and brittle as to splinter at the most gentle pressure in any direction other than the one in which it is ordained to move. Playing it is to tiresomely re-analyse the ever-shifting boundaries of interaction. The very first level kills you if you stray outside the invisibly defined battle zone; later you are gifted with an entire canyon to roam – assuming your horse remains above ground level.
At one point, I found myself stuck on a beach while angry locals swarmed through the jungle behind. The sign above my AI partner said, 'Follow'. However, he had stopped. I'd been told there were some boats on the beach, which would seem like a mission-critical observation, were it possible to interact with them. “Keep running, Mason!” shouts my AI partner, apparently unaware that we are hemmed into this tiny sandy deathzone by invisible walls. Several reloads later, I discover that I have to press F on my companion and initiate an ending cutscene. Ah.
This seems like a shame because it torpedoes one of Black Ops 2's most ambitious endeavours. At key points during the game you are given choices which dramatically change its outcome. But so trammelled are you in the interim that you may not realise your own power.
When the opportunity arose to execute someone, I couldn't work out how to decline – or even if I could. I tried shooting other people in the room, but the gun just didn't fire. I tried to wait the decision out, but eventually I assumed there was only one interactive option available. Bang. Sorry. Deciding whether or not to kill someone should be dramatic, but here it felt more like attempting to interpret faded washing instructions. Can I tumble dry this?
Still, such pivotal moments, when they work, do perk interest in the otherwise daft plot as it maniacally flings itself around history, occasionally stamping on the bits of it wingnuts don't like. Despite all the techno-gobbledegook, conspiracy, brainwashing and betrayal, Black Ops 2 presents a paint-by-numbers world, in which the primary colours are fear, jingoism and self-righteous aggression. In this version of reality, Islamic terrorists are elided with South American socialists, hackers and anti-capitalist protesters.
The game's arch-villain, Raul Menendez, is a product of American interventionism gone awry, but if there's a warning there, it's subsumed by the batshit fervour of his personal quest for revenge. Menendez is not a nice man (you can tell because he has a scar) and his response to his violation by America is to go around yelling and kneecapping people, so it's hard to sympathise with him. That we are only encouraged to worry about American foreign policy inadvertently creating Menendez-like monsters is itself troubling, but I suppose people whose lives were just quietly and terribly ♥♥♥♥ed don't make exciting antagonists.
After this calamitous introduction to the campaign, however, Blops 2 settles down. Its set-pieces become more coherent (if not the plot) and the majority of its novelties work. Except this time, there are no egregiously annoying infinite spawns. Indeed, the game sidesteps many of the series' clichés. Turret sections are subverted almost the instant they begin, as are other staples: the slow-motion breach and clear, the last-second gun-toss.
Elsewhere, futuristic gadgetry brings welcome variety. You can target enemies with a fleet of drones or hunker behind shambling quadrupedal mechs. Their power is most visible in the radical addition of Strike Force, a simplistic RTS gamemode which runs in parallel to the campaign. Using a high-altitude view, you capture points, defend them, protect convoys and rescue hostages. At any point you can dive into the brain of a soldier or robot and take direct control. The major weakness is the AI – the lamentable pathfinding is all the more visible in the top-down view – but its incompetence obligates you to get your hands dirty, and so creates the delightful tension between strategy and ground tactics. It's messy, perhaps, but fun: rarely in a Call of Duty game do you get the entire toybox to play with all at once.
Black Ops 2 also manages occasional spectacle, despite a creaking engine. The recreation of a Yemeni hillside township is both visually and spatially fascinating, a wonderful chaos of alleys and stairwells, offering as much vertical variation as horizontal. Elsewhere, an exclusive, floating mega-resort has been taking notes from Brink's super-white sea-faring skyline – a dazzling, crisp utopia which is disturbingly cathartic to smash.
Exploring that Yemeni township is all the better in multiplayer. In fact, everything is better in multiplayer. Add a few real people, and levels that were inert backdrops to the campaign now reveal a more delicate construction: multiple strata and intertwining paths, every space run through with dozens of sightlines to keep you on your toes. On the deck of a burning aircraft carrier, your objective is to minimise your exposure, skipping between coverpoints, constantly craning this way and that to ensure you aren't being flanked. A railway station generates an ongoing flow of combat through multiple, looping routes. Rarely do you find a position which isn't in some way compromised, forcing continual movement.
Myriad multiplayer modes are divided and duplicated among a variety of playlists, although most of the new additions, like the roaming king-of-the-hill gametype Hardpoint, are fairly unadventurous reconfigurations of existing rulesets. The 'party game' playlist contains the most outlandish departures from regular Call of Duty gunplay – here you earn extra bullets with kills or automatically cycle through the game's armoury.
Treyarch have made some canny rebalancing decisions: the special rewards formerly known as Killstreaks have evolved into Scorestreaks. Helping your team with objectives now contributes to earning UAV surveillance, drone strikes and other devastating powers. The unlockable-arms-race seems less painful for new players, too, thanks to an ample starting kit.
This is all to the good – but is it a reinvention worth $60/£40? The menus are biased toward gamepad controls and the lack of dedicated servers is regrettable.

I've been a fan of the Hitman franchise since the first title was released many years ago.  Anyone who's followed the games over the years will probably agree on two things:  1)  Bloodmoney is the best, and 2) We don't talk about Absolution.
If you loved Hitman 2, Contracts or Bloodmoney, you'll love this.  If you thought Absolution was great then you might like this.  Also, shame on you for liking Absolution.
HITMAN brings almost all the great bits of Bloodmoney, the few good bits from Absolution and mashes them into a fresh feeling game.  It's had a tricky launch with some pretty appalling optimization and unusual release scheduling but those problems seem to have been ironed out now.  The game looks and plays great!
Pros
-Though limited in number, the levels are huge, beautifully designed and incredibly detailed not only aesthetically but mechanically.  The game is less gritty than Absolution/Contracts and feels much more like Bloodmoney 2.0.
-The sheer number of approaches, techniques and possibilities for each assassination/objective is what Hitman is about and there's no shortage of things to discover here.  The game is deserving of it's 'Assassination Sandbox' tag.  The game is in no way linear like Absolution was.
-The disguise system in Absolution was completely broken/awful.  This has been re-worked and fixed.  That said, playing Suit Only is very achieveable and just as fun.
-The Challenges system is incredibly rewarding and keeps each level's replay value high whilst unlocking new gadgets/weapons/opportunities.
-The Contracts system, which was Absolution's one saving grace, is a great content generator which coupled with Escalations and  Elusive Targets mean there's plenty of new hits to be planned and played.
-Professional difficulty mode makes the game far more challenging.  Experienced players may find the standard difficulty a little too forgiving.
-The game retains it's notorious dark sense of humour.
Cons
-The game does require an online connection to play.  Now, I don't have any issues with this as my connection is fine, but I think it's a poor design choice.
-Reliance on tools (screwdriver/wrench) is a little annoying sometimes, especially as 47 cannot start with these items so you have to find them.  I'm hoping some buys 47 a multitool for Xmas.
-The voice acting is great, but they re-used the same few people too much and it's noticeable sometimes.
-Two things are missing from Bloodmoney which is a shame: 1) WA2000 doesn't come in a suitcase and 2) You cannot take hostages.  Two minor but really fun mechanics in my opinion.
Overall this is arguably Hitman as it's finest.  It captures almost everything that made Bloodmoney the game everyone loves whilst bringing new ideas and mechanics.  Most importantly I feel like IOI have built a fantastic foundation which they can build on with new chapters.  I don't expect to see a brand new Hitman game any time soon, instead I think we'll see the biggest and best Hitman game here.

HITMAN is a unique stealth experience that will require patience, knowledge and effort. This game is not for the lighthearted.
HITMAN is the best stealth game I've played in years, this is mostly thanks to some of the best level design in stealth games, the levels fit multiple play styles. And the stories expressed through these levels makes the game an immersive experience.
It's really rewarding and interesting to overhear conversations with your target, not only it reveals more behind the story which is usually interesting but it gives useful information that you could use to take out your target. It's a one of a kind game.
HITMAN also allows for many different ways to take out your target, it can be as easy as a sniper shot or something more unique like getting a set of lights to drop on your target. Long story short, if you think of a way to take out your target, you can probably do that in HITMAN.
My only gripe with the game is that there are not enough levels, even though they are very big and well detailed I felt like there needed to be more levels. The levels in the game, however, do have high replayability which is what increases the playtime.
Overall, this is still a great game. Stealth games have become more and more mainstream but HITMAN seems to straddle a line between accessibility and hardcore for people who loved Blood Money. This is easily the best HITMAN game to date.

It was very hard for me decided if I should make a positive or negative review or not. There are a lot of really great aspects about this game, but I feel like the downsides really hold it back too much. The level designs, generally, are gorgeous and varied. From private villa's to busy city streets. The graphics are very good, and this definitely has a greater aesthetic than previous games in the series. There are a LOT more items and ways to interact with the environment than previously, which makes it very interesting. And of course, the voice acting of the main cast is exquisite. I heard once they were thinking about not using Bateson and honestly that would have ruined it for me. His voice always reminds me of all the reasons I love this series, and ultimately pushed me over to a positive review.
The negatives however are quite steep. The biggest problem is that the UI is TERRIBLE. One of the worst video game UI's I have ever seen. Navigating the menu is confusing and organizing inventory is a nightmare. There was no quick inventory, or inventory wheel, no assigned slots. If you wanted that soda can you found twenty minutes ago you better open your entire inventory and work through it one by one. I praised the level designs before, but more often than not they were unnecessarily frustrating. You might find a piece of information telling you to head to the interrogation room, only to run around for an hour looking for it, because it is not in any of the places you would think of. Also, despite the 999 ways to kill each target I often would turn around and suddenly find myself with the target, completely alone. Once I nudged one off a ledge while walking towards another target. This happens semi frequently and takes away the challenge. And BUGS! Sometimes I would have to restart an entire mission because my target froze mid conversation, or because one clipped through a wall and I couldn't reach them.
However one of my biggest issues was the lack of immersion. Though I praised the voice acting of the main cast, the voice acting of the NPC's is terrible. The actual dialogue is good, but the wrong voices are constantly popping up. The number of english accents coming from the native people of Thailand felt actually kind of racist. My did half the people in Morocco sound southern? Why did the one guy actually named "The Texan" sound like he was from Minnesota? It all feels really out of place.
The story has a lot of promise, but it doesn't make sense for most of this season. The first several cut scenes were just confusing. While the last cut scene left me with chills, I had wished they all made me feel that. If you like the Hitman series, this one is okay. It definitely doesn't play as well as Absolution, but the levels are more interesting and I think the story has a lot of promise.
Enough settings to make it as challenging as you like (Way more fun with instinct disabled imo). Just as good as Blood money.

Looking for a realistic zombie game, but sick of wandering around the barren wastelands of Cherno?  Look no further.  No More Room in Hell is definitely worth your time.  You and seven other players are tasked with either surviving for a certain amount of waves (if you've read World War Z, you'll understand why) or get from point A to point B to escape the hordes.  Along the way, you'll find various weapons, from melee to firearms, to makeshift explosives.
Melee weapons come in either blunt or bladed.  Which ever one you pick though, it'll require you to get in close and risk getting bitten.  And yes, you can get infected in this game.  Infection will slowly dim your screen until you die and turn on your teammates (the infection can be staved off with pills, but only temporarily).  Regardless, you'll want to take out the zombies in a single, clean blow to the head.  Right clicking will let you do a heavy attack and left click will do a light attack.  Repeated blows will drain your stamina quickly.  If zombies get too close, you can shove them away with the 'c' button.  Or you can run.  Running is a better strategy to avoiding infection all together.
Ranged attacks are also effective.  There is no general ammo in this game.  Each gun uses it's designated, real-life ammo.  An m1911 will use .45 rounds, a winchester will use .357.  Each ammo box has a distinct look to help you, but memorizing which box is which will be the first thing you should do.  Hoarding ammo, but realizing you can't use half of it is the first mistake many people will make.  Keep what you need and get rid of or share what you don't (if you've ever played Zombie Panic, you'll know what to do).  Each gun has it's ups and downs.  Pistols are light weight and ammo is plenty.  Shot guns are a beast at close range and rifles tend to have scopes that make aiming easier.  The key is to find a combination of melee and ranged weapon that suit you.  Then again, since items are randomly spawned, you may just have to make do with what you find.
There are three types of zombies: standard walker, runner, and child.  The first one poses little risk unless you get surrounded.  But the second and third, be aware of them.  They will approach you quickly, giving you little time to melee them and increasing your risk to getting bitten.  The child especially.  With their lower height, it is easy to not notice them.
No More Room in Hell is an extremely team-dependent game.  It is very much possible for a single person to run through a map, clearing objective after objective.  But the game really shines when you join a random server and everyone works together.  You share ammo, give pills to those who need it, and split up to cover the various entrances of a building.
TL:DR - This game is a definite must play for anyone that's looking for a zombie survival game.

Quite possibly one of the greatest video game modifications ever made, MINERVA embodies some of the best sensibilities and philsophies modding has to offer. Taking advantage of the Half-Life 2 assets, mechanics and narrative to produce an almost immaculate experience that fits neatly into the greater Half-Life continuum; and featuring some truly ingenious, intricate and at times, stunning level design that truly rivals Valve's own work.
Ostensibly, MINERVA is "Valve-quality", considering its creator, Adam Foster, was hired by Valve to work on Half-Life 2: Episode Three in late 2008. He also did level design for Portal 2, which I thought was rather unfortunate. In any case, though the MINERVA series never got past this first chapter, its legacy does live on at Valve. And you can play it if you own HL2: Episode One. And you should probably do it.
